articles.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question every week to the candidates running for City Council in the November 3 election. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Wednesday, September 16, and were asked to reply with a 200-word response. Week 4 question: What, in your view, are the city’s top 3 infrastructure needs? If elected to the council, which of these needs would you prioritize addressing? And why? Adam Hundt (AdamHundt.com) The top 3 infrastructure needs for Piedmont are: first, mitigating risk from hazards that could affect residents’ housing; second, the renovation and modernization of city buildings (including Police and Fire departments) and the improvement of sewer and storm drain infrastructure; third, the upkeep of roads and enhancements to crosswalks and bike pathways to ensure resident safety and mobility. First, I support the Fire Department’s outreach work with residents to address hazards by switching from gas to home electrification and managing vegetation on one’s property to reduce wildfire risk. Piedmont’s 2025 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) noted the near 100% likelihood of catastrophic wildfires occurring in the next year or every year. Second, aging infrastructure is not up to code and challenges city departments’ ability to provide resident services. Piedmont Police and Fire departments need modern facilities that adequately accommodate personnel and equipment. The Recreation Department, which provides programming for children, needs repair. Piedmont must improve its city sewers to meet obligations from a Consent Decree Order. The Regional Water Quality Control Board has stormwater management requirements. Third, Piedmont must continuously maintain its roads; enhance crosswalk, sidewalk, and path safety and accessibility for pedestrians and bicyclists; and reduce speeding. Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) We live in a beautiful, historic town, but our infrastructure requires aggressive stewardship to keep Piedmont functioning at a high level. Three critical needs stand at the top: Sewers and Storm Drains: We lead neighboring cities in complying with federal sanitary sewer mandates, but 30% of the project remains. We must stay on track using State Revolving Fund low-interest loans, while preparing storm systems for El Niño. Pavement Management: Staff excels at securing state and county revenues, but rising construction costs outpace funding, causing our Pavement Condition Index (PCI) score to slip. We must inject more capital here; every dollar spent on maintenance saves up to ten dollars in future reconstruction. Aging Civic Buildings: Modernizing facilities far exceeds current revenue. I echo the Budget Advisory Committee’s guidance: ongoing planning, quantification, and strict prioritization are vital given long lead times. If elected, I will prioritize Pavement Management. While sewer compliance is mandated and facility upgrades require long-term planning, road maintenance offers the most immediate fiscal leverage. Letting streets deteriorate creates a compounding liability. Prioritizing preservation now protects tax dollars from being wasted on catastrophic road failures, keeping Piedmont safe and fiscally sound. Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) Given the age of our infrastructure, Piedmont has more maintenance and capital needs than available dollars. As a result, identifying, prioritizing, sequencing, and funding infrastructure projects is a continuous discussion between the city administrator, city council, and residents. articles.text: On Friday, September 18, the annual Medieval Faire was held at Piedmont Middle School. The Medieval Faire is an event for 7th graders as a way to experience what life was like during Medieval times. The school tradition dates back over 30 years. The students elected a king, queen, and nobility, and everyone dressed in period costumes. The monarchy and nobility made speeches welcoming everyone, and different classes performed during the “banquet” of cookies and juice. Lastly, everyone went to the pickleball courts where Medieval games were set up. One of the classes spent their social studies periods making games for the faire: Fortune Telling, Ring Around the Rosie, Donut on a String, Soak-a-Serf, Cornhole, and Hoop Rolling, taking place on the pickleball courts. Some of the most popular games were Soak-a-Serf, where someone stood in a pillory while others pelted them with sponges, and Donut on a String, a competition for the first to finish a donut suspended in the air by a string without their hands. Overall, most people thought that the fair was a fun way to see how it was in Medieval times, reinforcing the things they learned in social studies. (See additional articles and photos on pages 8 and 9)
articles.title: 7th Graders host annual Medieval Faire

For this year’s race, the Post will send one question every week to the candidates running for City Council in the November 3 election. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on Wednesday, September 16, and were asked to reply with a 200-word response. Week 4 question: What, in your view, are the city’s top 3 infrastructure needs? If elected to the council, which of these needs would you prioritize addressing? And why? Adam Hundt (AdamHundt.com) The top 3 infrastructure needs for Piedmont are: first, mitigating risk from hazards that could affect residents’ housing; second, the renovation and modernization of city buildings (including Police and Fire departments) and the improvement of sewer and storm drain infrastructure; third, the upkeep of roads and enhancements to crosswalks and bike pathways to ensure resident safety and mobility. First, I support the Fire Department’s outreach work with residents to address hazards by switching from gas to home electrification and managing vegetation on one’s property to reduce wildfire risk. Piedmont’s 2025 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) noted the near 100% likelihood of catastrophic wildfires occurring in the next year or every year. Second, aging infrastructure is not up to code and challenges city departments’ ability to provide resident services. Piedmont Police and Fire departments need modern facilities that adequately accommodate personnel and equipment. The Recreation Department, which provides programming for children, needs repair. Piedmont must improve its city sewers to meet obligations from a Consent Decree Order. The Regional Water Quality Control Board has stormwater management requirements. Third, Piedmont must continuously maintain its roads; enhance crosswalk, sidewalk, and path safety and accessibility for pedestrians and bicyclists; and reduce speeding. Tom Ramsey Incumbent (vote4tomramsey.com) We live in a beautiful, historic town, but our infrastructure requires aggressive stewardship to keep Piedmont functioning at a high level. Three critical needs stand at the top: Sewers and Storm Drains: We lead neighboring cities in complying with federal sanitary sewer mandates, but 30% of the project remains. We must stay on track using State Revolving Fund low-interest loans, while preparing storm systems for El Niño. Pavement Management: Staff excels at securing state and county revenues, but rising construction costs outpace funding, causing our Pavement Condition Index (PCI) score to slip. We must inject more capital here; every dollar spent on maintenance saves up to ten dollars in future reconstruction. Aging Civic Buildings: Modernizing facilities far exceeds current revenue. I echo the Budget Advisory Committee’s guidance: ongoing planning, quantification, and strict prioritization are vital given long lead times. If elected, I will prioritize Pavement Management. While sewer compliance is mandated and facility upgrades require long-term planning, road maintenance offers the most immediate fiscal leverage. Letting streets deteriorate creates a compounding liability. Prioritizing preservation now protects tax dollars from being wasted on catastrophic road failures, keeping Piedmont safe and fiscally sound. Bill Reichle (ReichleforPiedmont.com) Given the age of our infrastructure, Piedmont has more maintenance and capital needs than available dollars. As a result, identifying, prioritizing, sequencing, and funding infrastructure projects is a continuous discussion between the city administrator, city council, and residents. Photos by Anne Smith and Jay Russell 7th Graders host annual Medieval Faire By Milana Miller On Friday, September 18, the annual Medieval Faire was held at Piedmont Middle School. The Medieval Faire is an event for 7th graders as a way to experience what life was like during Medieval times. The school tradition dates back over 30 years. The students elected a king, queen, and nobility, and everyone dressed in period costumes. The monarchy and nobility made speeches welcoming everyone, and different classes performed during the “banquet” of cookies and juice. Lastly, everyone went to the pickleball courts where Medieval games were set up. One of the classes spent their social studies periods making games for the faire: Fortune Telling, Ring Around the Rosie, Donut on a String, Soak-a-Serf, Cornhole, and Hoop Rolling, taking place on the pickleball courts. Some of the most popular games were Soak-a-Serf, where someone stood in a pillory while others pelted them with sponges, and Donut on a String, a competition for the first to finish a donut suspended in the air by a string without their hands. Overall, most people thought that the fair was a fun way to see how it was in Medieval times, reinforcing the things they learned in social studies. articles.text: I strongly recommend Piedmont voters support Measure GG on this November ballot. Measure GG is a “transfer tax,” a one-time assessment collected when property is sold or ownership is transferred. The current Piedmont transfer tax was set in 1993. It has not been updated in 33 years. The transfer tax is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale and is often split between the buyer and the seller. Piedmont does not have sales tax or any significant commercial tax revenue, so the transfer tax is a critical source of income and represents 10% of the annual operating budget of the City. Proceeds from Measure GG will stay in Piedmont and support our core City services through the City’s General Fund. The City uses those revenues to partially pay for repair of aging City buildings, streets and sidewalks, parks, public safety and recreation. Our neighboring communities of Oakland, Berkeley, Emeryville, and Richmond have all increased their transfer taxes far higher than Measure GG. While Piedmont home prices have risen in the last few years, maintenance expenses and construction costs for roads, sidewalks and storm drains have risen even faster. As a former Councilmember and Mayor, and now Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, I have had a front row seat to City revenues and expenditures for the past 14 years. I can attest that the City Council has taken, and continues to take, a conservative approach to budgeting and expenditures. A long-overdue increase in the transfer tax would provide the City with revenue to continue to provide essential services and maintain the basic City infrastructure upon which we all rely. Please join me in voting YES on Measure GG. – Bob McBain, Former Mayor Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee

articles.text: I am writing in support of Measure GG, which will appear on the November 3 ballot. Piedmont is a remarkable community because of the things we have built and maintained together—excellent public safety, responsive police and fire services, beautiful parks, well-maintained streets and sidewalks, and the many community services that contribute to the quality of life we value so highly. Measure GG provides an important source of funding to help preserve those services for the future. The measure would increase Piedmont’s one-time real property transfer tax from 1.3% to 1.75% and is expected to generate approximately $1.5 million annually in additional general tax revenue. What I particularly appreciate about this approach is that it is a onetime tax paid when a property changes hands, rather than an annual tax on every Piedmont homeowner. The cost of the transfer tax can also be negotiated as part of a real estate transaction. For those of us who live in Piedmont, the value of our community is not simply the homes we own. It is the security of knowing that our police and firefighters are there when we need them. It is the quality of our parks, roads, sidewalks and public spaces. It is the investment we make in maintaining the infrastructure and services that make Piedmont such a special place to live. The City has identified significant ongoing needs, including aging buildings, infrastructure, parks, stormwater systems, roads and sidewalks, in addition to essential public safety and emergency services. I believe maintaining these services is an investment in the community we all care about. Measure GG provides an opportunity to help ensure that Piedmont continues to be the safe, beautiful and exceptionally well-served community we know and love. I encourage my fellow Piedmonters to vote YES on Measure GG this November. Sincerely, –Teresa Baum, Realtor
articles.title: A stronger Piedmont starts with protecting what makes our community special

articles.text: Join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) on Tuesday, September 29, for a candidate forum. It will feature candidates on the Piedmont City Council ballot in the November 3, 2026, General Election. The forum will be held at 7:00 p.m. in the City Council chambers and in overflow space as needed. It will include the following five candidates running for three positions: Nancy Beninati, Nancy Bostrom, Adam Hundt, Tom Ramsey, and Bill Reichle. Piedmont voters can learn more about the City Council forum at lwvpiedmont.org. Registration is required to attend the live forum, as space is limited. The forum will also be broadcast and recorded on KCOM. After the forum, the recording will be available on LWVP’s website, on LWVP’s YouTube channel, and through the websites of KCOM and the City. A LWVP representative will moderate the forum. It will include questions from the public. Questions will be reviewed to ensure a range of topics and issues. Ballot dropoff locations will open October 6. If you have moved or changed your party or your name, you can update your registration online. The last day to register to vote is October 19. There are three ways to vote in Alameda County: 1) mail your ballot, 2) drop off your ballot at a secure ballot drop-box in the county, or 3) vote in person or drop off your ballot at any vote center in the county. The list of vote centers will be updated as the Registrar of Voters confirms the sites. There will likely be a ballot drop-box in central Piedmont next to the mailbox near the Piedmont Community Church. There will likely be a vote center in Piedmont at the Veterans Memorial Building at 401 Highland Avenue. A limited number of additional early 10-day in-person Alameda County vote centers will also be open starting October 24. articles.text: What is the Real Estate Transfer Tax? The transfer tax is a one-time assessment collected when property is sold or ownership is transferred. Transfer tax revenue in Piedmont funds day-to-day costs for police, fire, emergency response, public works, recreation, and other services, as well as the maintenance and replacement of aging infrastructure and facilities. Who pays the Transfer Tax? Piedmont’s transfer taxes are typically split equally between buyer and seller when a home is sold, although the parties may negotiate a different arrangement. How would Piedmont’s rate compare with neighboring cities? Measure GG would bring Piedmont’s rate more in line with neighboring cities. In Oakland, the rate is 1.75% for sales between $2 million and $5 million and 2.5% for sales above $5 million. In Berkeley, the rate is 2.5% for sales of $1.6 million or more. What prompted the City to update the transfer tax? Piedmont has had a local transfer tax since 1968. As other neighboring cities have modified theirs, Piedmont’s transfer tax has not changed since 1993, which was 33 years ago. The City is facing a long-term gap between the cost of maintaining existing city services, facilities, and infrastructure and the revenues available to support them. Piedmont has no significant revenue from retail, and the cost of rehabilitating City buildings, parks, streets, sidewalks, stormwater drains and other infrastructure are rising. The increase was recommended by the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, after the City Council asked that they explore options for addressing Piedmont’s long-term needs.
articles.title: Measure GG: Transfer Tax FAQ

articles.text: What would Measure GG do? Measure GG would increase Piedmont’s Real Estate Transfer Tax rate from 1.3% to 1.75% of the sale price of real property – from $13 to $17.50 per $1,000. If approved by a majority of voters, the new rate would take effect July 1, 2027. Measure GG is estimated to generate $1.5 million in additional revenue annually. Actual revenue will vary based on the number of sales and sales price.

Attendees will enjoy a day of food, music, art, and community traditions throughout Piedmont Park from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. The festival kicks off the fall season for Piedmont families. The Edibles Contest has been part of the Harvest Festival since the beginning and remains its centerpiece. Each year, Piedmont’s community creativity and talent shine as tables fill with homemade breads, pies, cookies, jams, and homegrown produce. To enter, residents can download the entry form at piedmont.ca.gov/EdiblesContest and drop their entry off with a label at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:30 to 10 a.m. on the morning of the festival. This year’s Harvest Festival will feature an expanded Farmers’ Market, including local honey, flowers, vegetable starts, skincare products, and more. The Watermelon Eating Contest will return this year after last year’s success. Competitors will line up and eat a watermelon as fast as they can; the first one done wins. Sign-up is on-site, and the competition starts at 1 p.m. Scarecrow Alley will be crowded with student scarecrows to be auctioned. All auction proceeds benefit Beach, Havens, and Wildwood. Families can buy their kids a wristband in advance at PiedmontStore.org. A wristband gets you unlimited carnival games, one walk-through at the Cake Hop, and one snow cone. articles.text: The Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival celebrates its 25th year this Sunday, September 27. The festival will take place on an open stage in front of the Piedmont Community Hall starting at 11 a.m. This free city-sponsored event will be held in conjunction with the Harvest Festival and the School Carnival. For 25 years, the festival has celebrated Piedmont’s rich musical talent. articles.text: Mina Herrgott Girl Scout Troop #33521, made up of 15 high school juniors, will host a garage sale on Sunday, September 27, selling interesting used items from their homes to promote sustainability while fundraising for their activities. The garage sale will take place at 39 Craig Avenue, just a few blocks away from the park, from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m. The garage sale will coincide with the Harvest Festival, the yearly gathering of music and food in Piedmont Park. This gives people enjoying the Harvest Festival an opportunity to explore vintage clothes, children’s toys, sports gear, and handmade objects, from jewelry to ceramics. Girl Scout Troop #33521 was started in 2017 and has grown from a few students at Wildwood to almost 20 members from Piedmont and Oakland. They have done a variety of activities and gone on many adventures, ranging from camping to learning from Piedmont’s firefighters. Their earlier years were characterized by badge earning – first aid, babysitting, woodworking, eating healthy, and more. Many of the members completed a Silver Award in middle school. Girls spent more than 50 hours addressing a community issue. Two girls advocated to reduce food insecurity, another pair built a website about animal care, and one pair created a brochure to support new immigrants in the East Bay. Now students at Piedmont High School, Head Royce, and College Preparatory, they’re focused on volunteering and earning their Gold Awards, the most prestigious award in Girl Scouts and the next step after their Silver Award. Girl Scouts pursuing a Gold Award need to have at least 80 hours of work with prominent experts to create a profound, lasting impact on their community in an area of their choice. Some examples of Gold Award projects include supporting girls in a male-dominated sport, increasing excitement about math for kids, and educating people to empower introverts. Girl Scout Troop #33521 invites you to their Garage Sale Fundraiser. Please stop by to give these amazing items a new home and, in doing so, support these young entrepreneurs. Girl Scout Troop #33521 on its annual camping trip. They are at Tomales Bay, waiting to see bioluminescence in the water

articles.text: An Adults-Only (21+) Evening of Live Art for Bay Area Artists A local artist is live painting a piece for a guest at Drawn Together. Children’s Fairyland announces the return of its “artsiest party of the year.” Drawn Together will take place on Friday, September 25, from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. For this special evening, Fairyland opens exclusively to adults ages 21 and over, offering a rare opportunity for grown-ups to explore the magical world of Fairyland, a place typically reserved for children and their families. Tickets are now on sale. An intimate evening of live art, cocktails, and creative connection. The 21-and-over event invites art lovers to watch more than 50 local artists and industry professionals create original, Fairyland-inspired artwork live throughout the park. As the night winds down, the energy shifts into a wildly spirited art sale, where guests can take home a piece created that very evening for just $50. “It’s an open-air art gallery meets a bar meets a theme park meets a party meets an art sale,” said Fairyland’s Artistic Director Shannon Taylor of the one-ofa-kind event, which blends the whimsy of Fairyland’s storybook setting with a full slate of adult entertainment. Drawn Together is an adultsonly playground, featuring cocktails, food trucks, live art being made in real time by local visual artists, puppet shows, live music, tarot card readings, artists’ meet-and-greets, an infamously spirited art sale, and an evening showing of Fairyland’s current puppet production, The Three Little Pigs in the 1920s. Guests can explore Fairyland’s iconic storybook sets, from Willie the Whale to the Alice in Wonderland card maze. Tot-sized rides and animal areas will be closed for the evening. Guests who would prefer a guaranteed place are welcome to purchase a Patron Ticket. Patron Ticket holders will receive a numbered, limited-edition Children’s Fairyland print created exclusively for Drawn Together 2026, along with early entry to the event. It gives guests a chance to avoid the lines, speak with artists before the crowds arrive, and secure a piece of art early, all while donating to Children’s Fairyland. P roceeds f rom D raw n Together will support the people, programs, and spaces that make Children’s Fairyland magic possible year-round — from free field trips for under-resourced communities to hands-on workshops that bring creativity to life for young visitors. Tickets are $35 for general admission, $30 for members, and $100 for Patron. Tickets and event information can be found on Fairyland’s website: https:// secure.fairyland.org/4337/4338.
articles.title: Children’s Fairyland to host Drawn Together event

articles.text: The new phone policy at Piedmont High School, which forces students to keep phones and personal internet-connected devices in backpacks for the entirety of school days, has caused unforeseen consequences as students try to adjust to a different campus environment. After six weeks of the new policy, many students are expressing frustration over the restriction of their phones. According to the 2026-2027 student handbook, the current board of education policy limits cell phone usage during the school day to only a “dumb phone,” a phone equipped only with text and call features. Students began to see the new policy’s enforcement on day one of school, August 10, with cell phones being confiscated by school staff and Campus Supervisor Darnell Reed. “The phone policy has been very effective so far,” junior Cassidy Carter said. “Especially with the scaring tactic of phones being taken to the office, and the threat of having to turn your phone in every day at the beginning of the school day.” Many students are frustrated the policy was created to begin with, citing bigger issues that the school should be focusing on instead. “I don’t think it addresses an actual issue, if anything it’s more work for the teachers,” junior Maika Ting said. “They’re the ones having to enforce it and our old policy didn’t really have any issues.” With each violation of the phone policy, consequences increase. The first offense causes phones to confiscated for the day and comes with an email to parents. Further disciplinary action include revoking phone privileges for the remainder of the year, daily phone drop-offs, and assignments to progressive disciplinary. A fourth offense results in ineligibility for school activities. “The punishments are a little too harsh. It’s likely that many students will get their phones taken since we are slightly reliant on them,” Carter said. “It’s unfair to have to turn them in in the mornings on only the second offense.” Classes such as yearbook and journalism occasionally require cell phone use, which has caused frustration and difficulty when classes are given exceptions, according to students. “It’s necessary to have them on you at all times for pictures, interviews, or notes.” Carter said. “Administrators didn’t really understand that there was no need for a change.” Students also rely on their cell phones to contact family members throughout the day, and the phone policy limits their ability to do so. “I don’t think they [the administration] understand that students use their phones as a way to talk to their parents at school,” sophomore Olivia Nealon said. “Many people rely on lunch to talk to their parents about after school plans.” With lunch being the only period where students can go off campus and use their phones, there has been a decrease in students spending lunch on campus, changing the campus atmosphere in an unexpected way. Students said there are possible improvements to be made to make the policy more effective and sustainable for further years. “Having a hard reset for a number of phone offenses at different times throughout the school year would be better,” Carter said. “Or some other punishment that is a little more lenient for students.” Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student intern writer with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: PHS phone policy too spartan for some students

articles.text: Librarians provide warning about upcoming state cuts Piedmont librarians published a Letter to the Editor in the September 2 Piedmont Post describing the imminent lose of the COMPASS program at the end of this school year. Educators and librarians are currently calling on state legislators to restore funding for the California Online Media Program for Access and Student Success (COMPASS), a statewide program that provides K-12 students and teachers with free access to high-quality, vetted online research resources. The 2026-27 state budget eliminates COMPASS funding after July 1, 2027, ending the state’s $5.5 million annual investment in the program. COMPASS databases include Encyclopedia Britannica, PBS videos, PebbleGo, Gale, National Geographic for Kids, ProQuest, and TeachingBooks. Media resources slated to be lost include encyclopedias, research databases, and scientific journals. “We cannot imagine doing our work of teaching media literacy and research skills without this program,” Piedmont librarians stated. Since 2018, COMPASS has provided free access to research and curriculum resources to California’s public schools. The program’s resources are verified by teachers and credentialed school librarians. Since its launch, the program has received over 700 million searches. California ranks 49th nationwide in school librarian staffing, with nearly 10,000 students for each librarian, according to research by the Institute of Museum and Library Services. Without librarians or research tools, K-12 students will have to fend for themselves. According to a CalMatters article the state allotted funds for COMPASS in earlier budget versions but is directing the funding elsewhere. Instead, $5 million of the funding is going toward the state’s new dyslexia screener. Read more at Calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2026/06/ school-libraries-california/ The cost of replacing COMPASS will be dramatically higher if schools and districts are required to purchase the resources independently. According to the California State Library, individual schools subscribing to comparable COMPASS materials would spend more than $216 million annually. To send Governor Newsom an email urging him to restore this resource visit: Saveschoollibrarians.org/compass2026.
articles.title: California’s COMPASS research resources to be eliminated

articles.text: Ariel Rodriguez Many high schools throughout the country will be hosting the PSAT in October, but what is the PSAT? PSAT stands for Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test, essentially the precursor to the SAT. Like the SAT, the PSAT is a digital, adaptive test that includes a Reading & Writing section and a Math section. Both the SAT and PSAT are 2 hours and 14 minutes long. There are also some major differences between the PSAT and the SAT. The PSAT is only offered once per year, in October, and is typically hosted by your high school. The SAT, on the other hand, is offered eight times per year at test centers throughout the country. The maximum scaled score on each section of the PSAT is 760; the maximum scaled score on each section of the SAT is 800. If you are a junior taking the PSAT, your scores could qualify you for National Merit Commendation or National Merit Semifinalist. Many schools will also allow sophomores to take the PSAT, but only scores from junior year can qualify for national merit recognition. Exact score cutoffs are determined by state in the year following the PSAT taken. So, a junior taking the PSAT Fall 2026 will not find out if they have received national merit commendation or semifinalist status until 2027. Commended students are typically within the top 3-4% of testers; semifinalists are typically within the top 1% of testers. Historically, California has been one of the states with the highest cutoffs. Students who are National Merit Semifinalists can apply to become National Merit Scholars. National Merit Scholar status makes you eligible for different scholarships: some from the National Merit Scholarship Corporation, some from private corporations, and others from colleges and universities themselves. While there are some perks for students who score in the top percentiles on the PSAT, for the vast majority of students, the PSAT mainly functions as a practice test. If the PSAT is being offered at your school, go ahead and take it and put in a good faith effort, but don’t put undue stress on this test. Instead, use it as an opportunity to gain more information that will empower you to understand how standardized tests may become part of the bigger picture for college admissions. Ariel is the Co-Director of College Consulting and Emily is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel has worked in undergraduate admissions at both public and private universities. For more information, please visit www. studysmarter.com, email info@ studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.
articles.title: Putting the PSAT into Perspective

It’s likely that many students will get their phones taken since we are slightly reliant on them,” Carter said. “It’s unfair to have to turn them in in the mornings on only the second offense.” Classes such as yearbook and journalism occasionally require cell phone use, which has caused frustration and difficulty when classes are given exceptions, according to students. “It’s necessary to have them on you at all times for pictures, interviews, or notes.” Carter said. “Administrators didn’t really understand that there was no need for a change.” Students also rely on their cell phones to contact family members throughout the day, and the phone policy limits their ability to do so. “I don’t think they [the administration] understand that students use their phones as a way to talk to their parents at school,” sophomore Olivia Nealon said. “Many people rely on lunch to talk to their parents about after school plans.” With lunch being the only period where students can go off campus and use their phones, there has been a decrease in students spending lunch on campus, changing the campus atmosphere in an unexpected way. Students said there are possible improvements to be made to make the policy more effective and sustainable for further years. “Having a hard reset for a number of phone offenses at different times throughout the school year would be better,” Carter said. “Or some other punishment that is a little more lenient for students.” Ayla Blanford is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student intern writer with the Piedmont Post. Putting the PSAT into Perspective By Emily Thompson and Ariel Rodriguez Many high schools throughout the country will be hosting the PSAT in October, but what is the PSAT? PSAT stands for Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test, essentially the precursor to the SAT. Like the SAT, the PSAT is a digital, adaptive test that includes a Reading & Writing section and a Math section. Both the SAT and PSAT are 2 hours and 14 minutes long. There are also some major differences between the PSAT and the SAT. The PSAT is only offered once per year, in October, and is typically hosted by your high school. The SAT, on the other hand, is offered eight times per year at test centers throughout the country. The maximum scaled score on each section of the PSAT is 760; the maximum scaled score on each section of the SAT is 800. If you are a junior taking the PSAT, your scores could qualify you for National Merit Commendation or National Merit Semifinalist. Many schools will also allow sophomores to take the PSAT, but only scores from junior year can qualify for national merit recognition. Exact score cutoffs are determined by state in the year following the PSAT taken. So, a junior taking the PSAT Fall 2026 will not find out if they have received national merit commendation or semifinalist status until 2027. Commended students are typically within the top 3-4% of testers; semifinalists are typically within the top 1% of testers. Historically, California has been one of the states with the highest cutoffs. Students who are National Merit Semifinalists can apply to become National Merit Scholars. National Merit Scholar status makes you eligible for different scholarships: some from the National Merit Scholarship Corporation, some from private corporations, and others from colleges and universities themselves. While there are some perks for students who score in the top percentiles on the PSAT, for the vast majority of students, the PSAT mainly functions as a practice test. If the PSAT is being offered at your school, go ahead and take it and put in a good faith effort, but don’t put undue stress on this test. Instead, use it as an opportunity to gain more information that will empower you to understand how standardized tests may become part of the bigger picture for college admissions. articles.text: On Saturday, September 12, the Piedmont Makers hosted a season kickoff and watch party for the unveiling of the 2026-27 FIRST Tech Challenge theme at the new community robotics and maker space on 10th Street in FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) challenges middle and high school students to design, build and program robots to compete in a new game each year. Working with mentors, students develop engineering skills, teamwork and strategies for competition. A local non-profit dedicated to K-12 STEAM education, the Piedmont Makers offers hands-on learning opportunities through robotics, maker programs, teacher grants and community events. The organization has expanded beyond Piedmont, with programs serving over 1,000 students from 139 schools across the Bay Area during the 2026- 2027 season. Piedmont Makers’ programming starts in kindergarten and continues through high school. “It’s a really amazing program that impacts a lot of kids for a very long time,” says Paul Morrison, the co-leader of the Piedmont Makers FIRST Tech Challenge. The 7,000-square-foot 10th Street facility serves as a hub for the local maker and robotics community. The space provides a full-size robotics practice field and access to specialized equipment like CNC routers, and has hosted over 30 robotics teams throughout the Bay Area in the past year. Highlander Robotics, Piedmont Makers’ capstone high school team, first had the idea: a full-size, community-accessible robotics practice field. The team opened one at a temporary space in Oakland, giving Bay Area teams that used to drive to East Palo Alto for practice a home in the East Bay. When rent rose at that location, the team partnered with Piedmont Makers to find a long-term site. With grants from the PG&E Corporation Foundation, the KLA Foundation, and over one thousand volunteer hours from the team, the 10th Street facility opened in the fall of 2025. From the beginning, the vision for the new space extended beyond just serving its own Images courtesy of FTC team #37264 Members of FTC team #37264, CTRL-ALT-Defeat! L-R: Jeremy Block, Kai Chiles, Tristan Lu, Parsa Tarapore, & Jack Dove teams. “We’re always thinking about how we can expand our impact,” says Piedmont Makers co-president Ben Stein. “The impetus for investing in the 10th Street facility was not just to serve a single team or chapter; it was the goal of creating regional infrastructure for youth throughout the whole Bay Area. That’s the real magic.” For Kai Chiles, a middle school student and member of FTC team #37264 CTRL-ALT-Defeat!, the 10th Street space offers a chance to learn from older students. “The space is cool because we get to see the older teams practice and how their robots work,” he said. “The reveal was exciting, and I’m very interested to see how everyone’s robots are going to look this season.” His teammate Tristan Lu echoes the enthusiasm, saying, “I’m very excited for this FTC season. Right after the reveal, we started immediately building and modifying our robot for the competition.” The Piedmont Makers ecosystem is powered by a broad community of students, parents, mentors and partner teams. “The heroes of the Piedmont Makers program are really the kids and our volunteer parents,” says Stein. “We have roughly 300 volunteers, along with teams from across the region contributing labor, parts, and other support. At the end of the day, it’s about building a village to support the amazing work all these kids are doing.” To learn more about the Piedmont Makers or to get involved as a volunteer, visit piedmontmakers.org Images courtesy of FTC team #37264 Co-leaders of the Piedmont Makers FTC Laura Chu and Paul Morrison unveil the season’s theme to the FTC teams.

articles.text: What could a 7th grader love more than getting to skip 6th period to eat wafers, play games and dress up in internet-bought cloaks, dresses and polyester Piedmont Middle School’s annual Medieval Faire, given on the 18th of September, in the first year of the reign of King Leo Sahuc and Queen Ember McCall, was full of joy and festive chaos. It was a period where you could be anyone from the Medieval Ages, from archbishops to the rats carrying the bubonic plagues. Everyone dressed in colorful attire. Some favorites were the plague doctors, dressed in deep, black robes (sable, if you may) and those horrifying crow masks. Another interesting garment to note was the riding cloak. It’s such a beautifully cut piece of fabric, trimmed at the ankle and crowning the shoulders, pinned together with an elegant brooch. The vibrant hoods and capes added a certain swashbuckling effect to costumes. With crow masks and cloaks discussed, I still must ask what could a medieval faire be without its fair share of fair maidens? There were several glamorous dresses, featuring deep blues and rich greens worn by our nobles and queen. These flowing dresses allowed for a very stately gait, present in all the faire’s activities. And although the faire is over, surely all medieval apparel will be remembered. articles.text: The Piedmont-based non-profit Orion Fund will host its 20th annual Golf Tournament and Banquet at Chardonnay Golf Club in Napa on Saturday, October 24. Tickets are affordable and go to the best of causes, supporting college students undergoing medical emergencies in California. The Orion Fund non-profit started at the behest of Piedmont moms two decades ago following the death of PHS graduate Orion Trott from cancer at the age of 21. They have awarded more than $850,000 to college students in times of urgent need. The Orion Fund provides grants for students amidst any health crisis including organ transplants, car crashes and cancer diagnoses. The Orion Fund primarily serves low-income students without family support, many of whom are first-generation college students and working while enrolled. “We put a safety net under them so that they can recover and complete a hard-won education,” said Orion Fund President Pam Hirtzer. Since the Orion Fund began in 2004 it has assisted 500 college students with grants, so kids battling an injury or setback can stay enrolled in college. The Orion Fund has sent tuition to more than 65 schools in California, supporting local kids of all demographics, under any medical crisis, for any academic pursuit. Grant winners have also applied their funds to keep their health insurance or pay their rent while ill. Twenty-seven grant recipients already selected for the next year depend upon the continued support of donors to the Orion Fund. “It is seriously difficult to fundraise for non-profits in this day and age. We can’t help everybody, and have to turn kids away that would otherwise qualify,” said Hirtzer. A tee-time in the October 24 golf tournament and a seat for the banquet dinner costs $165; this also includes cart rental and range balls. The shotgun start begins at 12:00 p.m. and at 5:00 p.m. there will be a banquet dinner, along with an auction, tournament awards and a golden raffle. This year’s top prize in the raffle is a goals. The Chardonnay Golf Course in Napa is the site of the 20th annual Orion Fund Golf Tournament on October 24.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Waking up before sunrise for practice. Carrying two backpacks from class to class. Finishing homework in the backseat of a car on the way to an away game. For student-athletes at Piedmont High School, the school day doesn’t always end when the final bell rings. Practices, games, and workouts can last well into the evening, leaving athletes scrambling to find time for schoolwork whenever they can. Water polo player senior Raffaello Banin said managing school work during the water polo season can be difficult, especially when games and practices take up much of the day. “I try to be super efficient overall when I have time to work and sometimes get homework done in the car on the way to games,” Banin said. For some athletes, that efficiency means less free time to relax. Basketball player senior Taylor White said her schedule requires her to fit schoolwork in whenever she gets the opportunity. “Managing school and a sport can be a challenge sometimes, but mostly I do my homework during my free periods, in the car while going home, and sometimes I set my alarm to wake up early in the morning to catch up on anything I missed,” White said. The challenge can become more complicated for athletes who compete outside of PHS. Many student-athletes participate in club sports, adding another layer to an already busy schedule. For volleyball player junior Olivia Stevens, the timing of the school and club seasons helps make the commitments more manageable. “School season is August-October and club is November-May, so it works out,” Stevens said. “For beach volleyball, it’s harder because it’s spring season and it overlaps [with club], but it’s still manageable.” Even when seasons do not directly overlap, the workload can be exhausting. White said club basketball is more laid back than her school season, but travel can make it demanding. During school basketball season, practices and workouts can add another physical challenge to the school day. “The school days can be tiring after a workout from the previous day,” White said. “Since we have workouts right after school, it just depends on my mood. But other than that, school season is exciting.” Despite the time commitment, athletes said their sports provide experiences that make the busy schedules worthwhile. For Banin, one of the biggest differences between club and school sports is the connection among teammates. Knowing teammates from school already creates a stronger sense of community. “School sports is a bigger commitment [than club sports], but the team is also more connected because we see each other every day,” Banin said. “Club is good though, because you meet new people and it’s fun.” White said basketball has given her the opportunity to build relationships while also competing against high-level competition athletes from around the country. “The experience and opportunity to travel across the country playing against some of the best competition and future college players is really exciting. I get to see how I match up against some of the best players,” White said. For PHS student-athletes, balancing academics and athletics often requires fitting study sessions and homework in whenever there is time , and achieving success both as an athlete and as a student requires physical and mental strength. The sacrifices that athletes make show up both in the classroom and on the field, the court, or the pool. Julia Stokes is a junior at Piedmont High School and a student writer intern for the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: The double life of student-athletes

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team won one of four matches at the Vintage Valley Tournament at Vintage HS in Napa on Friday and Saturday, September 18-19. All three losses were separated by two goals or less; they fell 9-8 to Clayton Valley Charter and beat Marin Catholic 11-8 on the opening day, while losing 12-10 to Sequoia and 12-11 to San Marin the following day. The batch of results brings the Highlanders’ record to 5-6 overall with eight matches left in the regular season. It was a strong tournament for junior Henry Stein, who had 24 goals over the four-match span, including nine goals in their 12-11 loss to San Marin. Goalie Dylan Jerez was also instrumental in keeping the matches close, recording 35 saves throughout the tourney. Official quarter-by-quarter score lines were not provided for the tournament matches. 9-8 loss to Clayton Valley Charter Piedmont fell 9-8 in the opening match of the tournament. Clayton Valley led 4-0 through the first quarter and 6-2 by halftime. Then, Piedmont roared back in the third quarter with four unanswered goals to knot things up at 6-6 going into the final period. . However the Ugly Eagles outscored the Highlanders 3-2 in the fourth to win it. Final stats: Stein led with five goals and three assists. Rylan Patty had two goals, two assists, and two steals. Dylan Jerez finished with 11 saves, two steals, an assist, and scored once as a goalie. 11-8 win vs. Marin Catholic The Highlanders claimed its only win of the tournament 11-8 over Marin Catholic in their second match. Final stats: Stein had five goals and two assists. Patty had five goals, one assist, and one steal. Henry Van Den Bos had one goal and an assist. Oliver Hurwitz had one assist and one steal. Graham Smith had two steals. Travers Kemp had one steal. Raffi Banin had one assist. Jerez had six saves, four steals, and two assists. 12-10 loss to Sequoia Piedmont returned on Saturday and lost a narrow 12-10 battle to Sequoia. Staff Photos The boys’ water polo team won one of four matches at the Vintage Valley Tournament in Napa.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Newhall Community Park in Concord for the 2026 De La Salle Nike Invitational on Saturday, September 19. The Highlanders’ boys’ team finished 22nd of 31 schools, while the girls were 18th of 22. “The De La Salle Nike Invitational was our third meet of the season and another opportunity to see how our runners are progressing as we start to head into the middle of the season. We are still only in September. We are continuing to train, build durability and learn how to race,” explained coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The objective isn’t to be at our best right now—it is to keep progressing so that we are running our best when the important championship meets arrive later in the season. Saturday gave us another encouraging indication that we are moving in the right direction.” Junior runner Dresden Schulte-Sasse led PHS for the third straight meet. He finished 50th of 204 athletes with a time of 17:06.9 on the three-mile course. “Dresden led Piedmont over the three-mile course, becoming our No. 3 junior performance by a Piedmont runner at Newhall Community Park. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team took a one-sided 40-14 loss to Aragon for Homecoming Night on Friday, September 18 at Witter Field. The result brings their record to 1-3. The Highlanders were dealing with several important injuries to starters going into the game. They were without running back Rehan Mumtaz, receiver and safety Diego Hurwitz, linebacker Max Fujimoto, cornerback Owen Curran, and starting linebacker and receiver Mason Gray left the game with an injury. “We had a lot of people out, but the effort was there. Our numbers are low and we have to get some bodies back. You see how it played out; those are all great players for us and heavy contributing starters. I was just hoping to get through this game healthy, but that’s football,” coach Jordan Seiden said. PHS’ young roster faced growing pains, including sophomore quarterback Cyrus Emanuelson tossing some interceptions. He was able to respond well in the game’s final drive, leading the Highlanders to a touchdown. “One thing about Cyrus that I love is he is unflappable. He shakes things off and is on to the next play. Being a young quarterback, he could’ve easily gone into a hole and tanked, but not Cyrus. He has a huge heart and loves the game, he’s just going to continue to grow. My message to Mateo Long scoring a touchdown for Piedmont. George Saunders reaches for a ball against Aragon. He scored Piedmont’s final touchdown. Staff photos Piedmont suffered a rough 40-14 loss to the Aragon with a bulk of its starters missing due to injuries. him is to just keep growing and keep getting better. That’s the same with the rest of the team,” Seiden said. Game Recap After a scoreless first quarter, Aragon scored on a 12-play, 71-yard series. They converted a 4th-and-goal from the four to make it 6-0 with 11:10 left in the second quarter following a missed extra point. Piedmont scored on its ensuing possession with an eight-play, 72 yard drive. It featured 37-yard pass from Cyrus Emanuelson to Gray on 3rd-and-10 from their own 45. After that, Colby Hong ran the ball 18 yards, while Emanuelson threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Mateo Long with 8:15 on the clock. A missed two-point conversion kept it deadlocked at 6-6. PHS had good field position after Henry Brennan recovered a fumble at Aragon’s 45, but Piedmont turned over on downs after gaining just four yards. From there, AHS blew the game open with 34 unanswered points. They scored twice more in the second quarter to lead 20-6 at the half, and extended to 40-6 with an interception return for a touchdown with 2:37 left in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s final touchdown came with 1:12 remaining in the game. Starting at their own 42, the drive started with a 33 yard pass to George Saunders. On 2nd-and-10, Saunders took a 17-yard reception to the eight, and then connected with Emanuelson again for an eight-yard touchdown catch. Hong ran the ball in for a successful two-point conversion for a final score of 40-14. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-3 overall) visits Moreau Catholic in Hayward on Friday, September 25 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team came away with a one-sided 46-0 shutout of San Lorenzo on Thursday, September 17 at Witter Field. The result marked its third win in four games, bringing their record to 5-5 and 3-1 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. “The offense is coming along and the defense is improving every game. I think tonight was a good correction from our last loss, and the girls never wanted to leave the field,” said coach Beth Black. It was a strong game allaround for the Highlanders, logging six interceptions on the night by Sydney Latvala, Cory Minor, Maddie Lee, Skye Prata Baack, and two by Bea Nackley. “We’re forcing turnovers and we showed we’re hungry for the ball,” Black said. Prata Baack had a productive game with a touchdown reception and a one-point conversion on five receptions. She broke catches of 21-, 29-, 15-, and 12-yards. “It’s my first year playing, so it was hard to adjust in the beginning. Now, as a team, we’ve had so much time together and we’re feeling that connection. We’re able to execute, the energy was really good tonight. Getting to know each other and learn our styles of play is really helping,” Prata Baack said. Game Recap Piedmont’s Sydney Latvala recorded an interception on the second play of the game. Prata Baack then took a 21-yard reception to the Grizzlies’ five, but SLZ was able to nab an interception of its own. After forcing a punt, PHS got its first score of the game with 47 seconds left in the first quarter with an eight-play, 66-yard drive. It capped off with a nine-yard touchdown pass from Edie Elmquist to Cea’naiya Alexander on a corner route, making it 7-0 after a successful one-point conversion on a pass to Agatha Filha Gama. Bea Nackley grabbed an interception on San Lorenzo’s next drive, returning it to the one 18 seconds into the second quarter. On second down, Elmquist took a keeper up the middle for the touchdown with 10:26 left, making it 13-0 after an unsuccessful conversion. PHS’ defense forced a threeand-out, leading to six-play, 45 yard drive that resulted in a 19-yard touchdown run by Mafi, who also converted the one-point try on a run to make it 20-0 with 4:07 left in the half. Another three-and-out gave Piedmont a short field at the SLZ 31 with 1:46 remaining. After a 16-yard run by Elmquist, she hit Prata Baack for a 15-yard touchdown pass with 1:08 left. Elmquist converted the one-point try to make it 27-0. Staff Photos Skye Prata Baack celebrates a touchdown reception against San Lorenzo. Bea Nackley made two interceptions against San Lorenzo. Nea Mafi runs in a touchdown against the Grizzlies.

articles.text: Photos by Graham Smith Piedmont captains Ernie Hildreth (#6), Jeb Burden (#29), Alex Covian (#69) and Keliti Havea (#72) led the Highlanders to a 22-7 win over Aragon. The Piedmont Highlander JV team defeated Aragon 22-7 Friday, September 18, overcoming a 7-6 halftime deficit with a strong second half on both sides of the ball. Led by their four captains, the Highlanders shut down Aragon’s offense and took control after halftime. Aragon’s only points came on a first-half interception return. Piedmont’s defense held the Dons scoreless for the rest of the game, forcing four turnovers and making plays whenever Aragon threatened. Gael Fierro gave the Highlanders a big boost with two interceptions, including a pick-six that gave Piedmont momentum. His second interception helped keep Aragon from getting anything going through the air. Fierro was awarded the team’s turnover chain after the game. articles.text: Los Tranquilos Nipomo-based band Los Tranquilos perform at Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) this Friday. The free concert is part of the museum’s Friday Nights series. OMCA hosts free community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout the year, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. The band Los Tranquilos features brother duo Manny and JJ Martinez, as well as longtime friend Cameron Porter. Established in the summer of 2022, Los Tranquilos create both universal and historical tracks with sounds heavily inspired by 60s and 70s “romanticas” soul, psychedelia from Mexico and Latin America. The event continues in the museum’s amphitheater with Caja Mágica’s all-vinyl DJ set, featuring a vibrant selection of Latin American records from the ’60s and ’70s across a range of genres. Visitors can also connect with Bike East Bay in the museum garden to learn more about the organization’s efforts to create safer, more accessible streets throughout the East Bay. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Visit https://museumca.org/ to learn more. ®

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2026-27 season with Legally Blonde The Musical, based on the popular 2001 film, running now through October 11. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods, a sorority president who enrolls at Harvard Law School after being dumped by her boyfriend and ultimately proves herself while working on a case. No’eau Kahalekulu directs the production, with choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes and music direction by Camden Daly. The production features a 25-person company of Bay Area performers. “If you loved this movie in 2001, I promise it’s even more fun with a live band and an audience. The show moves at a whip fast pace and is full of laughs and seriously impressive dance and vocals,” said Kimberly Dooley, Artistic Director of Berkeley Playhouse. “Legally Blonde defies stereotypes and celebrates female teamwork, empowerment and above all else ... authenticity.” Kahalekulu said the character of Elle Woods has remained a favorite since the film’s release. “Elle Woods has been my comfort character since 2001. If she can get into Harvard and keep her sparkle, the rest of us can handle whatever’s in front of us,” said director No’eau Kahalekulu. “We’ve all gotten a little scared to be big and silly and sincere in public lately. This production is an invitation back into it. Like the show says, being true to yourself never goes out of style.” Scenic design is by Sarah Phykitt, with costumes by Ashley Renee and lighting by Sophia Craven. The musical is based on the novel Legally Blonde by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film of the same name. The cast also includes two dogs: Latke the Pomeranian, making a theatrical debut as Bruiser Woods, and Stella, a three-yearold French bulldog mix, as Rufus. Tickets are available through Berkeley Playhouse online at https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse presents Legally Blonde The Musical now through Oct. 11

articles.text: Photo courtesy of American Conservatory Theater The cast includes Danny Collins as Thornhill. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) opens its 2026-27 season with a theatrical adaptation of Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, showing onstage now through October 18. The production is adapted and directed by Emma Rice. Rice previously directed A.C.T.’s Brief Encounter and Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s The Wild Bride. Rice’s production uses seven performers, live music, movement and theatrical effects to tell the story of Roger Thornhill, an advertising executive who is mistaken for a Cold War spy and forced to flee across the country. The production features a 1950s-inspired soundtrack and a theatrical recreation of the film’s famous Mount Rushmore sequence. The cast includes Danny Collins as Thornhill, Evangeline Dickson as Mrs. Townsend and understudy, Patrycja Kujawska as Eve Kendall and others, Simon Oskarsson as Valerian and others, Katy Owen as the Professor and others, Bryony Pennington as Anna and others, and Karl Queensborough as Phillip Vandamm and others. Sam Archer will take over the role of Valerian and others beginning October 10. “What makes Emma Rice’s North by Northwest so exhilarating is that it isn’t trying to recreate Hitchcock’s film frame for frame,” said Andy Chan Donald, A.C.T.’s artistic producing director and acting artistic director. “Instead, it captures the wit, suspense, and cinematic scale of the original while embracing everything that makes live theater extraordinary.” “The result is a production that honors a beloved classic while becoming something entirely its own — a thrilling reminder that the stage can be every bit as breathtaking as the silver screen,” Donald added. The original North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant and Eva Marie Saint, follows Thornhill as he is pursued across the country after being mistaken for a government agent. Directed by Hitchcock and released in 1959, the film is widely regarded as one of the director’s major works. North by Northwest will run at A.C.T.’s Toni Rembe Theater now through October 18. Post-show conversations are scheduled for September 29, October 4 and 7. Pride Night will take place October 7, with an open-captioned performance on October 10. A tasting event is scheduled for October 6, and PlayTime, an interactive theater workshop, will take place before the October 17 matinee. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: A.C.T. presents North by Northwest now through Oct. 18

articles.text: 250 Years, Indigenous Futures installation view Haines Gallery at San Francisco’s Fort Mason presents 250 Years, Indigenous Futures, a group exhibition featuring work by eight Native American artists. The exhibition features Victoria Grace Canby, Jordan Ann Craig, Sky Hopinka, Brad Kahlhamer, Terran Last Gun, Jamie Okuma, Wendy Red Star and Keith Secola. The artists work across painting, drawing, sculpture, photography and film. The works draw from a wide range of sources, including Piikani painted lodges, Northern Cheyenne beadwork, the 1969- 71 occupation of Alcatraz Island by the Indians of All Tribes, the annual Crow Fair, horror films and archival photography. Among the artists featured is Marin-based Victoria Grace Canby, whose new works on paper depict the Three Sisters — corn, beans and squash — as a model of resilience, healing and collective care. Jordan Ann Craig’s paintings combine references to Northern Cheyenne beadwork and quillwork with the work of modernist painter Agnes Martin. Sky Hopinka’s film Sunflower Siege Engine connects the occupation of Alcatraz with Cahokia Mounds in Illinois, while Brad Kahlhamer’s Pima Air + Space features birds, horses and masked figures rendered in acrylic, ink and pencil on a bedsheet. Terran Last Gun created a series of works inspired by the geometric designs of Piikani painted lodges, while Jamie Okuma’s Of Love and Sacrifice: Motherhood combines intricate Payómkawichum (Luiseño) beadwork with imagery from the 2018 horror film Suspiria. The exhibition takes its title from the writings of Standing Photo courtesy of Haines Gallery Rock Sioux historian Philip J. Deloria and his colleagues, who have argued for understanding Native peoples through “the lens of futurity.” The exhibition similarly considers Indigenous creativity and knowledge as active forces shaping contemporary life and the future. Haines Gallery, a resident of Fort Mason since 2022, is dedicated to providing a platform for emerging and internationally established artists from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North and South America. 250 Years, Indigenous Futures is on view now through Saturday, November 7, 2026 at Haines Gallery located in Building C, on the first floor of the Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture. Admission is free. Visit https://fortmason.org/ event/haines-gallery-250-yearsindigenous-futures/2026-09-22/ to learn more.
articles.title: Haines Gallery explores Indigenous futures in new group exhibition

articles.text: The San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Orchestra jointly announced last week that they have reached a tentative agreement on a new four-year contract. The agreement, reached on September 17 after a week of negotiating by both parties, spans August 1, 2026 through July 31, 2030 and is still subject to ratification, according to the company. The orchestra strike forced the cancellation of the September 12 opening-night performance of Simon Boccanegra, as well as the annual free Opera in the Park concert scheduled for September 13. The musicians’ strike also postponed the company’s annual fundraiser to November. San Francisco Opera’s 104th season opened this Tuesday, September 22, with Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra. Thea Musgrave’s Mary, Queen of Scots opens tomorrow, Thursday, September 24, in a new co-production directed by Stewart Laing and led by debuting conductor Clelia Cafiero. “I am deeply grateful that we have reached a tentative agreement on a new contract, one that addresses important structural changes while providing a fair agreement for our Musicians,” San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock said in a press release. “We look forward to welcoming our talented company members and guest artists, as well as our cherished patrons and donors, back to the theater. Most of all, we look forward to coming together again and reconnecting through the collective beauty of the arts,” Shilvock added. For more information about San Francisco Opera’s 2026–27 season, visit www.sfopera.com.
articles.title: SF Opera and orchestra reach tentative contract agreement

articles.text: Saturday, September 26 – November 1 Oakland Art Association gallery show Oakland Art Association presents Hopes and Dreams, a curated show that encompasses everyone’s most precious and intimate desires for the future. It can be a dream vacation, a dream come true, a dream for the future of the world or just your part of it. Hope knows no bounds, hope for change, for healing, a brighter future, or for world peace. OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties whose mission is to encourage artistic endeavor in the community, support public school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. The Opening Reception will be from 1:00 – 4:00 p.m. on Saturday, September 26, free and open to all. For more information, see www.oaklandart.org. Saturday, September 26, 6:00 p.m. Ezequiel Barrera and Carl Blake piano recital As part of his residency in the SF Bay Area, virtuoso pianist and composer Ezequiel Sebastian Barrera from Mexico City will perform a recital, assisted by local pianist Carl Blake in a performance of Barrera’s Fantasia Mexicana for one piano-four hands. Ezequiel has performed extensively to critical acclaim in diverse venues around the world including US, Canada, Mexico, Central America, Chile, and Germany. The program includes works by Beethoven, Ravel, and Villa-Lobos as well as original compositions by Barrera. A wine reception will follow the recital to which everyone is cordially invited. $25 Advance tickets are available at https:// www.ticketsignup.io/Barrera. Sunday, September 27, 7:30 p.m. Festival Opera Vocal Salon Walnut Creek’s Festival Opera Association continues its 2026 season with the first of three events in this year’s Salon Series, which will celebrate the launch of Festival Opera’s new Resident Artist Program with a concert of arias and scenes featuring the exceptional talents of our inaugural class of resident artists, followed by a wine reception where you can meet the artists. Resident artist sopranos Marielle Leiboff and Rachel Nelson, mezzo-soprano Phoebe Dinga, tenor Spencer Greene, baritone Liam Daley, and pianist Daniel Lockert will showcase arias and scenes from operas composed by Verdi, Handel, Mozart, Strauss, Massenet, Bizet, Lehar, Leoncavallo, Tesori, and Bernstein. Doors will open at 7:00 p.m. Please buy advance tickets for this show or for the series at https://tinyurl.com/FestivalSalon1. Saturday, October 3, 7:00 p.m. Mads Tolling with Kenny Washington Two-time Grammy Award-winning Danish violinist Mads Tolling returns to PCA with prolific pianist John R. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington for the fourth time the three of them will perform together. The trio will perform their own music as well as that of composers Chick Corea, Ornette Coleman, and the group Toto, along with songs from the American Songbook, including the Temptations, Carol King, and jazz greats like Thelonious Monk and George Gershwin. Advance tickets are recommended, as this show is likely to sell out, and are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/jazzviolin, and doors will open at 6:30 p.m. Friday, October 9, 6:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture A Friday night Extravaganza! Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his hometown of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western Art. As he moved through his forties, this sculptor, painter, architect, and poet of the High Renaissance would continue to yield sculptural masterpieces and explore the art of architecture at San Lorenzo, the parish church of the Medici family. In 1534, he moved to Rome and only returned to Florence after his passing almost another thirty years later. articles.text: It’s kind of fun trying to be anonymous. Ogden Nash was convinced that it’s kind of fun to be extinct. I’m not sure that I agree with him on that one. But being anonymous is lots of fun. Especially if you are a music critic. You get to eavesdrop on conversations and ask innocent questions pretending that you don’t know very much. I had intended to write an article about being anonymous. That idea changed on Sunday afternoon during the violin recital of Marcio Candido. His violin recital in the Piedmont Center for the Arts was a one-man show devoted entirely to the unaccompanied violin sonatas of J.S. Bach. Candido is a very friendly person and possesses enthusiasm and a love for his art. He expresses these things musically and verbally. The solo sonatas of Johann Sebastian Bach are regarded as the Old Testament of violin music. They are indispensable. Candido began his program with Bach’s monumental Partita No. 2. Modern violinists approach music in general as if music is an antiseptic art. They strive for perfection. In spite of their perfection, their approach lacks the human element. Candido comes from a different school entirely. From the moment he places his bow on the strings of his violin, the music comes to life. No composer in the history of music had more rhythm than Johann Sebastian Bach. His music must dance. It doesn’t need a thump thump thump beat, but it must have a beat that conveys rhythm in a dancing way. When Marcio Candido plays Bach, it comes to life. His concept is expansive. The audience was receptive to everything the violinist played. Of particular interest was the movement known as the chaconne. Toward the middle of the movement the tonality changes from minor to the major key. When it returns to the minor key, violinists do not know what to do. Burr and Grammy-nominated vocalist Kenny Washington for the fourth time the three of them will perform together. The trio will perform their own music as well as that of composers Chick Corea, Ornette Coleman, and the group Toto, along with songs from the American Songbook, including the Temptations, Carol King, and jazz greats like Thelonious Monk and George Gershwin. Art historian Michael Stehr presents a spirited, illustrated 50-minute lecture exploring Michelangelo’s work in his hometown of Florence, Italy. At the age of 29, he would put the finishing touches on his David, likely one of the most recognizable sculptures in Western Art. Dick Carter introduced Matthew Hawk, a new participant joining the walk that morning. Announcements done, Dick turned the reins over to Jim Kellogg, who would lead the walk. Jim started by noting that the morning would focus on old and new architecture in the Piedmont City Center. We think of the “old” city center as built from about 1900 to 1920, but many “new” additions have been made, and when done well the two blend together to add to the beauty and value of our city. The first stop was the beautiful courtyard of Piedmont Community Church, where Don Ashburn, PCC associate pastor, met the walkers and talked about the heritage of the church. PCC was formed in 1910 as the first non-denominational church west of the Mississippi. The first example is the second level office and administration wing above the arched walkway, designed in 2005 by Piedmont architects Bill and Vicky Kendrick in Spanish Mission style, with detailing that integrates seamlessly with the original building. Dick Carter introduced Matthew Hawk, a new participant joining the walk that morning. Announcements done, Dick turned the reins over to Jim Kellogg, who would lead the walk. Jim started by noting that the morning would focus on old and new architecture in the Piedmont City Center. We think of the “old” city center as built from about 1900 to 1920, but many “new” additions have been made, and when done well the two blend together to add to the beauty and value of our city. The first stop was the beautiful courtyard of Piedmont Community Church, where Don Ashburn, PCC associate pastor, met the walkers and talked about the heritage of the church. PCC was formed in 1910 as the first non-denominational church west of the Mississippi. The original goal, which still applies today, was to be a church that reflected the diversity of a Piedmont that was growing and drawing people from all parts of America. Jim then talked about Albert Farr’s 1917 design, with the sanctuary and Guild Hall opening onto the courtyard, each with Spanish Mission style bell towers, the sanctuary with a copper roofed chancel dome, and the two connected by a mission style arched walkway. Additions that were not part of Farr’s original design have added a great deal to what is seen today. The first example is the second level office and administration wing above the arched walkway, designed in 2005 by Piedmont architects Bill and Vicky Kendrick in Spanish Mission style, with detailing that integrates seamlessly with the original building. The walkers took a group photo there. The group then proceeded into Route map the sanctuary, which is Farr’s original Spanish Mission style with open wood roof trusses, stucco walls and Spanish carved wood detailing. Here too, new elements add to what we see today. First is the stunning stained glass leaded window collection on the side walls, designed and built by James Hubbell in 1998 to replace the original windows that were showing their age. The Piedmont walkers take a group photo at Piedmont Community Church. large narthex Psalm 23 window is also new, redesigned in 2017 after the original stained glass began falling out of the lead frames and onto the floor. Something had to be done. The leaded glass work was done by The Hyland Studio in Santa Clara, one of the few remaining stained glass artisans in Northern California. Next is the large projecting bay at the chancel choir loft, under the chancel dome, added in 2005 as part of the Kendricks’ remodel, which also brought three new octagonal chancel windows designed by Hubbell. And last is the church’s grand organ. The church decided in 1957 that a grand organ was needed, and it was built to order by Mathias P. Moller, with pipe ranks up to 32 feet high and installed in a wood sound box behind the chancel screen. Moller immigrated to America from Denmark in 1892, and his shop built organs for the West Point and Naval Academy chapels. This just goes to show that immigrants to America can add significant value to our culture. In due course, however, all good things get old. By 2018 the console keys were sticking, the air bellows were wheezing and the pipes were leaking, and a complete restoration was required, done by Hupalo and Repasky Master Organ Builders in San Francisco. Walkers lined up to poke their heads into the wood sound box on the side of the chancel and see the inner workings of a grand organ. The group was then off down Highland Avenue, pausing at 1900 Oakland Avenue, the Rackcliffe-Coffin House, built in 1899.
