articles.text: On Monday, September 14, the First Mondays Reading Group met inside the Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. This was actually the second Monday of the month, as the Labor Day holiday had pushed their meeting back a week. The group received an excellent turnout of 24 participants to discuss their August book, Horse, by Geraldine Brooks. Horse is a 2022 historical fiction novel by Australian author Geraldine Brooks. She interlinks three periods with the thoroughbred racehorse Lexington and the enslaved person who groomed him in the 1850s. This is a story of slavery and social justice through the lens of art related to the horse’s celebrated life. The novel takes place in three periods: 1850s pre-Civil War Kentucky, 1950s New York, and 2019 through a painting discovered by Theo, a Nigerian-born Georgetown University graduate student. Brooks blends real history with her fictional story of an enslaved groom named Jarret who nurtured an extraordinarily strong connection with Lexington. This legendary horse won seven of its eight races, was the fastest horse for twenty years, and produced hundreds of race-winning offspring. The painting is rooted in real artwork produced by artists of the time, like itinerant painter Thomas J. Scott. Upon Lexington’s death, the horse’s skeletal remains were rearticulated, displayed for some time by the Smithsonian Museum, stored away for decades, and then rediscovered. Lexington’s importance to racing and breeding was largely forgotten until the 1970s. The novel brings together many different topics: slavery and freedom, the hidden brutality behind the sport of horse racing, the constant pull of greed, the development of the genre of equine art, New York City art galleries, interracial romance, and contemporary police brutality against people of color. Horse was well received by critics and also the reading group. It was noted that Brooks was initially a reporter, and the deep research she did to present Lexington’s history and also the novel’s human characters, with some license taken in historical accuracy, was appreciated. Readers appreciated that the author resurrected a largely lost past. The group valued how Brooks wove the different characters and time periods together to present her social justice message. Readers liked how she blended the actual histories of the book’s characters with her fictionalized enhancements. Readers agreed that the histories of the horse and characters were better than the fictional elements. It was expressed that Brooks seemed to add a romantic component to satisfy her readers. It was noted that the love story might make the book more sellable as a movie where the characters Jarret and Lexington might be more fully developed. Jarret’s powerful commitment to the horse was also noted. He preferred to remain enslaved rather than lose his connection to the horse. Many readers would have preferred Brooks stay with Lexington and the horse’s real history. In fact, one reader only read the chapters dealing with Lexington and Jarret and skipped those dealing with the story’s romantic relationship. It was said that a good writer makes the reader care about a book’s characters, and this might have been a criticism of the book. One topic of discussion was Brooks’ use of the common, contemporary writing technique of jumping back and forth between multiple time periods. While some readers had an issue with it, most readers generally thought Brooks did it well and filled in gaps that increased their understanding of her narrative. Some readers didn’t realize how racist and brutal horse racHorse by Geraldine Brooks ing was during this period, but they did recognize that some elements of it remain today. Brooks brought the racism of today front and center with a shocking murder that connected the fear and discrimination that Jarret and Theo shared over the generations. The murder brought Lexington’s story home to our times. Readers generally liked Horse, but a reader of Brooks’ other works felt it might not be her best book. However, the group agreed they learned a lot from the book and that Horse had provided for a good discussion. That also made it a good book for the First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected Freezing Order by Bill Browder for October, and The Correspondent by Virginia Evans for their November read. After Dick Carter presented three fiction candidates, the readers selected All Creatures Great and Small by James Herriot for their December book. With all their business done, they took a group photo in the circle outside the Community Hall. The readers will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on October 5 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. Among those participating were Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Marj Blackwell, Peggy Shultz, Judy Love, Susie Backer, Rob White, Kristin Howard, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Adrienne Hamlin, Bella Almanzan, Orrel Lanter, Darby Gragg, Melba Yee, Sandy Threlfall, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, Claudia Cate, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Mary Holt and Russell Van Herik, who were there for the first time.

articles.text: On July 25, Beach Play Field in Piedmont was filled with colorful team banners, soccer balls, laughter and plenty of cheering as children and families came together for a special CoachArt Field Day. The event brought together patients from Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland and their siblings for a morning of adapted sports, games and community. Led by CoachArt volunteers and Piedmont teens, and supported by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Field Day gave children an opportunity to play, connect and simply enjoy being kids. CoachArt provides free adaptive lessons in arts, athletics and STEM for children affected by serious illness. Volunteer mentors create safe, encouraging experiences tailored to each child’s needs. For families navigating serious illness, those experiences can help restore moments of childhood that might otherwise be lost. George Saunders, a longtime CoachArt volunteer and Piedmont High School junior, proposed the idea for a Piedmont Field Day and, along with CoachArt National Program Director Erick Rodriguez, brought the event together from the ground up. George and fellow students from Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School, Jonah Cha Foster, Joaquin Fierro, Emmy Hong and Jane Saunders, volunteered their time at the July event, helping organize activities, work with the teams and make the morning welcoming for every participant. The Piedmont Recreation Department was instrumental in making the Field Day possible. Liam Kelly, Recreation Supervisor, helped coordinate the event, provided props and materials for the activities, and issued a permit allowing CoachArt to use Beach Play Field. Participants were given CoachArt T-shirts and divided into teams, each assigned its own color. Before the athletic activities began, children and volunteers worked together to create colorful banners representing their teams. Over snacks and conversation, the teams got to know one another, creating connections before heading out onto the field. When it was time to play, teams rotated through a series of adapted activities, including soccer, Wiffle ball and relay races. Volunteer coaches and student volunteers helped participants take part at their own pace, creating an atmosphere where everyone could contribute and have fun. One CoachArt parent commented, “My family has been wearing their CoachArt T-shirts proudly and has been sharing about the program with family and friends. My daughter feels super supported by the experience.” For the Piedmont students who volunteered, the day offered a chance to give back to their community while helping create an enjoyable experience for participants and their families. Saunders commented, “I am so happy that this idea came to life. It was fun and meaningful to see the Piedmont and CoachArt communities come together for a great day!” The morning wrapped up with more time for the children and volunteers to spend together, along with raffle prizes for participants. CoachArt’s Executive Director, Molly Dirr, said, “The CoachArt families had a great time and enthusiastically shared that they would love to do it again!” Saunders hopes to make the Field Day an annual end-of-summer event in Piedmont and plans to roll out similar field day events in other CoachArt communities throughout the United States. pages.text: Wednesday, September 23, 2026 23 Adventures in Scouting Why Scouting Matters By Brad Cardon Many of my most cherished childhood memories came from Scouting. I went all the way through, earning my Arrow of Light and achieving the rank of Eagle Scout, like my dad before me. I grew up in San Diego with a core group of friends whom I met in first grade through Scouting. We camped, explored, learned new skills, and, most importantly, spent time together. Scouting gave us a chance to disconnect from school, sports, and everything else going on, and simply be kids. I’m still friends with many members of this Scouting group today—we have a group chat where we connect nearly daily, and we make a point of getting together at least once a year. Irreplaceable. I wanted that same experience for my two boys, now in fifth and second grade. I’m thrilled that they love Cub Scouts. It gives them a chance to get outside, put their feet in the dirt, play with sticks, sleep in a tent, and discover that having fun doesn’t require a screen. My second grader’s favorite experience is camping at Rock City on Mount Diablo. I barely saw him as he was having so much fun with his friends. My fifth grader also loves camping, but his favorite tradition is the Pinewood Derby. We’ve worked together on his car every year in our garage—it’s great father-son time. We’re a big sports family. Between soccer play dates, basketball practices, flag football games, and regular season and travel ball schedules, our calLandry (right) with friends in Muir Woods Landry Cardon at his first Webeloree, Bort Meadow Landry Cardon at the Piedmont Council Pinewood Derby Landry with his dad, Brad, at the Kirby Cove Cub Scout overnighter The Cub Scout Den at the Piedmont Fire Department Cub Scouts hike in Reinhardt Redwood Regional Park Beau Cardon and a friend at the Piedmont Council Pinewood Derby Brad & Marissa Cardon with their boys Landry and Beau hiking in Austria endar gets busy. But I believe kids can—and should—do both. Scouting doesn’t have to compete with sports—it complements it. Scouting isn’t competitive, which is a nice change for kids. Cub Scouts gives kids a place to try something new without worrying about whether they’ll be good at it or even do it correctly. The Cub Scout motto is “Do Your Best,” which says a lot about what Scouting is all about. As a parent and volunteer, I love what Scouting teaches: leadership, citizenship, service, helping others, and appreciation for nature. Yet I also love seeing kids smile and helping them create experiences that they’ll carry with them. I’m especially grateful for the parents who lead our pack. They are creative, dedicated, and committed to making every meeting and event fun. Scouting has a way of bringing out the best in people. For our family, Cub Scouts is one of the few places where the goal is simply to be together, get outside, and have a good time. You don’t have to do everything. You just have to show up, bring a good attitude, and do your best. And sometimes, that’s more than enough. Landry & Beau Cardon at Crater Lake, Oregon

articles.text: A family orders from the Gyro food truck. Families lay out blankets on the park’s lawn after receiving their food from the trucks. Hundreds of Piedmonters flocked to Piedmont Park on Friday, September 18, to enjoy the third Food Truck Friday. From 5 to 8 p.m., residents lined up to try savory foods and listen to music with their friends and family. The event preceded Piedmont High School’s Homecoming, allowing families to grab dinner before heading to the football game. Five food trucks were available on Highland Avenue for attendees to choose from. They included Golden Gate Gyro, Sausage King, El Gran Taco Loco, Crazy Empanadas Truck, and Pineapple Whips. These trucks provided a wide selection of sweet and savory foods, like pineapple drinks, hot dogs, empanadas, burritos, and gyros. From this reporter’s view, the most popular trucks were El Gran Taco Loco and Golden Gate Gyro, with lines extending deep onto the lawn. Piedmonters laid out their blankets for a picnic on the park’s grass after getting their food. Kids ran around the lawn and played at the tot lot nearby. The event gave many the chance to step back and have a nice evening catching up with friends The reporter’s meal of a regular burrito and horchata drink from El Gran Taco Loco. A man surveys the menu from the Sausage King food truck. and family. This reporter sampled the regular burrito and horchata from El Gran Taco Loco. The truck offers three meats for your burritos or tacos: chicken, beef, and pork. I decided to choose the chicken. The burrito came with beans, chicken, rice, and pico de gallo, and two spicy salsas on the side. The burrito was well cooked, and the chicken had that perfect grilled taste. The salsas were the perfect amount of spice to balance out the sweet horchata drink. Overall, I give the meal four out of five stars. The Rec Department will host a movie in the park on September 25, Elio, an animated kids’ movie that follows a young boy’s journey through space with different aliens. pages.text: Wednesday, September 23, 2026 27 Piedmont hosts third Food Truck Friday A family orders from the Gyro food truck. Families lay out blankets on the park’s lawn after receiving their food from the trucks. By Jake Lannon Hundreds of Piedmonters flocked to Piedmont Park on Friday, September 18, to enjoy the third Food Truck Friday. From 5 to 8 p.m., residents lined up to try savory foods and listen to music with their friends and family. The event preceded Piedmont High School’s Homecoming, allowing families to grab dinner before heading to the football game. Five food trucks were available on Highland Avenue for attendees to choose from. They included Golden Gate Gyro, Sausage King, El Gran Taco Loco, Crazy Empanadas Truck, and Pineapple Whips. These trucks provided a wide selection of sweet and savory foods, like pineapple drinks, hot dogs, empanadas, burritos, and gyros. From this reporter’s view, the most popular trucks were El Gran Taco Loco and Golden Gate Gyro, with lines extending deep onto the lawn. Piedmonters laid out their blankets for a picnic on the park’s grass after getting their food. Kids ran around the lawn and played at the tot lot nearby. The event gave many the chance to step back and have a nice evening catching up with friends The reporter’s meal of a regular burrito and horchata drink from El Gran Taco Loco. A man surveys the menu from the Sausage King food truck. and family. This reporter sampled the regular burrito and horchata from El Gran Taco Loco. The truck offers three meats for your burritos or tacos: chicken, beef, and pork. I decided to choose the chicken. The burrito came with beans, chicken, rice, and pico de gallo, and two spicy salsas on the side. The burrito was well cooked, and the chicken had that perfect grilled taste. The salsas were the perfect amount of spice to balance out the sweet horchata drink. Overall, I give the meal four out of five stars. The Rec Department will host a movie in the park on September 25, Elio, an animated kids’ movie that follows a young boy’s journey through space with different aliens. The next Food Truck Friday will be on October 16. Families wait in long lines to order their food. articles.text: Short-term priorities include regularly scheduled maintenance and replacement projects, as well as fixing unplanned hazards that — if left unaddressed — could lead to more costly repairs or liability exposure. These include items like street paving, sidewalk repair, and hazardous tree removal, and should be planned for in the annual budget. Medium-ter m pr ior ities include larger capital repairs, ADA upgrades, new equipment, technology, and upgrades that are known but may be beyond the reach of the current-year budget. Sequencing of these projects can change with the availability of municipal funding, limited state and regional grants, and community fundraising efforts. Long-term infrastructure needs (10+ years) include replacing or rebuilding older city buildings, particularly our fire and police stations. These buildings are in use 24 hours a day, are expensive to maintain, and are suboptimal for their current needs. While rebuilding these facilities would require significant financial and logistical planning, it may also present an opportunity to consider additional civic assets such as a library or senior center. articles.text: Editor, I write to enthusiastically express my support for Nancy Beninati, Tom Ramsey, and Bill Reichle for Piedmont City Council. All three of these candidates are proven leaders in our community. Nancy and I worked closely together as volunteers with the League of Women Voters of Piedmont where she served as President. Her leadership, collaborative spirit, and support of our community are unwavering, not just with the League, but also through serving on multiple Piedmont Commissions. Her professional background as a supervising attorney at the California DOJ and lecturer at UC Berkeley make her exceedingly qualified and ready to work on the issues most important to Piedmont residents. Tom and I have served on the City Council together since December of 2024. He always puts the residents of Piedmont first and has a positive, solution-oriented outlook. He is the epitome of a good public servant and good steward for our city’s funds. Bill is also a longstanding volunteer in Piedmont, supporting our schools that are a cornerstone in our community. His experience as Assistant Vice Chancellor at UC Berkeley makes him highly qualified to make the decisions required of Councilmembers in a way that best serves Piedmont. I urge my fellow Piedmont voters to cast their votes for Nancy, Tom, and Bill for Piedmont City Council. – Lorrel Plimier

articles.text: Editor, I am pleased to endorse Nancy Beninati for Piedmont City Council. Nancy brings the kind of experience and perspective that would strengthen our City Council. Her public service at the California Department of Justice, combined with her work as a UC Berkeley lecturer in law and public policy, Nancy understands government, policy, and the importance of thoughtful decision-making. Just as importantly, Nancy has been actively involved in the Piedmont community for decades. She has served on the Civil Service Commission, as President of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, and currently as a Recreation Commissioner. She has also volunteered in our schools and youth sports as her high school boys have grown up in Piedmont. Nancy understands what makes Piedmont such a wonderful place to raise a family, and she cares about preserving that sense of community. I look forward to working with Nancy on the City Council. She will bring a thoughtful, collaborative approach, listen to different perspectives, and work with her colleagues to find common ground and get things done for Piedmont. I strongly encourage Piedmont voters to join me in electing Nancy Beninati to the City Council. – Conna McCarthy Vice-Mayor, City of Piedmont

Nancy Beninati (NancyforPiedmont.com) I believe Piedmont’s top infrastructure needs are reflected in the City’s most recent budget: maintaining and improving our streets and sidewalks, upgrading our stormwater and sewer systems, and maintaining and modernizing our public facilities, including parks and recreational facilities. I support the City’s focus on these areas, while also considering public safety, emergency preparedness, and sustainability throughout these projects. I care about the Piedmont community, and with aging infrastructure and ongoing maintenance needs, we have a responsibility to take care of what we have while planning thoughtfully for the future. Places like our Community Hall, pool, parks, and other City facilities are part of what makes Piedmont special. They are where friends and families gather, make memories, and build community, and they should remain vibrant and welcoming. If elected, I would listen to residents, review the City’s capital improvement plans and financial projections, and work with City staff and fellow councilmembers to determine which projects should receive attention first. I would consider condition, public safety, urgency, community impact, available funding, and long-term financial consequences. I want to help take care of the Piedmont we have today while making thoughtful choices about the Piedmont we leave for the next generation. Sunny Bostrom-Flemming In my opinion, the most important infrastructure issues are the ones directly related to safety. At least twice a week, I ride my bike down Oakland Ave on the way to Trader Joe’s, having to dodge cracks in the pavement and potholes big enough to drown a baby chihuahua. Like the city of Alameda, I also recommend a citywide speed limit of 25 miles per hour, and less where posted. The issue of the state mandate requiring 587 new housing units in Piedmont is going to require all of our best effort to provide infrastructure for police, fire, and schools. If the same housing mandate rule applied in Oakland, where they have a current population of 440,000, they will have 80,000 people added that will need housing, education, police, fire, and infrastructure. Any city with this type of situation would have tremendous infrastructure challenges, but I am confident that Piedmont, with its population of men, women, and children of good will and hard work, can meet this challenge. In its early days Piedmont was thought of as “Queen of the Hills,” with somewhat densely packed elite homes surrounded by pastoral farmland and panoramic vistas. The Waldo property, from Park Way to Blair and from Vernal Avenue (Highland Avenue today) to the backyards of the houses on Bonita Avenue, was part of farmland owned by Walter Blair, and the only parcel of pastureland west of Vernal. Blair’s daughter Florence Blair inherited the property and continued to use it as pastureland until she died in 1925. That was the end of the old pastoral landscape attached to Piedmont’s city center. The parcel was developed as a new neighborhood, Waldo Avenue, and all of the homes were built within a two year period by 1928. The plan made use of consistent front yard setbacks and two story massing that melded varying colors and styles into a very popular neighborhood, one that integrates well into today’s Piedmont City Center. The group continued south on Bonita Avenue past several other notable old homes, then past Havens School, built in 2010 and designed by Piedmont architect Mark Becker in traditional Spanish Mission Revival style. The walk concluded at the observation deck at the north end of the Piedmont Community Swimming Pool, which is available for use by everyone. The group used it as a chance for a brief rest and to admire the spectacular view, greatly appreciated by all. Walking on Wednesdays meets every week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues). The program is free and open to all, and new walkers—along with their K-9 best friends—are always welcome. Registration is required. For more information or to sign up, visit https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or call (510) 420-3070. articles.text: This past week, the Post spoke with Piedmont Firefighter union leaders about the current state of their contract negotiations with the city. Currently, they’re working without a contract and face serious recruitment and retention problems. To address this, union leaders have proposed adding compensation and retirement benefits to bolster their recruitment. According to the Union, City leadership has rejected several collaborative proposals and refused to discuss specific issues. “The pool of applicants is shrinking, but the jobs are not. There’s not less work to be done, and if anything, there’s more because call volumes only go up. Now we’re just at a place where recruitment is tough, fire service-wide. The onus is on the employer to be attractive to employees,” said Union President Brian Gidney. According to the Union, the department is understaffed, which has caused staff to work heavy overtime. In this field, overtime is different than a traditional 9-to-5. Firefighters work 24 to 48 hours at the station, Piedmont fire and medical response teams being sent out on a call.
articles.title: Piedmont Firefighters voice frustration in negotiations for a new deal with the city

articles.text: The City of Piedmont held a ceremony on Friday morning, September 11, commemorating the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Washington, DC, in which 3,000 people lost their lives. The commemoration took place in front of the Fire Station at 8:30 a.m. The ceremony began with the fire department hoisting an American flag at half-mast to honor the lives lost. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen came to the podium to give her remarks on the 25th anniversary of the attack on September 11, 2001. “Twenty-five years ago today, our country changed in the space of a single morning. For those of us who remember that day, it feels like a line drawn through The Fire Department hoisted the American flag at half-mast to honor the victims of the September 11 attacks. our own lives. There is the world we lived in before, and the world we’ve lived in since. Most of us can still tell you exactly where we were when we heard, who we called. What the sky looked like. That kind of memory doesn’t fade. It becomes part of who we are,” said Mayor Andersen.

articles.text: Each election cycle the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question to the candidates running for City Council every week until election day. The five City Council candidates vying for three open seats received the question on September 1 and were asked to reply with a 200-word response. Week 3 question Do you support Measure GG? Why? If this measure passes, how would you prioritize the funds generated by the measure? Nancy Beninati (Nancyforpiedmont.com) I support Measure GG, which would increase Piedmont’s real estate transfer tax by 0.45 percentage points, from 1.3% to 1.75%. The tax is paid only when a property is transferred, not annually. As a licensed California Real Estate Broker, I am familiar with real estate transactions and transfer taxes. articles.text: During the September 9 Piedmont School Board meeting three University of California, professors from Berkeley spoke in support of reinstating the SAT as a requirement for undergraduate admission to the UCs. The board’s resolution asking the UCs to bring back standardized tests brought the lauded professors to Piedmont’s City Hall, including Noble Prize winner Dr. Randy Schekman. “I have seen in recent years a precipitous decline in the performance of my [Intro Biology] students,” said Dr. Schekman. Schekman, a professor of molecular and cell biology at the University of California, Berketeins in our cells. “We don’t know to what we can attribute this, but the indications are, that it may be attributable to the loss of that requirement for an SAT test,” added Schekman. Dr. Sabeeha Merchant, a 40 year-tenured plant biology professor and researcher at both UCLA and Cal also spoke eloquently in favor bringing the test back. articles.text: After two years serving as Padre Grande of the Beach Dads Club, and more than six years attending the Pancake Breakfast with my family, I have learned that the secret ingredient behind this tradition is not the batter or the butter. It is the people and community partners who make it possible. I want to offer an equally heartfelt thank you to Village Market, Mulberry’s Market and Piedmont Grocery. Each has generously supported the Pancake Breakfast and helped make this tradition possible. Between commercial griddles, the Fun Zone, entertainment, equipment and other hard costs, the event simply would not remain affordable without the collective support of all three. They are not just vendors. They are community partners, and we are deeply grateful to each of them. One of the best pieces of advice I received came from my wife, Zeena Fakoury, who serves on the Piedmont Education Foundation board. She reminded me early on that the goal is not maximizing the profit margin. It is maximizing the fun factor. If the kids are excited and want to stay, parents have more time to mingle, connect and actually get to know one another. Dads end up standing shoulder to shoulder making it happen, and families leave wanting to return the following year. That is the win. A special thank you also belongs to Principal Anne Valva, whose energy and support have strengthened these events year after year. Beach is incredibly fortunate to have a leader who understands how much these shared experiences matter. And then there is the Fire Department, whose visits and genuine engagement with the kids these past few years can only be described as quite possibly the coolest thing to happen on a playground at 8 a.m. in a very long time. None of this happens without volunteers. For 21 years, generations of Beach dads have hauled equipment, mixed batter, worked the griddles and cleaned the playground. For me, being part of that tradition carries a deeper meaning. My daughter Dalia is now in fourth grade at Beach, and my son Zane is in sixth grade at Piedmont Middle School. By the time I entered sixth grade, I had already moved four times, with roughly a dozen more moves still ahead of me before eventually finding this community. I know how much it means to find a place that welcomes you and feels like home. Serving as Padre Grande has been one small way to give something back and help other new kids and families feel that same sense of belonging. So, whenever possible, please remember to start local. The businesses we support are often the same businesses quietly supporting our children, schools and traditions. And three cheers to the Beach Dads Club: the dads who built this tradition, the dads carrying it forward today and the next generation waiting to leave its own mark. Give a bunch of dads a few griddles, an early alarm and the full support of a community, and it turns out they can make a little magic on a playground. Thank you to Village Market, Mulberry’s Market and Piedmont Grocery, Principal Anne Valva, the Piedmont Fire Department and every volunteer who continues to show up. You are the secret ingredient behind the Pancake Breakfast, and we could not do it without you. –Rob Doebelin Padre Grande #20 & #21 Beach School Dads Club
articles.title: The secret ingredient of 21 years of pancakes

articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident and conservation leader Cameron Wolfe will be honored by the Sonoma Botanical Garden (SBG) as its 2026 Gala Honoree & Legacy Leader at its annual gala in Glen Ellen, CA on October 3. Wolfe, who was a partner at the San Francisco office of Orrick, Herrington and Sutcliffe, LLP, became associated with Sonoma Botanical Garden in 2000, then named Quarryhill Botanical Garden, when the Garden’s visionary founder, Jane Davenport Jansen, passed away unexpectedly. Piedmont doyenne Helen Breck was on the Garden’s Board and recruited Wolfe to help the Garden weather legal matters related to Jansen’s death. Wolfe continued to provide pro bono legal services to the Garden and eventually served two 6-year terms on its Board and two years as the Board President. “Cameron stepped forward at a pivotal moment in the Garden’s history and has remained a steadfast champion for more than 25 years,” said Jeannie Perales, Executive Director, SBG. “His leadership, generosity, and commitment to conservation have helped the Garden endure and thrive. We are deeply grateful and proud to honor his remarkable legacy.” Wolfe is renowned for his volunteer efforts around Piedmont as well. He joined the Piedmont Recreation Committee in the late ‘60s and served two years as its Chair. In that role, he helped establish the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. He and his wife, Fran, organized Piedmont’s first Tree Lighting Ceremony in conjunction with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Most importantly, he secured the school-owned property at the corner of Hampton and LaSalle for the City of Piedmont and helped raise funds for the ballpark and playfield there. Wolfe has served on the Piedmont Education Foundation Board and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation where he continues to serve Cameron Wolfe, Jr. as an Advisor. Wolfe’s interest in the environment also led him to serve on the League to Save Lake Tahoe Board for 25 years. He and his wife Fran served as trustees for the Yosemite Fund for over 10 years. They are also long-time supporters of Save the Redwoods League and in 2012, Cameron commemorated a redwood grove in Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park to Fran – the Fran B. Wolfe Grove. The Gala will be held at the Sonoma Botanical Garden in Glen Ellen on October 3, 2026. Tickets and information are available at https://sonomabg.org/garden-gala-2026/. About Sonoma Botanical Garden Founded in 1987, Sonoma Botanical Garden (SBG) is a woodland experience where East meets West, celebrating the beauty and importance of Asian and California native plants. Nestled in the Sonoma Valley, the Garden’s 63 acres feature a unique Asian woodland, a California native oak savanna, and a Cabernet vineyard. Its mission is to inspire appreciation and understanding of Asian and California native plants and promote their conservation in natural habitats and gardens. Visit sonomabg.org for details. articles.text: Earlier this month, Patty Dunlap, President of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF), welcomed a full room of Trustees and advisors to the new board’s first meeting. Dunlap is serving her third year as President to help wrap up several projects underway before the next leadership change. Since the new Board took office on July 1, they’ve had a busy summer. The Spring Campaign for the Nature Play Area has proved extremely popular with Piedmonters, with donations crossing $70,000. Work is well underway at the Main Park Tot Lot, where the Nature Play Area will be installed, as well as the return of the swings. It is not too late to help make these projects a spectacular success, and additional contributions are very much appreciated. PBF is in its 62nd year of initiating and supporting projects for the safety, sustainability, and beautification of Piedmont. The organization has eight Trustees, three from the City of Piedmont, including the Mayor, the Vice Mayor, and the Chair of the Park Commission, and five from the Piedmont Garden Club. PBF has 29 advisors this year, including representatives from four other garden clubs in Piedmont: Hoe and Hope; Highlanders Garden Club; East Bay Garden Club and Home Gardeners. Measure GG The first item of business at the PBF meeting was consideration of the Measure GG Transfer Tax. Former Mayor Bob McBain, Chair of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, explained the measure; the tax is a one-time tax applicable only to the transfer of real estate. The committee unanimously recommended a modest tax increase to bring Piedmont’s transfer tax more in line with those of other East Bay jurisdictions. After a thorough discussion of the proposal, the Trustees unanimously voted that PBF endorse the measure and recommend a YES vote on November 3. Bringing back a Piedmont tradition The other important item on the agenda was consideration of a principal focus for PBF’s Fall campaign. Nancy Kent, Piedmont’s Parks and Projects Manager, outlined several city needs, prompting Vice President Marilyn Weber to propose reviving PBF’s original Holiday Greeting Fund. Under the initiative, community members donate to PBF – honoring friends and neighbors – with proceeds funding city projects throughout the year. The Trustees unanimously approved the proposal. Details for the campaign will be highlighted in the Fall Brochure arriving this November. Donor names and accompanying tributes will be published in early 2027. People can make contributions to PBF at any time through the PBF website, PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org. Cameron Wolfe, Patty Dunlap, and Bob McBain visit the Naturescape project in Piedmont’s main park. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: In November Piedmonters will vote to decide their next City Council members and decide on crucial measures that could impact the region. On the ballot is a transit tax measure called the Public Transit Revenue Measure, which would impose a sales tax for 14 years to fund public transportation systems in the region. At the Piedmont City Council meeting on September 8, AC Transit representatives discussed the potential impacts if the measure fails to pass and the current financial struggles that AC Transit is facing. AC Transit covers 364 square miles, and serves more than three million riders monthly, in 13 cities and eight unincorporated communities in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. According to Ryan Lau, the External Affairs representative at AC Transit, their costs have risen, and their revenue has flattened, causing a budget deficit. “When the cost of running our bus network rises faster than the revenue supporting it, it results in a fiscal cliff,” said Lau. “Our regional sales tax revenue has flattened, and our fare revenue growth has slowed. At the same time, fuel costs have gone up by 28%. Bus maintenance parts have increased by 14%, and the cost of buying new buses has surged by 35%.” With the increased costs, AC Transit is reportedly operating at a budget deficit. Over the next four years, AC Transit faces a $200 million deficit, which is roughly $50 million a year beginning in 2027. “Without a long-term sustainable funding source, we’re looking at service reductions of up to 16%, and those are unavoidable. We’re also looking at potential human costs, with layoffs projected to affect up to 300 employees,” said Lau. Piedmont would see service reductions to Lines 12, 18, 88, P, and V. The service reductions include reducing frequency to 30 minutes on weekdays and hours of operation from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. The Transbay lines P and V would face reductions in westbound morning trips and eastbound afternoon trips. These reductions would go into effect if the transit tax measure in November does not pass. If approved by voters, the measure would impose a transit sales tax of 1.0% in San Francisco and 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties. It would generate an estimated $980 million annually for Bay Area buses, trains, and ferries. AC Transit’s share would be $52 million a year. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, September 16, 2026 How a transit tax may impact Piedmont By Jake Lannon In November Piedmonters will vote to decide their next City Council members and decide on crucial measures that could impact the region. On the ballot is a transit tax measure called the Public Transit Revenue Measure, which would impose a sales tax for 14 years to fund public transportation systems in the region. At the Piedmont City Council meeting on September 8, AC Transit representatives discussed the potential impacts if the measure fails to pass and the current financial struggles that AC Transit is facing. AC Transit covers 364 square miles, and serves more than three million riders monthly, in 13 cities and eight unincorporated communities in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. According to Ryan Lau, the External Affairs representative at AC Transit, their costs have risen, and their revenue has flattened, causing a budget deficit. “When the cost of running our bus network rises faster than the revenue supporting it, it results in a fiscal cliff,” said Lau. “Our regional sales tax revenue has flattened, and our fare revenue growth has slowed. At the same time, fuel costs have gone up by 28%. Bus maintenance parts have increased by 14%, and the cost of buying new buses has surged by 35%.” With the increased costs, AC Transit is reportedly operating at a budget deficit. Over the next four years, AC Transit faces a $200 million deficit, which is roughly $50 million a year beginning in 2027. “Without a long-term sustainable funding source, we’re looking at service reductions of up to 16%, and those are unavoidable. We’re also looking at potential human costs, with layoffs projected to affect up to 300 employees,” said Lau. Piedmont would see service reductions to Lines 12, 18, 88, P, and V. The service reductions include reducing frequency to 30 minutes on weekdays and hours of operation from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. The Transbay lines P and V would face reductions in westbound morning trips and eastbound afternoon trips. These reductions would go into effect if the transit tax measure in November does not pass. If approved by voters, the measure would impose a transit sales tax of 1.0% in San Francisco and 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties. It would generate an estimated $980 million annually for Bay Area buses, trains, and ferries. AC Transit’s share would be $52 million a year. This would help protect the existing bus services and prevent layoffs. “If the ballot measure fails, there are going to be a tremendous number of unexpected consequences,” said Paul Kincaid, Assistant General Manager of AC Transit. “This contingency service plan is the best that we can do right now, and we hope that we will be able to throw it in the trash come November.” AC Transit is hosting a public hearing on October 14 at 2 p.m. and 6 p.m. Bay Area residents can give formal public comment on all of AC Transit’s proposed plans. Residents can submit comments through email, phone, or mail. All of AC Transit’s contact information can be found on its website, along with its contingency plan at https://www.actransit.org/contingency-plan. articles.text: The California State Board of Education (SBE) has started accepting applications for its 2027-28 Student Board Member for current juniors. The chosen student will debate and vote on statewide education policies that directly affect millions of students across the state. A California public high school student has been selected to serve a one-year term on the State Board of Education every year since 1969. The role will require the person to attend bi-monthly meetings in Sacramento. Hotel and meals are completely covered, plus the representative will earn a $100 daily stipend. The term runs from August 1, 2027 to July 31, 2028. The representative will attend roughly six 2-day board meetings across the state over the course of the year. The application package is on the State Board of Education Student Member Recruitment Page at Cde.ca.gov/be/ms/mm/sbestudentmember.asp Completed applications must be turned in by Friday, September 25, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Email completed application packages to sbe@sbe.ca.gov or submit it directly via the SBE Online Portal.
articles.title: Student Rep for State School Board application due 9/25

articles.text: At the September 9 School Board meeting the board announced progress in the search for a new, permanent superintendent. Following a request for proposal for search firms the board received four applications and has selected Leadership Associates to conduct the search. Leadership Associates conducted the search four years ago which led to the hiring of Jennifer Hawn. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans will lead the search. School Board President Ruchi Medhekar noted that Leadership was chosen for their network and their experience in California. “A reason why California experience specifically was important was because the rules in California are very nuanced and different. The way that we do our budgeting is nuanced,” said Medhekar. The board hopes to announce a new superintendent by December 9 with the first day on the job starting January 1, 2027. “As a reminder, when we did this the last time around there was a whole phase with community input, surveying, meetings. That’s all going to happen again. There’s a timeline for that,” explained board Vice President Michael Malione. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans confirmed that he will be in charge until the new person is found. “I will be here until the new superintendent starts. The last superintendent search only lasted a couple of months. The process started in February and went until May. By starting now, we’re hoping we’ll have more candidates applying for the position,” Evans told the Post.
articles.title: School district starts search for new superintendent

articles.text: During the September 9 school board meeting members of the Piedmont Education Foundation presented a check large in dimensions and sum to the school district. PEF members bestowed a record $4,355,000 check to the board to support Piedmont schools this year. It was the largest in the foundation’s history. The check pools together the efforts from every donor, volunteer, and event participant from the Giving Campaign, Spring Fling, the Harvest Festival, Dress Best for Less, business sponsors, and endowment support. For the 2026-27 school year, the PEF grant to PUSD accounts for 16% of teacher salaries, while also supporting paraeducator and teaching aides, counselors and specialists, health and wellness programs, special education, professional development and classroom supplies. “To understand the critical role of the Giving Campaign, you have to really look at what kind of funding goes to PUSD. 61% comes from the state and federal funding. Twenty-nine percent comes from parcel taxes and local fees, and that leaves a funding gap of about 10% to 9% in order to keep our schools at the excellent place that they are, so this year the gap is $2,528. That is more than it’s been ever,” explained PEF Board Member Kim Hunter. Bridget Schreiber, chair of the Education Foundation also acknowledged a grant made by a former Havens teacher. “We were also deeply moved by the continuation of a $25,000 annual professional development grant bequest from Pamela Wells Raffanelli, now in its third year of a four-year, $100,000 commitment honoring a cherished Piedmont teacher (Raffanelli) who chose to leave a legacy for Piedmont educators,” said Schreiber. While presenting the check, PEF introduced this year’s Giving Campaign chairs, Bindu Lokre, Brook Meakins, and Ellie Sommers. This year’s campaign will launch on Tuesday, September 22. To learn more about this year’s Giving Campaign and how to support Piedmont’s public schools, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org. No one on September 10, 2001, knew what the next morning would bring, either,” Mayor Andersen continued. “But we do know this: in every generation, there are people who step forward when it matters most, who run towards danger instead of away from it because a stranger needs help. It takes a special kind of person to have that strength. So today, we remember those we lost. We honor those who answered the call. And we give our deepest thanks to those who continue that commitment now.” Chief Brannigan gave an emotional speech thanking all the first responders and civilians who helped their fellow man in a time of terror. He honored those who lost their lives in the attack and those who rescued the victims in the aftermath. “For me, 9/11 ignited a very deep obligation. An obligation to the firefighters, police officers, flight attendants and pilots, the rescue workers, civilians, ferry captains, the National Guard; I have an obligation to all who stood up and responded, to all those who survived, and to all those who perished. I have an obligation to put aside my fear, to harness my skills, and to be ready to do what it takes when the bell tolls. That’s what the past 25 years have meant to me,” said Chief Brannigan. At the end of Chief Brannigan’s speech, he directed the crowd to read from the paper slip they were given. The crowd read 25 names that were chosen at random from the total 3,000 victims. articles.text: PHS beats San Leandro 3-1, falls to San Marin Piedmont split its last pair of matches to bring its record to 11-5. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches by 3-1 scores, beating San Leandro at Binks Rawlings Gym on Tuesday, September 8 but falling to San Marin two days later in the Mustangs’ home gym. The results bring Piedmont’s record to 11-5 as they enter the midway mark of the season. Regardless of PHS achieving nine of its wins in best of three tournament play, they are bound to win their most matches since 2017’s team went 16-8 and got the No. 7 seed in D4 North Coast Section. Although PHS lost to San Marin, the match was against last year’s Div. 3 NCS finalist, which returned its entire starting lineup. Piedmont played well against the Mustangs, winning the second set and holding a lead in the third of its 25-16, 17-25, 26-24, 25-13 loss. “The message after (the match) was that we played a strong team. This is a very strong Piedmont team and we competed with them. We had a shot at beating a team that Piedmont historically hasn’t had a big chance against,” co-head coach Jason Mongue said. Maika Ting led offensively in both matches with 13 kills against San Leandro and eight against San Marin. They also got big contributions against SL with eight kills by Lucia Dorsey and Izara Dando, seven by Sofia Meyer, and five by Fiona Olsen. Charlotte Bailey had six kills against San Marin and Meyer had five. “High-performing volleyball teams are defined by having two dominant outside hitters. We’re a small school, especially compared to high schools in our league. We’re running a really fast offense, we’ve pushed them from Day 1 to run a high tempo offense. It’s still new to a lot of the kids, but they are showing a lot of improvement,” said Mongue. 3-1 over San Leandro Piedmont dropped the first set but won the next three, 24-26, 25-23, 25-13, 25-18. Staff Photos PHS trailed 23-20 in the first set and led 24-23 with two kills by Meyer and one by Dorsey. However, the Pirates scored three straight to win. In the second set, both teams traded points until Piedmont established a strong 21-13 lead. At 24-20, SLHS scored three straight to make it 24-23, but PHS closed the set with a kill by Meyer. Final stats: Olsen recorded five kills and three digs. Ting recorded 13 kills, three aces and six digs. Bailey recorded four kills and three digs. Alyson Huynh recorded one ace and 31 digs. Carina Vora recorded six aces and 17 digs. Dando recorded eight kills and four digs. Hazel Schaeffer recorded 12 digs and one assist. articles.text: It was a dramatic ending for Piedmont High in its 20-14 loss to Salesian on Friday, September 11 at Witter Field. With 13 seconds left in the game, the Pride connected the go-ahead touchdown on a 13-yard pass, where quarterback Izeah Buchanan fit a ball to the back of the end zone to receiver Sal Guerra for a leaping catch over three Highlander defenders. PHS led 7-6 by halftime and 14-6 at the start of the fourth quarter, and was in control for much of the game. However, Salesian cut the deficit to 14-12 with 7:10 left in the game before landing the game-winner. “Our defense played great, but it’s a game of a play here and there that gets you. We have a lot of injuries we’re trying to overcome, but that’s no excuse. Salesian is one of the best coached teams in the Bay Area. It’s just one of those games, we were right there,” coach Jordan Seiden said. “Salesian’s a good team. We showed we can hang with them, we just have to finish… Incredible play by their receiver, for sure. We had three people on him and he made a helluva catch. It’s one of the plays where we’ve got to get the stop, it was a coin-flip,” senior safety and receiver Diego Hurwitz reflected on the final score. Piedmont got into the red zone while leading 14-12 but couldn’t finish the drive at 4th-and-7 at the 17. They also got to Salesian’s eight early in the second quarter, but failed to convert a 4th-and-6. “We got into the red zone with three minutes left but couldn’t finish the job. Not running the right. It comes down to Salesian getting a long run near the end. It’s just little things that are fixable, but signs of a young team,” Seiden said. Still, there were a lot of bright spots for a Piedmont High team that lost to Salesian 41-17 last season and 46-14 in 2024. Sophomore quarterback Cyrus Emmanuelson got his first start of the season, completing 50 percent of his passes for 210 yards and two touchdowns. Hurwitz also logged his third touchdown of the season with 85 yards on three catches. “Frustrating loss, but I like the effort we put in tonight, we just gotta finish. I really appreciate my coaches and teammates believing in me. I’m learning what parts of the field I should attack, I really enjoy throwing over the middle right now,” Emmanuelson said. “It was a helluva game. The o-line maybe had its best game, Cyrus was dishing out passes and didn’t have a lot of pressure. We’re mastering the playbook, the more you run it, the more you execute. With our passing game, Cyrus is getting a lot better at reading defenses and knowing what to do, and when to do it,” Hurwitz said. Game Recap After back-and-forth possessions, Salesian struck first at the end of the first quarter on a 44-yard drive, taking a 6-0 lead after a blocked extra point. On Piedmont’s ensuing possession, Colby Hong returned a short kickoff to the 47. Cyrus Emanuelson throwing a touchdown pass to Diego Hurwitz.

pages.text: 10 10 Wednesday, September 16, 2026 Sports Volleyball record soars to 11-5 PHS beats San Leandro 3-1, falls to San Marin Piedmont split its last pair of matches to bring its record to 11-5. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches by 3-1 scores, beating San Leandro at Binks Rawlings Gym on Tuesday, September 8 but falling to San Marin two days later in the Mustangs’ home gym. The results bring Piedmont’s record to 11-5 as they enter the midway mark of the season. Regardless of PHS achieving nine of its wins in best of three tournament play, they are bound to win their most matches since 2017’s team went 16-8 and got the No. 7 seed in D4 North Coast Section. Although PHS lost to San Marin, the match was against last year’s Div. 3 NCS finalist, which returned its entire starting lineup. Piedmont played well against the Mustangs, winning the second set and holding a lead in the third of its 25-16, 17-25, 26-24, 25-13 loss. “The message after (the match) was that we played a strong team. This is a very strong Piedmont team and we competed with them. We had a shot at beating a team that Piedmont historically hasn’t had a big chance against,” co-head coach Jason Mongue said. Maika Ting led offensively in both matches with 13 kills against San Leandro and eight against San Marin. They also got big contributions against SL with eight kills by Lucia Dorsey and Izara Dando, seven by Sofia Meyer, and five by Fiona Olsen. Charlotte Bailey had six kills against San Marin and Meyer had five. “High-performing volleyball teams are defined by having two dominant outside hitters. We’re a small school, especially compared to high schools in our league. We’re running a really fast offense, we’ve pushed them from Day 1 to run a high tempo offense. It’s still new to a lot of the kids, but they are showing a lot of improvement,” said Mongue. 3-1 over San Leandro Piedmont dropped the first set but won the next three, 24-26, 25-23, 25-13, 25-18. Staff Photos PHS trailed 23-20 in the first set and led 24-23 with two kills by Meyer and one by Dorsey. However, the Pirates scored three straight to win. In the second set, both teams traded points until Piedmont established a strong 21-13 lead. At 24-20, SLHS scored three straight to make it 24-23, but PHS closed the set with a kill by Meyer. Final stats: Olsen recorded five kills and three digs. Ting recorded 13 kills, three aces and six digs. Bailey recorded four kills and three digs. Alyson Huynh recorded one ace and 31 digs. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team wrapped up a busy week. They won two of three matches at the James Logan Tournament in Union City on Saturday, September 12, while they swept Albany 7-0 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Monday, September 14. At the tournament, PHS beat Granada 6-1 and Hayward 7-0, but lost 4-3 to host school James Logan. “A lot of tennis lately. We played three matches at the James Logan Tournament and won two of them. We played with just 10 girls for all three matches as it was an SAT testing day. We also swept Albany and played really well,” said coach Jim Landes. It was a strong week for freshman starter, Maddy Huynh, who won all four of her matches. “Maddy is already really good Staff Photos Piedmont freshman Maddy Huynh won all four of her matches over the last week. Faith Chin won her matches against Albany, Hayward, and Granada. Amalia Angulo won at singles against Albany, and all three doubles matches at the James Logan Tournament. as a freshman and is going to get better,” Landes said. 7-0 over Albany Faith Chin appeared at No. 1 singles, winning 6-4, 6-1. Maddy Huynh won 6-3, 6-3 at No. 2, Leela Sivakumar won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 3, and Amalia Angulo won in three sets at No. 4 by scores of 6-3, 6-7 (9-7), 10-1. At doubles, Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio won 6-1, 7-6 (7-2) at the top spot. Ella Thomasson and Mai Pham won 6-0, 6-3 at No. 2, while Layla Reed-Miguel and Amelia Oldrin won 6-2, 6-1 at No. 3. 7-0 over Hayward It was a clean 7-0 sweep for Piedmont. They didn’t lose a single game at No. 2 or No. 3 singles, including Faith Chin and Huynh winning their matches 6-0, 6-0 respectively. Ellia Sharafi won in three sets at No. 3, 2-6, 6-4, 10-4. Ruthven won her No. 1 match by default. At doubles, Amalia Angulo and Chiara Silvio won 8-4 at the No. 1 spot. Piedmont followed up with 8-0 shutout wins by No. 2 doubles team Ella Thomasson and Paige Chin, and the No. 3 team of Penelope Welch and Katie Pham. 6-1 over Granada Piedmont won two matches at singles, lost one, and won another by default. Faith Chin won 6-1, 6-1 at the No. 2 spot, while Huynh won 6-1, 6-3 at No. 3. Although Ruthven lost 6-0, 6-4 at No. 1, PHS claimed No. 4 by default. At doubles, Angulo and Silvio won 8-1 at No. 1 and Thomasson and Paige Chin won 8-0 at No. 2. Piedmont also won No. 3 by default. 4-3 loss to James Logan PHS won two of four singles matches and one of three at doubles. At singles, Huynh won 6-3, 6-0 at the No. 2 spot, while Angulo won in three sets at No. 4 by scores of 6-2, 5-7, 10-6. Faith Chin lost 6-4, 6-1 at No. 1, while her younger sister, Paige, lost 6-1, 6-0 at No. 3. At doubles, Thomasson and Pham won 8-4 at No. 2. Ruthven paired with Silvio at No. 1, losing 8-6. Welch and Sharafi lost 8-4 at No. 3. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-1 overall) hosts Berkeley today, September 16, at 3:30 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team claimed their first victory of the season in a close 12-6 win over the Salesian Pride on Friday, September 11 at Witter Field. “Hungry” is the best way to describe Piedmont’s result. The Highlanders completely shut down Salesian’s pass game, only allowing 31 passing yards throughout the game. On Salesian’s opening drive, defensive tackle Keliti Havea stuffed a run up the middle on a 4th-and-2 to force a turnover on downs. Quarterback Gio Lopez proceeded to throw a 36-yard touchdown pass to Mateo Morgan, completely burning Salesian’s coverage. It was one of several clutch catches by Morgan on the afternoon. The Highlanders led 6-0 after an unsuccessful two-point conversion and the score remained the same by halftime. Salesian recovered an onside kick to start the second half. But on the Pride’s ensuing possession, Morgan was able to make an interception. During the play, Pride’s quarterback was clobbered by linebacker Ernie Hildreth to enable Morgan’s pick. Later on, free safety Robbie Koch made a leaping interception to give the Highlanders the ball again. Koch was making his first start at safety and receiver. Salesian was able to tie the game 6-6 on a fake jet sweep, leading to a 34-yard run to score. A failed two-point conversion kept the game tied. The Pride tried for another onside kick, but PHS recovered to give itself great field position. On the next drive receiver Will Dietrick broke two tackles on a reverse play, and ran the ball 45 yards to Salesian’s three. Running back Ernie Hildreth punched the ball into the end zone on a toss to the left side. The touchdown was enabled by left guard Keliti Havea, giving Hildreth a huge lead block. Head coach Pouyan Assadi highly praised the offensive line after the game: “I thought the O Line had an outstanding game with Keliti leading the troops.” On the ensuing kickoff, Keliti ripped the ball out of the kick returner’s hands for a strip-fumble and recovery to secure the Highlanders’ win. Keliti was awarded the “I Got That Dawg in Me” chain after the game by Coach Pouyan for his performance. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-2 overall) hosts Aragon on Friday, September 18 at 4:00 p.m. at Witter Field Robbie Koch lines up at receiver. He had an interception in his first start at safety. Photos by Graham Smith Mateo Morgan had a touchdown and an interception against Salesian.

articles.text: Hola from Madrid and Lisbon! In years past, the Post has taken its summer vacation abroad to Spain and Portugal, visiting some of the best sites for a day full of walking. Should you ever find yourself in Iberian Country, here are a couple of places to consider for getting your steps in. Madrid’s historic El Retiro Park Madrid makes for the perfect city to walk off all the calories from tapas. Should you ever find yourself in the Spanish Capital, make your way to Parque de El Retiro. El Retiro Park was created in 1630; it is famous for its landscape, architecture, fountains, and countless statues commemorating its past. It’s a huge park at 350 acres and a popular destination for locals and tourists alike with an estimated total of 15,000 trees. You can easily take a full day walking around the park, finding fountains, sitting areas, grassy knolls, and shaded spots to hide from the sun. Perhaps the most popular feature of El Retiro Park is the Estanque Grande de El Retiro, or the Great Pond of the park. The pond is 280 meters long, 140 meters wide, with restaurants along the edges, bands looking for tips, and boats wading around the water. Standing tall at the east edge of the Great Pond is the Monumento a Alfonso XII—the largest monument of the park. The monument is 30 meters high, 86 meters long, and 58 meters wide. At its center is the casted bronze equestrian statue of King Alfonso XII, who was the King of Spain from 1874-1885. Palacio de Cristal is one of the most popular sites of the park. With its own pond, it’s a place where many tourists will be taking selfies, or enjoying another band playing music for tips. Parque Eduardo VII to Praça do Comércio in Lisbon Portugal is considered a great city for walking and hiking. The streets are tightly packed together with rolling hills similar Take a detour to A Ginjinha, a historic watering hole featuring Portugal’s famous ginjinha, a cherry infused liquor. The location was made in 1840.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera has postponed its annual Opera Ball, the company’s largest fundraising event, following a strike by members of the San Francisco Opera Orchestra. The ball, originally scheduled for September 12 at San Francisco City Hall, will now take place Thursday, November 12. The red-carpet evening will include cocktails, dinner and dancing inside City Hall, but will no longer include an opera performance. The post ponement was announced September 1, after the orchestra said its musicians would not perform unless the opera and the orchestra reached a new collective bargaining agreement by the opening of the season. The two sides had been in negotiations over a successor agreement after their previous contract expired July 31. San Francisco Opera leadership said postponing the gala would give the negotiations more time while removing uncertainty for guests, donors and the numerous outside vendors involved in producing the event. The event had originally been planned as the opening-night celebration for the Opera’s 104th season. Guests were to begin the evening with cocktails and dinner at City Hall before crossing Van Ness Avenue to the War Memorial Opera House for a performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra, followed by an after-party at City Hall. Instead, Opera Ball will stand on its own as a fundraising event in November. Matthew Shilvock, General Director of San Francisco Opera, said the new date would allow the gala to proceed without uncertainty surrounding the labor negotiations. “I am deeply grateful to all those involved for pivoting to this new November date, particularly the co-chairs and host committee who are working tirelessly to make this such a special fundraiser,” Shilvock said. “We feel that this is the best decision to ensure that this critical fundraising event can continue, free of any uncertainty, while at the same time giving negotiations the space needed to proceed ahead of what promises to be a beautiful opening of Simon Boccanegra on September 12. I am deeply grateful to all those attending Opera Ball for their understanding as we make this adjustment.” The orchestra strike subsequently forced the cancellation of the September 12 opening-night performance of Simon Boccanegra, as well as the annual free Opera in the Park concert scheduled for September 13. The company has since listed Simon Boccanegra performances beginning September 16 at the War Memorial Opera House. The Opera Ball has long been an important source of funding for both San Francisco Opera and the San Francisco Opera Guild. Proceeds support the Opera’s artistic programming and the Guild’s K-12 education programs. The 2026 ball was also to honor the late Diane B. Wilsey, who served as Opening Weekend Grand Sponsor for 20 years, supporting Opera Ball, the season-opening performance and Opera in the Park. The original event was to feature the opening of Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra, a political drama set in 14th-century Genoa. Music Director Eun Sun Kim was scheduled to conduct, with Mongolian baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat in the title role, soprano Eleonora Buratto as Amelia and Maria, tenor Joshua Guerrero as Gabriele Adorno and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn as Jacopo Fiesco. For the November event, the Opera says additional details will be announced in the coming weeks. The event will be held entirely at City Hall and will not include a staged opera performance.
articles.title: SF Opera postpones annual Opera Ball amid orchestra strike

articles.text: The annual Flower Piano festival concludes Sunday, September 20, with a closing-day celebration at the San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park. The festival brings a dozen pianos to the garden’s 55 acres, inviting visitors to explore the grounds while listening to music among the plants and flowers. The final-day celebration at the garden’s Celebration Garden, transformed into the “Flower Piano Lounge,” runs from noon to 7:30 p.m. and features performances by Mariah Parker’s Indo Latin Jazz Ensemble, The Kevin Gerzevitz Trio and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble. Mariah Parker’s Indo Latin Jazz Ensemble performs from 1 to 2 p.m., followed by The Kevin Gerzevitz Trio from 3 to 4 p.m. and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble from 5 to 7 p.m. Throughout the festival, professional musicians and community partners perform at pianos located throughout the garden, with open-play periods allowing visitors to sit down and play themselves. The music ranges from classical and jazz to Afro-Cuban and other genres. Sunset Piano, which presents the festival in partnership with the San Francisco Botanical Garden, places grand and baby grand pianos throughout the garden each year. Visitors can bring blankets or foldable chairs for lawn seating. A limited number of chairs will also be available. General admission to Flower Piano is included with admission to the San Francisco Botanical Garden. The Flower Piano Lounge is a separate ticketed experience. Visit https://gggp.org/flowerpiano/ to purchase tickets. Kev Choice closes out this year’s festival.
articles.title: Flower Piano ends at Golden Gate Park Sept. 20

articles.text: Festival Opera will open its annual Salon Series September 27 with a concert featuring the inaugural class of its Resident Artists at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The 7:30 p.m. performance features sopranos Marielle Leiboff and Rachel Nelson, mezzo-soprano Phoebe Dinga, tenor Spencer Greene and baritone Liam Daley, accompanied by Festival Opera pianist Daniel Lockert. The program includes opera arias, scenes and contemporary works by composers including Handel, Mozart, Verdi, Leoncavallo, Lehár, Richard Strauss, Massenet, Rachmaninoff, Jeanine Tesori and Leonard Bernstein. The Salon Series is a trio of concerts presented Septemand Lila Khazoum with Lockert. The program will include excerpts from operas including Macbeth, The Magic Flute, Anna Bolena and Lucia di Lammermoor, with costumes and props incorporated into the performance. The final concert, held November 22, will feature baritone Efraín Solís, making his Festival Opera debut, accompanied by San Francisco Opera pianist Marika Yasuda. The program will include works by French, Mexican, Argentine and Russian composers, along with the world premiere of Borders of Dreaming, a newly commissioned song cycle by Colombian composer Juan Sebastián Cardona Ospina with text by Michael Colbruno. Tickets are $40 per concert or $95 for all three. Visit festivalopera.org/salon-series to purchase tickets. Mezzo-soprano Phoebe Dinga ber through November, all performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Each performance is followed by a reception with the artists. The series continues October 25 with “Operatic Mad Scenes,” featuring sopranos Aura Veruni

articles.text: Photo by Memento Moda Nick Rossi performs jazz and salsa from the Swing Era. The Treasure Island Museum will host a swing dance fundraiser on Saturday, September 26, to support the museum’s educational programs and historical exhibitions. Held from 7 to 10 p.m. at the museum, 39 Treasure Island Road in San Francisco, the evening will celebrate the glamour of the Swing Era and the golden age of air travel. The event is organized by the Treasure Island Museum Board. Live entertainment will be provided by the Nick Rossi Swing Six, a jazz and salsa ensemble specializing in music from the 1930s and 1940s. Guests will also enjoy classic cocktails from Gold Bar Distillery and a onenight-only exhibition featuring rarely displayed artifacts from the museum’s Pan American Airways collection. The museum, housed in a historic building dating to the height of the Swing Era, will serve as the backdrop for the evening’s festivities. Attendees are encouraged to wear festive or vintage-inspired attire, although period dress is not required. Prizes will be awarded for the most authentic and creative vintage outfits. Proceeds from the fundraiser will benefit the museum’s educational programming and ongoing efforts to preserve and interpret the history of Treasure Island through exhibits and public outreach. The fundraiser will take place Saturday, September 26, from 7 to 10 p.m. at the Treasure Island Museum, 39 Treasure Island Road, San Francisco. Tickets are available at https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/our-swing-dance-benefit-inhistoric-building-one. ®
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum hosts swing dance fundraiser Sept. 26

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents The Cook, showing onstage now through October 11. Directed by Berkeley Rep Associate Artistic Director David Mendizábal, The Cook follows an aristocratic Cuban family that flees Havana for Miami on the eve of Fidel Castro’s revolution, leaving their mansion in the care of their devoted cook, Gladys. Gladys promises to protect the home until the family returns. For 40 years, she kept her promise while enduring personal loss, political upheaval and the changing fortunes of Cuba. When the aristocrats’ daughter eventually returns, Gladys confronts the sacrifices she has made for a relationship that has been forgotten. “I’m thrilled to be bringing Eduardo Machado’s play The Cook to life at Berkeley Rep and opening our 2026/27 season with this timely play,” said Mendizábal in a press release. “A landmark work in the American theatrical canon by a Latine playwright, the play illuminates Cuba’s complex history surrounding Fidel Castro’s revolution through richly drawn characters, focusing on their Photo by Ben Krantz Daniel Duque-Estrada and Yesenia Iglesias in Eduardo Machado’s The Cook. humanity, dreams, and ambitions. It is a deeply moving story about belonging and survival and asks the question, who has the greater claim to a nation’s identity—the people who stayed or those who were forced to leave?” The cast includes Gisela Chipe as Adria/Lourdes, Daniel Duque-Estrada as Carlos, Yesenia Iglesias as Gladys, Georgina Morillo as Elena/Rosa and Ashton Muñiz as Julio. Understudies are Luis Kelly-Duarte, Morillo, Monica Rose Slater, Omar Stewart and Courtney Thomas. Machado is the playwright, with Tanya Orellana as scenic designer, Toni-Leslie James as costume designer, Mextly Couzin as lighting designer and Mikaal Sulaiman as sound designer and composer of original music. Matthew Armentrout is the wigs and hair designer, and Adi Cabral is the voice and dialect coach. The Cook runs now through Sunday, October 11. Visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s The Cook playing now through Oct. 11

articles.text: Play ends Sept. 20 Marin Theatre opens its 60th season with the Bay Area premiere of The White Chip, a play about alcoholism and recovery, running now through September 20. Written by Sean Daniels and directed by Marin Theatre Executive Artistic Director Lance Gardner, the play follows Steven, a successful theater director whose career and personal life are increasingly affected by his struggle with alcohol addiction. After his drinking disrupts his relationships and professional life, Steven begins the process of recovery by accepting Alcoholics Anonymous’ white chip, which is given to people marking 24 hours of sobriety or expressing a desire to stop drinking. The play draws on Daniels’ own experiences with addiction and recovery. Gardner, who will mark 20 years of sobriety in 2027, said the production has personal significance for him. “The White Chip isn’t my story, but the decision to produce it is a very personal one,” Gardner said in a press release. “2027 will mark 20 years of sobriety for me. Making the choice to abstain from drugs and alcohol opened the doors that led me to the helm of Marin Theatre and probably saved my life.” Gardner said the play addresses the stigma surrounding addiction and recovery through its combination of comedy and drama. “The White Chip confronts the stigma of addiction and recovery head on with a hilarious and heart wrenching story which has the power to enlighten and inspire audiences whether or not they’ve experienced this kind of thing firsthand,” he said. The White Chip premiered at Merrimack Repertory Theatre before productions at New York’s 59E59 Theater and MCC Theater. It has since been produced by theaters around the country. Benjamin Clark will make his Marin Theatre debut as Steven. His regional theater credits include Asolo Repertory Theatre, Barrington Stage Company, Round House Theatre, Olney Theatre Center and Everyman Theatre. Danny Scheie and Lyndsy Kail round out the cast, portraying people in Steven’s life. Scheie previously appeared at Marin Theatre in The Cherry Orchard and Lady in the Dark and directed the theater’s productions of Splittin’ the Raft and The Pavilion. Kail has performed with California Shakespeare Theater, Center Repertory Company and San Jose Stage Company, among others. The White Chip will be performed at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. in Mill Valley. Subscriptions for Marin Theatre’s 2026-27 season are available through www.MarinTheatre.org or by calling 415-388-5208. Benjamin Clark, Lyndsy Kail and Danny Scheie in Marin Theatre’s The White Chip. Photo by David Allen
articles.title: Last chance to see Marin Theatre’s White Chip

articles.text: The film Pressure examines the most tense 72 hours of World War II, a stint when the weather forecasts were the most crucial piece of intelligence in the war. Directed by Anthony Maras and based on David Haig’s stage play of the same name, Pressure stars Andrew Scott and Brendan Fraser. Scott plays Captain James Stagg, a meteorologist tasked with predicting the weather to determine whether the D-Day invasion can happen at all. Brendan Fraser plays General Dwight Eisenhower, the Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force for Western Europe and D-Day. The entire invasion hinges upon the weather report, and Scott plays that pressure with a controlled desperation that never dips into melodrama. The movie is carried through conversation in two rooms across a handful of days showing professional respect fraying under the weight of an impossible decision. The best part of the film occurs when Stagg holds his ground against men with more rank and less humility, especially Chris Messina as rival forecaster Irving Krick, a man filled with plenty of confidence and no caution. The historical details feel authentic, and the music score helps heighten the tension. The movie stumbles a bit with some historical inaccuracies. There are a few too many liberties taken with the real timeline and the real people involved. Eisenhower’s real D-Day address trimmed down for the film didn’t help either; the full speech carries more weight than what made the cut. The movie title’s double entendre speaks of pressure in both the war room and the meteorological sense. If you like historical dramas that trust dialogue over spectacle, this movie is for you. Pressure builds adequate tension, and the behind-thescenes weather reporting adds something new to a well-documented war battle. Pressure . Directed by Anthony Maras. Starring Andrew Scott, Brendan Fraser, Kerry Condon, Chris Messina, and Damian Lewis. Rated PG-13. 1h 40min. Released in 2026. Watch it now on Peacock, Amazon Prime, and AppleTV. The 2026 film Pressure stars Andrew Scott and Brendan Fraser.
