pages.text: 18 Wednesday, September 16, 2026 The History of Piedmont The first house in Piedmont was built by brothers William and Walter Blair and was on Highland Avenue (then called Vernal) between Blair Avenue and Park Way. By Gail G. Lombardi Introduction During the City of Piedmont’s Centennial in 2007, the Piedmont Post, in cooperation with the Piedmont Historical Society, began printing stories and photos of the earliest history of the city from its founding in 1907, its growth resulting in part from the earthquake and fire in San Francisco in 1906, and the city’s earliest settlers. For families who have moved to Piedmont since 2007, when the city’s Centennial was widely celebrated and publicized, the series of history pieces by historian and researcher Gail Lombardi may prove insightful, providing a look at the earliest settlers, and why people have chosen to move to Piedmont for more than a century. Walter Blair, Piedmont’s first pioneer Walter Blair was Piedmont’s enterprising first settler who played an important part in the early development of today’s city. He built the first house in the Piedmont hills (see photo) and established a dairy and rock quarry. In the 1860s, long before bridges spanned the Bay, he developed the first horsecar line bringing visitors and picnickers into the Piedmont hills. Many of these visitors enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to build their homes here. Walter was born in 1830. Blair realized that a hard surface was needed for these roads. Always the entrepreneur, Blair hired Chinese laborers to quarry rock from a basalt outcropping near his dairy and sold crushed rock to lay over the muddy, dusty streets in Oakland. Today, the eucalyptus trees he planted still grow along the cemetery border on Moraga and in Dracena Park. As a successful businessman, Blair rebuilt his cabin in 1862 into the large gabled house with gardens as seen in the photo. Walter Blair married and soon moved to downtown Oakland. He leased the house to the Arthur Bowman family. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers tour homes On the hottest day of early September, about 40 hardy humans and five canine companions braved the sun, gathering at the Exedra to answer a burning real estate question: Does a home’s architect actually affect its market value? Leading the Sept. 9 Walking on Wednesday tour was Moya Robinson, a local Realtor uniquely qualified to tackle the subject. Robinson guided walkers past seven Piedmont residences designed by prominent architects, comparing their historic selling prices against average market trends. The goal was to see if architectural pedigree consistently drives a premium price—and the answer, it turns out, is nuanced. The tour focused on master builders active during Piedmont’s prime development era between 1907 and 1940. Among them was Oakland-raised Julia Morgan (1872–1957), a UC Berkeley civil engineering graduate and the first woman licensed as an architect in California. Renowned for designing Hearst Castle, Morgan crafted roughly 10 distinguished residences in Piedmont within 15 years of the city’s founding. Walkers also examined works by Albert Lincoln Farr (1871– 1947), known for Craftsman and Georgian residences, as well as civic landmarks like Piedmont City Hall, the Exedra monument, and Piedmont Community Church. Other featured architects included John Hudson Thomas (1878–1945), master of Arts & Crafts and European revival styles, and Joseph Francis Ward (1898–1970), who partnered with Farr starting in 1922. Setting out south on Highland Avenue and turning east onto Sierra Avenue, the group arrived at 12 Sierra Ave. Designed by Thomas in 1914, the Arts & Crafts home features steep rooflines, prominent gables, grouped windows, and traditional millwork. When it sold in 2008, marketing materials prominently featured Thomas’ name. Further up the street, a pair of Julia Morgan designs highlighted her architectural range. Built in 1925, 45 Sierra Ave. presents strong horizontal lines, lowpitched rooflines, broad eaves, and stucco walls—a geometric contrast to Thomas’ work. pages.text: Wednesday, September 16, 2026 19 Features WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers tour homes by famous architects By Lori Austin On the hottest day of early September, about 40 hardy humans and five canine companions braved the sun, gathering at the Exedra to answer a burning real estate question: Does a home’s architect actually affect its market value? Leading the Sept. 9 Walking on Wednesday tour was Moya Robinson, a local Realtor uniquely qualified to tackle the subject. Robinson guided walkers past seven Piedmont residences designed by prominent architects, comparing their historic selling prices against average market trends. The goal was to see if architectural pedigree consistently drives a premium price—and the answer, it turns out, is nuanced. The tour focused on master builders active during Piedmont’s prime development era between 1907 and 1940. Among them was Oakland-raised Julia Morgan (1872–1957), a UC Berkeley civil engineering graduate and the first woman licensed as an architect in California. Renowned for designing Hearst Castle, Morgan crafted roughly 10 distinguished residences in Piedmont within 15 years of the city’s founding. Walkers also examined works by Albert Lincoln Farr (1871– 1947), known for Craftsman and Georgian residences, as well as civic landmarks like Piedmont City Hall, the Exedra monument, and Piedmont Community Church. Other featured architects included John Hudson Thomas (1878–1945), master of Arts & Crafts and European revival styles, and Joseph Francis Ward (1898–1970), who partnered with Farr starting in 1922. Setting out south on Highland Avenue and turning east onto Sierra Avenue, the group arrived at 12 Sierra Ave. Designed by Thomas in 1914, the Arts & Crafts home features steep rooflines, prominent gables, grouped windows, and traditional millwork. When it sold in 2008, marketing materials prominently featured Thomas’ name. Further up the street, a pair of Julia Morgan designs highlighted her architectural range. Built in 1925, 45 Sierra Ave. presents strong horizontal lines, lowpitched rooflines, broad eaves, and stucco walls—a geometric contrast to Thomas’ work. It sold in 2013 with Morgan’s name as a primary selling point. Next door, 49 Sierra Ave., constructed in 1914, displays classic Tudor influences with steep cross-gables, half-timbering, and leaded windows. Currently undergoing renovation, the house spurred discussion on how modernization—like updated wiring, roofs, kitchens, and baths—must balance with historical preservation. Morgan’s legacy was key to its 2023 sale. Ascending Mountain Avenue, the group surveyed 284 Mountain Ave., designed by Farr in 1914. The substantial Arts & Crafts estate features dramatic gables and a prominent chimney. While it sold off-market in 2015—leaving the influence of Farr’s name uncertain—walkers noted the Route of last week’s walk neighborhood’s architectural variety, including the midcentury modern home at 300 Mountain Ave., formerly owned by Raiders icon Al Davis. At 235 Mountain Ave., another Farr design from 1912, showcases a blend of Craftsman, Georgian, and Colonial elements. With brick and shingle exteriors, multi-pane windows, and formal gardens, the home’s 2021 sale explicitly highlighted its architect and immaculate preservation. Reaching Sea View Avenue, the tour stopped at 2 Sea View Ave., a 1924 French Mediterranean estate by Farr. Boasting an arched entrance, stone surround, and formal gardens, its architectural lineage was a centerpiece of its 2025 sale. The tour concluded its house stops at 55 Sea View Ave., designed in 1924 by Farr & Ward. The grand Tudor estate features red brick, leaded glass, carved woodwork, and twin bronze lions flanking the entrance. Known locally as the Otis Spunkmeyer house—formerly owned by company founder Kenneth B. Rawlings—it sold in 2024 after a meticulous restoration. “At this level, architecture becomes part of the identity of the estate—not simply a feature of the house,” Robinson noted, calling 55 Sea View a prime example of pedigree, scale, and preservation converging. So, does the architect add value? Robinson concluded the answer is “probably,” but not a definitive yes. While all seven homes commanded prices above the average for similar Piedmont properties, buyer preferences, condition, and modern upgrades remain vital factors. A second tour exploring additional historic homes is planned for November. Walking on Wednesday meets weekly at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra. The program is free and open to the public. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Antioch Court will become one of Oakland’s newest outdoor salsa destinations as Montclair Village brings a full afternoon of dancing, live DJ sets and beginner-friendly instruction to the Village Plaza as part of its popular Picnic on the Plaza series. The free event, Salsa & Sangria, is on Sunday, September 20, from noon to 4 p.m. at 2066 Antioch Court, Oakland, CA. The event will feature a professionally installed dance floor, salsa instruction from the Oakland Salsa Club, music by Dímelo DJ, and hosting by Candi Martinez. The event is designed to make salsa dancing accessible to everyone, from experienced dancers to people stepping onto a dance floor for the very first time. “Picnic on the Plaza is about creating opportunities for people to come together in the heart of Montclair Village,” said Daniel Swafford, Executive Director of the Montclair Village Association. “This event takes that idea one step further by inviting people to get up and dance together. You don’t need experience, a partner, or even fancy dance shoes—just come ready to have fun.” The afternoon kicks off with an Open Floor DJ set from noon to 1 p.m., followed by Absolute Beginner’s Salsa Lessons from 1 to 2 p.m. The afternoon culminates with a Salsa Social from 2 to 4 p.m., giving participants the chance to put their newly learned steps into action. The salsa celebration is also an opportunity to experience Montclair Village as a walkable neighborhood destination. Visitors can stop by the Sangria Bar, grab lunch, snacks, and beverages from more than 20 local restaurants and eateries, or pick up fresh food and other offerings at the Village Farmers’ Market before settling in at community tables throughout the plaza. The event also highlights the work of the Oakland Salsa Club, whose mission includes providing free dance education to historically marginalized and underserved communities in Oakland. More information about the event is on MontclairVillage.com.
articles.title: Montclair Village turns Antioch Court into a salsa dance floor

articles.text: Kirsten Hanafee married Andy George of London, England, on May 30, 2026, in Puglia, Italy. Kirsten is the daughter of former Piedmont residents Claire Kostic and David Hanafee. She graduated from Piedmont High School in 2007 and obtained her degree in international relations at USC in 2011. In 2016, she moved to London, where she met her future husband. Kirsten currently works for Uber UK in corporate advertising. Andy, originally from Lincolnshire, England, graduated from Ravensbourne University in London and is co-founder and managing director of Lost Village, a globally influenced music/art/food/experience festival that is world renowned. The couple will honeymoon in Seoul, South Korea, and Japan this fall. They reside in London. Four of the seven bridesmaids were Piedmont High School classmates: Taylor Fleshman, Caitlin Chee, Kelsey Haffercamp and Sarah Balkissoon. Her brother Sean Hanafee (PHS Class of 2010) was a groomsman and served as emcee. Many Piedmonters made the trip to Italy to celebrate Kirsten and Andy’s wedding, including Patty and Carter Dunlap, Frank and Michele Helm, Sue Farley and Michael Levine, Alanna and Jack Dittoe, Robin Wu and Reagan Louie, Kate Morrow, Mary Beth and Terry Mayo, K and Lou Buty, and Melanie and Tyler Johnston.
articles.title: Kirsten Hanafee marries Andy George in Italy

articles.text: Nathan & Co celebrates 20 years in Oakland with a new home on Piedmont Avenue Nathan & Co, the Oakland-based gift and home retailer known for its colorful mix of gifts, home accessories, children’s merchandise, and locally inspired finds, is moving into a new flagship location on Piedmont Avenue, just across the street from the store it has called home for the past 18 years. Nathan & Co expects to open its new Piedmont Avenue flagship on Saturday, October 10, 2026. The move comes as Nathan & Co celebrates its 20th anniversary in Oakland. Earlier this year, owner Nathan Waldon announced that the Piedmont Avenue store would close after selling its longtime building and facing a significant increase in occupancy costs. What initially felt like the end of an era quickly turned into an unexpected new beginning when a nearby storefront became available. “We were heartbroken at the thought of leaving Piedmont Avenue,” said Waldon. “This is where Nathan & Co started 20 years ago. It’s our neighborhood, our community, and such an important part of our story. Then, almost out of nowhere, this wonderful space opened up directly across the street. It felt like the universe was telling us we weren’t finished here yet.” The new store, formerly home to Cotton Basics, is being completely refreshed and redesigned for Nathan & Co. The space will feature new lighting, fixtures, signage, a dedicated gift-wrapping area, and a warm, modern interior reflecting the retailer’s evolving aesthetic. The move also allows Nathan & Co to remain close to the customers and neighboring businesses that have supported the company since its early days. “We’ve been touched by the The company’s College Avenue store will remain open and recently underwent an exterior refresh. reaction from the neighborhood,” Waldon said. “When people thought we were leaving Piedmont Avenue, there was an enormous outpouring of love. Being able to tell everyone that we’re actually staying, and essentially moving across the street, has been one of the happiest surprises of my retail career.” Nathan & Co opened in Oakland in 2006 and has grown into a locally recognized independent retailer with locations on Piedmont Avenue and College Avenue in Rockridge. Over the years, the stores have become known for an ever-changing assortment of gifts, children’s products, home goods, jewelry, greeting cards, Oakland-inspired merchandise, and complimentary gift wrapping with a strong focus on personal customer service. “This new store brings together everything I’ve learned over many years in retail,” Waldon said. “It feels fresh and new, but it still feels completely like Nathan & Co. Most importantly, we get to begin our next 20 years right here in Oakland.” Founded in Oakland in 2006, Nathan & Co is an independent gift, home and lifestyle retailer with stores on Piedmont Avenue and College Avenue. The company offers a curated assortment of gifts, home accessories, children’s products, greeting cards, locally inspired merchandise, and unexpected finds, all presented with a distinctly Oakland point of view.

articles.text: Art was born in Jersey City, New Jersey, to working-class parents, Oscar and Ida Shartsis, in 1945. In 1949, his family moved to Los Angeles’s San Fernando Valley to chase the aerospace boom of postwar California. Art thrived: he was valedictorian of North Hollywood High School and went on to the University of California, Berkeley, which he later called the most formative experience of his life—and where he was again chosen as valedictorian, delivering the 1967 commencement speech that made national headlines. From there he went to Berkeley Law, where he met Mary Jo, and after a brief stint as an associate at Morrison & Foerster, co-founded the firm Shartsis & Friese with Bob Friese in 1975. Mary Jo joined them shortly after, leaving a more prestigious firm behind, and became one of the pioneering women in the San Francisco legal profession. Art approached his life with an intensity of purpose, pursuing excellence in everything he took on, whether it was public office, the courtroom, or representing the board of one of the world’s most valuable companies. On the board of the Bay Area Rapid Transit District, he was the leading advocate for making the system accessible to riders with disabilities. In addition to his professional accomplishments, Art will be remembered for his generous spirit and the pride he took in giving back to his communities. Some of his greatest fulfillment came from coaching Cal’s mock trial team, a commitment he kept for two decades, and Berkeley Law later honored him and Mary Jo with its highest alumni award. He found the greatest joy in the successes of those whose lives he Arthur J. Shartsis touched. Art also had a lifelong passion for photography. Early in his career he represented the photographer Imogen Cunningham, which led him to represent other prominent artists and co-found what is now California Lawyers for the Arts. His love of fly fishing led him to help found the Henry’s Fork Foundation, which continues to protect its namesake Idaho trout river to this day. In his later years he took up garden design, spending nearly two decades building the gardens that surround his Piedmont home. He also loved playing cribbage and watching his children and grandchildren’s sporting events. Art was predeceased by his wife of nearly fifty years, Mary Jo Shartsis. Later in life he married Stephanie, who shared his love of the garden and helped reshape much of it in his final years. She survives him along with his sister, Loretta Shartsis; his sons Alexander, Matthew, and Benjamin; his daughters-in-law Kim and Melanie; his grandchildren Aidan, Sophie, Fern, Hawk, and Savannah; and countless colleagues, students, and friends.
articles.title: Arthur J. Shartsis, distinguished trial lawyer, passed away at age 80

articles.text: The Piedmont Unified School District Board of Education will conduct a public hearing and adopt a Resolution in compliance with Education Code 60119(c) mandating that the governing board of school districts must hold a public hearing in order to receive funding for textbooks and instructional materials that are consistent with the Curriculum Framework adopted by the State Board of Education. The public hearing will be conducted at the Regular Board meeting on Wednesday, September 23, 2026 which begins at 7:00 p.m. in person at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, and via Zoom webinar. PUSD September 12, 2026 Office of the Superintendent 760 Magnolia Avenue Piedmont CA with the department long term. “We proposed a plan that would have provided just employee medical coverage from the time of retirement untill 65, when they became eligible for Medicare, just basically to bridge that gap. The retirement plan is designed around people retiring at 57. If you were to look statistically, people don’t work much past that in this job. It’s a physical job,” Gidney continued. “We actually based our proposal off of the system that the City of Alameda has for their employees, and the City of Berkeley also has a system. So we took those two systems and tried to right-size it for Piedmont, but it got nowhere.” The Union and the City of Piedmont have not yet reached an agreement. The city made its final offer on July 8, but the union voted against it. As a result, the city has officially declared an impasse, which may enable it to impose a one-year contract on employees if an agreement cannot be reached. “We’ve said the standards for what firefighters get in terms of compensation and benefits have really changed, and if we want to be competitive, we need to change along with it,” Gidney said. “We invited the city to collaborate, and there’s been no movement. They answered that they weren’t interested in talking about any of those things. Everything got shut down. Everything was non-negotiable.” Gidney, Borges, and Union Vice President Brian Protheroe expressed their worry that if the department continues on this trend, they face a future threat of being browned out. “It’s almost like we’re dancing on the train tracks, and eventually a train’s going to come by. Yeah, and I feel like the city keeps saying, ‘I don’t see a train.’ We’re like, no, but we’re the ones on the track. I can tell you, like, we feel the rumble,” Gidney said.

As a Councilmember, I would listen to residents and work with city staff and my Council colleagues to make thoughtful, fiscally responsible decisions about the best use of city resources. Adam Hundt I am running for City Council to, first, provide access to affordable home electrification and energy efficiency upgrades that increase home values and lower monthly bills; second, support new housing development; and third, generate new sources of revenue for the City of Piedmont. I support ballot Measure GG, which helps Piedmont maintain fiscal health. I support using funds for three purposes. First, renovating or replacing aging buildings and facilities, such as the Recreation Building, Fire Station and Police Department, and parks and tennis courts. Second, projects that enable compliance with regulatory requirements to control stormwater runoff. Unfortunately, state funding may not cover costs. Third, road repair and street safety. City scores on the Pavement Condition Index (PCI) declined in recent years. The Piedmont Safer Streets report recommended addressing crosswalk safety, bikeways, and speeding traffic. If allocated to these purposes, funding will address critical issues with city infrastructure and positively affect home values and residents’ quality of life. Additionally, I will work to incorporate private funding for city projects, engaging with groups such as the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization and Piedmont Beautification Foundation. I will seek cost-efficient solutions, such as speed humps/bumps, a less expensive and simpler solution than street redesigns. According to the Union, as of September 1, they’re averaging 40 overtime shifts per person in the first eight months of this year. With approximately 60 normally scheduled shifts during that same period, firefighters have already worked 100 shifts — 167% of their normal schedule. “It’s not just hard on the people here, but our families too,” said Union Secretary Brittany Borges. “You’re leaving your partner at home to do all the stuff alone, and these guys are missing moments with their kids because they’re here. We did sign up for that. That is what we agreed to. But this is an excessive amount that could be fixed, and we’re trying to put things on the table to help, but it’s being shot down and disregarded.” The union has put forth a plan to help with recruitment and retention to solve their understaffing issue. They’ve proposed introducing longevity pay to help incentivize employees to stay long-term. This is a benefit the Piedmont Police Department has in place, and the Union believes they can reach a similar agreement. “We put forward a proposal that would have given some pretty modest pay incentives in years six and seven, with a little bit of a bump at year 10 to try and encourage people to get to that place,” said Gidney. They’ve also proposed retiree medical benefits. According to the Union, because of the California Pension Reform Act in 2012, the City of Piedmont discontinued retirement medical benefits for new employees in 2018. The current average retirement age for firefighters is around 57 years old, leaving an eight-year gap without medical benefits before receiving Medicare at 65. This poses a problem for some employees, causing them to leave rather than stay with the department long term. “We proposed a plan that would have provided just employee medical coverage from the time of retirement untill 65, when they became eligible for Medicare, just basically to bridge that gap. The retirement plan is designed around people retiring at 57. If you were to look statistically, people don’t work much past that in this job. It’s a physical job,” Gidney continued. “We actually based our proposal off of the system that the City of Alameda has for their employees, and the City of Berkeley also has a system. So we took those two systems and tried to right-size it for Piedmont, but it got nowhere.” The Union and the City of Piedmont have not yet reached an agreement. The city made its final offer on July 8, but the union voted against it. As a result, the city has officially declared an impasse, which may enable it to impose a one-year contract on employees if an agreement cannot be reached. “We’ve said the standards for what firefighters get in terms of compensation and benefits have really changed, and if we want to be competitive, we need to change along with it,” Gidney said. “We invited the city to collaborate, and there’s been no movement. They answered that they weren’t interested in talking about any of those things. Everything got shut down. Everything was non-negotiable.” Gidney, Borges, and Union Vice President Brian Protheroe expressed their worry that if the department continues on this trend, they face a future threat of being browned out. “It’s almost like we’re dancing on the train tracks, and eventually a train’s going to come by. Yeah, and I feel like the city keeps saying, ‘I don’t see a train.’ We’re like, no, but we’re the ones on the track. I can tell you, like, we feel the rumble,” Gidney said. Should you ever find yourself in Lisboa, an easy walk for all ages goes straight through the heart of the city from Parque Eduardo VII, down Avenida da Liberdade and Rau Augusta to the historic Praça do Comércio and edge of the Tagus River for just 2.1 miles of walking. The path nears its end down R. Augusta Avenue to the Arco da Rau Augusta. Starting at Park Eduardo VII makes it a slight downhill course to Praça do Comércio. Parque Eduardo VII is 64 acres and just north of Avenida da Liberdad. It is famous for its intricate hedge work, flanked by long walkways to the left and right. At the observation deck at the top of the park, you can see a statue of Marquês de Pombal and the Tagus River off in the distance. From there, venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores (Monument to the Restorers). The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. Take a tasty detour after the Monumento aos Restauradores to A Ginjinha, is an historic openfront bar that opened in 1840. That’s where you can sip Portugal’s famous cherry liquor. The location was publicized by travel journalists Anthony Bordain and Rick Steves. Head down R. Augusta Avenue where you can find several gift shops and restaurants on your way to the Arco da Rau Augusta and Commerce Square. In the center of Praça do Comércio is a monument to King José I, created in 1775. Your journey ends across the street from Commerce Square at Cais das Colunas, a pier named after the two columns on the edge of the Tagus River. Parque Eduardo VII in Lisbon, Portugal is a famous site for its intricate hedges. It’s also a great place for a view of the city. One of the most visited locations in Lisboa, is Commerce Square with its large monument to King Jose I.

articles.text: As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. The exercise provides step-by-step instructions and discussion prompts in a short video that families, housemates, and neighbors can use to transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. The short exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect: • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of • • • evacuation A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfirePlan. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. The at-home evacuation exercise is one part of the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. Last year, the department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving residents a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide year-round public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. The department also recently led the development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a five-year roadmap that identifies steps the city can take to reduce the effects of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.
articles.title: Fire Dept. asks residents to complete wildfire evacuation plans

articles.text: better at attacking than understanding, punishing than healing, tearing down than building up, seeking revenge over pursuing restoration. I am left to wonder when, having invested so heavily in the weapons of war, we invest in the work of beating swords into plowshares, spears into pruning hooks? When do we prioritize restoration over revenge? I know the word is misused, misapplied and misunderstood, yet, I would suggest that at some point we need to get serious about forgiveness. I would argue that to escape the cycle of toxic animosity that grips us, we must forgive, we must release those who have done us wrong from the debt they owe. I would suggest that unless we want to forever worship at the altar of the God named “Get Even,” we need to apply the teaching of Jesus that forgiving “seventy times seven” is the only path to enduring peace. In some ways it is easier to call for forgiveness at an international level than it is to practice it in our communities, our congregations and our personal lives. Yet, if forgiveness is not a personal practice, it is hypocritical to suggest that it is a path to world peace. Thus, let me end with the invitation for each of us to consider who it is that we need to forgive and how it is we need to be forgiven and then, before too much time goes by, put the words “I am sorry” and “You are forgiven” to use and in our own way, seek to heal rather than to punish. Jim Hopkins in Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.
articles.title: Religion Corner

articles.text: Earlier this year the Piedmont City Council appointed Leslie Mendez as Piedmont’s new Planning Director, replacing Kevin Jackson who retired. Mendez holds a master’s degree in City and Regional Planning from the University of California, Berkeley, and a bachelor’s degree in environmental studies from Brown University. She is a former planning manager for the City of Albany, a planning manager for the City of San Rafael, and spent 13 years as a planner with the City of Berkeley. Mendez decided she was ready for a new challenge as the director of a city’s planning department. “I thought it was an amazing opportunity to become a director in a city,” said Mendez. “It’s a fun puzzle to apply planning, especially in our current mandates that we’re having and how to integrate the values of the community and reflect those values while still meeting state mandates.” Her former boss, Jeff Bond – the retired Community Development Director from the City of Albany – pushed her to take this role after serving as Piedmont’s Interim Planning & Building Director. “My previous boss and mentor acted as interim (in Piedmont), so he was touting the fun it would be for me, and I don’t say that sarPlanning & Building Director Leslie Mendez

articles.text: Labor Day is a recognition of both the important role labor unions have played in the well-being of our nation and its working families and of the value of work itself. It is on the value of work, and its corollary, the value of rest, that I would offer a few thoughts. The creation stories of Genesis celebrate the goodness of the world we inhabit. Included in that goodness are work, toil, labor and rest. In the first story human beings, having been created in the image of God, are given the work of being fruitful and multiplying, of filling the earth and exercising dominion “over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the air and over every living thing that moves upon the earth.” The questions “How well have we done in the work given us?” as well as “How well are we doing in that work?” are worthy of serious consideration. The answers must include the recognition that the exercise of dominion has often been mistakenly understood as exercise of domination and that our labors have thus undermined, rather than enhanced, the well-being of God’s creation. Still, there is meaning, purpose and joy to be found in “tilling and keeping” the earth, as the second story of creation describes the work we have been given. Wendell Berry, who died this week at age 92, said it well. “The care of the Earth is our most ancient and most worthy, and after all our most pleasing responsibility. To cherish what remains of it and to foster its renewal is our only hope.” Tilling and keeping the earth takes many forms. As Wendell’s life demonstrated, it includes sinking our hands into the soil, putting our hearts into our words, putting our best into our communities and putting our souls into our relationships. Whether we are employed or not, Labor Day, like the stories of creation and like the testimony of Farmer Berry, reminds us that we, all of us, are here because we have something to give and that there is a time both to give of ourselves, and to rest from giving. Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.
articles.title: Of Labor Day and Labor

As Wendell’s life demonstrated, it includes sinking our hands into the soil, putting our hearts into our words, putting our best into our communities and putting our souls into our relationships. Whether we are employed or not, Labor Day, like the stories of creation and like the testimony of Farmer Berry, reminds us that we, all of us, are here because we have something to give and that there is a time both to give of ourselves, and to rest from giving. articles.text: This past week the fencing around the Piedmont Park tot lot has been removed marking the completion of the new ADA path and landscaping. The next stage of the project will include installing new swings and a nature play area funded by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. According to the city, there is a delay on the manufacturer’s end in delivering the new swing set. The city expects the swings to arrive in November. The new path cuts through the former grassy area between the Exedra Plaza and Piedmont High School campus, connecting with the path in front of the tot lot. Fresh grass has been planted on the left side of the path, while the right side has playground wood chips. The location where the swings will be installed is currently a dug-out hole surrounded by cement stairs with signage and tape to keep the public from entering. The sand surrounding the area has been removed and will be replaced with ADA fiber matting. During installation of the new swings, the climbing structure, The new ADA path with wood chips and newly planted grass on either side. lawn area, Exedra Plaza, and restroom will remain open. The memorial benches are within the construction zone and will be reinstalled after the project is completed. Modernscape Innovations was awarded the $156,364 contract to complete the first stage of this project. The swing equipment and ADA fiber matting installation is anticipated to be awarded separately via a California Multiple Award Schedule (CMAS) agreement. The swings will be bucket swings similar to the original swings. Once the equipment arrives in November, installation will take two weeks to complete. This project is in response to the longstanding community request to rebuild the swings that were removed in 2024 due to structural rot. The current plan is to expand the swing zone to meet modern safety requirements. The dug-out area where the new swing equipment and ADA fiber matting will be installed.

articles.text: Jairo, pronounced Cairo, is a handsome, 4-year-old German Shepherd mix. He starts his day with bursts of zoomies and playbows, along with a few pets. It’s clear to his foster that he was well-loved and cared for by his former family who had to reluctantly surrender him when they lost their housing. Jairo is proving to be a perfect house guest. He is house trained and non-destructive when left alone. He has great leash manners and knows the sit command. He may become a bit bouncy when he gets too excited with his person, but responds well to redirection. Jairo weighs 80 pounds. He may be a bit shy and hesitant to interact when meeting new people, but warms up quickly. He is looking for an adopter to continue his journey building trust — someone who can take their time, read his cues, and let him connect on his timeframe. Given his timid nature, he’s best suited for an adult-only home or one Jairo is a handsome, 4-year-old German Shepherd mix. with older children. To see a video of him and learn more about him, check out mountainfosters on Instagram. To meet Jairo, submit your adoption questionnaire online on Oakland Animal Services shelter’s website and you will be contacted by his foster to arrange a meet-and-greet. articles.text: Denver and Cordelia quickly decided they belonged together forever, and we have to agree. The two had an immediate connection, and now spend their days cuddling, grooming, and quietly looking after one another. Denver is a goofy Siamese with a tiny squeak of a meow. He loves lounging on your chest and following Cordelia around. Cordelia is the capable “big sister” of the pair — a floofy tuxedo who gives nose kisses, naps with her chin resting in your hand, and sleeps belly-up with her tongue peeking out. This pair loves to play, often engaging in friendly wrestling matches. Both cats eat special diets and take daily medication easily, and Cordelia also receives eye drops twice a day. Their foster says, “She is quite used to taking her eye drops and will sit in your lap for them. She’s the easiest cat I’ve ever Adopt Denver and Cordelia through Cattown Oakland medicated.” This duo makes those little extra efforts worthwhile — Cordelia is quick to purr and Denver “loves to be taken care of.” You simply must meet these affectionate, mellow companions — they’re ready to make your house a true home. Denver and Cordelia are neutered/spayed, vaccinated, and microchipped. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland. org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: More than 25 years ago, a few community members dedicated themselves to bringing a new pool to Piedmont. Josh Bernstein, Russ Hafferkamp, and Clarence Mamuyac identified the community’s need for aquatics and worked to bring a new pool to the “There just wasn’t enough pool space,” said Bernstein. “Piedmont was and is still one of the only school districts in our area that doesn’t have their own At first, the group wanted to help the School District build a pool on campus, but were eventually shot down due to the School District’s concern over liability and maintenance. They decided to set their sights on the Piedmont “It became apparent that we had a much broader interest in aquatics in Piedmont than the pool (Piedmont Swim Club Pool) could really sustain. We had a new developing water polo team, we had a really good high school aquatics program, and there was a growing number of new families that wanted to have the same aquatic experiences that were available in Orinda, Lafayette and Moraga,” said Hafferkamp, then the assistant coach of Cal’s At the time, the Swim Club’s Pool was unfit to host aquatic sports. It was considered a “relic,” and the group believed it needed to be addressed. They proposed renovations to accommodate aquatic sports and expand space for swimmers. “We contacted Clarence Mamuyac, who was a very active architect in the aquatics field and lived in the community, and he was supportive of the idea. He helped us build a 3D model of what the facility would look like with drawings and renderings, and we had a series of public meetings and public presentations inside the community about our plan,” said Hafferkamp. Not everyone was supportive of this plan to renovate the pool and there was pushback from the leaseholders of Piedmont Swim Club. “We were met with equal parts opposition, equal parts support, and equal parts apathy. “Apathy kind of won the day,” said Hafferkamp. “The problem was the Piedmont Swim Club. They had the lease from the city on the pool, and they didn’t want to make any changes. What they had done at the time was remove the gutters from the old Piedmont pool during a renovation project, which rendered the old swimming pool unfit for swimming competition,” Bernstein explained. “They were trying to force the swim teams out, and it worked. They couldn’t hold swim meets at the old Piedmont swim club. That became a problem because we had the swim team here in town, and the kids were working out in this substandard pool. They (Piedmont Swim Club) were afraid they were going to lose their swim club, and they wouldn’t have any place to swim during construction.” Their project and ideas were shut down. It took years before the community would think about a new pool again. It was only when the swim club lost its lease to the city that the idea of a new pool gained traction. “Eventually, they lost their lease, and that’s when things started to change. Once the Recreation Department (under Mark Delventhal) took things over, there was an opportunity,” Bernstein said. There was a community movement of those who recognized the value of aquatics; many of whom were previously against the idea of a pool were now on board. “The community recognized the future value of aquatics, and the reality that the old pool was a relic and needed to be addressed,” said Hafferkamp. A new pool was approved, and after years of planning and construction, the Community Pool was built. Bernstein and Hafferkamp believe the work they did with Mamuyac paid off. “I think that the homework that we did in the beginning helped when Betsy Andersen came along, and she was able to really take it from this concept that we had to a real project,” said Bernstein. He and Hafferkamp were very appreciative of the work Mayor Andersen and the city did to bring this project to fruition. When Bernstein showed up for the pool’s opening day, he reflected on the years of hard work his group put into the idea of a new pool. Seeing it completed was an emotional moment Josh Bernstein gives a thumbs-up on the opening day of the Community Pool. for him. “I got choked up on the first day when we came to go swimming. It was such a long time coming. To see that concept that started in our kitchen become a reality and such an unbelievably impressive reality. It was an emotional experience for me,” said Bernstein. It was only when the swim club lost its lease to the city that the idea of a new pool gained traction. “Eventually, they lost their lease, and that’s when things started to change. Once the Recreation Department (under Mark Delventhal) took things over, there was an opportunity,” Bernstein said. There was a community movement of those who recognized the value of aquatics; many of whom were previously against the idea of a pool were now on board. “The community recognized the future value of aquatics, and the reality that the old pool was a relic and needed to be addressed,” said Hafferkamp. A new pool was approved, and after years of planning and construction, the Community Pool was built. Bernstein and Hafferkamp believe the work they did with Mamuyac paid off. “I think that the homework that we did in the beginning helped when Betsy Andersen came along, and she was able to really take it from this concept that we had to a real project,” said Bernstein. He and Hafferkamp were very appreciative of the work Mayor Andersen and the city did to bring this project to fruition. When Bernstein showed up for the pool’s opening day, he reflected on the years of hard work his group put into the idea of a new pool. Seeing it completed was an emotional moment Josh Bernstein gives a thumbs-up on the opening day of the Community Pool. for him. “I got choked up on the first day when we came to go swimming. It was such a long time coming. To see that concept that started in our kitchen become a reality and such an unbelievably impressive reality. It was an emotional experience for me,” said Bernstein. According to the National Park Service, the arch sits smack dab in the middle of one of the nation’s busiest bird highways: the Mississippi Flyway. articles.text: On Sunday, August 23, more than 100 Girl Scouts and their families gathered in Piedmont Park to kick off the new scouting year at the annual ice cream social and sing-along. The ice cream social was hosted by Head-Royce and Piedmont High School tenth grade Senior Troop 33587, who served scoops of vanilla, chocolate, and rainbow sherbet with a variety of toppings, including sprinkles, whipped cream, crushed Oreos, and chocolate chips. While enjoying their ice cream on the lawn, PHS twelfth grade Ambassador Troop 30713 led the girls in singing traditional Girl Scout songs. This year’s singalong was the final time for these Ambassadors to host the yearly tradition before they graduate. The Ambassador Scouts belted out classic camp tunes, starting with “Make New Friends” and diving into lively repeat-after-me songs like “There Was a Great Big Moose.” The younger scouts were invited to lead the group with songs they picked like “Over the Deep Blue Sea.” Service Unit 303 Girl Scouts gathered in a friendship circle to close the event as the girls are ready for a year of building courage, confidence and character. Girl Scouts kicked off the new scouting year with an ice cream social and sing-along event in Piedmont Park. Lucy Allen (front left), Jeannie Choi, Skye Prata-Baack, Kate Tong and Emma Chan; Charlotte Phung (back left), Junie Worthen, Maya Evans, Victoria Mbise, Sicheng Wu. Girl Scouts from Piedmont, Oakland, and Emeryville end the event with a friendship circle.
articles.title: Girl Scouts Ice Cream Social at Piedmont Park

articles.text: Registration is underway for the Fall 2026 session, with classes beginning September 14. Piedmont Adult School offers a wide range of community classes designed to make learning enjoyable and accessible for adults of all ages. Whether you want to explore a big idea, discover a new practice or simply taste some really good chocolate, there’s still time to join us and learn something new and valuable this fall. Spaces are still available for classes including: • Understanding Modern Art — Make more sense of what you see in museums and galleries! Explore the artists, ideas and movements that shaped modern art and learn some of the vocabulary that can make looking at and talking about art more enjoyable. No previous art background is needed. • Philosophy as a Way of Living — Explore how ideas from some of the world’s great philosophical traditions can help us think about the questions that matter in everyday life, from our values and choices to what gives life meaning. • Mindfulness in Motion: Zen and the Japanese Sword (Budo Zen) — Discover a different approach to mindfulness through movement. This class combines Zen meditation with Iaido, a classical Japanese sword art practiced with bokken (wooden swords). Through guided sword movements, concentration and meditation, you’ll explore ways to develop greater focus, awareness and inner calm. No martial arts or meditation experience is necessary. • Wild Chocolate: Taste the Amazon — Taste four premium chocolates made from sustainably sourced Amazonian cacao and discover how where cacao grows influences its flavor. A certified chocolate taster will guide you through the tasting while sharing the story of chocolate that supports rainforest preservation and local communities. • Eat for Your Body Type — Learn more about your individual body type and explore how making thoughtful food choices can support your health and well-being. Come learn something new, expand your horizons, and meet great people at Piedmont Adult School this fall! Register today at piedmontadultschool.org or call 510-594-2655 for more information.

articles.text: Sophomore Girl Scout Troop #33587 started their scouting year by camping for two nights at Point Reyes the last weekend of August. They started at the Palomarin Trailhead and hiked 5.5 miles in with an elevation gain of about 1,000 feet to Wildcat Campground. This was their 24th camping trip as a troop and the longest backpacking hike so far. The hike took the girls past Bass Lake and through forests lit by the setting sun. The girls arrived at the campsite in the dark and were greeted by the moon rising over a ridge and Venus glowing in the west over the Pacific Ocean. By day, the girls were visited by a fox, an elk and flocks of California Quail. The girls also earned merit badges by drawing in nature as part of the Mind, Body badge. Juliette Edesses (left) and Emma Syhabout Photos by Carolyn Pan Girl Scouts in Troop #33587 take the Palomarin Trail towards Wildcat Campground in Point Reyes. Pictured are Victoria Mbise (left), Emma Syhabout, Juliette Edesses and Charlotte Phung. Troop #33587 backpacked 5.5 miles to reach Wildcat Campground in Point Reyes. Victoria Mbise (left), Charlotte Phung, Emma Syhabout and Juliette Edesses stop for a photo as the sun sets over Bass Lake. A gray fox walks by Piedmont Girl Scouts during their backpacking trip in Point Reyes. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, September 9, 2026 By Carolyn Pan Sophomore Girl Scout Troop #33587 started their scouting year by camping for two nights at Point Reyes the last weekend of August. They started at the Palomarin Trailhead and hiked 5.5 miles in with an elevation Girl Scouts backpack to Point Reyes gain of about 1,000 feet to Wildcat Campground. This was their 24th camping trip as a troop and the longest backpacking hike so far. The hike took the girls past Bass Lake and through forests lit by the setting sun. The girls arrived at the campsite in the dark and were greeted by the moon rising over a ridge and Venus glowing in the west over the Pacific Ocean. By day, the girls were visited by a fox, an elk and flocks of California Quail. The girls also earned merit badges by drawing in nature as part of the Mind, Body badge. Juliette Edesses (left) and Emma Syhabout Photos by Carolyn Pan Girl Scouts in Troop #33587 take the Palomarin Trail towards Wildcat Campground in Point Reyes. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont High hosted its first water polo match since 2019 on September 3 against James Logan. Staff Photos Thursday, September 3 was a monumental day for Piedmont High’s water polo team. The boys’ team hosted James Logan HS at the Piedmont Pool for a regular season match, marking the first time the team has done so since 2019. The Highlanders fell in double-overtime 8-7 to the Colts, but the game result hardly impacted the team’s joy on Thursday night. For people who have been connected to the program, like coach Rik Krumins who was an assistant coach on that 2019 squad, playing at home was an emotional experience. “We all worked so hard for this. I love this sport, and the fact we’re here is kind of weird. There are a lot of people who put blood, sweat, tears into this facility. One thing I talked with the team about was past teams were literally knocking on doors to tell people,” Krumins said. Piedmont’s current players were in elementary school the last time the school hosted a water polo match. “Tonight means a lot to everyone. We’ve had to commute long distances for practice, but the team has so much passion and everyone was willing to do it. This is definitely going to help get more people involved, younger people involved, and grow the program,” senior Colin Amen said. The Highlanders’ match against James Logan was a battle of two D2 North Coast Section qualifiers, and Thursday certainly had a playoff atmosphere. According to online records, Piedmont High has never hosted a playoff game at the Piedmont Pool. Before the closure, PHS received high playoff seeds from 2016 to 2019, but still played each match at pools outside Piedmont. For this year’s team, hosting a NCS match would be a major step forward. “It would mean so much to host a playoff game. Having that crowd really riles us up; it takes the intensity to a whole new level,” said junior Rylan Patty. “I’ve rarely heard a home crowd before. It’s great; I tried to get a lot of my friends to come out here. A lot of people don’t know how big water polo is to our community, but it’s a big sport in Piedmont. We have an awesome culture and it’s nice to share that with people,” Colin Amen said. Hearing a home crowd at Rylan Patty scores one of his three goals against James Logan. articles.text: Rehan Mumtaz totals 180 yards on offense Piedmont High’s football team captured its first win of the season with a 28-0 shutout of St. Mary’s at Witter Field on Friday, September 4. It was a strong defensive day for the Highlanders who had five quarterback sacks, four tackles for loss, and an interception. It marked the school’s first shutout since October 2024 when they beat Dougherty Valley 41-0. “We probably could’ve played a cleaner game, but it’s hard to complain about a 28-0 shutout. The defense played really well, so it was good to see them rallying around and tackling. We’re a young team, and momentum is big for a young team, so now it’s about keeping the guys focused,” Coach Jordan Seiden said. It was a good response for PHS following its season-opening loss to Napa, where the winning side gained 314 yards on the ground. “During practice this week, we knew we had to work on the run game. We knew that if we stopped the run, we’ll be able to defend the pass and we really trust our pass coverage. We really just worked on defending the run so we can force them to pass,” senior linebacker Colby Hong said. Senior running back Rehan Mumtaz had his way with the Panthers’ defense, switching the field and putting opposing players on skates. He recorded 130 rushing yards on 12 carries, to go along with three receptions for 50 yards and two touchdowns. “We usually start off the season pretty slow, but once we find our zone, things really get going. Our line blocked so well today, I can’t give enough gratitude to them. Running becomes instinct at this point, I’ve practiced so many times that finding the lanes becomes second nature,” Mumtaz said. Game Recap St. Mary’s opened the game with a long drive down to Piedmont’s nine-yard line, but their series stalled on 4th-and-4. The Highlanders turned over on downs at their own 41, but wasted no time getting the ball back. On the Panthers’ first play, Piedmont’s Owen Curran intercepted a long pass at their own 12 with 20 seconds left in the first quarter. Staff Photos Diego Hurwitz (2) celebrates a touchdown with Henry Brennan (6) and Mason Gray (28). Rehan Mumtaz during his 35-yard touchdown reception against St. Mary’s. He had two touchdown catches, 130 rushing yards, and 50 receiving yards.

articles.text: Piedmont has boosted its record to 10-4 overall. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches over the past week. They shut out Redwood Christian 3-0 on Tuesday, September 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym Two days later they fell to Salesian 3-2 in a heated five-set match bout 3-2 at Salesian in Richmond. The results improves Piedmont’s record to 10-4 overall, which eclipses last year’s total of nine wins. “When we’re at our best, we’re getting pressure from all three hitting spots. It starts with our middles and opens up. We continue to see them just getting better,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. Despite the loss to Salesian, outside hitter Maika Ting had a strong performance, logging a season-high 24 kills. “Maika’s been super consistent and has shown great improvement in terms of knowing when to take a little bit off and when not to,” Glass said. 3-0 over Redwood Christian It was a clean 3-0 sweep for Piedmont over the Eagles, winning by scores of 25-9, 25-14, 25-14. In the first set, PHS established an 18-5 lead at one point, including two kills by Maika Ting, Sofia Meyer, and Charlotte Bailey. Fiona Olsen and Lucia Dorsey also had individual kills and blocks. Piedmont continued the momentum into the second set, leading 9-0 until Redwood Christian got its first point. The run included three aces by Carina Vora, a block by Dorsey, and another kill by Olsen. RCHS inched closer to make it a 12-7 deficit, but PHS extended to 24-12 from there before the Eagles added two more points. Both teams traded points in the third set with PHS leading 5-4. From there, Piedmont scored seven straight points to lead 12-4. The Highlanders extended the lead to 22-7 before Redwood Christian inched closer to 24-14. PHS closed the game with a thunderous kill by Olsen. Final stats: Olsen recorded seven kills and one block. Ting recorded four kills, six digs and two assists. Bailey recorded two kills. Allyson Huynh recorded one kill, five digs and one assist. Izara Dando recorded two kills. Hazel Schaeffer recorded one ace and five digs. Meyer recorded four kills, two aces and three digs. Nora Trombi recorded two kills, one ace, two digs and seven assists. Olivia Stevens recorded five kills, one ace and three digs. Staff Photos Fiona Olsen led Piedmont with seven kills against Redwood Christian. Maika Ting had 24 kills against Salesian. Dorsey recorded four kills and two blocks. Vora recorded five aces, one block, six digs and 15 assists. Mia Bechtel recorded two aces, six digs and four assists. 3-2 loss to Salesian Piedmont won the second and fourth sets, Match scores were 25-19, 18-25, 25-19, 24-26, 15-12. In the fourth set, both sides traded the lead multiple times until PHS built a 22-18 cushion. However, the Pride went on a four point run to tie it at 22-22. PHS had set-point at 24-23, but an error tied things up. After that, Piedmont scored two straight with a kill by Dorsey and a lane violation by Salesian to force a fifth set. Salesian took control in the fifth set to hold match-point at 14-9, but PHS scored three straight to make things interesting at 14-12. To end the match, Salesian called the number of its tall middle hitter, finishing with a spike. Final stats: Ting recorded 24 kills, six aces and eight digs. Bailey recorded five kills, two blocks and one dig. A. Huynh recorded 35 digs and 11 assists. Dando recorded four kills. Meyer recorded eight kills. Stevens recorded five kills, and five digs. Dorsey recorded five kills, three blocks and three digs. Vora recorded two aces, 20 digs and 26 assists. Bechtel recorded nine digs and 11 assists. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Moraga for the St. Mary’s Invitational at St. Mary’s College on Saturday, September 5. The boys team came away with an eighth place finish out of 25 schools, while the girls placed 10th of 24 teams. “Overall, it looked like what it was – the first race of the season,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “We saw a lot of good things, but we also learned some things about how we need to race better. We had runners who were aggressive early, but had a harder time maintaining that momentum through the second mile.” Senior Alex Schleuning led the way for the Highlanders in 26th of 178 runners in 10:47.02 on the two-mile course. Piedmont’s top-four runners were separated by just 14 seconds. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was next in, finishing 36th in 10:51.57. Having four runners that close together gives us a really good group to work with as we continue building toward the championship portion of the season,” Zirkelbach said. The girls’ squad was notably without three top runners, seniors Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray, and sophomore Kelsey Coleman. Sophomore Camille Hauser led the team placing 46th of 166 runners in 13:19.95. Alex Schleuning led the way for Piedmont, finishing 26th of 178 runners. “Camille Hauser ran 13:42 here last year, so she improved by approximately 23 seconds from her freshman season,” Zirkelbach said. Piedmont had all five of its best runners within 53-seconds of each other. Right behind Hauser was senior Cora Brozowski-Schrader in 47th with a time of 13:21.42. Junior Nikita Gorelik finished 55th in 13:29.41, fellow junior Viviane Oesterer was 69th in 13:50.26, while sophomore Madeleine Ewen rounded things out in 83rd in 14:13.06. “We have always put a lot of emphasis on developing a strong pack rather than relying on one or two runners at the front, and this gives us a good group to continue developing,” Zirkelbach said. pages.text: Wednesday, September 9, 2026 11 Piedmont volleyball improves to 10-4 Piedmont has boosted its record to 10-4 overall. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches over the past week. They shut out Redwood Christian 3-0 on Tuesday, September 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym Two days later they fell to Salesian 3-2 in a heated five-set match bout 3-2 at Salesian in Richmond. The results improves Piedmont’s record to 10-4 overall, which eclipses last year’s total of nine wins. “When we’re at our best, we’re getting pressure from all three hitting spots. It starts with our middles and opens up. We continue to see them just getting better,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. Despite the loss to Salesian, outside hitter Maika Ting had a strong performance, logging a season-high 24 kills. “Maika’s been super consistent and has shown great improvement in terms of knowing when to take a little bit off and when not to,” Glass said. 3-0 over Redwood Christian It was a clean 3-0 sweep for Piedmont over the Eagles, winning by scores of 25-9, 25-14, 25-14. In the first set, PHS established an 18-5 lead at one point, including two kills by Maika Ting, Sofia Meyer, and Charlotte Bailey. Fiona Olsen and Lucia Dorsey also had individual kills and blocks. Piedmont continued the momentum into the second set, leading 9-0 until Redwood Christian got its first point. The run included three aces by Carina Vora, a block by Dorsey, and another kill by Olsen. RCHS inched closer to make it a 12-7 deficit, but PHS extended to 24-12 from there before the Eagles added two more points. Both teams traded points in the third set with PHS leading 5-4. From there, Piedmont scored seven straight points to lead 12-4. The Highlanders extended the lead to 22-7 before Redwood Christian inched closer to 24-14. PHS closed the game with a thunderous kill by Olsen. Final stats: Olsen recorded seven kills and one block. Ting recorded four kills, six digs and two assists. Bailey recorded two kills. Allyson Huynh recorded one kill, five digs and one assist. Izara Dando recorded two kills. Hazel Schaeffer recorded one ace and five digs. Meyer recorded four kills, two aces and three digs. Nora Trombi recorded two kills, one ace, two digs and seven assists. Olivia Stevens recorded five kills, one ace and three digs. Staff Photos Fiona Olsen led Piedmont with seven kills against Redwood Christian. Maika Ting had 24 kills against Salesian. Dorsey recorded four kills and two blocks. Vora recorded five aces, one block, six digs and 15 assists. Mia Bechtel recorded two aces, six digs and four assists. 3-2 loss to Salesian Piedmont won the second and fourth sets, Match scores were 25-19, 18-25, 25-19, 24-26, 15-12. In the fourth set, both sides traded the lead multiple times until PHS built a 22-18 cushion. However, the Pride went on a four point run to tie it at 22-22. PHS had set-point at 24-23, but an error tied things up. After that, Piedmont scored two straight with a kill by Dorsey and a lane violation by Salesian to force a fifth set. Salesian took control in the fifth set to hold match-point at 14-9, but PHS scored three straight to make things interesting at 14-12. To end the match, Salesian called the number of its tall middle hitter, finishing with a spike. Final stats: Ting recorded 24 kills, six aces and eight digs. Bailey recorded five kills, two blocks and one dig. A. Huynh recorded 35 digs and 11 assists. Dando recorded four kills. Meyer recorded eight kills. Stevens recorded five kills, and five digs. Dorsey recorded five kills, three blocks and three digs. Vora recorded two aces, 20 digs and 26 assists. Bechtel recorded nine digs and 11 assists. articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team split its last two games, bringing their record to 2-5 overall. The Highlanders claimed a narrow 14-13 win over San Leandro at Witter Field on Thursday, September 3, and lost 38-0 to St. Ignatius of San Francisco at home on Saturday, September 5. Saturday’s game against St. Ignatius was Piedmont’s inaugural “Battle of the Bay” Highlander Showcase, which featured four games where one East Bay school took on one school from San Francisco. “A tournament like this is really good because we’re playing and watching more football. We’ve installed a lot in a little bit of time, so we’re looking forward to seeing how things look at the end of the season with the experience we’ve gained,” said defensive coordinator Hayley Adams, who filled in for coach Beth Black on Saturday. “This tournament means we’re taking this sport seriously. When the program started four years ago, it wasn’t very serious at first. Now, we’re here to play football and win games,” said quarterback Edie Elmquist. Against the San Leandro Pirates, PHS held an initial 8-0 lead after Agatha Filha-Gama recorded a safety late in the first quarter before Edie Elmquist hit Cea’naiya Alexander for a seven-yard touchdown midway through the second. San Leandro scored to end the first half. “Naiya was on the outside and was open in the corner. We’re moving the ball well; we’re working on blocking, seeing what the defense is doing, and then figuring out how that affects our plays and what we do,” Elmquist said. The Pirates went ahead 13-9 late in the third quarter, but Piedmont found the winner late in the game. Nearing the final minute Kate Tong had one interception and three pass defenses against San Leandro. Staff Photos Nea Mafi scored the gamewinning touchdown against San Leandro on an improvised 26-yard cutback run. of action, running back Nea Mafi made the play of the game. With the ball at SL 26, Mafi took an initial run to the left side, but turned the other direction with defenders converging on her. Using her speed, Mafi sprinted the opposite way to avoid pressure, evaded one defender, and then broke to the end zone to make it 14-13. 14-13 over San Leandro After back-and-forth possessions through the first quarter, Piedmont pinned San Leandro deep with a punt late in the first quarter. It led to Filha-Gama recording a sack in the end zone to give her team a 2-0 lead. Piedmont took over at their 25 midway through the second for its next score. Elmquist converted a critical 3rd-and-7 with an eight yard quarterback keeper, while Mafi later converted a 3rd-and-3 with an eight yard carry. On 3rd-and-goal from the SLHS seven, Elmquist stepped back for pass, initially looking left before turning to the right to find Alexander running a corner route for the touchdown, making it 8-0. San Leandro scored on its ensuing possession on 4th-andgoal from the 19 to end the quarter down 8-7. In the third quarter, San Leandro drove all the way down to Piedmont’s three, but the Highlanders held them without a touchdown. SLHS scored to end the third quarter after starting possession at Piedmont’s 25, scoring after four plays to go up 13-7. PHS had a chance to score after an interception by Kate Tong started a series at the Pirates’ 19, but Piedmont stalled out at the 23 following a penalty. Piedmont’s game-winning score came on the third play of its series. At the San Leandro 26, Mafi took a handoff to the Cea’naiya Alexander had a touchdown reception against San Leandro.

articles.text: William Bridges (4) Jeb Burden (81) Jojo Logwood (28) Although the Highlanders conceded a 26-13 loss to Casa Grande last week, their performance gave Highlander fans hope. The defense was quite strong and the offense picked up towards the end of the game. The Highlander defense came out in the first drive on fire. They set the tone on the first play of the game with a ferocious tackle for loss by Lethi Havea setting the Gauchos back 3 yards. The bottom line for the offense in the first half was turnovers. With two costly fumbles early in the game, the Gauchos put Piedmont on their heels with a passing TD and one touchdown on a run. With the Highlanders needing to score to stay alive, freshman Will Dietrich showed his speed and agility, taking the kickoff 70+ yards and putting the Highlanders in a prime position to go into halftime with some momentum. Along with his long kickoff return. Dietrich put the Highlanders in great position on just about every kickoff when he touched the ball despite playing with an injury. A combination of smart coaching by head coach Pouyan Assadi and quick runs by Ernie Hildreth enabled the Highlanders to convert on a fourth down with two seconds left in the first half. With an extra point by Gael Fierro the halftime score was 20-7. Special teams player Jojo Logwood came in with a full head of speed from the linebacker position and was able to block two CG extra points. With the Highlander defense trying to set the tone like they did in the first half, things were looking up as two penalties against Casa Grande’s offense resulted in a first and 25 on their own 20-yard line. But two miscues by Piedmont’s defense allowed a 23-yard catch, followed by a quarterback scramble to pick up the first down. It didn’t take long for the Gauchos to rip off a 54-yard touchdown run, the third TD of the game. With a Logwood extra point block the score was 26-7. Piedmont dominated the fourth quarter. Playing in Petaluma against a strong opponent, Piedmont showed grit and determination on both sides of the ball. Offensively, quarterback Gio Lopez led a commanding final drive, which ultimately resulted in a perfectly placed pass to wide receiver Gael Fierro on a slant route resulting in a touchdown. Fierro would go on to be the team’s leading receiver. The culmination of the fourth quarter came from a pass breakup by freshman Sebby Joseph. Coming to the team a little later than everyone else, he’s shown quick improvement. Injuries included severe leg cramping by linebacker and running back Ernie Hildreth, sidelining him for the rest of the game. Lev Keluva was pulled sharply while blocking on a Piedmont kick return, tweaking his back, but he was later able to return. Finally, freshman Will Dietrich came down hard on the ball after running for 70+ yards and needed a short break. Next week Piedmont will face a manageable opponent – Salesian High School – at 4 pm on Friday September 11 at Witter Field. Gio Lopez (25) Ernie Hildreth (1), Mateo Morgan (33), Will Dietrich (5), and Koli Faotusia (71) Photos by Graham Smith

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2026-27 season with Legally Blonde The Musical, based on the popular 2001 film, running September 11 through October 11. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods, a sorority president who enrolls at Harvard Law School after being dumped by her boyfriend and ultimately proves herself while working on a case. No’eau Kahalekulu directs the production, with choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes and music direction by Camden Daly. The production features a 25-person company of Bay Area performers. “If you loved this movie in 2001, I promise it’s even more fun with a live band and an audience. The show moves at a whip fast pace and is full of laughs and seriously impressive dance and vocals,” said Kimberly Dooley, Artistic Director of Berkeley Playhouse. “Legally Blonde defies stereotypes and celebrates female teamwork, empowerment and above all else...authenticity.” Kahalekulu said the character of Elle Woods has remained a favorite since the film’s release. “Elle Woods has been my comfort character since 2001. If she can get into Harvard and keep her sparkle, the rest of us can handle whatever’s in front of us,” said director No’eau Kahalekulu. “We’ve all gotten a little scared to be big and silly and sincere in public lately. This production is an invitation back into it. Like the show says, being true to yourself never goes out of style.” Scenic design is by Sarah Phykitt, with costumes by Ashley Renee and lighting by Sophia Craven. The musical is based on the novel Legally Blonde by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film of the same name. The cast also includes two dogs: Latke the Pomeranian, making a theatrical debut as Bruiser Woods, and Stella, a three-year-old French bulldog mix, as Rufus. Tickets are available through Berkeley Playhouse online at https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods. Music Lessons │ Band Instrument Rentals │ Sales and Repairs

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will celebrate the opening of its 104th season with the 51st annual Opera in the Park, a free outdoor concert this Sunday, September 13, at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. The concert begins at 1:30 p.m. and will feature the San Francisco Opera Orchestra conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim, along with singers from the company’s upcoming 2026-27 season. Scheduled performers include sopranos Eleonora Buratto, Sofia Gotch, Mary Hoskins, Toni Marie Palmertree and Heidi Stober; tenors Joshua Guerrero and Christopher Sokolowski; baritones Amartuvshin Enkhbat, Thomas Mole and Gabriel NatalBáez; and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn. The program will include arias and ensembles by composers including Verdi, Puccini, Donizetti, Glinka, Weber and Richard Strauss, as well as a selection from a movie musical. San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock will emcee the concert. The event, presented by the San Francisco Chronicle, typically draws more than 10,000 people to Golden Gate Park. Established in 1971 by former Opera General Director Kurt Herbert Adler, Opera in the Park has featured performers including Luciano Pavarotti, Montserrat Caballé, Marilyn Horne and Renata Scotto. A picnic contest, introduced last year, will return, with judges selecting the best-decorated or most elaborate picnic spread during the first half of the concert. Food and beverages will also be available for purchase. Children and families can visit Bearitone the Opera Bear’s Club House for coloring, crafts and lawn games. The event is free and does not require tickets. For more information, call (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera. com/operainthepark. The free concert is held at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Opera
articles.title: SF Opera performs free concert in Golden Gate Park this Sunday

articles.text: Presale tickets available online now Ramona Kelley in Oakland Ballet’s performance Luna Mexicana Oakland Ballet Company will perform Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Día de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. Visit https://oaklandballet. org to purchase tickets.
