The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods, a sorority president who enrolls at Harvard Law School after being dumped by her boyfriend and ultimately proves herself while working on a case. No’eau Kahalekulu directs the production, with choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes and music direction by Camden Daly. The production features a 25-person company of Bay Area performers. “If you loved this movie in 2001, I promise it’s even more fun with a live band and an audience. The show moves at a whip fast pace and is full of laughs and seriously impressive dance and vocals,” said Kimberly Dooley, Artistic Director of Berkeley Playhouse. “Legally Blonde defies stereotypes and celebrates female teamwork, empowerment and above all else...authenticity.” Kahalekulu said the character of Elle Woods has remained a favorite since the film’s release. “Elle Woods has been my comfort character since 2001. If she can get into Harvard and keep her sparkle, the rest of us can handle whatever’s in front of us,” said director No’eau Kahalekulu. “We’ve all gotten a little scared to be big and silly and sincere in public lately. This production is an invitation back into it. Like the show says, being true to yourself never goes out of style.” Scenic design is by Sarah Phykitt, with costumes by Ashley Renee and lighting by Sophia Craven. The musical is based on the novel Legally Blonde by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film of the same name. The cast also includes two dogs: Latke the Pomeranian, making a theatrical debut as Bruiser Woods, and Stella, a three-year-old French bulldog mix, as Rufus. Tickets are available through Berkeley Playhouse online at https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/. SF Opera performs free concert in Golden Gate Park this Sunday By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Opera will celebrate the opening of its 104th season with the 51st annual Opera in the Park, a free outdoor concert this Sunday, September 13, at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. The concert begins at 1:30 p.m. and will feature the San Francisco Opera Orchestra conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim, along with singers from the company’s upcoming 2026-27 season. Scheduled performers include sopranos Eleonora Buratto, Sofia Gotch, Mary Hoskins, Toni Marie Palmertree and Heidi Stober; tenors Joshua Guerrero and Christopher Sokolowski; baritones Amartuvshin Enkhbat, Thomas Mole and Gabriel NatalBáez; and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn. The program will include arias and ensembles by composers including Verdi, Puccini, Donizetti, Glinka, Weber and Richard Strauss, as well as a selection from a movie musical. San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock will emcee the concert. The event, presented by the San Francisco Chronicle, typically draws more than 10,000 people to Golden Gate Park. Established in 1971 by former Opera General Director Kurt Herbert Adler, Opera in the Park has featured performers including Luciano Pavarotti, Montserrat Caballé, Marilyn Horne and Renata Scotto. A picnic contest, introduced last year, will return, with judges selecting the best-decorated or most elaborate picnic spread during the first half of the concert. Food and beverages will also be available for purchase. Children and families can visit Bearitone the Opera Bear’s Club House for coloring, crafts and lawn games. The event is free and does not require tickets. For more information, call (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera. com/operainthepark. The free concert is held at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. Ramona Kelley in Oakland Ballet’s performance Luna Mexicana By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Ballet Company will perform Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Día de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. Visit https://oaklandballet. org to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony opens its 2026–27 season with Inheritance on Sunday, October 18, 2026, at 4 p.m. It marks the return of Music Director Laureate Kent Nagano to the orchestra for the first time since 2009. Held at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts (10 10th St, Oakland), the season-opening concert brings together works by Felix Mendelssohn and the world premiere of Vater unser by Argentine composer Alex Nante, a work dedicated to Berkeley Symphony and Nagano. The program opens with Mendelssohn’s The Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave), followed by the premiere of Vater unser. Pianist Mari Kodama then joins the orchestra for Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1. The program concludes with Mendelssohn’s Symphony No. 5, “Reformation,” whose finale is built on the chorale “Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott.” “In Vater unser, Bach’s melodies become a point of departure for an unbound process of orchestral amplification and harmonic elaboration,” said Nante. “One of my main interests as a composer is the evocation of light in sound, whether in meditative or ecstatic atmospheres.” Nante began his series of Bach-inspired works at Nagano’s encouragement, as the composer and conductor have collaborated frequently in recent years. Nagano led Berkeley Symphony for 31 years, from 1978 to 2009, shaping the orchestra into an internationally recognized Photo by Antoine Saito Conductor Kent Nagano is renowned for interpretations of clarity, elegance, and intelligence, with a repertoire spanning the classical, romantic, and contemporary eras. ensemble known for adventurous programming and commitment to living composers. His return to the podium reunites Nagano with an orchestra whose artistic identity he helped define for more than three decades. “As Berkeley Symphony looks toward its future, it is especially meaningful to welcome Kent Nagano back to the orchestra he helped shape,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton. “Kent remains a wonderful friend and champion of Berkeley Symphony, and we’re delighted to have him with us for this season opener. His return connects us to the orchestra’s history while reminding us that an inheritance is not simply something to preserve – it’s a foundation to build on as we imagine our future.” Berkeley Symphony’s 2026-27 season features three Mainstage Concerts and two Chamber Concerts, including two premieres. The next Mainstage Concert features Berkeley-born composer Gabriella Smith’s Desert Ecology, a response to the realities of climate change, on February 27 and 28, 2027. Following orchestra tradition, living artists make up over half of the season’s composers. Subscription packages and individual tickets are on sale now, with single tickets starting at $20. The season offers a full subscription (all three mainstage concerts plus both chamber concerts) and a mainstage subscription (all three mainstage concerts). Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by phone at (510) 841-2800.

articles.text: Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family. A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through December 6. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea. He exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The local exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moresby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Georgina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art in Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/papua-new-guinea-mathias-kauage.
articles.title: Mathias Kauage exhibition now on display at de Young

articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 15. Now in its 15th year, the three-night festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012. This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artists awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens. Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park. The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others. FGLM volunteers provide maintenance assistance as the city’s gardening staff has been reduced over time. The Autumn Lights Festival is the organization’s largest annual fundraiser. Tickets and additional information are available through the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt at https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/about/. Crystal Gardens by Studio One Art Center, 2025

articles.text: Ongoing through September 20 Book Club Art Show Gallery Hours This eclectic group of artists, The Book Club at Van Kleef’s, first met at Café Van Kleef in Oakland in 2005. Their show, For the Love of Art, includes works of 19 artists. Open Gallery Hours from 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through September 20. The show is free and open to all! Saturday, September 12, 6:30 p.m. Cuban Fusion Illustrated Book Talk Most people know the iconic voice of the Queen of Salsa, Celia Cruz, one of the world’s greatest ambassadors of Cuban music and culture, but what happened to Cuban music after successive waves of migration carried Cuban musicians, artists, and cultural producers across the globe? In this talk, Dr. Eva Silot Bravo examines how the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Eastern socialist bloc, and Cuba’s economic crisis of the ‘90s reshaped the trajectory of Cuban music. Drawing on the research behind Cuban Fusion: The Transnational Cuban Alternative Music Scene (Palgrave Macmillan, 2024), the presentation traces the evolution of trans-national Cuban jazz and fusion scenes over the past three decades, reshaping Cuban music into a truly global phenomenon. Reserve your seat for this fascinating event at https://www.ticketsignup.io/EvaBravo. Sunday, September 13, 7:00 p.m. Temescal String Quartet Concert A San Francisco Bay Area classical ensemble established in 2004 by professional musicians from the San Francisco Opera and Ballet Orchestras, founded by violinist Barbara Riccardi, the group will perform quartet masterworks by Mozart, Ravel, and the US premiere of a quartet by Jane O’Leary. Barbara will play alongside Dana Myers, violin, Linda Green, viola, and Nancy Bien, cello. Light refreshments will be available after the performance, and advance tickets are now at https://www.ticketsignup.io/TSQ. Sunday, September 20, 4:00 p.m. Marcio Candido solo violin Concert Award-winning Brazilian violinist Dr. Marcio Candido, who has performed worldwide as a soloist, chamber musician, concertmaster, and educator, will perform a program of 75–80 minutes of music that offers a strongly compelling musical journey, from the profound introspection of J. S. Bach’s D Minor Partita and its monumental Chaconne, through the radiant brilliance of the E Major Partita, to the architectural grandeur and triumphant conclusion of the composer’s Third Sonata. Recognized for his expressive artistry and versatility, Dr. Candido has appeared in major concert halls and music festivals around the world, and currently serves as Chair of the Music Department at Weimar University in California. Light refreshments will be offered, and advance tickets are now available online at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Candido. Saturday, September 26 to November 1 Oakland Art Association gallery show Oakland Art Association presents “Hopes and Dreams” — a curated show that encompasses everyone’s most precious and intimate desires for the future. OAA is a non-profit group of artists, photographers, and art supporters in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties whose mission is to encourage artistic endeavor in the community, support public school art education, and arrange show venues for our members’ artworks. The Opening Reception at PCA will be from 1:00–4:00 p.m. on Saturday, September 26, and is free and open to all! Saturday, September 26, 6:00 p.m. Ezequiel Barrera and Carl Blake piano recital As part of his residency in the SF Bay Area, virtuoso pianist and composer Ezequiel Sebastian Barrera from Mexico City will perform a recital, assisted by local pianist Carl Blake in a performance of Barrera’s Fantasia Mexicana for four hands, one piano. Ezequiel has performed extensively to critical acclaim in diverse venues around the world including US, Canada, Mexico, Central America, Chile, and Germany. The program includes works by Beethoven, Ravel, and Villa-Lobos as well as original compositions by Barrera. A wine reception will follow the recital to which everyone is cordially invited. $25 Advance tickets are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Barrera.

articles.text: Thomas Horn and Tom Hanks in Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close On September 11, 2001, four commercial airliners were hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists. Two crashed into the twin towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and one was brought down in rural Shanksville, Pennsylvania, by the extraordinary will of the onboard passengers. Known simply as 9/11, it is a day that will forever be remembered and memorialized. The moving and heartfelt film Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close opens with what has become an iconic image of 9/11: the falling man. We bear witness to an individual dropping some 106 stories through the air, unable, we assume, to escape a consuming fire and so chooses this unimaginable final outcome. Another image captured in the film, one that will forever be with us, is the scene of a brick wall. It’s only been a few days since the Twin Towers collapsed. In the dark of night the camera slowly moves from right to left, revealing countless photographs of the missing, along with hand-written messages, many a desperate plea to call home. At the foot of the wall are lighted candles and bouquets of flowers. In essence, the wall is a heartbreaking memorial to those who will likely never return, but we fear are lost forever amid the rubble and steel that now lies where the towers once stood. But there is more to this haunting and extraordinary film, one that tells the story of a nine-yearold boy, Oskar Schell (Thomas Horn), who lost his father on what he refers to as “the worst day.” School had let out early on Tuesday, September 11, for reasons that are initially unclear to Oskar. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, September 9, 2026 The Musical Gourmet Art needs nuance By Joseph Gold Where would the world be without nuance? Truly great art has nuance. That is one of the important ingredients. Picture a field of grass. It is green. But no two blades of grass have the same hue of green. Music used to require nuance. Now, thanks to pop music’s obsession with the electrical amplification, nuance has been relegated to the dictionary. It simply has ceased to exist. How sad. The reality of this was driven home to me in two pops-type concerts last week. A word of explanation is needed here. Many years ago, I knew one of the important Spanish dipThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet lomats of the 20th century. He was the Duke of Baena, and even though I knew him very well I always referred to him as “Your Excellency.” The Duke’s diplomacy was one of his strong points. One time he had a heated meeting with Generalissimo Franco. Diplomacy probably saved him from execution. I need his advice now on how to answer my opinion of pop music. One famous musician of the past responded by saying: “I like some of it very much.” The two concerts I attended were Tom Rigney’s fiddle concert with his ensemble known as Flambeau, and a concert entitled “Paris in Piedmont” presented by SonoMusette. The music was worlds apart, but the concerts shared many things in common. Each ensemble was thoroughly professional. They love to perform. It was most enjoyable to see their seamless timing as they moved from one musical selection to another. The mature audience was appreciative and enthusiastic from the outset. It is very gratifying to see things like this. But there was one drawback. Both concerts were so loud that the music was deafening. The volume was artificially created by artificial amplification not artistic ability. As I said before, the audience loved everything. It didn’t matter that they were becoming deaf. They loved it all. I, however, value my hearing and decided to depart. The music was still audible through closed doors while I was across the street. José María Ruiz de Arana y Bauer(1893-1985) was known as the Duke of Baena. He was a respected diplomat from Spain and a knowledgeable musical historian. His Excellency was a longtime friend of mine, and taught me the art of diplomacy. articles.text: High above Napa Valley, on the rugged slopes of Pritchard Hill, Chappellet Winery occupies a place that is both physically and historically distinctive. Founded by Donn and Molly Chappellet in 1967, the family winery was one of the pioneers of Napa Valley’s modern wine era and helped establish mountain vineyards as a source of some of California’s most distinguished Cabernet Sauvignon. Donn Chappellet came to winemaking with an ambitious goal: to produce wines that could stand alongside the great First Growths of Bordeaux. After selling his interest in a successful food-service company, he and Molly moved their family to Pritchard Hill, then an isolated and largely unproven piece of Napa Valley. Following the advice of legendary winemaker André Tchelistcheff, they planted vines on the steep, rocky terrain. It was hardly an obvious choice. Pritchard Hill is considerably warmer and more rugged than much of the valley floor, with elevations at the Chappellet estate ranging from about 800 to 1,800 feet. But those difficult conditions turned out to be an advantage. The thin, well-drained soils and varied elevations and exposures naturally limit vine vigor and produce small quantities of intensely flavored grapes. Today the estate is divided into 48 vineyard blocks, each reflecting differences in soil, slope and exposure. Chappellet’s first commercial Cabernet Sauvignon appeared in 1969, establishing a tradition that remains at the heart of the winery. Although the original vineyards also included Chenin Blanc, Riesling, Chardonnay, Gamay and Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon gradually became the estate’s signature. The winery’s Pritchard Hill Cabernet Sauvignon is now its flagship wine, produced from the finest fruit on the mountain. The winery itself is almost as memorable as the wines. Built in 1968, the unusual pyramid-shaped structure was designed by artist Ed Moses and architect Dick Keith. Partly hidden among the trees, it has become one of Napa Valley’s most recognizable winery buildings. articles.text: A new program called Weavers is getting Piedmont seniors and teens together for social visits aiming at intergenerational connectivity. The Piedmont chapter of Weavers was tested from April to June with more than 40 participants, thanks to the help of founding members and Piedmont students Allyson Huynh and Luca Laforte. Gloria Lee of Oakland founded the program along with Kristin Richmond, the co-founder of Revolution Food. Lee, who lectures at Cal and Stanford, contacted Ken Li, the Crew Advisor of Piedmont Community Service Crew to get the program off the ground. She was then introduced to PHS juniors Huynh and Laforte, meeting in March to discuss the launch. Huynh started a Weavers’ Instagram to recruit teenagers to participate and went door to door in Piedmont to find interested seniors. Lee explained the origination of the program. “My sons Corbin and Asher really benefited from their friendship with an older neighbor, who first invited them over to bake cookies when they were four and six years old,” she said. Richmond’s son Caleb similarly started a window washing business and noticed that the older adults hiring him enjoyed chatting more than they cared about clean windows. The Piedmont program in the spring started with six weekly visits between “Weavers,” teens, and “Silvers” (seniors), and each visit lasted 60-90 minutes. “We think it’s really important that these relationships are mutually beneficial. We saw other well-meaning programs out there that treat one person in the relationship as someone who needs Olivia Tran (left), Mary Carter, Dick Carter, and Elly Mak. to be taken care of — but no one really wants to be the recipient of charity,” said Lee. Helping one another and building community is at the forefront of this work. “While Weavers are able to lend a hand to Silvers with technology support, gardening, and light organizing. I have found that people really do enjoy just talking. It makes a difference in your day just to have a good long conversation with someone,” said Huynh. In the Spring pilot of Piedmont and Oakland region, there were 23 Weavers and 23 Silvers. Piedmont’s Dick and Mary Carter signed up for the program because they like the concepts of intergeneration connection and people helping one another. They also joined because of the recommendation to join from longtime friend Ken Li. “Just meeting and talking with these delightful, energetic young people is delightful,” said Dick Carter. “I think older adults who don’t have much contact and communications with teenagers would especially benefit and enjoy the program. However, everyone can benefit from having more contact with people who are different from them.” Carter also spoke of a reaffirmation that the future is in good hands after the meetings, a comment echoed by many of the Silvers participating. “Intergenerational community to me feels like everyone, regardless of age, having positive relationships,” said Huynh. “It feels like everyone coming together and being friends, making memories, and having fun. Having this kind of community is super important because really, everyone benefits.” “Weavers will have the opportunity not only to demonstrate their skills but also have those skills validated by an older adult with lots of life experience. One of the important things about this program is that both sides contribute and both sides benefit,” said Lee. All participants of the spring pilot signed up again for the fall sessions which begins this month. Teenagers and seniors who want to learn about the program can visit beaweaver.com or call 510-788-0260. Gael Pardi (left) and Asher Breeden. Nava Shaham (left) and Olivia Bailey. Co-founder Kris Richmond leads a focus group with Silvers (seniors) in Mill Valley, the site of the program’s second pilot.

articles.text: The Ghirardelli house and other stories on Highland and Bonita Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group drew 50 walkers and seven K-9 best friends to the Exedra for Part 2 of a walk they had enjoyed in early August. Mary Carter was back to lead, again drawing on her former Wildwood School Piedmont history lessons and Ann Swift’s 2007 Cottages and Castles – The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont for a second visit to historical, pre-1906 San Francisco Earthquake Piedmont homes. Swift’s book describes 173 of the city’s historic homes that qualified in 2007 as Piedmont Centennial Homes. August’s walk covered mostly Hillside Avenue; this one turned to Highland and Bonita. Mary started up Highland at 636, commonly known as “The Ghirardelli House,” one of the more noteworthy and beautiful homes in central Piedmont. George and Grace Howell built a Mission Style home there before 1903, then hired A.W. Smith to build a larger Tudor next door at 630 Highland on a lot they owned. In 1905 they sold 636 to Joseph and Ellen (Ellie) Ghirardelli, the son and daughter-inlaw of Domenico Ghirardelli, the Italian-trained chocolatier who emigrated from Genoa to Uruguay in 1838, came north for the Gold Rush, and founded his chocolate company where Ghirardelli Square stands today. Joseph, born in 1852, was the third of the Ghirardellis’ eight children. He worked in the family business and was in Santa Cruz when the 1906 earthquake struck. With no transportation available back to the East Bay, he set out on foot and died of a heart attack on the way. He never lived in the Highland Avenue house, which was then being remodeled from Mission Style to the Colonial Revival we see today. Ellie and their two daughters moved in once the work was finished. Back up Highland, the group passed 1900 Oakland Avenue — “The Rackliffe House,” built in 1899 with captivating witch’s cap turrets — and, across the street, the turreted Queen Anne at 225 Highland. John and Annie Hendry sold lots there to Maggie Perry in 1897; she built the house in 1898 and rented to the Hendrys, who eventually bought it from her. A 1910 proposal to line the street with retail stores set off a battle among the neighbors, and the widening that followed in 1911 claimed Annie’s front garden. She had the house put on rollers and moved with a significant setback so that her garden would never again be violated. At Highland’s corner with Moraga Avenue stands 7 Highland, built in 1907 by Frank C. Havens’ Piedmont Development Company to showcase homes and sell lots in Piedmont. Current homeowner Patty Edmonds came out to tell the walkers her family’s history with it: her mother and stepfather lived there 55 years until their passings, and Patty and her husband, Art, moved in later. She said the couple recently noticed a bulge around the front entrance and discovered the wire support for the stucco exterior had fully deteriorated after 120 years. It has been replaced, and the exterior will be painted soon to complete the project. Down Moraga and up Bonita, the walkers noted 24 Bonita, built in 1904 with deep eaves and brown shingles, and 42 Bonita, built in 1905 — a “hybrid house,” Mary said, originally wood-sided Colonial Revival until brown shingles added sometime after 1926 gave it a Craftsman look. Its owner, spotting half a hundred visitors outside, came out to see what was going on; the words “Wednesday Walkers” explained everything. He provided a little more information about the home but declined to be identified for this report. Farther along, 112 Bonita is a “twin house” to a Hillside home built in 1905. The Queen Anne “Berkenfeld House” at 227 Bonita has rooftop gargoyles, spindle work posts, corbels, and window panels. Its initial owner was one of the original Piedmont volunteer firefighters, who helped save a house at 116 Hillside — and possibly the block — during Among those participating were Moya Robinson with K-9 best friend Petunia, Albert Chen, Bill Ahern, Juliane Jacqueline, Kristin Howard, Audrey Sung, Matt Truesdell, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Rich Harms, Matt Gerhardt, Judy Love, Debbie Powell, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Cathy Laymon, Peggy Shultz, Noemi Alvarado, Vicki Trimbach, Pat Nicholas, Jim Kuo, Brian Hamlin, Denny McGee, Mary Ann Barnes, Greg Keller, Claudine Bach, Caskey Weston, Melba Yee, Chuck Oraftik, Rick Eigenbrode, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis, Sherry Jacobs, Mary Carter, Charlene Louie, Mary Henderson, Alan Jolly, Sanghi Wagner, Dan Sedonis, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Pat Keller, Bern Schild, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Christine Cumbelich with K-9 best friend Kobe, Anne Gritzer, Iris Chavarria, Al Chen with K-9 best friend Sherlock, and Eli Messinger walking with them for the first time.

Back up Highland, the group passed 1900 Oakland Avenue — “The Rackliffe House,” built in 1899 with captivating witch’s cap turrets — and, across the street, the turreted Queen Anne at 225 Highland. John and Annie Hendry sold lots there to Maggie Perry in 1897; she built the house in 1898 and rented to the Hendrys, who eventually bought it from her. A 1910 proposal to line the street with retail stores set off a battle among the neighbors, and the widening that followed in 1911 claimed Annie’s front garden. She had the house put on rollers and moved with a significant setback so that her garden would never again be violated. At Highland’s corner with Moraga Avenue stands 7 Highland, built in 1907 by Frank C. Havens’ Piedmont Development Company to showcase homes and sell lots in Piedmont. Current homeowner Patty Edmonds came out to tell the walkers her family’s history with it: her mother and stepfather lived there 55 years until their passings, and Patty and her husband, Art, moved in later. She said the couple recently noticed a bulge around the front entrance and discovered the wire support for the stucco exterior had fully deteriorated after 120 years. It has been replaced, and the exterior will be painted soon to complete the project. Down Moraga and up Bonita, the walkers noted 24 Bonita, built in 1904 with deep eaves and brown shingles, and 42 Bonita, built in 1905 — a “hybrid house,” Mary said, originally wood-sided Colonial Revival until brown shingles added sometime after 1926 gave it a Craftsman look. Its owner, spotting half a hundred visitors outside, came out to see what was going on; the words “Wednesday Walkers” explained everything. He provided a little more information about the home but declined to be identified for this report. Farther along, 112 Bonita is a “twin house” to a Hillside home built in 1905. The Queen Anne “Berkenfeld House” at 227 Bonita has rooftop gargoyles, spindle work posts, corbels, and window panels. Its initial owner was one of the original Piedmont volunteer firefighters, who helped save a house at 116 Hillside — and possibly the block — during See Wednesday Walkers on page 27 Mary Carter talking to the walkers Patty Edmonds and Mary Carter in front of Patty’s Home. articles.text: Gary Laymon, 68, of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully on July 24, 2026 after a nearly two-year journey with cancer. He was a cherished husband, father, son, brother, neighbor, colleague, and friend and he will be deeply missed. Gary was born in 1958 to Rose and Maurice Laymon in Indianapolis, Indiana. They moved to the Bay Area, where his younger sister, Nancy, was born in 1961. The young family lived between Mount Tamalpais and Mount Diablo, eventually settling in Danville. The Laymons were involved in their local church, and Gary loved going to the youth group. He also enjoyed singing in the church choir, bowling, playing golf, and doing yard work when he wasn’t pulling goofy pranks with his friends. He graduated from Monte Vista High School in 1976, and began pursuing a degree in Landscape Architecture at Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo that fall. After graduating, Gary landed a job with Guzzardo & Associates, a landscape architecture firm in San Francisco, where he would spend the next 46 years. He began attending First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley in the ’80s, meeting many dear friends and was involved in several fellowship groups. Through a young adult group, he met Cathy Ives, who invited him to a party marking the anniversary of the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. His world was rocked as through some blessed misread signals each believed the other to be flirting, and suddenly Gary saw his friend in a new light. They were together ever since the “Great Misunderstanding,” marrying October 3rd, 1992, and welcoming Emily in 1996, Claire in 1999, and Elissa in 2002. Gary was a devoted father, known for his silliness, humor, and sense of adventure. He shared with his daughters his love of the ocean, music, gardens, art, bike riding, and travel creating countless memories along the way. As a young family, the Laymons enjoyed bike rides in wine country, hikes in the East Bay Hills, annual trips to Half Moon Bay’s pumpkin patches, Disneyland trips, summer musicals at Woodminster theaters, sports games, innumerable dance recitals, and summers with extended family at Mount Hermon, where Gary had gone as a child. As the girls grew older, the family traveled together to France, Spain, and Italy, went wine tasting and bike riding, toured an excessive number of gardens and art museums, and took thousands upon thousands of photos. In 2000, Gary became partner and owner at The Guzzardo Partnership with his long-term colleague Paul Lettieri. Gary was passionate about landscape design and loved working with clients to bring projects to life. He also enjoyed mentoring and teaching colleagues who were newer to the profession. Any drive in the car with Gary inevitably included him pointing out the many, many projects he had worked on over the years. In his free time, Gary painted with acrylics, moving through phases of vineyards, palm trees, scenes from his travels, Gary with his paintings at the Piedmont Art Walk Piedmont resident Gary Laymon died on July 24, 2026, at age 68. surfboards and abstract pieces inspired by his favorite jazz compositions. He loved sharing his art, displaying it at church and participating in the Piedmont Art Walk over several years. Gary’s faith was integral to his life. He started the day with Bible study and prayer. He saw needs and felt led to help. He was known for being kind, humble, gentle, grateful and generous. He was involved in several projects at church and led work groups at CityTeam Oakland, an organization near and dear to his heart. Mostly, Gary loved the routine of the life he loved: commuting to work in SF by bike and ferry, church on Sunday with Cathy by his side and being the last to leave the sanctuary, never having chatted with quite enough people; drinking Peet’s coffee every morning from a cup he painted when the kids were young at Color Me Mine; creating immersive scenes from scripture in his garage-turned-studio space with his paint brush; marveling at the miracle of streaming music on Spotify; calling out “sunset alert!” in the house when the view was too stunning to miss; working hard in the yard, always wanting to make things more beautiful. It was never enough to marvel at something alone. Gary wanted to share his awe, share his vision, and share the beautiful things he created to the fullest extent possible. Gary is survived by his wife, Cathy Laymon of Piedmont; his daughters, Emily West (Nick) of San Diego, Claire Laymon of Piedmont, Elissa Laymon of San Francisco; his mother, Rose Laymon, of Walnut Creek, and his sister, Nancy Laymon, of Chico. He was preceded in death by his father, Maurice Laymon. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made in Gary’s memory to CityTeam Oakland. Gary with his family (from l to r) Nick, Emily, Cathy, Gary, Claire, Elissa
articles.title: Remembering Gary Laymon: Creating Beauty, Sharing Joy

articles.text: Abby graduated in 2020 from Piedmont High School and in 2025 from the University of Glasgow with a major in sociology. Abby was living and working in Scotland. She died July 26, 2026 in a scuba diving accident. Abby loved the ocean and its sea life. She also loved her friends, geocaching, music, travel and reading books. She had a great sense of humor and a joy for living. Abby is and will be sorely missed by her parents Faye Beverett and Charlie Wheeler. She is survived by uncles, aunts-in-law and cousins. If you wish to honor Abby’s memory, please consider a donation to a Scottish marine sanctuary: Seawilding: https://www. seawilding.org/, or COAST – Community of Arran Seabed Trust https://www.arrancoast.com/about/.
articles.title: Abigail (Abby) Wheeler

articles.text: James Richard Saunders, Jr., known as Jim to family and friends and “Pops” to his grandchildren, passed away peacefully at his home in Piedmont, California on July 11, 2026, surrounded by family. He was 82 years old. Jim was born on August 5, 1943, in Omaha, Nebraska. He grew up in Menlo Park, California, where he attended Menlo-Atherton High School. He went on to graduate from Johns Hopkins University before earning his medical degree from the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. While at Menlo-Atherton, Jim met Lynn, who would become his wife and lifelong partner. They were married for 59 years and built a life together while raising their three children and, in later years, enjoying the company of their six grandchildren, all of whom live within a mile. Jim practiced internal medicine for more than 40 years, spending the majority of his career with Oakland Medical Group. He took great pride in the lasting relationships he built with his patients, many of whom remained with him throughout his career. Medicine was more than a profession to Jim; it was a passion he cared deeply about and approached with dedication, compassion, and integrity. Outside of medicine, Jim had a lifelong love of the outdoors and stayed active through running, cycling, and hiking. He was a devoted Oakland sports fan and always knew the latest scores. Whether following the A’s, RaidJames Richard Saunders passed away peacefully on July 11, 2026. He was 82 years old. ers, or Warriors, he enjoyed keeping up with his teams through every season. Jim was also well known for his quick wit and sense of humor. Jim is survived by his devoted wife, Lynn; his son, Vince Saunders and his wife, Michelle, and their children, Henry and Charlie; his son, Jamie Saunders and his wife, Teebie, and their children, George and Jane; and his daughter, Ashley Stevanovic and her husband, Andreja, and their children, Luka and Nicholas. He was preceded in death by his parents, James and Marion Saunders, and his sister, Joanne. Jim will be remembered as a dedicated physician, a loyal friend, and a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His family will miss his humor, his steady presence, and the many ways he quietly showed his love over the years. In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the charity of your choice in Jim’s memory.
articles.title: James Richard Saunders, Jr., MD

In 2000, Gary became partner and owner at The Guzzardo Partnership with his long-term colleague Paul Lettieri. Gary was passionate about landscape design and loved working with clients to bring projects to life. He also enjoyed mentoring and teaching colleagues who were newer to the profession. Any drive in the car with Gary inevitably included him pointing out the many, many projects he had worked on over the years. In his free time, Gary painted with acrylics, moving through phases of vineyards, palm trees, scenes from his travels, Gary with his paintings at the Piedmont Art Walk Piedmont resident Gary Laymon died on July 24, 2026, at age 68. surfboards and abstract pieces inspired by his favorite jazz compositions. He loved sharing his art, displaying it at church and participating in the Piedmont Art Walk over several years. Gary’s faith was integral to his life. He started the day with Bible study and prayer. He saw needs and felt led to help. He was known for being kind, humble, gentle, grateful and generous. He was involved in several projects at church and led work groups at CityTeam Oakland, an organization near and dear to his heart. Mostly, Gary loved the routine of the life he loved: commuting to work in SF by bike and ferry, church on Sunday with Cathy by his side and being the last to leave the sanctuary, never having chatted with quite enough people; drinking Peet’s coffee every morning from a cup he painted when the kids were young at Color Me Mine; creating immersive scenes from scripture in his garage-turned-studio space with his paint brush; marveling at the miracle of streaming music on Spotify; calling out “sunset alert!” in the house when the view was too stunning to miss; working hard in the yard, always wanting to make things more beautiful. It was never enough to marvel at something alone. Gary wanted to share his awe, share his vision, and share the beautiful things he created to the fullest extent possible. Gary is survived by his wife, Cathy Laymon of Piedmont; his daughters, Emily West (Nick) of San Diego, Claire Laymon of Piedmont, Elissa Laymon of San Francisco; his mother, Rose Laymon, of Walnut Creek, and his sister, Nancy Laymon, of Chico. He was preceded in death by his father, Maurice Laymon. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made in Gary’s memory to CityTeam Oakland. Abby was living and working in Scotland. She died July 26, 2026 in a scuba diving accident. Abby loved the ocean and its sea life. She also loved her friends, geocaching, music, travel and reading books. She had a great sense of humor and a joy for living. Abby is and will be sorely missed by her parents Faye Beverett and Charlie Wheeler. She is survived by uncles, aunts-in-law and cousins. James Richard Saunders, Jr., MD James Richard Saunders, Jr., known as Jim to family and friends and “Pops” to his grandchildren, passed away peacefully at his home in Piedmont, California on July 11, 2026, surrounded by family. He was 82 years old. Jim was born on August 5, 1943, in Omaha, Nebraska. He grew up in Menlo Park, California, where he attended Menlo-Atherton High School. He went on to graduate from Johns Hopkins University before earning his medical degree from the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. While at Menlo-Atherton, Jim met Lynn, who would become his wife and lifelong partner. They were married for 59 years and built a life together while raising their three children and, in later years, enjoying the company of their six grandchildren, all of whom live within a mile. Jim practiced internal medicine for more than 40 years, spending the majority of his career with Oakland Medical Group. He took great pride in the lasting relationships he built with his patients, many of whom remained with him throughout his career. Medicine was more than a profession to Jim; it was a passion he cared deeply about and approached with dedication, compassion, and integrity. Outside of medicine, Jim had a lifelong love of the outdoors and stayed active through running, cycling, and hiking. He was a devoted Oakland sports fan and always knew the latest scores. Whether following the A’s, RaidJames Richard Saunders passed away peacefully on July 11, 2026. He was 82 years old. ers, or Warriors, he enjoyed keeping up with his teams through every season. Jim was also well known for his quick wit and sense of humor. Jim is survived by his devoted wife, Lynn; his son, Vince Saunders and his wife, Michelle, and their children, Henry and Charlie; his son, Jamie Saunders and his wife, Teebie, and their children, George and Jane; and his daughter, Ashley Stevanovic and her husband, Andreja, and their children, Luka and Nicholas. He was preceded in death by his parents, James and Marion Saunders, and his sister, Joanne. Jim will be remembered as a dedicated physician, a loyal friend, and a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His family will miss his humor, his steady presence, and the many ways he quietly showed his love over the years. Loud & Close Continued from page 16 Hanks), a call from the 105th floor of one of the towers where he has been attending a meeting. Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, observing the ceremony from a distance, his denial palpable. And so a year passes, and finally, reluctantly, Oskar enters his father’s den and begins to look through his things. And when taking down a box, he knocks a blue vase off the shelf, breaking it. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” And so attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book, and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept a secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt, but a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera takes their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can, to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous and at times fraught search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And, ultimately, why? Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close. Directed by Stephen Daldry. Starring Thomas Horn, Tom Hanks, Sandra Bullock, Max von Sydow. 2 hrs, 9 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Preserving Community and Sustainability: Responsibly meeting state housing mandates and future community needs while ensuring Piedmont remains a true home, not just a city. This requires investing thoughtfully in our infrastructure and planning Adam Hundt First, our community’s old homes are expensive to live in due to energy inefficiency. Although the median home value has risen, so has the Consumer Price Index (CPI). If elected, I will work to reduce monthly bills and increase home values through access to affordable electrification and energy efficiency programs. I will also work to lower the upfront cost of home upgrades that have a positive return on investment and improve our health by reducing exposure to gas. Second, Piedmont would benefit from new homes. In compliance with state mandate, the Council’s actions on housing have created opportunities for new development. New housing also increases diversity and grows the tax base. Third, to raise revenue, Piedmont should explore the possibility of introducing new small businesses and support ballot measure GG, which will provide funding for Piedmont’s essential services. This includes police, fire, and emergency medical response, park maintenance, and infrastructure. If elected, I will focus on these issues. Increasing home values and lowering living expenses will be my top priority. That said, I will Tom Ramsey Incumbent My view of the top three issues should always align with my neighbors because I don’t approach my role as a councilmember with any personal agenda. In my last four years on council, I know Piedmonters are focused on community safety, fiscal responsibility, and maintaining the beauty of our town. I tackle fiscal responsibility first because a solid financial foundation is required to deliver on any other priority. Currently, inflation and rising labor costs outpace our revenues. Since over 60% of city funding comes from a property tax base that doesn’t automatically keep pace, we must manage budgets meticulously. I am committed to working collaboratively with city staff, my neighbors, and colleagues to prioritize capital projects and essential facilities, steer our new community pool operations toward full cost-recovery, and consider new revenue sources and more creative funding. Our new emergency dispatch center serves as a perfect model. Completed on time and on budget, partially funded with federal grants, it stands as a seamless improvement to our city infrastructure — while directly enhancing community safety by maintaining rapid response times and allowing our operators to work more efficiently. I want to bring this blend of smart fiscal stewardship and community safety to all future projects in Piedmont. Nancy Bostrom No Response 62 63 64 65 66 67 READ IT IN THE POST ACROSS 51. They will continue to lead the classroom in its new home, bringing continuity and stability to the transition. The new location offers a light-filled, calm and inviting setting for the school’s play-based approach to early childhood learning. PPS remains the only licensed preschool of its kind in the area built around social-emotional learning as a core part of its curriculum. A day at Piedmont Play School Each day at PPS blends structured and child-led play, giving children space to explore, build friendships, and develop independence alongside caring, familiar teachers. PPS’s play-based, mixedage curriculum is intentionally designed to strengthen the social and emotional skills that matter most as children grow. Mixedage classes encourage younger children to learn from older peers and give older children opportunities to lead and mentor — building confidence, empathy, and communication skills. Educators increasingly point to strong social-emotional foundations as a key predictor of success when children enter TK and Kindergarten, where academic and behavioral expectations have never been higher. PPS’s approach is designed to help prepare children for that transition both academically and emotionally. Teacher Michelle Ritchie has been with Piedmont Play School since 2013. A Co-Op model built for busy families PPS operates as a light co-op by design. Families are asked to contribute in small, manageable ways rather than large time commitments, making it possible for working parents to still be present and engaged in their child’s classroom experience. Many parents describe their volunteer hours as some of the most rewarding time they spend with their kids. For PPS President & CEO June Groboske, the co-op model is about more than the preschool. It’s the starting point for a much longer relationship between families and their community. “Our co-op model is where a lifelong connection to our school community begins,” said Groboske. “PPS parents discover early on what meaningful school involvement looks like. Working side by side with teachers and other parents gives families a firsthand appreciation for the school, classroom, and community dynamics, helping parents learn how to best support teachers and students alike. That strong foundation naturally carries forward — so many of our PPS parents go on to serve as parent board officers, school committee chairs, and active community leaders throughout PUSD.” With this move to Clarewood Drive, PPS parents, alumni, and teachers preserved a philosophy of early childhood education, a group of beloved teachers, and a place where families can be genuinely involved in their children’s earliest school experiences. The comfort in knowing the school will carry on, paired with genuine enthusiasm for what’s ahead, has echoed throughout the PPS community as the school settles into its new space. To learn more about PPS, please visit piedmontplayschool. org. Follow along: @piedmontplayschoolca on Instagram. Students enter Piedmont Play School at age 2 usually with enrollment designed as a two-year experience preparing them for Transitional Kindergarten or Kindergarten. articles.text: As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. The exercise provides step-by-step instructions and discussion prompts in a short video that families, housemates, and neighbors can use to transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. The short exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect: • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of • • • evacuation A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfirePlan. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. The at-home evacuation exercise is one part of the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. Last year, the department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/ Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving them a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide year-round public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. The department also recently led the development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a 5-year roadmap that identifies steps the city can take to reduce the effects of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.
articles.title: Fire Dept. asks residents to complete wildfire evacuation plans

The at-home evacuation exercise is one part of the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. Last year, the department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/ Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving them a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide year-round public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. The department also recently led the development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a 5-year roadmap that identifies steps the city can take to reduce the effects of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole. articles.text: Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of each candidate to help residents make informed voting decisions. For this year’s race, the Post will send one question to candidates running for City Council every week until election day. The School Board election was cancelled due to a lack of candidates to challenge the incumbents. This week, only City Council candidates were sent a question. The five city council candidates vying for three open seats were sent the question on Monday, August 24, and were asked to reply with a 200-word response. Week 1 Question: Who are you, why are you running, and name one thing you have worked on in Piedmont that voters can look up? Tom Ramsey Incumbent My wife and I drove from the Midwest to California in an old Volkswagen bus on our honeymoon. Luckily, that thing made it to the Bay Area, and eventually we moved to Piedmont in 1997, where we raised our two daughters. Professionally, I’ve been a licensed California architect since 1990, and now I work for a national real estate advisory firm. I am running for re-election because experienced leadership makes a difference. My focus remains on rigorous fiscal oversight, maintaining balanced budgets, and prioritizing public safety. I am committed to smart planning—navigating state housing mandates while preserving Piedmont’s historic charm. During my seven years on the Planning Commission, I worked with the team that completed a comprehensive update to our city’s Design Guidelines. That document is actively shaping how we preserve our neighborhood integrity today. On the City Council, we updated those guidelines to stay ahead of state mandates and code changes, providing design guardrails to manage growth responsibly. Since you elected me to the City Council in November 2022, it has been an honor to work alongside you to keep Piedmont safe, vibrant, and connected. I would be grateful for your vote to continue serving our community.

articles.text: The Beach School Dads Club hosted its 21st annual Pancake Breakfast on Sunday, August 30 in grand proportion and style. Thousands of pancakes cooked up by the dads fueled a morning of non-stop games, music and fun as an army of kids and parents arrived early and stayed late. Beach Dads’ Club President Rob Doebelin brought even more carnival games this year to celebrate the 21st birthday. A 20-foot inflatable slide was put to early and frequent use by kids of all ages. The morning included music by DJ Criddy (Chris White) accompanied by Angelo Moore, a founding member and frontman of the band Fishbone. Moore serenaded the crowd on saxophone while walking among the revelers. He created his own lyrics about endless pancakes and the carnival-like atmosphere of the event. The sun wasn’t visible until 11 a.m. but that didn’t keep kids from lining up for the popular
articles.title: 21st Beach Dads’ Pancake Breakfast goes big

articles.text: Four more years for Thomasson and Medhekar Veteran school board members Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar are running unopposed in the November 3 General Election as incumbent candidates. Without anyone running in opposition, the city has decided to suspend the election. Medhekar and Thomasson will be awarded with renewed four year terms on the board. The nomination period was open from July 13, and nomination documents were due by August 7. Previous superintendent Jennifer Hawn announced her departure from the district in the middle of that period on July 25. The two incumbents filed their nomination papers on July 20 and will be elected to four more years without any opposition. Thomasson has already spent a year as board president and Medhekar is currently the board president. This current roster of the board with Max Roman, Susy Struble and Michael Malione will remain consistent for the next two years. articles.text: We, the teacher librarians of PUSD, are reaching out for community support regarding the recent elimination of funding for COMPASS, a resource that provides California students and educators with equitable access to vetted online research and curriculum resources – including encyclopedias, databases, journals, and educational content. Simply put, we cannot imagine doing our work of teaching media literacy and research skills without this program. The COMPASS program has provided our K-12 students with high-quality research and media resources for almost a decade. We need lots of voices to speak out in favor of restoring this important funding! Click here (https://www.saveschoollibrarians.org/compass2026) to send Governor Newsom an email voicing your support! articles.text: Six-year-old Pepita also goes by the nickname “Miss Cat America” and it’s easy to see why. This graceful brown tabby somehow looks perfectly poised at every angle — even while launching herself through the air after a wand toy! This clever, enthusiastic huntress loves leaping after toys, and her stealthy ambushes are adorably serious. After playtime, she’s happy to take a catnap, or follow the people in her life from room to room like a faithful sidekick. Pepita plays hard and feels her feelings deeply. She can get startled and overwhelmed easily. While daily anxiety medication helps her stay relaxed (and is easily mixed into her meals) she will also rely on her adopter to read her body language and guide her back to a calm state. This affectionate, curious Adopt Pepita through Cat Town. girl is looking for a quiet, adult-only home where she can be the one and only cat — and a person who will appreciate everything that makes her unmistakably Pepita. Are you ready for a sweet and loyal companion? Let us know! Pepita is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: Millie is a sweet mixed breed pup with a gentle personality and a lot of love to give. This 8-year-old is looking for a home for her golden years. Millie enjoys exploring her surroundings and takes a thoughtful approach to meeting new dogs and people. She would be most comfortable as the only dog in the home where she can soak up all the attention and continue to build confidence. This 40-pound girl would make a wonderful companion for someone looking for a calm, affectionate dog. Millie is ready for a loving home where she can enjoy her golden years with those who will appreciate her sweet spirit. If you’re looking for a loyal, grateful companion, Millie may be the match for you! Millie is a sweet mixed breed pup with a gentle personality. Submit your adoption questionnaire online at Oakland Animal Services and you will be contacted by her foster who can tell you much more about Millie and arrange a meet-andgreet with her if you like. For more information about adoption or fostering, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: In a planned turf replacement, the company FieldTurf, located in Montreal, arrived at Hampton Park and began removing the existing well-worn artificial turf on Monday, August 24, on the first phase of replacing the field. The field will be closed to the public throughout the duration of the project, which is estimated to take three weeks. The rest of the park will remain open. The City’s artificial fields are serviced twice a year through a contract with FieldTurf’s maintenance staff. During their most recent visit, the turf maintenance staff reported substantial tears in the path between second and third bases. There is concern for the players’ safety if the field is not replaced. FieldTurf noted that the quality of the turf blades has degenerated to the point that it’s challenging for the turf to hold the sand and cork infill. Artificial turf has an approximate life expectancy of 8-10 years. Hampton Field’s turf field was installed in 2016, marking 10 years with the turf in place. The field’s new design has been coordinated with the consultant Lloyd Engineering to ensure the changes meet the Recreation Department’s needs. “We understand the bases are high-wear zones; those areas have been designed so that if, in 2-3 years, they need to be replaced, the carpet can be cut, removed, and replaced in a less than awkward scenario,” said Park Director Nancy Kent. FieldTurf provided the turf for Witter Field and the Linda Beach Field and will be replacing the Hampton Field turf. The contract was awarded to the company for $171,824. FieldTurf is using its machinery to dig up the old turf field at Hampton They’re using rolling equipment to guide the dug-up turf to a neat pile. FieldTurf is rolling up the turf to make removal easier.
articles.title: Hampton turf replacement project underway

articles.text: New pool schedules in Piedmont will expand lap swim hours throughout the week. The updated fall schedule increases both hours and available lanes, with at least five lanes available until 6 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays and until 7 p.m. on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Thursdays. Lap swim at the competition pool is available: Monday 6 a.m. - 1 p.m.; 2 p.m. - 7 p.m. Tuesday 6 a.m. - 1 p.m.; 2 p.m. - 7 p.m. Wednesday 6 a.m. - 1 p.m.; 2 p.m. - 6 p.m. Thursday 6 a.m. - 1 p.m.; 2 p.m. - 7 p.m. Friday 6 a.m. - 1 p.m.; 2 p.m. - 6 p.m. Saturday 7 a.m. - 9 a.m.; 11 a.m. - 8 p.m. Sunday 7 a.m. - 6 p.m. Altogether, the expansion increases lap swim hours at the Competition Pool by more than 10%, bringing the total baseline availability to 80 hours per week. Swimmers should confirm schedules online before visiting. Schedules may shift further as the city seeks to optimize pool availability. High school sports (water polo) will impact competition pool availability on some days. The first year of operations at the Community Pool is a period of learning and adjustment. The pool staff is continuously monitoring use patterns.

articles.text: Chief Teaching & Learning Officer, Exploratorium A few weeks into the new school year, families are settling into familiar rhythms. We’re hearing from teachers, adjusting to new schedules, and getting a sense for what kids will be learning this year. We might be feeling excited, nervous, or a little of both. It can be daunting to know the best way to support kids and teens as they head back to school. As they get older, we may have less visibility into the classroom, less familiarity with the content they’re learning, or hear less directly from them. But what if a new school year was also an invitation for us, as parents and caregivers, to become learners again? Imagine a young child asks you why the sky is blue. You might already know something about how gases in the air scatter sunlight, or you might quickly look it up on your phone. But consider what happens when you instead say, “I’m not sure. What do you think?” That simple, curious response can open a completely different conversation. Instead of moving quickly from question to answer, we can linger in the space between. We can make a guess, look more closely, test an idea, change our minds, and figure something out together. Meeting questions with curiosity and an intention to understand is a form of inquiry-based learning, and it doesn’t require a science lab or a lesson plan. It can happen when a child wonders why the moon is visible during the day, why some songs get stuck in their head, or how an algorithm decides what they see online. Ask another question. Make a prediction. Look for evidence together. Let one question lead to another. Older kids may be less likely to wonder aloud, but they still have BIG questions about themselves, others, and the world around them. Create space to hear what’s on their minds, and meet their questions with that same spirit of curiosity. Invite them into your questions, too, even if the immediate response is an eye roll! At the Exploratorium, this kind of curiosity-driven, inquiry-based learning is at the center of everything we do. This summer, my team welcomed dozens of teachers from across California to spend several weeks learning and experimenting with us. We work with educators in all 58 California counties, giving them opportunities to step out of their role as experts and become learners again. They investigate things, follow their own questions, try ideas that don’t work, and bring that spirit of inquiry back to their classrooms. We like to imagine a world in which all adults are lifelong learners. Our kids are growing up with instant access to the most expansive set of information in history. Classrooms, technology, and education are – and should be – changing because of this. Curiosity, creativity, and connection remain essential. It will be the humans in the next generation who keep asking questions who will lead us forward. So this school year, support the kids in your life to be inquisitive by showing them what that looks like. Let them hear you say, “I’ve never thought about that before.” Wonder out loud. Be willing to try something and get it wrong. Our kids have plenty to learn this year. So do we. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life. A family gets up close and curious at the Exploratorium’s Skin Scope exhibit.
articles.title: Back to school, back to inquiry

The Animal Ambassadors program lets kids get up close and personal with their favorite animal ambassadors on the outdoor campus. Featuring 11,000 games, kids and adults will have a great time and get educated on video game programming as well. Play thousands of games on original hardware and check out one-of-a-kind pieces of gaming history. MADE is open W-Su, and into the evening 9:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday nights for nocturnal gaming fun. Oakland Museum of California Museumca.org 1000 Oak Street, Oakland; 318-8400 The OMCA’s “Nature Playspace” is geared for kids ages 2 to 5, along with their families and caregivers. Children under 12 years of age can visit the Museum for free as long as they are accompanied by an adult over 18 years old. OMCA is open Wednesday - Sunday 11:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. Friday Nights at OMCA have started back up every Friday, for free live music in a family friendly environment and Off the Grid food trucks. On Friday, September 4, come dance to Pher, the three-time Grammy-winning collaborator, perform his contemporary R&B, jazz, and soul with heartfelt storytelling. Oakland Zoo Oaklandzoo.org 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland; 632-9525 The Oakland Zoo is open every day from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Our own local zoo sets the standard for world-class animal care in captivity. Guests will marvel at the many species taking residence at the zoo, while learning about conservation in the wild. Take the gondola to the amazing boardwalk of the California Trail, for viewings of wolves, buffalo and bears. Amusement rides, including a brand new electric train, are open as well. Make sure to buy tickets in advance for timed-entry.

articles.text: The Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center’s fall fundraising campaign is off to a strong start thanks to a generous $30,000 gift from Dress Best for Less (DBFL). “The emotional well-being of teenagers plays a key role in their success and happiness, and DBFL is proud to support the Wellness Center in achieving this goal,” said DBFL President Nagisa Yamamoto. The donation will fully offset the cost of a Wellness Center counselor, helping keep mental health and wellness services free and accessible to Piedmont students.
