articles.text: 30+ Kidlit Creators join this year’s event More than 30 of the Bay Area’s kidlit (children’s literature) creators will fill Children’s Fairyland with storytelling magic on Saturday, September 19 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The park celebrates books, book lovers, and the people who bring books to life. Librarian and host of Reading Rainbow, Mychal Threets, and this year’s Caldecott Medal winner, Cátia Chien, bring the annual Children’s Book Festival into a class of its own. The festival brings together young readers, writers, and artists for a joyful day of storytelling, meet-and-greets, book signings, and interactive programming, all included with general admission. Speakers at the 2026 Children’s Book Festival: • Cátia Chien, illustrator, 2026 Caldecott Medal Winner and a Golden Kite Award winner. • Joanna Ho, author, recipient of the Asian/Pacific American Award for Children’s Literature Honor, a Golden Kite Award, and more. • Cindy Derby, illustrator, and recipient of a 2021 Caldecott Honor and Golden Kite Award. • Randy Ribay, author, co-winner of the Michael L. Printz Award and winner of the Asian Pacific American Library Association Medal. • Mychal Threets, beloved librarian, author, mental health activist/advocate, and host of revived children’s TV show Reading Rainbow. • Youth Writers Workshop led by author Natasha Tripplett. Guests will have the opportunity to participate in hands-on An attendee finishes a comic book strip at cartoonist Jen De Oliveira’s table at 2024’s Children’s Book Festival. activities hosted by the Oakland Public Library. The festival also spotlights Fairyland’s Youth Writers’ Workshop, where young authors (ages 8–12) will share their original stories in an anthology, presenting alongside their mentor, local author and educator, Natasha Tripplett. Independent local bookseller Books on B will be on site for guests to browse and purchase books. “Books are just the beginning,” said Vicky Chen, senior director of education and community. “Books open the door to creativity, empathy, connection, belonging, and so much more. We’re thrilled to celebrate the stories that bring us together, build bridges across communities, and spark the imagination of every child who walks through our Fairy Gates.” Throughout the park, families can meet authors and illustrators, hear stories read aloud by the creators themselves, watch illustration demos, and shop for books from the Books on B pop-up shop. The event will be emceed by beloved educator Peter Limata, host of “Storytime with Mr. Limata.” Additional community programming includes hands-on activities from local literacy partners, art-making stations, and family literacy resources. “There’s nothing quite like watching a child fall in love with books,” said Angela Moffett, Fairyland’s librarian and a member of the Caldecott Award Selection Committee. “The Children’s Book Festival gives young readers a chance to meet the people behind the pages, discover new favorites, and feel the joy of being a part of a community that values literacy and the art of storytelling. For children who love books, and all lovers of children’s literature, the book festival at Fairyland is truly the best day of the year.” Tickets and more information are available on Fairyland’s website: https://fairyland.org/ book-festival/.
articles.title: Children’s Fairyland welcomes 9th Annual Children’s Book Festival

articles.text: On Wednesday, August 26, a coalition of states reached a $17 billion settlement with Meta in a Child Safety Trial. The states of California, New Jersey, Kentucky, and Colorado alleged the tech giant designed its apps (Instagram and Facebook) to be addictive to kids and knew about the risks those platforms posed, but hid that information from the public. The states accused Meta of designing algorithms that encourage compulsive use with features such as infinite scroll, photo filters, and the “like” button. The states claim the company knew the platforms were addictive to kids, but publicly downplayed the risks. The states also accuse Meta of violating the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, by collecting data from users under 13 without parental consent. According to the State of California Department of Justice, the settlement requires Meta to pay up to $17 billion in penalties to the states over 10 years and to make significant changes to how its platforms operate to make them safer for minors. If approved by a judge, a few of these changes would include: • A default daily time limit of two hours for users under 18, which can only be lifted by a parent. • An enhanced mechanism for teens to report potentially harmful content and a requirement that Meta respond to 90% of those reports within six hours. • A ban on displaying likes or reactions to users under 18. • An option for users under 18 to have a non-personalized feed, meaning a feed that doesn’t use an algorithm to target them with content aimed to keep them endlessly scrolling. • A commitment from Meta to maintain, review, and improve existing teen content safety measures. California will receive up to $2.1 billion if the settlement is approved, according to a statement from Attorney General Rob Bonta. Meta will set aside some of the settlement money to address mental health harm to kids, while the California Legislature and governor will decide how to spend a portion. “We have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of difference for children and their families,” said Bonta. The Post spoke with two high school students to understand their feelings about being directly targeted by social media companies. “It’s honestly not surprising hearing about the Meta safety violations,” said PHS student Julia Stokes. “The effect of social media is definitely noticeable in our generation; it’s become integrated into every aspect of our lives.” “It feels terrifying in a sense to know they are trying to look me up in the media, and it was created specifically for my generation. I feel manipulated and scared for what else these large companies can do with mass amounts of power,” added PHS student Ayla Blanford. Both said they would like to see the government target other social media companies that are likely committing the same acts as Meta, but quieter. They hope that the federal government provides further restrictions on social media to protect the younger generation as they enter the online space earlier and earlier in their lives.
articles.title: States get $17 billion settlement with Meta in Child Safety Trial

articles.text: Piedmont High won its second Highlander Volleyball Tournament at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, August 29, going 5-0 with straight-set wins over St. Helena, The Bay School, HeadRoyce, St. Patrick, and Elsinore. Although all of those wins have come from best-of-three style tournament games instead of the typical best-of-five format, the Highlanders have already matched last year’s win total when it finished with a 9-12 record. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont got its first win of the season in a 7-0 victory over University. Piedmont High’s flag football team captured its first win of the season on Tuesday, August 25 when visiting University in San Francisco. It was a defensive 7-0 victory. They followed up two days later with a 41-0 loss at Witter Field to Las Lomas, which was last year’s No. 1 seed in the Division 1 North Coast Section bracket. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 1-3 to start its season. Of the four games, three of their opponents featured in last year’s NCS postseason, including Acalanes reaching the D2 championship and Las Lomas being D1 semifinalists as the top seed. “We’re learning that we can catch it and go long. We know there are better possibilities in the future,” said coach Beth Black. Against University, Piedmont got it done with defense. Their game-winning score came early in the fourth quarter when Nea Mafi intercepted a pass near the Red Devils’ end zone. It led to quarterback Ellie Elmquist hitting Agatha Filha-Gama for a short-yardage touchdown. Four games into the season Black has her eyes on Cea’naiya Alexander, who had an interception and 62 receiving yards against Las Lomas. “Naiya was phenomenal on all sides. If that grows with the other players, then the network continues. She’s bringing everything she has to practice and to the game, our goal was to connect with her on long passes. One of the big things to sharpen up overall is the energy level and to get a message across that they are just as fast as the girls on Las Lomas. We have to show that speed,” Black said. PHS now looks ahead to the start of its Western Alameda County Conference schedule, while also hosting the first “Battle of the Bay” Highlander Showcase on Saturday, September 5. Four games will be played at Witter Field when one East Bay team will face off against a school from San Francisco. Piedmont faces St. Ignatius at 10:30 a.m. and Oakland Tech plays George Washington of SF at 9:00 a.m., Bishop O’Dowd plays University at 12:00 p.m., and Berkeley plays Lowell at 1:30 p.m. 7-0 over University Piedmont got its touchdown when Mafi intercepted a pass near University’s goal line in the early minutes of the fourth quarter. Down around the one, Ellie Elmquist found Filha-Gama for a short-yardage touchdown reception. It was the team’s first offensive touchdown of the season. Final stats: Elmquist had 56 passing yards, 63 rushing yards, and one touchdown pass. Alexander had one reception for eight yards and 12 rushing yards. Mafi had 59 rushing yards, three tackles, one sack, one interception, and three pass defenses. Skye Prata-Baack had four receptions for 36 yards, and one tackle. Zayda Weber had one reception for five yards. Maddie Lee had seven tackles and two sacks. Cory Minor had 12 tackles, Kate Tong had six, Bea Nackley had five, Sophia Puckett had four, and Carmela Dilauro had three. Cea’naiya Alexander reels in a long pass against Las Lomas. She also had an interception.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross-country team returns to toe the line on Saturday, September 5 at the St. Mary’s Invitational at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. The girls team is back after reaching last year’s Division 4 CIF State Championship, placing 18th of 25 teams. It marked the first time the school has sent a full girls squad since 2019. Only two members of last year’s girls team departed with the Class of 2026, Skylar Best and Cora Chun. The squad is set to bring back several key runners: Leighton Mand, Viviane Oesterer, Amalia Gray, Cora Brozowski-Schrader, Nikita Gorelik, and Kelsey Coleman – providing the Highlanders a solid group of returning runners. Camille Hauser and Madeleine Ewen are also making their mark. “They should be a strong team, but the caveat is always everyone staying injury free,” said coach Dresden Schulte-Sasse (right) is emerging as a leader for the boys’ cross country team. Cora Brozowski-Schrader has been named a captain for the girls’ cross country team. Photos by Jenni Tsoi-Best Leighton Mand returns as a four-year starter. She was Piedmont’s leadrunner at the 2025 D4 CIF State Championship. Steve Zirkelbach. “The team is led by Leighton, Amalia, and Cora, with Nikita, Viviane, and Kelsey also returning. Camille Hauser and Madeleine Ewen also round out our top-eight and we’re very excited about them.” Mand is a four-year varsity starter. She was the Post’s 2025 Sophomore of the Year and our honorable mention for 2024 Freshman of the Year. She was the lead runner at State for Piedmont, finishing 96th of 205 runners with a time of 19:52.3 on the 5,000 meter course. She was a key runner throughout last year’s campaign and earned the Post’s Athlete of the Month in September, October, and November. She battled an injury during the spring track season but looks to be recovered to start the fall. “She and Amalia had some recurring pain in her feet, so we continue to monitor those. They are getting close to 100 percent, it’s coming around and we’ll have to see what happens this weekend to determine where everyone is,” Zirkelbach said. Zirkelbach also named Brozowski-Schrader a team captain. Coleman burst onto the scene as a freshman in 2025. “Cora has looked strong, she’s looking really good in training. She’s a captain with Leighton. Kelsey is back with us and she is right up there in our top-seven. It’s hard to determine just how everything will shake out; it’s a close group,” Zirkelbach said. The boys’ team will have to compete without senior Sebastien Swain who suffered a broken toe. One runner who is looking ahead for a big season is junior Dresden Schulte-Sasse, who reached the track NCS Bayshore Area Championship last spring in the 1600 and 3200. “Seb unfortunately had an accident and broke a toe this summer. Dresden is looking like possibly our strongest runner. He’s looking really good. He got a lot stronger over the summer and is very interested in trying to be at the top of the heap,” Zirkelbach said. Other returning runners include junior Aaron Bennett and senior Alex Schleuning. Both reached the NCS Bayshore 3200 in track. Schulte-Sasse was 14th of 24, and Schleuning was 19th, and Bennett 20th. “We’re looking to Aaron and Alex,” Zirkelbach said. “Aaron is looking strong; he’s very focused and is very committed. We had a 3200 time trial, and Dresden came out on top with Alex and Aaron behind him.” Also emerging for the boys are Dylan Wallway, Luca LaForte, and Jack Shim as the team’s possible best-six. “We have Dylan returning as a sophomore and Luca LaForte will be emerging this season. Jack Shim is looking pretty strong and I’m excited to see what he can do,” Zirkelbach said.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team got its season started in impressive fashion with a pair of victories on back-to-back days. They hosted Acalanes to a 7-0 sweep on Wednesday, August 26 and followed up with a close 4-3 win over Marin Catholic the next day. “The season has begun and we are off to a good start. After playing two scrimmages last week, we were warmed up and won both our matches,” coach Jim Landes said. It was a terrific week for No. 1 singles starter, sophomore Ella Ruthven, who beat two opponents to whom she lost last year. Ruthven was the Post’s honorable mention for our 2026 Freshman of the Year award. Ruthven won in three-sets over Acalanes’ Elisabetta Sokolova, 6-1, 5-7, 11-9, and also beat Marin Catholic’s Christiane Zuber in straight sets, 6-2, 6-1. “In the second set [against Sokolova], I lost some of my consistency and she started making more of her forehand. When it came to the tiebreak, I just tried to stay consistent and target her backhand,” Ruthven said after beating Sokolova. Last year, Ruthven lost in three sets to Sokolova and in two sets to Zuber. Playing with consistency Ruthven got the better of them this time around. “This helps with my confidence and keeping a constant energy. I want to stay confident with my aggressiveness on the court,” Ruthven said. The clinching match on Wednesday against the Dons came from senior captain Faith Chin at No. 2 singles. articles.text: Piedmont looks to regroup after a disappointing loss to Napa in the season opener. It was a rough start to the season for Piedmont High’s football team, losing 28-7 to Napa at Witter Field on Friday, August 28. PHS scored the game’s final touchdown with 8:39 left in the fourth quarter. “Our youth showed up at the worst time. But it’s a lesson; we’re a young team and didn’t have our best week of practice. It’s all about how we push each other in practice,” coach Jordan Seiden said. “Finishing” will be the word of the week for Seiden as Piedmont looks ahead toward hosting St. Mary’s on Friday, September 4. PHS had chances to capitalize in short-yardage situations, but struggled to get the ball across the line or hold off Napa on the defensive side. They got down to the two-yard line after a big catch and run by Rehan Mumtaz midway through the first quarter, but failed to score. In the second quarter, a fumbled snap on 3rd-and-1 led to a turnover on downs. They got to the Napa 29 early in the third quarter, but the drive stalled after that. Defensively, PHS couldn’t stop the run as Napa gained 314 of its yards on the ground. Napa gashed Piedmont with a 60-yard touchdown in the first quarter, and a 30-yard touchdown in the final seconds of the second quarter in a 4th-and-3 situation. They also converted two fourth downs on their way to their fourth score. “We’ve got to finish. It’s a part of being young and not understanding the importance of an inch in a game of inches. The message is to finish and they are going to get tired of hearing that word. We got down the field multiple times and only came away with one touchdown,” Seiden said. The St. Mary’s Panthers are coming off a 41-6 loss to Diablo Valley and finished 1-9 last season, perhaps giving the Highlanders a chance to get back on track. Game Recap Napa struck first on a fiveplay, 61 yard drive that capped off with a six-yard touchdown carry. On Piedmont’s ensuing drive, Mumtaz broke a 32 yard run on a screen down to the two-yard line, but things died after that. Staff Photos A loss of five yards on 1st-andGoal led to a false start on second down. A three-yard loss made things bleaker before quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster ran to the 10. An incompletion on fourth down turned it over with 6:07 left, leading to a four-play drive that resulted in a 60-yard touchdown run after nearly two minutes— making it 14-0. PHS drove to the Napa 47 on its next possession, but two sacks resulted in a punt on 4th-and-20. At the end of the second quarter, Napa scored on a 30-yard carry as time expired on an end-around in a 4th-and-3 situation. In the third, Piedmont started the quarter by driving 31 yards to the Napa 29, but three incompletions ended things. Napa scored its final touchdown with 10:30 left in the fourth quarter on a 12-play, 45 yard drive that featured two fourth-down conversions. John Bunje recovered a fumble with 8:52 left at the Napa 12 to help out the offense. Cyrus Emanuelson completed a pass to Owen Curran down to the one, leading to Colby Hong punching the ball into the end zone. Final stats: Cha-Foster had 128 passing yards. Emanuelson had 57 passing yards, completing five of six passes. George Saunders had five receptions for 123 yards. Mumtaz had three receptions for 47 yards, to go along with 24 rushing yards. Bunje had a fumble recovery, Curran had a pass defense. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1 overall) hosts St. Mary’s at Witter Field on Friday, September 4 at 7:00 p.m. George Saunders turns a reception up field in the fourth quarter. Jonah Cha-Foster breaks the pocket on a quarterback run.

articles.text: The Piedmont Highlanders JV football team suffered a loss in their season opener to the Napa Grizzlies, falling 22-6 on Friday, August 28. Piedmont’s offensive line gave quarterbacks Ernie Hildreth and Gio López strong protection throughout the game, allowing both quarterbacks to finish without any interceptions. The Highlanders were led by team captains, Ernie Hildreth (1), Alex Perez (69), Lev Kuluva (18), and Gio López (25) On the opening kickoff, Gael Fierro sent the ball deep, and Lev Kuluva (18) burst downfield through Napa’s blockers to the 17-yard line, forcing Napa to begin its first drive 83 yards from the end zone. Throughout most of the first half, Piedmont’s defense kept Napa off the scoreboard. Piedmont right tackle Ozem Fitzgerald came up with a huge fourthdown quarterback sack in the red zone, while captain Ernie Hildreth relayed defensive calls from Coach Assadi and helped lead the Highlanders to several key stops. With just two seconds remaining in the half, Napa connected on a controversial touchdown pass near the edge of the end zone. The play left Piedmont players and spectators questioning if the receiver had reached the end zone, but the touchdown stood, giving Napa an 8-0 lead heading into halftime. Coming out of halftime, Piedmont’s Will Dietrick returned the opening kickoff 17 yards, setting up the Highlanders’ offense at their own 40-yard line. Despite battling an injury suffered earlier in the game, Dietrick continued to fight through the pain and contribute for the Highlanders. The Grizzlies forced a turnover on Piedmont’s next possession, but the Highlanders’ defense made them work for every yard. Despite several key stops, Napa eventually broke through for a touchdown to extend its lead. Another kick return late in the third by Will Dietrick gave the Highlanders possession at their own 23-yard line. Despite the long field ahead, quarterback Gio López handed the ball off several times to running back Joseph Logwood, who helped move Piedmont downfield and into field position at Napa’s 38-yard line. Quarterback Gio López then fired a deep pass to Lev Kuluva, who made a diving 14-yard reception to carry the Highlanders’ momentum to Napa’s 24-yard line. Keeping the momentum alive, López dropped another dime, this time lofting a fade to Gael Fierro, who rose above the defender and caught a 24-yard touchdown pass to put the Highlanders on the board for the first time. Although the Highlanders failed on a 2-point conversion attempt, they were still in the game. With hope still alive, the Highlanders attempted to win the ball back and mount one final scoring drive. However, Napa regained possession and added one final touchdown at the end of the game, sealing the 22-6 loss for Piedmont. Key players include Gio López, who helped lead the Highlanders’ offense and threw Piedmont’s lone touchdown pass, and Gael Fierro, who led the team in receptions. Ernie Hildreth and Will Dietrick each recorded eight tackles to lead the defense. Next week Piedmont returns home to face Gunn High School of Palo Alto at 4:00 p.m. at Witter Field. The team looks to bounce back and get its first win of the season. Lev Kuluva (18) Photos by Graham Smith Gio López (25) Gael Fierro (15)

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) opens its 2026-27 season with a theatrical adaptation of Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, bringing the 1959 spy thriller to the Toni Rembe Theater beginning September 22. The production is adapted and directed by Emma Rice. Rice previously directed A.C.T.’s Brief Encounter and Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s The Wild Bride. Rice’s production uses seven performers, live music, movement and theatrical effects to tell the story of Roger Thornhill, an advertising executive who is mistaken for a Cold War spy and forced to flee across the country. The production features a 1950s-inspired soundtrack and a theatrical recreation of the film’s famous Mount Rushmore sequence. The cast includes Danny Collins as Thornhill, Evangeline Dickson as Mrs. Townsend and understudy, Patrycja Kujawska as Eve Kendall and others, Simon Oskarsson as Valerian and others, Katy Owen as the Professor and others, Bryony Pennington as Anna and others, and Karl Queensborough as Phillip Vandamm and others. Sam Archer will take over the role of Valerian and others beginning October 10. “What makes Emma Rice’s North by Northwest so exhilarating is that it isn’t trying to recreate Hitchcock’s film frame for frame,” said Andy Chan Donald, A.C.T.’s artistic producing director and acting artistic director. “Instead, it captures the wit, suspense, and cinematic scale of the original while embracing everything that makes live theater extraordinary.” “The result is a production that honors a beloved classic while becoming something entirely its own — a thrilling reminder that the stage can be every bit as breathtaking as the silver screen,” Donald added. The original North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant and Eva Marie Saint, follows Thornhill as he is pursued across the country after being mistaken for a government agent. Directed by Hitchcock and released in 1959, the film is widely regarded as one of the director’s major works. The show will run at A.C.T.’s Toni Rembe Theater from September 22 through October 18, with press night scheduled for September 23. Post-show conversations are scheduled for Sept. 29, Oct. 4 and Oct. 7. A tasting event is scheduled for Oct. 6, and PlayTime, an interactive theater workshop, will take place before the Oct. 17 matinee. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets. The cast of North By Northwest includes Danny Collins as Thornhill.
articles.title: A.C.T.’s North by Northwest opens Sept. 22

articles.text: Photo by Chris Hardy Danny Scheie, Benjamin Clark and Lyndsy Kail in White Chip. Marin Theatre opens its 60th season with the Bay Area premiere of The White Chip, a play about alcoholism and recovery, running now through September 20. Written by Sean Daniels and directed by Marin Theatre Executive Artistic Director Lance Gardner, the play follows Steven, a successful theater director whose career and personal life are increasingly affected by his struggle with alcohol addiction. After his drinking disrupts his relationships and professional life, Steven begins the process of recovery by accepting Alcoholics Anonymous’ white chip, which is given to people marking 24 hours of sobriety or expressing a desire to stop drinking. The play draws on Daniels’ own experiences with addiction and recovery. Gardner, who will mark 20 years of sobriety in 2027, said the production has personal significance for him. “The White Chip isn’t my story, but the decision to produce it is a very personal one,” Gardner said in a press release. “2027 will mark 20 years of sobriety for me. Making the choice to abstain from drugs and alcohol opened the doors that led me to the helm of Marin Theatre and probably saved my life.” Gardner said the play addresses the stigma surrounding addiction and recovery through its combination of comedy and drama. “The White Chip confronts the stigma of addiction and recovery head on with a hilarious and heart wrenching story which has the power to enlighten and inspire audiences whether or not they’ve experienced this kind of thing firsthand,” he said. The White Chip premiered at Merrimack Repertory Theatre before productions at New York’s 59E59 Theater and MCC Theater. It has since been produced by theaters around the country. Benjamin Clark will make his Marin Theatre debut as Steven. His regional theater credits include Asolo Repertory Theatre, Barrington Stage Company, Round House Theatre, Olney Theatre Center and Everyman Theatre. Danny Scheie and Lyndsy Kail round out the cast, portraying people in Steven’s life. Scheie previously appeared at Marin Theatre in The Cherry Orchard and Lady in the Dark and directed the theater’s productions of Splittin’ the Raft and The Pavilion. Kail has performed with California Shakespeare Theater, Center Repertory Company and San Jose Stage Company, among others. The White Chip will be performed at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. in Mill Valley. Subscriptions for Marin Theatre’s 2026-27 season are available through www.MarinTheatre.org or by calling 415-388-5208. Music Lessons │ Band Instrument Rentals │ Sales and Repairs

Sam Archer will take over the role of Valerian and others beginning October 10. “What makes Emma Rice’s North by Northwest so exhilarating is that it isn’t trying to recreate Hitchcock’s film frame for frame,” said Andy Chan Donald, A.C.T.’s artistic producing director and acting artistic director. “Instead, it captures the wit, suspense, and cinematic scale of the original while embracing everything that makes live theater extraordinary.” “The result is a production that honors a beloved classic while becoming something entirely its own — a thrilling reminder that the stage can be every bit as breathtaking as the silver screen,” Donald added. The original North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant and Eva Marie Saint, follows Thornhill as he is pursued across the country after being mistaken for a government agent. Directed by Hitchcock and released in 1959, the film is widely regarded as one of the director’s major works. The show will run at A.C.T.’s Toni Rembe Theater from September 22 through October 18, with press night scheduled for September 23. Post-show conversations are scheduled for Sept. 29, Oct. 4 and Oct. 7. A tasting event is scheduled for Oct. 6, and PlayTime, an interactive theater workshop, will take place before the Oct. 17 matinee. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ to purchase tickets. Photo by Chris Hardy Danny Scheie, Benjamin Clark and Lyndsy Kail in White Chip. By Allyson Aleksey Marin Theatre opens its 60th season with the Bay Area premiere of The White Chip, a play about alcoholism and recovery, running now through September 20. Written by Sean Daniels and directed by Marin Theatre Executive Artistic Director Lance Gardner, the play follows Steven, a successful theater director whose career and personal life are increasingly affected by his struggle with alcohol addiction. After his drinking disrupts his relationships and professional life, Steven begins the process of recovery by accepting Alcoholics Anonymous’ white chip, which is given to people marking 24 hours of sobriety or expressing a desire to stop drinking. The play draws on Daniels’ own experiences with addiction and recovery. Gardner, who will mark 20 years of sobriety in 2027, said the production has personal significance for him. “The White Chip isn’t my story, but the decision to produce it is a very personal one,” Gardner said in a press release. “2027 will mark 20 years of sobriety for me. Making the choice to abstain from drugs and alcohol opened the doors that led me to the helm of Marin Theatre and probably saved my life.” Gardner said the play addresses the stigma surrounding addiction and recovery through its combination of comedy and drama. “The White Chip confronts the stigma of addiction and recovery head on with a hilarious and heart wrenching story which has the power to enlighten and inspire audiences whether or not they’ve experienced this kind of thing firsthand,” he said. The White Chip premiered at Merrimack Repertory Theatre before productions at New York’s 59E59 Theater and MCC Theater. It has since been produced by theaters around the country. Benjamin Clark will make his Marin Theatre debut as Steven. His regional theater credits include Asolo Repertory Theatre, Barrington Stage Company, Round House Theatre, Olney Theatre Center and Everyman Theatre. Danny Scheie and Lyndsy Kail round out the cast, portraying people in Steven’s life. Scheie previously appeared at Marin Theatre in The Cherry Orchard and Lady in the Dark and directed the theater’s productions of Splittin’ the Raft and The Pavilion. Kail has performed with California Shakespeare Theater, Center Repertory Company and San Jose Stage Company, among others. The White Chip will be performed at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. in Mill Valley. Subscriptions for Marin Theatre’s 2026-27 season are available through www.MarinTheatre.org or by calling 415-388-5208. The cast of North By Northwest includes Danny Collins as Thornhill. articles.text: Branford Marsalis returns to San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium with jazz vocalist Dianne Reeves for a week devoted to the music of John Coltrane in honor of the centennial of his birth. The Branford Marsalis Quartet and Dianne Reeves will release a tribute album which revisits John Coltrane’s seminal 1963 collaboration with Johnny Hartman. Marsalis’ quartet includes bassist Eric Revis, Joey Calderazzo on piano and Justin Faulkner on drums. Marsalis is a highly regarded composer and tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known jazz musicians. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughan Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras including those in Chicago, Detroit, Düsseldorf and North Carolina as well as the New York Philharmonic. Reeves is known for her wide-ranging voice, improvisational skill and ability to move between jazz, R&B, gospel, Latin and pop. She has won five Grammy Awards, including three consecutive awards for Best Jazz Vocal Album and another for her work on the soundtrack to George Clooney’s 2005 film “Good Night, and Good Luck.” She has performed with artists and ensembles including Wynton Marsalis and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and the Berlin Philharmonic. In 2002, she became the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s first creative chair for jazz. To purchase tickets, visit www.sfjazz.org, or call the box office at 415-788-7353. Performance times vary. articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden’s outdoor summer concert series Sunset Sessions continues Thursday, September 17 with a performance by The Real John Gary. The Real John Gary is an East Bay alt-country one-man-band project of Drew Clinard. Clinard performs creative covers of Bob Dylan, Gillian Welch, Lucinda Williams, Neil Young, John Prine and more country, folk and Americana. The series features free live music on the garden plaza along with extended evening nursery hours. Admission to the plaza and concerts is free while paid admission is required to access the garden. Garden members receive free admission year-round. Food and beverages, including craft beer from Headlands Brewing, will be available for purchase. Mi Casita Mexican Cuisine will be serving food and sweet treats. Located in Walnut Creek, the Ruth Bancroft Garden is one of the nation’s best-known dry gardens and was the first garden preserved by the Garden Conservancy. Founded by horticulturist Ruth Bancroft, the 3.5-acre botanical garden features more than 2,000 species of drought-tolerant plants from California and arid regions around the world, including agaves, aloes, cacti, succulents, yuccas and proteas. The garden’s collection highlights plants adapted to dry climates and has helped showcase water-wise gardening practices in California’s Mediterranean climate. The nonprofit garden continues to serve as a resource for visitors interested in drought-tolerant landscaping and conservation. The concert begins at 5:30 p.m. and ends at 7:30 p.m. For more information, visit https:// w w w. r u t h b a n c r of t g a r d e n . org/sunset-sessions-concertseries-page/. The Real John Gary

articles.text: The Flower Piano festival will return to the San Francisco Botanical Garden September 10 through 20, bringing live performances and public piano installations to the 55-acre garden. The annual event features 12 grand and baby grand pianos placed throughout the garden, where visitors can attend scheduled performances, watch community groups perform or play the instruments during designated open play sessions. Flower Piano was created in 2017 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Fortissimo and Dean Mermell in collaboration with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The festival has since become an annual event at the botanical garden. This year’s lineup includes daily performances by La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9, and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, whose repertoire blends hip-hop, jazz and classical music. The San Francisco Ballet School is also scheduled to perform in this year’s festival. The school’s performances will give audiences an opportunity to see ballet students perform in an outdoor setting as part of a festival that combines music and community programming. The 2026 festival also includes an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, featuring seating, food and beverages, and evening performances. During open play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels to use. Attendees are encouraged to bring picnic blankets as seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and tickets, is available at https://gggp.org/flowerpiano. The beloved Flower Piano festival returns to Golden Gate Park this month.

articles.text: Ongoing through September 20 Book Club Art Show Gallery Hours This somewhat eclectic group of artists, The Book Club at Van Kleef’s, who first met at Café Van Kleef in Oakland in 2005, presents a show called For the Love of Art which includes works by about nineteen artist members and friends, and will hold Open Gallery Hours from 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. on most Saturdays and Sundays from August 15 through September 20 (except August 22 & 30). The show is free and open to all! Saturday, September 5, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Piano Trio Please note this event is on Saturday, not the usual Sunday! To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative (story line) that ties each tune on the program into the theme for the month. For Autumn Leaves, for example, many of the tunes, such as Autumn Leaves (1947), September in the Rain (1937), Autumn In New York (1934), have an obvious connection to the autumn theme. Other tunes such as I’ve Got the World on A String (1932) and Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams (1931) do not have such an obvious connection. The narrative ties these tunes and all the tunes on the show into the autumn theme. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Saturday late afternoon in our Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Advance tickets are $26.44 at https://www.ticketsignup.io/ Leaves, or pay $30 at the door, cash or check ONLY. Sunday, September 6, 4:00 p.m. SonoMusette Concert SonoMusette’s long-awaited return to Piedmont Center for the Arts promises an evening that will transport the audience into the heart of Paris through the songs of Edith Piaf and other iconic performers of the period. This is more than a concert, it’s a voyage back in time to the cabarets and jazz clubs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where stories of love, loss, and life were sung with passion. With SonoMusette, every performance invites you to feel the pulse of Parisian life and to fall in love with these unforgettable songs all over again. Mimi Pirard ~ vocalist, Robert Lunceford ~ accordion, Jan Martinelli ~ piano, Tami Pallingston ~ upright bass, Kendrick Freeman ~ drum set. Advance tickets are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Pirard. Saturday, September 12, 6:30 p.m. Cuban Fusion Illustrated Book Talk Most people know the iconic voice of the Queen of Salsa, Celia Cruz, one of the world’s greatest ambassadors of Cuban music and culture, but what happened to Cuban music after successive waves of migration carried Cuban musicians, artists, and cultural producers across the globe? In this talk, Dr. Eva Silot Bravo examines how the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Eastern socialist bloc, and Cuba’s economic crisis of the ‘90s reshaped the trajectory of Cuban music. Drawing on the research behind Cuban Fusion: The Transnational Cuban Alternative Music Scene (Palgrave Macmillan, 2024), the presentation traces the evolution of trans-national Cuban jazz and fusion scenes over the past three decades, reshaping Cuban music into a truly global phenomenon. articles.text: Inspiration is elusive, to say the least. So, seeking wisdom, I asked my 11-year-old granddaughter to enlighten me. Miriam offered to write today’s article. “Hold your horses” after I said “I need your thoughts.” She thought a minute, and said that Dolly Parton was an inspiration. While that quality comes in many forms, it should be a positive breath and not a reaction to negativity. In these respects, Dolly Parton was the embodiment of the positive. Any negatives were handled with humor and diplomacy. Well… How about the good things she accomplished? As we all know, she died a few days ago at the age of 80. While rumors of ill health circulated, Dolly presented a positive picture of good health. She even took to social media saying: “I ain’t dead yet.” Despite the cancellation of concerts, she presented her fans a hopeful medical outlook. Miriam knows that I appreciate classical music. Do I like country music? I certainly do, and I am drawn to the older country music songs. Dolly Parton was a “country music star.” This is a small issue because Dolly Parton was a huge success. She had dignity and sincere musicality. How I wish the current crop of classical musicians had these qualities. In life, everyone experiences hurdles, which are necessary in our art. Dolly Parton had more than her share of hurdles to overcome. She experienced poverty and parental illiteracy in the beginning. This situation resulted in autobiographical songs which stress her love for family and beyond. These songs offer advice for life. Her song “Coat of Many Colors” is a perfect example of her underlying philosophy. Dolly Parton performing at the Grand Ole Opry, April 24, 2005. Dolly unified musical genius and human universality in music and in life.

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, September 2, 2026 The Musical Gourmet Dolly Parton could have been The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet a successful diplomat because she knew what to say, and what not to say, and often used appropriate humor to defuse a delicate situation. Religion was probably a major force in her life, but in application, religion was truly humanistic. As for politics, she kept these separate from publicity. I learned this the morning that she was able to draw in the warring factions of the Democrats and the Republicans. Born into poverty, she learned not to waste her money. Millions were given to best advantage many charities. She established a bird sanctuary, enabled universities and medical associations to do research, helped children in general and encouraged people to read by establishing a book foundation for young readers… As you can see, she also influenced others to be generous. The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame wanted to include her. She was very diplomatic in saying: “Thank you for the honor, but please do not include me. I am a country musician, not a rock ‘n’ roll roller.” Dolly Parton’s persona was flamboyant and at the same time dignified. I regard her as a musical genius with a generous humanity. articles.text: Most people spend their lives searching for connection. Whether it comes from family, friends, or strangers, the need to feel seen by someone is universal and fundamental. Rental Family, directed by Hikari, explores this through an unusual premise: a company in Tokyo, Japan that rents out actors to fill emotional roles in people’s lives. What begins as a hard to swallow idea gradually becomes a heartfelt story about grief, loneliness, and the relationships that The film follows Phillip Vanderploeg (Brendan Fraser), a struggling American actor living in Japan. With little success, Phillip’s agent instructs him to go to a job, but gives him no context for what it’s about. The job lands him at what he believes to be a performance in a real event, but to his surprise, it is not. It is revealed that the event has been arranged through Rental Family, a service that allows clients to experience moments, milestones, and more that they otherwise wouldn’t be able to have. After his first gig, Phillip is offered a position by the founder of the Rental Family agency, Shinji (Takehiro Hira). His first assignments challenge Phillip’s understanding Mari Yamamoto and Brendan Fraser in Rental Family of deception and authenticity. Aiko (Mari Yamamoto), a fellow co-worker and actor, helps him understand that what he is doing can still provide something necessary for the client, even if it’s fake. He joins Rental Family full-time, stepping into the lives of strangers who need emotional support they have been deprived of in the real world or can’t seem to find elsewhere. As Phillip continues taking on new roles, his understanding of success in life and as an actor begins to morph into something new. His agent eventually informs him that he has landed a role in a major television production, his long-awaited break. But the people he has met through Rental Family force him to question what success really means: the performances seen by millions, or the ones that work to subtly and quietly impact one single life. Aiko challenges his belief that authenticity and sincerity are always the same, reminding him that people still deserve comfort, even when it is paid for. Two relationships become central to Phillip’s journey. The first is Kikou Hasegawa (Akira Emoto), an aging actor losing his memory. The second is Mia Kawasaki (Shannon Gorman), a young girl whose mother hires Phillip to pose as her father. What begins as temporary work becomes deeply personal as Phillip grows attached to both 801 MAGNOLIA Avenue, piedmont 94611 The San Francisco Bay Area’s Ambassadors of French Chanson Featuring Parisian singer Mimi Pirard, SonoMusette authentically recreates the moody and evocative sound of the Paris music scene of the mid-20th Century. SonoMusette’s renditions of these timeless French classics provide a freshness and excitement that is contemporary, yet faithful to the spirit and tradition of the original artists. Inspired by the great performers of the era, such as Edith Piaf, Jacques Brel, Charles Trenet, and Django Reinhardt, and contemporary musicians such as Zaz and Patrick Bruel, SonoMusette brings French Chanson to the “moderne” era. pages.text: Wednesday, September 2, 2026 17 MOVIE REVIEW Rental Family — a heartfelt story Toddler Storytime By Larissa Edel Most people spend their lives searching for connection. Whether it comes from family, friends, or strangers, the need to feel seen by someone is universal and fundamental. Rental Family, directed by Hikari, explores this through an unusual premise: a company in Tokyo, Japan that rents out actors to fill emotional roles in people’s lives. What begins as a hard to swallow idea gradually becomes a heartfelt story about grief, loneliness, and the relationships that matter most. The film follows Phillip Vanderploeg (Brendan Fraser), a struggling American actor living in Japan. With little success, Phillip’s agent instructs him to go to a job, but gives him no context for what it’s about. The job lands him at what he believes to be a performance in a real event, but to his surprise, it is not. It is revealed that the event has been arranged through Rental Family, a service that allows clients to experience moments, milestones, and more that they otherwise wouldn’t be able to have. After his first gig, Phillip is offered a position by the founder of the Rental Family agency, Shinji (Takehiro Hira). His first assignments challenge Phillip’s understanding Tuesday, September 8 — 10:15 – 10:30 a.m. Songs, active rhymes and stories especially for ages 18 months to 3 years. Aiko (Mari Yamamoto), a fellow co-worker and actor, helps him understand that what he is doing can still provide something necessary for the client, even if it’s fake. He joins Rental Family full-time, stepping into the lives of strangers who need emotional support they have been deprived of in the real world or can’t seem to find elsewhere. As Phillip continues taking on new roles, his understanding of success in life and as an actor begins to morph into something new. His agent eventually informs him that he has landed a role in a major television production, his long-awaited break. But the people he has met through Rental Family force him to question what success really means: the performances seen by millions, or the ones that work to subtly and quietly impact one single life. Aiko challenges his belief that authenticity and sincerity are always the same, reminding him that people still deserve comfort, even when it is paid for. Two relationships become central to Phillip’s journey. The first is Kikou Hasegawa (Akira Emoto), an aging actor losing his memory. The second is Mia Kawasaki (Shannon Gorman), a young girl whose mother hires Phillip to pose as her father. What begins as temporary work becomes deeply personal as Phillip grows attached to both PIEDMONT AVENUE BRANCH 80 Echo Avenue, Oakland, California 94611 Phone: (510) 597-5011 of them. The film, however, constantly reminds the viewer that these relationships have limits. Every role must end, thus creating quiet tension as Phillip grows closer to Kikou and Mia and the boundaries between performance and reality begin to blur. At its heart, Rental Family asks whether comfort loses meaning simply because it is fabricated instead of authentic. Phillip learns that kindness remains real even when it begins as a performance. The relationships may be temporary, but the emotions they create are not. In a world where loneliness is ever present, the film suggests that connection no matter how unexpected or unconventional is always worth pursuing. The film has also already earned significant recognition on the festival circuit, including Audience Awards at events such as the Middleburg Film Festival and the Chicago International Film Festival, as well as the Breakthrough Director Award for Hikari at Woodstock. articles.text: The voices of nearby students and the fragrance of local botanicals wafted through the air as the Walking on Wednesdays (WoW) group gathered at the Exedra for our weekly trek through Piedmont, a good turnout of 40 walkers and four K-9 best friends for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s latest walk. Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup and his canine companion, Kojak, led the walk. Jack’s goal was to shepherd the group down to Linda Park to meet Park and Project Manager Nancy Kent at the oak woodland there. Along the way he introduced the walkers to some of the fragrant plants in our urban landscapes. We all know the adage to “stop and smell the roses,” but Jack explained how their scent reaches our noses. A rose’s perfume is produced by specialized cells in the petals that manufacture volatile organic compounds, molecules that evaporate easily, which is why you can smell a rose from a distance. Roses use their scent to attract pollinators like bees and beetles, and it is strongest in the morning when they are most active. Jack then introduced us to one of his favorite fragrant garden plants, lemon verbena, and brought along a bag of leaves for us to squeeze and sniff. Gently crushed, the leaves release a distinctive citrus fragrance, similar to freshly grated lemon zest, from volatile oils stored in tiny glands. Some group members reported drinking lemon verbena tea, and someone had even tried lemon verbena ice cream, an elegant treat. Our olfactory senses on overdrive, the group headed down Park Commissioner, Jack Fischrup, and his canine companion, Kojak Nancy Kent at Linda Park Among those participating were Linda Linehan, Pat Nicholas, Matt Gerhardt, Peggy Shultz, Judy Love, Audrey Sung, Rick Eigenbrode, Sherry Jacobs, Nancy DeRoche, Brian Hamlin, Adrienne Hamlin, Lori Austin, Leilani Ching, Melba Yee, Stella Houston, Nancy Henn, Mary Carter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Mark Davis, Juliane Jacqueline, Marica Arthurs, Noemi Alvarado, Pat Keller, Nancy Kent, Joan Jung with K-9 best friend JT, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, Lisa Euphrat, Dave DeRoche, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Echa Schneider, Bern Shield, Greg Keller, Jeff Chew, Mike Henn, Moya Robinson, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friends Brie and Leica, and Dick Carter.

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, September 2, 2026 Features WEDNESDAY WALKERS - MAIN Walking on Wednesday Stop and smell the roses: Walking on Wednesday tours Piedmont’s fragrant plants By Lori Austin The voices of nearby students and the fragrance of local botanicals wafted through the air as the Walking on Wednesdays (WoW) group gathered at the Exedra for our weekly trek through Piedmont, a good turnout of 40 walkers and four K-9 best friends for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s latest walk. Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup and his canine companion, Kojak, led the walk. Jack’s goal was to shepherd the group down to Linda Park to meet Park and Project Manager Nancy Kent at the oak woodland there. Along the way he introduced the walkers to some of the fragrant plants in our urban landscapes. We all know the adage to “stop and smell the roses,” but Jack explained how their scent reaches our noses. A rose’s perfume is produced by specialized cells in the petals that manufacture volatile organic compounds, molecules that evaporate easily, which is why you can smell a rose from a distance. Roses use their scent to attract pollinators like bees and beetles, and it is strongest in the morning when they are most active. Jack then introduced us to one of his favorite fragrant garden plants, lemon verbena, and brought along a bag of leaves for us to squeeze and sniff. Gently crushed, the leaves release a distinctive citrus fragrance, similar to freshly grated lemon zest, from volatile oils stored in tiny glands. Some group members reported drinking lemon verbena tea, and someone had even tried lemon verbena ice cream, an elegant treat. Our olfactory senses on overdrive, the group headed down Park Commissioner, Jack Fischrup, and his canine companion, Kojak Nancy Kent at Linda Park Walking route Magnolia Avenue toward the Piedmont Police Department. Right outside the back door is a camphor tree, whose eucalyptus or menthol fragrance comes from the aromatic oils in its leaves, twigs and wood. Jack produced a bag of camphor leaves so that we could smell them for ourselves. The same oil turns up in muscle pain ointments, vapor rubs and medicated lip balms. The WoW members continued down Magnolia to the Piedmont Swim Club. The garden outside the main entrance is planted with California natives, including Cleveland sage, whose fragrance, one of the most powerful among the state’s native sages, combines sage, pine, camphor and a hint of spice. Many walkers rubbed their fingers on the leaves to release the aromatic oils, which also help make the foliage less attractive to herbivores. Our next fragrance stop was at the corner of Magnolia and Jerome avenues, where the front garden contained three types of lavender: English, French and Spanish. Rubbing a sprig breaks the tiny oil glands that cover the flowers, releasing a burst of aroma. Even after the plant dries the glands remain intact, which is why dried sachets can smell wonderful for years. Five fragrant plants under our noses already, the group continued down Magnolia to Grand Avenue, crossed the street and headed north to Linda Avenue, then turned left and walked up to meet Nancy Kent at Linda Park, which is gradually being restored to an oak woodland. Oak woodlands are one of the most distinctive natural features of Piedmont, a living connection to the landscape that existed here long before the city was developed. Nancy showed the walkers photographs from 1971 of a barren hillside with a few straggly oak trees that has become the oak woodland of Linda Park today. She explained that the slope, now a lush carpet of fescue grass, was hydro-seeded with four varieties of wildflowers, and neighbors have provided lots of California poppy seeds. In the spring the hill is a colorful mosaic of the different blooms. She asked that visitors give the understory plants a chance to establish themselves, walking gently on the grass or sitting on the benches provided. We left Linda Park and walked back down Linda and Grand, crossing the street at Ace Hardware to explore the bioswale at Grand and Fairview avenues, a landscaped channel that captures, slows and filters stormwater runoff from streets and parking lots. Completed in October 2025 to comply with Alameda County’s clean water program for Piedmont, it required the city to dig down 24 inches to the proper soil profile and plant vegetation that filters runoff before it flows into the Bay. articles.text: There are plenty of wineries in Napa Valley with impressive histories, but few can match the combination of family continuity, historic vineyards and a genuine sense of place found at Trefethen Family Vineyards. The Trefethen story began in 1968, when Eugene and Catherine Trefethen purchased a neglected property just north of the town of Napa. At the time, Napa Valley had fewer than 30 operating wineries, and the couple’s decision to invest in vineyards proved remarkably farsighted. Their purchase was tied to the establishment of the Napa Valley Agricultural Preserve, an effort that helped protect the valley from development and preserve its agricultural character. At the center of the property was an abandoned 19th-century winery originally known as Eshcol. Built in 1886, the handsome wooden structure was designed as a gravity-flow winery, with grapes entering at the upper level and wine moving downward through the building. The Trefethens painstakingly restored the structure, which today is regarded as the only surviving 19th-century wooden three-level gravity-flow winery in Napa Valley. The family’s first commercial wines appeared in 1973, made by Eugene and Catherine’s son John and his wife, Janet. Chardonnay quickly became one of the winery’s calling cards. The 1976 Trefethen Chardonnay received extraordinary international recognition when it was named “The Best Chardonnay in the World” at the 1979 Gault Millau Wine Olympics in Paris. What makes Trefethen parLorenzo Trefethen is part of the third generation of family to run the winery. ticularly interesting today is its commitment to estate-grown wine. The family’s main ranch encompasses about 400 acres of vineyards divided into 49 individual blocks, with soils ranging from deep valley-floor loam to rocky alluvial deposits. The vineyards lie entirely within the Oak Knoll District, one of Napa Valley’s coolest growing regions. Afternoon breezes and nighttime fog from San Pablo Bay help moderate temperatures, allowing grapes to ripen slowly while retaining natural acidity. That cool influence helps explain the characteristic Trefethen style: wines that emphasize balance, freshness and foodfriendly acidity rather than sheer power. Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon remain important, but the estate also grows Riesling, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Cabernet

Today the winery is in its third generation, with siblings Hailey and Lorenzo Trefethen helping guide the family business. Their challenge—and opportunity— is to preserve what has always made Trefethen distinctive while continuing to learn from the vineyards. Lorenzo, who was the host for our tasting, is knowledgeable about the winery’s history and culture and is passionate about keeping Trefethen at the highest level of quality. In an industry increasingly dominated by large corporate ownership, Trefethen remains something increasingly rare: a Napa Valley winery where the family name on the bottle is still the family name on the farm. • 2025 Trefethen Dry Riesling Trefethen has long been one of the rare Napa wineries that specialize in making Riesling and they have perfected the art. The dry Riesling is spicy, delicious and hard to put down, opening with gregarious scents of citrus, melon, peach and honeysuckle. The light-bodied palate is dry and shimmery, balancing racy acidity with citrus fruit and flinty undertones, and it has a long, spicy finish. • 2022 Trefethen Chardonnay Katie’s Acre Initial wafts of hay, flint and crème brûlée give way to melon, peach and jasmine aromas. The full-bodied palate is bursting with fragrant flavors, and its oak is seamlessly integrated. Silky in texture, its generosity is complemented by bright acidity, and it has a long, layered finish. The Trefethen Cabernet Sauvignon is made in the medium weight classic style. • 2021 Trefethen Cabernet Sauvignon Reserve Cherries, cranberries and hints of mocha and earth mark the nose of the Trefethen Reserve Cabernet. It’s a polite, restrained wine, smooth and silky in texture, medium-bodied, with a streamlined shape on the palate that tapers into a long, elegant finish. True to the winery’s historic style it’s not a big, in-your-face Napa Cab but one that prioritizes balance, elegance and refined, finegrained tannins. • 2022 Trefethen Petit Verdot So glad to see the Trefethens bottling this often-overlooked varietal. Opaque purple-colored, the Petit Verdot bounds boldly out of the glass with warm blueberries and kirsch notes plus hints of charcoal, garrigue and dried herbs. It is powerful and full-bodied with ample tannins on the finish. Delightful now, this wine will improve for two decades in the cellar. • 2022 Trefethen Dragon’s Tooth This is a unique blend of Malbec, Petit Verdot and Cabernet Sauvignon. It leads with a heady bouquet of resinous herbs, botanicals and toasted accents set against a black-fruited core with chalky overtones. A sleek, succulent mouthfeel follows, closing with a lifted finish marked by fine-grained woody tannins and a bright spine of acidity. This unusual combination really works. • 2023 Trefethen Block Party This Bordeaux blend is a beauty, wafting from the glass with aromas of cassis, plums, espresso, anise and violets. Medium to full-bodied, deep and concentrated, it’s velvety and layered with powdery tannins and a long, penetrating finish. Perfect to accompany a grilled ribeye steak. articles.text: Missy the Australian Shepherd holds an impressive sustained stay while balancing a cup of water on her rear for a photo shoot. One of the modern dog owner’s favorite pastimes is taking photos of, or with, their pup. And who could deny them? Dogs are the cutest, and we want to preserve our memories of them as thoroughly as possible. Although snapping a quick photo of your dog on the move or getting their attention with a treat are easy enough, there are some simple tricks your dog can learn that will take photos to the next level. All you need are some treats, a camera for practice, and a little patience. Contrary to popular belief, eye contact is not natural for dogs and must be taught. While tricks such as “watch” request eye contact, maintaining a steady gaze can mean something very different in dog language—it can be a cue to back off. Training sustained eye contact is simple but must be done intentionally. Use a happy, excited tone to maintain your dog’s interest, and reward often, giving verbal cues such as “look” or “what’s this?” With practice, your pup will learn that looking at you means good things are coming. The extended “stay” is a must

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is watching one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers movies in a comfortable setting with lively discussion afterwards. September’s film, Monsieur Ibrahim Et Les Fleurs Du Coran, is a touching and heartwarming French film from 2003, directed by François Dupeyron. It tells the story of a friendship between a Jewish teenager named Momo, played by Pierre Boulanger, and a Turkish Muslim grocer, Monsieur Ibrahim, played by Omar Sharif. The film is set in a working-class neighborhood in 1960s Paris. Momo lives with his lawyer father, who struggles with severe depression, and cannot meet Momo’s emotional needs after his mother leaves them. Momo, their meal provider, faces a tight household budget, and resorts to occasional thefts from Monsieur Ibrahim, the local ‘Arab’ grocer. Despite noticing these thefts, Monsieur Ibrahim decides to support Momo by encouraging a gradual increase in their friendship. Through their daily shop interactions, Momo finds solace and a sense of security with his newfound connection to the grocer whose wisdom, consistent patience and thoughtful observation creates a stable, non-judgmental environment, a stark contrast to Momo’s cold and hostile home life. A pivotal moment in the film occurs when Momo’s father abandons him, leaving behind only a short note and a small sum of money on the kitchen table. Momo, while keeping his father’s absence a secret from Monsieur Ibrahim, deepens his connection with the grocer by sharing experiences and learning from his new friend’s unique interpretation of the Koran. Eventually, Monsieur Ibrahim learns of Momo’s father’s abandonment, and seizes the opportunity to broaden Momo’s understanding of the world by impulsively buying a car, and inviting Momo to embark on a road trip to Turkey to visit his hometown. Momo’s encounter with a Sufi troupe performing the whirling dervishes dance helps him mature and embrace a broader understanding of a different culture. Later, as their car approaches Monsieur Ibrahim’s town, he asks Momo to get out so he can enter his birthplace alone for the first time in many years. The film then unfolds showing how Momo later accepts a new life back in his Paris neighborhood as the inheritor of his friend’s legacy. Director François Dupeyron skillfully evoked nostalgia in this film. With a delicate yet never sentimental touch, he introduces us to two individuals from vastly different ages and backgrounds in an engaging and insightful manner. Pierre Boulanger and Omar Sharif, the two stars, complement each other perfectly, making for an enjoyable viewing experience as we watch them work together. Monsieur Ibrahim will be shown on Thursday, September 10 at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The movie is free to anyone 18 and over. Our next movie is The Grand Budapest Hotel, a 2014 comedy/drama, to be shown on October 8 at 1 p.m.

Begin on a leash if you have to, creating gentle tension to discourage moving forward, and always place your dog back in the same spot if they get up. Practice at longer distances as your pup gets better, and gradually introduce distractions, such as dropped food. A reliable stay gives you those precious extra seconds to frame the perfect shot. Teaching your pooch to “chin prop” takes your photos to the next level. Using a treat, lure your pup’s nose down until their chin is braced on the desired place, such as the arm of the couch or a fun prop. A common verbal command for this may be “head down.” Once mastered, this trick can create especially sweet, thoughtful-looking portraits. A few other camera-friendly tricks include having your dog hold an item in their mouth, sit “pretty” on their hind legs with front paws in the air, tilt their head on cue, or, for the ambitious canine photographer, hug a person or item. Remember that great dog photography is as much about patience as it is about technique. Keep photo sessions short and fun, reward generously, and never force a pose. Combining these tricks and commands is the final step to creating top-quality photos—and memories—that will last a lifetime. articles.text: This summer Piedmont Scouts in Troop 4 completed an exciting backpacking trip through the Sierra Nevada mountains. Over the course of seven days, 54 miles and 10,500 feet of elevation gain, the trek took us through numerous lakes and mountain passes in the Ansel Adams and Yosemite Wildernesses. Every day brought new scenery, from dense forests and open mountain meadows to towering granite peaks and clear alpine lakes. Some of the most memorable views came when we reached a high point on the trail and could look back over the valleys and lakes we had hiked past. Each day began with breakfast before we packed up and left camp around 10 a.m. We would hike for several miles, stopping for lunch along the trail before continuing toward our next campsite. Although carrying a backpack for miles and climbing steep mountain passes can be tiring, the scenery made the effort worthwhile. Reaching the top of a pass was especially rewarding, since it felt like the hardest part had been completed (even though the downhill was usually just as hard). Since most Scouts on the trip were sleeping in hammocks, we rigged tarps over them whenever it looked like it might rain. On one occasion, the rain actually began, accompanied by hail, putting our setups to the test. Fortunately, everyone stayed dry until the storm passed, thanks to our scouting skills. At camp, there was plenty to do besides setting up and cooking dinner. We swam in the cold mountain lakes, played Prepared for rain at Vandenburg Lake cards, talked with each other, and relaxed in our hammocks after an eventful day on the long trails. Our route took us through high mountain terrain, with many campsites at altitudes above 9,000 feet and four mountain passes, with the highest, Red Peak Pass, reaching over 11,200 feet. Our route started at Isberg Trailhead in Sierra National Forest, and led us through two miles of burned out forest to the beginning of Ansel Adams Wilderness. We stayed at Cora Lake that night and on the second day hiked 10 miles over Isberg Pass into Yosemite National Park. We followed that day with another grueling 10 miles up and over Red Peak Pass to Ottoway Lake where we finally gave ourselves a break. The elevation made hiking more difficult, especially on the steep climbs, but it also gave us some of the best views of the trip. From the higher parts of the trail, we could see across huge stretches of wilderness, with mountains, forests, and lakes filling the landscape. Despite how far we could see, we figured that there were only a handful of people in the entire view, given that we sometimes hiked entire days without seeing more than one or two people. On the last day of the trip, we woke up, packed our gear, and left camp by 7 a.m. The lake where we were camping was still more than nine miles from the exit, so we had to hike quickly. Things became even more interesting when we discovered that the trail we had planned to take was closed. Instead, we followed a long dirt road that eventually brought us back to our cars in Ottoway Lake at sunrise the early afternoon. Along the way, we even had to deal with the unexpected obstacle of cows chasing us down the road, giving us another convincing reason to hike speedily. The wilderness was very different from normal life. Being away from the internet and everyday distractions made it possible to focus on the people around us and the incredible wilderness we were exploring. The challenging hikes made the relaxing evenings at camp more enjoyable, and experiencing the mountains together made the trip an adventure that everyone could share. articles.text: The Number 11 streetcar on the right-of-way between Linda and Sunnyside Avenues in 1948. was what then was the newly built Transbay Terminal in San Francisco. Cars travelled east and west on the top level of the bridge. Electric trains served other parts of the East Bay. The A Train covered downtown Oakland, and the B Train travelled through the Lakeshore and Trestle Glen neighborhoods. The E Train went to Berkeley to the Claremont Hotel. In Berkeley, the F Train travelled on Shattuck to Solano, the G Train served Westbrae, the H Train travelled on Monterey Avenue, and the K Train ran on College Avenue. Today, some AC Transit buses use the same letters to identify their routes. End of the Line The last Piedmont streetcar operated until 1948. With the proliferation of automobiles after World War II, electric streetcars were no longer considered efficient. Buses, later run by AC Transit District, took over the streetcar routes. The C Train continued to run to San Francisco until 1958 when streetcars on the Bay Bridge were discontinued. The Oakland Tribune described this poignant time as “sad, exuberant, quiet, noisy, confused and orderly.” That last ride was standing room only. Homeowners along the train’s route came out to wave goodbye, as the motorman saluted back. The C Train at the small Oakland Avenue station at Latham that provided shelter to waiting passengers in 1940. Legacy The Number 11 and 12 streetcar lines and the C Train also left a legacy of vacant right-ofway land. The right-of-way for the Number 11 between Sunnyside and Linda became the beautifully landscaped Linda Park and the energetic Linda Avenue Dog Park across from Beach School. The Number 12 streetcar on Fairview Avenue had no dedicated right-of-way. When the C Train stopped running, its right-of-ways were filled with houses. Today, three narrow houses occupy the right-of-way along Latham. The land between Ricardo and York became more back yard space for adjacent houses. New houses were built on York near Arroyo. The C Train also shared the right-of-way on Arroyo with the Number 10 streetcar before it As the C Train curves to the right toward its route to Latham and Oakland, the Number 10 streetcar descends Arroyo toward Piedmont Avenue.

articles.text: Bill Reichle I am a fourth-generation Californian and lifelong East Bay resident. My wife Julie grew up in Piedmont, and we moved here in 2000 when our daughters were in preschool. I was immediately impressed by Piedmont’s beautiful neighborhoods, its civic pride, and the spirit of volunteerism. I am a graduate of UC Berkeley and have an MBA from California State University, East Bay. As Assistant Vice Chancellor at UC Berkeley, I helped manage many of the departments that mirror Piedmont’s city administration, including police, facilities, and capital strategies. The City of Piedmont does an outstanding job providing services and programs to its residents cost-effectively. The level of service we enjoy is under increasing pressure from inflation, complex mandates from Sacramento, and aging City infrastructure. I am running to address these challenges to sustain Piedmont’s small-town character that residents value. I have served on the board of directors for several organizations that Piedmonters support: Piedmont Education Foundation, Camp Augusta, PHS Boosters, and the Piedmont Youth Soccer Club. Today, I enjoy volunteering to help Dress Best for Less (DBFL) set up their “Bag Sale” on the last Saturday of each month, raising funds to support our schools. Nancy Beninati (nancyforpiedmont.com) I am a 20-year Piedmont resident, an active working mom, civil rights attorney, and UC Berkeley lecturer. I know and care about this community because I’ve volunteered in our classrooms, coached youth sports, and raised my family here. I am running for City Council because public service is important to me. For 27 years at the California Department of Justice, I have worked to protect the rights of Californians and find practical solutions to difficult problems. I want to bring that experience home to Piedmont and put it to work for our community. My commitment to public service led me to serve as President of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. I worked to bring our community together around important issues, organizing voter forums and educational programs where residents could hear directly from candidates, community leaders, and experts. I also advocated for community interests before the City Council. I currently serve on the Recreation Commission and previously served six years on the Civil Service Commission. articles.text: Happy September, all! THE PIEDMONT PREMIUM While external economic headlines fluctuate, Piedmont’s real estate market continues to operate in a strategic league of its own. This enduring desirability has long rested on what makes Piedmont special: top-ranking public schools, hyper-responsive city services, and an unmatched quality of life. Yet, the current momentum is being amplified by an exceptionally well-capitalized class of buyers. Equipped with substantial liquidity and the ability to close quickly with cash, these buyers are moving with remarkable speed. The result is a market operating at peak performance. Today, virtually every well-presented listing is met with immediate, intense demand, routinely commanding multiple competitive offers within days of hitting the market. For homeowners, this alignment of scarcity and affluent demand ensures Piedmont remains an absolute stronghold for sellers. MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: If you own a condo, there were some important changes to condo financing rules this August that are worth knowing about. Since the tragic condo collapse in Surfside, Florida in 2021, lenders have paid much closer attention to the safety, finances, insurance, and deferred maintenance of condo buildings. That has made financing difficult in some projects that were previously easy to lend on. The new rules create two very different paths. Condo projects with 10 units or fewer now have a much simpler approval process, while projects with 11 or more units face a more detailed review than ever before. For owners in larger buildings, issues with insurance, building finances, major repairs, or litigation could limit the financing available to future buyers or make refinancing more difficult. If you own or are considering buying a condo, understanding whether the project itself qualifies for financing has become just as important as whether you qualify for a mortgage.

Doebelin said turning the schoolyard into an enormous party was way too much fun, but identified a larger importance. “What I appreciate most has nothing to do with pancakes. For Doebelin, the Beach Dads Club has provided great lasting friendships in a fast-paced modern world. “It has created real friendships, connection and community in a way I never expected when I first got involved. articles.text: The city is surveying residents to improve their visits to the Piedmont Community Pool. After years of planning, the first year of operations allows the city to test assumptions, learn how people actually use the pool, and make adjustments. The community’s feedback will help the city identify what changes will have the most impact for pool users. The survey is available at piedmont. ca.gov/PoolSurvey and will be open for responses through September 30. The survey asks about your experience using the pool so far – what’s working well, and where could things be better across several areas: • Planning your visit: schedules, registration, check-in • Hours of operation and programming • Facility comfort • Reserved open swim at the activity pool The survey also asks users to identify the one change that would most improve their experience. The city will review survey responses alongside attendance data to continue adjusting pool operations and programming. Campers inspect their LEGO spaceship at the STEM Minecraft LEGO class.
articles.title: Piedmont wants to hear about residents’ experience at the new Community Pool

articles.text: The Recreation Department said the introduction of new classes were a huge factors for the increase in campers this summer. The program hosted over 300 camps, adding 73 new camps from the last year. This brought in over 4,300 campers throughout the 10 weeks of summer programming. Each of the camp offerings grew, with Camp Everything as the most popular. “We expanded capacity, added new camps, and partnered with six new camp providers,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Camp Everything was especially attractive to families because of its affordable rate, free early drop-off, optional extended care, camp shirts, weekly field trips, and pool days.” Incorporating aquatics into weekly programming drew in large numbers of participants. The Community Pool’s summer programming hosted 286 classes between June and August. This amounted to 816 participants, among them were 573 children participating in classes. “The pool contributed to the increase in campers by adding weekly swimming to Camp Everything. The popularity of the new Community Pool showed the value of incorporating aquatics into future camps,” said Putzer.
