articles.text: The Wildwood Dads’ Club fired up the barbecue on campus last week, welcoming back Piedmont families to the new school year. The dads took over the lower playground to host the fun on Thursday, August 20 as part of a school night event that fed the whole family. The Dads like to have a little fun so they dressed up as hot dogs, mustard and other condiments. Kids rode bikes and played on the playground and blacktop. The Bay Area’s nice August weather helped boost attendance, with many parents coming to let their kids run free at school with their newly reunited friends. The event focused on camaraderie more than fundraising. It let parents catch up with each other about family vacations over the summer and tips on how to get back into the rhythm of the school year. More than a dozen dads volunteered at the event, making sure the burgers and dogs were well distributed and no one went hungry. The club welcomed kindergarten dads to the fold replenishing its roster after graduation from 5th grade turned a group of dads into alumni last May. Up next for the club will be its annual Pumpkin Patch in October, supplying the local region with everything needed for Halloween in one stop at Coaches Field. Wildwood Dads’ Club Officers dressed in BBQ costumes for the Welcome Back Barbecue on August 20. Pictured are Nimesh Singh (left) (Treasurer), Grady Snyder (Officer Emeritus), Alex Danoff (Co-President), Dave Rochwerger (Secretary), Darren Rees (Vice President), and Sergio Serna (Co-President) A Celebration of Life is scheduled for John Morrison on Saturday, September 12, at 2 p.m. in the John Morrison Gymnasium at Piedmont Middle School, 740 Magnolia Avenue. The longtime middle school principal died on August 7, 2026, at the age of 84.

articles.text: Mary was a much-loved member of the church where I serve as the Interim Pastor. She touched many in her long life. Her memorial service was truly a celebration of life. One of the people who eulogized her at that service was her brother-in-law. He spoke warmly of family travels and gatherings. He said that Mary taught him to savor a glass of wine and a leisurely dinner. He said she taught him that “life is more than a hot dog eating contest.” The most famous hot dog eating contest in the world is Nathan’s which takes place on Brooklyn’s Coney Island on the Fourth of July. The men’s record holder is Joey Chestnut who ate 76 hot dogs and buns in ten minutes in 2021. The women’s record holder is Miki Sudo who consumed 51 in 2024. Hot dog eating contests are about speed and conspicuous consumption. It seems that savoring, relaxing, resting and reflecting are not high values at hot dog eating contests. In his instruction to his followers about how best to live their lives Jesus said, “Behold the birds of the air” and “Consider the lilies of the field.” Behold and consider are not hurry words. They are not rush words. They are not consume frantically words. They are not hot dog eating contest words. They are slow down words, take a moment words, cool your jets words. A literary character who comes to mind is Agatha Christie’s somewhat eccentric detective, Hercule Poirot. Poirot is small of stature, large of head and absolutely committed to going slow, considering methodically and taking time to do nothing more than to think, to engage the “little gray cells” of his brain. He often irritates his associates with his refusal to rush around searching for clues and his commitment simply to contemplate. Poirot is not a hot dog eating contest sort of detective. In urging his community to perceive the amazing, complex, diverse and beautiful body that is church, the apostle Paul writes, We have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: prophecy, in proportion to faith; ministry in ministering; the teacher in teaching; the encourager in encouragement; the giver, in sincerity; the leader in diligence; the compassionate in cheerfulness. We cannot see this amazing grace, this amazing giftedness, without slowing down to behold, without pausing to consider. Acting like we are in a hot dog eating contest is a guarantee that we will miss the profound vision that is our life together. Let us consider. Let us behold. Let us press pause on our hot dog eating contest lives. Instead, let us set our gaze on the goodness of life and so embrace lives that are good. Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland.
articles.title: A word about hot dogs

articles.text: As the weather turns hotter and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. The fire department recommends downloading a checklist for preparing your yard at piedmont. The East Bay hills have experienced multiple significant wildfires in September and October in the last 150 years. Those events and recent wildfires across California have taught us that our communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, which helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. You can do your part by taking a few simple protective measures in your yard every fall. Make time in the next few weeks to prepare your property: • Clear debris and flammable materials. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your yard. Clear leaves and pine needles from roofs, gutters, and the ground. articles.text: The best practice in vegetation management is to remove all vegetation within five feet of your home. Even if this is not currently feasible for you, taking protective measures in your yard will increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire and reduce risk to our whole community. Use this checklist to prepare your yard. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! articles.text: Last week, the city conducted another pathway repair project in the upper Dracena, alongside Dracena Avenue near the bridge. Construction and demolition began last week, and the city poured concrete on Monday, August 24, to finish repairs on the path. The pathways were demolished last week due to cracking. The Public Works Department rebuilt the path’s structure with wooden and metal frames to provide long-term stability. Earlier this summer, Piedmont conducted a pathway repair project in upper Dracena along Park Way. The repairs were in response to cracking in the original asphalt path from age and damage. The city has undertaken substantial pathway repair work to improve safety and access in Piedmont’s parks over the past few years – including projects at Crocker Park, Piedmont Park, and a large portion of the pathways in upper Dracena two years ago. Once the concrete is set, the pathway will reopen for walkers. A leashed dog disregards the wet cement and gives the path some paw prints. The rebuilt pathway before the cement pour. Public Works workers smoothing out the freshly poured cement.
articles.title: Dracena Park pathways repaved near Dracena Avenue

articles.text: At 12 years old, Cece knows exactly what she wants: quality time with her favorite people, plenty of affection, and your undivided attention. This tortie lovebug will happily settle onto your chest, gaze directly into your eyes, and remind you with a little meow that your phone or laptop really can wait. Cece is happiest wherever you are. She’ll greet you, follow you around the house, and lounge beside you—or preferably on your chest. Her foster describes her as “a lover through and through.” As a senior, Cece has a couple of health needs to monitor. She has mild heart disease that currently requires no medication, diet changes, or exercise restrictions, but she’ll need annual check-ins with a veterinary cardiologist. Adopt Cece through Cat Town Cece’s wholehearted companionship makes it all too easy to understand that in her opinion, you’re the most important being in the world. She may prefer to be your one and only cat, and would love a calm, indoor-only home with someone ready to give as much affection as she does. Could that be you? Cece is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: Skippy is a 10-month-old mixed breed puppy with an enthusiastic personality and a love for learning. Although he can be exuberant and bouncy when excited, Skippy is easily redirected with treats. He enthusiastically practices “sit,” “down,” and “paw.” He’s highly food motivated, though he’s still learning polite treat manners. Skippy loves showing off his athleticism when prompted by tackling fun “barkour” exercises on outdoor furniture. He enjoys games of chase with other dogs in his doggie playgroup and would do well with appropriately matched canine companions or as a solo dog with dog friends outside the home. Skippy is looking for an active home that will embrace his playful spirit and continue helping this smart young dog grow into a wonderful companion. He weighs 62 pounds. Come meet Skippy at OakSkippy is available for adoption from Oakland Animal Services land Animal Services this Thursday 12 - 6:30 p.m., Friday 12 - 3 p.m., Saturday 11 a.m. - 4 p.m. or Sunday 12 - 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog within 25 pounds of Skippy’s weight must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2026 5 BUSINESS SPOTLIGHT By Jake Lannon Quality Body & Fender was founded in 1979 by David and Angie Perez. After moving in 1984, they’ve been at their current location at 2510 Martin Luther King Jr. Way for the last 42 years. David Perez was honored by California’s Hispanic Chamber of Commerce for his dedication and services to the Hispanic community as a renowned Latino Quality Body & Fender business owner. Today it is still a family-run business with Jacqueline Perez Kalafate as the GM and Michael Perez assisting Angie. Jacqueline entered the business as a kid, answering phones in the office and washing windows for 10 cents. It was after Jacqueline finished college that she took the business seriously and dedicated time to help out her father. “I believe he started to entice me, telling me he needed some help in the office, and I came to work after finishing college. I had a different career, so I helped in the office one day a week, and that was it. Then he needed two days a week. In 2010, he asked me to come three days a week, and because I had another job, I said, okay, well, let me commit to a year, and I will work full time. And if I like it, I’ll stay on,” said Jacqueline. Jacqueline spent that time Jacqueline Perez with her experienced office staff ATLAS HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY Old Fashioned Service and High-Quality Installations Jacqueline and her mother Angie Perez standing in front of their certifications, showcasing their longstanding reliability. handling contracts and learning to write estimates, eventually becoming an official estimator and manager for the business. Jacqueline would take over the business after her father fell ill and passed away in 2020. Ever since, Jacqueline and her family have carried their father’s legacy and dedication to the community through the business. “My father was born and raised in Oakland, and he was very ingrained in the community at different levels. No one was below him. He respected everyone at the same level, and that showed through with our customers,” Jacqueline continued. “We have people that are struggling, but we help them repair their car just as we would for the CEOs. We understand that everyone’s car is very important to them. We are compassionate enough to know that no one wants to see us. We’re not someone who wants to be visited; it’s stressful and overwhelming. But we have a staff that is trained to be compassionate and empathetic to them, to make this process easier.” According to Jacqueline, it’s this customer-focused approach that differentiates them from other repair shops. Their extensive experience and customer-first approach help people feel their vehicle is in safe hands. “The experience, and the connection we have with our customers and the staff that we employ. We have a person who speaks Chinese and Spanish. We’ve had French in the past, Cantonese, and just being able to service everyone from wherever they come, treating them with the same level of respect is something you don’t get in a lot of places,” said Jacqueline. They are a repair facility for Oakland Honda, Berkeley Honda, Oakland Kia, and Oakland Acura. They do work for Toyota, Volkswagen, and Subaru. They do work on all makes and models of foreign and domestic cars. The shop works with the City of Piedmont to repair its city-owned vehicles and recently started working with the City of Oakland. The business is Platinum Certified, a designation for collision repair professionals who maintain high levels of role-relevant training and complete safe, quality repairs. “We don’t like to deliver a car to a customer unless we are satisfied with it, and we see imperfections in a car that most people don’t. I think when customers know that we do that, they appreciate it a little more because they realize, oh, they care. They’re not just pumping me out and taking my money,” said Jacqueline. The Perez family wants the community to know they are dedicated to helping customers in their lowest moments. “We’re here for you so that we can help you when your kids get into an accident. We are your neighbors, and why not trust your neighbors when you’re dealing with something so important to your daily life? Come down, check us out, and get an estimate. You may not be ready to get it repaired now, but down the line, we are here for you,” she said. Readers can find more information about Quality Body & Fender at their website: www. qualitybf.com. articles.text: The Beach School Dads Club will host its 21st annual Pancake Breakfast this Sunday, August 30. The campus will be turned into a breakfast festival of fun for families starting at 9 a.m. with an army of grills churning out hot cakes with music, games and the Chalk Art Festival also on site. Returning Dads Club President (Padre Grande) Rob Doebelin, pulled out all the stops last year and continues the momentum by bringing out Angelo Moore, founder and frontman of Fishbone to join and possibly serenade the party on saxophone. Music will also be supplied by a DJ. “21st birthdays are a big deal. The Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast is officially old enough to party, so we feel some responsibility to act accordingly,” said Doebelin. Last year’s event featured a dunk tank and this year the flyer mentions “water surprises.” In cryptic fashion the flyer encourages prospective attendees to “Bring a towel.” Doebelin confirmed there will be a Fun Zone again and that the Good Eggs Market returns for attendees to take home goodies and groceries after eating their fill of hotcakes. The Beach Padres are offering all teachers, staff and their families to eat for free. The Padres are also encouraging firefighters and police officers to come by and eat free as a small gesture of appreciation. Food for the events is being provided by Piedmont Grocery, Mulberry’s Market, and Village Market. “Every single year, those three local institutions come through for us in a big way, and we’re incredibly grateful for their continued support of the Pancake Breakfast and the Beach community,” said Doebelin. “They’ve become part of the tradition at this point.” The Premium Pancake Toppings Bar will also be fully loaded. “Nutella, whipped cream, chocolate chips, berries, sprinkles and enough sugar to make the rest of Sunday somebody else’s problem,” said Doebelin. The pancakes, bacon, sausage, coffee and fruit salad are worth attendance on their own, but for the organizers, a larger reason compels them. “For more than two decades, dads have been showing up, flipping pancakes, volunteering, doing occasionally ridiculous things for the amusement of children and, somewhere along the way, building friendships of their own,” added Doebelin. The Beach Dads Club will celebrate 21 years of philanthropy, pancakes and community this Sunday, August 30 from 9:00 a.m.-12:30 p.m. at 100 Lake Avenue on the Beach Elementary School campus. Staff Photo Pancake options will include chocolate chip, oatmeal, blueberry and buttermilk. Photo from the 2022 event.

It’s a casual chance to learn more about PIE, connect with other families raising neurodivergent and disabled kids, and enjoy some good food together. Jean Fagin, PUSD’s Director of Special Education, will be there to connect with the community. Jean Takazawa, PUSD’s Director of Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEIB), will also be on hand to talk about the Affinity Mentorship program. Attendees will be able to learn about the Adaptive and Sidekicks afterschool programs. Bring a dish or just an appetite for this family friendly event helping parents increase their support network. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Nina Schwab graduated from Piedmont High in 2024 as the school’s only diver in its history. She intended to attend Carleton College in Minnesota and in March that year she made history for her college by winning the Division 3 NCAA title in the one-meter dive. She was also the runner up in the three-meter dive in a field of 16 divers. Upon entering her junior year, Schwab transferred to the University of Michigan “It’s definitely been a whirlwind. Being a national champ was super exciting, but I wanted a little more from the sport which is why I transferred to Michigan. I’m very excited about it and also a bit nervous. I’ve been spending the summer training with the team,” Schwab said. It marked her second consecutive year to reach the D3 NCAA Championship. She earned firstteam All-American honors as a freshman, finishing third of 29 in the 1-meter dive with a score of 438.20. You would think Schwab’s success as a diver is indicative of a long career that started in her childhood. But Nina only began diving when she was a junior at Piedmont High. During high school, Schwab decided to switch sports from gymnastics after suffering multiple fractures to her back. Her aunt was a former diver and helped lead Nina to make a decision about her athletic career. Looking back to her junior year in high school, becoming a Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, won the Division 3 NCAA Championship in the one-meter dive with Carleton College in March. national champion may have not been on her radar. “I really didn’t have a lot of expectations going into a new sport. My coach said it was possible, but I really didn’t expect to do it in college at all. I was injured all the time and lost my love for gymnastics. My aunt, who dove for the University of Minnesota, recommended the sport, so I just thought I’d try it out. And now here we are,” Schwab said. In 2024 as a high school senior, she finished fourth of 16 divers at the North Coast championships and 16th of 28 in State Championship. Just two years later, she became the best diver in her collegiate division and is now Nina Schwab reached two D3 NCAA Championships at Carleton College.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team’s season got off to a scorching start on Monday, August 24. Playing on the road at American High in Fremont, the Highlanders demolished the Eagles in a one-sided 18-7 win. The PHS offense was humming with a 12-3 lead by halftime while forcing several turnovers mid-pool and launching successful counter attacks one after another. “Our defense was focusing on a press in the lane, and we did a good job of that in the first half,” said coach Rik Krumins. “In the second half, we got into our position and then kind of relaxed. We want to continue being ball hawks. I was impressed with the boys. We got out on the counter, and got into the right areas.” Despite the win, Piedmont went down a man 13 times on the day, including conceding four 5-meter penalty attempts. “I’m not comfortable with the amount of penalties. We want to make sure we’re not in a bad spot so the referees make a call easily,” Krumins said. Still, the PHS defense was stout, including sophomore goalie Dylan Jerez who made 12 saves. “Dylan is one of the most consistent players on the team. He holds us down on defense and we can always rely on him. He’s a great leader in terms of communication,” junior Rylan Patty said of his teammate. Jerez was pinpointed by threeyear starting goalie and Class of 2026 graduate, Luke McAuliffe. “He played summer polo at CCU. At our end-of-season banquet, Luke said, ‘Dylan is the next guy.’ Luke kind of trained him last season so he’s ready to go,” junior Henry Stein added. The Highlanders are off for a week before visiting Newark Memorial on Tuesday, September 1, but look toward a monumental Thursday, September 3 when hosting their first match in Piedmont since 2019. Piedmont’s players were in elementary school the last time PHS hosted a game. Staff Photos Henry Stein had five goals, five assists, and four steals in Piedmont’s season-opener. “I had some great memories at the old Piedmont Pool. Now, the big thing I’ve been noticing is that we’re all so happy to be at the new pool. I don’t want to take it for granted, and want to put as many hours as I can in the pool,” Patty said. “Hopefully the crowd shows up and I see all my friends come to the game to support us. It’s going to be great,” Stein added. Match Recap Piedmont led 6-0 through the first quarter and 12-3 by halftime. They scored five more in the third quarter to go up 17-4, finishing with one goal in the fourth quarter and conceded three. In the first quarter, PHS had three goals by Stein, two goals by Henry Van Den Bos, and one by Patty to hold a commanding 6-0 advantage. Ven Den Bos scored again early in the second quarter before American got its first goal at the 5:43 mark. From there, PHS went on a four-goal scoring run to lead 11-1 with 2:44 left. Stein assisted Van Den Bos, Patty added another, Stein assisted Raffi Banin, and Colin Amen assisted Stein. Later on, Jack Dahling assisted Graham Smith to make it 12-2 with 1:27 left. PHS scored another four straight goals in the third by way of Stein assisting Walker Wilson, Stein assisting Patty, Van Den Bos assisting Stein, and Stein assisting Van Den Bos. Leo Maltz got Piedmont’s 17th goal following a steal and breakaway. Dahling scored Piedmont’s final goal with 2:06 left in the fourth quarter by way of a five-meter penalty shot. Final stats: Stein scored five goals, five assists, and four steals. Van Den Bos had five goals and two steals. Patty had three goals and two steals. Banin had one goal, one assist, and four steals. Wilson, Dahling and Smith had one goal and steal. Amen had one assist and steal. Jerez had 12 saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) visits Newark Memorial on Tuesday, September 1 at 5:30 p.m. They also host James Logan in Piedmont on Thursday, September 3 at the same time. Rylan Patty had three goals and two steals against American. Henry Van Den Bos also scored five goals with two steals vs. American.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s flag football team looks to rebound after two losses to start the season. Piedmont High’s flag football team got its season started against two strong teams over the last week. The Highlanders hosted Hercules on Tuesday, August 18 in a 19-6 loss. They also fell 33-0 at home against Acalanes two days later. Hercules was the No. 7 seed in last year’s D2 North Coast Section playoffs, and Acalanes was the No. 2 seed. Things won’t get much easier tomorrow, August 27, when they face Las Lomas, last year’s No. 1 seed in the Div. 1. The hope is that the difficult start to the season will tune Piedmont up ahead of September 1’s Western Alameda County Conference opener against Mt. Eden in Hayward. “We’re starting the season against some difficult North Coast Section teams. What we hope is that it sharpens us up for our league schedule, so we’re going to see what we’ve got,” said coach Beth Black. Despite the rough start, Piedmont’s defense had some moments against Hercules. Their only score came by way of a 44-yard interception return for a touchdown by new safety Cea’naiya Alexander after the ball was deflected into the air. It’s a solid start for a critical position that is up for grabs after the role was vacated by three-year starter and Class of 2026 graduate Dahlia Osman. “At safety, we’re going to try a couple of different players there. We have good candidates and we’re figuring out who is best for that position,” Black said before the start of the season. 19-6 to Hercules Both teams traded possession throughout the first quarter in a defensive battle. Hercules got within the Piedmont 10-yard line on its first possession, but a big tackle for loss by Sydney Latvala eventually led to Hercules throwing an incompletion on 4th-andgoal. Edie Elmquist prepares to pass. Maddie Lee lines up on defense.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team is off to a strong start to the season. After opening their campaign with a close 3-2 loss to Berean Christian at home on Thursday, August 20, they followed up by going undefeated (4-0) at the Stockton Classic hosted by Edison HS to win their bracket on Saturday, August 22. At Stockton, they closed with a 25-20, 25-20 win over Manteca in the finals. In their second match against Lathrop, they lost the first set 25-13 before responding with 25-7, 15-9 wins to close. In the semifinals against Edison, they similarly lost the first set 25-14 but bounced back with 25-11, 15-8 wins. “Overall, we really showed a lot of growth. It’s great to win, but the team really got better over the weekend. Against Lathrop, we got beat badly in the first set… but we showed resilience and adjusted to the pressure,” said co-head coach Mike Glass. “Edison was another case where we saw a lot of growth on the team with defensive adjustments. Our strong play against Edison carried into Manteca where we didn’t have any service errors the entire game.” Maika Ting was instrumental offensively throughout the tournament with 16 total kills in four matches. Piedmont’s service game was strong, including libero Allyson Huynh with 14 aces. Mia Bechtel finished the final match over Manteca with an ace. “Maika had 16 kills and only two hitting errors. Allyson was our ace leader with 14 aces and only a single serving error. In our final match against Manteca we had no serve receive errors,” co-head coach Jason Mongue added. The tournament success was a nice rebound after the season-opening loss to Berean Christian. PHS dominated the first set 25-13, and held leads in the second, third, and fifth sets before dropping each. “We’ve only had two weeks of practice, and there are a lot of new players on this team. It’ll take some adjusting, but I’m confident our success will come quickly and we’ll bond really fast,” Huynh said following the match. 2-0 over Manteca In the first set, both teams traded points with Manteca holding an early 5-3 lead. From there, Piedmont eventually took the lead by scoring six of seven points to go up 9-6 with two kills by Bailey, one by Maika Ting, and a block by Sofia Meyer. Holding a 14-11 lead, PHS rallied another six of seven points to extend the gap to 20-12 with another two kills by Bailey and one by Lucia Dorsey. Near the end of the set, Manteca scored three straight to cut the deficit to 24-20, but Bailey finished the set with a winning spike. It was a similar start to the second set with Manteca taking an 8-7 lead. PHS regained the lead at 9-8 with an ace by Mia Bechtel and never relinquished. At 13-11, the Highlanders scored six straight points to go up 19-11 with kills by Dorsey, Bailey, and an ace by Carina Vora. With a 23-16 lead, Manteca scored four straight to cut Piedmont’s lead to 23-20. From there, PHS scored via a service error and finished the tournament with an ace by Bechtel. 2-1 over Edison Piedmont defeated the hosting school in three sets by scores of 14-25, 25-11, 15-8. Glass credits the turnaround to their defensive shift and leadership by Huynh at Staff Photos Allyson Huynh had 14 aces in four matches at the Stockton Classic.

articles.text: and Ariel Rodriguez The school year is starting again, and this time of transition can feel both exciting and overwhelming. As we enter the new school year, we have the unique opportunity to make a fresh start: new classes, new teachers, and, perhaps, a new perspective. Here are some steps to help you start the school year feeling empowered. Step 1 – Reflect For many of us, the start of the school year can feel like a mad scramble, but setting aside even a few minutes to reflect on the previous school year can make a meaningful difference. Ask yourself, “What worked well last school year and how did that make me feel?” Then, ask yourself, “What was challenging last school year and how did that make me feel?” Write down a few responses for each question. Keep your responses brief, but try to be specific. Here are some examples: • “having a separate binder for each class helped me feel organized” • “we usually run late on Monday mornings which makes me feel anxious” Step 2 – Plan If something is working for you, don’t change it! Acknowledge how helpful it’s been and re-commit to that behavior going forward. Once you identify a challenge, acknowledge that it exists and work to make changes. If Monday mornings feel frantic and stressful in your household, write down some ideas for how you might be able to change that: • “pick out Monday’s outfit on Sunday” • “pack my backpack on Sunday evening” • “do homework on Saturday and Sunday so that I don’t have to stay up late on Sunday night to finish everything” After you’ve made your list of ideas, pick one or two to try. Step 3 – Check in For the last month, you’ve used Sunday to pick Monday’s outfit and to pack your backpack. Do you feel less stressed? Are you making it to school on time? If the answer is yes — congratulations! You’ve found a behavior that helps you overcome a challenge. Keep doing what you’re doing. If the answer is no, that’s OK. Go back to your list and try another idea from your brainstorm until you find something that does work for you. This process of checking in with yourself is especially helpful during times of transition and can help you feel empowered to grow not only as a student but as a person! articles.text: After-school enrichment classes are often described by what children are learning: basketball, chess, art, science, coding, or another skill. But the real value of a quality enrichment program goes far beyond the content When we teach children, we are also creating a culture. We use positive reinforcement, consistent routines, clear expectations and discipline to help children understand how to succeed—not just in an activity, but in a group. Students learn to listen to instruction, accept professional coaching, work alongside different personalities and independently check whether they are doing what has been asked of them. These are skills that carry into the classroom, onto athletic teams and eventually into the I have worked with Piedmont children and families for almost 30 years, and that experience has given me a deep understanding of the needs and expectations of this community. My path to running a sports organization, however, has not been a traditional one. As an athlete, I have been the worst player on my team, the best player on my team and just about everything in between. That perspective matters. I know what it feels like to be the child who immediately understands a skill, and I know what it feels like to struggle while everyone else seems to be getting it. I was also a middle school teacher, where I learned firsthand that children have different learning modalities. One explanation will not reach every child. Good teaching requires finding different ways to communicate, demonstrate, motivate and connect. My approach can sometimes appear contradictory. I am very strict about following our rules and meeting our expectations. At the same time, I bring a childlike zaniness to what we do and am usually more than willing to make fun of myself. Children should know that their instructor is in charge, but they should also know that the instructor cares about them and enjoys being there. of great enrichment: discipline without intimidation, high expectations with encouragement, and structure combined with joy. Ultimately, we may be teaching a sport or activity, but our larger responsibility is helping children become more confident, coachable and independent. When we combine discipline, love and plenty of fun, the lessons of an after-school class can last long after the class itself is over. articles.text: Folks attend a guided tour through the redwoods that surround Chabot as they learn about the land and its history. Redwood Regional Park, which surrounds Chabot Space & Science Center, is abundant in beautiful plant and animal life. A visit to Chabot offers the opportunity to learn about the wonders of our galaxy and the fascinating ecosystem of the planet we call home. Surrounding Chabot is a stunning and lush landscape filled with many types of animals, plants, and geology. One of the most famous plants in the area are the coast redwoods. These magnificent giants and the land that they sit on remind us of the rich history in the East Bay and that science is actively around us. A Giant’s History There was once a time when redwood trees were found across North America. In the past, the redwoods of the East Bay once reached from the Oakland Hills to Moraga. A group of especially tall redwoods, dubbed the Navigation Trees, acted as landmarks that helped safely guide ships through the San Francisco Bay. Unfortunately, due to a combination of changing climates and an increase in housing during the 1800s, a significant number of redwoods in the East Bay no longer exist. However, the descendants of these incredible ancient giants can be found predominantly in the Redwood Regional Park that surrounds Chabot. Redwood Regional Park encompasses the grounds of Chabot and is one of the many beautiful parks in the East Bay Regional Park District. The land within these parks is the ancestral home to a diverse group of indigenous people who are descended from Ohlone, Bay Miwok, and Delta Yokuts ancestral tribes. Members of the groups held an in-depth knowledge of the plants and animals in the areas where they lived. The vast knowledge of these groups fueled their ability to expertly manage the land in ways that would benefit and enhance all living things in the area. Today, the descendants of these groups are actively involved in the preservation and restoration of their ancestral lands. The Science of Redwoods Coast redwoods belong to the cypress family and are the tallest trees in the world. Hyperion, a coast redwood in Humboldt County, California, stands at 380 feet high, making it the tallest tree known in the world! To put that into perspective, the planetarium dome here at Chabot is 70 feet high. Even if we were to stack five planetarium domes on top of each other, it still would not quite reach the height of the tallest coast redwood. Coast redwoods are evergreen plants, which means their foliage stays green and functional year-round. The thick and resistant bark of coast redwoods has given these exquisite giants the ability to withstand fire. These beautiful giants are also conifers, which means they produce cones and needles. Despite their unusual appearance, the needles of redwoods are technically their leaves. Redwood needles are flat and pointed on both ends, providing the critical function of photosynthesis. Experience the History & Science Firsthand Experience an unforgettable evening of nature, history, and stargazing with our Hike & Sip series, a program designed for adults 21 and over. On Saturday, August 29th, explore the majestic Redwood forest, guided by Chabot’s knowledgeable outdoor educators, and learn about the ecosystem, the cultural heritage of the Ohlone peoples, and Oakland’s rich history. After your hike, unwind on Chabot’s Observation Deck with drinks and charcuterie. End the night with stargazing through telescopes (weather permitting) and star stories brought to life under the night skies. Visit chabotspace. org for more information on this incredible experience!

articles.text: KidNuz Editor in Chief News — the good, the bad, the fake — is everywhere, all the time. It’s on our phones, feeds and in our faces 24/7. And while that can be overwhelming for adults, it’s downright distressing for children who haven’t yet developed the skills to look beyond scary headlines, clickbait, and partisan spin. And yet they see it, hear it, and feel it. Today’s kids desperately need — and deserve — an antidote; someplace they can go to get informed, not afraid. So we created it. KidNuz, a nonprofit news organization for kids, produces a free, 7-minute, 6-story daily news podcast that meets kids where they are. It’s fun and factual, timely and nonpartisan, and age-appropriate for kids 8-13 years old who want to know what’s going on in the world — not what’s wrong with the world. Every weekday during the school year, our team of Emmy-winning journalists delivers the latest news from politics, science, sports, the animal kingdom and more. Much of the coverage is top of mind, important, and impactful, while some of it is just plain reassuring: people are more alike of my emotional reaction to it, it helps me to hear (KidNuz’s) simplified version to have a baseline conversation with my son. articles.text: Alicia Mason stars as Effie in Shotgun Players’ Iphigenia in Splott. Shotgun Players has extended its production of Iphigenia in Splott, Gary Owen’s one-person play inspired by Euripides’ Iphigenia in Aulis, through Saturday, August 29. Directed by Michelle Talgarow, the production marks the company’s first one-person performance and follows Effie, a modern-day version of Iphigenia who lives in the working-class town of Splott in Wales. Effie stumbles through life before facing a choice between selfless sacrifice and the welfare of her community. The production explores the socioeconomic conditions of the working class through Effie’s experience of systemic failure, Talgarow said. “Don’t let the title fool you, this isn’t just a retelling of the ancient Greek myth,” she added. “It is a sharp, modern thrill ride set in working-class Wales. It’s just one actor on stage for 75 minutes, and she will absolutely blow you away with her energy, wit, wry humor, and a story that feels incredibly urgent right now.” Alicia Mason stars as Effie. Talgarow returns to Shotgun Players after directing the company’s 2024 production of Thirty-Six. The production follows the release of Effi o Blaenau, a Welsh-language film adaptation that premiered at the Glasgow Film Festival in March of this year and received a full U.K. theatrical release in June. Tickets are available for purchase at www.shotgunplayers. org/show/iphegenia/ or by calling the box office at 510-841-6500.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre opens its 2026-27 season with Eduardo Machado’s The Cook, running September 4 through October 11. Directed by Berkeley Rep Associate Artistic Director David Mendizábal, the play follows an aristocratic Cuban family that flees Havana for Miami on the eve of Fidel Castro’s revolution. The family leaves its mansion in the care of Gladys, their cook, who promises to protect the home until they return. Gladys keeps her promise for four decades, despite experiencing loss and witnessing the changes brought by the revolution. When the family’s daughter eventually returns, Gladys is forced to confront how much she has sacrificed for a relationship that may no longer hold the same meaning. “A landmark work in the American theatrical canon by a Latine playwright, the play illuminates Cuba’s complex history surrounding Fidel Castro’s revolution through richly drawn characters, focusing on their humanity, dreams, and ambitions,” Mendizábal said in a press release. The cast includes Gisela Chipe, Daniel Duque-Estrada, Yesenia Iglesias, Georgina Morillo and Ashton Muñiz. Understudies include Luis Kelly-Duarte, Georgina Morillo, Monica Rose Slater, Omar Stewart, and Courtney Thomas. The production features scenic design by Tanya Orellana, costume design by Toni-Leslie James, lighting design by Mextly Couzin and sound design and original music by Mikaal Sulaiman. Visit berkeleyrep.org to purchase tickets. Photo courtesy of Berkeley Repertory Theatre Yesenia Iglesias as Gladys in The Cook. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

articles.text: Festival Opera will open its annual Salon Series September 27 with a concert featuring the inaugural class of its Resident Artists at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The 7:30 p.m. performance features sopranos Marielle Leiboff and Rachel Nelson, mezzo-soprano Phoebe Dinga, tenor Spencer Greene and baritone Liam Daley, accompanied by Festival Opera pianist Daniel Lockert. The program includes opera arias, scenes and contemporary works by composers including Handel, Mozart, Verdi, Leoncavallo, Lehár, Richard Strauss, Massenet, Rachmaninoff, Jeanine Tesori and Leonard Bernstein. The Salon Series is a trio of concerts presented September through November, all performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Each performance is followed by a reception with the artists. The series continues October 25 with Operatic Mad Scenes, featuring sopranos Aura Veruni and Lila Khazoum with Lockert. The program will include excerpts from operas including Macbeth, The Magic Flute, Anna Bolena and Lucia di Lammermoor, with costumes and props incorporated into the performance. The final concert, held November 22, will feature baritone Efraín Solís, making his Festival Opera debut, accompanied by San Francisco Opera pianist Marika Yasuda. The program will include works by French, Mexican, Argentine and Russian composers, along with the world premiere of Borders of Dreaming, a newly commissioned song cycle by Colombian composer Juan Sebastián Cardona Ospina with text by Michael Colbruno. Tickets are $40 per concert or $95 for all three. Visit festivalopera.org/salon-series to purchase tickets. All Salon Series concerts are held at Piedmont Center for the Arts.
articles.title: Festival Opera opens Salon Series at PCA September 27

articles.text: Finding happiness isn’t so difficult. All you need to know is where to go. Perhaps this sounds simplistic and perhaps it is. I suggest that it is best to sidestep the news media in general. They are very good at acknowledging the kamikaze ardor for the bad. Fortunately, the Piedmont Post is a rare exception. I suggest that happiness is certainly not contemplating the misery of another. Some people and some organizations know this. One of them is the Musicians’ Union. Every year, they host a “thank you luncheon” for lifetime members of the union. For many years the rendezvous was at Nick’s Rockaway Beach restaurant. It is interesting to note that Nick’s is celebrating 99 years of successful dining pleasure. That’s rather a long time to enjoy success. Please note that quite a few of the musicians are of a very advanced age. If I heard correctly, the oldest musician in attendance was also 99 years old. The day began with a very pleasant drive to Pacifica. Then we saw lots of friends. A band had been engaged to entertain us and they played nonstop. After about an hour, we sat down to enjoy lunch. Dining has been described as eating good food in good company and that’s the way it was on Monday. Nick’s is a very pleasant restaurant and they serve excellent food abetted by excellent service. Portions are very large. The union picked up the tab so I cannot tell you about the price but I think that it was very reasonable. Everyone in attendance was offered the choice of chicken, fish, or prime rib. Debbie and I chose one fish and one prime rib. Take a look at the accompanying photograph of the prime rib. It was just about the best I have ever had, and it overflowed the plate. Kudos to Nick’s and kudos to the Musicians’ Union for knowing how to show appreciation. Finding happiness can be a simple equation. When you enjoy music with good friends and good food you have found one version of happiness. Bring those three things together and you have a very good recipe. This glorious prime rib is an example of the food at Nick‘s Rockaway Beach restaurant. It was delicious and so big that Samson could’ve used it in battle.
articles.title: In quest of happiness

articles.text: An exhibition featuring Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau, a painting widely regarded as a landmark of modern art, leaves the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on SepThe exhibition, titled Matisse’s Femme au chapeau: A Modern Scandal, opened May 16 and examines the history, reception and lasting influence of the 1905 portrait, which is part of SFMOMA’s permanent collection. The painting debuted at the Salon d’Automne in Paris in 1905 and became associated with Fauvism, the first French avantgarde art movement of the 20th century. The exhibition explores the work’s historical context, subject, provenance and circulation through exhibitions and publications, while also considering its impact on later generations of artists. “We are thrilled to have this opportunity to share the full story of Matisse’s Femme au chapeau—a painting that is emblematic of the artist’s radical break from convention in the early years of his career,” Janet Bishop, SFMOMA Chief Curator, said in a press release. “Arguably SFMOMA’s most art-historically significant work of art, Femme au chapeau began sending shockwaves through the art world as soon as it left Matisse’s studio and has captivated viewers ever since,” Bishop added. The exhibition also traces the painting’s ownership history. American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein acquired the work in 1905 while living in Paris. It later entered the collection of Michael and Sarah Stein, who brought it to the Bay Area in 1935. The painting was first exhibited in the United States at the San Francisco Museum of Art, now SFMOMA, in 1936. It entered the museum’s collection in 1991 through a bequest from Elise S. Haas. “Par t of our vision at SFMOMA is to encourage our visitors to see the world— and art—in new ways,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “With stunning paintings by Matisse and his peers, as well as work by some of the most exceptional artists working today, this exhibition promises to captivate SFMOMA visitors.” Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/ for more information. A museum patron views Henri Matisse’s work included in SFMOMA’s newest exhibition.
articles.title: Last chance to see Matisse’s Femme au chapeau at SFMOMA

articles.text: Ongoing through September 20 Book Club Art Show Gallery Hours This somewhat eclectic group of artists, The Book Club at Van Kleef’s, who first met at Café Van Kleef in Oakland in 2005, presents a show called For the Love of Art which includes works by about nineteen artist members and friends, and will hold Open Gallery Hours from 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. on most Saturdays and Sundays from August 15 through September 20 (except August 22 & 30). The show, as are all of PCA’s art exhibits, is free and open to all! Saturday, September 5, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Piano Trio Please note this event is on Saturday, not the usual Sunday. To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative (story line) that ties each tune on the program into the theme for the month. For Autumn Leaves, for example, many of the tunes, such as Autumn Leaves (1947), September in the Rain (1937), Autumn in New York (1934), have an obvious connection to the autumn theme. Other tunes such as I’ve Got the World on a String (1932) and Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams (1931) do not have such an obvious connection. The narrative ties these tunes and all the tunes on the show into the autumn theme. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Saturday late afternoon in our Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 p.m. Advance tickets are $26.44 at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Leaves, or pay $30 at the door, cash or check ONLY. Sunday, September 6, 4:00 p.m. SonoMusette French Music from Paris SonoMusette’s long-awaited return to Piedmont Center for the Arts promises an evening that will transport the audience into the heart of Paris through the songs of Édith Piaf and other iconic performers of the period. This is more than a concert, it’s a voyage back in time to the cabarets and jazz clubs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where stories of love, loss, and life were sung with passion. With SonoMusette, every performance invites you to feel the pulse of Parisian life and to fall in love with these unforgettable songs all over again. Mimi Pirard ~ vocalist, Robert Lunceford ~ accordion, Jan Martinelli ~ piano, Tami Pallingston ~ upright bass, Kendrick Freeman ~ drum set. Advance tickets are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Pirard. Saturday, September 12, 6:30 p.m. Cuban Fusion Illustrated Book Talk Most people know the iconic voice of the Queen of Salsa, Celia Cruz, one of the world’s greatest ambassadors of Cuban music and culture. In this talk, Dr. Eva Silot Bravo examines how the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Eastern socialist bloc, and Cuba’s economic crisis of the ‘90s reshaped the trajectory of Cuban music. Drawing on the research behind Cuban Fusion: The Transnational Cuban Alternative Music Scene (Palgrave Macmillan, 2024), the presentation traces the evolution of transnational Cuban jazz and fusion scenes over the past three decades, reshaping Cuban music into a truly global phenomenon. Reserve your seat for this fascinating event at https://www. ticketsignup.io/EvaBravo. Sunday, September 13, 7:00 p.m. Temescal String Quartet Concert A San Francisco Bay Area classical ensemble established in 2004 by professional musicians from the San Francisco Opera and Ballet Orchestras, founded by violinist Barbara Riccardi, the group will perform quartet masterworks by Mozart, Ravel, along with the US premiere of a quartet by Jane O’Leary. Barbara will play alongside Dana Myers, violin, Linda Green, viola, and Nancy Bien, cello. Light refreshments will be available after the performance, and advance tickets are now at https://www.ticketsignup.io/TSQ. Watch this space and our website Join our mailing list & donate.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2026 21 Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts Ongoing through September 20 Book Club Art Show Gallery Hours This somewhat eclectic group of artists, The Book Club at Van Kleef’s, who first met at Café Van Kleef in Oakland in 2005, presents a show called For the Love of Art which includes works by about nineteen artist members and friends, and will hold Open Gallery Hours from 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. on most Saturdays and Sundays from August 15 through September 20 (except August 22 & 30). The show, as are all of PCA’s art exhibits, is free and open to all! Saturday, September 5, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Piano Trio Please note this event is on Saturday, not the usual Sunday. To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative (story line) that ties each tune on the program into the theme for the month. For Autumn Leaves, for example, many of the tunes, such as Autumn Leaves (1947), September in the Rain (1937), Autumn in New York (1934), have an obvious connection to the autumn theme. Other tunes such as I’ve Got the World on a String (1932) and Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams (1931) do not have such an obvious connection. The narrative ties these tunes and all the tunes on the show into the autumn theme. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Saturday late afternoon in our Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 p.m. Advance tickets are $26.44 at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Leaves, or pay $30 at the door, cash or check ONLY. Sunday, September 6, 4:00 p.m. SonoMusette French Music from Paris SonoMusette’s long-awaited return to Piedmont Center for the Arts promises an evening that will transport the audience into the heart of Paris through the songs of Édith Piaf and other iconic performers of the period. This is more than a concert, it’s a voyage back in time to the cabarets and jazz clubs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where stories of love, loss, and life were sung with passion. With SonoMusette, every performance invites you to feel the pulse of Parisian life and to fall in love with these unforgettable songs all over again. Mimi Pirard ~ vocalist, Robert Lunceford ~ accordion, Jan Martinelli ~ piano, Tami Pallingston ~ upright bass, Kendrick Freeman ~ drum set. Advance tickets are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Pirard. Saturday, September 12, 6:30 p.m. Cuban Fusion Illustrated Book Talk Most people know the iconic voice of the Queen of Salsa, Celia Cruz, one of the world’s greatest ambassadors of Cuban music and culture. In this talk, Dr. Eva Silot Bravo examines how the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Eastern socialist bloc, and Cuba’s economic crisis of the ‘90s reshaped the trajectory of Cuban music. Drawing on the research behind Cuban Fusion: The Transnational Cuban Alternative Music Scene (Palgrave Macmillan, 2024), the presentation traces the evolution of transnational Cuban jazz and fusion scenes over the past three decades, reshaping Cuban music into a truly global phenomenon. Reserve your seat for this fascinating event at https://www. ticketsignup.io/EvaBravo. Barbara will play alongside Dana Myers, violin, Linda Green, viola, and Nancy Bien, cello. Light refreshments will be available after the performance, and advance tickets are now at https://www.ticketsignup.io/TSQ. Last chance to see Matisse’s Femme au chapeau at SFMOMA By Allyson Aleksey An exhibition featuring Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau, a painting widely regarded as a landmark of modern art, leaves the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on September 13. The exhibition, titled Matisse’s Femme au chapeau: A Modern Scandal, opened May 16 and examines the history, reception and lasting influence of the 1905 portrait, which is part of SFMOMA’s permanent collection. The painting debuted at the Salon d’Automne in Paris in 1905 and became associated with Fauvism, the first French avantgarde art movement of the 20th century. The exhibition explores the work’s historical context, subject, provenance and circulation through exhibitions and publications, while also considering its impact on later generations of artists. “We are thrilled to have this opportunity to share the full story of Matisse’s Femme au chapeau—a painting that is emblematic of the artist’s radical break from convention in the early years of his career,” Janet Bishop, SFMOMA Chief Curator, said in a press release. “Arguably SFMOMA’s most art-historically significant work of art, Femme au chapeau began sending shockwaves through the art world as soon as it left Matisse’s studio and has captivated viewers ever since,” Bishop added. The exhibition also traces the painting’s ownership history. American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein acquired the work in 1905 while living in Paris. It later entered the collection of Michael and Sarah Stein, who brought it to the Bay Area in 1935. The painting was first exhibited in the United States at the San Francisco Museum of Art, now SFMOMA, in 1936. It entered the museum’s collection in 1991 through a bequest from Elise S. Haas. “Par t of our vision at SFMOMA is to encourage our visitors to see the world— and art—in new ways,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “With stunning paintings by Matisse and his peers, as well as work by some of the most exceptional artists working today, this exhibition promises to captivate SFMOMA visitors.” Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/ for more information. A museum patron views Henri Matisse’s work included in SFMOMA’s newest exhibition. articles.text: A scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day starring Tom Holland as Spider-Man Spider-Man: Brand New Day has set the world on fire since its release. The film is on track to reach the top five grossing films of all time, currently sitting at $2.2 billion globally. This movie comes off the heels of Spider-Man: No Way Home, which resets the universe around Peter Parker, as at the end of the film everyone forgets who he is and that he is Spider-Man. Brand New Day focuses on the inner workings of Spider-Man and Peter Parker and how Parker’s lack of a personal life has blurred the line between being Spider-Man and being Peter Parker. The film starts with a montage of Spider-Man fighting crime and arresting the top crime syndicates in New York. Between each clip of Spider-Man, we see Peter (Tom Holland) watching videos on his best friend’s Instagram. He watches Ned (Jacob Batalon) and MJ (Zendaya) living their best lives at MIT without him. You can feel the despair on Peter’s face as he watches these videos, but continues to tell himself that this is for the better, as they’re safer without him around. We immediately go into a giant action set piece where Spider-Man chases a stolen tank through the city. Once the tank breaks through the wall of the Department of Damage Control, it is revealed that the driver is an old woman with no recollection of what happened. It is then that Peter realizes through his spider sense that something is wrong. He follows these people throughout the building as they’re seemingly being mind-controlled and eventually confronts the telepath. articles.text: This summer, one of the most anticipated movies of the year was released in theaters: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. Nolan’s rendition of The Odyssey is an ambitious adaptation of a story that has endured for nearly 3,000 years. Like every major retelling of Homer’s epic, it raises familiar questions about what should remain faithful to the original and what can and should be reinterpreted. Nolan’s version is particularly interested in the difference between the Odysseus painted as a clever hero and favorite of Athena and the Odysseus who is utterly flawed as he fights to return home to Ithaca. Odysseus is one of the earliest trickster figures in Western literature. His greatest strengths are not physical power but cunning, endurance, and his ability to understand the people around him. He survives the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens, and seven uncertain years with Calypso, yet his journey is repeatedly prolonged by his own hubris and poor decisions. Unlike Achilles, whose heroism is straightforwardly tied to glory and battle, Odysseus lies, manipulates, and kills. His eventual return to Penelope, Telemachus, and Ithaca is therefore more complicated than a simple heroic homecoming. This portrayal of Odysseus must grapple with the consequences of his actions that led to the fall of Troy: the destruction and betrayal of the most sacred and human tradition, the breaking of Zeus’ Law, or xenia, which is a binding code of hospitality and mutual respect between a host and a stranger. pretenses and letting the Greek army enter into and subsequently ravage Troy, Odysseus’ actions led to the downfall of civil society as he knew it. His return to Ithaca becomes a story about justice, responsibility, and atonement, instead of a detoured journey home through the Mediterranean. articles.text: Piedmont Roundup Market Observations, Insider Wisdom & The Week in Piedmont Real Estate As students head back to class, the City has quietly rewritten the Civic Center’s traffic choreography. Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues is now one-way northbound toward Oakland, drivers can no longer turn onto Bonita from Oakland, and the Havens Elementary drop-off zone that used to live on Bonita has been eliminated. If you’re a Havens family, the main show has moved to Highland Avenue, where loading zones now line both sides of the street and a crossing guard helps the littlest Piedmonters across. The changes hit Havens families hardest but ripple through every route to the other schools and facilities in the Civic Center. Review your usual drive before the first bell and allow extra time in week one, because the first week of a new traffic pattern is always chaos wearing a polite smile. The Piedmont Police Department will station staff at the Bonita/Oakland intersection during that first week to assist with the transition, which is cityspeak for “we know this is going to be a mess, please be patient.” In the News: Pool Parking Pushback June of this year, from very smart young journalists at The Highlander comes a well-put-together parking pushback. When will municipal government learn that revolutions are built on inconvenienced citizens? Piedmont’s pool parking, which is near Piedmont’s schools, is already drawing pushback from students, and the complaints are not hard to understand. The city converted 30 spaces to two-hour parking and stepped-up enforcement, which means fewer longterm spots for PHS, MHS, and PMS students and staff. The Highlander editorial argues the result will be more tardies, more tickets, and more frustration for teachers who already deal with limited parking. It also notes that the new pool does not justify making weekday school parking worse, especially when swim and water polo practices themselves run about two hours. The bigger issue is process. Students say many only learned about the changes after getting ticketed, and a student petition to reverse the decision quickly gathered hundreds of signatures. If you want people to support civic change, start by not making their daily lives harder. Real Estate From the Trenches I went undercover on Monday’s broker’s tour last week, asking questions for this column. It turns out that none of the agents I visited knew I write this column. I wanted to chalk it up to them being busy but then I realized none of the ones I visited get the Post delivered to their homes. I did meet some of the residents on that tour and got some suggestions about how to make this a better column. I am listening. The best suggestion was to add a list of all addresses that changed hands for the month, akin to a police blotter. I’ll make sure to add all the ones that actually make the Multiple Listing Service (MLS). My favorite thing heard on tour came from a resident, wearing orange Crocs, who was very excited about the view of the lake from one of the properties on tour. Children have a way of cutting through the sales pitch to the important things. Did You Know Piedmont, yes, this Piedmont, has a lake. Most of us know the local landmarks, but there’s a secret hidden right behind the homes on Sotelo Avenue: Tyson Lake. Originally created in the early 20th century by George H. Tyson, who dammed a small local creek to build a private swimming hole, it remains one of the city’s bestkept secrets. Today, the lake is strictly private — managed by a neighborhood association rather than the city — and serves as a scenic (some say haunted) retreat for the surrounding homeowners. It’s a staple of local lore and often highlighted during Walking Piedmont tours, but don’t go looking for a public entrance; there isn’t one. The issue has been addressed — do I need to disclose it and how should I do it? pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, August 26, 2026 I’ve called the Bay Area home since 2007, when I moved here from Sacramento to be closer to my then-boyfriend, now husband. I may be a transplant, but our family’s roots in the Bay run deep. My husband’s mother was born in San Francisco and attended Bay Area schools, and his grandfather, Sam Johnstone, founded NorCal Supply in 1950, a family business my husband continues to run today. Grandpa Sam was also a USF Hall of Famer who believed deeply in giving back to the community and his alma mater. That tradition is something we’re proud to continue with our own family. Today, we’re raising three boys who attend Crocker Highlands schools and The Renaissance International School. I’m a proud Platinum Sponsor of my kids’ soccer club and believe that being part of a community means showing up for it, not just living in it. That philosophy carries into my real estate business, too. My selling style may be a little unconventional, and I like it that way. When I returned to real estate full-time, longtime Piedmont residents Steve and Corki Recht gave me a twoweek listing opportunity to sell their home at 83 Hazel Lane. Rather than disrupting their lives with months of preparation, staging and open houses, I took a quiet, highly targeted approach. We sold the home off-market for $5.5 million, all cash, with no staging and no open house. Corki had plenty of friends deeply rooted in Piedmont real estate, but she saw something in me and gave this gal an opportunity. I’m incredibly proud that I exceeded her expectations. I’m high-energy, I think outside the box, and I strongly believe that great real estate marketing has evolved. There are old-school ways of selling homes, and there are new-school ways. I combine relationships and neighborhood knowledge with social media, storytelling, creative exposure and aggressive grassroots marketing to get properties noticed.
