articles.title: Paws through time: Walking on Wednesdays explores Piedmont’s dog park history

pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2026 27 Features Walking on Wednesday Paws through time: Walking on Wednesdays explores Piedmont’s dog park history By Dick Carter Forty-three eager walkers and two canine companions turned out at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s “Dog Days of August” walk—a brisk, history-packed trek celebrating the town’s four-legged friends. Walk leader Sean Brient kicked off the morning by naming Piedmont Park as his favorite local spot, where he and his husband walk their dog, Pip, nearly every day. (Pip herself skipped the excursion, preferring to sleep in.) Unlike the fenced dirt lots common in neighboring cities, Piedmont offers lush green spaces where dogs can run, sniff and socialize while their owners walk the trails. As Sean guided the group down into Piedmont Park, he shared how these parks evolved. When Piedmont incorporated in 1907, early parks were designed as landscaped civic grounds and natural creek corridors, not designated dog parks. In those early decades, dogs roamed without leashes, expected simply to remain “at heel” or under control. A post-World War II surge in dog ownership led to regular routines and informal walking groups. As the city grew, safety concerns prompted Piedmont’s first official leash law in 1970. After a group photo beneath a massive eucalyptus tree, the walkers pushed down the hill, across Witter Field, up the steep 100 block of El Cerrito Avenue, and down Magnolia and upper San Carlos avenues. Pausing on lower San Carlos, Sean pointed out an architectural curiosity: why the street splits into upper and lower sections. To navigate the steep hillside without aggressive excavation, planners split the roadway. The design preserved level driveway access for homes and created a scenic, tree-lined median in between. The group pressed on down Sean Brient Talking to Walkers on Dog Trail in Dracena Park Route map Oakland Avenue, crossed at Jerome Avenue, and wound along Cambridge Way and Ricardo Avenue to Dracena Park, heading straight to the off-leash area to hear the rest of the story. In 1974, the city designated four official off-leash zones: Blair Park and portions of Dracena and Linda parks. Rather than building traditional fenced enclosures, Piedmont selected natural areas already favored by dog owners— wooded spots with trails and minimal interference with athletic fields. Fences were added to Linda Park in the 1990s, though environmental and water-quality issues forced its closure in 2025. Following habitat restoration, Linda Park reopened as an on-leash space. To balance freedom with responsibility, Piedmont added an off-leash permit system in 2000, requiring dog owners to purchase a permit and show proof of licensing and vaccinations. Sean noted that doing his research revealed a sweet local reality: some dog-walking groups have included the same neighbors for decades. The parks aren’t just thoroughfares; they are community hubs. Walking dogs echoes the spirit of Walking on Wednesdays—getting outside, moving together and building connections. After thanking Sean for the lively tour, the group looped along Dracena, Blair, Hillside and Bonita avenues, returning to Exedra Plaza refreshed and inspired. Walking on Wednesdays meets every week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues). The program is free and open to all, and new walkers—along with their K-9 best friends—are always welcome. Registration is required. For more information or to sign up, visit https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or call (510) 420-3070. Among those participating were Rich Harmes, Dick Carter, Shirley Nakao, Mary Carter, Lori Austin, Juliane Jacqueline, Judy Love, Jasmine Cai, Mike Gallant, Sean Brient, Joan Jung with K-9 best friend JT, Kat Lang, Ken Moy, Noemi Alvarado, Sherry Jacobs, Helen Dong, Brian Hamlin, Charlene Louie, June Yee, Albert Chen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Denny McGee, Kristin Howard, Quincy Dong, Ken Hubbert, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Max Becker, Mary Ann Barnes, Mark Davis, Pat Nicholas, Rick Eigenbrode, Brenda Ferrero, Debbie Powell, Jim Kellogg, Dan Scdonis, Alissa Quan, Mary Henderson, Brian Henderson, Peggy Shultz, Sanghi Wagner, and Cathy Laymon. The group was pleased to have City of Piedmont Finance Director Kiran Bawa walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: John Philip Morrison died peacefully on August 7, 2026 at the age of 84. After a long and remarkable life filled with family, friends, accomplishments, laughter and service to others, John Philip Morrison died peacefully surrounded by family on August 7, 2026 at the age of 84. John was born June 1, 1942 in San Francisco, and grew up in Vallejo, California. In his youth he enjoyed spending summers on his grandparent’s ranch, hanging out with his car club and devoting hours of practice to becoming a ranked tennis player, a sport he enjoyed throughout his life. In 1960 John was admitted to Cal with honors and received a degree in Spanish and French. He went on to earn his Masters Degree in Education and an Administrative Credential at San Francisco State University. His remarkable career in education began in his home town at Vallejo High School where he taught Spanish before moving on to Vandenberg High School as a Spanish teacher and tennis coach. After receiving his Administrative Credential, he was hired at Piedmont High School as a dean before coming to Piedmont Middle School as vice principal. He eventually served as principal for 27 years. As middle school principal Mr. Morrison understood that a successful school environment was far more than rules and discipline. John Morrison is a legend. In my life, there are few people that I hold in such high esteem. John Morrison in his Letter Jacket. He served as principal of Piedmont Middle School for 27 years.
articles.title: Obituary

articles.text: John treated Piedmont Middle School like it was his family. He did his best to make sure that he surrounded himself with smart, capable, and kind people. He had an easy laugh and was quick with a joke. He showed interest in everybody and wanted to know their families. If I ever needed anything or I was struggling, I knew that John was there to support me and offer guidance. Not many people know this about him, but John was a fierce ping-pong player. In all his years, he never once lost to a middle school student. He may have lost to a middle school teacher once… –Ted Scherman Retired middle school teacher and tennis coach trict and community. John was also a prominent leader in the antique car community, serving both as the regional president for the Bay Area Horseless Carriage Club and the national president of the Horseless Carriage Club of America. My colleagues may know him best as a longtime volunteer for our Fourth of July committee. Year after year, John arranged all of the antique cars for elected officials, both city council and school board, to ride in for the annual parade. –Betsy Smegal Andersen Mayor, City of Piedmont In the days following his recent passing, it became abundantly clear just how many lives he touched throughout his career. Former students, teachers, staff, colleagues, friends and members of the community remembered a man who was funny, kind, fair and deeply heartfelt in the manner in which he cared for and mentored those around him. His students remembered him not simply as a principal, but as their principal. He had a knack for finding just the right approach to help students feel like they belonged — whether it was involving them in the AV club, playing ping pong with them at lunch time or tutoring them in woodshop. . .just to name a few. Colleagues admired the community he built with his compassion and leadership. Teachers and staff respected his sense of humor and fairness. He was honored by the Rawlings Foundation and received the Educational Inspiration Award and by the Ann Martin Center as a Youth and Education Advocate in a Lifetime Achievement Award Ceremony in 2007. John’s love of old cars brought another community into his life. Over the years he occupied almost every board position in the Bay Area Horseless Carriage Club and in the National Horseless Carriage Club of America, serving as their President in 2002 and Chairman of the Board in 2003. He appreciated beautifully preserved automobiles and the lifelong friendships he made with people who were also passionate about them. What might have begun as a conversation about car parts at swap-meets could quickly become a friendship that lasted for decades. He delighted in chauffeuring newlyweds, especially former students, in his beautifully restored 1905 and 1913 Cadillacs. I had the pleasure to spend more than 25 years working with John on the 4th of July Parade. That is a long time to spend with someone, and every moment with John was exciting because he was excited. He knew every car and he knew every driver, and he worked meticulously on describing each vehicle. He mailed, he emailed and he called, checking his list twice. It was perfection! And then on the day of the parade he was there to welcome them, get them in the lineup and off they went, one by one. John and I became wonderful friends during this time as well as other times of the year. His smile was always one that said ‘I am so glad to see you!‘ Memories are treasured because of people like John. He is forever on my mind and in my heart. –Carla Betts 4th of July Parade Committee Chair for 25 years Betty C. Howard Award winner John Morrison and City Volunteer of the Year Carla Betts at the City’s volunteer reception in 2016. For several summers when he wasn’t working on home restorations, he and Carolee organized and chaperoned bicycling trips for local youth to England, France, Ireland and Holland. John loved travel and especially the evenings spent in youth hostels interacting with foreign students. Each evening the students cheered as he handily won match after match of ping-pong often landing shots with his non-dominant hand or on his knees! Flashing his ever-present rascally smile, he also enjoyed entertaining international travelers by telling his famous “dad jokes” in English, French and Spanish. You can be sure he was laughing the loudest! As meaningful as his career and extra-curricular hobbies were, it was John’s family that was the center of his life. His exuberant joy was ever-present whenever he spent time with his family. He was married for 43 years to the love of his life, Carolee. He was best friend to his brother, Lane, and adored by his sister, Polly. He was a beloved father, step-father, grandfather, father-in-law and great grandpa. He was Uncle John to many nieces and nephews. John is predeceased by his parents Edwin and Pauline, and his daughter-in-law ConI was blessed to have known John for over 50 years; first when I was a student at Piedmont High and later as a colleague and dear friend. He was a consummate cheerleader for those around him…. Family, friends, faculty, community members, and students. His contributions to Piedmont are legendary. His gentle, wise and supportive nature permeated all he did. John was happiest when he was helping others, often working quietly behind the scenes. He was proud of Piedmont and the many organizations who had the benefit of his devotion. Piedmont has lost an icon; a citizen in the truest sense of the word. And I have lost a treasured friend. –Mark Delventhal Former longtime Piedmont Recreation Director John Morrison also served our community for two decades as the beloved principal of Piedmont Middle School. He was well known for hiring amazing teachers, including my mother and staff, and building a strong sense of teamwork and belonging. After his retirement, he stayed active and supportive of our school disHis love of cars became part of Piedmont’s beloved Fourth of July Parade. John helped organize and lead the parade of antique and vintage automobiles down Highland Avenue for many years. He was honored by the city of Piedmont to serve as Parade Grand Marshal with his wife Carolee in 2001. It was a perfect fit for him: old cars, good friends, and an entire community gathered together. As a member of Piedmont Community Church, he served on the pastoral nominating committee, participated in several homebuild trips in Mexico, putting his Spanish fluency and handyman skills to good use, and assisted with the Senior Citizens Program on Monday mornings. John Morrison in antique car

It was defined by the people he gathered around him, the lives he helped, the friendships he made, and the laughter he brought along the way. John leaves behind more than memories; he leaves people who are better off because he has been a part of their lives. A Celebration of Life is scheduled for Saturday, September 12th, at 2 pm in the John Morrison Gymnasium at Piedmont Middle School, 740 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont. Donations, if you wish, may be made in John’s memory to the Alzheimer’s Foundation, the Piedmont Education Foundation or the Piedmont Community Church. I was blessed to have known John for over 50 years; first when I was a student at Piedmont High and later as a colleague and dear friend. He was a consummate cheerleader for those around him…. Family, friends, faculty, community members, and students. His contributions to Piedmont are legendary. His gentle, wise and supportive nature permeated all he did. John was happiest when he was helping others, often working quietly behind the scenes. He was proud of Piedmont and the many organizations who had the benefit of his devotion. Piedmont has lost an icon; a citizen in the truest sense of the word. And I have lost a treasured friend. –Mark Delventhal Former longtime Piedmont Recreation Director John Morrison also served our community for two decades as the beloved principal of Piedmont Middle School. He was well known for hiring amazing teachers, including my mother and staff, and building a strong sense of teamwork and belonging. After his retirement, he stayed active and supportive of our school disHis love of cars became part of Piedmont’s beloved Fourth of July Parade. John helped organize and lead the parade of antique and vintage automobiles down Highland Avenue for many years. He was honored by the city of Piedmont to serve as Parade Grand Marshal with his wife Carolee in 2001. It was a perfect fit for him: old cars, good friends, and an entire community gathered together. As a member of Piedmont Community Church, he served on the pastoral nominating committee, participated in several homebuild trips in Mexico, putting his Spanish fluency and handyman skills to good use, and assisted with the Senior Citizens Program on Monday mornings. articles.text: at first, but once they start pedaling, with the bay breeze on their backs, before they know it, they’ve gone farther than they thought possible. That sense of accomplishment builds lasting confidence. As a parent, I value the unstructured outdoor time Scouts provides. So much of modern childhood is scheduled and directed. On a campout, once tents are set up, kids get to explore, figure things out, and entertain themselves, making their own fun. I love being part of it as both a parent and a den leader. Watching Scouts progress from first-time clumsiness to proficiency is a joy. It also connects parents; building friendships on the trail or around a campfire lets us create experiences none of us could easily provide alone. They love camping — Mt. Diablo is a favorite spot — and biking on the Bay Trail. They especially enjoy learning skills that feel a little dangerous, like using knives, building campfires, cooking, and archery. When my children camp under the trees and stars, a wonderful shift occurs: screens disappear from their thoughts. When children are given a compelling outdoor environment, they’re too busy having fun engaging with nature. This is true for both my fourth-grade daughter and my seventh-grade son, who has since moved on to Scouts. Following in her brother’s footsteps, my daughter, already busy with swimming and ballet, fell in love with Cubs in her own right. articles.text: At the City Council meeting on Monday, August 17, Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies gave a presentation to council members on issues of concern with e-bikes in the community. Shavies pointed out the lack of education on e-bikes and is concerned that parents may not know what they’ve purchased. California recognizes three different e-bike classes: • Class 1: Pedal assist, up to 20 mph, no minimum age, helmet required under 18 • Class 2: Throttle & Pedal assist, up to 20 mph, no minimum age, and helmet is required if under 16 • Class 3: Pedal assist, up to 28 mph, minimum age 16, helmet required for all ages Shavies and his staff are seeing e-vehicles that surpass these classes and California’s legal parameters. The red flags for parents are bikes that lack operable pedals, modified throttles, and energy to increase their power and speed significantly. These are classified as e-motos. “California DMV now specifically recognizes off-highway electric motorcycles or e-motos as off-highway motor vehicles, subject to certain OHV requirements. That distinction is important because parents may see two wheels and an electric motor and reasonably think I bought my child an e-bike. But what they actually purchase may have capabilities much closer to a motorcycle,” said Chief Shavies. articles.text: This summer, a group of young soccer players from Piedmont traveled to Sweden and Denmark to compete in two of the world’s largest and most respected international youth soccer tournaments: the Gothia Cup and the Dana Cup. The local players included Eloise McDowell (PSC GP U12), Pierce McDowell (PSC BP U12), Kate Nealon (AFC), Josh Nealon (LAMO), Lola Ruthven (AFC), Kellan Ruthven (PSC BP U12), Ramsey Stull (PSC BP U12), and Troy Wallway (PSC BP U12). The players represented National Soccer Academy (NSA), an organization that has brought teams to these prestigious tournaments for 35 years. The trip gave the Piedmont athletes an opportunity to compete internationally, experience Scandinavian culture, and build friendships with players from around the world. The Gothia Cup, held annually in Gothenburg, Sweden, began in 1975 and has grown into the world’s largest and most international youth soccer tournament. In a typical year, approximately 1,900 teams from about 75 countries compete in nearly 5,000 matches played on more than 100 fields throughout Gothenburg. One of the tournament’s highlights is its opening ceremony, during which thousands of players enter the stadium wearing their club uniforms and carrying their national flags. The celebration creates an atmosphere similar to a major professional sporting event. Although the level of competition is high, the Gothia Cup is about more than winning. Its broader mission is to bring young people together regardless of nationality, religion, or background, using soccer as a shared language. Following the Gothia Cup, the players traveled to Hjørring, Denmark, for the Dana Cup. Founded in 1982, the Dana Cup is Denmark’s largest sporting event and one of the world’s leading youth soccer tournaments. Each summer, it welcomes approximately 1,000 teams and 20,000 players and participants, along with thousands of supporters, referees, and volunteers. Teams from around 56 countries take part. The Dana Cup begins with an opening procession through the streets of Hjørring. Players march together wearing their club colors and carrying flags before entering the stadium. The tournament offers age divisions for both boys and girls and is known for its international atmosphere, well-organized matches, quality fields, and emphasis on equality, friendship, respect, and unity. Competing against teams from different countries introduced the Piedmont players to a variety of playing styles. Some opponents relied on speed and physical play, while others emphasized technical ability, possession, and quick passing. The experience challenged the players to adjust their strategies, communicate effectively, work together, and remain confident under pressure. The benefits of the trip also extended beyond the soccer field. Traveling internationally with a team encouraged responsibility, independence, time management, and respect for other cultures. For the Piedmont players, the Gothia Cup and Dana Cup were much more than ordinary soccer tournaments. The experience gave them a chance to test their abilities at a high level, represent their local clubs and community, and create friendships and memories that may last a lifetime.
articles.title: Piedmont youth soccer players compete in Sweden and Denmark

articles.text: Caltrans has published its findings on the potential effects of lifting the truck ban on Highway I-580. The study indicates that there would be no benefits for residents in East or West Oakland in terms of a healthier environment. However, it highlights significant advantages for the freight industry. Caltrans has released a feedback survey for residents to voice their opinions. It can be found at the following link: https://www.surveymonkey. com/r/i580TAS-Survey. According to the 2025 WOCAP Report. Heavy and medium-duty trucks on I-880 contribute the least PM 2.5, at levels the EPA does not consider harmful. Local streets and industrial sites account for most pollution, as does road dust. Whether trucks use 880 or both freeways will not change ‘local’ conditions. Truck Volumes The Study estimates that if the truck ban were lifted today, we would see some 4,400 trucks per day on I-580. Over a 16-hour day (6 a.m.- 6 p.m. is when most truck travel occurs), that amounts to one truck every 13 seconds. State Route 13 (the Warren Freeway) would see 900 trucks (compared to 400 now). Tunnel Road would expect 270 heavy trucks; Hesperian, Hegenberger and 150th would each see 400+ trucks each day. Other arterials such as High St, Park, 14th Avenue and Fruitvale were not deemed significant but, as the study team acknowledged, the model-assessed impacts may not be reality. Even a small number of additional trucks on some of these streets may have outsized impacts. Ashby Avenue could expect 190 additional trucks and Grand Ave about 140 more trucks between Harrison and MacArthur Blvd. Speed Lifting the truck ban on I-580 would result in higher speeds for trucks on all freeways in the network. Some 67% could travel at speeds of over 60mph (only 49% can do so with the ban). The commercial speed limit on California highways is 55mph. The study noted truckers would need to ‘be more careful’ in tighter turns while driving on 580s on and off ramps. The study flagged this: “Increasing the number of trucks traveling at speeds greater than 55mph…could increase the severity of truck-involved collisions…” It also acknowledged speeds on local streets could increase, which presents a challenge to ‘determine how changes in truck speeds could impact collision severity. Air Quality The Study’s fundamental premise was to evaluate potential improvements in air quality in East and West Oakland, with a focus on improved health outcomes. The finding that lifting the ban on I-580 would not improve health outcomes for these communities is relevant. Exposure to Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5, a measure of air quality, shows that the Study Area as a whole has equivalent exposure. Structural Capacity The Study’s assertion that I-580 is structurally capable of handling heavy-duty trucks was based on the overhead clearances being sufficient and on its use by buses. The 100 or so buses that use I-580 daily weigh 45- 54 pounds. This is not equivalent to thousands of trucks weighing up to 80,000 pounds. Highway 880 was built in the late 1950s specifically as the region’s freight corridor. The Port, Airport, and Oakland-San Leandro-Hayward area industrial hubs evolved in tandem. Highway 880 is maintained as a ‘state of the art’ freight corridor. Highway 580, built just a few years later, 1) replaced the segment of MacArthur Blvd that previously served as Highway 50, and 2) was designated as a ‘Scenic Highway’ and NOT for trucks. One of the agreements was to honor the 1951 truck ban between Grand Ave and San Leandro. The Study’s assertions about the number of trucks on both highways with and without the ban, today and in 2035, use a dated traffic model. It also ignores disincentives that providing new capacity promulgates. For example: • The Port’s freight tonnage today is 15-20% lower than in 2016, but the number of heavyduty trucks serving the Port increased 5-10%. • The trucking industry structurally adapts to increased capacity, and the trend is for smaller, more frequent deliveries with more trucks. The fundamentals of road congestion law and economics tell us industry scales operations to capacity. • Carriers that currently move goods at night will shift to daytime hours • More road capacity disadvantages rail and other clean strategies, economically Implying lifting the truck ban on I-580 will improve health in East and West Oakland is inaccurate and misleading. Lifting the truck ban on I-580 will not change the number of trucks or the most congested parts. Conditions will worsen for 580 while 880 will see minor improvements. Only the freight industry wins. Several elected officials have taken a stand against lifting the ban. The “No Big Rigs” organization hopes to get all the area State senators, assembly representatives, County and local officials to do the same.
articles.title: Are 4,400 trucks in I-580’s future?

They’ve got to be defined by the first word – news.” – Arthur Sulzberger Jr. b. 1951 New York Times puplisher Are 4,400 trucks in I-580’s future? By Wendy Silvani Caltrans has published its findings on the potential effects of lifting the truck ban on Highway I-580. The study indicates that there would be no benefits for residents in East or West Oakland in terms of a healthier environment. However, it highlights significant advantages for the freight industry. Caltrans has released a feedback survey for residents to voice their opinions. It can be found at the following link: https://www.surveymonkey. com/r/i580TAS-Survey. According to the 2025 WOCAP Report. Heavy and medium-duty trucks on I-880 contribute the least PM 2.5, at levels the EPA does not consider harmful. Local streets and industrial sites account for most pollution, as does road dust. Whether trucks use 880 or both freeways will not change ‘local’ conditions. Truck Volumes The Study estimates that if the truck ban were lifted today, we would see some 4,400 trucks per day on I-580. Over a 16-hour day (6 a.m.- 6 p.m. is when most truck travel occurs), that amounts to one truck every 13 seconds. State Route 13 (the Warren Freeway) would see 900 trucks (compared to 400 now). Tunnel Road would expect 270 heavy trucks; Hesperian, Hegenberger and 150th would each see 400+ trucks each day. Other arterials such as High St, Park, 14th Avenue and Fruitvale were not deemed significant but, as the study team acknowledged, the model-assessed impacts may not be reality. Even a small number of additional trucks on some of these streets may have outsized impacts. Ashby Avenue could expect 190 additional trucks and Grand Ave about 140 more trucks between Harrison and MacArthur Blvd. Speed Lifting the truck ban on I-580 would result in higher speeds for trucks on all freeways in the network. Some 67% could travel at speeds of over 60mph (only 49% can do so with the ban). The commercial speed limit on California highways is 55mph. The study noted truckers would need to ‘be more careful’ in tighter turns while driving on 580s on and off ramps. The study flagged this: “Increasing the number of trucks traveling at speeds greater than 55mph…could increase the severity of truck-involved collisions…” It also acknowledged speeds on local streets could increase, which presents a challenge to ‘determine how changes in truck speeds could impact collision severity. Air Quality The Study’s fundamental premise was to evaluate potential improvements in air quality in East and West Oakland, with a focus on improved health outcomes. The finding that lifting the ban on I-580 would not improve health outcomes for these communities is relevant. Exposure to Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5, a measure of air quality, shows that the Study Area as a whole has equivalent exposure. Structural Capacity The Study’s assertion that I-580 is structurally capable of handling heavy-duty trucks was based on the overhead clearances being sufficient and on its use by buses. The 100 or so buses that use I-580 daily weigh 45- 54 pounds. This is not equivalent to thousands of trucks weighing up to 80,000 pounds. Highway 880 was built in the late 1950s specifically as the region’s freight corridor. The Port, Airport, and Oakland-San Leandro-Hayward area industrial hubs evolved in tandem. Highway 880 is maintained as a ‘state of the art’ freight corridor. Highway 580, built just a few years later, 1) replaced the segment of MacArthur Blvd that previously served as Highway 50, and 2) was designated as a ‘Scenic Highway’ and NOT for trucks. One of the agreements was to honor the 1951 truck ban between Grand Ave and San Leandro. The Study’s assertions about the number of trucks on both highways with and without the ban, today and in 2035, use a dated traffic model. It also ignores disincentives that providing new capacity promulgates. For example: • The Port’s freight tonnage today is 15-20% lower than in 2016, but the number of heavyduty trucks serving the Port increased 5-10%. • The trucking industry structurally adapts to increased capacity, and the trend is for smaller, more frequent deliveries with more trucks. The fundamentals of road congestion law and economics tell us industry scales operations to capacity. • Carriers that currently move goods at night will shift to daytime hours • More road capacity disadvantages rail and other clean strategies, economically Implying lifting the truck ban on I-580 will improve health in East and West Oakland is inaccurate and misleading. Lifting the truck ban on I-580 will not change the number of trucks or the most congested parts. Conditions will worsen for 580 while 880 will see minor improvements. Only the freight industry wins. Several elected officials have taken a stand against lifting the ban. The “No Big Rigs” organization hopes to get all the area State senators, assembly representatives, County and local officials to do the same. READ IT IN THE POST

The city will show the movie Flow on a large projector in the Main Park starting at 8 p.m. The food trucks will range from sweet and savory foods along Highland Avenue. The food truck lineup is: Golden Gate Gyro; Chick—Go; Shamal Burgers & More; Lola’s Spanish Cuisine; Yummi BBQ; Bay Area Halal Eats; More Life Ice. Bring a blanket and low chairs. articles.text: Giovanni and Francesca are bonded 2-year-olds described as “funny, sweet, and cuddly.” This charming duo are a joy to have around! Gio is a “gentle giant” who loves belly rubs and will purr in your lap so enthusiastically that he’s been known to roll right onto the floor! He has tiny vampire fangs, a raspy whisper-meow, and silently moves through the house until playtime, when he stalks wand toys. Although he’s much bigger than his sister, he never bullies her for food, lets her take her turn in play, and even shares treats! Franny is a playful little dynamo with an impressive vocabulary of squeaks, mews, and trills. She loves staying near people, whether she’s sitting on your desk while you work, snuggling against you on the couch, or asking to chase after her favorite feather wand. She’s even invented her Adopt Giovanni and Francesca through Cat Town own game of tossing a foam soccer ball down the stairs and chasing after it! These two will need a little extra time to feel comfortable with new people, but once you’re in their circle, prepare for plenty of love! Giovanni and Francesca are neutered and spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: Radar is a German Shepherd Dog mix of about a year and a half with a wonderful balance of independence and affection. He enjoys exploring the world at his own pace, and happily returns to his favorite people for love and attention. He enjoys pets and sometimes even resting his head in a lap. This 70-pound cutie is smart and treat motivated. He plays well with other canines in his doggie playgroup, displaying appropriate social skills with other dogs. Radar enjoys sniffari walks and investigating the world. He is making progress on his loose-leash walking with guidance. Radar could join your existing pack, or be your cherished solo dog. Come meet him at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 7 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or SunRadar is an independent explorer with a snuggly side day between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Radar must be brought to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.

articles.text: On Wednesday, August 12 Piedmont School Board held its first regularly scheduled meeting of the school year. The meeting’s headline event was the official naming of Donald Evans as interim superintendent. Changes to the faculty were noted and Facilities Director Pete Palmer gave a summary of projects completed over the summer. The meeting began with a new speaker. PHS math teacher Sam Coburn is now the co-president of the teachers union, APT, and will represent district teachers alongside Dr. Elise Marks. The co-presidents have welcomed 31 new teachers to the district this year. Marks said it was “by far the largest number current teachers can remember.” Marks conjectured it was the largest in the history of the district aside from years when new schools were opened. The changes may be most acutely felt at the middle school, where there are 11 new staff members following the retirement of seven teachers. There are also many changes within class assignment at PMS, as many are teaching new classes. “Of course we have our bellto-bell no cell phones policy,” said Coburn. “So far students seem to have gotten the message and understand what is expected of them.” Coburn announced new standardized STAR testing for every grade level multiple times a year, provided by Renaissance. With new AP and Honors courses available at PHS, Marks cautioned this year would “be a bit of a living experiment.” “Workloads in honors classes are going to take a serious step up,” said Marks. “The challenge in terms of intellectual demand and in terms of sheer homework time is going to be fierce. Some sophomores have signed up for something accelerated every single period of the day.” A presentation by Facilities Director Pete Palmer summarized 25 construction projects completed over the summer. Priority 1 projects included: new asphalt on P.E. Hill, the modernization of three elevators, a TK classroom and bathroom at Wildwood, and the rekeying of all classrooms for the first time in 20 years (around 1000 doorways). Palmer expects a wet winter this year and accordingly, there was some roof repair at Havens. Palmer defined Priority 2 projects as items that seek to avoid huge costs before facilities fail. “Stephanie [Griffith] and her crew replaced the core switch from the district office over to the STEAM building. That basically runs the entire internet for our whole district, so that was quite an accomplishment,” said Palmer. More changes include the addition of two “jumbotrons” inside Binks Rawlings Gym. Thanks to PEF funding, an observation deck was installed at the Witter softball field. A new play structure was built at Havens School with funding from Havens Parents Club. An itemized list with costs of all the facility projects conducted over summer can be viewed at: Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/Attachment. aspx?S=36030373&AID=164677 1&MID=75386 Courtesy of PHS Principal David Yoshihara’s parent newsletter Smore.com/n/wk21b A graphic illustrates the recourse for students’ usage of smart phones on the PHS campus. Havens students received a new playground over the summer.

Registration for the Fall 2026 session of Piedmont Adult School opens Monday, August 17 at 9:00 a.m. Classes begin Monday, September 14 and run through December 19. articles.text: Dr. Donald Evans was welcomed back to Piedmont and confirmed as the interim school superintendent during the first school board meeting of the year, on August 12. Evans was on hand to symbolically take the torch from Jennifer Hawn and begin his second one-year term guiding the school district. “There are so many emotions going through my mind right now. I feel so good about being here, this is my family,“ said Evans. Board President Ruchi Medhekar called the approval of Evans a full circle moment, and characterized the work with Evans as “joyful and full of laughter.” “[Evans has] deep expertise, and a true understanding of this community and what this community needs,” said Medhekar. The return of Evans received the stamp of approval from Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) Co-President Elise Marks as well. “Dr. Donald Evans, who we know from a very happy experience in 2022-23, is an incredibly steady hand at the wheel as we navigate this time of transition. It’s a huge relief to have him joining us again. We are eager to get back to work together,” said Marks. Board member Lindsay Thomasson called Evans’ arrival “the silver lining” to Supt. Jennifer Hawn’s quick departure. Both Thomasson and Medhekar started their board of education tenures at the start of 2023 when Evans was at the helm of the district. “You came to Piedmont four years ago when the district was on extremely shaky ground. I’m happy to share that you are now walking into a much stronger and more stable district,” said Thomasson. “This is a special place and so having the opportunity to come back and continue your [Hawn’s] work and the board’s vision and mission for this district and to work with all of you again, means so much to me,” said Evans. Medhekar informed the public that the board did their due Dr. Donald Evans returns as interim school superintendent. diligence in the hiring process. She stated that the board interviewed two other candidates for the Interim Superintendent in the two weeks following Hawn’s announcement. “I’m excited and joyful, I’ll add a little bit of heart to that joy and try to mix it up and create this amazing environment that you already have here,” said Evans.
articles.title: School board welcomes return of Donald Evans as interim superintendent

articles.text: On Saturday, September 26, from 6:30 to 9:15 p.m., community members will have a unique opportunity to explore that question with some of the people working at the forefront of artificial intelligence. “AI: Will It Save or End the World?” will take place at the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School and will feature a screening of the acclaimed 2026 documentary The AI Doc, followed by a live panel discussion and audience Q&A. The panel brings together four technology and media leaders: • Jeff Bleich: The Chief Legal Officer at Anthropic, brings a perspective from one of the world’s leading AI companies and from his extensive experience in law, government, and technology. • Marco Casalaina: VP Products, Core AI and AI Futurist at Microsoft, leads Microsoft’s AI Futures team, which identifies emerging AI trends and develops products for the next generation of artificial intelligence. He previously led teams across Azure AI, including Azure OpenAI, Responsible AI and AI Studio. • Clara Shih: founder of New Work Foundation and advisor to Meta Business AI, is the former CEO of Salesforce AI and a TIME100 AI honoree. • Emily Chang: host and executive producer at Bloomberg Media and one of the country’s best-known technology journalists, will moderate the discussion. The evening is intended not as a technical seminar, but as a community conversation about questions increasingly confronting families, students, educators and businesses. Is AI developing too quickly? How will it change education and the careers today’s students are preparing for? Which jobs will disappear, which will be transformed, and which new ones will emerge? Can increasingly powerful AI systems be trusted? And how can society capture the enormous potential benefits of AI while managing its risks? Those questions may be especially relevant for high school students, who are encouraged to attend, as the film and panel will address how AI could affect university choices, careers and the skills young people will need in a rapidly changing economy. The program will begin with a screening of The AI Doc, which examines the opportunities and dangers presented by artificial intelligence. Following the film, Chang will lead the panelists in a discussion before opening the conversation to questions directly from the audience. For a community located just a few miles from the center of the AI revolution, the subject is particularly close to home. Whether you believe artificial intelligence will usher in an era of unprecedented innovation, worry that the technology is advancing faster than society can manage, or simply want to understand what all the excitement is about, the evening offers Piedmont residents a chance to hear directly from people helping shape AI’s future. Sponsored by Piedmont Unified Schools, Piedmont Parents Network, and Piedmont Makers, tickets are available with a $50 donation per person, with all proceeds going to Piedmont Boosters and PUSD. Learn more and buy tickets at: https://piedmontstore.org/products/ai-will-it-save-or-end-theworld.
articles.title: Piedmont AI event asks: Will Artificial Intelligence save—or end—the world?

The panel brings together four technology and media leaders: • Jeff Bleich: The Chief Legal Officer at Anthropic, brings a perspective from one of the world’s leading AI companies and from his extensive experience in law, government, and technology. • Marco Casalaina: VP Products, Core AI and AI Futurist at Microsoft, leads Microsoft’s AI Futures team, which identifies emerging AI trends and develops products for the next generation of artificial intelligence. He previously led teams across Azure AI, including Azure OpenAI, Responsible AI and AI Studio. • Clara Shih: founder of New Work Foundation and advisor to Meta Business AI, is the former CEO of Salesforce AI and a TIME100 AI honoree. • Emily Chang: host and executive producer at Bloomberg Media and one of the country’s best-known technology journalists, will moderate the discussion. The evening is intended not as a technical seminar, but as a community conversation about questions increasingly confronting families, students, educators and businesses. Is AI developing too quickly? How will it change education and the careers today’s students are preparing for? Which jobs will disappear, which will be transformed, and which new ones will emerge? Can increasingly powerful AI systems be trusted? And how can society capture the enormous potential benefits of AI while managing its risks? Those questions may be especially relevant for high school students, who are encouraged to attend, as the film and panel will address how AI could affect university choices, careers and the skills young people will need in a rapidly changing economy. The program will begin with a screening of The AI Doc, which examines the opportunities and dangers presented by artificial intelligence. Following the film, Chang will lead the panelists in a discussion before opening the conversation to questions directly from the audience. For a community located just a few miles from the center of the AI revolution, the subject is particularly close to home. Whether you believe artificial intelligence will usher in an era of unprecedented innovation, worry that the technology is advancing faster than society can manage, or simply want to understand what all the excitement is about, the evening offers Piedmont residents a chance to hear directly from people helping shape AI’s future. Sponsored by Piedmont Unified Schools, Piedmont Parents Network, and Piedmont Makers, tickets are available with a $50 donation per person, with all proceeds going to Piedmont Boosters and PUSD. Learn more and buy tickets at: https://piedmontstore.org/products/ai-will-it-save-or-end-theworld. AI WILL IT SAVE OR END THE WORLD? FOUR OF THE WORLD’S LEADING AI EXPERTS. ONE STAGE. ON NIGHT. RIGHT HERE IN PIEDMONT.

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads’ Club (WWDC) invites the larger Piedmont school community to their Welcome Back BBQ at Wildwood’s lower playground this Thursday, August 20, 5:30-7:30 p.m. Volunteer dads will handle everything, including supply shopping, setup, grilling, working the cashier and even cleaning up after the event. The annual Welcome Back BBQ is a fun community event that kicks off the new school year and welcomes families back to Wildwood. Keep an eye out for dads in fun costumes, and the always-popular inverted dunk tank may even make an appearance, weather permitting. Kids of all ages will have the lower playground at their disposal for games and play mixing backto-school and an endless summer. Despite ever-increasing food costs, WWDC makes a concerted effort to keep the BBQ prices low so that families can relax and enjoy a fun evening together without breaking the bank. The menu includes burgers, hot dogs and veggie burgers with sides and condiments to match. The Dads Club is excited to kick off another year of fundraising and community-building. The 2026-27 WWDC officers are: • Co-Presidents: Alex Danoff and Sergio Serna • Vice President: Darren Rees • Secretary: Dave Rochwerger • Treasurer: Nimesh Singh • Social Chair: Scott Zengel • Officer Emeritus: Grady Snyder All funds raised will support the school – recent projects at Wildwood that WWDC has helped fund include new water fountains/water bottle fillers, a new A/V system in the auditorium, and PE supplies. For more information on the Wildwood Dads’ Club and to join the email list go to Wildwooddadsclub.org. articles.text: August’s iteration of the Indie Next List has a a good variety of genres, with many new powerhouse fiction reads for summer. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving and supporting their local communities with brick and mortar locales to buy books and give patronage to literature. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland 699 Bellevue Avenue, Oakland; 452-2259 Fairyland has just the right stuff to spark a child’s imagination. The park is open Wednesday-Sunday; 10:00 a.m.-4:00 p.m. From the rides to the petting zoo and Alice in Wonderland maze, a day of fun is a few blocks away from Piedmont. All shows on the stage of Fairyland’s Storybook Puppet Theater are original productions, featuring scripts, costumes, music, and sets designed by their talented puppeteers. Check website for show schedules and special events. Cartoon Art Museum 781 Beach Street, San Francisco Kids will bubble up at the chance to learn about cartooning at the Cartoon Art Museum. The museum houses 7,000 original pieces in its permanent collection. Kids of all ages and skill levels can join cartooning workshops at Cartoon Art Museum, the oldest such museum on the West Coast. Stop by on a First Tuesday of the month, which are “pay what you wish” days at the museum. They are open daily, except Wednesday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

articles.text: The shoulder pads and helmets are on for the Piedmont High football team as they get ready for the season opener on Friday, August 28 against Napa at Witter Field. The Highlanders return after reaching last year’s Division 7 North Coast Section Championship, but this year they have big positions to fill on offense and defense. Piedmont’s big changes start at the quarterback position after Jimmy Lagios transferred to Monte Vista. Head coach Jordan Seiden still hasn’t named the starter between sophomore Cyrus Emanuelson and junior Jonah Cha-Foster. He will get a better look at how each thrower handles live reps in their Saturday, August 22 scrimmage with Redwood Christian, Emerald, Weston Ranch, and Alameda. “This is the first time we won’t have a Lagios at the quarterback spot in five years. Cyrus has come so far, I can’t even quantify how far he’s developed. Jonah is an incredible athlete and might be our fastest player, Rehan Mumtaz included, who set the school record in the 100,” Seiden said. Emanuelson is making the step up from junior varsity and has been a consistent face at practice since the spring program opened up at the end of the 2026 school year. He’s been working with a quarterbacks coach, and has shown noticeable improvement with his delivery and poise. “When I got the news Jimmy was leaving, I started putting in a lot of work. At first, I didn’t have a lot of confidence and didn’t think I could compete at a varsity level. Over time, I started working with a coach and was getting a lot of support from my teammates. Now, my confidence is way up,” Emanuelson said. Cha-Foster is a much different type of quarterback as a dualthreat weapon. Although he had less time with the team due to his baseball schedule this summer, he has varsity experience as their primary backup last season and gives an added wrinkle to the offense with his running ability. “I’m just going day-by-day, keeping my head down, and looking to my teammates for support. I played baseball over the summer, but in between games I was throwing the football and studying the playbook, so I’m feeling prepared. I’m a dualStaff Photos Cyrus Emanuelson, a sophomore, is competing for the starting quarterback role. Jonah Cha-Foster, a junior, is also battling for the starting quarterback spot. threat player, when I’m in we do a lot of RPOs and read-options,” Cha-Foster said. Both quarterbacks effectively split first-team reps in practice this week. Seiden goes into the scrimmage keeping a sharp eye on the quarterback position, knowing it’s an important time for either player to take control. “I’m focused on my own game. My mentality is to just keep competing, keep improving, making the right reads, the right decisions, and just be confident in what I’m doing,” Emanuelson said. “I just need to do what I do and compete. I know I’m a good player, so I just have to believe in myself,” Cha-Foster said. As for the rest of the offense, Rehan Mumtaz makes the obvious step up the depth chart following the graduation of running back Xavier Henderson. George Saunders will be a focal point on both offense and defense. After that, Diego Hurwitz and Max Fujimoto will feature more heavily at wide receiver, while the Post’s 2026 Sophomore of the Year, George Saunders, is also expected to get more targets. “It’s all about the work and working as a team. As an upperclassmen, you have to take initiative and point players in the right direction. I hope to get some targets on offense and do what I did last year on defense. I’m definitely getting more involved offensively at the receiver spot,” Saunders said. Seiden called Saunders the defensive Player of the Year in 2025 when he earned first-team All-League honors after notching four interceptions. He’ll continue being a focal point of the defense. “George was our defensive MVP from last year, he’s going to be incredible on both sides. He’ll play a little bit of everything on defense, we can put him anywhere on the field,” Seiden said. Seiden also thinks this could be one of their strongest defenses in his five years coaching the team. “Defense will be a catalyst for us. If we can hold teams to 14 points, we’re going to be great. The secondary might be our most talented group we’ve had; Mateo Long and Owen Curran will be our corners, Diego Hurwitz at safety, Mason Gray in that rotation, George can play everywhere, and Colby Hong is an AllLeague returner at linebacker,” Seiden said.
articles.title: Football team ramping up for season opener

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team is back in action for the 2026 season with its first official matches set for Saturday, August 22 at the James Logan Tournament in Union City. Piedmont, the defending Western Alameda County Conference champions, must replace five players from last year’s roster, but brings back most of the lineup. At singles, Piedmont must replace their former No. 2 and 3 starters, Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum. Ella Ruthven, who was the Post’s Honorable Mention for Freshman of the Year, will enter her second season at the No. 1 spot, while senior Faith Chin bumps up to No. 2. “Ella will be our No. 1 again. Faith Chin is returning and will be our No. 2,” coach Jim Landes said. Landes said incoming freshman Maddie Huynh is emerging in the order. She’s the younger sister of Samantha Huynh who graduated last year and appeared at No. 1 doubles. Junior Leela Sivakumar will line up at No. 4 singles, a spot she held last season. “Maddie is a freshman and is very good, she’ll be my No. 3. Our fourth singles player will probably be Leela, who also played at No. 4 last year,” Landes said. With the doubles lineup, Class of 2026 graduates include former No. 1 starter Samantha Huynh, the No. 2 doubles team of Maddie Tran and Inara Mehta, along with Lila Rosen who typically appeared with the No. 3 team. Piedmont brings back Emma Chan as one half of the No. 1 doubles team that won last year’s WACC Individual Tournament Doubles title, while she is currently teaming up with Chiara Silvio – who is a junior and entering her third year on the team. Doubles could have a slew of first-year varsity players making an impact, including sophomore Ellia Sharafi, junior Layla Reed-Miguel, sophomore Mai Pham, and sophomore Penelope Welch. Landes said they are still figuring things out on the doubles order. “Doubles is much more muddled at the moment. I have 10 girls and they are all pretty good. I was thinking Emma and Chiara would be our No. 1 doubles, but they lost in a challenge match yesterday to Ellia and Layla. We may juggle the teams, but it looks like Mai and Penelope will also start,” Landes said. Piedmont has a pair of scrimmages against Los Lomas yesterday, and Miramonte today, August 19. Then they will travel to the James Logan Tournament on Saturday, August 22 for the official start of its season. PHS will get its Western Alameda County Conference schedule started on September 16 when hosting Berkeley. Landes thinks Alameda and Bishop O’Dowd will be their biggest competition in defending their league title. “We should be good against Castro Valley and Berkeley again. Alameda is going to be tough and O’Dowd may have some new players. We beat O’Dowd twice last year, but it’s going to be closer this year. We split with Alameda last year, but they might be strong,” Landes said. Staff Photos Emma Chan won last year’s WACC Doubles title. She returns as a senior. Ella Ruthven returns to the No. 1 singles spot as a sophomore. Faith Chin, a senior, locks down the No. 2 singles spot.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team returns after going 16-9 last season. They will host their first match in Piedmont since 2019. For the first time since 2019, Piedmont High will feature its water polo teams in town at the Piedmont Pool across the street from the school. It’s a hallmark moment for the team that has emerged as a perpetual contender in the Western Alameda County Conference and North Coast Section despite not having a pool at home. “It’s a joy to be back at the pool,” coach Rik Krumins said. “The facility is top notch, so Rylan Patty is back as a leading scorer from last season. we are all thrilled to be there. It feels like home base and it’s fun to interact with everyone there. It sort of feels like moving into a new apartment; we’re figuring out where everything is and where we all start to hang out.” During their time away from the Piedmont Pool, the high school won WACC title in 2022 and won the 2023 Division 2 North Coast Section title. Both of those teams never truly felt the love from a home crowd until their postseason runs, but now, Krumins is noticing how having a home pool gives them the attention they deserve. “It’s fun to see the guests show up. There were a bunch of kids at the little pool watching us practice, so hopefully there’s some organic water polo love going on there,” Krumins said. Last year’s squad finished its season with a 16-9 overall record and reached D2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 1 seed while taking third place in the WACC Tournament. Although they bring back a young roster, they’ll be highlighted by important leading scorers and starters from last season like juniors Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, along with sophomore Ben Kappes. “We’re young. We have our juniors in Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, but after that it’s a sophomore heavy class. The goal is to develop everyone and within the next couple of years we’ll be back on top, that’s the goal,” Krumins said. Piedmont must replace at least two outfield players who graduated with the Class of 2026, including Elles Kreickhaus and Zach Dupree. Sophomore Walker Wilson got critical minutes as a freshman, while Krumins also highlighted sophomores Henry Van Den Bos and Graham Smith. “Walker Wilson played last year, he’ll play quite a bit. Graham Smith played club all summer long and has made tremendous strides. Henry Van Den Bos has been working really hard all summer. We’re throwing new ingredients in the pot and hoping it comes out positive,” Krumins said. As for the goalie role, Piedmont must fill in a critical spot held by three-year starter Luke McAuliffe. The Class of 2026 graduate was the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year after leading PHS to the 2023 D2 NCS title. Between the pipes will be another sophomore, Dylan Jerez, who Krumins says was a standout player in a preseason tournament they played in Hawaii. “Dylan Jerez is outstanding. He’s been playing club for three or four years. I took a team out to Hawaii in August and he shut people down. We placed third and a lot of that had to do with Dylan, he’s an outstanding goalie,” Krumins said. The PHS season starts on Monday, August 24 when visiting American High in Fremont. They play again on September 1 at Newark Memorial and will host their first match at the Piedmont Pool on Thursday, September 3. Henry Stein returns as a junior after being a leader in goals and assists last year.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team returns to Binks Rawlings Gym tomorrow, Thursday, August 20 against Berean Christian. The squad does so with a new head coach, Mike Glass, who took over the boys’ squad last season. Glass inherits a squad that looks poised for success in 2026. Last year’s team went 9-12 and accomplishing the school’s first berth in North Coast Section since 2018, falling in a five-set match to No. 9 Urban as the No. 8 seed in the opening round of the D4 bracket. The 2025 team featured eight sophomores and a freshman, all of which have returned to the varsity lineup. At outside hitter, juniors Maika Ting, Olivia Stevens, and Sofia Meyer return to the fold, as does three-year varsity senior Fiona Olsen. Ting was last year’s leader in kills, logging a gamehigh of 17 in 2025. “There’s a core set of juniors who are going to be stars for this team. Maika is clearly one of our leaders, and we’ll split time with Maika, Olivia Stevens, and Sofia Meyer. With Olivia, she’s been a starting libero, so this is a change in focus but she has all the right tools,” Glass said. PHS proved to be rich at the setter role last season with junior Allyson Huynh and freshman Carina Vora. Now in 2026, Huynh will be getting time at her natural libero role as Piedmont’s defensive leader, while Vora will continue at setter. Huynh earned an honorable mention for AllLeague honors as a sophomore last year. “Allyson is going to be a team leader. She’s been the team’s starting setter, but we are having her change to her natural position. She plays libero for club, we want her to do what she does best. We’re looking at three setters with Carina, Nora Trombi, and Mia Bechtel. All three of them Staff Photos Maika Ting returns as the team’s leader in kills last season. are neck-and-neck, so right now, they will be splitting the time and we’ll see who can develop as the season goes on,” Glass said. Along the middle, Glass is looking at juniors Lucia Dorsey and Izara Dando, along with freshman Charlotte Bailey. “We have Lucia, she has a lot of upside and is very athletic. She hits the ball hard. Izara Dando is also in the mix at middle and oppo, she’ll get looks at both. And then we have Charlotte Bailey, she’s 6 foot 3. pages.text: Wednesday, August 19, 2026 13 Boys’ water polo team can finally host home matches Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team returns after going 16-9 last season. They will host their first match in Piedmont since 2019. By Jonathan Comeaux For the first time since 2019, Piedmont High will feature its water polo teams in town at the Piedmont Pool across the street from the school. It’s a hallmark moment for the team that has emerged as a perpetual contender in the Western Alameda County Conference and North Coast Section despite not having a pool at home. “It’s a joy to be back at the pool,” coach Rik Krumins said. “The facility is top notch, so Rylan Patty is back as a leading scorer from last season. we are all thrilled to be there. It feels like home base and it’s fun to interact with everyone there. It sort of feels like moving into a new apartment; we’re figuring out where everything is and where we all start to hang out.” During their time away from the Piedmont Pool, the high school won WACC title in 2022 and won the 2023 Division 2 North Coast Section title. Both of those teams never truly felt the love from a home crowd until their postseason runs, but now, Krumins is noticing how having a home pool gives them the attention they deserve. “It’s fun to see the guests show up. There were a bunch of kids at the little pool watching us practice, so hopefully there’s some organic water polo love going on there,” Krumins said. Last year’s squad finished its season with a 16-9 overall record and reached D2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 1 seed while taking third place in the WACC Tournament. Although they bring back a young roster, they’ll be highlighted by important leading scorers and starters from last season like juniors Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, along with sophomore Ben Kappes. “We’re young. We have our juniors in Rylan Patty and Henry Stein, but after that it’s a sophomore heavy class. The goal is to develop everyone and within the next couple of years we’ll be back on top, that’s the goal,” Krumins said. Piedmont must replace at least two outfield players who graduated with the Class of 2026, including Elles Kreickhaus and Zach Dupree. Sophomore Walker Wilson got critical minutes as a freshman, while Krumins also highlighted sophomores Henry Van Den Bos and Graham Smith. “Walker Wilson played last year, he’ll play quite a bit. Graham Smith played club all summer long and has made tremendous strides. Henry Van Den Bos has been working really hard all summer. We’re throwing new ingredients in the pot and hoping it comes out positive,” Krumins said. As for the goalie role, Piedmont must fill in a critical spot held by three-year starter Luke McAuliffe. The Class of 2026 graduate was the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year after leading PHS to the 2023 D2 NCS title. Between the pipes will be another sophomore, Dylan Jerez, who Krumins says was a standout player in a preseason tournament they played in Hawaii. “Dylan Jerez is outstanding. He’s been playing club for three or four years. I took a team out to Hawaii in August and he shut people down. We placed third and a lot of that had to do with Dylan, he’s an outstanding goalie,” Krumins said. The PHS season starts on Monday, August 24 when visiting American High in Fremont. They play again on September 1 at Newark Memorial and will host their first match at the Piedmont Pool on Thursday, September 3. Henry Stein returns as a junior after being a leader in goals and assists last year. articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team returns to the gridiron at Witter Field this week for its fourth year of activity, remaining one of the most popular sports at the school with around 60 athletes spread across its program. They played their first game light night, August 18, against Hercules and host Acalanes tomorrow, August 20, at 7:30 p.m. PHS finished 5-13 last season and must replace six graduates from the Class of 2026. But returning to the fold is junior quarterback Edie Elmquist for her third-year as a starter, giving the Highlanders a strong presence at one of the most important positions in the game. “She truly owns the leadership skills. We threw her in as a freshman, and then she learned more about the team as a sophomore. This year, she’s such a strong presence as a leader and people feeling confident around her. She’s feeling confident in herself, so we named her one of our captains. That’s going to bring the whole team up,” coach Beth Black said. Anjali Bowers also returns as a senior. She played the cenEdie Elmquist returns as the starting quarterback role in her third year as a starter. Kate Tong is a returning senior. Flag Football is back for its fourth year of activity. Staff Photos ter role last season and earned an honorable mention for AllLeague. “Our other captain is Anjali Bowers. She and Edie work really well together; she spent a lot of time at center and was solid from the start. She improved over the summer as well,” Black said. Black is also being cognizant of not overworking Elmquist at the quarterback role with intention of the junior starting as a defensive player as well. With that, PHS wants to be more effective in the running game. “We want to start our rungame earlier this year. I don’t want to wear Edie out because she wants to play on both sides of the ball,” Black said. Key receivers Piedmont must replace from 2025 include Malia Williams and Stephanie Lee. Back with the team is senior Kate Tong, who scored a touchdown last season and brings considerable speed to the receiver role. Black also identified Agatha Filha, Bea Nackley, Corey Minor, and Maddie Lee as players who could contribute more heavily. “We’ve got a lot of speed that we can take advantage of. We’ve got Agatha and Bea back for our seniors. Corey Minor is a solid player on both sides of the ball. Maddie Lee also has a lot of innate moves on the field, she knows where to go,” Black said. Defensively, Black faces the ultimate task of replacing starting safety Dahlia Osman, who closed her PHS career with 24 interceptions and was the squad’s leading tackler. “Bea will get time on defense. Carmela Dilaura will also be an important defensive player on the front line. But at safety, we’re going to try a couple of different players there. Dahlia is hard to replace, but I know we have good candidates and I’m going to figure out who is best for that position,” Black said. PHS loaded up its schedule with some tough competition before breaking into their Western Alameda County Conference schedule. Hercules was the No. 7 seed in the D2 NCS Tournament last year, Acalanes reached the D2 championship as the No. 2 seed, while August 27’s game against Las Lomas is against last year’s D1 semifinalist that went 25-1. “We’re starting off against some powerful teams, so we’re going to see what we’ve got and what we need to work on. It sharpens us up for our league schedule,” Black said.

articles.text: In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at Parker Terrill of California’s track and field team, Xander Schulte-Sasse of Chico State’s track and cross country teams, Evan Byun of Wesleyan’s swimming team, and Owen Blanford of UC Santa Cruz’s swimming team. ship, Byun reached the finals as part of the 200 freestyle, 200 medley, and 400 medley relay teams. Wesleyan finished 11th of 22 schools with a time of 1:29.80, his 400 medley team was 20th in 3:35.28, and were 22nd in the 200 medley in 1:37.73. He was also 31st of 39 in the 50 breast in 27.12, and 31st of 35 in the 200 breast in 2:10.35. XANDER SCHULTE-SASSE Chico State Xander Schulte-Sasse, PHS Class of 2025, is embarking on his sophomore year on Chico State’s cross country and track teams. In October last year Schulte-Sasse was a member of the Wildcats’ 2025 California Collegiate Athletic Association Cross Country championship team. Chico State won with a collective time of two hours, three minutes, and 12 seconds, beating second-place Cal Poly by 23 seconds. Although Schulte-Sasse wasn’t among Chico’s top five runners to score, he finished the race 33rd of 97 with a time of 26:09.5. On the track and field team, Schulte-Sasse featured in the 5K at Azusa Pacific’s Franson Last Chance event in May, finishing 39th of 110 runners in 14:46.85. The Owls went 7-18 the previous season and Govert started all 25 games, averaging 25 minutes per game. She scored 54 total points, 63 rebounds, 25 assists, 18 steals, and one block. In the 2023/2024 season, Govert appeared in 17 games and recorded a career high of 11 points, to go along with 13 assists and 12 steals. She earned Centennial Conference Academic Honor Roll honors. As a freshman, she averaged 24.8 minutes per game with 54 points and 94 rebounds. With Piedmont as a senior, Govert’s team reached the D4 NCS Championship as the No. 2 seed, losing to No. 1 Marin Academy in the finals.

articles.text: When visiting Chiang Mai and the northern province of Thailand, it’s clear to see the region’s cultural ties to elephants with countless merchants having trinkets, clothing, and jewelry of elephants on display. If you’re visiting Chiang Mai, travelers are bound to run into offices for sanctuaries looking to lure in tourists, so it is important to do your research to ensure you’re investing your experience with the right company which treats its elephants ethically. With that, the Post visited Into The Wild Elephant Camp on the outskirts The Post visits an elephant sanctuary on the outskirts of Chiang Mai, Thailand. Walking through a thick jungle in Doi Inthanon National Park. Another look at one of Into The Wild Elephant Camp’s seven elephants. of Chiang Mai. In Thailand, elephants are tied to the nation’s history in religion and royalty. They are considered guardians of Buddha, Earth and Thailand’s temples. They were also used in ancient wars to defend the country, while ownership of them was considered a sign of status. However, the species has decreased from the 300,000 wild elephants during the 20th century to an estimated 3,084-3,500 now with an estimated 4,000 in captivity. When choosing an elephant sanctuary to visit, it’s important to decide against places that host rides, keep their elephants in enclosed areas, and has a proper diet for the elephants—all of which is considered animal cruelty. Elephants, which have a typical lifespan of 60-70 years, can have a severe drop in life expectancy when kept in improper conditions, with some cases as high as a 50 percent drop. Into The Wild Elephant Camp have seven elephants in a large encampment about 40 miles outside of Chiang Mai in the Doi Inthanon National Park. Their elephants are in an open space alongside the Mae Tian River, allowing you to learn about the species, its history, and natural habitat. As the guides at Into The Wild explained, it is difficult to release domesticated elephants back into the wild given they are intelligent creatures with good memories, meaning they will seek out humans in order to get food. pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, August 19, 2026 Back to School in Piedmont Piedmont Cub Scout recruiting season begins Piedmont Scout Council’s Cub Scouts welcome new families and youth in grades K-5. Pack open houses are a great opportunity to meet adult leaders, make new friends, and learn about the adventures that await your family. articles.text: Mountain Music is a premier independent music shop located at 4444 Piedmont Ave. in Oakland, just down the street from the iconic Mountain View Cemetery. Shop proprietor Adam Lipansky is a trained luthier who performs precise, in-house string instrument repairs alongside a team of expert technicians. Lipansky has been a musician, music teacher, and luthier for over 35 years, faithfully serving the Bay Area previously through Adam’s String Shack and now through A Mountain Music student is pictured taking piano/keyboard lessons at Music Lessons │ Band Instrument Rentals │ Sales and Repairs Mountain Music. In March 2020, he expanded the business into a full-scale brick-and-mortar retail establishment alongside his wife, Felicia Lipansky, who runs the back of house. Together, the Piedmont residents have built a thriving local hub dedicated to serving the needs of Bay Area musicians and families alike. The storefront specializes in sourcing unique, rare, and vintage instruments and gear, while also maintaining a diverse selection for beginners and advanced players. This curated collection has earned the store a dedicated word-of-mouth reputation and a loyal following of repeat customers. “Mountain Music is the kind of place where you actually feel good spending your money,” one local patron noted. “Instead of leaving with a feeling that you’ve contributed to some massive, faceless supply chain, you feel like you’ve contributed to a living, breathing community of cool people. I couldn’t recommend the shop more highly.” Beyond rare retail finds, Mountain Music actively invests in the community by offering tailored one-on-one music lessons with independent teachers, affordable school band instrument rentals, and reliable walk-in maintenance. The repair shop provides top-of-the-line work without the long wait times or the need for an appointment, ensuring that technicians work closely within each customer’s personal budget. The shop’s repair techs cover amp, turntable, keyboard, pedal, home audio, and string and band instrument repairs. Another satisfied customer shared, “Adam is a very knowledgeable man who’s truly out to help you and your kids make more music. Whenever I get a guitar, I bring it here to have Adam give it a setup.” This dedication to music education is visible in their robust instructional programs. Mountain Music offers a wide variety of in-house lessons for students ages 5 and up, spanning beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels. They also provide a seamless band rental process to help local families prepare their children for the upcoming school year. To encourage new students, the shop is running a special promotion throughout the month of August, offering a 50% discount on a single trial music lesson. Whether you are looking to fix a beloved vintage guitar, rent a trumpet for the school year, or pick up an instrument for the very first time, Mountain Music meets every customer where they are on their musical journey. To sign up for a lesson, visit https://www.mountainmusicstore.com/lessons.htm. For gear, repairs and rentals, visit Mountain Music at 4444 Piedmont Ave. in Oakland, or call (510) 655-2263 or email mountainmusic4444@ gmail.com.
