articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals closes out its 2026 season with Rumors, running August 28 through 30. Rumors is a farcical play by Neil Simon that premiered in 1988, following four wealthy couples arriving at a large New York townhouse for the tenth wedding anniversary party of the city’s deputy mayor, Charley Brock, and his wife, Myra. The guests discover that the host has accidentally shot himself in the earlobe and his wife is missing, leading to frantic miscommunications and accusations. Woodminster Summer Musicals events are held at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. Woodminster is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals at the amphitheater for over 50 years, traditionally featuring three to four plays or musicals over summer months and is Oakland’s longest continually running live theater. Producers Associates, Inc., the nonprofit organization that organizes the summer festival, also offers a “Kids Come Free” program designed to make live theater affordable for families. Several thousand free tickets are given to children and teens each season. Visit https://www.woodminster.com/2026-season to purchase tickets. Performances begin at 8 p.m.
articles.title: Rumors closes out Woodminster Summer Musicals Aug. 28-30

articles.text: Photo courtesy of The Exploratorium The children’s science museum becomes an adult playground every Thursday evening. Visit San Francisco’s Exploratorium every Thursday evening to experience the science museum “after hours.” After Dark is a recurring adults‑only event that transforms the museum into a late‑night playground of science, art and sensory exploration from 6 to 10 p.m. Guests aged 18 and up are invited to wander through more than 700 interactive exhibits focused on science, technology, engineering and more. With the lights dimmed, guests can explore the museum’s classic galleries, a live DJ set, themed programs and alcoholic and nonalcoholic drink options at cash bars. “It’s kind of like an adult playground,” Sam Sharkland, senior program developer at the Exploratorium, told ABC7. “It’s 18 and older, we have cocktails available and lots of extra programming, so you can almost be a kid or scratch that scientific curiosity that you may have lost.” Each Thursday features a different theme or special programming. Previous nights have included Sexplorations, talks tied to science and culture, live performances, and temporary exhibits. For more information, visit https://www.exploratorium. edu.
articles.title: Visit Exploratorium every Thursday evening for After Dark

articles.text: Center Repertory Company Artistic Director Matt Morrow Center Repertory Company launches its 2026-27 season with Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie, beginning Sunday, September 6 and running through Sunday, September 27. The 1944 semiautobiographical play follows a cast of characters in St. Louis: Tom Wingfield, an aspiring writer trapped in a warehouse job, supports his mother, Amanda, a former Southern belle, and his sister, Laura. Amanda, anxious about her daughter’s future, becomes determined to find her a romantic partner. Set against a backdrop of economic hardship and family tension in the 1930s, the play explores memory, desire, responsibility and the difficulty of escaping the past, and is an allnew production directed by Center Repertory Company Artistic Director Matt Morrow. “The Glass Menagerie was one of the first plays I read as an adolescent. Its heart-wrenching and poetic story made me fall in desperate love with the power of theatre,” Morrow said in a press release. “Four decades later, this exquisite masterpiece still haunts me, and I’m thrilled to launch my third season with Center Rep by directing it for the first time.” The cast includes Nancy Carlin, Alanna Darby, Rob Fagin, and Cody Sloan. The creative team includes Meg Neville as costume designer, Spense Matubang as lighting designer, Yi-Chien Lee as scenic designer and James Ard as sound designer. A “Director Chat” will be held before the September 11 performance at 6:30 p.m. A “Cast Chat” will be held September 23 following the performance. Performances are held at Walnut Creek’s Lesher Center for the Arts beginning Sunday, September 6 and running through Sunday, September 27. For more information, visit centerrep.org.
articles.title: Center Rep presents The Glass Menagerie Sept. 6-27

articles.text: Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc features 75,000 hand-made bamboo kites. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) unveils Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc, the largest installation of Hashimoto’s career, with a public celebration tomorrow, Thursday, August 20. The art installation combines nearly 75,000 hand-made bamboo kites suspended together into a cloud canopy, covering the museum’s ground floor admission-free gallery from floor to ceiling and wall to wall. The unveiling will feature a conversation between the artist and SFMOMA Curator of Architecture and Design, Joseph Becker, as well as a sound performance by Nico Georis. “This giant arc of kites, color and pattern will be at once chaotic and meditative, playful and considered—a generous artwork that invites viewers to spend time in the gallery. It will be an enticing, intriguing overture to the museum itself,” said Hashimoto about the project. “Our mission at SFMOMA is radical hospitality for all—these efforts include filling over 45,000 square feet of free public space with irresistible contemporary art,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Hashimoto’s enveloping and breathtaking commission in our free-to-visit Roberts Family Gallery promises to welcome visitors of all ages, imbuing all who experience it with a sense of wonder and awe.” The event begins at 6 p.m. and admission is free. Visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ jacob-hashimoto-giant-arc/ to learn more.
articles.title: SFMOMA unveils Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc tomorrow

articles.text: Tickets for performances available online now Music at Kohl Mansion announced its 44th season, featuring eight performances by internationally acclaimed chamber music ensembles and artists from October 18, 2026 through May 2, 2027. The Burlingame concert series will present Sunday evening performances at 7 p.m., showcasing returning ensembles alongside debut appearances by several artists. Performances are held in the historic Kohl Mansion, also known as The Oaks, which was built in 1914 and is located at 2750 Adeline Drive in Burlingame. The mansion was listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its architecture and social and cultural significance to the local area in 1982, and provides a unique and intimate setting for chamber music concerts. “Our 44th season honors the rich traditions of chamber music while looking ahead to an exciting and dynamic future,” Music at Kohl Mansion Executive Director Patricia Kristof Moy said in a press release. “We are thrilled to welcome remarkable artists from across the United States and Europe and to invite audiences into the uniquely personal experience that chamber music offers.” Hope, commissioned by Music at Kohl Mansion and premiered in 2020. The work by composer Jake Heggie and librettist Gene Scheer will be performed by the Miró Quartet with mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz. “Every performance becomes a shared journey between artists and listeners,” Moy said. “Just as important, we remain committed to extending that experience beyond the concert hall through collaborations with community partners, bringing the transformative power of live music to people of all ages and backgrounds throughout our region.” Season tickets are available online at www.musicatkohl.org. Neave Trio performs on November 15. Among the season highlights are the Music at Kohl Mansion debuts of the Neave Trio on November 15 and the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet on January 17, 2027. The Neave Trio will perform a program featuring works by early 20th-century Croatian composer Dora Pejačević, while the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet will present the local premiere of Hard Winter/ Holler and Stomp by violist and composer Kenji Bunch. The season will also include a holiday program by the Philharmonia Baroque Chamber Players and conclude May 2 with an encore presentation of Intonations: Songs from the Violins of Wolfman was a noted cannibal. Many musical luminaries contributed to a useful book entitled “Culinary Harmony.” This book includes favorite recipes from some of the world’s finest classical musicians. Historically, we remember some things named for Nellie Melba, the famous opera singer. Perhaps you have heard of Melba toast or peach Melba. One of the greatest singers of all time was Enrico Caruso. He was a noted gourmand with a generous helping of gluttony. He slurped up spaghetti à la Caruso most enthusiastically. His feminine counterpart was Luisa Tetrazzini, who is known for the Italian dish named for her: Chicken Tetrazzini. The great Russian basso Feodor Chaliapin liked any food as long as he had plenty of booze. Current opera stars like Jessye Norman love desserts of all kinds. Our local operatic superstar Frederica von Stade prefers salads. The elegant tenor Robert White offered a recipe for portobello mushroom pasta. articles.text: Project Hail Mary provides proof that a movie can be about averting doomsday while making time for laughs and real heart. Directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, based on the book by Andy Weir, Project Hail Mary stars Ryan Gosling as a scientist, Ryland Grace, who wakes up alone in space with no memory of how he got there. Ryland’s mission: figure out why the sun is dying and come up with a way to fix it before it’s too late. It’s a big task for one guy and a spaceship. Ryan Gosling carries this movie. A lot of the film is just him alone on a ship, and he makes that work through sheer performance, mixing humor with real desperation so you never lose interest even when it’s just one guy talking to himself. The best part is the moment he meets Rocky, an alien he ends up teaming up with. That scene fills the heart of the film as their chemistry grows. Watching two completely different beings, with the same mission and existential fear, figure out how to trust each other, is more than all the space effects combined. The science in this movie feels real. The science provides adequate explanation for a motion picture, especially when compared to movies like Jurassic World or The Mandalorian. Daniel Pemberton’s score stands out without the viewer noticing it’s there. Where the movie stumbles is the earthbound flirt scenes. They feel forced and out of place compared to everything happening in space. If you like sci-fi that’s funny but not too serious, this movie is for you. Project Hail Mary earns its ambition, and Rocky alone makes it worth the watch. Project Hail Mary. Directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller. Written by Drew Goddard. Starring Ryan Gosling. articles.text: Here Be Dragons. And now, once again, as Horowitch argues, the stars are changing, again unfamiliar, and looking ahead we find ourselves wondering if out there, in the still unknown Here be dragons. Is this truly the end of something? Are we experiencing a techiedriven redefinition of literacy? Horowitch points out that for millennia we have communicated solely by voice until the transformative advent of the printed word and soon thereafter reading. “Reading has never been natural,“ she argues. “Humans have no innate cognitive machinery designed to string letters into words, and connect them to their real world and analogues. To read, people had to repurpose regions of their brain used for speech and object recognition.” History tells us that this process began some 6,000 years ago in Mesopotamia. However, for millennia thereafter most of the world’s population was illiterate until, as has been mentioned, in the mid-15th century Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press and literacy became a mass phenomenon. Horowitch goes on to opine that writing is a process wherein, the message is detached from the messenger, “allowing for a more dispassionate spread of information than was possible in oral societies. Writing forces the author to slow down and reflect. Written language tends to employ more sentence structure and vocabulary than spoken language. And unlike speech, it doesn’t disappear into the ether. Readers can return to a text and plumb it for new meaning and understanding.” Horowitch turns to Walter J. Ong, a historian and Jesuit priest, who stated that “writing, more than any other single invention, has transformed human consciousness…” Literacy has created the conditions for “inner concentration, extended focus, and logical deduction.” It allows for a “new kind of rational, linear and analytical thought.” I would add that literacy, beginning at an early age, nurtures our ability to imagine. Horowitch goes on to remind us that “America’s Founders used a print document to construct their new nation and believed that the system they had devised would work precisely because citizens would be informed readers… Early on, Americans came to see staying informed as a civic duty and even a moral imperative.” But there remains a caveat, one perhaps not fully understood or anticipated by those same Founders: Access to literacy was denied to large numbers of Americans, in particular the South, where preventing Black literacy was a cornerstone of white supremacy. 801 MAGNOLIA Avenue, piedmont 94611 The San Francisco Bay Area’s Ambassadors of French Chanson Featuring Parisian singer Mimi Pirard, SonoMusette authentically recreates the moody and evocative sound of the Paris music scene of the mid-20th Century. SonoMusette’s renditions of these timeless French classics provide a freshness and excitement that is contemporary, yet faithful to the spirit and tradition of the original artists. Inspired by the great performers of the era, such as Edith Piaf, Jacques Brel, Charles Trenet, and Django Reinhardt, and contemporary musicians such as Zaz and Patrick Bruel, SonoMusette brings French Chanson to the “moderne” era. pages.text: Wednesday, August 19, 2026 21 COMMENTARY MOVIE FOR ADULTS By Chris Honoré Part 4 While reading Rose Horowitch’s 28-page essay I found myself wondering why her thesis was so compellingly unsettling. I soon realized that she was asking me to share her view of a world not only in flux, but one that I had simply taken for granted, and one that continues to define so much of my life, meaning the richness offered through literacy. I cannot imagine a world in which words, books, magazines, newspapers and writing are not deeply valued. Or a world in which an ongoing attempt to understand why some descriptive sentences are simply pedestrian, utilitarian, while others resonate with a memorable beauty. In the words of E.B. White and William Strunk, authors of the very approachable and instructive text, The Elements of Style, this remains still a “high mystery.” Language is, of course, dynamic: new words and sentences appear, find a grammatical/usage niche, while others are discarded. “And writers,” Strunk and White acknowledge, “often find themselves steering by stars that are disturbingly in motion.” Ancient cartographers, when pondering the unknown, beyond the blue water horizon, simply wrote on their parchment maps: The end of reading is here Here Be Dragons. articles.text: In a Napa Valley dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, Lang & Reed has spent more than three decades making a persuasive case for another member of the Cabernet family: Cabernet Franc. Founded by John and Tracey Skupny, the St. Helena winery has built its reputation almost entirely around this often-overlooked Bordeaux grape, producing wines that emphasize fragrance, freshness and balance rather than sheer power. The Skupnys came to Napa Valley from the restaurant world, where they had worked as sommeliers in Kansas City. After moving to California in 1980, John held winemaking and executive positions at several prominent Napa wineries. His fascination with Cabernet Franc grew during those years, particularly after encountering a compelling barrel of 100 percent Cabernet Franc at Niebaum-Coppola in the early 1990s. The experience convinced him that the variety could stand on its own. The first Lang & Reed Cabernet Franc was made in 1993 and the winery was formally established a few years later. The name Lang & Reed comes from the Skupnys’ two sons, J. Reed and Jerzy Lang, underscoring the family character of the enterprise. Today, son Reed Skupny is part of the winemaking team, bringing a new generation into the family business. What distinguishes Lang & Reed is its determination to show Cabernet Franc as a distinctive grape rather than merely a blending component. The wines typically display the variety’s characteristic aromas of dark berries, violets, herbs and earth, along with lively acidity and relatively restrained alcohol. A San Francisco Chronicle review described the North Coast Cabernet Franc as combining the herbal and floral qualities associated with the Loire Valley with a distinctly California character. The winery works with vineyards in Napa Valley, Alexander Valley and Lake County, using different sites to capture the range of Cabernet Franc’s personality. Its more ambitious bottlings can Lang & Reed Winery 1244 Spring St. St. Helena, CA 94574 Open 10-5 Everyday but Sunday langandreed.com The Lang & Reed tasting room is just off Main Street in St. Helena. be structured for extended aging, while the North Coast Cabernet Franc is intended to be approachable and food-friendly. In recent years, Lang & Reed has expanded its focus to include Chenin Blanc, another variety with strong Old World roots and relatively modest representation in California. The addition makes sense: both grapes share the Skupnys’ preference for wines with energy, character and a strong sense of place. For wine drinkers tired of Napa wines built solely around power and richness, Lang & Reed offers something refreshingly different. Its Cabernet Francs demonstrate that Napa Valley can produce wines of perfume, subtlety and elegance— and that sometimes the most interesting wines come from grapes willing to play a less familiar role. • 2023 Lang & Reed Chenin Blanc Napa Valley, $75 The nose offers aromas of fresh melon, apple and sweet citrus elements with a hint of flint and petrol. Medium-bodied, the palate is delightfully textured, offering good weight with complexity and precision. The wine will remain food friendly for many years to come. • 2023 Lang & Reed Chenin Blanc Mendocino, $35 Enchanting nose of peaches, apricots and honeysuckle struts from the glass. In the mouth you get pineapple and a touch of honey. It is medium-bodied but plump and silky, with a long satisfying finish. I preferred this wine to the Napa Valley Chenin and at half the price it is a great value. • 2023 Lang & Reed Chenin Blanc Talmage, $60 Named after a small Mendocino County town where the grapes come from, the Talmage is a selection of the best barrels. It has a huge boisterous nose of stone fruit and pears with hints of jasmine. On the palate it is big and viscous, filling the mouth with juicy, ripe fruit. Complex and layered the finish goes on for days. This is the best New World Chenin Blanc I have tasted. Great work. Lang & Reed Chenin Blanc is an excellent version of the varietal. Lang & Reed made their reputation on Cabernet Franc. • 2023 Lang & Reed Cabernet Franc North Coast, $60 The North Coast Cab Franc opens with aromas of crushed red and black currants, cherries and leather with wafts of earth and bay leaves. The palate is medium to full-bodied with great varietal expressions and a chewy frame, finishing long and lively. • 2023 Lang & Reed Cabernet Franc Napa Valley Two Fourteen, $90 Very French in style this wine reminded me of a Right Bank Bordeaux. Offering up aromas of leather, earth, dark berries and mint framed by a touch of oak, its medium to full-bodied, fleshy and polished, concluding with a long, delicate finish. Perfect partner to beef Bourguignon. articles.text: August 12, 1839, was an important date in California history. On that day the pioneer John Sutter arrived at the confluence of the Sacramento and American Rivers to establish Sutter’s Fort, the founding, as it is generally reckoned, of California’s capital city, Sacramento. Accompanying Sutter were ten Hawaiians, three sailors, and one bulldog. One hundred eighty-seven years to the day later, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, another large party, 55 walkers and six K-9 best friends of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group, met at the Exedra to walk the caminos (streets) of Piedmont. Matt Gerhardt was the intrepid leader of the walkers last Wednesday. Intrigued by Piedmont’s streets with Spanish names, he decided to introduce them to his fellow walkers, every one of them, in fact, except Alta. Why not Alta? Because alta means “high” or “upper” in Spanish, and the group was reluctant to do that much uphill walking on a sunny summer day. With California history swirling through our heads, we marched from the Exedra, turned down Vista Avenue (vista, “view”), and headed north on Bonita Avenue (bonita, “pretty”) past the Frank C. Havens elementary school playground. It was the first week of school after summer vacation, and the children sounded happy and excited to be back. Crossing Oakland Avenue, we continued along Bonita, turned left on Blair Avenue toward Dracena Quarry Park, and then right on El Cerrito Avenue (“little hill”), which, as its name implied, was only the slightest of climbs. Dracena sounds as if it could be Spanish too (cena means “dinner”), but it is actually the name of a plant species, an appropriate name for Piedmont’s second-largest park. We took the group photo at the corner of El Cerrito and Ricardo Avenue, Ricardo being simply the Spanish for Richard, at the southwest corner of the park. Next the walkers traveled a short distance up Ricardo to a hidden passage connecting the street to York Drive below. Emerging from that green, shaded tunnel of shrubs, we continued down to Manor Drive and made a right turn to Arroyo Avenue (arroyo, “creek”). Then came another hidden passage, from Arroyo to Ramona Avenue, another Spanish given name. The walkers clambered down the stairway onto Ramona and turned uphill toward Estrella Avenue (estrella, “star”). We followed that leafy, treelined street until it ended at Moraga Avenue, and there we encountered a confluence of three Spanish-named streets: Bonita, Estrella, and Moraga. Not quite as momentous as Sutter reaching the meeting of the American and Sacramento Rivers 187 years ago, but still a pretty cool street sign, and “Bonita Estrella,” or Beautiful Star, would make a fine name for one of the Moraga family’s descendants. And what does moraga mean? It can be a bundle, like a bundle of harvested wheat, or, in southern Spain, a beach barbecue. But our street, like the town of Moraga over the hill, almost certainly honors a Californio family of the pre-Gold Rush Bay Area, and an interesting lot they were. The first Moraga in California was the patriarch, José Joaquín Moraga, second in command to General Juan Bautista de Anza in the Royal Spanish Army, who in 1776 became the comandante of San Francisco. His son Gabriel, also a soldier, traveled throughout Northern California and named many of its rivers, including the Sacramento, the very river beside which Sutter’s Fort would later rise. The town of Moraga was named for Gabriel’s son Joaquín, one of his fourteen children and the namesake of the original commander. Getting a good workout of our leg muscles, the walkers trudged up Moraga Avenue along what felt like a mountain trail to Monte Avenue (monte, fittingly, “mountain”), then climbed to Mesa Avenue, which, as its name promised, was flat as a table (mesa). Whew! From there it was all downhill on Pala Avenue to Highland. And at the corner of Pala and Highland we saw a man wielding a shovel, pala means exactly that, which gave us all a chuckle. Some of us will think of Pala as “Shovel Street” from now on. The walkers who remained after all those hills ambled back along Highland Avenue to the Exedra, where we thanked Matt for an excellent tour of the caminos of Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: The Greenhouse Salon The Greenhouse Salon, located at 4319 Piedmont Ave, was founded by Sean Berry, a stylist with over 18 years of experience. Berry wants the salon to create a community of hairdressers who are passionate about education and try to give back to the community. The salon attempts to accomplish these goals by selling ethically sourced haircare and styling products through Davines. Berry grew up in Sacramento amongst a family with a deep art background. His grandfather was an art professor, his father a woodworker, and his mother a strong influence on his early journey in art. “She didn’t really want us watching TV. It was either playing outside or creating something, and so it just kind of came naturally to me to do things with my hands and design things,” said Berry. Around 20 years ago, Berry found himself working in a restaurant without a clear goal of what he wanted to do. It was when he was sitting at his salon with his hairstylist of 21 years that they had a heart-to-heart conversation and Berry realized what he wanted to do. “Through that conversation, I The Greenhouse Salon waiting room Sean Berry, founder of The Greenhouse Salon decided to go to beauty school, ended up liking it, and now I’ve been doing it for 18 years. I had no clue that’s what I wanted to do, but instantly just really enjoyed it,” said Berry. Berry attended the Federico Beauty Institute in Sacramento, and on his third day of beauty school Berry found his passion for product knowledge and ethically sourced products. “I actually had a Davines educator come into my classroom on the third day of beauty school, and she taught a product knowledge class about part of their product line. And I was like, ‘I’m obsessed with this company,’ and ‘I want to do what she’s doing,’” Berry continued. “And then six months outside of beauty school, I became an educator with that company, and I’ve just fallen in love with them. articles.text: Making recalls exciting and theatrical rather than repetitive obedience drills One of the most common dog training pain points for owners is recall. Whether it’s an emergency or not, your pup is always distracted along the way or seems to say, “Just a minute,” before responding—a minute that quickly turns into an eternity. The most essential part of recall training is the handler’s behavior and reactions. Below are some tips to increase your dog’s responsiveness and avoid common pitfalls that may be contributing to your dog’s unwillingness to come when called. The key to training your dog to move toward you without fail is to make it worth their while— in short, you have to get excited! Your dog has no reason to want to move your way unless you seem eager and interesting. Make sure your body language is inviting by bending over toward your dog. You can clap your hands or pat your thighs to seem even more encouraging. Always use a happy, high-pitched voice when calling your dog. If you are having trouble with this, squeal with delight as soon as your dog begins moving your way. This makes you much more interesting than any other distraction around and reinforces the dog’s recall with positive attention. When your dog gets to you, make sure you reward them right away. This can be with physical affection and praise or with treats. Remember that the reward must be given within three seconds of compliance. One common pitfall owners encounter is accidentally teaching the dog to associate coming when called with extra work. Avoid putting your dog through a predictable obedience routine, such as asking them to sit every time they get to you. After praising your dog, they should be dismissed to return to their play the majority of the time. Similarly, make sure that you are not leashing your dog and ending play every single time you call them. If your dog is giving you a hard time with recall, never reprimand A collie puppy comes running to her owner when called. the dog when they finally get to you. Even if your dog takes an eternity to complete their recall, ensure that compliance is met with praise each time—no matter how annoyed you are. While it is important to have a system in place that eventually teaches your dog that disregarding recall is not an option, reprimanding the dog when they finally comply gives mixed messages. Following these tips will not only improve your dog’s response but your relationship as well. One of the best parts of owning a dog is the unconditional excitement with which they greet you every day. By offering this in return whenever you call them, you will enrich your interactions with your furry friend and take irritation out of the equation. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call (510) 507- 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. articles.text: their secluded house in Danville that he came to call his “final home and harbor.” Of all the places Eugene O’Neill called home during his restless life, the Tao House (which is what he named his Danville abode) was the one that held him the longest, and the refuge where he wrote his last plays, including Long Day’s Journey into Night, an autobiographical glimpse into his troubling life. O’Neill’s interest in Eastern thought and his wife’s passion for Oriental art and décor inspired the name “Tao House.” The house combined a Spanish colonial exterior of abodeThe Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a Turkish lunch at Meyhouse Restaurant & Jazz Club. Pictured are: (left side of table): Nedra Shumway, Judy Wang, Gayle Young, Mary Buller, Edith Hereso, and Jim Ayotte; (right side of table): Sandra Ponce, Gloria Wilmer, Greg Jurin, and Piedmont Pictured for the Piedmont Seniors in front of Eugene O’Neill’s Tao House are: (front row, L to R): Piedmont Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, Nedra Shumway, Edith Hereso, Gayle Young, and Judy Wang; (back row, L to R): Sandra Ponce, Ranger (and tour guide) Geraldine Finton, Jim Ayotte, Greg Jurin, and Mary Buller. like blocks with an interior of deep blue ceilings and red doors, tiled or black-stained floors, and Chinese furniture. Because Carlotta’s eyes were overly sensitive to light, most of the shades were kept drawn. The darkness and the ghostly images reflected by colored mirrors create a shadowy, enclosed atmosphere that can be unsettling to visitors. Though the O’Neills rarely spent a night away from Tao House, especially when the “Master,” as Carlotta called him, was at work, the couple was far from reclusive as they were visited by relatives, friends, and O’Neill’s old theatre colleagues. Still, he mostly immersed himself in his plays, working on several at a time. Shut away by thick walls and three doors leading to his study, Carlotta ensured that his isolation was undisturbed to allow his creative energy to flow unchecked for days, even weeks at a stretch. During the tour, the Piedmont Seniors also got the opportunity to visit the surrounding grounds of the house, including a mid-19th century barn which is currently used to conduct an annual fundraiser to showcase O’Neill’s plays. The Seniors also visited the gravesite of O’Neill’s dog Blemie, who was considered a “surrogate child” for both himself and his wife, Carlotta. O’Neill even wrote a “Last Will and Testament” for Blemie from the dog’s perspective as if Blemie was speaking directly to Eugene and his wife. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors then boarded their “caravan” for a trip to the Bishop Ranch in San Ramon to have lunch at Meyhouse Restaurant & Jazz Club. Here, the group ventured from having standard American fare to having a delectable Turkish lunch. Afterwards, the group had time to meander around the local shops before returning home. All in all, it was another relaxing, and educational day for all! If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. The Piedmont Seniors get a tour of the Tao House living room. Pictured (r to l) are: Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, Sandra Ponce, Nedra Shumway, Jim Ayotte, Greg Jurin, Mary Buller and tour guide Geraldine Finton. Seated on the couch is Eugene O’Neill.

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, August 19, 2026 Seniors Piedmont seniors take a “Long Day’s Journey” to visit historic home of legendary playwright Eugene O’Neill The Piedmont Seniors’ latest excursion was a trip to Danville to get a private guided tour of the home of four-time Pulitzer Prize-winner Eugene O’Neill, a National Historic Site. The house is only accessible through a National Park shuttle bus to the property, with a gated private entrance. O’Neill, renowned for being America’s most exciting dramatist, is the author of such plays as his 1940 play, The Iceman Cometh, and Ah, Wilderness!. In 1936 O’Neill was even awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature. It was with this stipend that he and his wife Carlotta were able to build their secluded house in Danville that he came to call his “final home and harbor.” Of all the places Eugene O’Neill called home during his restless life, the Tao House (which is what he named his Danville abode) was the one that held him the longest, and the refuge where he wrote his last plays, including Long Day’s Journey into Night, an autobiographical glimpse into his troubling life. O’Neill’s interest in Eastern thought and his wife’s passion for Oriental art and décor inspired the name “Tao House.” The house combined a Spanish colonial exterior of abodeThe Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a Turkish lunch at Meyhouse Restaurant & Jazz Club. Pictured are: (left side of table): Nedra Shumway, Judy Wang, Gayle Young, Mary Buller, Edith Hereso, and Jim Ayotte; (right side of table): Sandra Ponce, Gloria Wilmer, Greg Jurin, and Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein. Pictured for the Piedmont Seniors in front of Eugene O’Neill’s Tao House are: (front row, L to R): Piedmont Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, Nedra Shumway, Edith Hereso, Gayle Young, and Judy Wang; (back row, L to R): Sandra Ponce, Ranger (and tour guide) Geraldine Finton, Jim Ayotte, Greg Jurin, and Mary Buller. like blocks with an interior of deep blue ceilings and red doors, tiled or black-stained floors, and Chinese furniture. Because Carlotta’s eyes were overly sensitive to light, most of the shades were kept drawn. The darkness and the ghostly images reflected by colored mirrors create a shadowy, enclosed atmosphere that can be unsettling to visitors. Though the O’Neills rarely spent a night away from Tao House, especially when the “Master,” as Carlotta called him, was at work, the couple was far from reclusive as they were visited by relatives, friends, and O’Neill’s old theatre colleagues. Still, he mostly immersed himself in his plays, working on several at a time. Shut away by thick walls and three doors leading to his study, Carlotta ensured that his isolation was undisturbed to allow his creative energy to flow unchecked for days, even weeks at a stretch. During the tour, the Piedmont Seniors also got the opportunity to visit the surrounding grounds of the house, including a mid-19th century barn which is currently used to conduct an annual fundraiser to showcase O’Neill’s plays. The Seniors also visited the gravesite of O’Neill’s dog Blemie, who was considered a “surrogate child” for both himself and his wife, Carlotta. O’Neill even wrote a “Last Will and Testament” for Blemie from the dog’s perspective as if Blemie was speaking directly to Eugene and his wife. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors then boarded their “caravan” for a trip to the Bishop Ranch in San Ramon to have lunch at Meyhouse Restaurant & Jazz Club. Here, the group ventured from having standard American fare to having a delectable Turkish lunch. Afterwards, the group had time to meander around the local shops before returning home. All in all, it was another relaxing, and educational day for all! If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 a.m. to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: Last year, Americans over 60 reported losing $7.7 billion to online criminals, a 59% jump in a single year, across more than 201,000 victims. The average loss was $38,500. More than 12,000 people lost over $100,000 each. And because federal researchers estimate that fewer than one in twenty victims ever reports the crime, the real number is far higher. These aren’t strangers in faraway places targeting careless people. They are targeting our parents, our neighbors, and increasingly, us. What’s changed: artificial intelligence. The “grandparent scam” used to rely on a panicked, muffled voice and a bad connection. Today, a scammer needs only a few seconds of audio, pulled from a Facebook video or a voicemail greeting, to clone your grandchild’s voice convincingly. The call comes at 11 p.m. There’s been an accident. Don’t tell Mom and Dad. Please hurry. THIS HAPPENED TO MY PARENTS. It’s real. To this day, my mom, Chase’s grandmother, is certain that the person calling was in fact Chase. It was not, but the voice sounded exactly like him. The FBI logged thousands of AI-related fraud complaints last year, with losses in the hundreds of millions. The technology is inexpensive, widely available, and improving monthly. The four that cost seniors the most: • Investment fraud. Now nearly half of all senior losses. Often begins as a friendly text “sent to the wrong number,” builds into a months-long relationship, then introduces a fake trading platform showing spectacular returns. The account balance is a screenshot. The money is gone. • Tech support scams. More than $1 billion lost last year. A pop-up or call claims to be Apple, Microsoft, or your bank and requests remote access to your computer. • Romance scams. Built patiently over weeks on Facebook, Instagram, or dating apps — then the emergency arrives. • Recovery scams. The cruelest category. Someone contacts a victim shortly after a loss, claims they can retrieve the stolen funds, and takes what’s left. A note for anyone buying or selling a home: wire fraud remains a serious threat in our industry. Criminals monitor transaction email and send fraudulent wiring instructions days before closing. Never wire funds based on emailed instructions. Call your escrow officer at a number you already have and verify verbally. Six habits that actually work: 1. Pause ten minutes. Urgency is the weapon. Every legitimate request survives a ten-minute delay. No scam does. 2. Hang up and call back on a number you already have — never the one provided to you. 3. Choose a family code word. A phrase only your family knows. Ask for it before you send anything. 4. Never grant remote access to your computer, and never send cryptocurrency to anyone you met online. Legitimate institutions do not ask you to deposit cash into a crypto kiosk. 5. Talk to someone before you act. Isolation is the scammer’s greatest ally. Seniors who call a family member first are dramatically less likely to lose money. 6. Report it — always. File at ic3.gov or call the Justice Department’s Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11. There is no shame in being targeted by a professional. Please forward this to your parents and children, friends and neighbors. Then call them, and talk it through. articles.text: There’s a persistent misconception that getting older means becoming less capable of learning something new. But in the performing arts, age can bring something else to the table: a lifetime of experiences to draw upon. Radhika Rao sees that firsthand teaching improv at Stagebridge in Oakland, the nation’s oldest performing arts organization for older adults. In fact, working with Stagebridge performers has changed the way Rao thinks about improv itself. “As we get older, our experiences get richer. We have all this backstory,” she says. Rather than emphasizing quick thinking or landing the cleverest line, Rao teaches for “presence of mind rather than speed or memory.” “You don’t have to chase the joke,” she says. “It’s about telling authentic stories, and the humor comes naturally.” Improv teacher Greg Philippi recently came to a similar conclusion after looking at aging, memory and long-form improv. “What matters more than memory is your ability to notice, associate, listen, and respond in the moment,” he wrote in The Armadillo Lab. Older improvisers, he Radhika Rao (center) and her students play 3 Headed Expert argues, have an advantage that’s easy to overlook: a much larger library of human experience. Research into creative aging suggests that participating in the arts may have benefits beyond the stage. The landmark Creativity and Aging Study, led by psychiatrist Gene Cohen, followed older adults participating in professionally led arts programs. Compared with a control group, participants reported better overall health, fewer doctor visits and greater social activity. But creativity as we age isn’t only about health. There’s something to be said for continuing to surprise ourselves with what we can learn and do. Stagebridge offers classes throughout the year, and this fall there are plenty of opportunities to do just that. Students can tell a story without words in Visual Comedy, dig into text and character in Monologues Through the Ages, or create stories for children using puppets and music. There’s also Shakespeare, songwriting, tap, musical theatre, folk dance and, of course, improv. Rao sees something else older adults bring to the stage. “As you get older, you stop worrying so much about what other people think,” she says. “My students bring that sort of permission to the stage.” Perhaps that’s a creative advantage worth celebrating. Stagebridge fall classes begin the week of Sept. 7 at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, across from Whole Foods near Lake Merritt. Need-based scholarships are available and class sizes are limited. Learn more and register at stagebridge.org/classes. Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama, My neighbor told me I should get a data wiper to remove my personal information from the internet. What is that, and can it help protect my identity and cut down on spam? – Angel, Oakland Dear Angel, I think your neighbor is talking about an automated personal data removal service. And though it provides some protection and can cut down on some spam it is not a fix-all. Let’s talk about what this kind of service is, what it does and what it doesn’t do. A personal data removal service can help protect your identity by scrubbing your personal details from data broker sites, and people search directories. The idea behind it is to reduce your digital footprint, which can cut down on targeted spam, and also lowers the risk of “doxxing” which is publishing someone’s private information online without their permission. They save you the trouble of contacting these data brokers and requesting that your information be scrubbed or erased. These services scan online public directories for your name, phone number and address and send requests to these brokers to delete your private files. Because in some cases this activity is automated, the services can do it much more quickly and efficiently than you can do it yourself. And they also will run regular scans because deleted data often returns. This can also reduce spam calls, text and junk mail, but it doesn’t eliminate them altogether. It also can remove your home address and family information from public search engines. These data removal services also continuously monitor these data brokers and request deletion automatically. Now for what they don’t do. They do not block hackers from stealing passwords or opening fake credit cards in your name. They also don’t erase things in public records like government registries, social media posts, and any court cases that have your name associated with them. They don’t replace the need for credit freezes, identity theft and dark web monitoring, and you still need to use very strong passwords or better yet passkeys. So, is it worth it to invest in one of these services? I personally am trying one to see if it reduces my spam. I already have credit monitoring and identity theft protection and have my credit frozen. If you decide to invest in one of these services, you will be asked to provide your legal name, address, phone number and email addresses. Most of them allow you to add at least one or two more email addresses. And most have a 30-day money back guarantee. Here are some highly rated companies, with some notable differences: 1. Incogni: (incogni.com). This is the one that I use. I have a family plan, for my husband and kids. This is $179 a year for one user. Incogni uses “set it and forget it” automation and covers 420+ brokers. 2. DeleteMe: ( joindeleteme. com) The cost for this is $129 a year for one user. This one uses human privacy experts to scrub personal information. This service requires a bit more oversight from users. 3. LifeLock by Norton: This is a very different service than the previous two. LifeLock monitors your credit, financial accounts and the dark web and offers insurance if your identity is compromised. LifeLock does not scan the web to remove your personal information and reduce your digital footprint but instead, works to protect you from the real-world consequences of stolen data. The plans start at a bit over $10 for the Core plan. Services like Incogni or DeleteMe and LifeLock can work well together: Incogni or DeleteMe reduces the amount of personal information available online, while LifeLock monitors for misuse. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the lives of hundreds of children each summer. Letters sent home by kids at Camp Augusta. Enjoy some glimpses into a day at Camp Augusta. Two months, 8 weeks, 61 days—that’s the duration Camp Augusta brought the magic to children during the summer of 2026. Throughout this period, the community has forged enduring friendships, empowered campers to develop new skills, and created memories destined to be cherished for summers to come. From soaring through the air to dominating lively water gun battles, the excitement has been relentless. A camper rides their electric skateboard full speed to end the summer. For Stephanie Chase it’s lamb shanks. And the list goes on and on. The noted violinist and teacher Josef Gingold is happy with simple scrambled eggs. Many years ago I was in a car with Gingold. He was in the front passenger seat, and I was in the back seat. Gingold put his arm over the top of the seat, leaned back and said to me: “I’ve always wanted to meet you.” I was surprised by this and asked him why. He responded by saying: “Isn’t it obvious… Josef Gingold… Joseph Gold.” Over many years restaurants have gotten better and better. It helps when you psychoanalyze a restaurant and know what to order. If you’re still undecided, take the advice of Jascha Heifetz. If you think the restaurant is not particularly good, order ham and eggs. Even a bad restaurant can’t ruin ham and eggs. Be sure to enjoy life and eat a good meal in good company.

I refuse to have that be a thing here,” Berry continued. “I think that’s what sets us apart is just the culture to be supportive and welcoming. It’s a hard thing to curate in our industry. My biggest focus is making sure that everyone that works here and walks in the door is welcome, supported, and lifted.” Berry not only has his own salon but has co-founded an education company with his co-worker Julie Tomczek. The company Propagation Education focuses on helping stylists with 5+ years of experience teach advanced color theory and chemistry classes. Tomczek mainly teaches in the classroom while Berry is on the salon floor teaching students fresh out of beauty school. New clients on their first visit have the opportunity to begin with a brief consultation. During your first visit, we reserve extra time for an in-depth consultation, a customized service plan, and education on at-home care. This helps the stylist review their client’s history and hair goals, making the appointment feel “seamless and relaxed.” Interested readers can visit The Greenhouse Salon’s website to sign up for their first appointment: https:// thegreenhousesalon.beauty/. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School (PMS) students returned to campus last week, for Walkthrough Registration in the Buzz Redford Gym. With a new administration and new faculty, the back to school annual event at 740 Magnolia Avenue had renewed energy, excitement and sounds as speakers blasted music fit for a celebration. New Principal Jamie Van Kleeck and new Assistant Principal Adam Saville led by example, working a table to interface directly with students by handing out and explaining new class schedules for the year. Students lined up in an orderly fashion in the gym with their parents to get their schedules. The calm ensued until the sights of old friends now standing at new heights with new haircuts brought students to life. Community tables inside the gym also offered parents and students with extracurricular activities and affiliation. The Piedmont Post hosted its first table at Walkthrough Registration informing the denizens of Piedmont about ways to contribute to the newspaper. Middle School sports signups, the Piedmont Parents Network (PPN) and The Wellness Center also had community booths in the gym eager to reach new participants. New sixth graders at PMS entered the Walkthrough Registration with fresh eyes, seeing their new campus filled with life Principal Jamie Van Kleeck and Assistant Principal Adam Saville helped students with questions while handing out class schedules.
articles.title: PMS Walkthrough Registration

articles.text: Piedmont students returned on Monday, August 10 in Piedmont at each of the district’s six campuses. K-12th grade students have resumed their traditional morning schedules as they marched through town to school in time for the sound of the first bell at 8:30 a.m. Piedmont Unified School District delivered some welcome news earlier this week as the board announced Donald Evans’ return as the interim superintendent. Evans came out of retirement in 2022 to steer the district from the top administrative position for one year. Evans’ familiarity with the district provides much needed stability while the school board conducts another search for a permanent superintendent. At Beach Elementary backto-school brought the traditional first-day-of-school new outfits and new shoes. These were topped with new backpacks containing unused pens, pencils and notebooks. Students reunited with old friends on the Beach blacktop, wasting no time in greeting familiar faces with bear hugs, high fives and grins of grandeur. Beach students posed for first day of school photos in front of a large Hollywood-style photo backdrop in the form of notebooks. Beach students lined up in front of their new classrooms, some with flowers in hand for their new teachers.
articles.title: School is back in session

articles.text: In 2024, the wooden swings in Piedmont Park’s tot lot were removed due to structural rot. The swings posed a risk to the people who used them and needed to be removed. Ever since then, the community has been outspoken about their desire to return the swings to the park. After years of waiting, the community is finally getting what they want. This past week, the city began construction on the tot lot to return the swings and add an ADA path. The climbing structure, restrooms, and upper lawn are open during construction. Memorial benches have been temporarily removed and safely stored. Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) President Patty Dunlap spoke with the Post to explain the importance of the swings in Piedmont Park and tot lots in general. “Swings are much more than playground equipment; they are part of the soundtrack of childhood,” said Dunlap. “PBF and the community’s enthusiasm to replace the swings says something important about Piedmont. articles.text: Pending school board approval during the August 12 meeting, the board has selected Donald Evans as Piedmont Unified School District’s interim superintendent for the year. Dr. Evans came out of retirement to be Piedmont’s interim superintendent during the 2022-23 school year, after Randy Booker’s departure and before Jennifer Hawn. “[Evans] has a tremendous amount of experience, serving as the superintendent of Berkeley Unified School District for six years before retiring in 2019, and as the superintendent of Hayward Unified School District before that,” the board said in an August 9 press release. Since Evans last served as the leader of Piedmont schools in 2023, he has stayed busy in retirement. He was the interim superintendent in 2024 in Albany and has worked with the California Collaborative for Educational Excellence. Evans also provides executive coaching for district leaders in the Bay Area and has been a lecturer at California State University, East Bay since 2022. Dr. Evans’ career in education began in the classroom as an elementary school teacher before finding his niche in administration as a vice principal and then a principal. He received his bachelor’s degree from University of Delaware, his master’s from United States International University, and earned his Doctorate of Education from the University of California, Berkeley. ”We are thrilled to welcome him back to the district, where he has well-established relationships with our administrators and staff,” stated the board. With Evans’ arrival, the district won’t skip a beat following Hawn’s departure for Cupertino. Evans joined Hawn on the Piedmont campus for the first day of school on Monday, where he was greeted by parents happy to see his familiar face. Donald Evans (left), pictured with School Board President Ruchi Medhekar and outgoing superintendent Jennifer Hawn, will be Piedmont Unified School District’s interim superintendent for the second time.
articles.title: Donald Evans returns as interim school superintendent

Dr. Evans came out of retirement to be Piedmont’s interim superintendent during the 2022-23 school year, after Randy Booker’s departure and before Jennifer Hawn. “[Evans] has a tremendous amount of experience, serving as the superintendent of Berkeley Unified School District for six years before retiring in 2019, and as the superintendent of Hayward Unified School District before that,” the board said in an August 9 press release. Since Evans last served as the leader of Piedmont schools in 2023, he has stayed busy in retirement. He was the interim superintendent in 2024 in Albany and has worked with the California Collaborative for Educational Excellence. Evans also provides executive coaching for district leaders in the Bay Area and has been a lecturer at California State University, East Bay since 2022. Dr. Evans’ career in education began in the classroom as an elementary school teacher before finding his niche in administration as a vice principal and then a principal. He received his bachelor’s degree from University of Delaware, his master’s from United States International University, and earned his Doctorate of Education from the University of California, Berkeley. ”We are thrilled to welcome him back to the district, where he has well-established relationships with our administrators and staff,” stated the board. articles.text: Part 3 Rose Horowitch, The Atlantic magazine journalist, continues to build her case, affirmatively stating that not only have we arrived at the end of reading, but that its “decline cuts across age groups, gender and education levels. Even the demographics that traditionally read the most – retirees, women, and college graduates – Horowitch also points out that “Americans get much less of their news through reading than they once did. In 1975, about half of 20-somethings said that they read the newspaper every day. Today, less than 10 percent do … and 40 percent say they prefer to watch or listen to online news rather But let’s pause for a moment and examine what Horowitch means when she refers to this change as a “literacy crisis,” or “the end of reading.” Her choice of words is not intended to be hyperbolic; rather she is drawing our attention to a profound social transformation, not dissimilar from that which occurred post-Gutenberg. She refers to this moment not as one in which we cannot decode individual words. In fact, she suggests, “Americans are reading more words than ever before. What has changed is what they read and how.” And therein, as the Bard long ago stated, “is the rub.” I recall an image from a period film, set during the Great Depression, which showed a silent room full of seated, unemployed men looking for work, each reading a newspaper. It was the worst of times for many, made manifest in that room of white sails. But that was then, and this is now. Clearly those waiting today for an appointment, an interview perhaps, or for a subway (or seated on a subway), or even at a dinner table are looking intently down at a small screen. Each, as Horowitch describes, is “bombarded with emails, text messages, X posts, Reddit threads, Instagram captions.” She refers to this beckoning cascade of messages as an “explosion of textual fragments” that compete with devoting our attention to longer written works that convey rich and complicated information. Horowitch goes on to cite Maryanne Wolf, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCLA, who states that “people are losing the ability to think deeply about writing. That doesn’t mean they are forgetting how to decode individual words. Rather, they are losing the higher-order abilities of comprehension and synthesis. America, in other words, isn’t illiterate. It’s postliterate.” capable, warm, tender and personable. I was in such good hands. So, I sit here a few days after surgery with a heart full of wonder at the invention of such a device and deep gratitude to God and his helpers who guided me through this experience. In a day and time in which it is so easy to feel overwhelmed by the problems surrounding us – by the corruption, incompetence and mean-spiritedness of our current government, by the degradation of our planet’s environment, by the wars and poverty we read about every day. I want to always remember how tremendously blessed I am. From my privileged perspective of someone who has resources and insurance and lives in a country and city where the medical standards are so high I must never forget the blessed state of my existence. Every time I start to worry or complain I want to remember the event this week – a day of miracle and wonder. Bill McNabb is the retired former Senior Pastor of Piedmont Community Church.

articles.text: Since 2023, Piedmont’s home electrification rebates have supported 90 gas-to-electric appliance conversions and electrical panel updates. Over the same period, home electrification has gained ground locally. In 2025, permits for heat pump and heat pump water heater installations surpassed their natural gas equivalents for the first time. But natural gas use in Piedmont homes still accounts for around half of community-wide greenhouse gas emissions, and continued progress is needed to meet the city’s climate goals. Updates to the rebate program take what the city has learned from the first three years and put it to work by expanding the projects the city supports, improving access to higher rebates, and focusing city funds where they can have the greatest impact. Projects eligible for rebates now include solar paired with battery storage, standalone battery storage, gas meter removal, and smart electrical panels: • Heat pump water heater: $800 standard rebate; up to $2,000 for income-qualified • Solar + battery system: $2,000 standard rebate; up to $5,000 for income-qualified • Electrical panel improvements: $900 standard rebate; up to $2,250 for income-qualified • Gas meter removal: $2,500 for all eligible households Under the new eligibility rules, heat pump heating and cooling rebates are limited to incomequalified households. City data showed that these projects were moving forward without a rebate, while rebates appeared to play a greater role in heat pump water heater projects. Redirecting those funds allows the program to support more projects and better target assistance where it can make a difference. Sustainability Award honoree Jeff Fucigna with his heat pump water heater Sustainability Award honoree Brandon Bercovich with upgraded electrical panels For residents who already submitted a permit application for a heat pump project that would have qualified under the previous rules, the city is providing a grace period and accepting applications for the standard rebate until October 1. The city has expanded eligibility for higher, “income-qualified,” rebate amounts. Previously, income-qualified rebates were tied to CARE or FERA eligibility, which applies to only about 2% of Piedmont households. In three years, just one rebate was issued at the income-qualified level. Analysis found that these limits were not reaching many households that may still face financial barriers to electrification. Now, households earning up to 120% of Area Median Income (roughly $195,000/year for a 4-person household) can qualify for a new “moderate-income” rebate tier. Households that qualify for CARE or FERA will continue to receive the highest rebate amounts. Before starting a project, review current rebate amounts and eligibility requirements at piedmont.ca.gov/Electrification-Rebates. Rebates are firstcome, first-served, and funding is not guaranteed.
articles.title: Expanded home electrification rebates available

Now, households earning up to 120% of Area Median Income (roughly $195,000/year for a 4-person household) can qualify for a new “moderate-income” rebate tier. Households that qualify for CARE or FERA will continue to receive the highest rebate amounts. Before starting a project, review current rebate amounts and eligibility requirements at piedmont.ca.gov/Electrification-Rebates. Rebates are firstcome, first-served, and funding is not guaranteed. articles.text: Ready for a new best friend? So is Koala! This 11-year-old tabby quickly overcomes her shyness to become a devoted companion—often curling up as the little spoon for movie night. Koala is wonderfully expressive. She’ll make soft eye contact and meow sweetly to invite you to follow her around the house, sometimes flopping down mid-walk for a surprise cuddle. When she’s at her happiest, she kneads enthusiastically, purrs loudly, and occasionally drools as she makes biscuits. This darling old lady knows what she likes, and that is to be the only cat in a calm, indoor-only home, complete with her favorite litter box set-up (low sides, please!). Her daily medication and love of routine help her stay confident and comfortable. Adopt Koala through Cat Town. Although she’s not a kitten anymore, Koala still has a playful side. She loves chasing her wand toy near you and goes wild for catnip. After a quick burst of play, she’s ready to settle in with an adoring gaze for close snuggles. Koala is ready to reward you with endless affection— and plenty of cuddles. Koala is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. articles.text: At the city’s Park Commission meeting on August 5, the commission announced that the Hampton Field turf replacement project is underway. The project is expected to start within the next two weeks. Hampton Field has shown significant wear and damage in the heavy-use zones. The city’s artificial fields are serviced twice a year through a contract with FieldTurf’s maintenance staff. During their most recent visit, the turf maintenance staff reported substantial tears in the path between second and third bases. There is concern for the safety of youth players if the field is not replaced. FieldTurf also noted that the quality of the turf blades had degenerated to the point that it made it challenging for the turf to continue to hold sand and cork infill. Artificial turf has an approximate life expectancy of 8-10 years. Hampton Field’s turf field was installed in 2016, marking 10 years with the turf in place. FieldTurf, the firm that provided the turf for the Linda Beach Tot Lot and Witter Field at the high school, will be replacing the Hampton Field turf. The contract was awarded to the company for $171,824. During the Park ComThe severe damage to the turf field between second and third base mission’s meeting, Parks Director Nancy Kent said that once the construction starts, she expects the installation to take one week. Hampton’s damaged turf field
articles.title: City to replace turf field at Hampton after 10 years

articles.text: I’ve been thinking a lot lately about connection as a muscle. For most of human history, and honestly for most of our own lives, until pretty recently, we got a lot of tiny social “reps” without trying very hard. When we walked into a store, we talked to the cashier. If we got lost, we asked someone for directions. We chatted with the person next to us in line or made small talk with the barista while waiting for our regular coffee order. We walked through the world without earbuds in our ears and a phone in our hand. And while none of these interactions felt especially meaningful because they honestly weren’t, they served a very important purpose. They were moments of connection reps. Tiny moments of eye contact, noticing another person, saying something, responding, adjusting, laughing, recovering from awkwardness. And all those reps added up. Today, a lot of those moments have quietly disappeared. We order through apps and use self-checkout. We text instead of call. We put in earbuds and fill every pause by looking at a screen. Again, none of these things are bad. They are convenient and I use all of them, but I do wonder what happens when we stop doing the little lifts. Because then, when we need to do the big connection lifts, they somehow feel much harder. Things like starting a conversation with someone new or inviting a potential friend to coffee. Or walking into a room where you don’t know anyone and then asking a question that might feel vulnerable. These are all heavier connection lifts. And if our connection muscles have been slowly atrophying, it makes sense that they would feel harder than they used to. So maybe, the answer is not to start with the biggest, bravest version of connection. Maybe we need to start doing little reps again. This month’s experiment is simple: look for one tiny social interaction each day that you would normally skip. For instance, say something to the cashier instead of looking at your phone and remember to ask the barista how their day is going. Try to take out your earbuds on a walk and choose to make one phone call instead of sending a text. The goal is not to become wildly extroverted or strike up deep conversations with strangers; it’s to simply exercise the connection muscle. Connection is not only built in the big moments, it is built in hundreds of tiny acts of social courage and attention that teach us, over and over again, how to be with other people. And the good news about muscles is that even when they get a little weak, they can get stronger again. We just have to notice and then start doing the reps again. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Summer experiment: Exercise our connection muscles

pages.text: Wednesday, August 12, 2026 7 PMS Registration Continued from page 1 for the first time. Retired seventh grade teacher Ted Scherman and current P.E. teacher Tim Wisnewski hosted 6th grade boot camp orientation for 49 students the week before, to ease some of the new school anxiety. Piedmont Post papergirl and 6th grader Zoë Selor found the Post’s booth and summed up her take on the registration event. “I didn’t expect it to be so loud,” she said. After these 6th, 7th and 8th graders received their new class assignments with wide eyes they compared classes with newly reunited friends. The party spilled out onto the patio where the music blared and students lingered with renewed vigor displacing their dog days of summer melancholy. Outside, students spun a wheel of fortune for new school supplies and enjoyed food from a taco truck on Magnolia. Many tried to guess how many M&Ms and other candies were inside of mason jars, hoping to win the bounty of sugar on the first day of school, when the correct quantities are announced. The 2026 Walkthrough Registration at PMS may have been the most raucous and exciting iteration yet, setting the stage for a year to come filled with fun. Outside of the gym, students played Jenga and guessed at how many pieces of candy were inside of jars. Piedmont Post Executive Editor Misha Edel and his daughter Larissa, who is also a Post contributor, worked the newspaper’s booth on August 7. pages.text: 8 8 Wednesday, August 12, 2026 School is Back Continued from page 1 The Beach Parents Club unveiled their new shirts for the year, adorned with the school’s mascot, the friendly French Bulldog Oliver. The school at 100 Lake Avenue is anchored by Anne Valva, who enters her fifth year as the principal and 15th in the district. She is now the longest-tenured principal in the district. At Beach, outgoing Superintendent Jennifer Hawn stopped by with interim Superintendent Evans. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich and School Board President Ruchi Medhekar also graced the Beach campus early Monday morning, overseeing the start of Piedmont’s top-ranked elementary site. At Wildwood and Havens students readopted their familiar routes walking to school, this time with one more grade and fresh summer tans to their credit. Havens students returned to find a brand-new playground and tested out the equipment heartily before the first bell. Both Wildwood and Havens will benefit this year as principals Amy Fry and Susanne Reed enter their second years guiding their students and staff. Piedmont Middle School started the first day with many new faces in the faculty room replacing retirees. Piedmont High School students moved up the ladder towards graduation by one more rung. Teenage students likely had the most difficulty adjusting from summertime schedules and back to early morning alarm clocks. Piedmont has kept the same instructional calendar from last year. August 10 marks one of the earliest starts in the Bay Area, tied with Oakland Unified. Piedmont is not the earliest in the state to start the race to 180 instructional days though. Some schools in Tracy started last week and Stockton Unified brought students back on July 30. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council’s Cub Scouts welcome new families and youth in grades K-5. Pack open houses are a great opportunity to meet adult leaders, make new friends, and learn about the adventures that await your family. Cub Scouts do fun activities like: • Building and racing Pinewood Derby cars • Camping under the stars • Hiking Bay Area trails • Exploring reptiles and wildlife with programs like Tree Frog Treks • Learning outdoor skills like fire building and knot tying • Making friends and giving back through community service You can also meet local Pack leaders at elementary school back-toschool events in August and September. Scouting has been a proud Piedmont tradition for generations, with nearly 20% of local youth participating. Questions? articles.text: On Tuesday, August 4, Piedmont hosted its National Night Out to celebrate the public safety departments that help keep the city safe. Millions of neighbors take part in National Night Out on the first Tuesday in August across thousands of communities in all 50 U.S. states, U.S. territories, Canadian cities, and military bases worldwide. The annual event was hosted at the Exedra in Piedmont Park, with multiple tables set up to engage with the community. Police officers and firefighters were walking around the Exedra speaking with community members and answering any questions they had. At the tables, they had public safety-themed coloring books, pinwheel spinners, pens, stickers, hand sanitizer, junior firefighter helmets, and more. There were lawn games and giveaways that attendees could participate in. An ice cream truck was parked on Highland Avenue for guests to enjoy. Refreshments like popsicles were available in coolers in front of the tables at the Exedra fountain. Next to the ice cream truck was Fire Engine 1 parked for children to explore the inside. A Piedmont kid reaches out for a fist bump from Sergeant Kristina Foster after receiving his public safety-themed sticker. Officer Alain Trias talks with attendees and hands out stickers. Officers set up tables at the Exedra fountain to speak with residents.
