articles.text: last individual section championship for the girls’ squad. When I arrived at the Post, one thing was made clear; Piedmont High is a tennis school. At the time, the Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team was pushing one of the longest undefeated league title runs in the state and possibly the country at around 20 years. Now in 2026, how has the school’s top discipline changed? Is PHS still a tennis school, or have other teams caught up? RUNNING SPORTS TENNIS In 2018, PHS extended its league unbeaten run with one of its most talented teams including eventual Cal Golden Bear Makenna Thiel finishing her sophomore year before returning to the team as a senior in 2021. The girls’ squad was the No. 1 seed in the 2018 D2 NCS Team Tournament and the favorite to secure a sixth-straight title before poor air quality set in from the fire in Paradise. The boys’ team, meanwhile, had won five NCS titles (2009, 2012, 2014, 2015, 2017) in a nine-year span from 2009-2017. Piedmont High snapped a seven year WACC Foothill division title drought with the girls’ team in 2025. The boys, meanwhile, last won a regular season league title in 2018. Tennis continues to excel on an individual basis. Lucas Smolko graduated from Piedmont High in 2026 as our Athlete of the Year. He’s the only athlete in WACC history to win two and three straight singles titles, and also won the Division 2 NCS singles championship in 2026. In the fall of 2025, Class of 2026 graduate Samantha Huynh and Class of 2027 senior Emma Chan won the school’s first-ever WACC Doubles title. Tanya Kononova won a WACC singles title in 2022 and reached the 2023 finals. PHS Class of 2024 graduate Monte Imburg and Class of 2026 member Nate Welch won the WACC Doubles title in 2024. Thiel won the WACC singles title in 2021. Emily Becker and Audrey Call’s 2019 D2 NCS doubles title is the Both the track and cross country programs have held a steady spot atop the school. Since 2018, we’ve named 12 track/cross country stars to our year-end Athlete of the Year awards, including Reece Proctor in 2018, Sophia Zalewski in 2020, Ellie Black, Jack Stein and Parker Terrill all featured in 2022, Parker Long in 2023, Breah Bell was our honorable mention in 2024, Nia Kim and Miguel Long were our 2025 winners, along with Sam Shelby and Sebastien Swain as honorable mentions, while Claire Aubrecht was our 2026 winner. The cross country team has sent at least one athlete to the State Championship going back 37 years. Last year, PHS sent its girls’ team, marking an end of a six year drought for the girls’ and four-year absence for the school as a whole. The boys’ team last reached state in 2021 when they were led by Stein. As for the girls, they won four NCS Championships (2014, 2015, 2017, 2019) from 2014-2019. Track and Field hasn’t claimed an NCS team banner since 1943, but excels individually. Aubrecht and Swain lead the charge for the track team going into the spring of 2027. Aubrecht is fresh off a fifth-place finish in the 200 at the NCS Meet of Champions, while Swain was eighth in the 800 at the Meet of Champions. Is Piedmont still a tennis school? Pictured is Piedmont’s 2017 NCS title-winning team. BASKETBALL It’s now been over 20 years since Bryan Gardere led Piedmont High to back-to-back State titles in 2004 and 2005, but basketball has continued to produce quality players in both girls’ and boys’ teams while competing for titles. Boys Basketball reached the NCS Finals in 2024 and 2025, while girls’ basketball has won four straight league titles. Of all sports at the school, basketball currently has the most graduates playing collegiately. SOCCER Staff Photo Piedmont basketball has been among the most successful at sending athletes to compete in college. Pictured in 2023 are Perséas Gioukaris (left), Trinity Zamora, Eva Levingston, and Natalia Martinez. All four went on to play collegiately. PHS girls’ cross country team qualified for the State meet. Cross Country has sent at least one individual athlete to State for the last 37 years. Natalia Martinez and Trinity Zamora are at San Diego State, Eva Levingston is at Robert Morris University, Perséas Gioukaris played at SF State, Samantha Smith is at Macalester, Hannah Govert featured Bryn Mawr College, Erinn Gardere attends UT Tyler, Maddie Hill attended Rocky Mountain College before returning to Laney, while Adrienne Blackwell and Lindsey Wirgler also featured at Laney. Maddy Meadows also graduated from William Jessup in 2025. JoJo Murphy recently graduated from Seattle University, A.J. Harris plays at Emory University, Britt Burden plays at USC, Ravi Silverberg is featured at Macalester College and Dillon Casey recently joined Occidental College. Luke Harris and Luke Barrett wrapped up their collegiate careers at Carleton and St. Mary’s College. Barrett is the only recent PHS athlete to turn professional, now playing at AMW Arka Gdynia of Poland. In NCS, Piedmont’s boys’ last won the D4 title in 2020, while the girls last won the D4 crown in 2023. The girls’ team is among the best in the State, receiving two consecutive NCS Open Division and D1 CIF State berths. The boys’ soccer team claimed the 2025 D5 CIF NorCal title in a 4-1 win over Williams. It marked the team’s third title banner in four years after the school won D4 NCS titles in 2022 and 2023. Girls’ soccer, meanwhile, also won the D4 NCS crown in 2023. Former boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan departed the school in 2024 as its most successful soccer coach of all time. In addition to two NCS first-place banners, Sullivan’s teams won WACC Shoreline Division titles in 2019, 2021, and 2022. He finished his time at the school with 87 wins, 19 ties, and 49 losses. New coach, Ben Russell, went 13-4-9 (W-T-L) overall in his first season in 2025 toward a D4 NCS Finals appearance and the D5 CIF NorCal title. Girls’ soccer has routinely competed in NCS, qualifying for the tournament for 15 straight years. PHS ended a two-decade NCS title drought in 2023 and also lost in the finals in 2018. articles.text: In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at Parker Terrill of California’s track and field team, Taylor Rolefson of Bates College’s swim team, her brother Tom Rolefson of Hamilton College swimming, and Samantha Smith of Macalester College’s basketball team. He reached the finals of the NESCAC Championship’s 50 meter breaststroke and 200 freestyle relay. In the breaststroke, Tom finished 19th of 24 finalists with a time of 26.17. To get there, he was 22nd of 39 in the prelims Macalester College Samantha Smith, PHS Class of 2024, enters her junior year at Macalester College. She was a two-year varsity member at Piedmont High. Macalester College went 3-21 last season. Smith appeared in all 24 games and started seven times, playing 17.7 minutes per game for 66 points, 42 rebounds, seven assists, six steals, and six blocks. In 2024/2025 as a freshman, Macalester finished 12-13 overall. Smith appeared in all 25 games for 399 minutes, 57 points, 34 rebounds, 11 assists, six steals, and two blocks. At Piedmont High, Smith helped the Highlanders win the 2023 D4 NCS title as a junior and claim back-to-back Western Alameda County Conference firstplace banners. She transferred to PHS as a junior after two years at Dublin.

articles.text: LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Piedmont High Class of 2026 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2030 We recently named Lucas Smolko our 2026 Athlete of the Year after finishing his Piedmont High career in illustrious fashion. He won the school’s first North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975 by claiming the D2 crown on May 9, and won his third consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title on May 1. He is the only repeat and three-time singles champion in the league tournament on the boys’ side. For the NCS title, Smolko defeated Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3. To get there, he shutout St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson 6-0, 6-0 in the opening round, won 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and shut down Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. His win over Chen was a rematch of Piedmont’s February 26’s match against Acalanes, where Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. For the WACC singles crown, he defeated Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-3 as the top seeded player. He was our honorable menLucas Smolko recently graduated from Piedmont High and embarks on his freshman year on UC Santa Cruz’s tennis team. tion for 2024 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Freshman of the Year. Piedmont High named Smolko the school’s boys’ Oustanding Senior Athlete in 2026. Lucas will continue his tennis career at UC Santa Cruz. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program has been cultivated by my UC Santa Cruz tennis coach. I am expecting to do specific strength training exercises multiple times a week and do 5k runs weekly. This conditioning has been easing me into all the training I will be doing with the tennis team. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My summer fitness goal is to prepare myself as much as possible for my tennis season. By the time I start college I want to be able to run a 5k in under 21 minutes as that will be weekly conditioning with the team. How are you measuring your development? When I am working on my cardio I go to the Piedmont track and time most of my runs to track progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with a private trainer once a week on strength training and lift weights at home as well. When working out I have been incorporating new workouts from the UCSC tennis coach that I will be using with my team. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished was reaching clay court nationals in Florida. It was very difficult to gain enough points to be accepted into the tournament. In addition to traveling and playing many tournaments I trained a lot in the weeks leading up to the event to prepare myself for playing on clay along with very hot and humid conditions. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I would advise younger athletes to set achievable goals in your sport and plan out how you can reach them. Giving yourself a level you want to reach or event

pages.text: 14 Wednesday, August 12, 2026 SUMMER WORKOUT - MAIN Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 19th year. Current and former college athletes as well as high school athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. JASPER SCHUETZ Cycling LUCAS SMOLKO Tennis Piedmont High Class of 2026 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2030 We recently named Lucas Smolko our 2026 Athlete of the Year after finishing his Piedmont High career in illustrious fashion. He won the school’s first North Coast Section Individual Tournament singles title since Barry Gilbert in 1975 by claiming the D2 crown on May 9, and won his third consecutive Western Alameda County Conference singles title on May 1. He is the only repeat and three-time singles champion in the league tournament on the boys’ side. For the NCS title, Smolko defeated Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3. To get there, he shutout St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson 6-0, 6-0 in the opening round, won 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and shut down Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. His win over Chen was a rematch of Piedmont’s February 26’s match against Acalanes, where Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. For the WACC singles crown, he defeated Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in straight sets by scores of 6-2, 6-3 as the top seeded player. Piedmont High named Smolko the school’s boys’ Oustanding Senior Athlete in 2026. Lucas will continue his tennis career at UC Santa Cruz. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program has been cultivated by my UC Santa Cruz tennis coach. I am expecting to do specific strength training exercises multiple times a week and do 5k runs weekly. This conditioning has been easing me into all the training I will be doing with the tennis team. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My summer fitness goal is to prepare myself as much as possible for my tennis season. By the time I start college I want to be able to run a 5k in under 21 minutes as that will be weekly conditioning with the team. How are you measuring your development? When I am working on my cardio I go to the Piedmont track and time most of my runs to track progress. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with a private trainer once a week on strength training and lift weights at home as well. When working out I have been incorporating new workouts from the UCSC tennis coach that I will be using with my team. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished was reaching clay court nationals in Florida. It was very difficult to gain enough points to be accepted into the tournament. In addition to traveling and playing many tournaments I trained a lot in the weeks leading up to the event to prepare myself for playing on clay along with very hot and humid conditions. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I would advise younger athletes to set achievable goals in your sport and plan out how you can reach them. Giving yourself a level you want to reach or event Piedmont High Class of 2026 Cal Poly Class of 2030 Jasper Schuetz graduated from Piedmont High last spring and has been the stalwart of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team since his days in middle school. As a senior, Schuetz concluded his high school career by finishing fifth of 76 riders in the NorCal Interscholastic Cycling League’s High School Championship’s Varsity Boys race on May 17. He began his journey with Piedmont MTB in 8th grade. Over the past four years, he swept the Freshman category in his first season, winning every race and the Championship. As a sophomore, he led JV1 in the East Bay/Central League and 4th in the NorCal. And during his senior year, he was the Varsity Leader for the East Bay/Central League. As an independent rider, he won the Grasshopper Series Junior title, won the U18 Lost and Found (100 miles), the U18 Heart of Gold (73 miles and 10,000 feet of climbing), the Wente 2-person relay in 2025, and placed second in the U18 Rad Dirt Fest in Trinidad, Colorado (113 miles). In May, he competed in the 206-mile Life Time Unbound Gravel race in Emporia, Kansas—considered the premier gravel event in youth mountain biking. He rode 11 hours and 50 minutes to place 53rd overall in a field of 1,251 riders, and also 14th in the Male 16-29 category. Schuetz is set to continue riding on Cal Poly’s cycling team. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program consists of riding bikes around the Bay Area, surfing, and enjoying time outside. I also challenge myself with long rides up to 150 miles. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals are to stay healthy, sleep a bunch, eat clean, and stay in good cardiovascular shape. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development on Strava, where I track all my rides and look at my stats through the app. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working completely alone. I love the freedom to do whatever I want throughout the week, and I find myself doing something I enjoy every day. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I completed the Unbound Gravel 200-mile race in under 12 hours in the pouring rain on May Jasper Schuetz graduated from Piedmont High and was a premier member of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team. He’ll continue his cycling career at Cal Poly. 31st in Emporia, Kansas. It was brutal. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Do what you love to do with your friends. Never make a sport a burden or something you dread doing; always try to make it something you look forward to at the end of the day. There will always be something challenging about it, but you have to zero in on what makes the sport so special to you. JACK MEYJES Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2026 Bates College Class of 2030 Jack Meyjes graduated from Piedmont High as a three-year starter on the baseball team and two-year starter in football. In baseball Meyjes finished last season with a .329 batting average. He recorded a team-leading 25 hits, 22 RBIs, and two triples, along with 12 runs scored and three doubles. On the mound, he also led the squad with 28 strikeouts and logged two wins. In 2024 as a sophomore, Meyjes was the winning pitcher in Piedmont’s regular season WACC Foothill title clinching 7-5 win over Berkeley. On the football gridiron, Meyjes typically lined up as a receiver, helping PHS reach the D7 NCS title game. As a senior, he was credited with 19 receptions for 328 yards and six touchdowns. He’s off to continue his baseball career at Bates College. What is your workout program this summer? I’m in the gym six days a week. Throughout those six days, I work out all muscle groups and have one dedicated day for plyometrics. I sprint for 3-4 of those days as well. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals are to prepare to become a collegiate pitcher with more, overall stamina, strength and balance. How are you measuring your development? Every week I am testing myself to do more reps/weight than the week prior. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work by myself using what I’ve learned that works best for me as a pitcher. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone was bench pressing 280 pounds. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Stay in the gym so you can stay on the field! Your best ability is your availability. Staff Photo Jack Meyjes recently graduated from PHS and is set to continue his baseball career at Bates College.

articles.text: The Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat & Wat Phra That Doi Suthep [Reprinted from August 2023] Welcome travelers, hikers, and traveling hikers! Thailand is home to some of the thickest jungles in the world. Luckily, the outskirts of Chiang Mai provide a scenic hike through a Thai jungle on its way to a pair of historic Buddhist temples. The Monk’s Trail, also known as the Wat Pha Lat Trail, takes hikers to a hidden temple, Wat Pha Lat, within the Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is just 0.8 of a mile but ascends a steep 550 feet in elevation gain. During the hike to Wat Pha Lat, hikers pass under groves of bamboo with insects making noise around you, while also passing a small waterfall on your way to the temple. articles.text: “Big Picnic” closes out festival’s 89th season Public Enemy Stern Grove Festival will conclude its 89th season next weekend with its annual Big Picnic Weekend, featuring performances by hip-hop group Public Enemy on Saturday, August 15, and soul singer Al Green on Sunday, August 16. The concerts will take place at Sigmund Stern Grove, a natural amphitheater surrounded by eucalyptus, redwood and fir trees at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. Founded in 1938, Stern Grove Festival is the West Coast’s longest-running free outdoor music festival. The summer concert series has presented more than eight decades of performances spanning music, opera, theater and dance. The Big Picnic Weekend serves as the festival’s annual fundraiser. While general admission to Stern Grove Festival performances is free, picnic table seating for the final weekend is available for purchase, with proceeds supporting the festival and helping keep its concert series free for more than 110,000 people who attend the festival each summer. Public Enemy will headline Saturday’s concert. Formed in Long Island, New York, in 1985 and led by Chuck D and Flavor Flav, Public Enemy was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2013 and is known for albums including “It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back” and “Fear of a Black Planet.” Sunday’s lineup will be led by Al Green, the Grammy-winning soul singer best known for hits including “Let’s Stay Together,” “Tired of Being Alone” and “Take Me to the River.” Green, whose career began in the 1960s, was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1995. His performance will also feature Oakland singer Goapele and The Glide Ensemble, the gospel choir associated with San Francisco’s Glide Memorial Church. Doors open at noon both days, with performances beginning at 2 p.m. Picnic table seating remains available for the Big Picnic Weekend. Table purchases are considered donations to Stern Grove Festival and are nonrefundable. Visit https://www.sterngrove. org/big-picnic to purchase picnic table tickets. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet School students will perform at the Flower Piano festival at the San Francisco Botanical Garden in September as part of the annual outdoor music event. The festival is scheduled for September 10 through 20 at the 55-acre garden and will feature 12 grand and baby grand pianos placed throughout the grounds. Visitors can attend scheduled performances, watch community groups perform and play the pianos themselves during designated open-play sessions. The San Francisco Ballet School is among the performers scheduled for this year’s festival. The school’s performances will give audiences an opportunity to see ballet students perform in an outdoor setting as part of a festival that combines music and community programming. Flower Piano was established in 2015 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Ffortissimo and Dean Mermell in partnership with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The event has since become an annual festival at the botanical garden. Other performers scheduled for the 2026 festival include La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9 and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble. The ensemble’s repertoire combines hiphop, jazz and classical music. The festival also will feature an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, with seating, food and beverages, along with evening performances. During open-play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels. Organizers recommend that attendees bring picnic blankets because seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and ticket information, is available through the Gardens of Golden Gate Park at https://gggp. org/flowerpiano/. The San Francisco Ballet School is among the performers scheduled for this year’s festival.
articles.title: SF Ballet School students to perform at Flower Piano festival

articles.text: San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild will open the company’s 104th season with its annual fundraising gala “Opera Ball” on September 12. The evening will begin with a cocktail reception and dinner at San Francisco City Hall before the opening night performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra at the War Memorial Opera House. An after-party at City Hall will follow the performance. Proceeds from the event will benefit San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s artistic and K-12 education programs. This year’s Opera Ball is dedicated to Diane B. Wilsey in recognition of her 20 years as Opening Weekend Grand Sponsor, supporting Opera Ball, the season-opening performance and Opera in the Park. “Opera Ball is more than the opening night of the opera season, it is one of the Bay Area’s defining fall galas,” co-chairs Sydney Leung and Jennifer Walske said in a joint statement. “Most importantly, every ticket supports our house of creativity, San Francisco Opera, and brings the transformative power of music education to K–12 students throughout the Bay Area through San Francisco Opera Guild.” Music Director Eun Sun Kim will conduct the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and Chorus in Verdi’s political drama, which is set in 14th-century Genoa. The cast includes Mongolian baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat in the title role, soprano Eleonora Buratto as Amelia and Maria, tenor Joshua Guerrero as Gabriele Adorno, and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn as Jacopo Fiesco. The production is directed by Katherine M. Carter in Claus Guth’s staging from Hamburg State Opera. For tickets, visit sfopera.com, call (415) 864-3330 or visit the Box Office in the lobby of the War Memorial Opera House at 301 Van Ness Avenue. San Francisco Opera’s annual fundraiser benefits education programs in San Francisco.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera Ball launches company’s 104th season Sept. 12

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse concludes its 2025-26 season with the Tony Award-winning musical Hairspray, running now through September 12. Set in 1962 Baltimore, Hairspray follows teenager Tracy Turnblad as she pursues a spot on the popular television program “The Corny Collins Show.” After achieving her dream, Tracy uses her newfound platform to challenge racial segregation and advocate for integration. The musical features a score by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman, including songs such as “You Can’t Stop the Beat,” “Good Morning Baltimore,” “Welcome to the ‘60s” and “I Know Where I’ve Been.” The book is by Mark O’Donnell and Thomas Meehan. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English directs the production, with Phaedra Tillery-Boughton serving as associate director, Dave Dobrusky as musical director and Phoenyx Rose as choreographer. “In San Francisco Playhouse’s new production, we will reimagine Hairspray with a sharper edge, stripping away some of its bubblegum sheen to restore the subversive bite of John Waters,” English said in a press release. “This production leans into the story’s racial politics and cultural satire, examining Baltimore’s fight for integration through our contemporary lens.” Based on the 1988 film by John Waters, Hairspray premiered at Seattle’s 5th Avenue Theatre before opening on Broadway, where it won eight Tony Awards, including Best Musical, and ran for more than eight years. The musical later opened in London’s West End, winning four Olivier Awards, and has since been adapted into a feature film and a live television production. Director Bill English said the production “becomes more than a feel-good musical… in an era marked by polarization, erasure, and the lingering shadows of racist ideology.” “It’s a defiant, joyful call to resistance, where dancing is protest and inclusion is revolutionary,” he added. Ella Ruth Francis will make her San Francisco Playhouse debut as Tracy Turnblad. Trevor March returns to the company as Link Larkin after appearing in “Into the Woods.” Jeffrey Brian Adams will play Corny Collins, while Samantha Rich portrays Penny Pingleton and Jordan Covington returns as Seaweed J. Stubbs. Jonathan Chisolm makes their Playhouse debut as Edna Turnblad alongside Ken Brill as Wilbur Turnblad. Mackenzie Macdonald will portray Amber Von Tussle, with Alison Ewing as Velma Von Tussle and Jeannine Anderson as Motormouth Maybelle. The cast also includes Rebecca Pingree as Prudy Pingleton, David Boyll as Mr. Pinky and Harriman F. Spritzer, Sanaiya Johnson and Suleika Onia Patton alternating as Little Inez, Kareem Jenkins as Duane, Kaila Dyson, Anese Jade and Cai Rodis as The Dynamites, and Sierra Bolar, Matt Letton, Gwen Tessman and Hunter Yocom as The Nicest Kids in Town. Visit https://sfplayhouse. org/2025-2026-season/hairspray/ or call the box office at 415-677- 9596 to purchase tickets. Cast of San Francisco Playhouse production of Hairspray

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater’s (A.C.T.) Twelfth Night leaves the stage this Sunday, August 16. Twelfth Night was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine, The Hollywood Reporter and The Washington Post. The play is a contemporary musical adaptation of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery. Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a duke. Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role while she finds her true love in the process. The production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic features an original jazz-funk score by Shaina Taub. The cast includes Nathan Bennett-Crump, Briana Bothello, Khalil Carim, Lucas Ceja, Laura Ferreira, Benjamin Grant, Mia Hangai, Ella Kim, Lourdes Verde Lombardo, Zoe Mastropasqua, Justina Mateescu and Keenan Moran. The play is directed by Dee Dee Stephens and choreographed by Meredith Joelle Charlson, with music direction by Amanda Dee. Twelfth Night is showing onstage at the Strand Theater in San Francisco now through August 16. Visit https://www. act-sf.org/whats-on/conservatory-shows/twelfth-night to purchase tickets.
articles.title: A.C.T.’s production of Twelfth Night ends this Sunday

articles.text: There is no doubt that music has evolved over generations. While some of us deplore the current state of affairs, there were charlatans in the past some of whom were immensely successful. A few of true intrinsic merit were overlooked. Even fewer were able to combine public acclamation and profound musical insight. Long ago, music was confined to churches. When music graduated to the concert hall, programs were very long. articles.text: A scene from Arrested Development Are you a fan of HBO’s Succession? Do you enjoy eccentric family dynamics where no one wins? Arrested Development should be the next show on your watchlist. As its narrator (Ron Howard) states at the top of every episode: “Now the story of a wealthy family who lost everything, and the one son who had no choice but to keep them all together. It’s Arrested Development.” Most sitcoms about families settle for warmth and comfort. Arrested Development, created by Mitchell Hurwitz, has almost none of the nostalgic familial dynamic, and that’s the point. The show follows the Bluths, a once-untouchably-wealthy Orange County family who ran the Bluth Company, a successful real estate development firm, until patriarch George Bluth Sr. (Jeffrey Tambor) is arrested for fraud and embezzlement. What’s left behind is his son Michael (Jason Bateman), the only Bluth who’s ever done an honest day’s work and is so dedicated to his father’s company that he and his son George Michael (Michael Cera) live in the attic of a model home unit. But he suddenly finds himself the last responsible adult in a family that’s never once considered being responsible. Michael’s attempts to keep the Bluth Company afloat quickly become secondary to the much larger problem of keeping his family from completely falling apart. His mother Lucille (Jessica Walter) is a martini-soaked social climber who cares more about preserving her lifestyle than dealing with the family’s imminent financial collapse. His sister Lindsay (Portia de Rossi) is a shopaholic with no job experience, married to Tobias Fünke (David Cross), a former licensed psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who lost his license after performing CPR on a man who didn’t need it and has since become obsessed with pursuing an acting career he is utterly unsuited for. Their daughter Maeby (Alia Shawkat) is a scheming teenager who constantly looks for new ways to get her parents’ attention, while Michael’s brothers are hardly any easier to manage. Gob (Will Arnett) is a magician whose ego far exceeds his talent, perpetually trying to prove himself to a family that rarely takes him seriously. And Buster (Tony Hale), meanwhile, is a socially stunted man-child whose sheltered upbringing has left him almost completely unequipped to function on his own.

articles.text: Ongoing through September 20 Book Club Art Show Gallery Hours This somewhat eclectic group of artists, The Book Club at Van Kleef’s, who first met at Café Van Kleef in Oakland in 2005, presents a show called For the Love of Art which includes works by about nineteen artist members and friends, and will hold Open Gallery Hours from 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. on most Saturdays and Sundays from August 15 through September 20. The show, as are all of PCA’s exhibits, is free and open to all! Thursday, August 13, 7:00 p.m. Nathan and Jessie Duo Concert Nathan Rivera and Jessie Andra Smith bring an unforgettable performance of jazzy folk music. The duo has traveled all over the world, sharing their music on streets and stages with their unique sound: a charming fusion of jazzy folk and blues on resonator guitar and accordion, with an interesting interplay of harmonies between the two voices, performing upbeat tunes rooted in the spirit of jazz, improvisation, humor, and storytelling. For advance tickets, see https://www.ticketsignup. io/NandJessie. Friday, August 14, 7:00 p.m. Danny Coots and Sonny Leyland Duo Concert Carl “Sonny” Leyland, Boogie-woogie hall-of-famer since 2010, blues and stride piano/guitar expert one-man band, partners here with Danny Coots, every musician’s dream percussionist; Danny has played drums in over 100 countries & on over 160 recordings of blues, jazz, & boogie-woogie music! Enjoy a memorable concert combining stride piano, classic jazz and ragtime, along with traditional boogie-woogie. Advance tickets are especially important for this show, available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/CarlDanny. Sunday, August 16, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Players Chamber Concert Music for Summer will include music composed by Mozart, Reicha, Bloch, and Hindemith, performed by a subset of Piedmont Chamber Orchestra’s musicians, including Susanne Rublein and Martha Stoddard, flutes; Shauna Revelli, violin; Gar Wei Lee, viola and piano; Elizabeth Sadewhite, cello; Allison Schwartz, oboe; Marcelo Meira, clarinet; Alexander Stepans, horn; and Adam Williams, bassoon. For a delightful afternoon in the gallery, featuring classic gems for strings, winds and piano, please reserve your FREE tickets at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/1993504672138. Saturday, September 5, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Piano Trio To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative (story line) that ties each tune on the program into the theme for the month. For Autumn Leaves, for example, many of the tunes, such as Autumn Leaves (1947), September in the Rain (1937), Autumn In New York (1934), have an obvious connection to the autumn theme. Other tunes such as I’ve Got the World on A String (1932) and Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams (1931) do not have such an obvious connection. The narrative ties these tunes and all the tunes on the show into the autumn theme. Don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Sunday late afternoon in our Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Tickets $25 at https://www. ticketsignup.io/Leaves or $30 at the door, cash or check ONLY. Sunday, September 6, 4:00 p.m. SonoMusette Concert SonoMusette’s long-awaited return to Piedmont Center for the Arts promises an evening that will transport the audience into the heart of Paris through the songs of Edith Piaf and other iconic performers of the period. This is more than a concert, it’s a voyage back in time to the cabarets and jazz clubs of SaintGermain-des-Prés, where stories of love, loss, and life were sung with passion. With SonoMusette, every performance invites you to feel the pulse of Parisian life and to fall in love with these unforgettable songs all over again. Mimi Pirard ~ vocalist, Robert Lunceford ~ accordion, Jan Martinelli ~ piano, Tami Pallingston ~ upright bass, Kendrick Freeman ~ drums. Advance tickets are available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/Pirard.

articles.text: If asks the question “if your imagination were dwindling from childhood, would you still remember your I.F. (Imaginary Friend)?” Ryan Reynolds takes the second leading role of Cal in this movie, which aims to answer the mystery of when kids’ imaginations stop ruling their reality and boldly asks “what happened to those invisible friends from our past?” Lead character 12-year-old “Bea” (Cailey Fleming) stumbles upon an entire network of retired imaginary friends on the top floor of grandma’s Brooklyn apartment. While at first unsure of her eyes Bea decides to employ herself as a talent agent for notbelieved-in-anymore creations of children’s imaginations. Now, this reporter has a toddler who called this the “Ghost” movie and she liked the imagery of the imaginary friends. The Betty Boop bumble bee, and Steve Carell’s character Blue, an enormous and happy-go-lucky purple monster, come to life with modern day graphics processing power. Reynolds plays the only-adult allowed into the kid world and his acting manufactured chemisRyan Reynolds and Cailey Fleming in a scene from IF try with mostly computer graphic characters. There is a backstory about Bea’s family that opens the film and gets a little too much screentime. This dad and daughter film critic team barely stayed on the couch waiting for the shiny characters, the “ghosts,” to first appear on the screen. There is good intrigue and mystery to the story and this film employes a worthy use of AI graphics development. It’s a cute story about never being too old to believe and there’s good intrigue to the development of the plot which is to relocate these unemployed Imaginary Friends. Younger kids three to maybe eight are the target audience, but there were enough surprises to keep a babysitter capable of following along. This dad and daughter duo actually finished this one, although it took two sittings. Just crossing the finish line is a win, so great job IF, you did the trick. The movie was requested ahead of reruns of Little Bus Tayo, so it earns a 7 out of 10. IF (2024). Directed by John Krasinski. Starring Cailey Fleming, Ryan Reynolds, and John Krasinski. Rated PG. 1 hour and 44 minutes. Now streaming on Paramount+, Netflix, Amazon Prime, YouTube, Google Play, Apple TV and Fandango.

articles.text: Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group had a very strong turnout of 55 walkers and six K-9 best friends at the Exedra for another special walk. As part of the group’s new initiative to ensure the longterm future of the activity, more walkers are leading walks. This morning Mary Carter was going to have the group check out the new student drop-off zones and parking around Havens School, and then take a look at beautiful old homes built before the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. Mary led the group across Highland Avenue, past the commercial center, and up the street to a spot across from Havens’ Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, where she pointed out the new “No Parking During School Hours” signs marking the new drop-off area for Havens students. There were cars parked there this morning, but when school starts next week that will be illegal. The group crossed at the Havens crosswalk to the front entrance, another drop-off zone, and then went around the corner on Oakland Avenue to the one for preschool, TK, and kindergarten students. The walkers then went down Bonita Avenue to the middle of the block, where a gate opens into the playgrounds. This gate is on the spot where the entrance to the original Bonita Avenue School stood when it was built in 1910. The school was later renamed for Frank C. Havens, who donated the land. Much of the original building was torn down in the 1950s, replaced in 1955, and later the campus was almost entirely rebuilt. The group continued down Bonita to the historic Wetmore House, the oldest surviving house in Piedmont. Jesse L. Wetmore built it in 1878 in a New Orleans architectural style, and this wonderful house narrowly escaped being torn down. When the last Wetmore daughter died in 1939, she left the property to her maid, Myrtle Brown, but Brown died while the will was in probate, which prevented her from taking ownership. The house sat vacant until 1942, when City officials wanted to raze it for a City parking lot. Mills College art instructor Alice Putnam Erskine stepped in, purchased the home at auction through a friend for $5,200, and saved it from the wrecking ball. Erskine ultimately secured the home’s permanent survival by getting it officially listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. It is the only property in Piedmont with this designation. Back in the 1870s, Wetmore built a similar Southern cottage next door as a wedding gift for his daughter, Blanche, and her husband, Dr. George Sherman. The Sherman Cottage later became a Christian Science Reading Room. The City acquired the building in 2003, and in 2011 it was converted into the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia. Then Mary led the walkers down Magnolia Avenue to the building that has been the home of the Piedmont Recreation Department for approximately 77 years. It was not the first building on the site. James Gamble, one of Piedmont’s first residents, bought land from Walter Blair and built a Victorian mansion on it sometime before 1883. It was Gamble who first used the Italian word “Piedmonte” to describe the hillside community that became the city of Piedmont. The name “Piedmont” remains, but Mary noted some street names have changed since then: Piedmont Avenue is now Magnolia Avenue, Vernal is Highland Avenue, and Amity is Craig Avenue. Gamble’s residence was destroyed, and a new house, owned by Ralph W. Kinney, was built on the site in 1912. pages.text: Wednesday, August 12, 2026 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Walkers visit the oldest house in Piedmont By Dick Carter Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group had a very strong turnout of 55 walkers and six K-9 best friends at the Exedra for another special walk. As part of the group’s new initiative to ensure the longterm future of the activity, more walkers are leading walks. This morning Mary Carter was going to have the group check out the new student drop-off zones and parking around Havens School, and then take a look at beautiful old homes built before the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. Mary led the group across Highland Avenue, past the commercial center, and up the street to a spot across from Havens’ Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, where she pointed out the new “No Parking During School Hours” signs marking the new drop-off area for Havens students. There were cars parked there this morning, but when school starts next week that will be illegal. The group crossed at the Havens crosswalk to the front entrance, another drop-off zone, and then went around the corner on Oakland Avenue to the one for preschool, TK, and kindergarten students. The walkers then went down Bonita Avenue to the middle of the block, where a gate opens into the playgrounds. This gate is on the spot where the entrance to the original Bonita Avenue School stood when it was built in 1910. The school was later renamed for Frank C. Havens, who donated the land. Much of the original building was torn down in the 1950s, replaced in 1955, and later the campus was almost entirely rebuilt. The group continued down Bonita to the historic Wetmore House, the oldest surviving house in Piedmont. Jesse L. Wetmore built it in 1878 in a New Orleans architectural style, and this wonderful house narrowly escaped being torn down. When the last Wetmore daughter died in 1939, she left the property to her maid, Myrtle Brown, but Brown died while the will was in probate, which prevented her from taking ownership. The house sat vacant until 1942, when City officials wanted to raze it for a City parking lot. Mills College art instructor Alice Putnam Erskine stepped in, purchased the home at auction through a friend for $5,200, and saved it from the wrecking ball. Erskine ultimately secured the home’s permanent survival by getting it officially listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. It is the only property in Piedmont with this designation. Back in the 1870s, Wetmore built a similar Southern cottage next door as a wedding gift for his daughter, Blanche, and her husband, Dr. George Sherman. The Sherman Cottage later became a Christian Science Reading Room. The City acquired the building in 2003, and in 2011 it was converted into the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia. Then Mary led the walkers down Magnolia Avenue to the building that has been the home of the Piedmont Recreation Department for approximately 77 years. It was not the first building on the site. James Gamble, one of Piedmont’s first residents, bought land from Walter Blair and built a Victorian mansion on it sometime before 1883. It was Gamble who first used the Italian word “Piedmonte” to describe the hillside community that became the city of Piedmont. The name “Piedmont” remains, but Mary noted some street names have changed since then: Piedmont Avenue is now Magnolia Avenue, Vernal is Highland Avenue, and Amity is Craig Avenue. Gamble’s residence was destroyed, and a new house, owned by Ralph W. Kinney, was built on the site in 1912. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, August 12, 2026 The Wine Corner Far Niente and Kenefick Ranch – Two sides of Napa Valley By Pierre DuMont It is hard to imagine two more different tasting experiences in the Napa Valley than Far Niente and Kenefick Ranch. And yet in one day last month my colleague Richard Wing and I experienced the two extremes of Napa Valley wine tasting. As you drive up a long driveway that takes you to Far Niente, you pass immaculately trimmed gardens and landscape nestled among redwoods and past a small lake. The old stone winery is majestic and everything you see says…class. The first thing you see after they hand you a glass of Chardonnay is the amazing classic car selection featuring vintage Jaguars, Alfa Romeos and Mercedes. The tasting takes place on an outdoor flagstone courtyard overlooking the lake and was hosted by the knowledgeable Reed Gomes who had well over a decade of experience at the winery and was a fount of information. Few Napa Valley wineries have a history quite as colorful as Far Niente. The handsome stone winery in Oakville dates to 1885, when pioneer vintner John Benson built the gravity-flow facility on a wooded hillside. The name he chose – Far Niente, Italian for “the sweetness of doing nothing” – seems almost deliberately at odds with the relentless work required to make great wine. Far Niente eventually fell into disuse, but the story changed dramatically in 1979 when Napa Valley entrepreneur Gil Nickel purchased the abandoned property and began an ambitious restoration. Nickel was determined not merely to revive an old winery but to establish Far Niente as one of California’s great estates. Wine production resumed with the 1982 vintage, producing both Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay. Those two varieties remain at the heart of the Far Niente style. The Cabernet Sauvignon comes from Oakville vineyards, where the combination of warm days, cooling evening temperatures and well-drained soils is particularly well suited to producing concentrated but balanced wines. The Chardonnay, meanwhile, has long been distinguished by its Burgundian influence. In 1981, Nickel imported Grand Cru Chardonnay cuttings from Burgundy, establishing a foundation for the elegant, richly textured style associated with Far Niente. The winery itself is almost as important as the wines. Its historic stone buildings and hillside caves have been carefully preserved, creating an atmosphere that recalls Napa’s pioneering era. This year, Far Niente has also completed a sensitive renovation of its Great Hall, updating the hospitality experience while retaining the character of the historic building. Far Niente today is hardly a newcomer trying to reinvent itself. Its appeal lies in consistenly beautifully made Cabernet and Chardonnay, an extraordinary setting, and a philosophy that favors refinement over fashion. In a Napa Valley that has changed enormously over the past four decades, Far Niente remains a reminder that some of the valley’s most enduring pleasures are the simplest ones—good vineyards, careful winemaking and time. Far Niente winery is nestled among the redwoods. Outdoor tasting at Far Niente overlooks a man-made lake. Far Niente focuses on Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. • 2024 Far Niente Chardonnay The Far Niente Chardonnay has a unique sense of freshness; its aromas blooming slowly as it airs in the glass and flint, toast, beeswax give way to scents of lemon and pineapple. The palate has a silky texture and explodes with layers of concentrated tropical fruit. Its generosity is complemented by fresh acidity that adds an ethereal sensation. • 2023 Far Niente Cabernet Sauvignon Oakville The deep garnet colored Oakville Cabernet has aromas of cassis, chocolate and red currants plus underlying notes of roses, tobacco and fresh herbs. Full-bodied, the palate has a taut, muscular core of youthful, expressive black fruit framed by firm, grainy tannins and tons of freshness, finishing long and savory. • 2022 Far Niente Cabernet Sauvignon Benson Vale The Benson Vale Cabernet, the winery’s flagship, exhibits a youthful dense, purple color as well as sweet notes of graphite, oak, forest floor, black currants and leather. This full-bodied, exceptionally elegant wine possesses well integrated, sweet tannin, enough acidity for balance and impressive purity. This should improve for three decades in the cellar. The estate vineyard of Kenefick Ranch in Calistoga • 2021 Far Niente Dolce Late Harvest Far Niente is one of the few Napa wineries to go to the trouble of making a late harvest botrytised wine. Crafted from a cuvee of 80% Semillon and 20% Sauvignon Blanc, the Dolce offers fragrant orange blossoms, honeycomb, and ginger scents with a core of orange marmalade, pears and spice cake. The palate is light on its feet with zippy freshness lifting the well-knit sweetness, finishing long with a skip in its step. Forgo dessert and serve this instead. Kenefick Ranch: A family vineyard in the Calistoga hills When we turned off Silverado Trail onto a small rough road, it was like entering a different world. It was serene and quiet; the normal traffic noise of Napa Valley was gone and we were in a Napa Valley from another century. Housed in an old wooden house is the tasting room for Kenefick Winery though we had our tasting sitting at a picnic table on a wooden deck overlooking the vineyards. There are still a few Napa Valley wineries where the vineyard comes before the tasting room, the brand and the marketing. Kenefick Ranch in Calistoga is one of them. The story began in 1978, when Dr. Tom Kenefick, a San Francisco neurosurgeon, discovered a 250-acre ranch tucked against the Palisades. He was drawn not only to the beauty of the property but to the possibility of farming it. Kenefick spent his weekdays practicing medicine and his weekends working the ranch, eventually taking viticulture classes at night. He approached grape growing with the analytical eye of a scientist, studying soils, rootstocks, disease and vine health with remarkable attention to detail. The estate today encompasses 125 contiguous acres in the Calistoga AVA, with volcanic soils, alluvial fans, varied elevations and several distinct microclimates. Over two decades, Kenefick replanted the vineyard with Bordeaux and Rhône varieties, including Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Viognier, Marsanne and Grenache Blanc. Kenefick Ranch began producing its own wines in 2002. The wines are made with an emphasis on balance rather than sheer power. Native yeasts, careful vineyard work and French oak are used to produce wines with soft tannins and naturally refreshing acidity. Winemaker Kent Jarman describes the goal as wines that are approachChris and Kali Kenefick run the Kenefick Estate. able when young but structured enough to reward a decade or more in the cellar. Tom Kenefick died in 2021, but his family remains deeply involved. His son Chris is now the second-generation owner and proprietor, working alongside his wife Kali and sister Caitlin to carry on their father’s vision. The family also works closely with the Garcia family, whose members have helped farm the property for decades. That continuity may be Kenefick Ranch’s greatest strength. In an increasingly corporate Napa Valley, it remains a family vineyard where the connection between the land, the people who farm it, and the wine in the bottle is still remarkably direct. • 2024 Kenefick Ranch Sauvignon Blanc The Kenefick Sauvignon Blanc from their estate vineyard reveals zesty scents of melon, grapefruit and key limes with touches of flint and dried herbs. Medium-bodied, it delivers mouth-filling citrus and mineral layers with oodles of freshness and great length. The perfect aperitif on a warm afternoon. • 2022 Kenefick Ranch Cabernet Franc “Caitlin’s Select” This is one of the best Cabernet Francs I have had from Napa Valley. It opens with wafts of menthol and rich cassis, with pure touches of earth, tobacco and exotic spices on the nose. The full-bodied palate is firm and grainy with bold, dark, black and red fruits and a mineral-laced finish. • 2022 Kenefick Ranch Cabernet Sauvignon This wine exhibits black currant fruit, a spicy, licorice, earthy bouquet, full body, and a sense of balance and grace without astringent tannin or high alcohol heaviness. It is a classic, concentrated Calistoga Cabernet Sauvignon that should drink well for 20 years.

articles.text: Art and music will fill every block of College Avenue when the Rockridge District Association presents Rock-N-Stroll on Saturday, August 22, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. This free, family- and pet-friendly celebration invites visitors to spend the day exploring one of Oakland’s most beloved business districts through live music, local art, shopping, dining, and neighborhood experiences. Unlike a traditional street festival, Rock-N-Stroll keeps the streets open while encouraging visitors to wander at their own pace. Stretching from Broadway to Alcatraz Avenue, the one-mile event transforms Rockridge into an interactive celebration where every storefront, sidewalk, and gathering space offers something new to discover. More than 50 local artists, over 20 live musical performances, artisan popups, wine and food tastings, children’s activities, demonstrations, exclusive promotions, and neighborhood restaurants create an experience that celebrates the businesses and creative spirit that define Rockridge. Rather than visiting a crowded vendor village or being packed in front of a single stage, at this festival visitors are encouraged to roam throughout the district, discovering dozens of businesses offering exclusive Rock-N-Stroll experiences. Market Hall will fire up the grill for fresh sausage sandwiches and prize wheel giveaways, while Bad Walter’s Bootleg Ice Cream pairs live music with kids’ crafts. Starter Bakery celebrates with Happy Hour specials on pastries and drinks, Belly will serve taco samples throughout the afternoon, and Redfield Cider Bar & Bottle Shop features Japanese wine tastings alongside an okonomiyaki pop-up. Shopping enthusiasts will find oneday-only promotions throughout the district. Art lovers will discover even more throughout the district with pop-ups placed across a full mile. Mercy Vintage showcases Oakland-based Palestinian artist Manar Harb alongside several guest artists, and the SLATE Contemporary Gallery will host a small works exhibition and sale with artists on-site throughout the day. Preserved, The Yoni Temple, In Full Swing Plus Sizes, Saffron Kitchen, Pegasus Books and numerous other merchants will host local artists, creating an art walk that extends the entire length of College Avenue. Families can also enjoy face painting, children’s craft stations, pup-friendly stops, photo opportunities, giveaways and interactive activities around nearly every corner, making Rock-N-Stroll a destination for visitors of all ages. Rock-NStroll celebrates Oakland’s thriving creative community with an Art Bazaar featuring more than 50 local visual artists of all ages exhibiting paintings, ceramics, jewelry, prints, textiles and handcrafted works inside and outside participating businesses. Rock-N-Stroll also showcases musicians whose performances are unlike anything audiences typically encounter. The performances will feature handpan artists, jazz, blues, soul, and rock & roll, indie folk, pop, rock, electronic music, DJs, violinists, and R&B. The majority of these artists have roots in the Bay Area and are happy to perform for their community. Par ticipating merchants throughout Rockridge will offer wine and food tastings, sidewalk pop-ups, artist demonstrations, exclusive sales, craft stations, children’s activities, prize wheels, and special promotions throughout the day. The Festival Fun Zone at College Avenue Presbyterian Church serves as the community gathering place throughout the day, featuring children’s crafts, a family photo booth, raffles for Rockridge e-Gift Cards, pup water stations and treats, and information about everything happening throughout the district. If you’re looking for family activities, check the website as merchants and local artists are hosting face painters, craft stations, workshops, giveaways for kids, and more. “Rock-N-Stroll is about celebrating the people and businesses that make Rockridge such a special neighborhood,” said Jody Colley of the Rockridge District Association. “Visitors can spend the day discovering incredible musicians, meeting local artists, supporting independent businesses and enjoying great food—all while experiencing the welcoming spirit that defines our community.” Admission is free. Visitors are encouraged to take BART to Rockridge Station or enjoy available street parking while spending the day exploring College Avenue from Broadway to Alcatraz Avenue. Rock-N-Stroll is made possible through the support of Crossroads, 1st United Credit Union, Kelly S. Wright State Farm Insurance, Page 11 Events, SLATE Contemporary Gallery, Rockridge Voice, Becker Boards, Oaklandside and BART. For the complete entertainment schedule, participating businesses and event information, visit RockridgeDistrict.com.

articles.text: On Monday, August 3, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had a strong turnout of 26 participants inside the Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. They were there to talk about their August book, The Art Thief by Michael Finkel. This non-fiction tells the true story of Stéphane Breitwieser, history’s most prolific art thief. For over six years, he stole nearly 240 artworks worth up to $2 billion from European museums. He stole these objects during broad daylight from small museums, castles, and churches. Unusually, he never sold any pieces; instead, he kept them in his room in his mother’s attic to admire. His girlfriend, Anne-Catherine Kleinklaus, was his accomplice and acted as his lookout during many of the robberies. They amassed roughly 239 items over 172 separate visits before being caught in 2001. Breitwieser was motivated entirely by an insatiable desire to live surrounded by pure beauty rather than to have wealth. He lived with his girlfriend in his dark, private room, where he felt like a king among priceless artifacts. He was finally caught after returning to a museum for what was supposedly his last theft. His capture led to a shocking conclusion when his mother panicked and destroyed or discarded many of the masterpieces. It’s not often that a reader thinks a non-fiction book is fiction. However, the story of Stéphane Breitwieser and The Art Thief is so amazing that initially that’s what one reader thought. Members of the group generally found the book to be fascinating. The chapters are short, and the book is an enjoyable, easy, fast, good summer read. Readers also found it to be a well-written book. Almost all readers gave it a thumbs up. However, liking the book didn’t mean readers liked the characters. The group thought this was a little unusual. In fact, there wasn’t a character in the book that they liked. Breitwieser was at the top of the list. He was selfish, obsessed, and even a psychopath. He rationalized his criminal behavior and was unable to control his obsessions and actions that harmed others. Breitwieser’s early family life, with a missing father who removed his beautiful works of art from Breitwieser’s life and a mother who seemed to care for nothing other than her son, damaged him. His grandparents were also party to it. There were no guardrails on Breitwieser. His family created a void in his moral character that enabled him to justify stealing anything that appealed to him. The readers thought Breitwieser’s mother was particularly contemptible because her attempt to hide Breitwieser’s crimes destroyed many of the stolen pieces. Breitwieser appreciated the beauty of what he stole. She didn’t. The readers thought she might have been protecting herself too because she must have had an idea that something her son was doing wasn’t right. Breitwieser’s behavior was also abetted by his girlfriend. She became his partner in crime and was a disappointing character in the story too. The mother and girlfriend received light punishments for their participation in the crimes, which was disapA photo of the real-life Stéphane Breitwieser, on whom the story is based Participating were Albert Chen, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, Laura Goldman, Bill Ahern, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Peggy Shultz, Lois Price, Tim Weishahn, Judy Love, Melba Yee, Ken Young, Marj Blackwell, Sandra Threlfall, Orrel Lanter, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Bella Almanzan, Rich Seigel, Robert White, Mary Carter, Hilary Honore, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Kristin Howard with them for the first time.

The group’s discussion expanded into other types of art theft, particularly larger ones. Colonial empires’ looting of less developed countries’ cultural and historical treasures was recognized, as was the unwillingness of their national museums to return the thousands of stolen objects they hold. Readers recognized that art is history and is culturally and even spiritually important for countries. These are crimes too. While most of the readers liked the book, not everyone did. For one, Breitwieser was a “parasite.” Other members of the group found him intolerable. Additionally, the author’s chronicling of his thefts was repetitive and not enjoyable. They would have also liked more information about the psychology behind this type of behavior. However, the readers seemed to agree that The Art Thief was a good book for the First Mondays Reading Group. It was one that most members would not have read, but it generated a stimulating discussion. It also raised important historical, cultural, and societal issues for us to think about. The group had previously selected Horse by Geraldine Brooks for September and Freezing Order by Bill Browder for October. After Phyllis Van Kranenburgh presented three fiction candidates, the readers selected The Correspondent by Virginia Evans for their November read. With all their business done, they took a group photo in the circle outside the Community Hall. Because Labor Day is September 7, the group will meet on September 14 at 1:30 p.m. at the Community Hall for their next discussion. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https://bit.ly/3R86PP4 or call the Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 to register. articles.text: With George Sr. behind bars and the family’s fortune rapidly disappearing, Michael becomes the reluctant center of the Bluth family’s increasingly ridiculous attempts to maintain their old way of life. Rather than dealing with the consequences of George Sr.’s crimes or accepting that their wealth is gone, the family continues spending, scheming, lying, and competing with one another as though nothing has changed. Michael is left trying to convince them that they can survive if they simply start acting like a normal, functional family, an idea that becomes increasingly impossible the longer he stays around them. What keeps this from being just a parade of terrible people doing terrible things is Michael. He’s not virtuous by any means, he’s controlling and self-righteous at times, but he’s trying. And the show frames that effort against a family that isn’t trying at all, which makes every small, doomed attempt to fix things land somewhere between hilarious and frustrating. But all of the subplots and gags, as maddening as they are for Michael, are incredibly entertaining to watch, because they aren’t separate. The absurdity of the Bluths is established almost immediately, but the show rarely treats their behavior as isolated punchlines. The jokes in the show are constantly colliding, and a joke from one episode can pay off four episodes later in a different context. Its writing is dense enough to reward close attention and is paired with a faux-documentary style: handheld cameras, sudden zooms, a wry narrator undercutting the characters’ lies in real time. Entrance to the monastery costs ฿100, which is just $2.85— it is also recommended to dress appropriately, so no tank tops. Some monasteries do not allow people wearing shorts as well, but if you’re traveling in July or August, some make exceptions like at Doi Suthep. At Doi Suthep are sweeping views of Chiang Mai from multiple overlooks on the grounds and several large statues of Buddha. Visitors are required to take shoes off when entering the primary section of the temple, where there’s a spectacular large golden Chedi, which towers 79 feet in height. Should hikers call it a day, you’ll end your hike at around 2.5 miles with over 2,000 feet in elevation gain. Taxis will be ready at the base of Doi Suthep to take patrons back into town. Heading back down the road and onto the trails makes it a 4.5 mile day of hiking. Keep in mind some steep sections coupled with usual wet conditions in Thailand could make things difficult for a descent. Hikers should wear proper footgear for tackling the Monk’s Trail and Pilgrim’s Trail, along with packing mosquito repellent to keep away the pesky critters. Rather than dealing with the consequences of George Sr.’s crimes or accepting that their wealth is gone, the family continues spending, scheming, lying, and competing with one another as though nothing has changed. Michael is left trying to convince them that they can survive if they simply start acting like a normal, functional family, an idea that becomes increasingly impossible the longer he stays around them. What keeps this from being just a parade of terrible people doing terrible things is Michael. He’s not virtuous by any means, he’s controlling and self-righteous at times, but he’s trying. And the show frames that effort against a family that isn’t trying at all, which makes every small, doomed attempt to fix things land somewhere between hilarious and frustrating. But all of the subplots and gags, as maddening as they are for Michael, are incredibly entertaining to watch, because they aren’t separate. The absurdity of the Bluths is established almost immediately, but the show rarely treats their behavior as isolated punchlines. The jokes in the show are constantly colliding, and a joke from one episode can pay off four episodes later in a different context. Its writing is dense enough to reward close attention and is paired with a faux-documentary style: handheld cameras, sudden zooms, a wry narrator undercutting the characters’ lies in real time. This kind of cinematography and screenwriting makes the show feel less like a sitcom and more like it’s eavesdropping on a family with no idea how absurd it looks from the outside. Arrested Development ran three seasons on Fox before cancellation in 2006, then returned on Netflix for a fourth season in 2013 and a fifth in 2018–2019. It won six Primetime Emmys and a Golden Globe, and its groundbreaking style can be seen all over modern single-camera comedy, from Community to 30 Rock. If you want a show that finds real comedy in a family actively failing each other — no lessons learned, no group hugs, just a son who won’t stop trying to save them — this is it. Arrested Development is currently available to stream on Netflix, with individual episodes available to purchase on Apple TV, Amazon Video, and Fandango At Home. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: Nature Play Area hand-drawn illustration by artist Ana Gadish-Linares Following the removal of the unsafe swings in 2024, Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s (PBF) Fall Fundraising Campaign successfully focused on securing funds for the swing replacement. The redesigned area will feature state-of-the-art materials for enhanced durability and safety, including new safety matting to replace the existing sand, upgraded ADA access and a refined perimeter for the swing area. To build on this momentum, the PBF Spring Campaign is now focused on creating a nature play area adjacent to the swings. This project will transform an underused section of the park into a vibrant outdoor learning environment featuring climbing logs, native plants, and hands-on natural play elements for children to explore. PBF has worked since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces that foster a strong sense of pride and community. In addition to its many valuable contributions to parks, tot lots, schools, and recreational facilities, PBF also brings the community together to celebrate the Piedmont Lights Up ceremony every December. PBF looks forward to sharing more updates as they work to improve the community’s outdoor spaces. To learn more about PBF’s efforts to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park, visit their website: https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/ways-to-give/.
articles.title: PBF partners with the city to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park

Good public spaces bring together people who might not otherwise meet, and they are one of the first places where children begin to understand that they are part of a larger group — a neighborhood. We should give them a place worthy of their enthusiasm,” said Dunlap. During the fundraising effort for the swings, two parents, Alex Corvin and Sally Baker Chapin, partnered with PBF to secure $5,000 in matching donations from the organization. They’ve lived in Piedmont their entire lives and believe it’s important to have a space to go with your little one and find others in similar situations. These places build new friendships that started as small talk between pushes on the swings. “We both grew up in Piedmont and care deeply about this community. Now, as parents of young kids, we understand the need for beautiful public spaces to gather with other families. The swings are a central part of the playground, and the more space we can give these kids to play and roam, the better,” said Corvin and Chapin. The project includes a nature play area fundraised by PBF. This is because the children will get to play and interact with nature, which teaches them more about the natural world. “Instead of everything being manufactured and directed, children will be able to interact with natural materials, explore, balance, build, imagine and make discoveries. A stick can become a magic wand, or a sword, or absolutely nothing at all, and that freedom is part of the point. It also doesn’t hurt if some of their memory-making involves getting a little dirty,” said Dunlap. The new project includes site demolition and removal of the sand where the swings used to be. They will install a new sidewalk, ADA playground fiber, handrails, storm drainage, and a nature play area funded by the PBF. The city expects the demolition work to take around six weeks. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn’s three-year tenure will be defined by increased academic rigor and significant policy shifts as she says goodbye on August 12. Hawn’s legacy will be seen and felt for years to come with expanded and enriched course offerings for AP and Honors courses, adding foreign language back to 7th grade and adding Latin in 5th grade. The elementary curriculum also received a shakeup, 4th grade music was replaced with Theater Arts and 5th grade instrumental music was almost doubled. The drama and theatre study will emphasize voice, movement, and storytelling while making connections to English Language Arts and social studies material. While in Piedmont, Hawn and her board, adopted a new evidence-based K–5 literacy curriculum with Spellography and Fish Tank Learning. As that English Language Arts program enters its second year a multi-year plan is set to benefit students learning to read and write. The board’s interest in jump starting this program deserves much credit too. Hawn’s team also put in a great showing toward their “Partnering Beyond the Classroom” goal by launching the Piedmont Alumni Network, which aims to connect graduates with current students. Under Hawn’s leadership experiential learning and field trips were increased across schools. New dual enrollment options at community colleges also moved learning off campus. Hawn did well to keep parents informed by authoring her bi-monthly Piedmont Pulse newsletter. Her openness to communicate with families and the press proliferated her messages. New selections for principals made under Hawn’s tenures are Jennifer Hawn’s last day as PUSD Superintendent will be August 12.
articles.title: Supt. Jennifer Hawn’s Piedmont legacy

articles.text: The Post welcomes Piedmont High students back to school! With the 2026-27 school year upon us, here is a look back to our favorite moments from last year. 1. Jennifer Hawn’s Piedmont legacy By Jay Russell Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn’s three-year tenure will be defined by increased academic rigor and significant policy shifts as she says goodbye on August 12. Hawn’s legacy will be seen and felt for years to come with expanded and enriched course offerings for AP and Honors courses, adding foreign language back to 7th grade and adding Latin in 5th grade. The elementary curriculum also received a shakeup, 4th grade music was replaced with Theater Arts and 5th grade instrumental music was almost doubled. The drama and theatre study will emphasize voice, movement, and storytelling while making connections to English Language Arts and social studies material. While in Piedmont, Hawn and her board, adopted a new evidence-based K–5 literacy curriculum with Spellography and Fish Tank Learning. As that English Language Arts program enters its second year a multi-year plan is set to benefit students learning to read and write. The board’s interest in jump starting this program deserves much credit too. Hawn’s team also put in a great showing toward their “Partnering Beyond the Classroom” goal by launching the Piedmont Alumni Network, which aims to connect graduates with current students. Under Hawn’s leadership experiential learning and field trips were increased across schools. New dual enrollment options at community colleges also moved learning off campus. Hawn did well to keep parents informed by authoring her bi-monthly Piedmont Pulse newsletter. Her openness to communicate with families and the press proliferated her messages. My tradition, though imperfect, is also one of good people doing good work. I was reminded of this when one of the members at Shell Ridge Community Church in Walnut Creek gave me a collection of prayers by the Reverend Walter I. Fishbaugh from his tenure (circa 1965-75) as pastor of Valley Baptist Church of Walnut Creek, one of the predecessors of Shell Ridge. The collection is titled Lord Have Mercy! 100 Prayers for hard times and hard hearts. The first prayer in the collection concludes with these words. “All we seem to achieve are brief interludes of insight — occasional episodes of faith’s firm grasp — and then the tumult and tempest resume. Speak the ‘Shalom! Be Still!’ we pray Thee, O God. Do not speak it to the storm but speak it to our souls. We do not ask that the buffeting cease. We do not expect to be spared the surf or the storm. We ask only that in the strain and stress we may know some reassuring familiarity — some continuing core of Eternal presence — some convincing trace of Thy faithfulness — so that in the midst of change we are not lost. Find us, O God, and go with us. Possess us and never let us go. Amen.” I do not know the precise struggles and strains in which the Spirit gave rise to these words. I know that I find them helpful and that I find myself grateful to Rev. Fishbaugh and for being, with him, part of the American Baptist story, a story both imperfect and impactful. Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland.
