articles.text: There has been a lot of noise about how homeowners should market their homes for sale. But the most important question is not whether every property should follow the same process. It’s which strategy will best position the seller and their home to achieve the right result. At Compass, we believe sellers should have a choice. They can place their home on the MLS immediately, or they can begin with a phased marketing strategy that allows them to test pricing, gather feedback, and prepare the property before it is presented to the The moment a home is listed on the internet via the MLS or another portal, the clock starts ticking and days on market begin accumulating. This is a statistic that everyone can now see. The asking price becomes an anchor from which buyers negotiate down. When a buyer sees the days on market increase, they perceive there is something wrong with the property. Moreover, public price cuts make the seller appear desperate, which further hurts the seller. Pre-marketing a home gives a seller the opportunity to ready their property, evaluate pricing, gather market feedback, and make informed decisions before their home makes its public debut on the MLS. New research found that homes that use pre-marketing, such as Private Exclusive or Coming Soon, before being listed on the MLS, sell for 4.6% more than homes that go directly to the MLS. They also sell faster and are significantly less likely to experience public price reductions. On a $1.5 million home, a 4.6% premium represents approximately $69,000. For a seller, that difference could become part of a down payment on their next home or provide additional retirement savings and greater financial security. The research findings make sense because a home that enters the public market with the right price, the right presentation, and stronger information on buyer demand is better positioned to succeed. Just as companies in other industries test products before a major launch, sellers should have the ability to gather information and refine their strategy before putting one of their most important financial assets on the market. No single approach will be right for every homeowner. Some sellers will want immediate and maximum public exposure. Others may value privacy, flexibility, or the ability to test the market before their public debut. Both choices should remain available. Real estate professionals, as trusted advisors, have a fiduciary duty to share with a seller the myriad opportunities available before listing directly on the MLS. The seller is not obliged to adhere to the rules of the listing aggregators or third-party websites that don’t have their best interests in mind. That may be one way, but it’s not the only way. At Compass, we offer clients a choice when selling their home, helping them confidently and successfully reach their goals, based on their individual needs. YOU, the homeowner, should decide the best approach to selling your home. Submitted by Kevin Patsel, Regional Vice President, NorCal, Compass

articles.text: Part two Last week I began what I hope will be a series of essays under the umbrella title The Only Constant is Change wherein I referred to the Gutenberg revolution which eventually led to the democratization of reading, an expanding access to books, and the extraordinary impact writing and reading had on countless Shortly after that first Post article appeared, I received by email a remarkable 28-page essay from a fellow Returned Peace Corps Volunteer. He had devoted several decades since returning encouraging those Peace Corps writers who sought to capture in prose the essence and meaning of those two years of service in some of the most challenging and The author of the essay, The End of Reading is Here, was The Atlantic Magazine journalist Rose Horowitch and can be found in the August, 2026 edition. And just under the title is the following caveat: “Optimists once believed that universal literacy was inevitable. Now it seems that the age of reading might be a short anomaly in human history.” When I received the essay I read and reread what was not a prediction of future outcomes, but an affirmative, well documented essay that we have indeed arrived at a second Gutenberg moment. Initially I approached Horowitch’s thesis with skepticism. My earliest memories are of yearning to read, and I soon began collecting comic books filled with graphic stories of superheroes. I was a devoted member of the Dell/Marvel Universe. As were my friends. Before long I had a library card and relished spending afternoons, when not playing ball at the local rec department field, at a small local library. And yet, there was that subtitle qualifier. That word “anomaly.” Horowitch points out that while Americans were once members of a proudly literate society, according to a National Endowment for the Arts comprehensive survey of the nation’s reading habits, “fewer than half of all adults reported having read a book of any kind in 2002. Only 38 percent read a novel or short story.” Horowitch goes on to say: According to an analysis of 236,000 responses to the American Time Use Survey it was found that “the proportion of Americans who read for pleasure on any given day fell from 28 percent in 2004 to 16 percent in 2023. (The study looked at people who had read a book, magazine, or newspaper; listened to an audiobook; or read an e-book.) Gambling has become a more common leisure activity than reading a book. Last year 57 percent of Americans placed a bet.” What has changed, and why? Part three to follow. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Enjoy a free performance of Shakespeare’s Richard III in Dracena Park on Sunday, August 9, presented by the Vallejo Shakespeare Group. The group will perform on Sunday, August 9, at 4 p.m. in Lower Dracena Park. The performance will take place in the quarry area, next to the grove of dawn redwoods. Seating is first come, first served and will be picnic-style on the lawn. Bring a blanket or a low beach chair to enjoy the performance. Friendly, well-behaved dogs are welcome but must be on leash. Parking is limited, so consider walking, biking, or carpooling to the performance. This performance marks the fifth appearance of Vallejo Shakespeare in Piedmont. Previous stagings include As You Like It (2025), The Winter’s Tale (2024), Hamlet (2023), and Henry V (2019). Established in 2010, Vallejo Shakespeare Group produces one live Shakespeare play each summer, with free performances in outdoor settings across the Bay Area. The troupe uses minimal sets and costuming, putting the focus on the dialogue and actors’ performances. For more information contact Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Do you love a calm routine and peaceful space? Are you known for being patient, observant, and appreciating life’s little moments? We think you’ll love Thomas. articles.text: Edric is a 5-year-old Australian Cattle Dog/Blue Heeler mix weighing 40 pounds with a bright mind and a fun-loving personality. During a short foster stay, Edric quickly learned “sit,” “down,” “bed,” “stay,” and “off,” and even appeared to understand “outside.” He also signaled when he needed to go outside. He thrives on interacting with people and loves learning new things. Since he is highly treat-motivated, training is fun and easy. Edric enjoys both independent exploring and interactive toy play. When playtime winds down, he happily leans in for all-over scratches and affection. While he may become a bit bouncy when excited, Edric settles down nicely with gentle petting. Edric would do well with appropriately matched dogs or as a solo dog with dog friends outside the home. articles.text: At the council meeting on July 20, councilmembers accepted the 2025 Annual Progress Report for the implementation of the Piedmont General Plan 6th Cycle (2023-2031) Housing Element programs. Interim Planning and Building Director Jeff Bond presented the report detailing the City’s ongoing progress toward meeting its State-mandated Regional Housing Needs Allocation. Last year was determined to be satisfactory, but the council was slightly concerned with the small decline in planning and building permits compared to the past four years. In 2025, the City completed construction of 14 new homes, all of which were accessory dwelling units (ADUs), which is an increase from the nine units completed in 2024. The City issued 15 building permits (14 ADUs and one SB 9 unit). City staff categorized the 15 permitted units as four very low-income, five low-income, three moderate-income, and three above-moderate-income units. These numbers are a decline from the previous four years, which saw over 20 planning permits and at least 16 building permits. 2025 falls short of the city’s goal to build 20 ADUs per year. Bond attributes this to the current state of the market, mortgage rates, and high construction costs. In addition to direct unit construction, Piedmont made significant progress implementing the 77 programs outlined in its Housing Element. Key achievements in 2025 included relaxing zoning restrictions for mixed-use development and adopting the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, adopted in October 2025, provides a framework for the construction of 132 new homes on City-owned land along Moraga Avenue, including road safety improvements, design and landscaping standards, and wildfire safety requirements. The city posted a request for qualifications in May 2026 to begin a search for a development team for Moraga Canyon. The report highlighted the average rent in Piedmont in 2025 was $2,473 per month, the same as reported in 2024. This is still down from the rent prices in 2023 ($2,609) and 2022 ($2,725). Piedmont’s average rent is less than the City of Oakland’s at $2,565 per month for a 769-square-foot unit. California has seen a slight increase in new housing permitted statewide. It’s up 2% from about 119,000 in 2024 to about 121,000 in 2025. There have been gains in affordable multifamily housing and ADU production. Low-income housing saw increases at all stages of development from 2024 to 2025. The number of entitled units increased by 122% from 1,511 to 3,350, permitted units by 7.6% from 3,492 to 3,758, and completed units by 36.4%, from 2,741 to 3,739. The state-mandated targets for the production of new units in Piedmont by the end of 2031 are 587 housing units in the following affordability categories: 238 above moderate income; 92 moderate income; 94 low income; and 163 very low income. Piedmont’s progress will be assessed by the Housing and Community Development department again in June 2027. R e c r e a t i o n 358 Hillside Ave. piedmont.ca.gov/recreation
articles.title: Piedmont progress report of the 6th cycle Housing Element

articles.text: As students return to school, families dropping off and picking up students at the Civic Center may need to adjust their routes due to recent circulation changes. Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues is now one-way (in the northbound direction). Families with students at Havens Elementary, Piedmont Middle School, and Millennium and Piedmont High Schools should review their usual route before the first day of school. Drivers can no longer turn onto Bonita from Oakland Avenue, and the Havens Elementary drop-off zone on Bonita has been eliminated. These changes apply most directly to Havens families but may also affect routes to other schools and facilities in the Civic Center. Highland Avenue is now the primary pick-up/drop-off area for Havens Elementary. Loading zones are available on both sides of the street, and a crossing guard is available to assist students crossing Highland. Families approaching Havens from the south part of town should use the new white curb zone, which was added in January, instead of turning on Vista or Craig. Parents should pull into the new white curb zone across the street from Havens to drop off their student. Under the new traffic pattern, allow extra travel time during the first week as drivers become The block of Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland was converted to one-way traffic heading toward Oakland Avenue. This change eliminated the Havens Elementary drop-off zone on Bonita and added 17 new parking spaces on the Havens Elementary side of the street. familiar with the changes. The Piedmont Police Department will have an employee at the Bonita/ Oakland intersection during the first week of school to assist during the transition. Secondary zones remain available on Oakland and Vista Avenues. Havens families should review the school’s updated pick-up/drop-off information before school begins and use Highland Avenue whenever possible. Traffic and pedestrian activity will increase throughout the Civic Center when school resumes. Drivers should slow down, follow posted signs and traffic laws, and watch carefully for students and other pedestrians. When picking up or dropping off students, the city and school recommend families: • Use designated loading zones and follow the restrictions posted on signs • Do not stop in travel lanes or other undesignated areas • Allow extra time and avoid unsafe turns or last-minute maneuvers • Remain alert for crossing guards and pedestrians at intersections With these new changes, families should plan their route for the first day of school to ensure they’re prepared. Families should contact their school to ask if their drop-off zones have changed or if there have been any changes to their usual route.
articles.title: City recommends families review Civic Center travel routes before school starts

articles.text: Every so often, nature gives us an opportunity to stop what we’re doing, look up, and wonder together. On August 12, a total solar eclipse will be visible from parts of Russia, Greenland, Iceland, and Spain for the first time since 1999. If you happen to be on a European holiday, consider this your reminder to step outside and look up. If not, there’s still plenty you can do to explore the science together from home. A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun, temporarily blocking the Sun’s light. Only people sitting directly within a narrow path will experience totality—when the Sun is almost completely hidden, and the sky turns to night—while those outside it will see a partial eclipse or none at all. One of the best places to see the eclipse next week will be in northern Spain, where the maximum eclipse will happen around 8:25 p.m. local time. Because the eclipse there will take place just before sunset, it will appear very low on the horizon—just about one hand’s width above the ground! This rare mix of an eclipsed Sun and the setting sky will produce vibrant sunset colors and a 360-degree twilight glow, making it one of the most visual and unforgettable sky shows of the century! One of the best ways to understand eclipses is through a simple hands-on activity. Using any broad or ring-shaped light that shines from multiple angles at once (your tween’s ring light would work great!), try the Exploratorium’s Science Snack A mother and son safely observe a solar eclipse during an Exploratorium watch party. Eclipses of the Ring Light to recreate the alignments of the Moon, Earth, and Sun. As you reposition the Moon, you’ll discover how eclipses occur, why the path of totality is so narrow, and the different types of shadows the Moon casts. As you play with light and shadow, share what you notice, what you wonder, and try new experiments based on what you want to learn next. What’s happening during an eclipse? Why don’t they happen every month? Why does the Moon sometimes appear to cover the entire Sun and other times only part of it? These kinds of conversations invite us to think like scientists, not by memorizing facts, but by observing, wondering, and building explanations together. Of course, nothing compares to experiencing the eclipse itself. On August 12, the Exploratorium will host a watch party featuring a live broadcast of totality from Spain, alongside scientists and eclipse experts who will help explain what’s happening as it unfolds. Although California won’t experience totality, families can still experience the excitement of this global event while learning the science behind it. Eclipses have a way of bringing people together, and next week is no exception. Let it be a reminder that some of the best learning happens when the world itself becomes the classroom. Sometimes all it takes is looking up, asking questions, and letting curiosity do the rest. To try the Eclipses of the Ring Light activity at home, visit the Exploratorium’s Science Snacks collection at exploratorium.edu/ snacks. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. She is a Nationally Board Certified Teacher with over two decades of experience in the San Francisco Bay Area. bonus to retire in 2026. articles.text: Incoming 6th grader Jack Detlefsen spoke to the Post about the benefits of the bootcamp. “Starting at the middle school seems a little easier now that I know where everything is. I’ve made some new friends already. I still have some worries about the change, but I’m excited for math class and to create projects in school,” said Detlefsen. Bootcamp used to be a fiveday camp with a large focus on academics, but now it runs for three days, with one group learning the ropes on Monday and Tuesday and the second group packing in all their preparation on Wednesday. Former teachers Scherman and Penny Sullivan, started the orientation camp in 2014, to help 6th grader feel comfortable on campus through games and team building activities. Also helping Scherman, Wisnewski and the 8th grade staffers this year was Ted’s son Julian, a PHS 2021 graduate. The camp starts with outdoor activities, to help smooth over the most glaring difference from elementary school- a lack of recess time. Bootcamp took over the Bern Courts, as students put their minds together to complete the Human Knot trials. Scherman’s academic and organizational tips in the MPR also served to get rid of the first day jitters. This extra preparation helps the new 6th graders make the big transition to the new campus with new colleagues, schedules and teachers. A little extra academic pressure is on the horizon as well, with students receiving letter grades for the first time. Although Scherman will not be teaching 6th, 7th or any grade this year, one more crop of new middle schooler got Scherman’s grand tour of their new academic home for the next three year. Incoming sixth graders put their heads together to try to solve a math riddle. New sixth graders welcome the Scherman family dog, Josie, during orientation

articles.text: Once a year, Oaklandish invites adults to relive the magic of Fairyland on their own terms. On Friday, August 14 from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., Fairyland opens its gates for the 14th annual Fairyland for Grownups, an evening of art, entertainment, and pure imagination – an adult-only event. Tickets are on sale now. Fairyland for Grownups transforms the beloved storybook park into an adults-only playground, featuring cocktails, food trucks, live art activations by local visual artists, puppet shows, live DJs, dancing under the stars, and special musical performances by Bay Area heavy-hitting artists. Guests can explore Fairyland’s iconic storybook sets, from Willie the Whale to the Alice in Wonderland card maze, and even ride the beloved Jolly Trolley. Tot-sized rides and animal areas will be closed for the evening. This year’s lineup includes: DJ SHELLHEART: A Bay Area powerhouse who has spun for the Warriors, Outside Lands, San Francisco Pride, and the Valkyries. DJ SHELLHEART will bring her signature blend of crowd-pleasing hits and immaculate vibes to keep the Merry Meadow dance floor alive all night long. DJ Red Corvette: She is a DJ, music director, and one half of the brilliant minds behind Women Sound Off. With a 10-year journey as a top-tier DJ, she’s rocked at many festivals, nightclubs, and branded events, leaving her mark across Cali and NYC’s hottest spots. Michael Sneed: An East Oakland rapper, producer, and vocalist who uses his vocal superpowers to share narratives about Black joy, personal malaise, reclamation, nostalgia, and the importance of friendships amid the swirling chaos of tech-fueled capitalism. Ovrkast: Oakland-reared rapper, producer, and director Ovrkast is known for his jazz-influenced, sample-heavy sound and fierce independence. After producing for Drake, Earl Sweatshirt, and MAVI, he debuted as a solo artist with Try Again (2020), RESET! (2023), and KAST GOT WINGS (2024) alongside Cardo. His acclaimed 2025 sophomore album, While The Iron Is Hot, cemented his multi-hyphenate status. Beyond music, he directs visuals via his production company, Angr Management, building a creative universe rooted in community and longevity. As part of the annual benefit, guests can purchase the limited-edition Oaklandish Fairyland “Starlit Tee,” featuring a vintage-inspired illustration of Fairyland icons and storybook sets, with delightful characters journeying within its world. The black tee features colorful depictions of “Happy Dragon,” Humpty Dumpty, Willie the Whale, and the famous Fairyland Shoe, accompanied by text that reads “Children’s Fairyland.” The shirt is available to purchase at Oaklandish retail stores and online at oaklandish.com. The event runs for four hours, with bars and activities set up throughout the park. Admission is $30 per person and $25 for Fairyland members. Beer, wine, and cocktails are available for purchase. A selection of Oakland’s finest food vendors will be on hand, offering a variety of delicious bites. Proceeds from Fairyland for Grownups support Children’s Fairyland’s mission to provide affordable access to all children, including outreach programs such as Fairyland for All, summer camp scholarships, and free field trips for underserved communities. While it’s okay to be a kid at heart, a valid 21+ ID is required to attend. Tickets are now available for purchase online at https://fairyland.org/fairyland-for-grownups/. pages.text: Wednesday, August 5, 2026 9 Annual Fairyland for Grownups event on August 14 Once a year, Oaklandish invites adults to relive the magic of Fairyland on their own terms. On Friday, August 14 from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., Fairyland opens its gates for the 14th annual Fairyland for Grownups, an evening of art, entertainment, and pure imagination – an adult-only event. Tickets are on sale now. Fairyland for Grownups transforms the beloved storybook park into an adults-only playground, featuring cocktails, food trucks, live art activations by local visual artists, puppet shows, live DJs, dancing under the stars, and special musical performances by Bay Area heavy-hitting artists. Guests can explore Fairyland’s iconic storybook sets, from Willie the Whale to the Alice in Wonderland card maze, and even ride the beloved Jolly Trolley. Tot-sized rides and animal areas will be closed for the evening. This year’s lineup includes: DJ SHELLHEART: A Bay Area powerhouse who has spun for the Warriors, Outside Lands, San Francisco Pride, and the Valkyries. DJ SHELLHEART will bring her signature blend of crowd-pleasing hits and immaculate vibes to keep the Merry Meadow dance floor alive all night long. DJ Red Corvette: She is a DJ, music director, and one half of the brilliant minds behind Women Sound Off. With a 10-year journey as a top-tier DJ, she’s rocked at many festivals, nightclubs, and branded events, leaving her mark across Cali and NYC’s hottest spots. Michael Sneed: An East Oakland rapper, producer, and vocalist who uses his vocal superpowers to share narratives about Black joy, personal malaise, reclamation, nostalgia, and the importance of friendships amid the swirling chaos of tech-fueled capitalism. Ovrkast: Oakland-reared rapper, producer, and director Ovrkast is known for his jazz-influenced, sample-heavy sound and fierce independence. After producing for Drake, Earl Sweatshirt, and MAVI, he debuted as a solo artist with Try Again (2020), RESET! (2023), and KAST GOT WINGS (2024) alongside Cardo. His acclaimed 2025 sophomore album, While The Iron Is Hot, cemented his multi-hyphenate status. Beyond music, he directs visuals via his production company, Angr Management, building a creative universe rooted in community and longevity. As part of the annual benefit, guests can purchase the limited-edition Oaklandish Fairyland “Starlit Tee,” featuring a vintage-inspired illustration of Fairyland icons and storybook sets, with delightful characters journeying within its world. The black tee features colorful depictions of “Happy Dragon,” Humpty Dumpty, Willie the Whale, and the famous Fairyland Shoe, accompanied by text that reads “Children’s Fairyland.” The shirt is available to purchase at Oaklandish retail stores and online at oaklandish.com. The event runs for four hours, with bars and activities set up throughout the park. Admission is $30 per person and $25 for Fairyland members. Beer, wine, and cocktails are available for purchase. A selection of Oakland’s finest food vendors will be on hand, offering a variety of delicious bites. Proceeds from Fairyland for Grownups support Children’s Fairyland’s mission to provide affordable access to all children, including outreach programs such as Fairyland for All, summer camp scholarships, and free field trips for underserved communities. While it’s okay to be a kid at heart, a valid 21+ ID is required to attend. Tickets are now available for purchase online at https://fairyland.org/fairyland-for-grownups/. articles.text: Music from some of Studio Ghibli’s best-known animated films will be performed at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco this Sunday, August 9. Sixth Station Trio presents an afternoon concert of chamber arrangements for violin, cello and piano, beginning at 2 p.m. in Samsung Hall. Tickets are included with general museum admission. Based in San Francisco, the Sixth Station Trio consists of violin, cello and piano musicians who have performed together since attending the Ruth Asawa San Francisco School of the Arts. The ensemble made its debut at Grace Cathedral in 2023 with a sold-out program featuring music from Studio Ghibli films. Founded in 1985, Studio Ghibli is one of Japan’s most influential animation studios, known for films that combine hand-drawn animation, imaginative storytelling and memorable musical scores. The program features music composed primarily by Joe Hisaishi, the longtime collaborator of filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki. The concert will include selections from films such as Howl’s Moving Castle, Spirited Away, Kiki’s Delivery Service, My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, Ponyo, Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, Laputa: Castle in the Sky, Arrietty and The Boy and the Heron. Audience members can expect to hear pieces including “Merry-Go-Round of Life,” “One Summer’s Day” and “A Town with an Ocean View,” as well as familiar Nintendo theme songs. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/sixth-station-trio-august-9/. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) newest exhibition Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs explores the evolving dialogue between movement and photography. Feel the Beat, on view now through January 31, 2027, highlights photography’s role in shaping how dance is recorded and remembered, and how dancers have inspired photographers to view movement in a different medium. The new exhibition includes items from SFMOMA’s permanent collection, opening with a gallery devoted to Irving Penn’s images of Anna Halprin and the San Francisco Dancers’ Workshop, as well as pictures that reflect Halprin’s experimental approach to dance. The second gallery turns to Kamaitachi, the partnership between Japanese photographer Eikoh Hosoe and Butoh founder Tatsumi Hijikata. The final section of the exhibition explores “nightlife,” with Malick Sidibé’s photographs of dancing at parties in Mali, as well as photos by Nan Goldin, Larry Fink, Janine Gordon, Weegee, Imogen Cunningham, Barbara Morgan, Robert Rauschenberg, Richard Avedon and more. For more information, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibitions/. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art Museum patron views Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs exhibit at SFMOMA.
articles.title: Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs on view now at SFMOMA

articles.text: Attendees dance in a historic building dating to the height of the Swing Era. The Treasure Island Museum will host a swing dance fundraiser on Saturday, September 26, to support the museum’s educational programs and historical exhibitions. Held from 7 to 10 p.m. at the museum, 39 Treasure Island Road in San Francisco, the evening will celebrate the glamour of the Swing Era and the golden age of air travel. The event is organized by the Treasure Island Museum Board. Live entertainment will be provided by the Nick Rossi Swing Six, a jazz and salsa ensemble specializing in music from the 1930s and 1940s. Guests will also enjoy classic cocktails from Gold Bar Distillery and a onenight-only exhibition featuring rarely displayed artifacts from the museum’s Pan American Airways collection. The museum, housed in a historic building dating to the height of the Swing Era, will serve as the backdrop for the evening’s festivities. Attendees are encouraged to wear festive or vintage-inspired attire, although period dress is not required. Prizes will be awarded for the most authentic and creative vintage outfits. Proceeds from the fundraiser will benefit the museum’s educational programming and ongoing efforts to preserve and interpret the history of Treasure Island through exhibits and public outreach. The fundraiser will take place Saturday, September 26, from 7 to 10 p.m. at the Treasure Island Museum, 39 Treasure Island Road, San Francisco. Tickets are available at https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/our-swing-dance-benefit-inhistoric-building-one.
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum hosts Swing Dance fundraiser Sept. 26

articles.text: Margaret Cho Comedian and actor Margaret Cho will perform her new stand-up show “Choligarchy” at Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Roda Theatre for a limited six-performance run September 15 through 19. The engagement marks Cho’s return to the East Bay with a new hour of political and personal comedy. Performances begin Tuesday, September 15, and continue through Saturday, September 19. Tickets went on sale to the general public July 31, following early access for Berkeley Rep subscribers. Cho describes “Choligarchy” as a return to her roots as a political comedian, drawing on current events and social issues. The show explores topics including politics, racism, sexism, homophobia and activism through Cho’s blend of sharp social commentary and personal storytelling. “I’m so frustrated with the state of the union, and I know the only weapon I have is humor,” Cho said in a press release. “We are being taken over by the richest people in the world, but the one thing they cannot afford is jokes at their expense. I want to fight fascism with everything I have. This will be my most blistering and brutally honest show yet.” A San Francisco native, Cho first gained national attention in the 1990s through her stand-up comedy and the television sitcom All-American Girl, the first U.S. network sitcom centered on an Asian American family. Over a career spanning more than three decades, she has earned five Grammy and Emmy nominations and built a reputation for tackling subjects such as identity, addiction, family and LGBTQ+ rights in her performances. In addition to stand-up, Cho has appeared in numerous television series and films, including Fire Island, The Flight Attendant, Hacks and Will Trent. Her recent film All That We Love premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival, and she is also set to appear in the second season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians. The Roda Theatre performances are scheduled for September 15 through September 19 at Berkeley Repertory Theatre. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Margaret Cho brings new stand-up show to Berkeley Rep in September

articles.text: The Grammy Award-winning gospel group Take 6 will return to San Francisco for a four-concert engagement at SFJAZZ’s Miner Auditorium from August 13 through 16. The Alabama-based sextet is known for its intricate a cappella harmonies, blending gospel, jazz, R&B, pop and blues. The performances celebrate more than 45 years of the group’s career, which has earned 10 Grammy Awards and established Take 6 as one of the most influential vocal ensembles in contemporary gospel music. Founded in 1980 at Oakwood College in Huntsville, Alabama, by tenor Claude McKnight, the group began by performing at churches before signing with Atlantic Records. Their self-titled 1988 debut album won three Grammy Awards and earned a nomination for Best New Artist. Over the decades, Take 6 has released 15 albums and collaborated with artists including Ray Charles, Ella Fitzgerald, Whitney Houston, Stevie Wonder and Jacob Collier. The ensemble has also contributed music to the soundtracks of films including Do the Right Thing and Boyz n the Hood, while performing for audiences around the world and multiple U.S. presidents. The group’s most recent album, Iconic, released on its independent Sono label, reached No. 1 on the Billboard Jazz Albums chart. The SFJAZZ concerts will feature founding members Claude McKnight and Mark Kibble alongside the current lineup, performing selections that showcase the group’s signature vocal arrangements and gospel-inspired repertoire. Visit https://www.sfjazz. org/tickets/productions/summer-2026/take-6/ to purchase tickets. Take 6
articles.title: Take 6 returns to SFJAZZ for four-concert run in August

articles.text: The Flower Piano festival will return to the San Francisco Botanical Garden September 10 through 20, bringing live performances and public piano installations to the 55-acre garden. The annual event features 12 grand and baby grand pianos placed throughout the garden, where visitors can attend scheduled performances, watch community groups perform or play the instruments during designated open play sessions. Flower Piano was created in 2015 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Ffortissimo and Dean Mermell in collaboration with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The festival has since become an annual event at the botanical garden. This year’s lineup includes daily performances by La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9, the San Francisco Ballet School and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, whose repertoire blends hip-hop, jazz and classical music. The 2026 festival also includes an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, featuring seating, food and beverages, and evening performances. During open play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels to use. Attendees are encouraged to bring picnic blankets as seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and tickets, is available at https://gggp.org/flowerpiano. The beloved festival returns to Golden Gate Park next month.
articles.title: Flower Piano returns to SF Botanical Garden in September

Flower Piano was created in 2015 by Sunset Piano founders Mauro Ffortissimo and Dean Mermell in collaboration with the Gardens of Golden Gate Park. The festival has since become an annual event at the botanical garden. This year’s lineup includes daily performances by La Gente SF, Sixth Station Trio, Tango No. 9, the San Francisco Ballet School and the Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, whose repertoire blends hip-hop, jazz and classical music. The 2026 festival also includes an expanded Flower Piano Lounge in the Celebration Garden, featuring seating, food and beverages, and evening performances. During open play periods, the pianos will be available for visitors of all ages and skill levels to use. Attendees are encouraged to bring picnic blankets as seating is not guaranteed. Additional infor mation, including the performance schedule and tickets, is available at https://gggp.org/flowerpiano. The beloved festival returns to Golden Gate Park next month.

articles.text: The Sheep Detectives is the best movie about intelligent sheep since Shaun the Sheep! With actors like Bryan Cranston, Hugh Jackman, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, director Kyle Balda had his work cut out for him, balancing a big cast while still making sure every character got their moment. Hugh Jackman’s character, George Hardy, lives a simple life as a shepherd for a flock of sheep to whom he gave individual names, treating them less like animals and more like a family he talks to every night. Despite his merits, he is not immune to smalltown drama, and it becomes clear early on that his quiet life is not as peaceful as it looks from the outside. All of the actors brought this world together; the proper voice actor for each sheep brings personality to the fuzzy fourlegged characters in the film. The soft and confident voice of Louis-Dreyfus gave her character, Lily, the proper attitude of a sheep prone to lead, but with much to learn. It was easy to root for Lily even when she was in the wrong. The great work of the casting directors, Lucy Bevan and Emily Brockmann, is Hugh Jackman as George Hardy in the Sheep Detectives heard and seen in every character, down to the smaller roles in the flock who still manage to feel like real personalities instead of background noise. One of the few problems is the pacing at the beginning and the ending. George dies at a strange time, about a quarter of the way through the movie, and the rest of the film feels rushed, as if it’s hurrying to fit the investigation and the ending into the time it has left. It’s not that the mystery itself suffers, but you can feel the arrow of time speeding up in a way that doesn’t quite match the careful setup at the beginning. The mystery stayed a mystery through the entire movie, which is exactly what a film like this needs to do to keep you guessing. All of the suspects had good motives and opportunities to kill George, so there was never a moment where the answer felt obvious. For a kids’ murder-mystery, the movie never loses its message: showing and telling those you love makes them better people. If you are into children’s mysteries and do not need to feel like the smartest detective in the room, this movie is for you. The Sheep Detectives . Directed by Kyle Balda. Starring Bryan Cranston, Hugh Jackman, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. Rated PG. 1h 49 min. Released in 2026. Watch it now on Amazon Prime.

articles.text: For more than four decades, North Berkeley Imports has quietly shaped the way Americans think about fine wine. Founded in 1979 and based in Berkeley, California, the importer has earned a national reputation for seeking out family-owned estates that faithfully express the character of their vineyards rather than chasing international trends. Its portfolio reflects a philosophy that great wines are made in the vineyard, with an emphasis on sustainable farming, traditional winemaking, and producers who are deeply connected to their land. Few importers have done more to introduce American consumers to the classic wines of France’s Loire Valley. North Berkeley Imports represents many of the region’s most respected growers, helping wine lovers discover everything from the mineral-driven Sauvignon Blancs of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé to the age-worthy Chenin Blancs of Vouvray, Savennières, and Anjou. The company’s selections consistently emphasize authenticity, balance, and value, proving that some of the world’s most distinctive wines need not be the most expensive. For retailers, sommeliers, and adventurous consumers alike, the North Berkeley Imports name has become a trusted guide to producers whose wines capture the unique terroir of the Loire and many of Europe’s other great wine regions. For many wine lovers, France’s Loire Valley is synonymous with elegant white wines that emphasize freshness, balance, and a remarkable sense of place. Stretching more than 600 miles along the Loire River from central France to the Atlantic Ocean, the region produces an extraordinary range of whites that are among the world’s finest values. Perhaps the best known is Sauvignon Blanc from the neighboring appellations of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé. These wines are celebrated for their vibrant citrus flavors, crisp acidity, and distinctive mineral character that reflects the region’s limestone and flint soils. They are natural companions to oysters, goat cheese, and fresh seafood. Farther west, Chenin Blanc reigns supreme. Few grapes are as versatile. In appellations such as Vouvray and Montlouis-sur-Loire, Chenin Blanc can produce bone-dry wines with notes of green apple, quince, honey, and chamomile, as well as sparkling wines and luscious dessert bottlings capable of aging for decades. In Anjou and Saumur, the grape takes on yet another personality, offering rich texture balanced by lively acidity. Near the Atlantic coast, the Melon de Bourgogne grape gives rise to Muscadet, a light-bodied white that is often aged “sur lie,” resting on its yeast lees to develop extra texture and a subtle bready complexity. It remains one of the classic partners for shellfish and is a favorite in the seafood restaurants of western France. What unites the Loire’s white wines is their emphasis on elegance rather than power. They are 1505 Shattuck Ave., Berkeley, CA retail@northberkeleyimports.com The Loire Valley is home to Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc and Muscadet.

articles.text: Last Wednesday, 49 walkers and two K-9 best friends gathered at the Exedra for a Piedmont Recreation Department Walking on Wednesdays outing featuring music, local history and a little climbing. As part of an effort to ensure the activity’s long-term future, more walkers are taking turns leading the group. Max Becker led this week’s walk. The group also thanked Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kellogg and Matt Gerhardt for leading walks in July. Mary Carter, Gerhardt, Jack Fischrup and Sean Brient will lead the four August walks, and Lori Austin has been helping write walk summaries. Becker grew up in Piedmont and attended Piedmont schools. After he and his wife returned from Washington, D.C., he joined Walking on Wednesdays to reconnect with the community. He also brought a musical background to the morning. For the past 15 years, Becker has performed internationally with the rock band SWMRS, which includes his younger brothers, Cole and Cade Becker. The band began while they were students at Piedmont High School. Rather than leading a walk focused on real estate, Becker planned a musical route through town and the high school campus. He handed out lyric booklets featuring two Beatles songs and one by Ben E. King, along with pens so walkers could autograph one another’s copies and “feel like rock stars for a little while.” Before leaving the Exedra, Becker led the group in Ben E. He handed out lyric booklets featuring two Beatles songs and one by Ben E. King, along with pens so walkers could autograph one another’s copies and “feel like rock stars for a little while.” Before leaving the Exedra, Becker led the group in Ben E. Max Becker with walkers in PHS Amphitheater Route map King’s “Stand by Me.” The walkers then headed down Highland and Wildwood avenues. At the top of the Wildwood steps, the group stopped to sing the Beatles’ “Here Comes the Sun.” They descended the steps to Witter Field, where youth soccer classes were underway and Piedmont High School assistant football coach Po Tauaho was working with young athletes in the weight room. The walkers crossed the top of the stadium and followed an access road past Bern Field, a small turf practice area above the stadium walkway. The Piedmont Soccer Club received permission several years ago to create the field on previously unused land. The route then joined the high school’s steep “PE Hill,” giving the walkers their main climbing exercise of the morning. From there, the group passed William “Binks” Rawlings Gymnasium, where Piedmont students play basketball, volleyball and badminton. The walkers continued to the central campus quad, which connects the school library, cafeteria and outdoor amphitheater. Becker led the group down into the amphitheater, where everyone took a seat and sang the Beatles’ “With a Little Help From My Friends.” The setting had personal significance for Becker. He said Piedmont High’s a cappella program and its longtime director, Joe Piazza, helped inspire him to become a singer. He also recalled that his high school band won a “Battle of the Bands” competition in the same amphitheater. The walkers asked for an encore, and Becker responded by performing “Lose It,” an original SWMRS song. The band was originally called Emily’s Army and released its first album in 2011. The walkers thanked Becker for leading a Wednesday outing unlike any the group had taken before. They then crossed the campus and returned to the Exedra, ending a walk that combined exercise, familiar Piedmont landmarks and a few songs that many likely continued humming on the way home. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. Among those participating were Denny McGee, Alicia Rivera, Debbie Powell, Charlene Louie, Albert Chen, Mary Ann Barnes, Quincy Dong, Joyce Ahern, Caskey Weston, Jim Kellogg, Bill Ahern, Helen Dong, Sanghi Wagner, Matt Gerhardt, Dan Sedonis, Audrey Sung, Peggy Shultz, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Claudine Bach, Bern Shield, Judy Love, Marcia Arthurs, June Yee, Kristin Howard, Mark Davis, Max Becker, Alissa Quan, Phil Witte, Sean Brient, Ken Hubbert, Ken Moy, Jasmine Cai, Sherry Jacobs, Stella Houston, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Marianne Jakus, Melba Yee, Noemi Alvarado, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, Tamil DeSellier, Chuck Oraftik, Mike Gallant, Dave DeRoche, Brian Hamlin, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Rachel Blanchard and Sue Tierney walking with them for the first time.

Oakland Zoo’s decades-long commitment to rescuing and caring for exploited big cats continues with the arrival and placement of five tigers. Oakland Zoo has successfully transferred these tigers after a private owner reached out to the Zoo for assistance, following their abandonment at his facility. The effort, in partnership with People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), to help these tigers began over a decade ago, tied to the closure of a private roadside facility known for mistreating and neglecting its animals. Since the passing of the Zoo’s previous rescued tigers, Mia and Lola, earlier this year, the Zoo has kept a habitat available to provide a home for future tigers in need. With this transfer, a female generic tiger now named Sitara (Hindi origins meaning star), estimated to be 13 years old, became a permanent resident of Oakland Zoo on July 9. Sitara remains strong, though she is experiencing some lameness in her left hind leg. Despite these difficulties, the Zoo’s Animal Care and Veterinary Team is working extensively to settle her in and help her adjust to her new surroundings. She started off with access only to her night house and temporary outdoor space, while settling in the new space and getting to know her Animal Care Team. Sitara is an older tiger with mobility limitations, so Oakland Zoo is approaching this transition slowly and thoughtfully. Over the past month, the team has adapted her habitat to support her geriatric stage of life, including comfort, mobility, and overall wellbeing. For now Sitara’s viewing decks will remain closed while she becomes familiar with her new surroundings. Docents are stationed outside of the upper deck to chat with guests about her journey. Sitara explored her new habitat for the first time on July 29. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, August 5, 2026 your Oakland Zoo welcomes new female tiger, Sitara Photo Credits Oakland Zoo Sitara, Oakland Zoo’s newest tiger resident, went out on habitat for the first time on July 29. Oakland Zoo’s decades-long commitment to rescuing and caring for exploited big cats continues with the arrival and placement of five tigers. Oakland Zoo has successfully transferred these tigers after a private owner reached out to the Zoo for assistance, following their abandonment at his facility. The effort, in partnership with People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), to help these tigers began over a decade ago, tied to the closure of a private roadside facility known for mistreating and neglecting its animals. Since the passing of the Zoo’s previous rescued tigers, Mia and Lola, earlier this year, the Zoo has kept a habitat available to provide a home for future tigers in need. With this transfer, a female generic tiger now named Sitara (Hindi origins meaning star), estimated to be 13 years old, became a permanent resident of Oakland Zoo on July 9. Sitara remains strong, though she is experiencing some lameness in her left hind leg. Despite these difficulties, the Zoo’s Animal Care and Veterinary Team is working extensively to settle her in and help her adjust to her new surroundings. She started off with access only to her night house and temporary outdoor space, while settling in the new space and getting to know her Animal Care Team. Sitara is an older tiger with mobility limitations, so Oakland Zoo is approaching this transition slowly and thoughtfully. Over the past month, the team has adapted her habitat to support her geriatric stage of life, including comfort, mobility, and overall wellbeing. For now Sitara’s viewing decks will remain closed while she becomes familiar with her new surroundings. Docents are stationed outside of the upper deck to chat with guests about her journey. Sitara explored her new habitat for the first time on July 29. Oakland Zoo’s rescue program extends far beyond any single case, and for over 30 years the Zoo has played a unique role among accredited institutions. The Zoo regularly supports law enforcement and animal welfare agencies through case consultation, emergency response, placement coordination, and, when possible, by providing a forever home. When the Zoo is unable to provide a home, it stabilizes rescued animals and coordinates with a network of accredited facilities to ensure appropriate lifelong care. Over the past few weeks, the Zoo has worked with partners, including Performing Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) in California and Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge in Arkansas, to place three of the tigers and determine the best possible outcome for all those transferred. Both sanctuaries are accredited by the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries (GFAS) and are members of the Big Cat Sanctuary Alliance. Each of the five tiger’s outcome reflects individualized holistic care decisions based on their health, behavior, and longterm welfare: A 14-year-old female white tiger, suffering from significant visual impairment due to inbreeding, received intermediate care at Oakland Zoo. Once she was physically prepared, she relocated to Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge. White tigers result from a rare genetic mutation called leucism. Breeding these tigers involves pairing two individuals with recessive genes to produce white-coated offspring. However, in these breeding programs, the animals are commonly related, leading to inbreeding that can cause myriad health issues, including blindness. A male, white-and-Bengal tiger mix, estimated to be 11 years old, and a male Siberian tiger mix, estimated to be 13 years old, were relocated to PAWS, which specializes in providing expert, lifelong care for older and physically challenged animals with complex needs. A female generic tiger, estimated to have been 16 years old, came to Oakland Zoo experiencing end-stage arthritis and spinal disease, causing extreme lameness and neurologic deficits in her hind limbs. She received intensive care at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital, but her condition did not respond to treatment despite continuous effort from the veterinary and animal care teams; ultimately, the kindest option for this tiger was humane euthanasia. The new resident, Sitara, has begun working with her Animal Care staff to train and develop the skills she needs to explore her new habitat. She is learning to navigate pools, a waterfall, raised platforms, grass, and vegetation - all things she hasn’t had before. The Zoo will continue to post updates on social media about her journey. Additionally, the Zoo is initiating a program to help her build trust and resilience in response to negative experiences with past caretakers, while monitoring her behavioral and mental health challenges. “Projects like this remind us that animal welfare is profoundly personal, and one of the most meaningful things we can do is change the life of one individual. These tigers have been given a future with greater stability, greater opportunity, and greater peace,” said Amy Phelps, Zoological Manager at Oakland Zoo. The Zoo has cared for numerous big cats, including tigers, for decades, providing a safe refuge and raising awareness among visitors, members, and the commuSitara lies in the grass of her habitat at the Oakland Zoo. nity about the challenges posed by private ownership and trafficked wildlife in human care. The arrival of these rescued tigers continues the legacy of more than a dozen Oakland Zoo big cat rescues and provides an opportunity to share new stories that inspire compassion and support higher standards and regulations for big cats and other captive wildlife nationwide. This latest effort follows over 30 years of the Zoo’s dedication to protecting wildlife and to closing facilities involved in the mistreatment, malnutrition, and inadequate care of exotic animals. Oakland Zoo has played a crucial role in rescuing and caring for a wide range of animals, including reptiles, amphibians, mammals, and birds. Since 2021, the Oakland Zoo has received more than 250 requests from wildlife agencies, advocacy groups, and animal rescue organizations for assistance with rescue operations. These efforts aim to support victims of the wildlife pet trade, roadside zoos, and other forms of trafficking. The Zoo’s commitment to rescues requires significant financial and staff investment, especially due to the unpredictable nature of the health and wellbeing of the individuals rescued. The zoo estimates that in 2025 they spent more than $100,000 on rescue work, work that is only possible through philanthropy. Progress has been made since the passage of the Big Cat Public Safety Act, signed into law in 2022, which has significantly contributed to animal protection efforts. The act has curbed private ownership and commercial breeding of big cats in the U.S. It has decreased “cub petting” operations and prevented new private owners from acquiring these animals, helping to reduce illegal activity and protect exotic wildlife. Sitara and the other recently transferred tigers serve as reminders that more can be done to protect big cats and to educate visitors and supporters about responsible choices. The core issue in the tiger crisis is the breeding of big cats to supply the cub-petting industry, including pay-to-pose photo opportunities. For more information, please see: oaklandzoo.org/endthetrade Sitara explores the pool in her new habitat. Sitara lounges on a platform.

articles.text: July 15, 1969 to July 25, 2026 Ronald Scott Mosbaugh passed away on July 25, 2026, after several years struggling through congestive heart and kidney failure. Known to everyone as Scott, he was born in Castro Valley’s Eden Hospital on July 15, 1969 to Nancy Heishman Mosbaugh of Castro Valley and Ronald Mosbaugh of Joplin, Missouri. A lifelong resident of the East Bay, he was raised in a multigenerational home in Castro Valley with his maternal grandmother and grandfather Helen and Harvey Heishman, his great-grandmother Lily Schatt and mother Nancy. He graduated from Castro Valley High in 1987, and attended Chabot College before getting his degree in history from Cal State Hayward. After graduation he contributed to multiple tech start up companies including art.com and Cytiva Software. In 2008 his life pivoted, as he bought his first home in Oakland, changed careers and married his girlfriend of three years, Elizabeth (Liz) Tuuri. Leaving the tech startups behind, he settled into the California Public Utilities Commission in San Francisco where he served under the last eleven commissioners, most recently Matt Baker, working until the day he died. Liz and Scott’s only child, Chris, was born three years later. The family moved to Piedmont in 2016 as Chris entered school. A lover of history, bad puns, Disney, Pixar, video and RPG board games, his favorite place in the world was Disneyland. His fondest memory was a three hour Ronald Scott Mosbaugh Friendsgiving dinner where he and a friend spent the entire meal speaking in nothing but puns. He enjoyed his time with his family (preferably at a Disney park) and was deadicated to paranormal investigating, always looking for signs of life beyond death. We hope he has found it peacefully now, somewhere as wonderful as the Magic Kingdom itself. He is survived by his mother Nancy, his father Ron, sisters Carrie and Sunny, brother Jeff, sisterin-law Kim, nephews Johnny and Conal, niece Shaelyn, sister-in-law Laura Tuuri, and his wife Liz Tuuri-Mosbaugh and son Chris. A memorial service will be held on the evening of August 24 from 4 to 7 p.m. at the Lake Temescal Boathouse. His family is grateful for the kindness and support shown during this time.
articles.title: Ronald Scott Mosbaugh

articles.text: Mark Edwin Feldkamp, the former Parks and Project Manager for the City of Piedmont, passed away peacefully on July 11, 2026. He was born on January 20, 1955, in Louisville, Kentucky. He graduated from Trinity High School in Louisville and earned a degree in landscape architecture from the University of Kentucky. He went on to build a successful career as a landscape architect in California, where his creativity, talent, and artistic vision left a lasting impression on clients, colleagues, and friends. Those who knew Mark will remember his wonderful sense of humor, his charming personality, his artistic spirit, and his generous heart. He had a gift for bringing beauty into the world through his work and warmth into the lives of those around him. Mark was preceded in death by his parents, Oscar Samuel Feldkamp and Martha Hurst Feldkamp, and by his husband, Jerold Grimm. He is survived by his sisters, Ruthmary Gaunt (Bart) and Joan Lett; his brother, Christopher Feldkamp (Debbie); along with Mark Feldkamp many extended family members and dear friends who will cherish his memory. A funeral mass was held on July 18 at St. Frances of Rome Catholic Church in Louisville, Kentucky. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Little Sisters of the Poor, 15 Audubon Plaza Drive, Louisville, Kentucky 40217. Mark’s kindness, laughter, creativity, and generous spirit will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing him.

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers movies in a comfortable setting with lively discussion afterwards. August’s selection is Finding Forrester, a 2000 portrayal of generational mentoring and friendship directed by Gus Van Sant and written by Mike Rich, who makes the art of writing the point of connection for the two principal characters. Sean Connery, age 70, in his role as William Forrester, is a reclusive occupant of an apartment in the Bronx overlooking a basketball court frequented daily by high school players of varying skill. Rob Brown, age 16, as Jamal Wallace, is the star of their games and uses his basketball skills to connect with friends and community, while keeping his intellect hidden to ensure his place in the neighborhood. Jamal breaks into Forrester’s apartment to satisfy his friends’ curiosity, but something goes wrong. Jamal leaves his backpack with his private notebooks in Forrester’s apartment. He discovers the writing samples, makes notes of both praise and criticism, and returns the backpack to Jamal. This exchange leads to a mentorship and a friendship that helps Forrester re-engage with the outside world, while sharpening Jamal’s writing skills and expanding his view of his future. Jamal’s high test scores at school expose his intellect and qualify him for a scholarship at an exclusive Manhattan prep school, where he enters a writing contest with a piece that included a few introductory comments by Forrester. By Sierra Berrick Any dog owner who is unfamiliar with the AKC Trick Dog program should take a second look. Apart from being a fun way to bond with your dog, many of the tricks taught in the program have practical value. In fact, several can cross over into service dog territory when trained reliably. A service dog is individually trained to perform tasks that actively mitigate its handler’s disability. Several tricks performed by advanced trick dogs can be adapted into mobility assistance tasks. Here are a few examples: Light – In this trick, the dog is trained to use its paw or nose to turn on a light, whether it’s a push-button lamp or a wall switch. This is especially helpful for handlers who have difficulty getting up due to pain, injury, or physical disability. Open door – The dog may interact directly with the door handle or pull a tug rope attached to the door. This trick becomes a valuable service dog task for handlers who cannot open doors independently, such as wheelchair users. Open drawer – Similar to opening a door, a dog can be trained to pull open a drawer. This task becomes even more useful when paired with retrieving an item from inside, such as medication or clothing. Put away items – The AKC Trick Dog program asks dogs to put toys into a designated container. Expanded into service work, this becomes a retrieval task, allowing the dog to pick up dropped objects or return items to PIEDMONT FLIX FEST Finding Forrester to play at next week’s Flix Fest on August 13 By Gerry Gragg One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. Carry an object – For handlers who cannot safely carry items because of a disability, a dog trained to carry objects can provide invaluable assistance. Dogs should be comfortable holding a variety of objects, including those with unusual shapes or textures. Remove the handler’s shoe – Although often amusing in a trick routine, this can be genuinely helpful for handlers who are unable to bend over or squat comfortably. The dog may use its mouth or paw to remove the shoe. Pay for it – Another crowdpleasing trick, this teaches a dog to retrieve the handler’s wallet. It can be expanded into an even more useful service task by teaching the dog to locate a misplaced wallet by scent before bringing it to the handler. While trick dog training is often viewed as entertainment, many trick behaviors naturally cross over into mobility assistance service dog work. Individuals with invisible disabilities—or disabilities they consider “mild”—may not realize they could benefit from a service dog or that they have already taught their pet the foundation for several useful service tasks. With reliable training and a disability-related purpose, yesterday’s trick can become tomorrow’s life-changing task. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: Finn Zijlstra, Zara Hinson, Josh Estrada, and Theodore Mehlinger Eisemon Happy people, a crew working together, operating a boat, docking and casting off, navigating, steering, cooking and washing dishes together, and bursting into song like in an old-fashioned Broadway musical. I was part of that joy as a guest for five of the 14 days of the annual Summer Cruise aboard the Sea Scout boat Seafox. Sea Scouts is part of Scouting America (formerly Boy Scouts of America) for all genders, ages 14 through 20. The scouts planned the cruise and sailed the 67-foot powerboat under the watchful eyes of US Coast Guard Licensed Skipper Ken Shupe, who started in scouting as a young boy and has been Skipper since 2014, growing the program from a few active scouts to more than two dozen. Skipper Shupe said that they average almost 90 days of water activities per year, from an inflatable Zodiac to rowing and sailing dinghies, 26-foot rowing whaleboats, a ski boat, a 41-foot sailboat, and a 67-foot powerboat. He said, “We are here to give scouts confidence to be leaders to their peers, communities, and future careers…” He emphasized that the scouts have “Fun and learn something along the way.” Sea Scout Ship 9 Committee Chair Will Pallas emphasized Sea Scouts’ coed youth leadership and maritime and life skills. Scouts learn about themselves, learn to work with others to get things done, and environmental stewardship. Elliot Tenorio, a rising tenth grader, said, “For me, this summer cruise was finding out who I am, and for that I am ever grateful for this opportunity. Sea Scouts for me has helped me in many ways ... and [I] will continue to participate for the years to come.” Beginning at the home dock of Ballena Bay in Alameda, the Photos by Michael James Mehlinger, Ken Shupe, William Pallas, and Joshua Estrada Sea Scout boat at the dock in West Sacramento Back: Officer Josh Estrada (left), Jim Mehlinger, Will Pallas, Brody Esquer, Yeoman Zara Hinson, Ken Shupe, Junior Officer Roman Rishin, Executive Officer Tory Troisi, Natalie, Gavin McCoy, Skipper Emerita Krisie Babcock Front: Galley Chief Sebastian Sanchez(left), Charlotte Hurowitz, Finn Zijlstra, Cameron Gambino, Bosun’s Mate Johnny Oey, Junior Officer Tatiana Orellena, Elliot Tenorio, Brandon Taylor, Officer Aaron Christman Not pictured but present on parts of the cruise: Sadie Cosby, Tiernan McClure, David Karp, Elizabeth Carhart, Mason Estrada, Officer Bee Christman, Executive Officer Alec Dru scouts cruised south to Santa Cruz and Monterey, then back under the Golden Gate Bridge to dock at Pier 39 in San Francisco. Junior Officer Sadie Cosby, a rising sophomore at Oregon State University where she is majoring in Environmental Science, said, “We’ve sighted over a dozen humpback whales, several pods of Pacific white-sided dolphins, and large flocks of migrating sooty shearwaters… We were treated to a blue whale sighting, and a pod of Risso’s dolphins.” In the spirit of environmentalism, the boat slowed, and scouts Elliot Tenorio (left), Aaron Christman, and Brandon Taylo Scouts operated the boat under the watchful eyes of Skipper Ken Shupe, Committee Chair Will Pallas, Executive Officer Tory Troisi, Executive Officer Alec Dru, and Skipper Emerita Krisie Babcock. Clockwise: Sadie Cosby steers under the Golden Gate Bridge; Brandon Taylor and Mason Estrada stand watch as lookouts. Zara Hinson, Johnny Oey, and Roman Rishin monitor the engines. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, August 5, 2026 Busy summer for Piedmont Sea Scouts By Michael James Mehlinger, Finn Zijlstra, Zara Hinson, Josh Estrada, and Theodore Mehlinger Eisemon Happy people, a crew working together, operating a boat, docking and casting off, navigating, steering, cooking and washing dishes together, and bursting into song like in an old-fashioned Broadway musical. I was part of that joy as a guest for five of the 14 days of the annual Summer Cruise aboard the Sea Scout boat Seafox. Sea Scouts is part of Scouting America (formerly Boy Scouts of America) for all genders, ages 14 through 20. The scouts planned the cruise and sailed the 67-foot powerboat under the watchful eyes of US Coast Guard Licensed Skipper Ken Shupe, who started in scouting as a young boy and has been Skipper since 2014, growing the program from a few active scouts to more than two dozen. Skipper Shupe said that they average almost 90 days of water activities per year, from an inflatable Zodiac to rowing and sailing dinghies, 26-foot rowing whaleboats, a ski boat, a 41-foot sailboat, and a 67-foot powerboat. He said, “We are here to give scouts confidence to be leaders to their peers, communities, and future careers…” He emphasized that the scouts have “Fun and learn something along the way.” Sea Scout Ship 9 Committee Chair Will Pallas emphasized Sea Scouts’ coed youth leadership and maritime and life skills. Scouts learn about themselves, learn to work with others to get things done, and environmental stewardship. Elliot Tenorio, a rising tenth grader, said, “For me, this summer cruise was finding out who I am, and for that I am ever grateful for this opportunity. Sea Scouts for me has helped me in many ways ... and [I] will continue to participate for the years to come.” Beginning at the home dock of Ballena Bay in Alameda, the Photos by Michael James Mehlinger, Ken Shupe, William Pallas, and Joshua Estrada Sea Scout boat at the dock in West Sacramento Back: Officer Josh Estrada (left), Jim Mehlinger, Will Pallas, Brody Esquer, Yeoman Zara Hinson, Ken Shupe, Junior Officer Roman Rishin, Executive Officer Tory Troisi, Natalie, Gavin McCoy, Skipper Emerita Krisie Babcock Front: Galley Chief Sebastian Sanchez(left), Charlotte Hurowitz, Finn Zijlstra, Cameron Gambino, Bosun’s Mate Johnny Oey, Junior Officer Tatiana Orellena, Elliot Tenorio, Brandon Taylor, Officer Aaron Christman Not pictured but present on parts of the cruise: Sadie Cosby, Tiernan McClure, David Karp, Elizabeth Carhart, Mason Estrada, Officer Bee Christman, Executive Officer Alec Dru scouts cruised south to Santa Cruz and Monterey, then back under the Golden Gate Bridge to dock at Pier 39 in San Francisco. Junior Officer Sadie Cosby, a rising sophomore at Oregon State University where she is majoring in Environmental Science, said, “We’ve sighted over a dozen humpback whales, several pods of Pacific white-sided dolphins, and large flocks of migrating sooty shearwaters… We were treated to a blue whale sighting, and a pod of Risso’s dolphins.” In the spirit of environmentalism, the boat slowed, and scouts See Sea Scouts on page 23 Elliot Tenorio (left), Aaron Christman, and Brandon Taylo Scouts operated the boat under the watchful eyes of Skipper Ken Shupe, Committee Chair Will Pallas, Executive Officer Tory Troisi, Executive Officer Alec Dru, and Skipper Emerita Krisie Babcock. Clockwise: Sadie Cosby steers under the Golden Gate Bridge; Brandon Taylor and Mason Estrada stand watch as lookouts. Zara Hinson, Johnny Oey, and Roman Rishin monitor the engines. Zara Hinson calls on the hand-held radio to raise the Helen Madere Memorial Bridge across the Sacramento River at Rio Vista. Docking at the Sacramento Yacht Club on the Sacramento River. Then, homeward bound, stopping to provision, scouts practiced boating skills, swam, went tubing, and learned to water ski. Bosun Finn Zijlstra, a rising high school senior, summed up his experience saying, “Twenty-four teenagers running a former workboat down the coast of California for two weeks sounds like an interesting way to spend your summer, but there really is no better experience. From learning how to operate small boats on Monterey Bay to swimming in the California Delta, our summer cruise let us spend time together in and on the water and build our boating skills. We run a unique program, and over the course of my time in scouts, I have seen the ways we are able to serve our community. I have no more important memories than my time on the The mast was a popular hangout spot amid radar, electronics, and other navigational equipment used by scouts to safely pilot the boat. The rise of sprinter Claire Aubrecht Claire Aubrecht set the world on fire as a junior, setting individual records in the 100- and 200-meter dash events, along with leading the 4x100 relay team to a new school record. She beat Lauren Remer’s 13-year record in the 200 meters multiple times, ultimately running a 25.46 at the NCS meet of Champions to finish fifth of seven finalists. Aubrecht broke Breah Bell’s 100-meter dash record of 12.55 in 2024 by finishing her season with a 12.39 at the Meet of Champions to place 10th of 23 runners. To qualify for state they placed third of 15 teams at the NCS Meet of Champions. 7. articles.text: Nature Play Area hand-drawn illustration by artist Ana Gadish-Linares Following the removal of the unsafe swings in 2024, Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s (PBF) Fall Fundraising Campaign successfully focused on securing funds for the swing replacement. The redesigned area will feature state-of-the-art materials for enhanced durability and safety, including new safety matting to replace the existing sand, upgraded ADA access and a refined perimeter for the swing area. To build on this momentum, the PBF Spring Campaign is now focused on creating a nature play area adjacent to the swings. This project will transform an underused section of the park into a vibrant outdoor learning environment featuring climbing logs, native plants, and hands-on natural play elements for children to explore. PBF has worked since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces that foster a strong sense of pride and community. In addition to its many valuable contributions to parks, tot lots, schools, and recreational facilities, PBF also brings the community together to celebrate the Piedmont Lights Up ceremony every December. PBF looks forward to sharing more updates as they work to improve the community’s outdoor spaces. To learn more about PBF’s efforts to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park, visit their website: https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/ways-to-give/.
articles.title: PBF partners with the city to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park

articles.text: With pots of steaming pasta and roasting trays of vegetables, members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew race around the kitchen of the Presbyterian Church on College Avenue as those in need of a warm meal gather outside. For this volunteer crew, Friday night dinners at the church are just one way students volunteer their time to serving others in the greater Bay Area. The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) was founded in the fall of 2004 by crew advisor Ken Li, with help from Piedmont parent Barbara Caruso. Through Li’s leadership and dedication to service, the crew has exponentially grown from six students to more than 150 students every year. Li said that what makes PCSC so special is that students have the opportunity to participate in countless diverse events, revolved around students’ schedules. Events range from cooking meals to relandscaping gardens, and even building houses. “The beauty of PCSC is that everyone can find a way to contribute. Whatever your hobby or skill may be, there’s something for you,” said VP of Parent Engagement junior Noah Baldwin. This freedom to choose events based on interests is exactly why Li said that most students come to realize that community service can be extremely enjoyable. “My experience is that there are a good number of people who join the crew with the idea that they’re joining to get hours and make themselves look good,” Li said. “But they find out that it’s actually a lot of fun and that they enjoy doing it with friends. They meet new people and they learn new skills that they are really proud of, and that it does actually feel good to be helping other people.” PCSC president senior Claire Aubrecht said that volunteering through PCSC has had a profound impact on members beyond completing service hours. “It certainly makes you very empathetic and it’s good for a student to talk and interact with people outside the actual school environment,” Aubrecht said. “Especially for Piedmont, we’re all similar in that way so meeting people who didn’t grow up with the same background we did, it puts into perspective what our privilege is.” For Aubrecht, those moments of connection have happened PCSC members Noah Sukeforth (left), Brent Bornkamp, Julian Tsai, and Toby Tsai work on a tiny house.
