Stevko Gardens Michelle Docter Miscellaneous Dick Carter Robert Hall Professional Services Jim Gardner Ed Kaplan HDR Remodeling McCutcheon Construction Seniors Anne Callahan Cookie Segelstein REVIEWERS Art Allyson Aleksey Anastasia Edel Dance Jaime Robles Film Chris Honoré Music Joseph Gold Paul Hertelendy Jaime Robles Wine Reviews Bill McNabb ADVERTISING Nancy Kurkjian 510-626-2468 Student Writer Crystal Vadker Samantha Pell Mira Sen CIRCULATION Call 510-652-2051 READ IT IN THE POST By Jim Hopkins I Kings 3:9 [Solomon] “Give your servant, therefore, an understanding mind to govern your people, able to discern between good and evil, for who can govern this great people of yours?” Shortly after he became King, Solomon had a dream in which the LORD appeared to him directly and said, “Ask. What shall I give you?” Most of us can rather quickly think of several ways we would answer the question. Among them might be — “The winning numbers for this weekend’s lottery.” “A long life with good health.” “Prestige and power.” “Inner peace.” “World peace.” “A better world for my children and grandchildren.” “Pickleball supremacy.” The list goes on. There are many ways we might respond to the question, some quite selfish and some quite selfless. It is a worthwhile exercise to live with the question for a moment. King Solomon’s response to the LORD is both interesting and instructive. He requests an “understanding heart to discern between good and evil. For who can judge this vast people of yours?” Wisdom is one way of summarizing Solomon’s request. Discernment is another. Empathy is still another. Whatever terms we use to describe his answer, it is clear that he understands that if he is to lead the people well he needs to connect with them at more than a surface level, that he needs to hear their hearts. To do this a hearing heart of his own is required. This realization leads to the questions: How is our “hearing heart” health? What might we do to improve it? The answers are not surprising. Prayer. Community. Service. These proven pathways serve to wake us up, to move us from dreaming about having an understanding heart to actually growing one. If I were to recommend a question to aid in the development of an understanding heart it would be “How can I serve?” After all, it was Solomon’s desire to serve well as king that inspired his search for an understanding heart. In the same way, our desire to serve our community can aid and improve our hearing heart health; aid and improve it even more than the assurance that we have the correct numbers for the next lottery would. These words of Steve Charleston say it well. Do what you know to be right Say what you know to be true. Protect what is vulnerable Share what is valuable. Trust your experience Grow your wisdom. Give what you can Receive what you can. Smile gently on your sorrow Weep quietly in your joy. Be your vision of who you are Become the hope you feel. articles.text: Residents looking to submit arguments for or against local measures appearing on the November 3, 2026 ballot need to send them to Piedmont City Clerk’s Office by 4 p.m. on Monday, August 3, 2026. One local measure will appear on Piedmont’s ballot: a proposal to increase the City’s Real Property Conveyance Tax, which is being retitled to “Real Property Transfer Tax” (“Transfer Tax”) from 1.30% to 1.75%. Direct arguments are limited to 300 words. Under state law, arguments may be submitted by eligible voters, qualifying organizations, or City Councilmembers authorized by the Council. If more than one argument is submitted for the same position, the City Clerk will select one for publication according to the priority order established by state law. Rebuttal Arguments for or against the measure must be submitted to the City Clerk’s Office by 4 p.m. on August 13, 2026. Rebuttals are limited to 250 words. Submissions must include a completed Argument/Rebuttal Submission Form and be provided in final form as both a wet-signed hard copy and an electronic Word document. This form is also available at the City Clerk’s Office. Arguments remain confidential until the filing deadline. Contact the City Clerk’s Office at (510) 420-3040 with questions or review Resolution No. 58-2026 for more information about the ballot measure for the Transfer Tax. Residents interested in running for one of three City Council seats or two Board of Education seats must file nomination documents in person by 5 p.m. on Friday, August 7, 2026. If an eligible incumbent does not file for reelection, the nomination period for that office only will be extended through 5 p.m. Wednesday, August 12, 2026. The nomination process can be complicated and filing deadlines are strict, so interested residents should contact the City Clerk’s Office at (510) 420-3040 or CityClerk@piedmont.ca.gov as soon as possible to get started. Find election information and a current candidate list at piedmont.ca.gov/vote2026. Find more information about the November 2026 election or running for office at piedmont.ca.gov/elections

articles.text: On Tuesday, August 4, Piedmont will host its National Night Out to celebrate the partnerships that help keep the city safe and connected. The event will be hosted at the Exedra in Piedmont Park from 5 to 7 p.m. Attendees will meet members of the Piedmont Police Department, Fire Department, and the city’s community partners for an evening of fun, conversation, and community spirit. Guests can participate in lawn games and giveaways. Light refreshments will be served. National Night Out is all about strengthening relationships between public safety agencies and the community. “Whether you’ve lived in Piedmont for years or are new to the neighborhood, we’d love to see you there,” said the Piedmont Police Department in a release earlier this week. To learn more about the event, visit https://natw.org/about/.

articles.text: On August 3, the City of Piedmont will start construction on upgrades to the Piedmont Park tot lot. The project will replace the tot lot swings and add a new ADA pathway to the swing area. Community members will see a chain-link fence around the section of the park between the Exedra and Piedmont High School campus. During construction, the climbing structure and restroom will remain open but will need to be accessed via Exedra Plaza. The sidewalk along Magnolia Avenue will remain open. The construction contract was awarded to Modernscape Innovations for $156,364. Modernscape is a family-owned business established in 2023. Construction is expected to take 5-6 weeks. The contract scope includes site demolition, sand removal, sidewalk installation, swing area curb and wall installation, handrail installation, storm drainage installation, and landscaping. It excludes the installation of the new swing equipment and new ADA playground fiber, which will be executed under a separate agreement with a certified playground equipment installer. The swing equipment and ADA fiber matting installation are anticipated to be awarded separately via a California Multiple Award Schedule (CMAS) agreement. The equipment has a 6-8 week lead time, and installation is anticipated to commence in October with approximately 2 weeks to complete. The project is funded in the FY26-27 City budget and supported by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). The PBF 2026 Spring Fundraising Campaign is focused on creating a Nature Play Area adjacent to the swings. This project is in response to the longstanding community request to rebuild the swings that were removed in 2024. The original wooden swing set was removed due to structural post-rot, which posed a risk for children. The current plan is to expand the swing zone to meet modern safety requirements and ADA accessibility. During construction, the climbing structure and restroom at the tot lot will remain open.
articles.title: Piedmont Park tot lot to undergo upgrades

articles.text: Busa is a one-year-old German Shepherd mix. This sweet girl is gentle and dog friendly. She could use some hearty meals and plenty of treats to help her fill out her lean frame. Busa took a little weekend getaway to a foster home and did wonderfully. She’s already mastered the art of quiet car rides, polite leash walking, and sleeping soundly in her crate overnight. Her foster host said her favorite things were leaning in for pets and sitting politely for rewards. Busa was a little timid at first, but she warmed up quickly and displayed her affectionate side. Come meet Busa at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 7 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Busa is a one-year-old German Shepherd mix. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Busa must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Adoptable Dog of the Week

articles.text: At 14 years old, Gandalf proves that senior cats absolutely rule. Want a reading buddy? Gandalf will fall asleep on your lap for hours and give you kisses if you massage the right spot on his nose! Want a playful pal? He’ll pounce his toys, and even bunny-kick them for good measure. Want a dinner companion? Gandalf adores being fed with a spoon — yet is not above sticking his entire nose into his wet food before grooming his damp little face. This affectionate boy has medical needs that are straightforward (and even cute) to manage: simply keep him indoors, give him a daily steroid pill in a spoon with his prescribed diet, sprinkle his daily pain medicine into his supper, and schedule regular vet checkups. He really makes it easy! He has his own way of Adopt Gandalf through Cat Town. showing that he’s had enough touch time (a little push with his nose to say “No Thank You”) and will do best in a home where he can get some personal space whenever he chooses — after all, balance is key to a happy life! Gandalf is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FIV-positive. Learn more by talking to our team! Inquire at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland. org.
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: Nature Play Area hand-drawn illustration by artist Ana Gadish-Linares Following the removal of the unsafe swings in 2024, Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s (PBF) Fall Fundraising Campaign successfully focused on securing funds for the swing replacement. The redesigned area will feature state-of-the-art materials for enhanced durability and safety, including new safety matting to replace the existing sand, upgraded ADA access and a refined perimeter for the swing area. To build on this momentum, the PBF Spring Campaign is now focused on creating a nature play area adjacent to the swings. This project will transform an underused section of the park into a vibrant outdoor learning environment featuring climbing logs, native plants, and hands-on natural play elements for children to explore. PBF has worked since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces that foster a strong sense of pride and community. In addition to its many valuable contributions to parks, tot lots, schools, and recreational facilities, PBF also brings the community together to celebrate the Piedmont Lights Up ceremony every December. PBF looks forward to sharing more updates as they work to improve the community’s outdoor spaces. To learn more about PBF’s efforts to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park, visit their website: https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/ways-to-give/.
articles.title: PBF partners with the city to restore the play area in Piedmont’s Main Park

articles.text: The Artemis II lunar flyby created palpable excitement and awe across the world. This historic event and crew had the incredible effect of inspiring all generations to become curious and passionate about space exploration. The newly announced crew of Artemis III will carry the torch of inspiration and enthusiasm for the future of space travel and exploration. Introducing the Artemis III Crew For the next phase of the Artemis program, NASA has selected a four-person crew to complete the mission. The Commander of Artemis III is NASA’s Randy “Komrade” Bresnik. Luca Parmitano from the European Space Agency has been selected as our Artemis III Pilot. Lastly, the Mission Specialists for Artemis III are NASA’s Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio. Together, the Artemis III crew will help pave the way for humans to return to the Moon’s surface in a more substantial and permanent way. The Artemis III Mission Planned to launch in 2027, Artemis III is a crucial step to take for humans to land on the Moon’s surface. The overall objective of Artemis III is to demonstrate critical systems for lunar landing. In other words, the tests and demonstrations done in Artemis III will ensure the safety of those landing on the Moon in future missions. The Artemis III crew will conduct and undergo several important tests and procedures. One of the first goals in the Artemis III mission is for the SLS rocket to launch the crewed Orion spacecraft into Earth’s orbit. Once in orbit, the crew will practice docking the Orion spacecraft with two lunar landers. Lunar landers will be used in future Artemis phases to bring astronauts to the Moon’s surface. The Artemis III Space Week participants crew will also spend more time on the Orion spacecraft than the Artemis II crew did to further evaluate the life support systems aboard. While taking place in Earth’s orbit, Artemis III will be one of the most complex missions NASA has tried so far. The Artemis Legacy The scientists and crew members involved in each phase of the Artemis program will play a pivotal role in the advancement of human space exploration. The Artemis program has reignited excitement and curiosity about space and science across generations. With each mission, new individuals are inspired to learn more about space and the importance of our place in the universe. A Week of Inspiration and Curiosity The Artemis program has created a ripple of excitement and passion for space exploration across the world. At Chabot Space & Science Center, we welcome everyone who has curiosity and enthusiasm for space and science. On Wednesday, July 29, Chabot begins its annual Space Week program, which celebrates the importance of STEM-related fields and those involved. During Space Week, Chabot brings in aerospace pros, real rocket parts, hosts space chats, and so much more. This stellar week of learning and discovery will end in a weekend of out-of-this-world fun with our Space Week Festival. Visitors will enjoy a celebration of exploration, discovery, and the wonders of the universe. Learn more about NASA’s Artemis missions and try your hand at interactive science demonstrations and creative crafts in an action-packed weekend of learning and imagination. From rocket science to real-world space missions, it’s your chance to get up close with the people, tools, and ideas pushing humanity beyond Earth! And don’t forget Cosmo Con. This year’s event is 18+ and is a celebration of all things science fiction complete with a cosmic cantina bar, a costume contest hosted by AfroComicCon, cult classic sci-fi episode screenings, star sketching in the planetarium and much more. Make sure you stop by the coolest corner of the multiverse! For more information about Space Week at Chabot, visit chabotspace.org/programs/ space-week/
articles.title: New discoveries await with Artemis III

In other words, the tests and demonstrations done in Artemis III will ensure the safety of those landing on the Moon in future missions. The Artemis III crew will conduct and undergo several important tests and procedures. One of the first goals in the Artemis III mission is for the SLS rocket to launch the crewed Orion spacecraft into Earth’s orbit. Once in orbit, the crew will practice docking the Orion spacecraft with two lunar landers. Lunar landers will be used in future Artemis phases to bring astronauts to the Moon’s surface. It’s so great to be able to help them feel comfortable, and that’s really what PCSC is all about,” Aubrecht said. Volunteering is only one side to PCSC. Because PCSC is entirely youth-led, Li said the hidden advantage to joining PCSC is the opportunity to take a leadership role. “The sky’s the limit. You could be an event leader and organize one particular event or be in charge of a series of events or a relationship with a partner organization. You could also be a crew officer (VP or President) or an assistant,” Li said. Leaders have certainly exemplified “the sky’s the limit” motto, leading service trips to Ethiopia, Italy, India, and most recently to Oregon. Baldwin participated in the week-long Oregon trip during spring break that resulted in the 14-person group building a shed for Willow Witt Ranch. “It was kind of like stepping away from normal community service and making something that was kind of ours,” Baldwin said. “You got to see the appreciation that the people had for the shed you had just built.” However, trips like these wouldn’t be possible without the help from parents, who play a fundamental part in running PCSC. There are options to participate in events, to mentor students, and to manage the technical aspects behind the scenes. “Community service is kind of an expression of our morals. It’s where the good in our hearts comes out in a world that has so much wrong with it,” Baldwin said. “Parents have experienced that. The fact that they’re showing up to still do good is a sign that our community that our world as a whole can grow and be better.” This spirit of compassion is exactly the atmosphere PCSC strives to create at events. articles.text: Within Piedmont’s FY2026- 27 budget, the city has introduced a new fine schedule for off-leash violations. The increase in fines is in response to community feedback on the lack of punishment for offenders. The new fines have been in place since July 1, 2026, and will stay in effect until the end of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. The City determined that the previous fines were ineffective at deterring people from committing off-leash violations. They have instituted an increase for repeat offenders, doubling the fine for a second violation and fivefold for a third offense. The new fine schedule for off-leash violations is: • 1st violation: $100 (same as previous) • 2nd violation within 24 months: $200 • 3rd violation within 24 months: $500 The City receives many complaints from community members about dogs running off-leash in on-leash areas. The escalating fines are intended to deter repeat offenders. All dogs in Piedmont must be leashed when in public, unless the pet has an Off-Leash Permit and is in an off-leash recreation area. Residents with an Off-Leash Permit for their pet can use it in the off-leash areas of Blair Park, Dracena Park, and Piedmont Park. To apply for a Dog License and Off-Leash Permit, an application is available on the City’s website or at the Police Department. A dog license may be obtained by mail. Residents can mail the application and proof of vaccination from their veterinarian to the Police Department. If you prefer to drop off the form in person, you can drop the form off at the lobby window during business hours. Readers can find further information on applications and off-leash dog areas on the City website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/police/ services/animal_services. articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost on the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on four athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Four who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included Henry Stein of the boys’ water polo team, Mattias Seelenberger of football, and Allyson Huynh and Carina Vora of the girls’ volleyball team. Staff Photos HENRY STEIN Water Polo Henry Stein, a rising junior, is set to be a key player on the boys’ water polo team. He returns as a leading scorer. The Highlanders reached last year’s D2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 1 seed, and finished with a 16-9 overall record. They fell in a heated overtime match to No. 9 Marin Academy, 10-9 in the NCS quarterfinals, and beat No. 16 St. Patrick Henry Stein was a leading scorer for the boys’ water polo team as a sophomore. 19-8 in the opening round. Some of his best games in 2025 included six goals in Piedmont’s 14-13 win over Carmel to claim third place at the Vintage Valley Tournament, he scored three goals and four assists in a 14-11 overtime win over Bishop O’Dowd, and had four goals and three assists in a 14-10 win over Castro Valley. He also scored twice in their playoff loss to Marin Academy. Stein earned an honorable mention for All-League. MATTIAS SEELENBERGER Football Mattias Seelenberger burst onto the scene as a junior kicker for the football team. He is a twosport athlete in football and soccer. On the gridiron, Seelenberger was a big part of the Highlanders going 8-5 and reaching the D7 NCS Championship game – the school’s first title-game appearance since 1976. Seelenberger was credited with scoring 35 total points for the team, including 29 extra points. In a 36-16 win over Aragon, the kicker converted a 41-yard field goal to earn him the Post’s Athlete of the Week honors. It marked the school’s longest field goal since 2015. ALLYSON HUYNH Volleyball Allyson Huynh was an important part of the girls’ volleyball team reaching new heights in 2025 as a sophomore. The squad received the school’s first berth in NCS since 2018 and finished with a 9-12 overall record. Huynh is primarily a setter and service expert. As the No. 8 seed, Piedmont lost to No. 9 Urban in the first round of the D4 Mattias Seelenberger emerged as a powerful kicker for the football team, landing a 41-yard field goal last season. Allyson Huynh was a key part of the girls’ volleyball team achieving its first NCS berth since 2018.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of UAE Team Emirates Tadej Pogačar solidified himself among the greatest cyclists of all time by capturing his fifth Tour de France title. He’s now one of five riders to do so. Tadej Pogačar cemented himself among the greatest cyclists of all time, capturing his fifth Tour de France title in seven years and third consecutive Yellow Jersey on Sunday, July 26. He has now matched five-time winners like France’s Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault, Belgium legend Eddy Merckx, and Miguel Induráin of Spain. At 27 years old, Pogačar has a chance to become the only six-time winner in the Grand Tour’s history. Pogačar won the tour with a commanding 6 minute, 26 second lead over Remco Evenepoel after initially claiming the Yellow Jersey on Stage 6. pages.text: Wednesday, July 29, 2026 13 SUMMER WORKOUT - MAIN Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 19th year. Current and former college athletes as well as high school athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. articles.text: With the new school year approaching, the Class of 2027 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. DIEGO HURWITZ Football Diego Hurwitz enters a critical senior campaign after missing much of his junior year due to an injury. He returns to the football team in an important role at receiver and defensive back. Staff Photos Diego Hurwitz is set to take a jump up the depth chart at receiver and defensive back in 2026. On the offensive side, Hurwitz is taking a big leap up the depth chart following the graduation of the school’s top two receivers last season in Cash Panico and Jack Meyjes. On defense, Jason Shum’s graduation opens a spot at safety, while Meyjes also played cornerback. Last season, Hurwitz was credited with five receptions for 131 yards, averaging 26.2 yards per catch, to go along with one touchdown. NIA JACKSON Basketball, Track & Field Nia Jackson ran the anchor lap of the 4x100 relay team that set a new school record. Beach Lorin returns as the basketball team’s leading scorer. Nia Jackson was a two-sport athlete in both basketball and track. She was a role-player on Bryan Gardere’s basketball team, while she emerged as one of the strongest sprinters on the track team. With the track and field team, Jackson was a part of the 4x100 team setting a new school record as the squad’s anchor alongside Claire Aubrecht, Akunna Iroh, and Darcy McKee. The team finished second of 19 schools at the NCS Bayshore Area Championship with a time of 49.21 seconds to set a new Piedmont High record. Her team also won the 2026 WACC Championship in a field of nine teams with a time of 49.76. In basketball, Jackson is set to be one of two seniors on the roster alongside Taylor White. Her best performance from last season was seven points, two rebounds, and two steals in a dominant 68-43 victory over Marin Catholic. BEACH LORIN Basketball Beach Lorin emerged as the basketball team’s second leading scorer, who coach Ben Spencer described as the “heir apparent” of their squad. He’ll be entering his third year on the varsity roster in 2026-27. The Highlanders went 19-9 and reached the D2 NCS Quarterfinals with the No. 4 seed. He scored a team-leading 16 points against No. 13 Urban in their opening round 55-46 win. Some of his best performances included 25 points in a 75-64 win over Castro Valley, 25 points in a 67-58 loss to Alameda, 21 points in a 62-52 loss to San Leandro, and 19 points in an 83-62 loss to University. We named Lorin our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in February.

NINA SCHWAB Carleton College Nina Schwab, PHS Class of 2024, won a Division 3 National Title in the one-meter dive with Carleton College of Minnesota in March. She logged a winning score of 465.65 in the finals after posting a second-place score of 437.60 in the preliminary round against a field of 29. Schwab also placed second of 16 in the 3-meter dive with a score of 484.35. To get there, she was first of 29 in the preliminary round with a 497.25. Nina also made school history when winning the MIAC Championship in the 1-meter dive. She wound up twice setting the school and MIAC Championship record as a freshman, scoring 464.10 points in the preliminary round and 475.40 points to claim the title in a field of 23. She was also second of 22 in the 3-meter dive with a score of 471.35. Schwab was Piedmont High’s only diver and competed in the 2024 CIF State Swimming Diving Championship in the 1-meter Emory University A.J. Harris, PHS Class of 2023, enters his senior year on Emory University’s men’s basketball team in Atlanta after helping the school reach the Division 3 NCAA Championship game. Emory went 27-4 with Harris an every-game starter. In the finals, the Eagles lost 75-73 to Mary Washington after the winning team hit a buzzer-beater to end the game. To get there, Emory beat Mississippi University for Women’s men’s team 87-73 in the opening round, beat Roanoke College 83-81 in overtime, won 101-80 over Yeshiva University in the Sweet 16, won 83-78 over Illinois Wesleyan in the Elite Eight, and won 72-58 over Christopher Newport in the Final Four. In 2025/2026, Harris started 30 of 31 games and had the thirdmost minutes on the team with 937. He logged 310 total points, 121 rebounds, 73 assists, and led the team with 47 steals. As a sophomore in 2024/2025, the Eagles finished 23-6 and reached the Elite Eight of the Division 3 NCAA Tournament before falling to Wesleyan University 61-58 in overtime. Harris appeared in all 29 games for 825 minutes, scoring 336 points by shooting 45 percent from the field and 33 percent from 3-pointers, to go along with 149 rebounds, 43 assists, 42 steals and seven blocks. Harris notched a career-high of 28 points in a 77- 71 win over Union College. He finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s All-Time leading scorer Photo courtesy of UC Davis Christian Taylor, PHS Class of 2023, enters his senior year at UC Davis.

articles.text: In this week of Hiking with Jon, The Post delves into our final of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe with the popular urban exploring adventure, Donner Pass, right outside of Truckee on the north side of Lake Tahoe. The Post typically covers Donner Pass in the winter time given the snow sheds on along the abandoned railway that give excellent cover from the harsh winters of the Sierra Mountains. During the spring and the summer, the location is an excellent place to walk for experienced hikers, elder seniors, and young children given the railway’s level surface. Now in late July and early August, the snow has since melted, providing a great place to take in the scenic beauty of the Sierra Mountains and urban art with graffiti and murals scattered around the walls. The abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco is presenting “Boom and Bust,” a photography exhibition examining cycles of growth, destruction and renewal in Northern California. The exhibition leaves this Sunday, August 2. The exhibition traces how California has been shaped by repeated periods of opportunity and upheaval, from the Gold Rush of the 19th century to the region’s rise as a global center of technological innovation. Through photography, “Boom and Bust” documents how the landscape has been built, damaged and rebuilt over time. Featured works chronicle major moments in San Francisco’s history, including the city’s reconstruction following the 1906 earthquake and fire, the construction of the Golden Gate Bridge and Bay Bridge, and the development of the South of Market neighborhood. Together, the images show how urban settlement and infrastructure projects have transformed the region’s physical and social environment. The exhibition also addresses the environmental forces that continue to threaten California’s habitability, highlighting how natural disasters and human development are closely intertwined. Since the 19th century, photographers have played a key role in recording these changes, using the camera to bear witness to both progress and vulnerability. The photographs underscore the resilience of the land and its residents, illustrating how communities have adapted to repeated challenges while continuing to reshape the region. Featured photographers include Janet Delaney, Willard E. Worden, Isaiah West Taber, Carleton E. Watkins, Peter Stackpole, Arnold Genthe and Eadweard Muybridge. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/boom-bust-photographing-northern-california#exhibition-preview for more information. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will launch Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc, the largest installation of Hashimoto’s career, with a public celebration on Thursday, August 20. The art installation combines nearly 75,000 handmade bamboo kites suspended together into a cloud canopy, covering the museum’s ground floor admission-free gallery from floor to ceiling and wall to wall. The unveiling will feature a conversation between the artist and SFMOMA Curator of Architecture and Design, Joseph Becker, as well as a sound performance by Nico Georis. “This giant arc of kites, color and pattern will be at once chaotic and meditative, playful and considered—a generous artwork that invites viewers to spend time in the gallery. It will be an enticing, intriguing overture to the museum itself,” said Hashimoto Artist Jacob Hashimoto about the project. “Our mission at SFMOMA is radical hospitality for all—these efforts include filling over 45,000 square feet of free public space with irresistible contemporary art,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Hashimoto’s enveloping and breathtaking commission in our free-to-visit Roberts Family Gallery promises to welcome visitors of all ages, imbuing all who experience it with a sense of wonder and awe.” The event begins at 6 p.m. and is free admission. Visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ jacob-hashimoto-giant-arc/ to learn more. Jacob Hashimoto: Giant Arc

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse concludes its 2025-26 season with the Tony Award-winning musical Hairspray, running now through September 12. Set in 1962 Baltimore, Hairspray follows teenager Tracy Turnblad as she pursues a spot on the popular television program The Corny Collins Show. After achieving her dream, Tracy uses her newfound platform to challenge racial segregation and advocate for integration. The musical features a score by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman, including songs such as “You Can’t Stop the Beat,” “Good Morning Baltimore,” “Welcome to the ‘60s” and “I Know Where I’ve Been.” The book is by Mark O’Donnell and Thomas Meehan. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English directs the production, with Phaedra Tillery-Boughton serving as associate director, Dave Dobrusky as musical director and Phoenyx Rose as choreographer. “In San Francisco Playhouse’s new production, we will reimagine Hairspray with a sharper edge, stripping away some of its bubblegum sheen to restore the subversive bite of John Waters,” English said in a press release. “This production leans into the story’s racial politics and cultural satire, examining Baltimore’s fight for integration through our contemporary lens.” Based on the 1988 film by John Waters, Hairspray premiered at Seattle’s 5th Avenue Cast of San Francisco Playhouse production of Hairspray Theatre before opening on Broadway, where it won eight Tony Awards, including Best Musical, and ran for more than six years. The musical later opened in London’s West End, winning four Olivier Awards, and has since been adapted into a feature film and a live television production. Director Bill English said the production “becomes more than a feel-good musical… in an era marked by polarization, erasure, and the lingering shadows of racist ideology.” “It’s a defiant, joyful call to resistance, where dancing is protest and inclusion is revolutionary,” he added. Ella Ruth Francis will make her San Francisco Playhouse debut as Tracy Turnblad. Trevor March returns to the company as Link Larkin after appearing in Into the Woods. Jeffrey Brian Adams will play Corny Collins, while Samantha Rich portrays Penny Pingleton and Jordan Covington returns as Seaweed J. Stubbs. Jonathan Chisolm makes their Playhouse debut as Edna Turnblad alongside Ken Brill as Wilbur Turnblad. Mackenzie Macdonald will portray Amber Von Tussle, with Alison Ewing as Velma Von Tussle and Jeannine Anderson as Motormouth Maybelle. The cast also includes Rebecca Pingree as Prudy Pingleton, David Boyll as Mr. Pinky and Harriman F. Spritzer, Sanaiya Johnson and Suleika Onia Patton alternating as Little Inez, Kareem Jenkins as Duane, Kaila Dyson, Anese Jade and Cai Rodis as The Dynamites, and Sierra Bolar, Matt Letton, Gwen Tessman and Hunter Yocom as The Nicest Kids in Town. Visit https://sfplayhouse. org/2025-2026-season/hairspray/ or call the box office at (415) 677- 9596 to purchase tickets.
articles.title: San Francisco Playhouse presents Hairspray through Sept. 12

articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) presents Twelfth Night, opening on Friday, August 7. Twelfth Night was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine, The Hollywood Reporter and The Washington Post. The play is a contemporary musical adaptation of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery. Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a Duke. Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role while she finds her true love in the process. The production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic feature an original jazz-funk score by Shaina Taub. The cast includes Nathan Bennett-Crump, Briana Bothello, Khalil Carim, Lucas Ceja, Laura Ferreira, Benjamin Grant, Mia Hangai, Ella Kim, Lourdes Verde Lombardo, Zoe Mastropasqua, Justina Mateescu and Keenan Moran. The play is directed by Dee Dee Stephens and choreographed by Meredith Joelle Charlson, with music direction by Amanda Dee. Twelfth Night is showing onstage at the Strand Theater in San Francisco August 7 through 16. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ whats-on/conservatory-shows/ twelfth-night to purchase tickets.
articles.title: A.C.T. presents Twelfth Night Aug. 7 - 16

articles.text: San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild will open the company’s 104th season with its annual fundraising gala “Opera Ball” on September 12. The evening will begin with a cocktail reception and dinner at San Francisco City Hall before attendees cross Van Ness Avenue for the opening night performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra at the War Memorial Opera House. An after-party at City Hall will follow the performance. Proceeds from the event will benefit San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s artistic and K-12 education programs. This year’s Opera Ball is dedicated to Diane B. Wilsey in recognition of her 20 years as Opening Weekend Grand Sponsor, supporting Opera Ball, the season-opening performance and Opera in the Park. “Opera Ball is more than the opening night of the opera season, it is one of the Bay Area’s defining fall galas,” co-chairs Sydney Leung and Jennifer Walske said in a joint statement. “Most importantly, every ticket supports our house of creativity, San Francisco Opera, and brings the transformative power of music education to K-12 students throughout the Bay Area through San Francisco Opera Guild.” Music Director Eun Sun Kim will conduct the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and Chorus in Verdi’s political drama, which is set in 14th-century Genoa. The cast includes Mongolian baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat in the title role, soprano Eleonora Buratto as Amelia and Maria, tenor Joshua Guerrero as Gabriele Adorno and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn as Jacopo Fiesco. The production is directed by Katherine M. Carter, who revived Claus Guth’s staging from Hamburg State Opera. For tickets, visit sfopera.com, call (415) 864-3330 or visit the Box Office in the lobby of the War Memorial Opera House at 301 Van Ness Avenue. The event is San Francisco Opera’s annual fundraiser benefiting education programs in San Francisco.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera Ball launches company’s 104th season Sept. 12

articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting next month’s Night Market on Friday, August 21. The free monthly event in San Francisco runs on select Fridays from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. through December, and features live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store on select dates. Fort Mason Night Market was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2026/ Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason in August.
articles.title: Fort Mason hosts Night Market on August 21

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, July 29, 2026 The Musical Gourmet Cult of personality By Joseph Gold We hear a lot about “cult of personality” these days. All too often, it is a rallying cry. In reality, the topic is not new. In fact, it has been with us since the beginning of time. Well… cults like this are often disconcerting. In music, there have been many who were so popular that they became cult figures, often negating their genius. Too often their personalities were misunderstood. Misconceptions abound. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet One in particular will get thoughts rolling. The scene is the harbor near Caracas, Venezuela in the year 1946. A friend of mine was there awaiting a passenger. On the same passenger liner was the famous Austrian tenor Richard Tauber. My friend saw Tauber strutting around, behaving in dictatorial fashion. He did not speak Spanish, and it seemed that no one understood him. I asked my friend if he volunteered to help and he said, “I didn’t want to be snubbed by Tauber.” My friend completely misconstrued the situation. Tauber’s personality was so strong that it went beyond the stage lights. That’s the way it is with some of our greatest entertainers. Another scene that stands out in music history concerns the very generous Czech violinist Jan Kubelik. He was in Chicago walking with a group of people led by his concert promoter. The story goes that Kubelik saw a poster of one of his competitors. Seemingly he flew into a rage and ripped the poster from its backing, shouting to everyone: “I’m your star! Why do you put up posters of non-entities?” That story has been repeated for more than 100 years. It is my opinion that the scene was completely humorous. Ambrose Bierce declared that self is the most important person in the universe. Many of the stories that are told about a great artist are just that…stories. These stories certainly make good publicity. But more often than not the really great artists are actually selfless and generous. Much of the publicity served to the public must be taken with a grain of salt. Ambrose Bierce had a humorous look at reality. articles.text: A Post reader recently asked whether the paper would ever again review/critique recently released feature-films which continue to open in those still familiar walk-in theaters. It was a question born of observation and curiosity. Yet, something has indeed changed, not only in the Post but also in this century-old compelling form of entertainment and its venue. This begs the questions: what is happening, and what does it mean? In thinking about the above I searched for an analogue, something equally transformative, even revolutionary. I decided on Johannes Gutenberg, who, in c.1450, invented movable metal type, a compatible oilbased ink, and a screw-down press. Reportedly, his first book was the Bible. Consider that before Gutenberg, copies of this much-coveted tome were painstakingly copied by hand. What Gutenberg’s stunning invention triggered was an explosion of accessible knowledge and soon the sharing of a spectrum of information leading to scientific inquiry, global exploration, advances in architecture and philosophy. It proved a Renaissance of creativity made manifest in the arts – theater, literature, and innovation. Reading was soon democratized. I would judge that we find ourselves in a similar period, a breathtaking invention/tech renaissance of sorts that began in the early 1900s and continues today. Consider the telegraph, photography (cameras, movie projectors), the railroad, automobile, telephone, the printing press as related to newspapers, radio, flight, space travel, television, the computer, Wikipedia, the Internet, email, iPhones and certainly more, all a kaleidoscope of change. And now A.I. Filmmaking/moving images with recorded sound/celluloid to digital — Hollywood has certainly not been exempt, now a kaleidoscope of streaming entertainment and information that is offered on platforms such as Prime, YouTube, Netflix, Disney+ being only four examples of many. Similar to the advent of books in the 1450s, we are experiencing an explosion of change: series, episodes, and a richness of storytelling, to include character development for writers and actors. For the audience, there’s extraordinary access. We now have available a massive, historical archive of films, documentaries and more. Will movies watched on high-tech, large screens at home be transformative? Will walk-in theaters be relics of the past? Likely. Consider that according to an industry poll, just-released movies are held in theaters only 30-45 days. And when they open, the announcement comes with a trailer/clip and the qualifier: “In Theaters Only.” Is this our Tech-driven Gutenberg moment? Perhaps.
articles.title: The only constant is change

articles.text: Supergirl (2026), directed by Craig Gillespie, is the second blockbuster movie in James Gunn’s DC universe, and it follows Superman’s cousin. Supergirl takes the viewer on a journey of revenge and self-discovery. We are learning who Kara Zor-El (Milly Alcock) is and who she wants to become after losing her family and friends in the destruction of her home planet Krypton. The film begins with Kara traveling with her dog Krypto to several planets to party and celebrate her 23rd birthday. The planets she travels to are red-sun planets, which take her powers away and allow her to let loose through drugs and alcohol. During one of her stops, Kara encounters Ruthye Marye Knoll (Eve Ridley), the last survivor of her family — who were murdered by Krem of the Yellow Hills (Matthias Schoenaerts), leader of a ruthless bandit group known as the Brigands. Ruthye requests Kara’s assistance in her quest for vengeance, but is denied. While the two are talking of Kara’s ship, Krem hijacks the vehicle and shoots Krypto with a poisonous dart when he tries to stop him. The poison paralyzes Krypto and leaving him with three days to live. Kara decides to pursue Krem to retrieve an antidote he keeps on him and reluctantly takes Ruthye with her. Before watching this movie in theaters, I was very excited to learn more about Kara and had high expectations for the film, especially after the success of Superman in 2025. After the was on screen. Supergirl was not all bad. The character designs and Kara herself are extremely bright spots. The aliens in every scene were distinctive and interesting. Every bar scene felt like the Cantina in Star Wars where all these different alien cultures came together to interact. These designs made the universe feel so unique and different on every planet that Kara went to. Throughout the film, we were given flashbacks into Kara’s life on Krypton, and we learned about how the planet was destroyed and the sacrifices her family made. Learning about how she had to abandon her family to save herself from the planet’s destruction was heartbreaking. Seeing Kara fall into self-destructive habits to escape bad memories and lose who she is was a compelling element of the movie. Watching Kara rediscover who she is and what she wants to become through Supergirl was the strongest part of the film. Not to mention the great action in the film; every time Supergirl can let loose and fight at full strength, it’s awesome. Overall, Supergirl failed to meet the high expectations I had for the movie before watching, but it’s still worth seeing if you care about the DC Universe. It is far from a bad movie, but also not a great one, paralyzed by being average. Supergirl. Directed by Craig Gillespie. Starring Milly Alcock, Eve Ridley, Matthias Schoenaerts, and Jason Momoa. 1 hr., 48 min. PG-13 (older kids, tweens). Released in 2026. Still playing in theaters. Supergirl starring Milly Alcock was released on June 26 this summer. movie ended, I left disappointed with the result. I felt there was so much potential in Supergirl’s story that they failed to capture. The villain Krem is one of the plainest and most boring antagonists I’ve ever seen in a superhero movie. His lack of personality or interest made the battles with Supergirl boring. Krem was just an evil guy who doesn’t talk much, and as a viewer, I just ended up not caring. The duo of Ruthye and Kara was not my favorite; it felt like the two actors lacked chemistry in their scenes, and I ended up disliking Ruthye as a character. The Ruthye revenge sideplot in the film was by far the weakest aspect. The character doesn’t do much in the film, and she didn’t blow me away with any extremely emotional moments. articles.text: Some of Sonoma’s finest wines come from places that are easy to miss, and Canihan Family Winery is one of them. Tucked among rolling vineyards just outside the town of Sonoma, Bill Canihan Jr. has spent the past two decades quietly building a reputation for handcrafted wines that reflect both the family’s history and the character of their certified organic estate vineyard. The story begins long before the first bottle was sold. Bill’s grandfather, August Siegrist, grew up working vineyards in Switzerland before immigrating to the United States. Although Prohibition ended his dream of becoming a winemaker, his love of wine was passed to future generations. In 1973, Bill Canihan Sr. purchased a 20-acre Sonoma property that remained unplanted for more than two decades before the family established vineyards in 1998. Today, Bill Canihan Jr. continues that legacy with a philosophy rooted in patience. The vineyards are dry-farmed and certified organic, grapes are harvested by hand, native yeasts carry out fermentation, and the wines are bottled without fining or filtration whenever possible. The goal is simple: allow the vineyard to speak for itself. Pinot Noir is the winery’s calling card. Produced from several Dijon and heritage clones, the wine balances vibrant red fruit with earthy complexity and bright natural acidity. Chardonnay offers freshness and precision rather than excessive oak, while limited sparkling wines have also attracted attention for their elegance and finesse. Their other specialty is cool climate Syrah bottled under the Exuberance label. The 2004 vintage of their Syrah was awarded “Best of Show Red Wine” at one of the world’s largest wine competitions, the San Francisco International Wine Competition. Despite earning awards and critical praise over the years, Canihan Family Winery remains intentionally small. Tastings are by appointment, giving visitors an opportunity to meet the people behind the wines and experience the relaxed pace that defines the estate. In a region often associated with luxury and spectacle, Canihan Family Winery demonstrates that authenticity, careful farming, and family tradition remain among Sonoma’s greatest strengths. • Canihan Brut Nature A charming sparkling wine with 75% Pinot Noir grapes and 25% Chardonnay made in Methode Champenoise style. It offers up lovely floral expressions along with a rich, almost tropical expression of fruit. This generous, seductive wine possesses excellent depth and lovely balance. • 2025 Canihan Rosé Sonoma Coast The Canihan Rosé opens with a lively and pretty nose, featuring subtle herbal accents set against aromas of strawberries and watermelon. The palate is straightforward yet refined, with impressive precision and concludes with an energetic, zippy finish. The perfect summer picnic wine. • 2025 Canihan Blanc de Pinot Noir Showing off a beautiful golden color the Blanc de Pinot Noir has a pretty brioche and citrus scented bouquet with subtle almond notes. The palate is balanced with nice melon fruit and a twist of sour lemon on the finish. (tasting by appointment only) 1340 Napa Road Sonoma, CA 95476 (415) 990 9270 Bill Canihan Jr. is proprietor of Canihan Winery.

The palate is balanced with nice melon fruit and a twist of sour lemon on the finish. Canihan Winery sits on a bucolic site east of the town of Sonoma. Canihan Winery (tasting by appointment only) 1340 Napa Road Sonoma, CA 95476 (415) 990 9270 The tasting room at Canihan is basic but gets the job done. Great partner to any fish or shellfish dish. • 2025 Canihan Viognier The wine leads with apricot, melon and honeysuckle aromas followed in the mouth with peach, apple and pear fruit flavors. It is round and viscous in the mouth with the voluptuous nature Viognier is famous for. Beautiful wine that needs no accompaniment other than a fine summer afternoon. • 2022 Canihan Chardonnay The Canihan Chardonnay is tangy and fresh, with a clear vein of acidity cutting through the stone fruit and sweet apple. Angular and nicely constructed, it shows balanced mineral contours, delivering precision and energy rather than breadth, with a finish that is rich, full and lingering. • 2022 Canihan Pinot Noir This deeply flavored Pinot Noir is made from a dry-farmed vineyard near the Carneros appellation. The cool climate provides a darkly floral, expressive bouquet introducing a broad, silken palate of cherry fruit that retains a welcome understated quality. The resonant finish captures an impressive array of savory and floral undertones, which I found quite enchanting. • 2022 Canihan Exuberance Syrah The Exuberance label is reserved for Canihan’s finest vintage selections. This cool climate Syrah reminds me of a fine Côte Rôtie from France’s Rhône Valley, avoiding the corpulence that some California Syrahs exhibit. It bursts onto the palate with a mélange of dark blueberry fruit, anise and spices. All the elements come together beautifully in the glass as the waves of fruit build towards the creamy textured finish. Bright floral notes of violets, pepper, leather and spices add further dimensions of complexity. Great with a beef or lamb daube. • 2016 Canihan Exuberance Syrah To get a sense of how the Canihan wines age, I was able to taste this 10-year-old bottle of their Syrah. It shows some of the complexity and mellowing that comes with bottle age but is very vibrant and youthful. It is velvety textured with nice layers of blackberry fruit, earth, licorice and a touch of chocolate. It is medium to full-bodied and has another decade ahead of it. Bill Canihan Jr. is proprietor of Canihan Winery. Canihan makes an elegant style of Chardonnay. The Sonoma Coast appellation is perfect for Pinot Noir. Canihan’s cool climate Syrah is elegant yet powerful.

articles.text: Matt Gerhardt The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a strong turnout of forty-three walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday. Matt Gerhardt, guest leader, invited the walkers to “tiptoe through the redwoods” with him. A longtime Piedmont resident who loves redwoods and our city’s hidden passages, he designed the walking route to include both. The walk began with a short stroll along the upper path in Piedmont Community Park to our first secret stairway, which headed up to Hazel Lane and merged onto Requa Road. That’s where we spotted our first gigantic coastal redwood tree — so magnificent that one exuberant walker gave it a big hug. Coastal redwoods, the type we see in Piedmont, are fast-growing and the tallest trees on Earth, often reaching 200 to 250 feet; the tallest, in Redwood National Park, tops out at 380 feet. The other type of redwood, the giant sequoia, grows in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California, such as in Yosemite and Sequoia National Parks, and is the largest redwood by volume. The walkers wound down Requa until it ended at Wildwood Avenue. After a block, they used the crosswalk at the top of Prospect Avenue to cross usually busy Wildwood, quieter than usual due to the summer break. After a steep walk downhill, Prospect ended at Harvard Road. That’s where we found our second enormous redwood tree and took the official group photo for the walk. On the hunt for more redwoods, the group turned onto Portsmouth Avenue and continued to Ranleigh Way, where the walkers discovered our second secret stairway. That stairway led up 42 steps to lower Wildwood Avenue, where the walkers halted momentarily at “The Five-Way Stop,” the junction of the four Ws: Wallace Road, Warfield Avenue, Wildwood Avenue (upper and lower), and Winsor Avenue. Then we headed past “The Camel House,” a local landmark — a beige Mediterranean-style home with brown dromedary (one-hump) camels painted on its walls under the roof line. The house doesn’t change hands very often, but when it does, the new homeowners inherit the stencils so they can carry on the cavorting camel tradition. After crossing Palm Drive at the foot of Wallace, the walkers entered our third hidden passage, a verdant tunnel of shrubs from Palm to Magnolia Avenue. Then the climb began! The group trudged up Magnolia one very long block to Jerome Avenue, where we caught our breath at a beautiful small redwood grove at the intersection of Jerome and Fairview Avenues. Fellow walker Route map and Piedmont Park Commission member Jack Fischrup estimated the trees to be thirty to fifty years old and explained how the two redwoods reproduce: coastal redwoods sprout from burls on their trunks, while sequoias drop seed pods that need fire to open them. Fifty years ago, government employees raked up the leaf litter; now they do controlled burns instead, helping new trees to sprout. This grove was planted on a former right-of-way of the Key System, the privately owned transit network that served the East Bay from 1903 to 1960. It connected local communities to San Francisco with an iconic network of streetcars and transbay ferries, and later via the lower deck of the Bay Bridge. pages.text: 22 22 Wednesday, July 29, 2026 Walking on Wednesday By Lori Austin and Matt Gerhardt The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a strong turnout of forty-three walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday. Matt Gerhardt, guest leader, invited the walkers to “tiptoe through the redwoods” with him. A longtime Piedmont resident who loves redwoods and our city’s hidden passages, he designed the walking route to include both. The walk began with a short stroll along the upper path in Piedmont Community Park to our first secret stairway, which headed up to Hazel Lane and merged onto Requa Road. That’s where we spotted our first gigantic coastal redwood tree — so magnificent that one exuberant walker gave it a big hug. Coastal redwoods, the type we see in Piedmont, are fast-growing and the tallest trees on Earth, often reaching 200 to 250 feet; the tallest, in Redwood National Park, tops out at 380 feet. The other type of redwood, the giant sequoia, grows in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California, such as in Yosemite and Sequoia National Parks, and is the largest redwood by volume. The walkers wound down Requa until it ended at Wildwood Avenue. After a block, they used the crosswalk at the top of ProsWednesday Walkers tiptoe through the redwoods pect Avenue to cross usually busy Wildwood, quieter than usual due to the summer break. After a steep walk downhill, Prospect ended at Harvard Road. That’s where we found our second enormous redwood tree and took the official group photo for the walk. On the hunt for more redwoods, the group turned onto Portsmouth Avenue and continued to Ranleigh Way, where the walkers discovered our second secret stairway. That stairway led up 42 steps to lower Wildwood Avenue, where the walkers halted momentarily at “The Five-Way Stop,” the junction of the four Ws: Wallace Road, Warfield Avenue, Wildwood Avenue (upper and lower), and Winsor Avenue. Then we headed past “The Camel House,” a local landmark — a beige Mediterranean-style home with brown dromedary (one-hump) camels painted on its walls under the roof line. The house doesn’t change hands very often, but when it does, the new homeowners inherit the stencils so they can carry on the cavorting camel tradition. After crossing Palm Drive at the foot of Wallace, the walkers entered our third hidden passage, a verdant tunnel of shrubs from Palm to Magnolia Avenue. Then the climb began! The group trudged up Magnolia one very long block to Jerome Avenue, where we caught our breath at a beautiful small redwood grove at the intersection of Jerome and Fairview Avenues. Fellow walker Route map and Piedmont Park Commission member Jack Fischrup estimated the trees to be thirty to fifty years old and explained how the two redwoods reproduce: coastal redwoods sprout from burls on their trunks, while sequoias drop seed pods that need fire to open them. Fifty years ago, government employees raked up the leaf litter; now they do controlled burns instead, helping new trees to sprout. This grove was planted on a former right-of-way of the Key System, the privately owned transit network that served the East Bay from 1903 to 1960. It connected local communities to San Francisco with an iconic network of streetcars and transbay ferries, and later via the lower deck of the Bay Bridge. The system’s original logo was a literal skeleton key: the teeth represented its ferry Kristin Howard hugs a redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane, which marked the entrance to the 1913 Ransom Bridges School for Girls, Piedmont’s first school. pier berths, the shank was the pier itself, and the three-pronged handle represented its core East Bay destinations — Berkeley, Piedmont, and Oakland. Leaving the redwood grove, the walkers crossed Oakland Avenue and headed uphill (again) to El Cerrito Avenue, then turned north to reach Blair Avenue, which skirts Dracena Quarry Park. articles.text: Sky the Aussie plays in a baby pool as he gets used to the water for the first time. As the summer heat arrives, many of us are eager to get our dogs into the water. While some pups are natural-born swimmers, others need a little more patience and a safe introduction to find their confidence. With these gentle tips, you can help your furry friend enjoy the water every day. First, remember that not all dogs are natural swimmers. If your pet is hesitant, never force them in. Always use a canine life vest and keep a helper nearby. It is best to start in calm water — like a pool with wide steps — for an easy entry and exit. Bring high-value treats to the water’s edge and reward your dog for just being near the pool. Use a happy, positive voice. Try to avoid overly reassuring phrases like “It’s okay,” which can actually validate their fear. Lure them onto the first step or into the shallows with treats. Ideally, your dog should stand comfortably in water up to its shoulders before moving deeper — a process that might take several days of practice. The first time your dog loses its footing can be a bit scary for them. To help them feel secure, support them with one hand under the chest and the other under the belly. Start with just a few seconds of floating before heading back to the stairs. Always let your dog leave the water whenever they want. As they get more comfortable, walk them around the pool. If they relax into a doggy paddle, loosen your grip and encourage them to swim a few feet toward your helper for more rewards. If they start to flounder, gently help them float. If a scary moment happens, just return to the edge to rebuild that confidence. Keep an eye out for signs of fatigue, since swimming is hard work for beginners. You might want to use a 20-foot long line if your dog swims more than a short distance from you. These simple steps will help ensure your pup’s first swim is a wonderful experience! Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC evaluator located in Oakland, California. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail.com or visit her website at www.oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors have been an established part of the Piedmont community since 1996 and will be celebrating their 30th year this September! This organization is sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, and is for Piedmont and Oakland residents who want to cultivate new friendships, explore new places and learn new things. Since Piedmont does not have an actual senior center, it becomes vitally important for the seniors to have a welcoming place to visit on a monthly basis. The purpose of the Piedmont Seniors’ program is to promote and strengthen the social and emotional well-being of seniors, as well as continuing to learn new things throughout one’s life. There are monthly meetings (usually on the fourth Wednesday of each month), and along with the business part of the meetings, there are speakers who talk about a variety of subjects that are of interest to our senior members. Recent topics have covered Medicare, elder fraud and abuse, decluttering and keeping up with the latest in technology. It has become challenging to keep up in today’s society as AI has dramatically changed how we deal with the changing world we live in. In addition to meetings, the Piedmont Seniors go on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. They have gone to theatre productions, a California Highway Patrol training academy, factory tours as well as numerous museums in the area. Next up for the busy group is a visit to the Eugene O’Neill Historic Site in Danville, a tour of the San Francisco City Hall and an A.C.T. theatre production in San A memorable excursion for the Piedmont Seniors was a trip to visit the San Francisco Bay Model in Sausalito. The Piedmont Seniors visit San Francisco’s Legion of Honor. Francisco. This is a great way to meet new people and prevent social isolation, which can be a real issue for those who are aging in place, many of whom have lost their spouses. Lunch and socializing is part of the excursion experience. During the school year, there is the “Juniors Helping Seniors” program, where high school students are willing to relinquish their lunch periods to help the Seniors solve technology issues on their devices. Another collaborative program that many of the Seniors have recently participated in is the “Weaver program.” This is where teens go to seniors’ homes to visit and help with a myriad of tasks in the home, such as gardening, computer help, lifting, and other tasks that can sometimes feel overwhelming. It really helps with intergenerational bonding and has been extremely successful to date! Both generations have much to learn and share! The Seniors also have extended travel programs available through Collette Vacations, the oldest tour company in the United States. Some of the upcoming trips include those to Tuscany, New York City, Eastern Canada, the colors of New England, and river cruising on the Rhine and Moselle Rivers. If you would like to find out more about the Piedmont Seniors group, please feel free to contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. It really helps with intergenerational bonding and has been extremely successful to date! Both generations have much to learn and share! The Seniors also have extended travel programs available through Collette Vacations, the oldest tour company in the United States. Some of the upcoming trips include those to Tuscany, New York City, Eastern Canada, the colors of New England, and river cruising on the Rhine and Moselle Rivers. If you would like to find out more about the Piedmont Seniors group, please feel free to contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Piedmont Seniors received a guided tour through the Hiller Aviation Museum in San Carlos. I scream! You scream! We all scream for ice cream! Yes, it’s always time for ice cream as the Piedmont Seniors visited the It’s-It factory in Burlingame.

articles.text: November 21, 1940 – December 31, 2025 Karl Christian Kardel, founder of Karl Kardel Company, preservationist, designer, builder, expert witness, husband, father, grandfather, and lover of life, passed away on December 31, 2025, at the age of 85. Born in Charlotte, Michigan, to Danish immigrant parents Hans and Karen Kardel, Karl was the fourth of five children. His early years were shaped by an international upbringing when his parents’ civil service work took the family to Bangalore, India. He attended Kodaikanal International School before returning to the United States at fifteen following his father’s death. He later moved his mother and sister to Berkeley, California, while earning a degree in political science at the University of California, Berkeley. In 1959, he founded Karl Kardel Company and began acquiring and renovating properties throughout Berkeley. Among his earliest undertakings was the transformation of a row of modest Spruce Street cottages into boldly saturated hues—a project that became emblematic of a broader creative renewal in the city. Karl was part of the cultural and architectural resurgence that helped redefine Berkeley. Known for historically informed restoration and a distinctive eye for color, his work balanced imagination with craftsmanship. His projects included the Woodland Opera House, the Legion of Honor, University House at UC Berkeley, the Berkeley Public Library, and the State Capitol Mall. Throughout his career, he continued to design and restore private and civic spaces across Northern California. Over time, his work expanded into forensic building analysis, and he became widely respected as an authority on building failure, waterproofing and envelope integrity, serving as an expert witness in cases nationwide. Karl was a respected figure in preservation, restoration, and the stewardship of historic buildings. His commitment to these fields extended beyond his own work through service to arts and preservation organizations throughout the Bay Area. Karl served on the board of Berkeley Repertory Theatre for many years. He also Karl Christian Kardel served on the board of State Fund Insurance. He believed that “all design is theater.” An avid classic car enthusiast and collector, Karl was active in the Rolls Royce Owners’ Club and The Classic Car Club of America. In 1983, he married Allyson Tynes Kardel, and together they built a life of more than four decades in Piedmont. Family was at the center of Karl’s life. Food, conversation, friendship, and dogs were central to family life. The table was full from top to bottom. Conversation mattered to Karl. He found deep pleasure in the garden and was a voracious reader throughout his life. He believed life should be beautiful and lived accordingly. He was previously married to Cecilia Spurgeon Alighieri, with whom he shared his three eldest children. Karl is survived by his wife, Allyson Tynes Kardel; his children, Cecilia Sissel Kardel, Kaj Emil Kardel, Camilla Kardel Sharma, Justin Tynes Kardel, Allyson Ashley St. Germain, and Lauren Alexandra Kardel; his grandchildren, Madeleine Simone Kardel, Ozzy Oakley St. Germain, Emil Albert Limenes, and Lucia Cali Limenes; his motherin-law, Elinor Ruth Smith; and his siblings, Hans Kardel and Karen Kardel. A celebration of Karl’s life will be held on July 30, 2026, at the Brazil Room in Berkeley. Those wishing to attend may contact the family. Karl leaves behind a devoted family, enduring friendships, and an imprint on the communities, places, and people he helped shape.

articles.text: Stagebridge springing from summer camp to fall classes Last week, Stagebridge’s Encore Performing Arts Summer Camp for Adults brought together storytellers, actors, singers, drummers and improvisers for an intensive week of classes. Some were already practicing artists while many came with no experience beyond a willingness to learn. Stagebridge welcomes all levels, and by Friday afternoon students took the stage for family and friends. For some, summer camp at Stagebridge is one unforgettable week. For others, like Sandy Lasky, it’s the beginning of something much bigger. More than a decade after enrolling in her first class, Lasky is still coming back. Lasky first signed up for a jazz chorus at Stagebridge because she loved singing harmony. She admits that prior to finding Stagebridge, she’d gone back to school “a hundred times” and earned several degrees. Eventually, she realized she wanted something different. “I didn’t want to sit,” she said. “I wanted to do. And this is a do place.” One class led to another. “It was so fun and the people are so welcoming and so nonjudgmental,” Lasky said. “They just allow you to explore what it is you think you might be interested in.” More than 10 years later, Lasky still calls the experience “revelatory.” “And now this is my community,” she said. Encore Performing Arts Summer Camp wrapped up July 17, but Stagebridge’s fall, winter and spring seasons offer a full lineup of classes, including innovative new offerings. Alongside returning favorites like acting, singing and musical theater are new offerings, including a podcasting class with Wayne Harris and workshops such as folk dancing and somatic voicework for creative aging. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland, inside the First Congregational Church of Oakland, Stagebridge is just across from Lake Merritt’s Whole Foods and steps from AC Transit Line 33. Registration opens Aug. 1 and fall classes begin Sept. 14. Scholarships are available. Class size is limited. Learn more and register at www.stagebridge.org. pages.text: 32 32 Wednesday, July 29, 2026 Supt. Hawn Continued from page 1 making change happen in Piedmont and, following modern employment trends for superintendents, leaves after only a few years. Current board members Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson helped conduct the previous search for a superintendent in 2023, which resulted in the hiring of Hawn. The naming of the next Superintendent will mark the fourth leader of Piedmont schools since 2022. Randy Booker served from 2015 until 2022. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans came out of retirement to serve from 2022–2023, and Hawn took the post from 2023–2026. Booker’s resignation came with relatively advance notice; he notified the board on May 13, 2022. Despite having the whole summer to conduct a search, the board elected to hire an interim superintendent for one year. Hawn achieved much in her time; she told the Post that she made sure no other candidate would outprepare her when applying for the job. She did extensive research on Piedmont by watching hours of board meetings and continued the fastidious work while employed. Hawn’s tenure ushered in higher standards of excellence and a focus on high-achieving academics. Her success in this is evidenced by the high number of 2026 PHS graduates admitted to the University of California – 48 in total. Fifteen recent Piedmont graduates are about to start their freshman years at UC Berkeley. The focus on rigor and improving the district rank did not come without resistance. Hawn supported the addition of AP and Honors courses at PHS. Hawn will not stick around to deal with the side effects of adding pressure to student workload, nor will she be here to see the impact of adding Latin studies to 5th graders or the much-debated bell-to-bell cell phone ban policy in action. Hawn proved to be a shrewd and fierce negotiator with the teachers, holding her ground in her first year at the negotiating table to the point that teachers declared negotiations at an impasse and threatened the first teacher strike in Piedmont’s history. Today’s board reaps the rewards and consequences of Hawn’s leadership. Many questions remain, and the board states its plan for the future will be developed in the coming weeks. The first board meeting of the new school year is on Wednesday, August 12 and will be Hawn’s last appearance as a Piedmont administrator. A farewell to Superintendent Hawn is planned to take place during the meeting. Will Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich, who was hired at the same time as Hawn, immediately step in? How have the priorities in the next search changed? Is a three-year term the new normal for school superintendents or can Piedmont find a person willing to make a longer-term commitment? Hawn gave a two-week notice before resigning and described her decision in her Piedmont Pulse newsletter (Smore.com/n/ db4tu). “This decision was not an easy one to make. Serving as Superintendent of PUSD since July 2023 has been one of the great honors of my career, and I leave with tremendous gratitude for what we have built together,” she said. Medhekar has indicated the board will pursue an interim Superintendent with more details to be shared at the August 12 board meeting. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Where in the World Are We? articles.text: Pete Palmer and the Piedmont Unified Facilities team have completed construction projects this summer to spruce up Piedmont school facilities. A new playground has been built at Havens, and a portion of P.E. Hill from the Binks Rawling Gym down past the Bern Courts has been repaved. Modernization of three district elevators is also underway. The elevators, one at Wildwood and two at Piedmont Middle School (PMS) were identified as nearing the end of their viability. The final elevator modernization project in the 500 building at PMS is scheduled to be completed by August 7. Although it is a City project, the conversion of Bonita Avenue into a one-way street in front of Havens has also been completed. Additional parking spots have been added on the block from Vista to Oakland, and barricades are in place to prevent drivers from turning onto Bonita Avenue from Oakland Avenue. Bonita is now a one-way street from Magnolia Avenue to Oakland Avenue. The new play structure at Havens was built by Ross Recreation Equipment for $211,477 and New slides and an impressive climbing dome await Havens kids returning to school in the fall.
articles.title: PUSD summer facility construction projects

articles.text: Over the past week, youth choirs from throughout the world came together for the Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. It was an unforgettable week of concerts, competitions, special events, and cultural exchange. Choral groups participated in solo performances and two group performances on the first and final days of the festival. During the week the groups competed in several categories: Children’s Historical Music Competition, Youth Historical Music Competition, Children’s Folk Music Competition, Youth Folk Music Competition, Gospel / Spiritual Music Competition, and Contemporary Music Competition. The solo competitions included: the Children’s Vocal Solo Competition and Youth Vocal Solo Competition. Outside of the competition events, awards were given to groups that showcased outstanding global citizenship and celebrated contributions of unique cultural significance. The Choir of Angels Award was given to the Austrian choir Singakademie
articles.title: GG International Choral Festival celebrates youth music in week of competition
