articles.text: Dale Edmondson, a much respected American Baptist pastor and personal friend, writes beautifully about entrusting those he loves to God’s care. He quotes an early spiritual guide, Francis Whiston, who prayed daily, “O God, I give my loved ones back to you for your taking or returning.” Dale continues, “He (Whitson) said, ‘Your loved ones aren’t yours. They’re not owned or possessed by you. They’re God’s and come to you as gifts. They enrich and shape and bring meaning to your life. Each day he urged, surrender them – indeed “entrust” them – to God’s keeping. And if, on the morrow, they are returned to you, rejoice in the gift. And if, on the morrow, they are not, you have already entrusted them to God’s care.’” In a similar way the writer of Colossians (Paul?) tenderly entrusts the well being of the community of Christ-followers in that ancient city to its members. “Therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience. Carjuzaa described briefly how America’s forefathers had struggled to establish the Declaration of Independence. He said that there are currently two narratives in the country, one about a form of patriotism that is good for everyone that contains the belief that people can effectively govern themselves. The other narrative is about nationalism that is based on domination and is led by a group of people that believe that people only need to be obedient to them. Lamba decided against running on the ballot to support Carjuzaa. In Lamba’s speech he described how the Declaration of Independence, besides laying out lofty principles, also listed the misdeeds of the King of England. articles.text: & D.J. Grubb Real Estate Decoded, July 2026 Last month, D.J. Grubb — President of The Grubb Company, fourth-generation East Bay native, and steward of the brokerage his father and uncle founded in 1967 — and I were both appointed to the Board of Directors of the Bridge Association of Realtors, which operates bridgeMLS, the cooperative listing platform serving the East Bay and surrounding Bay Area markets. We want to tell you why we said yes. And to do that, we need to tell you about the war being fought right now over who controls the way homes are bought and sold in America. You’ve probably heard some version of it — Zillow banning listings, Compass suing Zillow, a Chicago MLS cutting off data feeds, federal antitrust lawsuits flying in both directions. The media is covering it like a corporate cage match. Two tech giants, billions of dollars, lawyers everywhere. But here’s what that framing gets wrong: this fight isn’t about Zillow or Compass. It’s about whether you — the person actually buying or selling a home — get a fair shot at the market. Or whether the deck gets quietly stacked against you by people who benefit when you don’t know what you don’t know. Let’s break it down. What is the MLS and why should you care? The Multiple Listing Service — the MLS — is the cooperative database where brokers share listings with each other. When your agent lists your home, it goes into the MLS. When a buyer’s agent searches for homes, they search the MLS. Every offer, every counteroffer, every accepted bid — the MLS is the infrastructure underneath all of it. It was built on a simple, pro-consumer idea: the more buyers who see your home, the more competition you get, and the more money you walk away with. Basic auction theory. More bidders equal higher prices. Every time. No exceptions. The MLS is not glamorous. It doesn’t have a slick app or a Super Bowl ad. But it is the single most important piece of infrastructure in residential real estate, and right now, two of the largest companies in the industry are fighting over who gets to control it — and who gets to decide who sees what. Enter Compass: The private exclusive play Compass — which completed a $4.2 billion merger with Anywhere Real Estate (Coldwell Banker, Century 21, Corcoran, Sotheby’s) in January 2026 — is now involved in roughly 1 in every 5 home sales in the United States. That’s not a brokerage. That’s market infrastructure. Compass’s signature move is what they call the “Private Exclusive.” A home gets marketed within the Compass agent network — and only the Compass network — before it ever hits the public MLS. Compass frames this as seller empowerment. Seller choice. Privacy. Exclusivity. Here’s what it actually is: a mechanism for Compass to represent both the buyer and the seller on the same transaction. Think about what that means. If your home is listed as a Compass Private Exclusive, the only buyers who see it are buyers working with Compass agents. Which means when an offer comes in, there’s a very good chance it’s from another Compass agent. Which means Compass collects commission on both sides of the deal. Which means your agent’s brokerage just doubled its revenue on your transaction — while you, the seller, had a fraction of the potential buyer pool competing for your home. A Drexel University study of Bright MLS data found that homes marketed through the open MLS sold for 17.5% more than comparable homes marketed off it. 17.5%. On a $1.5 million East Bay home, that’s $262,500 left on the table. In exchange for what, exactly? The privilege of your listing staying “exclusive”? Enter Zillow: The white knight who isn’t Now here’s where we have to be straight with you, because we’re not here to sell you a narrative. Zillow isn’t fighting this battle for you. Zillow is fighting this battle for Zillow. Zillow’s business model runs on traffic — 235 million monthly users scrolling listings, clicking through to agents, selling lead data back to the industry. If listings disappear from Zillow because Compass keeps them in a private network, Zillow’s product gets worse, their traffic drops, and their revenue follows. Zillow’s Listing Access Standards — the policy that kicked off the legal war — were designed to protect Zillow’s data pipeline, not your equity. That said: a policy that serves Zillow’s interests can simultaneously serve yours. Zillow’s position — that any publicly marketed listing should be on the open MLS within 24 hours — is actually correct. Not because Zillow said so, but because the math says so. More exposure equals more buyers equals more competition equals more money for sellers. Zillow is the only company with enough market power to push back against Compass on a national scale. That doesn’t make them good. It makes them useful — for now, in this particular fight. The part that should actually make you angry In October 2025, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin sent direct messages to at least eight MLS boards across the country urging them to “discipline” Zillow — to cut off Zillow’s access to listing data if Zillow continued enforcing its standards. According to Zillow’s federal antitrust complaint, one of those MLSs, MRED in Chicago, had a Compass vice president sitting on its board. That Compass executive was telling Compass agents about board decisions before the board had formally voted. Let that sink in. A brokerage — one with a financial interest in limiting listing exposure — was using a seat on the cooperative MLS board to advance its own business agenda. The MLS then cut off Zillow’s access to 43,000 Chicago listings. Sellers in Chicago woke up with their homes invisible to a platform with 235 million monthly users, because a Compass VP made some phone calls. This is not competition. This is regulatory capture. And it’s exactly why who sits on local MLS boards matters enormously. Why this fight brought us to the Bridge Board Now you understand the stakes. And now you understand why we didn’t hesitate when asked to serve. Consider the contrast. On one side of the national story: Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Repairs on the foot path in Dracena Park were officially completed on July 7. The repairs were in response to cracking in the original asphalt path due to age and damage. The repairs took place in the upper canyon area near Park Way. Piedmont Public Works employees began demolition of the old path in late June, using machinery to dig up the cracked asphalt path. They lined the path with wooden planks as form boards. The City has undertaken substantial pathway repair work to improve safety and access in Piedmont’s parks over the past The damaged asphalt pathway before demolition. few years – including projects at Crocker Park, Piedmont Park, and a large portion of the pathways in upper Dracena two years ago. The pathway is currently open to the public and ready for walkers. Public Works employees digging up the broken pathway in the Upper Canyon area of Dracena Park. articles.text: Poor Eeyore is feeling gloomy. First he and his pal were tied up to a post outside Oakland Animal Services shelter and abandoned. Then his buddy was adopted and left him behind at the shelter. This tenderhearted pup is seven-year-old, gentle, and low energy. An 82-pound house hippo, Eeyore enjoys pets and cuddles, napping in the sun, and being in the company of other dogs during the shelter’s daily playgroup time. He’s easy to walk on leash, although he does occasionally decide he’d prefer to rest rather than move! Come see if Eeyore would be a fit for you by stopping by Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. You’d bring a ray of sunshine Eeyore is a seven-year-old tenderhearted pup into his life. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Eeyore must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Adoptable Dog of the Week

articles.text: Mr. Snuggles earned his name honestly: this 5-year-old cream tabby believes there’s no such thing as too much affection! He’ll follow you from room to room hoping for cuddles and he asks for ear scratches with an enthusiastic purr. This love bug is positive for FIV, so needs some simple care to live a long, healthy life: keep him indoors, feed a balanced diet, and schedule regular vet checkups. He’ll agree that three square meals a day are crucial for his happiness — while his sensitive stomach does best on a high-fiber diet, this sweet boy’s eagerness for suppertime can occasionally get the better of him. Keep his excitement in check with clear boundaries, puzzle feeders, and predictable feeding schedule. After snuggles, and after his mealtime puzzles, this little guy loves pouncing on wand toys, watching birds and squirrels from the window, making Adopt Mr. Snuggles through Cat Town biscuits on his favorite scratching lounge, and cuddling up to you at night (big surprise there). He may do well with another cat and is looking for a calm, indoor-only home where he can soak up all the love. Mr. Snuggles is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FIV-positive. Learn more about this lovebug at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Youth aquatics teams begin practices July 27 Lap and open swim schedules at the Piedmont competition pool will shift in the coming weeks as local youth aquatics teams begin their seasonal practices. Midday activity hours will change starting Monday, July 27, when the Piedmont High School water polo team starts pre-season practice. Starting August 10, hours will shift again as the PHS water polo team and Piedmont Swim Team fall-season practice schedules begin. From August 10 through October 30, the Competition Pool will be fully dedicated to water polo practice on weekday evenings and Saturday mornings from 9 a.m.- 11 a.m. Competition and Activity Pool schedules through October 30 are available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/pool. Hours are subject to change, so visitors are encouraged to check the website to confirm schedules before visiting. As a facility built to serve the full community, the pool provides space for recreation, fitness, swim instruction, and youth sports throughout the year – striving to balance water access across the diverse array of community aquatic needs. During the fall season, the Competition Pool will continue to offer over 61 hours of lap swimming and 66 hours of open swim availability each week. The Competition Pool is scheduled to be closed from 2 p.m.-8 p.m. for PHS Water Polo home games on the following dates (schedule is subject to change): • Thursday, September 3 • Wednesday, September 9 • Tuesday, September 22 • Thursday, September 24 • Tuesday, October 6 • Tuesday, October 20 The Activity Pool will remain open with regularly scheduled activities during the games. Spectators are welcome at water polo games. Those wishing to watch the game can enter at the Magnolia Avenue gate. A full list of planned closures is posted on the pool website. Find pool hours, schedules, and visitor information at piedmont.ca.gov/pool. Register for aquatics programs at rec.us/piedmont. As the youth aquatics teams begin fall practices, Piedmont’s competition pool hours will change to accommodate the teams. Once games begin in the fall season, the competition pool will be closed in the evening for the event.
articles.title: Competition pool hours to change

pages.text: Wednesday, July 22, 2026 5 Competition pool hours to change Youth aquatics teams begin practices July 27 By Jake Lannon Lap and open swim schedules at the Piedmont competition pool will shift in the coming weeks as local youth aquatics teams begin their seasonal practices. Midday activity hours will change starting Monday, July 27, when the Piedmont High School water polo team starts pre-season practice. Starting August 10, hours will shift again as the PHS water polo team and Piedmont Swim Team fall-season practice schedules begin. From August 10 through October 30, the Competition Pool will be fully dedicated to water polo practice on weekday evenings and Saturday mornings from 9 a.m.- 11 a.m. Competition and Activity Pool schedules through October 30 are available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/pool. Hours are subject to change, so visitors are encouraged to check the website to confirm schedules before visiting. As a facility built to serve the full community, the pool provides space for recreation, fitness, swim instruction, and youth sports throughout the year – striving to balance water access across the diverse array of community aquatic needs. During the fall season, the Competition Pool will continue to offer over 61 hours of lap swimming and 66 hours of open swim availability each week. The Competition Pool is scheduled to be closed from 2 p.m.-8 p.m. for PHS Water Polo home games on the following dates (schedule is subject to change): • Thursday, September 3 • Wednesday, September 9 • Tuesday, September 22 • Thursday, September 24 • Tuesday, October 6 • Tuesday, October 20 The Activity Pool will remain open with regularly scheduled activities during the games. Spectators are welcome at water polo games. Those wishing to watch the game can enter at the Magnolia Avenue gate. A full list of planned closures is posted on the pool website. Find pool hours, schedules, and visitor information at piedmont.ca.gov/pool. Register for aquatics programs at rec.us/piedmont. As the youth aquatics teams begin fall practices, Piedmont’s competition pool hours will change to accommodate the teams. Once games begin in the fall season, the competition pool will be closed in the evening for the event. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council Board Vice President of Programs, Karen Snow Hawkins, sat down with Betsy Smegal Andersen, Piedmont’s Mayor, to reflect on Scouting’s impact on Piedmont and why it continues to matter today. Q: Growing up in Piedmont in a Scouting family, and given your civic involvement over the years, you have a unique perspective on Scouting. What do you think has been its greatest contribution to the Piedmont community? Scouts contribute in so many ways, yet I’d say that one of its biggest contributions is how Scouting brings our community together. Whether it’s the Tree Lot, serving hot dogs and hamburgers at the Fourth of July celebration, or volunteering at community events, Scouting creates opportunities for all of us to connect. I also have to mention Eagle projects, as they require young people to look at their community and think about how they can make it better. That kind of reflection is valuable in itself. Every year, Eagle projects make a positive physical impact on our town—to our schools, athletics, and other organizations. I’m also proud that many Piedmont Eagle Scout projects benefit communities beyond Piedmont. These projects make a tangible difference while teaching young peoScouts Ellie Przybyla, Raven Oliver-Wheeler, and Grace StricklandReddy prepare hot dogs at the Troop 4 Hot Dog Stand during the Piedmont July 4th Celebration. Scout Elise High collects donated food for Scouting for Food, which benefits the Alameda County Community Food Bank, November 2025. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen (left) speaks at the Eagle Court of Honor in May for Piedmont Scout Gabriel Barbosa-Topete. Pictured also are Scouts James High, and Adelina Mbise. ple that they have the ability to create positive and lasting change in their community. Q: What are some of the aspects of Scouting that you believe make it an important and relevant program for youth today? From my perspective, one of the things that makes Scouting special is its vertical integration. What I mean by this is that younger Scouts work with older Scouts, learning from them and building friendships across age groups. Parents benefit too, as they get to know families with kids of different ages. Whether camping, hiking, or serving the community together, those shared experiences build community and create lasting relationships. I also value Scouting’s emphasis on the outdoors and stewardship. In an urban community like ours, any program that gets kids outside—whether it’s hiking, camping, or service—is incredibly valuable. And, perhaps most importantly, Scouting gives young people the chance to build real connections in a world dominated by screens. It’s hard to be on your phone when you’re hiking a trail or building a campfire! places where youth have opportunities like that. They’re also remarkably good public speakers, and that confidence comes from years of practice. Scouting teaches innumerable practical life skills—from first aid and emergency preparedness to personal management and wilderness survival. These skills will serve them well throughout their lives. Scouting also inspires youth to be good citizens in their local community and beyond. We need future leaders! As mayor, I often get invited to attend Eagle Scout Courts of Honor. It’s such a joy for me to proclaim a City of Piedmont Day in each Eagle Scout’s name, in honor of their commitment and achievement. How cool is it to have a day named after you. Q: You’ve interacted with Scouts for merit badges and Courts of Honor. What qualities have you seen Scouting develop in our youth? One of the things that always impresses me is the leadership skills our young people have developed through Scouting. articles.text: Many rising seniors are feeling a sense of urgency around their college application essays. Before writing a single sentence, however, it’s worth taking a step back. The strongest essays rarely begin with exceptional writing. They begin with thoughtful reflection. One of the biggest misconceptions about college essays is that students need to write about the most impressive, dramatic, or life-changing event they’ve ever experienced. In reality, admissions officers are not searching for extraordinary stories; they are looking for authentic people. articles.text: Rival Jonas Vingegaard crashes, withdraws from race Photo courtesy of UAE Team Emirates Tadej Pogačar is less than a week away from making history as a fivetime winner of the Tour de France. The 2026 Tour de France approaches the final week of action with just five stages remaining and Tadej Pogačar leading the race for the Yellow Jersey in the General Classification standings with a 4 minute, 32 second lead over Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel, If Pogačar wins it all, as expected, it will mark his fifth win of Le Grand Tour and third consecutive title. It will match him with five-time winners like France’s Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault, Belgium legend Eddy Merckx, and Miguel Induráin of Spain. A third consecutive title will become the first since Chris Froome did so from 2015 to 2017. So far this tour, Pogačar took control of the Yellow Jersey on July 9 in Stage 6’s 186.2-kilometer mountain course with a solo attack on the Col du Tourmalet to win the stage by two minutes and 38 seconds. He extended his advantage by 44 seconds with another mountain-stage victory on July 14’s Bastille Day Stage 10 from Aurillac to Le Lioran, beating Evenepoel by 32 seconds in the process. Pogačar’s top rival, Jonas Vingegaard of Denmark, crashed out of the event, He was sitting in second place of general classification and trailing by four minutes and 30 seconds. On Sunday’s Stage 15, Vingegaard took a tumble about 20 kilometers from the finish line, resulting in a broken collarbone. The incident notably occurred the following morning after anti-doping officials woke him up around 2:00 a.m. on race day for an unexpected drug test. The rider was never flagged for a positive test. In Tuesday’s Stage 16 time trial, Evenepoel gave himself some life by winning the stage

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Spanish National Team Wikipedia Spain lifted the World Cup trophy after beating Argentina 1-nil in extra time. It marks the nation’s second title. The 2026 FIFA World Cup officially came to a close on Sunday, July 19 with Spain upending defending champions Argentina 1-nil in extra time. It was a dominant game by the Spanish on their way to a second star, playing their stifling highly-possessive style to record 20 shot attempts with 12 on target while holding Argentina with a single shot attempt until the second period of extra time. It was interesting to see Argentina and Lionel Messi become the world’s super villain going into the final. Spain was largely cheered on by the entire world, including Argentina’s South American counterparts. Messi was overcome with emotion after the final whistle, knowing this is likely his last World Cup appearance at 39 years old. This year’s Coupe Du Monde was the most-watched in the tournament’s history, while the Final between Spain and Argentina raked in 1.5 billion viewers. It brought a lot of legendary moments that are difficult to quantify in our limited space available, but provided is some of the Post’s favorite moments. No Scotland, no party Starting off our list is the interactions from fans visiting the United States. There have been a lot of spectacular ones; Norway fan’s Viking Row, Japanese fans cleaning up entire sections, English being astounded by Texas BBQ, and the Dutch’s Oranje Fanwalk. But, perhaps nothing was as outstanding and hilarious as how the Scottish Tartan Army invaded Boston and was embraced by the city. The Scottish made headlines by drinking the city completely dry of beer, giving bar owners the best week of business in their history. Baseball fans got an example of how crazed European soccer fans are with the Scots belting out songs in the stands during the game, and over a half-hour past the final pitch in Fenway Park’s halls. After their visit, Boston and Glasgow officially launched their sister city partnership, signing an official letter to formalize their kinship. The moment was the epitome of the World Cup, where a game transcends sport and provides an example that foreign cultures are more related than the surface appears. The tiny country that could, Cabo Verde Cabo Verde was a prime example of FIFA hitting on its bet to expand the World Cup to 48 teams. The tiny African island of 550,000 was the Cinderella story of the tournament, achieving second place in its group with 0-0 ties against Spain and Saudi Arabia, along with a 2-2 draw against Uruguay. Goalkeeper Vozinha became a star, exploding his social media following from around 50,000 to over 15 million people. Although Cabo Verde exited the Round of 32 with a 3-2 loss to Argentina, Sidny Lopes Cabral landed one of the greatest shots in World Cup history to tie that match at 2-2 in extra time. The defending champions and finalists, Argentina, didn’t score the game-winner until nine minutes were left in overtime. The match goes down as a surefire World Cup classic. Mexico vs. England at The Azteca Speaking of World Cup classics, England’s 3-2 win over Mexico in the Round of 16 goes down Photo courtesy of The Straits Times The Scottish “Tartan Army” took over Boston and was completely embraced by the city. It was among the great fan interactions of this year’s World Cup.

articles.text: NIA KIM Track and Field Piedmont High Class of 2025 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2029 What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for the summer are to put on lots of muscle and improve my speed and explosiveness. I also want to improve on some of my basics like getting across the ring in shotput or certain form in the weight room. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my development by tracking my lifting numbers, sprint times, and how I feel during workouts. I’m also paying attention to my consistency and recovery. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working out on my own but following the summer training program given to me by my coaches at UCSC. While I’m on my own during workouts, I try stay updated with my teammates and what they’re doing and feeling. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I’ve accomplished is feeling much stronger and explosive, especially in the weight room. I’ve consistent increasing the weight I’m lifting and I’ve noticed that my power overall has improved. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I’d tell the younger/aspiring student-athletes to stay consistent and trust the process. Success can’t happen overnight. The small habits you build everyday make the biggest differences. Photo courtesy of UC Santa Cruz Nia Kim, PHS Class of 2025, enters her sophomore year on UC Santa Cruz’s track and field team. She was the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2025. Nia Kim, PHS Class of 2025, just finished her freshman season on UC Santa Cruz’s track and field team. She was The Post’s 2025 Athlete of the Year. She made it to the D3 NCAA Track and Field Championships on May 23, finishing 13th of 19 in the heptathlon, which is the compiled results for seven different events. She was sixth of 20 in the 100 meter hurdles, fifth of 20 in the high jump, 18th of 22 in the shot put, 11th of 19 in the 200 meter dash, fourth of 20 in the long jump, 19th of 20 in the javelin, and 11th of 18 in the 800. Kim set UC Santa Cruz’s record in the pentathlon, 60 meter hurdles, and long jump at the Wolf Pack Classic in February. Her 3,439 pentathlon score was the No. 6 total in the country. She logged a winning time of 8.78 seconds in the 60 meter hurdles in a field of eight at the Coast-To-Coast Athletic Conference Indoor Championships in February. She also won three events at the 2026 Coast-To-Coast Outdoor Championships in May, including the 100 hurdles in 14.19 over seven other finalists, the high jump at 1.57 meters against eight others, and the long jump at 5.77 meters in a field of 16. Kim was a breakout star on Piedmont High’s track and field team in her only year as a varsity athlete after joining the squad as a former gymnast. She became a Western Alameda County Conference champion in the 100 hurdles with a time of 15.62 seconds and the North Coast Section Bayshore Area champion in 15.19. What is your workout program this summer? My current workout program mainly consists of lifting. I try to lift three times a week and try to throw shotput twice a week. I am also starting to learn to pole vault because I’m going to try that next year! I also stretch and do rehab twice a week to keep mobility up and prevent any injuries that could occur. To qualify for State at the NCS Championship on May 9, Piedmont’s 200 medley team of Takazawa, Costello, Connor Carnazzo, and Cole Carnazzo finished fourth of 16 total finalists with a time of 1:32.91. The boys’ 400 freestyle relay team of Latronica, Secor, Costello, and Takazawa placed sixth of 16 finalists, clocking a 3:05.85 to reach State. On May 1 at the WACC Championships, Costello won four firstplace medals and made history in the process. At the meet, Piedmont’s 200 medley relay team with Costello, Takazawa, Cole Carnazzo, and Connor Carnazzo set a WACC record with a time of 1:31.81, winning the league title in a field of 15 teams. Individually at the WACC Championship, Costello won 50 free in 21.26 in a field of 51 swimmers and the 100 free in 46.44 in a field of 46. He was a member of the winning 400 free team alongside Takazawa, Cole Carnazzo, and Secor with a time of 3:09.02 against 16 other schools. What is your workout program this summer? This summer, I’m doing three strength-training sessions each week along with eight swim practices. Each swim practice is about 5,000 yards, so most of my time is spent building endurance, speed, and technique. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goals are to continue improving in the pool and become stronger in the weight room. I’m focused on making steady progress in both areas before my freshman season of college. How are you measuring your development? I measure my swimming progress through my race times at meets. In the gym, I track my improvement by increasing the weight I lift or the number of reps I can complete each week. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I train with my teammates in the weight room, which helps keep everyone motivated. In the pool, I practice with my club team under the guidance of my swim coach. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone was dropping more than two seconds in the 100 breaststroke about a month ago. I’ve put a lot of work into improving that stroke, so it was rewarding to see that progress in a race. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Focus on improving a little every day instead of expecting instant results. Progress isn’t always obvious, but consistently showing up and putting in quality work over time makes a big difference. Louisa Symkowick, PHS Class of 2025, is set to enter her sophomore season on Carleton College’s soccer team. She was a sophomore on Piedmont High’s 2023 D4 North Coast Section title team. Carleton College went 18-3-3 last season to win the Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference title with a 1-nil win over St. Catherine University on November 8. The Knights proved to be one of the best Division 3 schools in the country, reaching the Elite 8 before falling 2-1 to No. 7 University of Chicago on November 23. To get there, No. 16 seeded Carleton beat John Carroll University 1-0 in the first round on November 15, beat Lake Forest College 2-nil the next day, and upset No. 13 Swarthmore College in penalty kicks 4-2 on November 22. Symkowick appeared in 19 matches as a freshman for 475 total minutes. She scored once, recording six shots with three on target in the process. What is your workout program this summer? I was injured in practice last spring so I am focusing on my physical therapy this summer. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals this summer are to be recovered from my injury and ready to train in the preseason this August. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my development with small goals and trying not to rush things to allow my body to fully heal. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working with my physical therapist to be sure my form and reps are appropriately challenging. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished is getting playing time on a collegiate team that made it to the Elite Eight in the NCAA tournament. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? To younger, aspiring athletes I would say not to let injuries discourage you. They are just one moment in a larger sports journey. articles.text: In this week of Hiking with Jon, we delve into our fifth of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe with one of the most unique trails in Northern California. The Five Lakes Trail is a batch of alpine lakes in the Granite Chief Wilderness, just north of Lake Tahoe in Olympic Valley. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.8 mile hike in total and provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain. It’s a good location to get accustomed with hiking in high elevation. Our day starts at 6,450 feet of altitude, topping out at near 7,600 feet. It also connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Washeshu mountain peaks. To the left will be views of the pine-treed strewed mountains of Scott Peak and the mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak. But given the location is surrounded by resorts and the tourist towns of Truckee, Tahoe City, Kings Beach and other North Lake Tahoe destinations, this hike can be a traffic jam. I passed 105 other hikers in the trek toward the summit and another 51 on the way back toward the car—bringing an average of 31.5 people per mile. This means patience while passing others is of utmost importance. Long portions of the hike are less than six-feet wide, which makes stepping aside for groups a certainty. I passed at least three groups with more than 10-people and many families with children miserably making their way up the mountainside. Faster hikers may find themselves behind slower traffic without a clear pathway around. But at the summit, a group of five alpine lakes await. Despite the foot traffic, one can easily find isolated areas on one of the three swimmable lakes. Finding all three could be tricky for some. The largest lake lays right off the main trail; hugging its eastern shore leads to another interconnecting swimmable lake. Look for this sign off of Alpine Meadows Road to start the hike.

articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Garden will launch a new outdoor summer concert series, Sunset Sessions, on Thursday, August 6. The series will feature free live music on the garden plaza along with extended evening nursery hours. Food and beverages, including craft beer from Headlands Brewing, will be available for purchase. Admission to the plaza and concerts is free while paid admission is required to access the garden. Garden members receive free admission year-round. The opening performance on August 6 will feature bicoastal singer-songwriter Avery Chapman. Chapman’s music combines folk influences with pop songwriting, featuring personal lyrics and storytelling. She has released four albums, including her latest album, The Mainland, and studied music education and contemporary songwriting at the Frost School of Music at the University of Miami. In addition to her work as a musician, Chapman is also a music educator. Located in Walnut Creek, the Ruth Bancroft Garden is one of the nation’s best-known dry gardens and was the first garden preserved by the Garden Conservancy. Founded by horticulturist Ruth Bancroft, the 3.5-acre botanical garden features more than 2,000 species of drought-tolerant plants from California and arid regions around the world, including agaves, aloes, cacti, succulents, yuccas and proteas. The garden’s collection highlights plants adapted to dry climates and has helped showcase water-wise gardening practices in California’s Mediterranean climate. The nonprofit garden continues to serve as a resource for visitors interested in drought-tolerant landscaping and conservation. All concerts will be held Thursdays from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/sunset-sessions-concert-series-page/.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft Garden launches summer concert series Aug. 6

articles.text: Performances scheduled July 25 and 28 A concert will be held at the San Francisco Public Library’s Glen Park Branch this Saturday. Musicians from the San Francisco Symphony will perform a series of free small-ensemble concerts at libraries and community spaces across San Francisco this summer. The performances give audiences an opportunity to hear Symphony musicians in smaller, more intimate settings. Previous concerts have been held at the San Francisco Public Library’s Portola and Sunset branch libraries, as well as the Mission Cultural Center for Latino Arts. The San Francisco Symphony covers the full cost of the performances, allowing partner organizations to offer the concerts free of charge. The series is presented in honor of donor Frederic Smith, whose estate gift supports the Symphony’s community programming. The next concert will be held from 3 to 4 p.m. Saturday, July 25, at the San Francisco Public Library’s Glen Park Branch, 2825 Diamond St. Another performance is scheduled from 1 to 2 p.m. Tuesday, July 28, at the library’s Main Branch, 100 Larkin St. For more information about upcoming performances, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Community-Volunteer/Community-Chamber.
articles.title: SF Symphony brings free chamber concerts to city libraries

The festival also includes “American Apollo,” conducted by Kedrick Armstrong and directed by Nataki Garrett. The contemporary opera centers on Thomas Eugene McKeller, the Black model whose likeness inspired works by artist John Singer Sargent, and examines questions of history, identity and recognition. The cast features Markel Reed, John Bellemer, Marnie Breckenridge, Alexandra Armantrading and others. “Our 2026 festival celebrates the daring, diversity, and emotional depth that define West Edge Opera,” West Edge Opera Artistic Director Mark Streshinsky said in a press release. “From Britten’s eerie psychological drama to Handel’s heroic spectacle and Damien Geter’s contemporary voice, these works reflect our belief in the power of opera to speak through ages.” The festival runs August 1 through 16 at the Oakland Scottish Rite Center, 1547 Lakeside Drive in Oakland. Single day tickets are available for purchase online at https://www.westedgeopera.org/. West Edge Opera will return to Oakland this summer with its 2026 Summer Festival, presenting three operas at the Oakland Scottish Rite Center from August 1 through 16. Founded in 1979 as Berkeley Opera, West Edge Opera is an East Bay opera company that presents an annual summer festival in Oakland and produces both contemporary works and lesser-known operas alongside traditional repertoire. The company adopted its current name in 2014 and has staged performances at venues including the 16th Street Station, Bridge Yard and the Oakland Scottish Rite Center, where its summer festival is now held. The festival opens Saturday, August 1, and features Benjamin Britten’s “The Turn of the Screw,” George Frideric Handel’s “Rinaldo” and “American Apollo” by Damien Geter and Lila Palmer. The three productions explore themes of identity, resilience and self-discovery across different eras. “The Turn of the Screw,” conducted by Jonathan Khuner and directed by Mark Streshinsky, follows a governess caring for two children at a remote English estate as she confronts mysterious and unsettling forces. The cast includes Laura Bohn, Alex Boyer, Erin Neff and Alexa Sessler. Handel’s “Rinaldo,” conducted by Emily Senturia and directed by Keturah Stickann, tells the story of a hero navigating temptation and adversity. The production stars Kyle Tingzon, All operas take place at the Oakland Scottish Rite Center.
articles.title: West Edge Opera 2026 Summer Festival begins August 1 in Oakland

By Allyson Aleksey Musicians from the San Francisco Symphony will perform a series of free small-ensemble concerts at libraries and community spaces across San Francisco this summer. The performances give audiences an opportunity to hear Symphony musicians in smaller, more intimate settings. Previous concerts have been held at the San Francisco Public Library’s Portola and Sunset branch libraries, as well as the Mission Cultural Center for Latino Arts. The San Francisco Symphony covers the full cost of the performances, allowing partner organizations to offer the concerts free of charge. The series is presented in honor of donor Frederic Smith, whose estate gift supports the Symphony’s community programming. The next concert will be held from 3 to 4 p.m. Saturday, July 25, at the San Francisco Public Library’s Glen Park Branch, 2825 Diamond St. Another performance is scheduled from 1 to 2 p.m. Tuesday, July 28, at the library’s Main Branch, 100 Larkin St. For more information about upcoming performances, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Community-Volunteer/Community-Chamber. West Edge Opera 2026 Summer Festival begins August 1 in Oakland Shawnette Sulker, Nikki Einfeld, Sara Couden, Efraín Solis and Gabi Esquenazi. The festival also includes “American Apollo,” conducted by Kedrick Armstrong and directed by Nataki Garrett. The contemporary opera centers on Thomas Eugene McKeller, the Black model whose likeness inspired works by artist John Singer Sargent, and examines questions of history, identity and recognition. Single day tickets are available for purchase online at https://www.westedgeopera.org/. By Allyson Aleksey West Edge Opera will return to Oakland this summer with its 2026 Summer Festival, presenting three operas at the Oakland Scottish Rite Center from August 1 through 16. Founded in 1979 as Berkeley Opera, West Edge Opera is an East Bay opera company that presents an annual summer festival in Oakland and produces both contemporary works and lesser-known operas alongside traditional repertoire. The company adopted its current name in 2014 and has staged performances at venues including the 16th Street Station, Bridge Yard and the Oakland Scottish Rite Center, where its summer festival is now held. The festival opens Saturday, August 1, and features Benjamin Britten’s “The Turn of the Screw,” George Frideric Handel’s “Rinaldo” and “American Apollo” by Damien Geter and Lila Palmer. articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts will host an intimate evening of swinging jazz and acoustic folk music with San Diego’s acoustic duo, Nathan & Jessie, scheduled for Thursday, August 13, at 7:00 p.m.. This exclusive performance will offer Northern California audiences a rare sneak preview of the group’s highly anticipated upcoming studio album, “I’m at Home.” The San Diego-based duo Nathan & Jessie. Nathan & Jessie have cultivated a signature sound that seamlessly blends early jazz, folk traditions, and classic Americana swing. Driven by intricate fingerstyle guitar, soaring accordion melodies, and striking vocal harmonies, the duo delivers a performance style that is both nostalgic and thoroughly modern. Their upcoming album, “I’m at Home,” marks the next chapter in their catalog, expanding on their traditional roots with fresh original compositions and storytelling that captures the imagination. The concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts provides a perfect acoustic setting for this preview. Nathan & Jessie are a touring musical duo based in San Diego. Combining jazz, blues, folk, and Americana influences, they have spent years touring internationally, captivating audiences from street corners to grand concert halls. Their unique instrumentation and upbeat, joyful performances have established them as a prominent voice in the contemporary acoustic music circuit. Tickets are available online at https://www.ticketsignup.io/ NandJessie. Doors open at 6:30 p.m. and the event begins at 7 p.m.
articles.title: Folk duo Nathan & Jessie to perform at Center for the Arts

articles.text: Shotgun Players presents Iphigenia in Splott, a one-person play by Gary Owen adapted from Iphigenia in Aulis by Euripides, showing onstage now through August 23. Directed by Michelle Talgarow, preview performances begin July 25, with opening night August 1. The production marks the company’s first one-person performance and follows Effie, a modern-day version of Iphigenia who lives in the working-class town of Splott in Wales. Effie stumbles through life before facing a choice between selfless sacrifice and the welfare of her community. The production explores the socioeconomic conditions of the working class through Effie’s experience of systemic failure, Talgarow said. “Don’t let the title fool you, this isn’t just a retelling of the ancient Greek myth,” she added. Alicia Mason stars as Effie in Shotgun Players’ Iphigenia in Splott. “It is a sharp, modern thrill ride set in working-class Wales. It’s just one actor on stage for 75 minutes, and she will absolutely blow you away with her energy, wit, wry humor, and a story that feels incredibly urgent right now.” Alicia Mason stars as Effie. Talgarow returns to Shotgun Players after directing the company’s 2024 production of Thirty-Six. The production follows the release of Effi o Blaenau, a Welsh-language film adaptation that premiered at the Glasgow Film Festival in March and received a general U.K. theatrical release in June. Tickets are available for purchase at www.shotgunplayers. org/show/iphegenia/ or by calling the box office at 510-841-6500.

articles.text: There are many reasons why we go to concerts. If you attended the final concert of the Golden Gate International Choral Festival you’d know why. Simply stated, music brings international diversity together. You want proof … here it is. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival happens every three years and is organized by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. The festival is wonderful in every way. Choral groups from numerous countries converged in the East Bay and made beautiful music individually and together. It was a veritable United Nations, with choruses from Poland, Georgia, Catalonia, Finland, Estonia, Lithuania, Austria, the Czech Republic and the United States among many other countries. They sang their hearts out while wearing their national costumes and dancing to inspired choreography. They wore beautiful national costumes and exhibited many aspects of their cultures. This speaks to the individuality of each nation. At the end, all 400 singers joined forces for an exciting musical conclusion. Along the way the concert went from one high point to another, encompassing traditional folk music as well as complicated modern music. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Artistic Director Eric Tuan was present in a variety of roles. He is also a first class composer, as well as an inspiring conductor. Speaking of conductors, Kedrick Armstrong, the conductor of the Oakland Symphony, was clothing. They sang beautifully and the audience was enthusiastic.

If you attended the final concert of the Golden Gate International Choral Festival you’d know why. Simply stated, music brings international diversity together. You want proof … here it is. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival happens every three years and is organized by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. The festival is wonderful in every way. Choral groups from numerous countries converged in the East Bay and made beautiful music individually and together. It was a veritable United Nations, with choruses from Poland, Georgia, Catalonia, Finland, Estonia, Lithuania, Austria, the Czech Republic and the United States among many other countries. They sang their hearts out while wearing their national costumes and dancing to inspired choreography. They wore beautiful national costumes and exhibited many aspects of their cultures. This speaks to the individuality of each nation. At the end, all 400 singers joined forces for an exciting musical conclusion. Along the way the concert went from one high point to another, encompassing traditional folk music as well as complicated modern music. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Artistic Director Eric Tuan was present in a variety of roles. He is also a first class composer, as well as an inspiring conductor. Speaking of conductors, Kedrick Armstrong, the conductor of the Oakland Symphony, was Ellerhein Girls’ Choir won the Youth Historical Music Competition and the Youth Folk Music Competition. there and I had the opportunity to speak with him. His personality is a delight and he exudes the kind of encouragement which is conveyed to the musicians of his orchestra. Other noteworthy supporters of the arts were present. The festival has superlative organization. That’s the reason it’s so successful. Audience members were packed into the main auditorium at the Mormon Temple in Oakland. articles.text: Cary Elwes, Morgan Freeman, Denzel Washington, Andre Braugher, and Jihmi Kennedy in Glory Glory, adapted from the book titled Gallant Rush by Peter Burchard, is an award-winning film (nominated for five Oscars) and starring Matthew Broderick as Col. Robert Gould Shaw, Denzel Washington portraying Pvt. Trip, and Morgan Freeman in the role of Master Sgt. John Rawlins. The core of the narrative resides with the 54th Massachusetts All-volunteer Infantry, which was comprised of a regiment of Black soldiers, who attributed their freedom to join the Union Army because of Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation. Despite taking what can be referred to as literary license with the lack of gear, shoes and rifles, the story is accurate and familiar: the Black volunteers are paid less than the whites, and they were initially relegated to performing common labor instead of fighting the lethal battles against the “Rebs.” That changed when Col. Shaw stepped forward on July 18, 1863, and volunteered the 54th to take the lead on the well-armed Confederate Ft. Wagner, at the mouth of Charleston Bay. The casualties were devastating. But the bravery of the 54th opened the way for those Black soldiers that followed. Glory. Directed by Edward Zwick. Starring Matthew Broderick, Denzel Washington, Morgan Freeman, André Braugher. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated R/PG. Released in 1989.

Advance tickets are especially important for this show, available at https://www.ticketsignup.io/CarlDanny. articles.text: Guillermo del Toro’s reimagined Oscar-winning Pinocchio is based on the classic Carlo Collodi’s children’s book, written in 1883. But parents should know that this stop-motion version, while immensely creative, is not your grandfather’s Pinocchio. Disney or Pixar it’s not. The reframed story opens by introducing the audience to Geppetto (David Bradley), an elderly Italian woodcarver, and his much-adored young son Carlo. The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course with Carlo is at his side helping, his favorite pinecone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pinecone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one of the bombers has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned, knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding the boy in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pinecone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Duce, has now become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s gravesite and with an ax chops down the pine tree that his grown by Carlo’s tombstone. In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But there does appear in the early dawn, while Geppetto sleeps, a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him and the villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by del Toro and Mark Gustafsen. Stop-motion animation. Voiced by Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradle. 1 hr., 57 min. PG-13 (older kids, tweens). Released in 2022, Now streaming on multiple platforms. A scene from Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio

In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But there does appear in the early dawn, while Geppetto sleeps, a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him and the villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by del Toro and Mark Gustafsen. Stop-motion animation. Voiced by Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradle. 1 hr., 57 min. articles.text: On a warm July morning, 45 local walkers and three energetic K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra in Piedmont Park for the Recreation Department’s popular “Walking on Wednesdays” outing. Led by resident and landscape architect June Yee, the morning route promised an energetic climb, an insider’s look at local architectural history, and a hands-on lesson in neighborhood wildfire resilience. Setting off from the park center, the group made its way up Highland, Sierra, and Sheridan avenues. Navigating the scenic, winding residential turns of Richardson Way, Lakeview Avenue, and Poplar Way, the walkers emerged onto Mountain Avenue before beginning their steady ascent up Bellevue Avenue. While Bellevue is widely celebrated as one of Piedmont’s signature streets—known for its grand historic estates spanning Mediterranean, Tudor, Colonial Revival, and Georgian Revival styles—Yee paused the group at 33 Bellevue to highlight a striking modern departure. Built in 1937 for publication executive Milo Gates and his wife Virginia, the residence was designed by legendary UC Berkeley architect William Wurster. A true pioneer of Bay Area regionalism, Wurster famously rejected heavy European ornamentation in favor of clean lines, down her long driveway to enjoy a sweeping, side-yard view of the San Francisco skyline. Resuming their route, the walkers tackled the steep climb up Pacific Avenue, making brief turns onto Hagar and Mountain avenues to reach the Bell Avenue home of fellow walkers Peggy and Dana Shultz. The Shultzs’ property recently earned the Piedmont Fire Department’s Wildfire Resilience Award, drawing the attention of city staff members Echa Schneider and TV Station Manager Jeff Shaw, who were on hand to capture the visit for local communications. Dana Shultz walked the group through the deliberate steps he took to create a defensible space around his home following major seismic retrofits. Acting on advice from the fire department regarding regional east-to-west wind patterns, Shultz paid special attention to the home’s eastern elevation. He systematically cleared dense vegetation within five feet of the foundation, pruned tree branches to eliminate “fire ladders” that allow ground flames to reach the canopy, and applied fire retardant to the wooden entry gate. “Less is more,” Shultz explained, pointing out how simple choices—like the home’s stucco exterior—substantially lower wildfire risk without sacrificing classic Piedmont curb appeal. Following the informative discussion, Peggy and Dana welWilliam Wurster unadorned materials, and functional layouts that prioritized informal indoor-outdoor living. Wurster frequently collaborated with renowned landscape architect Thomas Church, designing homes with expansive windows and central courtyards that seamlessly brought nature inside. Current homeowner Sara Cumbelich greeted the group out front, sharing warm observations about what it has been like for her family to live in and care for the historic residence—only the second family to occupy it since its construction nearly nine decades ago—before joining the group for a quick photo. Continuing further up Bellevue, the excursion featured an unexpected local bonus. Nearby resident Alicia Kalamas stepped out to welcome the group and graciously invited everyone Participants: June Yee (Leader), Tom Yee, Melba Yee, Peggy Shultz, Dana Shultz, Jack Fichrup (with K-9 Kojak), Joan Jung (with K-9 JT), Sean Brient (with K-9 Pip), Deborah Curtin (with K-9 Brie), Mary Ann Barnes, Rick Eigenbrode, Lois Price, Matt Gerhardt, Alicia Rivera, Albert Chen, Jim Kellogg, Audrey Sung, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis, Phil Witte, Claire Anderson, Ken Hubbert, Judy Sokoloff, Cathy Laymon, Judy Love, Lori Austin, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Liz Dalrymple, Brian Hamlin, Stella Houston, Mary Carter, Sherry Jacobs, Marianne Jakas, Quincy Dong, Alan Jolly, Dan Scdonis, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Sanghi Wagner, Dick Carter, Jean Sokolow, and Pat Keller (with guest Morika Keller).

articles.text: With the exception of Burgundy, to my mind there is no finer place in the world to grow Pinot Noir and Chardonnay than California’s Russian River Valley. Nestled in the heart of Sonoma County’s Russian River Valley, Lynmar Estate has earned a reputation as one of California’s premier producers of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay while offering visitors an experience that celebrates both exceptional wine and sustainable farming. Founded in 1980 by Lynn and Margrit Fritz, the estate began with a vision of cultivating world-class Pinot Noir in the cool-climate vineyards surrounding Sebastopol. Today, Lynmar farms more than 100 acres of estate vineyards, with many vines planted on the rolling hills and Goldridge soils that have become synonymous with elegant Russian River Valley wines. Winemaker Pete Soergel has helped shape Lynmar’s distinctive style, crafting wines that emphasize balance, vibrant fruit, and a strong sense of place. The estate’s Pinot Noirs are known for layers of cherry, raspberry, and spice, supported by silky tannins and bright acidity. Its Chardonnays combine rich orchard fruit with crisp minerality and restrained oak, reflecting the cool coastal influence that defines the region. Visitors quickly discover that Lynmar offers more than a traditional tasting room. The winery’s beautifully landscaped culinary gardens supply herbs, vegetables, and edible flowers that complement thoughtfully prepared food-and-wine pairings. Seasonal tasting experiences allow guests to see firsthand how fresh ingredients can elevate both the wines and the dining experience. Sustainability remains central to Lynmar’s philosophy. The estate follows environmentally responsible farming practices designed to protect soil health, conserve water, and encourage biodiversity throughout the vineyards and gardens. These efforts have made Lynmar a model for balancing premium wine production with stewardship of the land. As Russian River Valley continues to gain worldwide recognition for cool-climate wines, Lynmar Estate stands as one of its signature producers. Combining meticulous vineyard management, skilled winemaking, and gracious hospitality, the winery offers visitors an authentic taste of Sonoma County while demonstrating why the region remains one of the world’s finest homes for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. 3909 Frei Road, Sebastopol, CA 95472 707 829 3374 lynmarestate.com The inviting Lynmar Estate Winery Lynmar Estate offers a variety of tasting experiences

articles.text: • 2021 Lynmar Estate Pinot Noir Quail Hill Vineyard A blend of 14 different Pinot Noir clones, the Quail Hill is quintessential Russian River Pinot. It gives up scents of raspberries, currants, tar, thyme and charcuterie with accents of lavender and black pepper. Medium-bodied, the palate has intense layers of dark, earthy fruits with a firm, finely grained frame and juicy freshness, finishing long and layered. • 2023 Lynmar Estate Pinot Noir Anista’s Blend Pale to medium ruby, it gives up bright aromas of cranberries, strawberries and earth with hints of underbrush and leather. The palate is light to medium-bodied and delicate with earth-laced fruits a sturdy frame and great freshness, finishing soft and supple. • 2022 Lynmar Estate Pinot Noir Monastery Burgundian in style, the Monastery bottling is in honor of the monks of Burgundy who first put the Pinot Noir grape on the map. It is scented of cranberries, dried flowers, dust, tobacco, herbs with hints of mushrooms. The palate is medium bodied and intense with very pretty layers, a gently grainy frame and a long, juicy, nuanced finish. My favorite.

articles.text: On Monday, July 6, the First Mondays Reading Group had a strong turnout of 26 participants at the Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly discussion. They were there to talk about their July book, Old Filth by Jane Gardam, published in 2004, a historical fiction and the first in a trilogy. It was selected as a “Best Book of the Year” by The New York Times Book Review and The Washington Post and shortlisted for the 2005 Women’s Prize for Fiction. In 2015, a BBC survey of literary critics from outside the United Kingdom ranked Old Filth among the 100 greatest British novels. It is the life story of Sir Edward Feathers, an eightyyear-old retired widower living a comfortable, quiet life in Dorset, England. The novel blends aspects of tragedy and comedy as Feathers reflects on his life from his early years in the British Raj to his legal career. He is struggling to come to terms with his wife’s recent death and trying to make sense of the past. Feathers is born in Malaya to a British colonial administrator father who drinks too much and a mother who dies just days after his birth. He grows up among the natives speaking their language and is quite content with his life, even though he is all but ignored by his father. Before his fifth birthday, Feathers is sent back to England to begin his proper education and to keep him safe from tropical fevers. He ends up in Wales in the care of foster parents and has practically no contact with his father. The “Filth” in “Old Filth” stands for “Failed in London, Try Hong Kong”, which is what Feathers did in his poor days just after World War II when he was new to the bar. Despite a long and distinguished career as a lawyer and judge, Filth feels dirty because of his childhood secret that he carries with him throughout his life. The readers generally liked the book, or found something to like about it, in a range of “loved it” to “really didn’t care for it that much.” Everyone agreed that Gardam is an excellent writer and that the book was well written. It is rich in language and economical in its communication. It’s a fast, but not necessarily an easy, read because Feathers and the novel are complex. Readers felt the story captured the times and places well. They enjoyed the descriptions of Malaya – which is now Malaysia and also British life at the time. This novel is an example of a genre of English storytelling of this period. Think Masterpiece Theatre. The decline of the British Empire is part of the story too. The history of the “Raj orphans,” children born to British expatriates living in British Empire colonies who were sent back to England for schooling, was new for some readers. They felt this experience affected Feathers throughout his life and others too, but it was an unfortunate, common part of life for a class of British people. Feathers’ long story from childhood to old age resonated with some readers. They could relate to his reflections and his dealings with his morality and thus with him as a character. Readers also liked how Feathers’ longtime adversary in his earlier work and personal life became his closest friend in his later years. It was a separate story of redemption and hope in a generally sad life. While a majority of the readers liked the book, there were others who “liked parts of the book but really didn’t care for it.” The story had a slow start and was “hard to get into.” It also moves around in time, with Filth looking back on a full life yet feeling an emptiness all the same. Some readers thought this bouncing around was skillfully done by the author, but, with so many characters in the book, it made the story hard to follow. However, a more significant issue for those readers on the negative side was that, while they The First Monday Reading Group read Jane Gardam’s Old Filth, the first of a trilogy. admired the author’s excellent writing, they didn’t care for the character of Old Filth. He was a shallow person and never seemed to understand his wife or remember his long-standing housekeeper’s name. His loneliness and isolation were not surprising considering his shaky emotional childhood, but they did not make him likeable. Why would you want to read the life story of a person you don’t care about? As Old Filth drew closer to the end, a childhood secret was revealed that makes Feathers more understandable. It also made some readers want to read the book again to see what they might have missed. The group had previously selected The Art Thief by Michael Finkel for August and Horse by Geraldine Brooks for September. After Laura Goldman presented three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected Freezing Order: A True Story of Money Laundering, Murder, and Surviving Putin’s Wrath by Bill Browder for October. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on August 3 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. Participating members were Dick Carter, Susan Southworth, Bob Hall, Marj Blackwell, Mike Henn, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, Adrienne Hamlin, Rob White, Peggy Shultz, Judy Love, Nancy Henn, Bill Ahern, Melba Yee, Orrel Lanter, Laura Goldman, Phil Witte, Heidi Schmidt, Ken Young, Susie Backer, Lois Price, Rich Seigel, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Lisa Euphrat, and Albert Chen. The group was pleased to welcome Claudia Cate, who was with them for the first time. Lois Price led the conversation for discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, who was away.

articles.text: Chicken curry stir-fry is an easy, casual dinner for summer nights. This quick stir-fry is inspired by a recent dinner with friends. I prepared a veggie-only side dish of stir-fried zucchini and cherry tomatoes for our alfresco gathering. It made an easy switch to a weeknight dinner by adding chicken for an all-in-one skillet meal. The “weeknight” in the recipe title translates to fast and easy. Using a prepared curry powder blend provides most of the flavors and marinating the chicken pieces beforehand is purely optional. I keep a few varieties of curry powder blends on hand; each has a distinct flavor profile. There are common ingredients – cumin, coriander, turmeric – but each blend brings a nuance from part of the world that inspired the blend. Stir fry dishes are easily adapted with substitutions. Any combination of meat and vegetables will work. For best results, remember the idea is to slice the meat and vegetables so they will be of similar size for even cooking. Weeknight Chicken Curry Stir-Fry INGREDIENTS • 1½ pounds boneless chicken, sliced into 1-inch pieces • 1 pound tender zucchini, about 5 - 6 young squash, sliced into 1-inch pieces • 15 cherry tomatoes • 1/2 white onion, diced in ½″ - ¾″ pieces • 2 - 3 teaspoons curry powder • Salt and cayenne pepper, to taste • 2 - 3 teaspoons ghee or vegetable oil that will withstand high heat, divided • Cilantro or green onions to garnish GOOD THROUGH AUGUST 2026 GOOD THROUGH AUGUST 2026

articles.text: give. Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony. And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; teach and admonish one another in all wisdom; and with gratitude in your hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.” (Colossians 3:12-17, NRSVUE) According to the writer of long ago, in the church, those to whom the life of the community is entrusted are to supplant the coerciveness of the empire with the care known best in households. In our time, we are entrusted not only with the care of our church, but the care of our nation. These are high and demanding callings in which we do well to keep the tender words of Colossians before us for, when we “clothe ourselves with love,” our congregations have a chance to against the Compass playbook being run on your neighborhood. And those boards are only as good as the people on them — people without a corporate agenda, who don’t benefit from double-ending deals, and whose only job is to serve the market. That’s what we’re there to do. What this means if you’re buying or selling in the East Bay A few practical things to know right now: If you’re a seller: Ask your agent directly — will this listing be on the open MLS from day one? If they suggest a “private exclusive” period, ask them to show you the math on what full market exposure has historically done for comparable homes. Then ask them who benefits if the deal double-ends within their network. You deserve a straight answer. If you’re a buyer: The fragmentation of listing data is real. In 2026, no single platform shows you everything. A good buyer’s agent has MLS access — not portal access — and can show you inventory before it hits Zillow, Redfin, or anywhere else. That’s a competitive advantage that still exists in a local cooperative MLS. In both cases: The best protection you have is an agent who is legally and ethically obligated to serve your interests — not their brokerage’s volume targets, not their company’s double-end rate, and not a private network’s deal flow.

articles.text: Compass International Holdings — never profitable in 14 years, freshly merged with Coldwell Banker, Century 21, Corcoran, and Sotheby’s, lobbying MLS boards across the country to run a private listing playbook that benefits their double-end deal flow at the expense of seller exposure. On the other side of the local story: The Grubb Company — nearly 60 years independent, locally owned, deeply rooted in Oakland, Piedmont, Berkeley, and Alameda, with no shareholders to answer to and no private network to feed. And those boards are only as good as the people on them — people without a corporate agenda, who don’t benefit from double-ending deals, and whose only job is to serve the market. That’s what we’re there to do. What this means if you’re buying or selling in the East Bay A few practical things to know right now: If you’re a seller: Ask your agent directly — will this listing be on the open MLS from day one? If they suggest a “private exclusive” period, ask them to show you the math on what full market exposure has historically done for comparable homes. Then ask them who benefits if the deal double-ends within their network. You deserve a straight answer. If you’re a buyer: The fragmentation of listing data is real. In 2026, no single platform shows you everything. A good buyer’s agent has MLS access — not portal access — and can show you inventory before it hits Zillow, Redfin, or anywhere else. That’s a competitive advantage that still exists in a local cooperative MLS. The Three Lions jumped out to a 2-nil lead with a pair of goals in quick succession by Jude Bellingham, but adversity hit when England went down a man. England sat deep after going to 10 players, and parked the bus even more after Raúl Jiménez put Mexico within a goal in the 69th minute. Although El Tri dominated possession in the second half with 72% of the ball, the Three Lions continuously sent away Mexico empty handed. In the end, it marked El Tri’s first loss at the Azteca since 2013 and only its third defeat in 89 appearances at the legendary stadium. Argentina’s comeback over England England’s defensive stance came back to bite them against Argentina in the Quarterfinals, losing 2-1 after holding a 1-nil lead with five minutes left in regulation. It was a testament that playing not to lose is a dangerous strategy. The Three Lions took its lead in the 55th minute when Anthony Gordon scored, but after that point, England elected to park the bus for the final 35 minutes of the game. From that point, England held just 12% of possession time, allowing Argentina to build itself back into the game. Enzo Fernandez scored a banger from outside of the box in the 85th, and then Lautaro Martinez put away a header after a perfect cross by Lionel Messi. DRC’s route to the Round of 32 The Democratic Republic of the Congo was another beneficiary of FIFA expanding this year’s tournament to 48 teams, marking their first World Cup appearance since 1974. They made it out of Group K by taking third after miraculously tying world giants Portugal 1-1 and upending Uzbekistan 3-1 on the last day of the group stage. They closed with a spirited performance in its 2-1 loss to England in the Round of 32, holding an initial 1-nil lead in the seventh minute before Harry Kane scored back-to-back goals in the 75th and 86th. Morocco stunning Netherlands Morocco’s penalty kick win over the Netherlands was another legendary moment from the Round of 16, representing the “step child” of sorts overtaking its conceited older brother. Before the tournament, former Netherlands star Rafael van der Vaart sparked controversy by stating: “Moroccan players who aren’t good enough to play for the Netherlands end up playing for Morocco.” The match was another example of one team playing “not to lose.” The Netherlands, famous for its ‘total football’ brand that relies on heavy possession, reverted after taking a 1-nil lead in the 72nd minute. The Dutch sat deep, seemingly playing for penalty kicks, allowing Morocco nearly 80 percent of possession in the second half and nearly 85 percent in extra time. It came back to bite them, as Issa Diop tied the match at 90+1 before the Moroccans won 3-2 in PKs. Norway’s Erling Haaland becomes global star Europeans know Erling Haaland of Manchester City well, but he arose to global superstardom at the World Cup. Haaland captured attention by embracing American culture, leading the Viking row celebration and put on a show with seven goals and leading Norway to the quarterfinals. He scored in the 86th minute to put Norway above Ivory Coast 2-1 in the Round of 32, while he bagged a brace in Norway’s 2-1 win as the underdog against Brazil in the Round of 16. Thanks to his effort, Norway entered the tournament as the world’s No. 31 ranked team and exited 12 spots higher at No. 19. Kylian Mbappé atop history This World Cup was a race between Lionel Messi and Kylian Mbappé to become the tournament’s all-time leading scorer. After scoring twice in France’s high-scoring 6-4 loss to England in the third-place final, Mbappé now sits alone with 22 in three World Cup appearances. Les Bleus fell short of the final after losing 2-nil to Spain in the semifinals, but it is now assured that Mbappé will hold the tournament’s scoring record for an entire generation of players. The redesigned area will feature state-of-the-art materials for enhanced durability and safety, including new safety matting to replace the existing sand, upgraded ADA access and a refined perimeter for the swing area. To build on this momentum, the PBF Spring Campaign is now focused on creating a nature play area adjacent to the swings. This project will transform an underused section of the park into a vibrant outdoor learning environment featuring climbing logs, native plants, and hands-on natural play elements for children to explore. The PBF has worked since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces that foster a strong sense of pride and community. In addition to its many valuable contributions to parks, tot lots, schools, and recreational facilities, PBF also brings the community together to celebrate the Piedmont Lights Up ceremony every December. PBF looks forward to sharing more updates as they work to improve the community’s outdoor spaces.
