articles.text: In her book “This Land Is Your Land: A Road Trip Through U.S. History” Yale historian Beverly Gage tells of the chair George Washington sat in while presiding over the Constitutional Convention at Independence Hall in Philadelphia. On the back of the ornate mahogany chair is a half-round sun, its rays peeking out over the horizon, carved into the wood and painted in gold. According to Gage, “Benjamin Franklin supposedly remarked that he pondered whether the sun was rising or falling on the nation that had been created.” On the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, many of us who inhabit the United States of America are wondering the same thing. Is the sun rising or setting on our republic? In this regard there are narratives and counter narratives. There are stories of brokenness and stories of blessing. There are testimonies of grief and testimonies of grace. There are outpourings of despair and offerings of hope. The seemingly conflicting descriptions and understandings are true. Ours is not an “either/or” history but a “both/and” history. There is ample reason to celebrate. There is ample reason to protest. We, who would be followers of Christ in this conflicted time can find insight and encouragement in the instruction given by the writer of the letter of 1 Peter near the end of the first century CE and the beginning of the second. “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of God’s own possession.” These words were not then, nor are they now, a political manifesto, a reason for arrogance, a call to superiority, or an invitation to believe ourselves exceptional. Instead, they are a statement of faith, an invitation to see ourselves as participants in God’s dream for the created order, to accept ourselves as a diverse throng working to connect heaven and earth, earth and heaven, to understand ourselves to be a living body brought together to celebrate God’s world of magnificent differences and to honor the many ways God is at work to save and to bless. As such, we have stories to tell about ourselves. We have many sins of which to repent. We have blessings for which to give thanks. We have heroes to honor. We have villains to acknowledge. We aspire to goodness even while we seem anchored to brokenness. We have questions to ask of our past, present and future. Who are we? Where have we been? Where are we going? Is the sun rising before us or setting upon us? In the midst of it all we have songs to sing: God Bless America. America the Beautiful. The Star Spangled Banner. This Land Is Your Land. Beverly Gage invites us to pay particular attention to This Land Is Your Land. “Woody Guthrie got it right when he said ‘This land is your land, from California to the New York Island, from the redwood forest to the Gulf Stream waters.’ But he knew that it wasn’t just yours or mine; it’s our land too. Whether we like it or not — this big, cruel and transcendent country of ours — we’re in it together. Let’s make of it what we can.” This land is our land. Together let’s let the songs we sing inspire us to make it a safe haven for mercy, a sanctuary for belonging, a household of welcome in which there is no greater priority than helping those who have been knocked down to get back up. Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland.
articles.title: Celebrating America’s 250th anniversary

articles.text: Editor: When I was growing up, I was the youngest carrier for The Boston Globe. I had several paper routes from elementary school through high school. Having something to do to earn money as a kid is a big deal. It teaches work ethic. It creates independence. Among the many things that make Piedmont such a special community is the Piedmont Post. Each week providing topical perspectives, cultural and sports updates, and a delightfully whimsical police log that reminds us how fortunate we are to live in this little donut hole of Oakland. Also each week, scores of local kids hit the streets Wednesday afternoons to deliver this paper. Sure, parents may help — reminders, umbrellas, rides — but a gig is a gig. It is a new responsibility and a check every two weeks. My kids had the good fortune to have this opportunity. First Lucy, then Maisy (a bit under the table), and finally Will. Today was the first Wednesday in more than 10 years that one of my children wasn’t out delivering the Post. It got me thinking: what a remarkable thing, this local newspaper. It keeps us informed. It brings our community together. And, perhaps without realizing it, it helps raise our kids. Thank you, Gray, and everyone at the Post, for making Piedmont a little better every Wednesday afternoon since 1998. –Robin Richardson 3756 Grand Ave., #203, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall Executive Editor: Misha Edel City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jake Lannon Ed Gilligan Evolette Mak, Intern SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. Each week providing topical perspectives, cultural and sports updates, and a delightfully whimsical police log that reminds us how fortunate we are to live in this little donut hole of Oakland. Also each week, scores of local kids hit the streets Wednesday afternoons to deliver this paper. Sure, parents may help — reminders, umbrellas, rides — but a gig is a gig. It is a new responsibility and a check every two weeks. My kids had the good fortune to have this opportunity. First Lucy, then Maisy (a bit under the table), and finally Will. Today was the first Wednesday in more than 10 years that one of my children wasn’t out delivering the Post. It got me thinking: what a remarkable thing, this local newspaper. It keeps us informed. It brings our community together. And, perhaps without realizing it, it helps raise our kids. Thank you, Gray, and everyone at the Post, for making Piedmont a little better every Wednesday afternoon since 1998. –Robin Richardson Collecting photos for Where in the World For 28 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in faroff places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post. com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. Celebrating America’s 250th anniversary By Pastor Jim Hopkins In her book “This Land Is Your Land: A Road Trip Through U.S. History” Yale historian Beverly Gage tells of the chair George Washington sat in while presiding over the Constitutional Convention at Independence Hall in Philadelphia. On the back of the ornate mahogany chair is a half-round sun, its rays peeking out over the horizon, carved into the wood and painted in gold. According to Gage, “Benjamin Franklin supposedly remarked that he pondered whether the sun was rising or falling on the nation that had been created.” On the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, many of us who inhabit the United States of America are wondering the same thing. Is the sun rising or setting on our republic? In this regard there are narratives and counter narratives. There are stories of brokenness and stories of blessing. There are testimonies of grief and testimonies of grace. There are outpourings of despair and offerings of hope. The seemingly conflicting descriptions and understandings are true. Ours is not an “either/or” history but a “both/and” history. There is ample reason to celebrate. There is ample reason to protest. We, who would be followers of Christ in this conflicted time can find insight and encouragement in the instruction given by the writer of the letter of 1 Peter near the end of the first century CE and the beginning of the second. “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of God’s own possession.” These words were not then, nor are they now, a political manifesto, a reason for arrogance, a call to superiority, or an invitation to believe ourselves exceptional. Instead, they are a statement of faith, an invitation to see ourselves as participants in God’s dream for the created order, to accept ourselves as a diverse throng working to connect heaven and earth, earth and heaven, to understand ourselves to be a living body brought together to celebrate God’s world of magnificent differences and to honor the many ways God is at work to save and to bless. As such, we have stories to tell about ourselves. We have many sins of which to repent. We have blessings for which to give thanks. We have heroes to honor. We have villains to acknowledge. We aspire to goodness even while we seem anchored to brokenness. We have questions to ask of our past, present and future. Who are we? Where have we been? Where are we going? Is the sun rising before us or setting upon us? In the midst of it all we have songs to sing: God Bless America. America the Beautiful. The Star Spangled Banner. This Land Is Your Land. Beverly Gage invites us to pay particular attention to This Land Is Your Land. “Woody Guthrie got it right when he said ‘This land is your land, from California to the New York Island, from the redwood forest to the Gulf Stream waters.’ But he knew that it wasn’t just yours or mine; it’s our land too. Whether we like it or not — this big, cruel and transcendent country of ours — we’re in it together. Let’s make of it what we can.” This land is our land. Together let’s let the songs we sing inspire us to make it a safe haven for mercy, a sanctuary for belonging, a household of welcome in which there is no greater priority than helping those who have been knocked down to get back up. articles.text: Beloved Scavenger Hunt returns to Oakland Families, book lovers, and local shopping enthusiasts are invited to spend July searching for one of the world’s most recognizable characters as Where’s Waldo? Local returns to Oakland’s Rockridge District from July 1–31. Participants of all ages can pick up a free Find Waldo Local Game Card at Pegasus Books (5560 College Ave.), any participating business, or download one online. As they discover miniature Waldos hidden inside participating shops, they’ll collect stamps, stickers, or signatures from each location. Presented by the Rockridge District Association in partnership with Pegasus Books and Market Hall, the free, month-long community scavenger hunt transforms Rockridge’s vibrant College Avenue business district into an interactive adventure featuring 26 locally owned businesses. Those who collect stamps from 20 or more businesses will be entered into prize drawings featuring gift cards, merchandise, and experiences donated by Rockridge businesses, including a $50 Rockridge e-Gift Card redeemable at more than 40 neighborhood merchants. The celebration concludes with a Where’s Waldo Local Party on Thursday, July 31, at 5 p.m. at Pegasus Books (5560 College Avenue). Participants can enjoy refreshments while winners are drawn for books, stickers, gift cards, and fun prizes. Winners do not need to be present to claim their prizes. “Where’s Waldo? Local is a fun way for families to explore the neighborhood together while discovering the incredible variety of independent businesses that make Rockridge such a special destination,” said Jody Colley, Rockridge District Association. “The event encourages residents and visitors alike to shop local, meet business owners, and experience everything the district has to offer.” The participating businesses represent a diverse mix of retailers, restaurants, specialty shops, salons, and community organizations, creating an engaging walking tour through one of Oakland’s premier shopping districts. Along the way, visitors can enjoy local dining, browse unique boutiques, and discover neighborhood favorites they may have never visited before. The Rockridge District is easily accessible via BART, with the Rockridge Station located in the heart of the business district. Participation is free, and Game Cards may be submitted anytime during July or brought to the July 31 celebration for entry into the prize drawings. For a complete list of participating businesses, game information, and event details, visit www.rockridgedistrict.com/wheres-waldo. pages.text: Wednesday, July 8, 2026 3 Daniel Gonzales Continued from page 1 a Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering from San Jose State University and is a registered Civil Engineer with the State of California. Gonzales grew up in the East Bay and was familiar with Piedmont before applying for the Public Works Director position. He found the community very appealing, and it was a serious factor in why he chose to work here. “Piedmont is the type of community that I find to be very appealing,” said Gonzales. “It’s small government, where you actually feel like you’re making a tangible difference, and that’s not always easy to see in larger communities, even mid-sized communities, but this is the type of community where I think they really value the type of work that gets done.” Throughout his time with the City, Gonzales has made major pedestrian safety improvements on Grand and Oakland Avenues, completing safe crossing upgrades at five of the top 10 priority locations identified in the 2021 Safer Streets Plan. Installed Piedmont’s first “green infrastructure” bioswale at Grand and Fairview and made major upgrades to the City’s storm drainage and sanitary sewer systems. Gonzales’s efforts have helped the city change to become more inclusive and accessible for everyone. “I would focus just on the concept of inclusivity. We’re trying to be something for many different groups,” said Gonzales. “I think we’ve really focused on ADA accessibility improvements, and that’s people of all walks of life, whether it’s age-related or whether it’s some other thing. That’s making sure everyone can access and enjoy our public spaces, our parks, our buildings, and really orienting ourselves towards that type of change.” In his time with Public Works, he oversaw the city’s completion of the new community pool and 9-1-1 Dispatch Center. Two projects that received historically significant investment. “It was a difficult project (the community pool). The reason you get into this type of profession is because you really focus on outcomes, and the outcome is that you want to have a wonderful facility that is sustainable and will be used again by a generation of Piedmonters, and that’s ultimately what we have,” said Gonzales. One of his favorite things to do is walk by the pool to see how much use it’s getting, and just see what a success it has ultimately been. Gonzales’s work on the Dispatch Center marked the most significant investment in public safety in Piedmont’s history. The upgraded technological infrastructure has helped first responders receive up-to-date information as fast as possible. “It is probably the most important facility we have in the entire city,” Gonzales continued. “I think taking really appropriate steps to take an outdated space and to upgrade it helps make our police and fire much more efficient and much more responsive to evaluate risk in a much quicker fashion, and to disseminate information to those who need it as quickly as possible. None of those things were possible with the old space.” When asked how he wants the residents to remember his time as Public Works Director, he had this to say. “I’m really proud of the fact that we have checked off many of the locations that were listed as high-priority intersections on our paid Piedmont Safer Streets report. The biggest need was our dispatch center, and we’ve addressed that. Of course, the pool had just passed when I was being hired, and it was obviously a major community priority. Looking to address those items that really were community priorities to implement those changes was really important to me,” said Gonzales. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department has scheduled classes for residents interested in learning the basics of CPR and first aid. Their CPR class is on July 15, and the first aid class is on July 19. The classes will be held at the Veterans’ Memorial Building. Piedmont Firefighters will teach all CPR classes. This is not a Red Cross or American Heart Association CPR class; this is an American Safety and Health Institute CPR certificate. “First aid training empowers people to better care for their families, neighbors, and the community by providing skills to help stabilize injuries and give confidence to help before professional responders arrive. I encourage all community members to learn this essential skill,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The class is $20 per participant. Advance registration is required. Register online on Community Pass: https://bit. ly/4gngGPX. Participants must be at least 14 years old to register— maximum class size: 16 students. Firefighter-EMT Nadder Shehadeh teaches two residents the basics of CPR.

articles.text: Residents interested in running for Piedmont City Council or School Board can pick up nomination documents with the City Clerk by appointment starting Monday, July 13. On November 3, Piedmont voters will elect candidates to fill two seats on the City Council and three on Board of Education. Councilmembers Jennifer Long and Tom Ramsey and Board of Education members Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson are eligible to run for a second term, while Mayor Betsy Andersen is termed out. The nomination process can be complicated and filing deadlines are strict, so interested residents should get started as soon as possible. If you’re interested in running: 1. Make an appointment to get your candidate documents: Contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040 or CityClerk@piedmont.ca.gov to schedule your appointment. At your appointment, the City Clerk will walk you through the nomination process, reviewing documents, deadlines, and rules. Plan to spend 30-60 minutes. 2. Review the basics of the process online: Prepare for your appointment by reviewing information about running for office on the City website. This will give you an idea of what to expect and an opportunity to identify questions you want to ask during your appointment. 3. File your nomination documents by August 7. Nomination documents must be filed in person at the City Clerk’s office. It’s a good idea to file documents early so you have time to correct any issues. A list of people who have pulled or filed nomination papers will be available at piedmont. ca.gov/vote2026. City Council and Board of Education are volunteer positions. To find more information about the November 2026 election or running for office, visit piedmont.ca.gov/elections.
articles.title: Candidate nomination period for November election opens July 13

articles.text: Prune trees, remove dead vegetation, and clear flammable materials As grazing goats arrive in Moraga Canyon to clear dead grasses on the hillside, it’s time to start preparing your own yard for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around your property. The gold standard for wildfire protection is to remove all vegetation within 5 feet of your home. However, even if this is not feasible on your property in the short term, you can do your part and increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire by taking a few simple protective measures in your yard. Make time over the next few weeks to prepare your property: • Create space between plants and your home: Remove branches that hang over your roof or are within 10 feet of your chimney. Prune plants away from buildings. Separate tree canopies by at least 10 feet. • Create space between plants: Trim trees so the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or three times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. This helps prevent fire from moving from the ground to the treetops, where it can spread more quickly. • Clear debris and flammable materials: Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your yard. Clear leaves and pine needles from roofs, gutters, and the ground. If you have eucalyptus trees in your yard, remove any shedding bark or leaves. Remove flamGoats eating grass at the Corporation Yard. mable materials, such as paint or propane containers, from under decks and away from buildings. Download a checklist for preparing your yard at piedmont. ca.gov/YardChecklist. If you need help identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Fire Department at (510) 420- 3030 to request an inspection. Using grazing goats to clear dry grasses is only one part of the vegetation management work Piedmont Public Works engages in year-round to mitigate wildfire risk. The goats followed a large fuel-load reduction project above the Corporation Yard in 2024 and 2025, which cleared out trees and removed low-lying vegetation on the steep hillside. Throughout the year, maintenance staff monitor and remove dead and dying vegetation in parks and public spaces. Annual street tree trimming prunes branches away from residents’ roofs. The Fire Department commits to staff training and conducts public outreach around disaster preparedness year-round. Last summer, the Department held a community wildfire evacuation exercise, giving staff across multiple departments and residents a hands-on opportunity to rehearse their role in wildfire response. The City is now updating its emergency operations training program based on what it learned during that experience. The City recently updated its local hazard mitigation plan (LHMP), which identifies longterm strategies to reduce damage to our community from natural disasters like wildfires, earthquakes, and floods. The adopted LHMP is now available at piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP. Find more information and links to additional resources on preparing your property for fire season at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. With questions, contact the Fire Department at (510) 420- 3030.
articles.title: Time to prepare your yard for fire season

articles.text: Jessica McDevitt Handsome Husky mix Palomino is looking for an adopter or foster. This medium-sized pup weighs 42 pounds and has gorgeous ice-blue eyes and a beautiful cream and gray coat. Palomino enjoys companionship, but is also happy to independently explore. This three-year-old absolutely loves running and can be found happily sprinting back and forth across Oakland Animal Services’ yard when he is given time outside. He takes treats politely and appreciates a tasty reward, with cheese his favorite reward. Palomino attends a shelter dog playgroup and gets along with the other canines. He would do well with appropriately matched dogs, or as a solo dog with dog friends outside the home. articles.text: When most people think about play, they picture sports, games, or kids running around outside. But psychiatrist and play researcher Stuart Brown discovered that play looks very different from one person to the next. Through years of research, he identified several “play personalities,” each describing a different way people naturally experience joy and curiosity. Some people are explorers. Some are storytellers. Some are creators. And some are collectors. If you’re a collector, you probably know exactly what that feels like. You save quotes that make you think. You take pictures of interesting signs and you are the one who always remembers odd facts. Maybe you tear articles out of magazines or keep a running list of books you want to read. You definitely have a drawer with 50 interesting colored rocks you have found over the years. You don’t necessarily know why something catches your attention. You just know it does. I don’t think enough of us give ourselves permission to collect things simply because they are interesting. Instead, if we are not by nature collectors, we tend to ask, “Will this be useful?” “Do I need this?” “When will I ever use this?” And these aren’t bad questions but they don’t inspire creativity. One of the things I’ve noticed about highly creative people is that they seem to carry around an ever-growing collection of interesting observations. A phrase they overheard in line at the grocery store or a photograph of peeling paint because they loved the colors underneath. Most of those little discoveries never become anything, but some do. And you don’t know which will be which. Think of your mind like a compost pile (odd analogy, but stick with me). Every interesting idea, image, conversation, question, or experience gets tossed in. Most of it quietly breaks down over time. But then, often when you least expect it, the magic of creativity happens and your brain combines a few of those old scraps into something entirely new. That process is nearly impossible to do if the compost pile is empty. So here is this month’s experiment: Become a collector. For the next week, don’t worry about producing anything. Instead, keep an eye out for things that make you pause and notice. It could be something you observe, like a fun cloud formation or a sentence in a book or a conversation overheard at the farmer’s market. Or it might be something physical, like a beautiful leaf on the ground or a really great color crayon. Write them down, take a picture or put them in a box! Don’t organize it and avoid deciding whether it matters or it’s somehow important. Just collect. You may never use most of what you gather. Then again, that’s exactly what makes collecting so powerful. You never know which tiny, interesting thing will become the beginning of your next big idea. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Creativity experiment: Collecting interesting things

Hello from the camp on Lake Vera! Session 3 has officially begun! We’ve jumped straight into our first two-week session of the summer, and all sorts of shenanigans are afoot. Camp Augusta has about 105 campers, 75% returning for their first 2-week session of the season. Many have been advancing in clinics across categories ranging from ropes to arts, circus, and weapons. articles.text: Two of Piedmont High’s rising seniors represented the school in several prestigious postseason events. Sprinter Claire Aubrecht and distance runner Sebastien Swain both ran at the 2026 Nike Outdoor Nationals on June 18-20 at the University of Oregon’s Hayward Field in Eugene. Swain ran at the Portland Track Festival at Lewis & Clark College on June 20-21 and Aubrecht ran at the USATF Junior Olympics at Monterey Peninsula College on June 25-28. The Nike Outdoor Nationals is a 36-year old event and a premier postseason meet with more than 5,000 athletes from high schools, middle schools, and club teams throughout the U.S. The Portland Track and Field Festival originated in 2008, designed for runners from the older masters level down to youth level. “Claire and Seb are looking to get recruited between now and the end of next season so they’re taking advantage of how in shape they are and seeing if they can make one last impressive mark for the season,” said Piedmont track coach Pouyan Assadi. Aubrecht was recently named the Post’s Female Athlete of the Year after setting the school’s 100-meter, 200-meter, and 4x100 all-time records. Competing in the 100 meter dash the Nike Outdoor Nationals, she finished 34th of 120 in the preliminary race in 12.50 seconds. Then at the Junior Olympics Qualifiers, she reached the finals to finish third of eight in 12.25. She was fourth of 22 sprinters in the prelims in 12.36. Although she qualified for the Junior Olympics National meet, she doesn’t plan on competing. “Claire’s Outdoor Nationals race showed off her top end speed and speed endurance, but she popped up out of the blocks a little early from her drive phase so she didn’t hit the time she had wanted there. She came back to qualify for the National Junior Olympics with a mark of 12.25, which is really impressive. She won’t race at the nationals event just because it’s been such a long season and it’s time to rest up and prepare for 2027,” Assadi said. Swain competed in the 800 at the Nike Outdoor Nationals, finishing 22nd of 115 runners in 1:55.48. He followed up at the Portland Track Festival’s 1500 meter event, finishing fifth of 17 in 4:02.11. Swain was our 2025 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year as a sophomore, but spent most of 2026 recovering from an injury. At the NCS Meet of Champions, he finished eighth of 11 in the 800 finals in 2:01.53 and was second of 29 in the prelims in 1:55.45. “It was great to see Seb run fully like Seb at the Nike Outdoor Nationals. He navigated the race well and set himself up in position to have a nice kick. He brushed up against his 800 PR from late April but more importantly he looked good doing it. And while I didn’t watch his 1500 in Portland, he again hit a time that was equivalent to his PR at the WACC championship in May,” Assadi said. Both runners look ahead to their senior seasons as they look to lock down their college prospects. “Both athletes are looking to run in college. Since I joined the staff five years ago, we’ve had 19 athletes compete in track in college. It’s been pretty incredible watching our kids become young adults and finding their way in college, too. We’re in a position where both the boys and girls teams are teed up to have really nice 2027 seasons. We shouldn’t just be good but we could be elite and quality for nationals if things go right,” Assadi said. Photos by Aaron Aubrecht (@csevenstudios) Claire Aubrecht and Sebastien Swain represented Piedmont High at the 2026 Nike Outdoor Nationals in Eugene, Oregon.
articles.title: Aubrecht & Swain compete in Nike Outdoor Nationals, Junior Olympic Qualifiers, Portland Track Festival

articles.text: Photo courtesy of SoccerWire The United States looked bad in its 4-1 loss to Belgium in the Round of 16. Despite its strong start to the World Cup, the Stars and Stripes are still looking for its first Quarterfinals berth since 2002. Wow, I should have stayed with to my original pre-tournament prediction of the United States losing to Belgium in the World Cup’s Round of 16. For all the momentum the Stars and Stripes established through the Group Stage and its Round of 32 win over Bosnia, it all fell apart against Belgium. It felt like the full U.S. Soccer experience; supreme optimism leading to supreme dread. It was fair to write off Belgium going into the R16. They looked woeful through the Group Stage with draws against Egypt and Iran, and had to mount a serious comeback from a 2-nil deficit against Senegal with two goals in the final five minutes of regulation before scoring the winner in the second period of extra time. Belgium manager Rudi Garcia made the bold call to leave out star players like Jeremy Doku and Kevin De Bruyne from the starting lineup against the U.S. and it worked out incredibly well. The United States’ loss looked much like its 5-2 defeat to Belgium back on March 28. Defensive mistakes led to each of Belgium’s goals; Sergino Dest allowed a ball to bounce in the box before the first goal, two defenders couldn’t close out Leandro Trossard’s cross for the second goal, Matt Freese had a blunder for the third goal, and a lazy clearance by Chris Richard resulted in the fourth. But the knockout stages have produced some World Cup classics. The tiny African island of Capo Verde had the defending champions Argentina on the ropes in the Round of 32, and then Messi and the Argentines mounted a comeback after trailing 2-nil to Egypt before winning 3-2 with each goals in the final 13 minutes on Tuesday. England’s 3-2 win over Mexico at the Azteca was another Round of 16 instant classic, while Belgium’s R32 comeback over Senegal is also in the discussion. We’ll be able to fully reflect on all the key moments of this spectacular World Cup after the conclusion of the final on July 19. Until then, here’s looking at the upcoming Quarterfinals matches before The Post returns from vacation on July 22. No. 1 France versus No. 6 Morocco (Thursday, 1 p.m.) I’m still taking France to win it all, but the route goes through scrappy Morocco—marking a rematch of 2022’s semifinal. For me, Les Bleus just has too much talent to be upset. I’m taking France by the same score as the 2022 semifinal, 2-nil. No. 3 Spain versus No. 8 Belgium (Friday, 12 p.m.) My pre-tourney prediction was Spain reaching the semifinals with a quarterfinals win over Belgium, and I’m sticking to it. But, the Spanish needs to find its scoring boots, having scored nine goals in this World Cup to Belgium’s 13. I’m going Spain, 2-1. No. 4 England versus No. 19 Norway (Saturday, 2 p.m.) This is arguably the most intriguing match of the Quarterfinals. Norway has been propelled by striker Erling Haaland, who the English teams know well with Haaland staring at Manchester City. Despite England being the much higher ranked side, and still being my finalist selection, this thing could easily go the other way if the Three Lions can’t lock down Haaland. Brazil definitely paid the price, will England too? I’m going England in another 3-2 thriller. No. 2 Argentina versus No. 13 Switzerland (Saturday, 6 p.m.) Argentina is riding high after its comeback win over Egypt, but they sure have looked vulnerable in their two knockout stage matches thus far. Of all the Quarterfinals, however, I think Argentina has the easiest route to the semifinals. Switzerland has some talented players, but I don’t think they have enough to lock down Messi and the Argentines. Still, it could easily go the Swiss’ way. My guess: Argentina, 2-1. Photo courtesy of CGTN.com Kylan Mbappé and France start the Quarterfinals on Thursday against Morocco.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Cal Athletics Tommy Ashton, PHS Class of 2025, just finished his freshman year on the California Golden Bears rugby team. TOMMY ASHTON Rugby Piedmont High Class of 2025 University of California Class of 2029 Tommy Ashton, PHS Class of 2025, just finished his freshman year on the University of California’s National Championship winning rugby team. He played football at Piedmont High, but made his most noise on the rugby field with Lamorinda Rugby. In 2026, the Golden Bears went 35-2 on their way to their 36-22 win over Navy to win the NCAA National Championship on May 2. He made two appearances this season, making his first career start in Cal’s 50-5 win over Fresno State on January 17, where he scored his first collegiate try (5 points). At Piedmont High, Ashton was a two-way starter on football as a running back offensively and linebacker defensively. He earned first-team All-League honors at both positions his senior year. He helped lead Piedmont to a 10-2 overall record, the WACC Mission Division title, and an appearance in the Division 7 NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seed. What is your workout program this summer? My workout plan this summer is directed towards building as much strength, mass, and size as possible. As an athlete in the offseason, I am not trying to be in “game shape” but rather to continue to build up the necessary muscle groups that help protect and improve my performance when that time comes. The core of my workout routine consists of heavy squatting, bench press, shoulder press, and power cleaning. These lifts help me build explosive strength and mass to protect my body when the season comes. What are your fitness goals for the summer? The goals I have set for myself this summer all revolve around size. I am focusing on gaining as much weight as possible prior to the upcoming season. With this goal, I am trying to add significant weight to every core lift within my program. How are you measuring your development? Measuring my development is very straightforward. Every workout/lift I do is documented in an app/database that keeps track of multiple variables such as weight, reps, and time. Each week, I aim to improve all these numbers to keep me on track to reach my goals. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Right now, in the summer, I am working out on my own, but every workout I do is guided with the help of my coaches electronically. I am tracking my weight, the weight of my lifts, and the number of reps I can do. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished was back squatting 385 pounds for 5 reps. In the sport of rugby, having a sturdy and strong base is key to my success in multiple aspects of the sport. articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost in the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on four athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Four who made a huge impact included , freshman Talia Perl of softball, Maika Ting of the girls’ volleyball team as a sophomore, junior Beach Lorin of boys’ basketball, and Ben Sorensen of baseball as a freshman. We’ll provide more athletes in the coming weeks. MALIA WILLIAMS Track and Field, Flag Football Malia Williams graduated from Piedmont High as a twosport athlete in track and flag football. She earned first-team All-League honors in the process. On the track team, Williams emerged as one of the best high jumpers in the Western Alameda County Conference. Williams was the league champion in the high jump with a leap of 4 feet, 10 inches against 12 other athletes. She logged the same high jump at the NCS Bayshore, which got her third of 21. At the NCS Meet of Champions, she was ninth of 18 with a five-foot jump. MAX FUJIMOTO Football, Baseball BEN KAPPES Water Polo Max Fujimoto is entering his junior year at Piedmont High and made his varsity debut on both the football and baseball teams as a sophomore in starting roles. On the football team, Fujimoto was a key contributor on both sides of the ball of their 8-5 team that reached the D7 NCS Championship game. Offensively, Fujimoto was credited with a team-leading 27 receptions, to go along with 214 yards and one touchdown. The baseball team went 8-16-2 with Fujimoto appearing in all 26 games, helping them receive the No. 6 seed in the D4 NCS postseason as their starting center fielder. He logged 14 hits, eight RBIs, scored 11 runs, and stole four bases. Ben Kappes emerged as a starter on Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team, helping them go 16-9 overall. They qualified for the D2 NCS postseason with the No. 1 seed, falling in a heated overtime match to No. 9 Marin Academy, 10-9, in the quarterfinals. To get there, they beat No. 16 St. Patrick 19-8 in the opening round. He scored two goals in their quarterfinals loss to Marin Academy. At the WACC Semifinals, he had one goal and three assists in Piedmont’s 14-13 loss to Castro Valley, while he had one goal, one assist, and one steal during Piedmont’s 10-4 victory over Encinal in the WACC Tournament’s opening round. Staff Photos Max Fujimoto was a starter in both football and baseball as a sophomore. Malia Williams won the WACC title in high jump as a senior. Ben Kappes was a freshman starter on the water polo team.

articles.text: In this week of Hiking with Jon, we delve into our fourth of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe with one of the tallest peaks in California at Washeshu Peak of Palisades Tahoe in Olympic Valley. If you’re in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a worthy and achievable mission to the million-dollar view atop Washeshu Peak while hiking at over 8,000 feet in elevation. Palisades Tahoe Olympic Valley is a popular destination for Piedmont residents on Ski Week. But during the summer months, the region becomes a prime hiking location with wildflowers and sweeping awe striking views of Lake Tahoe and the Desolation Wilderness. The name of the resort and mountain peak was changed from “Squaw Valley” and “Squaw Peak” due to the term being a racist and sexist slur. The change occurred following extensive research into the Washoe Tribe history, whose ancestral lands include Olympic Valley. Washeshu is in commemoration of the Washoe Tribe. Early literature from the tribe indicates the term Wa She Shu translates to “People from here.” Our day starts by taking the aerial tram ride up to High Camp, which gives another incredible view from the viewing platform back towards Lake Tahoe, a popular restaurant, outdoor games, a skating rink, and Olympic museum dedicated to the 1960 Winter Games. The large-scale pool and hot tub, unfortunately, have remained closed for several years due to extensive repairs. From High Camp, walking to Washeshu Peak is a two-mile straight shot and around 850 feet in elevation gain with the final 0.6 of a mile to the peak providing the sharpest ascent. The trail averages less than 10% gradient for the first 1.3 miles before making the climb to Washeshu Peak. At the 1.3 mile mark, hikers will come to a junction with a path on the left shooting upwards towards the Siberia Express ski lift, while the preferred trail on the right going takes you along the back-end toward Washeshu Peak. Palisades Tahoe’s staff advised the Post to take the trail on the right as opposed to the steep jaunt toward the ski lift on the left. Moreover, the trail on the The advised trail toward Washeshu Peak provides you with wildflowers and fluttering butterflies. right provided an unforgettable walk with bushels of wildflowers lining the path and butterflies fluttering unbothered around you. Off to your right will be the magnificent Granite Chief Mountain and the Desolation Wilderness. From Washeshu Peak, hikers get a clear view of Lake Tahoe and get a glimpse of Five Lakes while panning to the right. Pack a lunch to eat with the view. There are also mounds of shale enclosures to protect from the wind if needed. Returning to High Camp from Washeshu Peak will round out your day at four miles. articles.text: Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing, the most comprehensive retrospective to date of the artist’s body of work, is on view now at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA). The exhibition features half a century of work by Hassinger, including large-scale sculpture, site-specific installation, video, and performance, and will display more than twenty of her most notable works from the 1970s to the present. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing will be accompanied by an extensive exhibition catalogue, featuring new scholarly essays and previously unpublished documentation of her artwork. Notable displayed works include Love (2008), a site-specific sculpture composed of pink plastic bags inflated by human breath and filled with love notes; Beach (1980), a floor installation consisting of plaster and wooden dowels; and multiple sculptures that incorporate recently harvested tree branches which BAMPFA showcases in partnership with the University of California Botanical Garden. “Maren Hassinger’s practice has been of great influence for generations of artists,” Chief Curator Margot Norton said in a press release. “We are thrilled to finally bring her artworks and their stories from across her career together through our exhibition, and to showcase Hassinger’s profound contributions to contemporary art.” “Maren Hassinger’s work invites us to reflect on the beauty and complexity of human connection, through movement, material, and shared experience,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director, Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “Presenting this landmark retrospective at BAMPFA underscores our commitment to amplifying artists whose practices challenge conventions and inspire collective engagement across generations.” The retrospective will be on display at BAMPFA now through November 29. More information about this and other public programs can be found at bampfa. org. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing installation view at BAMPFA. Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing

articles.text: Production concludes company’s 2025-26 season Cast of San Francisco Playhouse production Hairspray. San Francisco Playhouse concludes its 2025-26 season with the Tony Award-winning musical Hairspray, running July 10 through September 12. Set in 1962 Baltimore, Hairspray follows teenager Tracy Turnblad as she pursues a spot on the popular television program “The Corny Collins Show.” After achieving her dream, Tracy uses her newfound platform to challenge racial segregation and advocate for integration. The musical features a score by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman, including songs such as “You Can’t Stop the Beat,” “Good Morning Baltimore,” “Welcome to the ‘60s” and “I Know Where I’ve Been.” The book is by Mark O’Donnell and Thomas Meehan. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English directs the production, with Phaedra Tillery-Boughton serving as associate director, Dave Dobrusky as musical director and Phoenyx Rose as choreographer. “In San Francisco Playhouse’s new production, we will reimagine Hairspray with a sharper edge, stripping away some of its bubblegum sheen to restore the subversive bite of John Waters,” English said in a press release. “This production leans into the story’s racial politics and cultural satire, examining Baltimore’s fight for integration through our contemporary lens.” Based on the 1988 film by John Waters, Hairspray premiered at Seattle’s 5th Avenue Theatre before opening on Broadway, where it won eight Tony Awards, including Best Musical, and ran for more than eight years. The musical later opened in London’s West End, winning four Olivier Awards, and has since been adapted into a feature film and a live television production. Director Bill English said the production “becomes more than a feel-good musical… in an era marked by polarization, erasure, and the lingering shadows of racist ideology.” “It’s a defiant, joyful call to resistance, where dancing is protest and inclusion is revolutionary,” he added. Ella Ruth Francis will make her San Francisco Playhouse debut as Tracy Turnblad. Trevor March returns to the company as Link Larkin after appearing in “Into the Woods.” Jeffrey Brian Adams will play Corny Collins, while Samantha Rich portrays Penny Pingleton and Jordan Covington returns as Seaweed J. Stubbs. Jonathan Chisolm makes their Playhouse debut as Edna Turnblad alongside Ken Brill as Wilbur Turnblad. Mackenzie Macdonald will portray Amber Von Tussle, with Alison Ewing as Velma Von Tussle and Jeannine Anderson as Motormouth Maybelle. The cast also includes Rebecca Pingree as Prudy Pingleton, David Boyll as Mr. Pinky and Harriman F. Spritzer, Sanaiya Johnson and Suleika Onia Patton alternating as Little Inez, Kareem Jenkins as Duane, Kaila Dyson, Anese Jade and Cai Rodis as The Dynamites, and Sierra Bolar, Matt Letton, Gwen Tessman and Hunter Yocom as The Nicest Kids in Town. Visit https://sfplayhouse. org/2025- 2026-season/hairspray/ or call the box office at 415-677- 9596 to purchase tickets. articles.text: Young Voices of the Philippines In a world where the power of music can inspire and cultivate excellence, the Young Voices of the Philippines (YVP) stands as a beacon of hope and creativity for countless children. This scholarship choir program, performing under the Treble Choir Association of the Philippines (TCAP), founded by Dr. Maria Theresa Vizconde-Roldan and Prof. Jude B. Roldan, has transformed lives by nurturing not only musical talent but also the holistic development of its young members. Their festival spotlight performance will take place Tuesday, July 14, at the Oakland Asian Cultural Center, Pacific Renaissance Plaza. YVP has received national recognition, being honored with the esteemed ANI NG DANGAL award from the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) and winning two consecutive AWIT AWARDS for Best Recording By a Child or Children. The choir is committed to promoting Philippine music and inspiring youth through community engagement. They lead choirs at festivals and initiate programs like Bisita at Awit ng Pagasa, a choral pilgrimage aimed at uplifting youth around the globe. In 2023, YVP made history by becoming the first choir from the Philippines to perform at Carnegie Hall’s Isaac Stern Auditorium/Perelman Stage. In addition to this historic performance, YVP won multiple first prizes at the 12th Golden Gate International Choral Festival USA. The choir also performed at the inaugural World Children’s Day in Rome, singing for Pope Francis at St. Peter’s Square. In celebration of Montserrat’s 1000th Anniversary, YVP performed at iconic venues in Spain, including the Abadia de Montserrat, La Sagrada Familia, and the Monestir de Sant Cugat. YVP has been highlighted in a premier spotlight at the Philippine Choral Directors Association National Convention. They have performed at national events, including the inauguration of the Philippine president, as well as festivals throughout the Philippines, the USA, Europe, and Asia. YVP regularly sings at the Immaculate Conception Cathedral of Cubao, sharing their passion for music with the community. Organized by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, the Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place locally from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ggf-concerts-2026.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of San Francisco Museum of Modern Art A museum patron views Henri Matisse’s work included in SFMOMA’s newest exhibition. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) new exhibition is focused on Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau, a painting widely regarded as a landmark of modern art. The exhibition, titled Matisse’s Femme au chapeau: A Modern Scandal, opened May 16 and is on view through September. The exhibition examines the history, reception and lasting influence of the 1905 portrait, which is part of SFMOMA’s permanent collection. The painting debuted at the Salon d’Automne in Paris in 1905 and became associated with Fauvism, the first French avantgarde art movement of the 20th century. The exhibition explores the work’s historical context, subject, provenance and circulation through exhibitions and publications, while also considering its impact on later generations of artists. “We are thrilled to have this opportunity to share the full story of Matisse’s Femme au chapeau—a painting that is emblematic of the artist’s radical break from convention in the early years of his career,” Janet Bishop, SFMOMA Chief Curator, said in a press release. “Arguably SFMOMA’s most art-historically significant work of art, Femme au chapeau began sending shockwaves through the art world as soon as it left Matisse’s studio and has captivated viewers ever since,” Bishop added. The exhibition also traces the painting’s ownership history. American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein acquired the work in 1905 while living in Paris. It later entered the collection of Michael and Sarah Stein, who brought it to the Bay Area in 1935. The painting was first exhibited in the United States at the San Francisco Museum of Art, now SFMOMA, in 1936. It entered the museum’s collection in 1991 through a bequest from Elise S. Haas. “Part of our vision at SFMOMA is to encourage our visitors to see the world—and art—in new ways,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “With stunning paintings by Matisse and his peers, as well as work by some of the most exceptional artists working today, this exhibition promises to captivate SFMOMA visitors this spring.” Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/ for more information. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

articles.text: Tickets available for shows now through July 19 Festival Napa Valley celebrated its 20th anniversary with a summer season that launched Friday, July 4. Tickets are available for shows now through July 19, featuring internationally known musicians, world premieres and cultural events across Napa Valley. The 2026 season will include performances by Renée Fleming, Wynton Marsalis, Time for Three, Ray Chen and Jean-Yves Thibaudet, along with the world premiere of The Judgment of Paris by composer Jake Heggie and librettist Gene Scheer. More than 200 artists will participate in concerts, dance performances and special events throughout the valley. Programming includes admission-free daytime concerts, evening performances, family events and the annual Taste of Napa celebration. “For 20 years, Festival Napa Valley has presented some of the world’s greatest artists on stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” Festival President and CEO Richard Walker said in a press release. “This anniversary season honors that legacy while expanding our artistic reach and community impact.” Among the season highlights is the Arts for All Gala at Nickel & Nickel Winery headlined by Marsalis. Fleming will appear in “Voice of Nature: The Anthropocene” and serve as keynote speaker for the Festival’s Music & Wellness Summit. Additional programming includes a performance of The Wizard of Oz with live orchestra accompaniment, a ballet program directed by Melanie Hamrick and a Symphonic Finale celebrating America’s 250th anniversary. “Festival Napa Valley is a beloved cultural tradition, uniting exceptional music, wine, food, and hospitality,” said Steven Stull, chairman of the Festival Napa Valley Board of Directors. “We welcome audiences from near and far to celebrate this milestone season with us.” For more information about Festival Napa Valley and to purchase tickets, visit www.festivalnapavalley.org. The music festival takes place at wineries and cultural venues across Napa Valley.
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley underway

articles.text: The Valley of the Moon Music Festival returns for its 12th season this summer with a program celebrating the music and global influences of Czech composer Antonín Dvořák. Titled Postcards from Dvořák, the festival will run July 11 through 26 at venues throughout Sonoma County, combining chamber music performances on historical instruments with outdoor concerts, lectures and family programming. Led by festival co-founders and directors Tanya Tomkins and Eric Zivian, the 2026 season explores the people, places and cultural traditions that shaped Dvořák’s music during his travels across Europe and the United States. “Dvořák is a natural choice to anchor our 12th season,” Zivian said in a statement. “While deeply rooted in musical tradition, he was remarkably open to cultural influences from around the world — traveling extensively and embracing new ideas in ways that were rare for a 19th-century composer.” “His openness, heartfelt musical voice, and deep respect for other traditions continue to inspire us,” Tomkins added. “For us, he represents the power of music to bring people together across cultures and communities.” The season features seven mainstage programs at Hanna Center Auditorium, beginning July 11 with “Bohemian Homeland,” an opening-night concert inspired by Dvořák’s roots in 19th-century Prague. The festival concludes July 26 with “Final Years: Going Home,” a finale celebrating Dvořák’s return to Bohemia. Other programs include “English Impressions,” exploring connections between English and Bohemian musical traditions, and “American Roots,” highlighting the composer’s years in the United States and the influence of African American spirituals and American folk music on his work. The festival also will present music by composers including Johannes Brahms, Felix Mendelssohn, Florence Price, Harry T. Burleigh and Leoš Janáček. Organizers said the programming reflects the festival’s ongoing effort to broaden the classical canon and highlight underrepresented composers. Guest artists this season include violinists Rachell Ellen Wong, Jennifer Frautschi, Elizabeth Blumenstock and Tien-Hsin Cindy Wu. The Amizia Quartet will return as the festival’s Fellowship Quartet-in-Residence. In addition to ticketed performances, the festival will offer pay-what-you-wish outdoor concerts, a free family concert at the Sonoma Community Center and pre-concert lectures curated by Kate van Orden. Tickets and passes are available online at valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org. Postcards from Dvořák will run July 11 through 26 at venues throughout Sonoma County.
articles.title: Valley of the Moon Music Festival runs July 11 - 26

articles.text: The Fourth of July is a festive day nationally. We in Piedmont celebrate like nowhere else. While it is popular in some places to be pessimistic, that is not the case in Piedmont. The annual Fourth of July parade is a picture of what we want to be. America is a country unique in the history of the world. How we achieved this status is a story in itself. Here is part of the story: If you are interested in sports, some of the most important historical heavyweight boxing championships were fought on the Fourth of July. But it is the world of music which can draw us together. The earliest composers in America were indebted to a European background. If they knew about indigenous sources, they side stepped them. A classic example is the music of Benjamin Franklin. Here in America, the earliest composer of note was Stephen Foster. Some segments of the population choose to contaminate his memory. Despite some of the lyrics, he was a melodist of supreme attainment. The short- lived pianist Louis Moreau Gottschalk continued down the musical line of Stephen Foster. However it was the Bohemian composer, Antonin Dvořák, who really unified all aspects of American music. This unification produced virtually all of the American music which came afterwards. Scott Joplin’s ragtime merged easily into the jazz era epitomized by Gershwin, which then became bebop, rock ‘n’ roll and onward ad nauseam. Along the way came important composers such as Irving Berlin and George M. Cohan. My father knew both of these composers. He thought that George M. Cohan was Jewish and he thought that his name was George M. Cohen. When I told him that George M. Cohan was an Irishman, my father said, “He spoke Yiddish to me.” Music in Europe always retained a formality. Concerts were in palaces, concert halls, and in opera houses. Some of that formality was continued in America. But we also had concerts in schools, churches and outdoor bandstands. American bands became famous. Think of the Gilmore band or the bands of John Philip Sousa. We are also notable for Photo of Center for the Arts banner in July 4 parade

articles.text: The live-action Moana premieres in theatres this Friday Moana is a family friendly animated feature by Disney. It is a lively Polynesian story about a strong-willed, adventurous girl named Moana (Auli’i Cravalho), 16, the daughter of her tribe’s chief, Tui (Temuera Morrison). Set on the Pacific island of Motunui, an emerald paradise, the story begins with Moana, looking toward the horizon, ever curious, wondering what’s beyond, understanding that for years her tribe has been afraid to venture past the reef that surrounds the island. But a strange cloud now hangs over the island. The fish are not as plentiful and the coconuts dry and tasteless. Moana’s grandmother, Tala (Rachel House), tells her that the ocean has chosen her to return the island’s goddess, Te Fiti, an idol stolen by the demigod, Maui (Dwayne Johnson), a millennium ago. Late at night, in the pale moonlight, Moana takes a beached canoe, called a camakau, and sets out, beyond the reef, in search of the hulking, overly confident demigod Maui (Dwayne Johnson). Her mission is to break the spell cast over her people. Moana is clearly Disney’s attempt to feature a young woman who does not need to be rescued by a prince, an almost iconic story line. Instead, the studio approaches the character of Moana with a light hand, A scene from Disney Animation studios’ Moana the inherent feminism subtle but compelling. Moana is independent, courageous and never burdened with an oppressive patriarchy. Actually, it is her destiny to become the eventual chief of her tribe. There is also no love story, no rugged islander waiting to marry her. Moana is simply a story of an empowered teenage girl on a quest. The directors of the film, John Musker and Ron Clements (The Little Mermaid, Aladdin) consulted with South Pacific locals, regarding their history and folklore. They also cast a wide net in search of the Hawaiian teen Auli’i Cravalho as the voice of Moana. As well, Dwayne Johnson, adding star power, has Samoan heritage. Voicing Moana’s father, chief Tui, is New Zealander Temuera Morrison of Maori background. Know as well that Moana is sprinkled with 10 songs, sung by Moana and Maui (as it turns out, Johnson has a solid voice). The music was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who wrote Hamilton. Plus, the animation is rich in tropical colors. Moana. Directed by John Musker and Ron Clements. Disney Animation Studios. With voices of Auli’i Cravalho, Dwayne Johnson and Rachel House. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. articles.text: Netflix’s Voicemails for Isabelle is not your typical romcom; it’s modern, edgy, heartbreaking at times, and portrays feminism in a way that movies should aspire to replicate. When I sat down on my couch to watch it, I expected it to be sappy and full of cliches. The premise itself is a trope: the heroine’s voicemails find their way to the love interest by accident, and then he falls for her. My assumption ended up being wrong. The movie didn’t start with a cute meet, but with a montage. The love story established was one between two sisters: Jill (Zoey Deutch) and Isabelle (Ciara Bravo). It is in the context of their relationship that we fall in love with both of them. Their personalities are clear from the first few lines, when the young versions of them freak out over Jill’s first kiss, and we see them shine through sisterly antics (burning food in the microwave, sharing choreographed dances, running to spend New Years’ together). Isabelle is also shown to suffer from cystic fibrosis. Although this is a major part of the plot, it takes a backseat in the montage. She is given a personality, one that isn’t “sick girl,” and that is a great choice on the filmmakers’ part. We feel the heartbreak even more when she *spoiler* passes away. Jill tries to move on, mostly by sending voicemails to her sister recounting her life, her job, and all the crazy things that have happened since Isabelle’s passing. What she doesn’t know is that the number has been reassigned to Wes (Nick Robinson), who lives on the other side of the country Zoey Deutch and Nick Robinson in Voicemails for Isabelle Jessie Andra Smith bring an unforgettable trilingual performance of swingin' bluesy jazzy folk. The duo has traveled all over the world, sharing their music on streets and stages with their unique sound. A fusion of jazzy folk and blues on resonator guitars and accordion, with an interesting interplay of harmonies between the two voices. Upbeat tunes rooted in the spirit of jazz, improvisation, storytelling, and humor. For advance tickets and more details, please see: https://www.ticketsignup.io/NandJessie .

articles.text: Ralph Fiennes in Conclave Conclave, the recipient of eight 2025 Oscar nominations, to include Best Picture, achieves what film does best: it takes the audience inside one of the world’s most secretive and centuries-old traditions. The church’s Cardinals, dressed in black and scarlet vestments, each with a large Pontifical cross, have been called to the Vatican from around the world. There they will gather behind locked doors in a cloistered conclave, tasked with the responsibility of selecting a new pope. Chosen to manage this densely ritualistic process is Cardinal Lawrence (Ralph Fiennes); his responsibility, we soon realize, is no small endeavor. The position of Pope is not only one of shepherding the millions of Catholics word wide, but one of power. Which Cardinal will be chosen, using paper ballots, while solemn is, as the narrative reveals, also Machiavellian, even touched by scandal and deception. With quiet sidebars, it can seem closely similar to a political gathering of sorts, these small huddles taking place behind closed doors or small huddles. These men of insistent faith are also just men who deal in the currency of secrets, touched by temptation, often conflicted when tested. Conclave is, ultimately, a captivating character study of Cardinal Lawrence who must reach beyond the conclave as he urgently attempts to discover the truth behind two whispered mysteries. This takes place while ballots are filled out and counted as the conclave waits to reach that necessary majority, and a plume of white smoke can be released from the much-watched chimney, signaling that a new pope has finally been elected. Conclave . Directed by Edward Berger. Starring Ralph Fiennes, John Lithgow, Stanly Tucci. 2 hrs. Rated PG. Released in 2024. Streaming on Netflix/ Prime/Fandango/apple tv.

articles.text: Small coastal towns have always been an excellent setting for eerily haunting stories told by people who are riddled with dark and stormy secrets. Whether it’s through the lens of haunted folklore, the odd disappearance, or legends whispered over pints of beer passed down through generations, audiences are time and time again fascinated by communities where something just doesn’t quite feel right. Widow’s Bay, born from the mind of Katie Dippold, embraces that fascination by blending supernatural mystery, sharp humor, and an unforgettable cast of characters to create a gripping comedy-horror show. Set on a remote New England island, the series follows Mayor Tom Loftis (Matthew Rhys), who is determined to make his struggling town the next Martha’s Vineyard by attempting to attract tourists despite the town’s insistence that it is cursed. Tom callously dismisses the island’s stories of ghosts, monsters, and ancient curses that Wyck (Stephen Root), one of the town’s most outspoken believers in its supernatural past, is constantly warning Tom about. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had an excellent holiday-week turnout of 47 walkers and five K-9 best friends last Wednesday at the Exedra. Dick Carter kicked things off by introducing a new participant and asking what was special about July 1. After a few wrong guesses, he revealed the answer: the year was half over. Happy Half New Year. Walkers marveled that 2026 was already halfway gone. Dick also announced that the next Second Thursday movie, “American Graffiti,” screens July 9 at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Announcements done, Dick handed the reins to Sherry Jacobs, dressed in a sequined red, white, and blue jacket she would wear three days later while leading the Wednesday Walkers in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade. Sherry is the first of several longtime walkers taking turns to help Dick shepherd the weekly walk. Fittingly, the group would also be the first in this year’s parade to cover the route. Sherry led them from the Exedra across Magnolia Avenue, left on Vista Avenue, and down to Bonita Avenue, where they stopped mid-block across from the Frank C. Havens Elementary School playground. On Bonita, Sherry explained that the City is reconfiguring this busy street over the summer before school resumes in the fall. Bonita will become a oneway, south-to-north thoroughfare with seventeen diagonal parking spaces and two disabled spaces on the west side. The current loading zone on the east side will be discontinued. A new loading zone for T-K and kindergarten students will go on Oakland Avenue, and two loading zones on either side of Highland Avenue will serve first- through fifth-graders. Sherry challenged the group to guess the project’s cost. A couple of guesses ran into the millions, but she reassured everyone the initial budget was $181,000. After a lively exchange about downtown congestion during school drop-off and pick-up, the group headed down Oakland Avenue to El Cerrito Avenue. Piedmont’s citywide parade began sixty years ago, in 1965, when Recreation Commission chairman Dick Johnson launched it. His El Cerrito Avenue neighborhood had been celebrating the Fourth since the mid-1950s with its own bicycle parade, watermelon-eating contest, and water-balloon toss. Mary Ellen Sherry and Dorothy Carter, who lived on the block and had experienced Fourth of July block parties on the East Coast, wanted one for their street and created the El Cerrito Avenue celebration. Longtime parade announcer Patty Edmonds and Wednesday Walker Dick Carter were El Cerrito Avenue kids at the time. Thinking Piedmont too quiet in summer, Johnson was instrumental in consolidating the various neighborhood parades into one citywide event. The 2026 parade marks America’s 250th year of independence, with a focus on community spirit, family fun, and civic pride. It features neighborhood floats, antique cars, and bands, along with a pancake breakfast and a big-band concert in Piedmont Park. articles.text: of dark chocolate, cedar, graphite, and subtle mint, supported In the center of Napa Valley, between Yountville and Rutherford, lies one of the world’s most celebrated wine-growing regions: the Oakville American Viticultural Area (AVA). Although it covers just over 5,700 acres, Oakville has earned an international reputation for producing some of the finest Cabernet Sauvignon on the planet and has become synonymous with excellence in California winemaking. Oakville’s story began in the late 1800s when pioneer Henry Walker Crabb established the famed To Kalon Vineyard, recognizing the extraordinary potential of the area’s deep, well-drained alluvial soils. The small community itself grew as a stop along the Napa Valley Railroad and took its name from the majestic valley oak trees that once blanketed the landscape. The Oakville AVA was officially recognized in 1993, but its reputation had been building for more than a century. What makes Oakville so special is its remarkable combination of climate, soils, and geography. Warm, sunny afternoons allow Cabernet Sauvignon to ripen fully, while cool evening breezes and morning fog drifting north from San Pablo Bay help preserve acidity and balance. Gravelly benchland soils along the western side of the valley provide exceptional drainage, encouraging vines to produce smaller berries with concentrated flavors and refined tannins. Oakville is home to many of Napa Valley’s most iconic wineries. Robert Mondavi Winery helped redefine California wine after its founding in 1966, while Opus One, a partnership between Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild, demonstrated that Napa Valley could rival the great wines of Bordeaux. Legendary estates such as Screaming Eagle, Harlan Estate, Dalla Valle Vineyards, Far Niente, and Heitz Cellar have further elevated Oakville’s global prestige. Their wines routinely command high scores from critics and are sought after by collectors around the world. Although Cabernet Sauvignon is unquestionably the star, Oakville also produces outstanding Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc, and Chardonnay. The finest Cabernets are known for their rich cassis and blackberry fruit, layers by polished tannins that allow the wines to age gracefully for decades. For visitors, Oakville offers more than world-famous wines. The scenic drive along Highway 29 passes historic wineries, vineyard-lined roads, and breathtaking mountain views that capture the beauty of Napa Valley. Whether tasting at an internationally renowned estate or discovering a small family-owned producer, guests quickly understand why Oakville occupies such a special place in the world of fine wine. For wine lovers, Oakville is more than an appellation—it is the benchmark against which many New World Cabernet Sauvignons are measured, a place where exceptional terroir and generations of winemaking craftsmanship continue to produce some of California’s most remarkable wines. On June 15 the Oakville Winegrowers Association held a tasting for the Trade and Media at the newly refurbished Robert Mondavi Winery. Nearly all the major wineries in the Oakville AVA were present. Many, many outstanding wines were poured but the following wines were the standouts. Far Niente Winery is one of the iconic properties in the Oakville AVA • 2023 Far Niente Cabernet Sauvignon The beautiful, striking Far Niente label certainly gets your attention, and you are not disappointed upon tasting. The wine exhibits a spicy, fragrant blueberry nose, rich concentrated, full-bodied flavors, with ripe tannin, licorice, smoke and red The vineyards of Oakville AVA are ideal for Cabernet Sauvignon
