Gravelly benchland soils along the western side of the valley provide exceptional drainage, encouraging vines to produce smaller berries with concentrated flavors and refined tannins. Oakville is home to many of Napa Valley’s most iconic wineries. Robert Mondavi Winery helped redefine California wine after its founding in 1966, while Opus One, a partnership between Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild, demonstrated that Napa Valley could rival the great wines of Bordeaux. Legendary estates such as Screaming Eagle, Harlan Estate, Dalla Valle Vineyards, Far Niente, and Heitz Cellar have further elevated Oakville’s global prestige. Their wines routinely command high scores from critics and are sought after by collectors around the world. Although Cabernet Sauvignon is unquestionably the star, Oakville also produces outstanding Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc, and Chardonnay. The finest Cabernets are known for their rich cassis and blackberry fruit, layers by polished tannins that allow the wines to age gracefully for decades. For visitors, Oakville offers more than world-famous wines. The scenic drive along Highway 29 passes historic wineries, vineyard-lined roads, and breathtaking mountain views that capture the beauty of Napa Valley. Whether tasting at an internationally renowned estate or discovering a small family-owned producer, guests quickly understand why Oakville occupies such a special place in the world of fine wine. For wine lovers, Oakville is more than an appellation—it is the benchmark against which many New World Cabernet Sauvignons are measured, a place where exceptional terroir and generations of winemaking craftsmanship continue to produce some of California’s most remarkable wines. On June 15 the Oakville Winegrowers Association held a tasting for the Trade and Media at the newly refurbished Robert Mondavi Winery. Nearly all the major wineries in the Oakville AVA were present. Many, many outstanding wines were poured but the following wines were the standouts. Far Niente Winery is one of the iconic properties in the Oakville AVA • 2023 Far Niente Cabernet Sauvignon The beautiful, striking Far Niente label certainly gets your attention, and you are not disappointed upon tasting. The wine exhibits a spicy, fragrant blueberry nose, rich concentrated, full-bodied flavors, with ripe tannin, licorice, smoke and red The vineyards of Oakville AVA are ideal for Cabernet Sauvignon The Oakville Winegrowers tasting was held at the newly refurbished Robert Mondavi Winery currant flavors. A classic Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon at the top of its game. • 2022 Rudd Cabernet Sauvignon “Samantha’s” This wine was the cream of the cream of the crop. The nose of vanilla, expresso, blackberries and smoke was enchanting. On the palate it was unbelievably rich with great intensity and power. The finish went on and on. This is a massive, powerful wine that should be laid away for five years minimum and will last thirty. • 2021 Oakville Ranch Napa Valley This Bordeaux blend is the wineries flagship wine. is a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petite Verdot, and Merlot. The wine however is much richer and riper than most Bordeaux’s bursting with fruit that leaps out of the glass. The nose is a combination of oak, cherries and black currant. It has a good balance of acidity and fruit, and the tannins are not overly harsh. Great effort. • 2021 Meyer Family “Le Bon Bon” Cabernet Sauvignon This small batch wine spends 35 months in new French oak. The wine’s opaque purple color is followed by a smoky, chocolaty, violet scented nose and deep, powerful full bodied blackberry fruit flavors. Lingering finish with smooth, supple tannins. • 2022 Gargiulo Vineyards “G Major Seven Study” Cabernet Sauvignon A Bordeaux style blend crafted from Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petite Verdot and Merlot This wine displays a dense purple color, followed by a gorgeous nose of blackberries, saddle leather and cigar box. This large scaled wine is bursting with concentration yet has a velvety, refined finish • 2023 Nemerever Cabernet Sauvignon This was a new wine to me and is made in small quantities. This wine exhibits a dark purple color, sweet, jammy blackcurrant-scented nose. The lush, juicy, succulent texture is crammed with glycerin and extract. With a smooth, rich texture, and a long savory finish, this medium-bodied, well-balanced Cabernet should drink well for 10-15 year • 2023 Nickel &Nickel Cabernet Sauvignon John Sullenger Vineyard This quality estate has established an enviable reputation for outstanding wines. A good lashing of French oak gives a warm vanilla flavor to the nose. Full bodied yet silky with layers of concentrated, highly extracted dark berry fruit this wine is exceptionally well balanced and already delicious. It will last well for a couple of decades in the cellar. • 2022 Plumpjack Cabernet Sauvignon This wine comes in either a screw top or cork finished bottle. It had a spot on cabernet nose and was balanced and medium bodied on the palate. More of an elegant style than some of the others in this review nevertheless it was perfectly constructed and delicious. A great food wine that calls out for a grilled steak. • 2023 Maybach Materium Developed by a family whose reputation is built on luxury automobiles the Materium is a wonder of wine engineering. The nose explodes out of the glass with notes of blackberry, vanilla, baking spices and earth. In the mouth you are greeted by plum, cassis, blueberry and anise flavors. It sports a huge, full-bodied palate of high extract and lots of tannin. It’s built to last 30 years if you can resist that long. texture, ripe tannin and enough structure for long aging. A sign of good things to come. • 2022 B Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon Oakville Located on the Oakville Cross Road next to some heavy hitter wineries B Cellars has flown under my radar until now and I was glad to make acquaintance with this delicious wine. An inky dark, opulent, blackberry nose proceeds a plum and raspberry fruit filled palate with a full luscious body. Great structure and balance with smooth tannins on the finish. • 2022 Goldschmidt Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon Game Ranch This shows beautiful aromas of blueberry, chocolate and cherries with lots of cassis and earth on the palate. The wine saw 17 months in new French oak and is bottled without fining which gives a good amount of tannin on the finish. Should improve in the bottle for a couple of decades. Can’t imagine a better partner to a grilled ribeye steak. Only 280 cases of the Ehrlich Cabernet Sauvignon were made • 2023 Ehrlich Cabernet Sauvignon Oakville Just 280 cases of this lovely wine were produced. The wine possesses a deep plum color as well as a sweet perfume of minerals, and cassis, and tons of blackberry fruit on the palate. It has medium to full body, excellent Tench is a small family owned winery with outstanding Cabernet Sauvignon • 2023 Tench Estate Cabernet Sauvignon This small estate has been around for a while but was new to me. Opaque purple in color, the wine has a brooding nose of minerals, cherries and blackberries. This leads to a smooth-textured, intense layered wine with superb depth and concentration and a decade of aging potential. Beautiful label too. • 2023 Baker & Hamilton Cabernet Sauvignon Dark purple in color, the nose reveals toasty oak, earth, in the mouth an amalgam of black fruits, plum and anise. Smooth textured, opulent, and full-flavored, the oak is fully integrated, and every element is in harmony. This delicious wine is approachable now but will cellar well for over a decade.

24 24 Wednesday, July 8, 2026 Parade Continued from page 1 where the annual pancake breakfast was underway. The group spoke about their excitement in performing their jazz standards this year. “It’s been fifty-one years in this parade; I’ve only been here twenty,” said one member of the band. “It’s been an amazing tradition, so we’re really happy to be a part of it.” The parade judges included 4th of July Committee Chair Kathy Kelleher, Grand Marshal Cora Wood, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, School Board President Ruchi Medhekar, and high school student Claire Aubrecht, who was the first high school student to judge in the parade. “It’s super cool that I get to do this and be able to participate in this way other than doing floats or just watching. I’m really excited to see some of the floats in this year’s parade,” said Aubrecht. The parade began with a police motorcycle driving in a zig-zag pattern to clear the way for the fire department’s fire engines. A color guard of Piedmont Scouts followed shortly after. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band strolled by next, playing their way down Highland Avenue to kick off the parade. The band was led by Allen Carr, who has been the band’s leader in the parade for 17 years and is the son of the founder. The first wave of classic cars came next, led by parade Grand Marshal Cora Wood, a long-time employee of the Recreation Department. Wood was with her family in a fire truck. Other cars held City Council members Andersen, Conna McCarthy, Lorrel Plimier and Tom Ramsey, as well as School Board members Medhekar, Michael Malione, Max Roman, and School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Alameda County Supervisor Nikki FortuPhotos by Jake Lannon Before the parade began, School Board Vice President Michael Malione, Mayor Betsy Andersen, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, School Board President Ruchi Medhekar, and Councilmember Tom Ramsey lined up for a photo in front of the classic cars. July 4 Parade Judges Claire Aubrecht, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, School Board President Ruchi Medhekar, Grand Marshal Cora Wood, and July 4th Committee Chair Kathy Kelleher. Grand Marshal Cora Wood gets out of the fire engine with her family. Barrelhouse Jazz Band musicians warm up in advance of the July 4 parade. Fire trucks and a police motorcycle start the parade. A 1929 Ford Model A pickup owned by the late Frank Swenson. 1938 Aston Martin owned by Joe Hurwich. WW II Flyers in a 1935 Rolls-Royce driven by WWII Reenactor Guillermo Sanchez. Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy and Peter Craigie in a 1967 Mustang owned by Martin Falarski. Councilmember Lorrel Plimier and husband Michael Plimier, riding in a 1970 Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme owned by Omar Rathford. Councilmember Tom Ramsey in a 2001 Morgan Plus 8 owned by Garrett Clifford. School board president Ruchi Medhekar with her daughters Amali, Liana, and Sana in a 1965 Mustang owned by Tom Straus. Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas with husband Brad Erickson in Elisabeth Straus’s 1964 Mercedes 230 SL. Oakland Rotary Club of Oakland #3 celebrates its longstanding efforts to help Oakland thrive. nato Bas was the last elected official to start the parade. Classic cars made their routine appearance, thanks to Roland Lazzarotto and the Bay Area Horseless Carriage Club, with cars ranging from 1909 to 1935. The Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital, owned by Piedmont resident Elizabeth MacDonald, wowed the crowd with its brilliant truck design. On top of the car was an American-themed top hat with red, white, and blue confetti attached. The front of the truck was decorated with confetti to create the face of a dog with its Piedmont Baseball & Softball Foundation with a large inflatable baseball on the top of their truck. tongue hanging out. The truck’s bed had American-colored balloons and bald eagles. The creative design won the hospital the Highland Saucer, the parade’s 2nd top prize. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team made an appearance with mini-stunts, performing jumps on mobile wooden ramps. The group won the Best Youth Entry for their fun riding. The Recreation Department won this year’s Best Theme award for their western take on the 4th of July. Some members held “Wanted” cutouts around their heads, and others rode on “horses” and danced around their vehicle. The car was covered with Western-themed items, like saloon doors, cacti, and old carriages. Silicon Valley Pipe Band, formerly Stewart Tartan Pipes and Drums, also made an appearance, playing various bagpipe standards as they marched down the avenue in rigid formation. Now based in Saratoga, the band was founded in San Francisco in 1980 and is considered by many to be the premier bagpipe band of the Bay Area. See Parade on page 25

Wednesday, July 8, 2026 25 Parade Continued from page 24 Following them was the Piedmont Swim Team, who brought a huge group of people to Highland Avenue. They sprayed bubbles and held swim team balloons. The team custom-made a silver piranha bicycle. The fish was large with a metallic body and a wide tail at the back. Their creative efforts earned them the Highland Spoon as the third best entry in the parade. The Oakland Strokes Rowing Club was the highest-energy group of them all, carrying their oars and shouting at the top of their lungs. Attached to their truck was a large 8-oar boat that had recently competed in the National Championships. Strokes’ members hung off the side of the rowboat with their oars and American flag-themed pants. Their energy and enthusiasm caught the attention of the judges, who rewarded them with this year’s Highland Cup, the top prize. The crowd favorite Balloon Platoon celebrated its 51st year of appearing in the Piedmont parade with a 21-mop salute in front of the judges’ reviewing stand. The Piedmont Pickleball team won Best Spirit for their American-themed car covered in Independence Day confetti. The group hoisted a net and played pickleball with it as they walked down Highland. The California Repercussions were the last musical performance of the parade, marching down Highland Avenue in their red and black uniforms. The 50-piece band, all UC Davis alumni, is made of equal parts brass, woodwinds, and percussion. The group was voted this year’s Best Band. The parade lasted just over an hour. An after-party was held in Piedmont Park, featuring live music by the Yacht Rockers party band while parade goers enjoyed picnics in the main park. The Walking on Wednesday group in the starting area of the parade, preparing to march down Highland Avenue. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band kicks off the first musical performance of the parade. The Balloon Platoon performs its famous 21 Mop Salute, celebrating 51 years in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. The Piedmont Park gymnasts acrobatically make their way down the parade route. The Piedmont Community Band marches down Highland Avenue wearing their classic red scarves. Silicon Valley Bagpipers play in their classic kilts. Piedmont Food Fest members show off their tasteful outfits and celebrate five years of successful events. The Piedmont Community Church celebrates with the community. The Piedmont Highlanders Bagpipe Band, led by Pipe Major Ellison Dunlap, Jr., produced a high-quality sound this year. The parade-goers follow the last car as they head towards Piedmont Park for a picnic and to listen to the live music from the Yacht Rockers. Nearby the Scouts in Troop 1 and Troop 4 sold hamburgers and hot dogs courtesy of Dave Larson and Piedmont Grocery.

articles.text: Troop 11 Scouts above Ropi Lake: Leo Shrago (left), Ryan Moon, Jojo Shim, Sasha Blum, Adlai Johnson, Charlotte Eisemon, Zoe Lacker, Veronica Shi, and Calliope Johnson. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 11 took a three-night backpacking trip to Desolation Wilderness near Lake Tahoe this summer. Nine middle school scouts and three adults went on this amazing adventure. We got the campsite of our dreams next to Lake of the Woods and went swimming almost every day. The first day, Sunday, we took a boat taxi across Echo Lake and then hiked the rest of the way to our campsite. On Monday, we went on our first day hike to Lake Aloha, known for its stunning crystal clear water and many granite islands. The lake was beautiful and some of us swam to an island in the middle. On Tuesday we hiked to Ropi Lake. We had fun wading in the water and eating our lunch in the shade, after a scorching hike on carved granite steps. Our final day was by far the most challenging. We hiked six miles up and down steep hills with rough terrain, and one particularly slippery rock that foiled most scouts. It was all worth it for the epic trip with views, lakes, and backcountry trails away from technology and civilization. Two Scout patrols cooked the food. The girls’ patrol’s favorite dish was pesto noodles made with instant ramen, and the boys enjoyed burritos. Not only was the food very good, we also learned about bear canisters and packing up food to fit a small space. We saw many animals: ducks, dragonflies, chipmunks, fish, and lizards. New and veteran scouts learned many things, some of which are requirements towards their next rank. Some of these things included cooking, cleaning, packing a bag, and finally we learned how to navigate using a map (and only got lost once along the way). Calliope Johnson cooks dinner for her patrol. It was the trip of a lifetime. It was fun, beautiful and we all learned a lot. Thank you to all the adults who put it together. Calliope Johnson is a member of Piedmont Scouting’s Troop 11. Piedmont Scouts swimming in Lake Aloha: Adlai Johnson (left), Sasha Blum, Leo Shrago, Ryan Moon, and Jojo Shim.
articles.title: Troop 11 backpacks in Desolation Wilderness

articles.text: Piedmont resident Amanda Reese died on June 24, 2026 at age 76. Piedmont resident Amanda Reese died on June 24, 2026. Born on May 24, 1950 in San Francisco, she was the daughter of Mortimer Hughes and Mary Alice Baker. Raised in Piedmont, she graduated from Piedmont High School, became a founding member of the Oakland Raiders’ Raiderettes, and attended the University of Nevada in Reno. She later joined her father and brother at Hughes & Hughes Jewelers, a San Francisco family business dedicated to a highend clientele—including the San Francisco 49ers—where she spent more than 30 years as a jeweler and eventual owner. On August 25, 2001, Amanda married her great love, Thomas W. Reese III, in Murphys, California. Together, they shared a wonderful life filled with adventure, cooking, camping, traveling, dancing, and attending concerts. They cherished hosting family gatherings and splitting their time between their homes in Piedmont, Los Barriles, Mexico, and Lake Tahoe. Amanda stood proudly alongside Tom throughout his distinguished 32-year career as an Oakland firefighter. Amanda was a deeply devoted mother and grandmother. Her marriage, close family bonds, and friendships spanning decades were the ultimate reflection of how she unconditionally showed up for the people she loved. Amanda was forced to slow down over the last six and a half years. Though illness altered her physically, her undefeated spirit and infectious humor never changed. Tom stood by her side with unyielding devotion, meeting every challenge with fierce loyalty and living as though no obstacle was ever too great to face by her side. Her perseverance, dignity, and quiet strength became a sanctuary and an inspiration to everyone who knew her. She is survived by her devoted husband, Thomas W. Reese III; her children, Corbie, Joshua, and Jenna; her grandchildren, Jack, Wylder, and Jett; her sister, Maryella Pegnato; and her sisters-in-law, Kathryn Walker, Vickie Reese, and Tish Reese. Amanda leaves behind a legacy of unconditional love, remarkable strength, and complete devotion to her family and friends. The love, encouragement, and warmth she provided will remain a guiding light in our lives forever. A Celebration of Life will be held in late August. Additional details will be shared with family and friends.
articles.title: Community mourns the loss of beloved Piedmont resident Amanda Hughes Reese

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, July 8, 2026 By Jay Russell July’s iteration of the Indie Next List has a double helping of romance novels fit for a beach chair. Checking out the Indie Next List is a good start towards finding the newest contemporary reads. The titles below received rave reviews from independent bookstore owners from across the country. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving and supporting their local communities with brick and mortar locales to buy books and give patronage to literature. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of inspired recommendations by picking 25 new releases called the “Indie Next List.” Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. July’s #1 Pick Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt by Ben Reeves was named a “Most Anticipated Book of the Summer” by People and BuzzFeed. Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt By Ben Reeves, Avid Reader Press/Simon & Schuster, Fiction “Unique, heartbreaking, and profound. This novel broke me in half but left me with immense gratitude for life, even for the toughest of times. You will want to share this with everyone you know.” —Barb Rascon, Page 158 Books, Wake Forest, NC Country People By Daniel Mason, Random House, Fiction “Entering the magical world of Daniel Mason is discovering the most perfect illustration of literature. The characters are quirky, the plot is inventive, and the landscape defies convention. Loved every page from beginning to end.” —Mary McBride, Monstera’s Books, Overland Park, KS The Shampoo Effect By Jenny Jackson, Pamela Dorman Books, Fiction “This is a juicy and fun summer read, but it also has wonderful depth of character and a truly thoughtful exploration of what happens to a tight-knit group of friends as they reassess their lives, negotiate adulthood, and raise their own kids.” —Debra Ginsberg, DIESEL, A Bookstore, Santa Monica, CA A Real Animal By Emeline Atwood, Catapult, Fiction “This novel follows Lucy as she navigates her twenties in the after- 25 Indie Next Best Reads of July math of an assault. PCSC Continued from page 1 and transformed the Veterans Hall into a pancake mecca. In total 30 PCSC students and adults volunteered time to make the event happen. Supporting the volunteer team with food donations were Piedmont Grocery and Village Market. Piedmont Grocery donates the sausages, orange juice, coffee, pancake mix, and the syrup. Village Market has donated fresh fruit for the pancake breakfast since PCSC took it over in 2016. While only one volunteer chef at a time can cook the hotcakes, other members of the crew made themselves useful by walking a large banner up and down Highland Avenue to promote the event. “Inside, it was warm and energetic. Everyone was mingling PCSC Co-VP of fundraising Lucas Bekele (left) and PCSC volunteer Danny King stand next to sign boards about the volunteer crew’s efforts. and coming together for a good cause,” said Huynh “The team was working really well together to keep up with the pancake and fruit demand.” By all accounts the pancakes, sausage, and fruit were delicious, providing sustenance to hundreds. The breakfast is the largest fundraiser for the crew, and the funds raised will directly support the many events the crew of 150 hosts. Li, who founded the crew in 2004 with help from Piedmont parent Barbara Caruso, is thankful for the large roster of student volunteers. He hopes to reach another market of volunteers – adults. “I get a lot out of this and I think there are lots of Piedmont adults who would enjoy it too. There’s an opportunity to make an impact on our youth and the surrounding community,” he said. Huynh and her co-VP of fundraising Nick Tam hit the streets to request donations for the Richmond Tiny House project. PCSC is building the management office for a village of houses that will house homeless and endangered youth. Student and adult volunteers can visit Pcservicecrew.org to find out more about the crew’s efforts and how to get involved. pages.text: 32 32 Wednesday, July 8, 2026 Widow’s Bay Continued from page 21 the town, supernatural believers like Wyck become more active, as they claim the island is “waking” from its slumber. The island itself quickly becomes one of the show’s greatest strengths. Foggy and blurred coastlines, coastal buildings with chipped paint hiding from the tourists, and a constant sense of something lurking just out of sight of the camera. These elements create an atmosphere that works to feel cozy but ever so slightly unsettling. But shortly after the arrival of Tom’s long awaited New York Times journalist, who Tom believes will help the island become more known, increasingly bizarre events begin unfolding around Tom and the occupants of the town. Patricia (Kate O’Flynn), the sharp-witted and loyal assistant of Tom, who often serves as a voice of practical reason, begins to lose her practicality as the island continues to “wake up” and wreak havoc on all the inhabitants. To complete the main ensemble of characters, Rosemary (Dale Dickey), who is known as the chain-smoking and gossiping local, becomes integral to the plot as she turns into a quasi-genealogist to help solve the mystery of the Widow’s Bay Curse. As Tom and his gang are forced to fight off the mounting monsters and curses haunting Widow’s Bay, the clock is ticking down for a solution to be found. The series slowly unravels the island’s mysterious origins and intertwined familial lineages all the while balancing genuine built-up suspense with plenty of ice-breaking comedic moments. What makes Widow’s Bay stand out is not simply its generic supernatural premise but the way it effortlessly blends classic jumpscare and thriller horror with timeless comedy. The humor throughout the show comes naturally via the loads of eccentric townspeople and their complete acceptance of the island’s strange traditions, with mystery continuously and steadily building each episode. Critics have praised the series for its unique tone, clever writing, and strong performances, highlighting how successfully it balances mystery, humor, and heartfelt moments. Matthew Rhys, Stephen Root, Kate O’Flynn, and Dale Dickey all deliver profoundly grounded and real performances that make the increasing absurdity of the events believable. They create a compelling dynamic with Tom’s skepticism contrasting Wyck’s blind belief and Patricia’s rationale clashing with Rosemary’s tall tales. Fresh off its first season debut, Widow’s Bay has already been renewed for a second season and has earned 5 nominations for the Television Critics Association (TCA) Awards and is a strong contender for the Emmys. For those looking for a series featuring small-town mystery, sitcom wit, and supernatural intrigue, Widow’s Bay is a perfect watch. It offers a refreshing take on familiar horror tropes without taking itself too seriously. Widow’s Bay. Created by Katie Dippold. Starring Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn, and Kevin Carroll. Rated TV-MA. articles.text: Fourth of July Parade at 11 a.m. Saturday The long-awaited 59th annual 4th of July Parade will be held this Saturday, July 4, starting at 11:00 a.m. This year’s parade lands on the 250th anniversary of the United States of America, marking a significant milestone in the history of this nation. The Parade will set out from the intersection of Highland & Park Way with a procession of classic cars, marching bands, and a variety of floats by local clubs and organizations, and march to the far side of Piedmont Park. After the parade, Piedmont Park will host a community picnic and a musical performance by the Yacht Rockers. The Fourth of July Parade is Piedmont’s largest annual event, drawing an estimated 3000-4000 participants and viewers each year. The theme of this year’s parade is “Independence Day the Piedmont Way.” Parade entries prepare for friendly competition as they compete for the Highland Cup, Highland Saucer, Highland Spoons, and the ribbon awards. articles.text: Starting on July 6, the block of Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland will be converted to one-way traffic heading northbound toward Oakland Avenue. The block will be closed to traffic on the morning of July 6, while the roadway is being restriped. Once the striping is complete the block will reopen as a one-way street. The conversion is the final of several measures the City has taken to improve safety, circulation, and the parking experience for visitors to the Civic Center. In addition to converting the street to one-way traffic, the new configuration will: • Eliminate the Havens Elementary drop-off zone on Bonita • Convert the parking spaces on the Havens Elementary side of the street from parallel to diagonal parking, which will add 17 new parking spaces • Add two new ADA parking spaces Earlier this year, the City added 30 additional time-limited parking spaces along Magnolia and Bonita Avenues. This doubled the short-term parking in the heart of the Civic Center. In an earlier phase, the City expanded the Havens Elementary School pick-up and drop-off areas on Highland Avenue, adding a second drop-off zone across the street from the school. The city’s goal is to improve safety and traffic flow in the Civic Center, particularly during school pick-up and drop-off hours, while providing the best possible experience for visitors. The City Council approved the circulation and parking changes in May 2025 after several months of discussion, including a community survey completed by 500 residents. The survey identified the expansion of short-term parking as a top need, with roughly half of respondents reporting parking in the Civic Center to be either “somewhat” or “very” difficult and over 80% of respondents reporting that they typically stay less than 2 hours. Workers rebuild the street on Bonita Avenue.
articles.title: One-way traffic on Bonita Ave. in Civic Center begins July 6

articles.text: Before starting a home improvement project that involves oil-based paint, stain, varnish, polyurethane, linseed oil, teak oil, or similar products, plan for safe storage and disposal of oily rags. As oil-based products dry, they release heat. When rags are bunched together, heat can build up and cause the rags to ignite without a spark or flame. This “spontaneous combustion” has caused multiple fires in Piedmont over the past three years. Piedmont Fire Department reminds residents, property owners, and contractors that oily rags should never be left in a pile, tossed in a trash can, or stored in a garage, shed, or work area without proper precautions. Always follow the instructions on the product you or your contractor uses. Before your next home improvement project, take a few minutes to plan for cleanup. If you are hiring someone to work on your property, talk to them about how they will store and dispose of oily rags during and after the job. Read and follow the disposal instructions on the paint, stain, varnish, oil, or solvent container. As oil-based products dry, they release heat. When rags are bunched together, the heat builds up and can ignite without a spark or flame. Plan where the oily rags will be safely stored while work is underway. Make sure oily rags are not left in piles, bags, trash cans, garages, sheds, or enclosed work areas. Confirm that oily rags will be removed from the property or handled safely at the end of each day. How to safely handle oily rags after using them: • Take rags outside and lay them flat in a single layer to dry. • Keep drying rags away from buildings, decks, fences, vehicles, and anything that can burn. • Weigh rags down so they do not blow away. • Once dry, place rags in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Follow the product manufacturer’s disposal instructions. Oily rags, oil-based paints, stains, solvents, and similar materials should not be placed in regular trash. Residents can use Alameda County household hazardous waste drop-off facilities for disposal of oil-based paints, stains, solvents, and similar materials. The closest drop-off facility is at 2100 East 7th Street in Oakland.
articles.title: Prevent house fires by making safe disposal of oily rags

articles.text: Zion Lutheran Church will host Tom Rigney and Flambeau for an afternoon arts and entertainment event on Saturday, August 29 at 5201 Park Blvd. in Piedmont. The concert is designed as a community-building cultural event, inviting neighbors, families, music lovers, and friends of Zion Lutheran Church to gather for an energetic live performance. Tickets are $30 for adults and $15 for children under 12. Food and drinks will be available for purchase on site. Tom Rigney, a Bay Area violinist, fiddler, composer, and bandleader, leads Flambeau in a spirited blend of American roots music. The band is known for fiery Cajun and zydeco twosteps, low-down blues, funky New Orleans grooves, Boogie Woogie piano, and roots rock and roll, with much of the repertoire composed by Rigney. “Tom Rigney and Flambeau bring people together, lifting spirits and creating lasting memories,” said Steve Harger, Director of Family Ministries at Zion Lutheran Church. “Tom, with his fiery fiddle, infectious rhythms, and joyful energy, fills the air. They will get your hands clapping, your toes tapping, and your feet moving!” Tom Rigney and Flambeau are known for an uplifting, danceable blend of American roots styles, including Cajun, zydeco, blues, New Orleans grooves, Boogie Woogie, and roots rock. Rigney’s fiddle-driven performances combine musical depth, high-energy showmanship, and a sound shaped by decades in the San Francisco Bay Area roots music scene. Tickets are available at www. zionlutheran.net ($30 adults; $15 children under 12). Food and drinks available to purchase.
articles.title: Tom Rigney and Flambeau to perform at Zion Lutheran Church

articles.text: Piedmont’s Community Pool is showing this year’s World Cup soccer games on the large screen above the pool. The games are usually in the afternoon during recreation swim or open swim periods. The city is complying with FIFA and US Soccer regulations. Many Piedmont residents have already come by the pool to lounge on a floatie while enjoying the World Cup. Currently, the World Cup is in the round of 32, the first knockout stage. The USA plays Bosnia-Herzegovina at 5 p.m. on Wednesday, July 1. The city does not plan to advertise these showings. Visitors planning to go to the pool to watch the World Cup games should call the pool staff in advance to confirm if a game is being played. Residents may call at the following phone number: (510) 420-3090. The competition pool is open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m., with a one-hour break between 1 and 2 p.m. To find more information about the competition pool’s open swim and recreation swim periods, readers can go to the city’s website: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/cms/One.aspx- ?por t alId=13659823&pageId=16935826#schedule.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Pool showing World Cup games

articles.text: Jessica McDevitt Petra is an 8-month-old puppy weighing 31 pounds with a sweet, mellow personality. This pittie mix can be a little shy when meeting new people and exploring new places, but Oakland Animal Services shelter volunteers have watched her confidence grow each day. Once she feels comfortable, she enjoys treats, gentle pets, and spending time near people. Volunteers describe her as sweet, gentle, and easy to handle. Petra enjoys leisurely walks and self-guided “sniffaris,” taking in the sights, sounds, and smells of the world around her. Petra loves exploring the shelter yard, watching birds, and investigating interesting sounds. If you’re looking for a gentle companion who will blossom with a little time and love, Petra may be the perfect match. Come meet Petra at OakPetra is an 8-month-old puppy with a sweet, mellow personality land Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 6:30 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Petra must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Adoptable Dog of the Week

articles.text: Seventeen school staff members retired as educators from the Piedmont Unified School District at the end of the 2025-26 school year. Five CSEA school employees retired and 12 classroom teachers said goodbye to hallway bells, backpacks and homework. Their efforts were acknowledged at length during the May 20 school board meeting. Retirees that attended the board meeting were acknowledged by their colleagues, former students and parents, and fans at large. Former Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer was on hand especially to thank a trio of valued colleagues – Christine Petersen, Melissa Cowan and Lianne Morrison. “I want to send warm regards to all the retirees, what an impressive group and what a change,” said Cramer. Christine Petersen began her career in PUSD in 1989 at the age of 23 and since then occupied a plethora of trusted roles throughout the district, including Wildwood Secretary, and CSEA President for seven years. She was also recognized by new CSEA President Amy Lee, board members and much of the entire room. “When you [Christine] joined Wildwood there wasn’t yet a Director of Facilities. You had no problem stepping in as the de facto Director of Wildwood, bringing your keen sense of what a clean, well kept school with all systems running, should look like,” said Cramer. “You have a way of staying in the hearts of so many students, colleagues and families,” Cramer said of Petersen. “Thank you for letting me work here my whole life. I loved it. I really don’t want to go but I’ll be around. The kind words were incredible. I feel so appreciated and cared for,” said Petersen. Piedmont Middle School At the middle school, immense staffing holes will also present Ted Scherman showed monk-like patience for 32 years in helping middle school students find their stride. themselves as veteran Alison Kelly, Camila Thayer and Ted Scherman have called it quits. Both librarians Gulassa and White, plus John White of the Green Team and P.E. teacher Best will retire. “If ever I use something that Ali created, which is all the time, I know it is flawless,” said colleague Lisa Brenneman. “Ali is a hard worker, and is one of the first on the campus every day. I admire so much about how she teaches.” Ted Scherman was serenaded by co-teacher for the last four years Ellen Breeden, who was also a student in Scherman’s first 6th grade classroom. “As a teacher, Scherman is one of the rare, magical educators where every single kid feels like they’re his favorite. He knows what sports they play, who their families are, what lights them up, what they are working through. He always encourages the shy kids to speak up more and the boisterous kids to see themselves as learners,” said Breeden. “It is bittersweet to talk about our retirees. We have many of them this year because we did offer a retirement incentive,” said Superintendent Hawn. That retirement incentive offered eligible teachers one full year’s salary in compensation to retire. In doing so PUSD makes a youth movement at the front of its classrooms. The unwavering efforts of this unique retirement class will be felt for years to come. Their lessons may be emulated and sustained by colleagues next year and their phone numbers and advice will be priceless commodities for continuing staff. Ali Kelly taught 8th grade English, reading, drama, and a Newspaper class in addition to 7th grade core.
articles.title: Seventeen to retire from Piedmont Unified School District

articles.text: A family takes a quiet moment outside the Exploratorium, slowing down to observe, connect, and notice. One month into summer, and most parents have probably heard some version of it: “I’m bored.” Depending on the day, those two words can sound anywhere from mildly annoying to completely alarming. But what if boredom isn’t actually the problem? What if it’s part of the solution? My father was famously never bored. Wherever he went, he carried a sketchbook. Airports, waiting rooms, even meetings, he was always drawing; people sitting nearby, objects on a table, a view from a window. We still have books of those sketches. What I remember most isn’t that he was making art, it’s that he was paying attention. Many of his drawings were unfinished. Some were little more than scribbles. But sketching gave him a way to exercise curiosity, observation, and patience. He wasn’t waiting to be entertained. He was engaging with the world around him. In our household, that’s the version of boredom I’ve tried to pass along to my daughters. I’ve often told them that boredom is a choice—not because there is always something exciting happening, but because there is always something to notice. No matter where you are, there is something to wonder about, examine more closely, or learn from. The challenge isn’t finding something interesting, it’s learning how to direct your attention toward it. Summer gives us the opportunity to practice this skill. During the school year, much of children’s time is structured for them. Adults decide where they need to be, what they need to accomplish, and often what they should pay attention to. Summer creates pockets of unstructured time that can feel uncomfortable at first. Without a schedule to follow or an assignment to complete, young people are left with a different challenge: deciding for themselves what deserves their attention. Research shows that boredom can help kids build emotional resilience and independence. In one study tracking early childhood development, Alana Anderson and Sammy Perone found that learning to navigate the uncomfortable lull of boredom is a primary way children practice “effortful control,” the critical behavioral skill required to manage restlessness, brainstorm their own activities, and build internal motivation without relying on an adult or a screen to entertain them (Anderson & Perone, 2024). Additionally, when external stimulation drops, the brain shifts into what neuroscientists call the “default mode network,” a reflective state that encourages daydreaming, connection-making, and problem-solving, making an empty afternoon the ultimate workspace for independent imagination. This summer, let your kids get bored, but also encourage them to get themselves un-bored. Resist the urge to stimulate or entertain your child when they tell you they’re bored. Instead, ask what they’ve noticed today that they hadn’t noticed before. Ask what they’re curious about. Ask what they’ve always wondered but never taken the time to investigate. At the Exploratorium, we often talk about curiosity as a habit. Like any habit, it grows stronger with practice. So this summer, don’t rush to fill every empty moment. Leave a little room for wondering and noticing. Sometimes the most important summer learning starts when there’s nothing planned at all. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, July 1, 2026 SchOOLs Seventeen to retire from Piedmont Unified School District By Jay Russell Seventeen school staff members retired as educators from the Piedmont Unified School District at the end of the 2025-26 school year. Five CSEA school employees retired and 12 classroom teachers said goodbye to hallway bells, backpacks and homework. Their efforts were acknowledged at length during the May 20 school board meeting. Retirees that attended the board meeting were acknowledged by their colleagues, former students and parents, and fans at large. Former Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer was on hand especially to thank a trio of valued colleagues – Christine Petersen, Melissa Cowan and Lianne Morrison. “I want to send warm regards to all the retirees, what an impressive group and what a change,” said Cramer. Christine Petersen began her career in PUSD in 1989 at the age of 23 and since then occupied a plethora of trusted roles throughout the district, including Wildwood Secretary, and CSEA President for seven years. She was also recognized by new CSEA President Amy Lee, board members and much of the entire room. “When you [Christine] joined Wildwood there wasn’t yet a Director of Facilities. You had no problem stepping in as the de facto Director of Wildwood, bringing your keen sense of what a clean, well kept school with all systems running, should look like,” said Cramer. “You have a way of staying in the hearts of so many students, colleagues and families,” Cramer said of Petersen. “Thank you for letting me work here my whole life. I loved it. I really don’t want to go but I’ll be around. The kind words were incredible. I feel so appreciated and cared for,” said Petersen. Piedmont Middle School At the middle school, immense staffing holes will also present Thinking Outside the Classroom In defense of boredom Ted Scherman showed monk-like patience for 32 years in helping middle school students find their stride. themselves as veteran Alison Kelly, Camila Thayer and Ted Scherman have called it quits. Both librarians Gulassa and White, plus John White of the Green Team and P.E. teacher Best will retire. “If ever I use something that Ali created, which is all the time, I know it is flawless,” said colleague Lisa Brenneman. “Ali is a hard worker, and is one of the first on the campus every day. I admire so much about how she teaches.” Ted Scherman was serenaded by co-teacher for the last four years Ellen Breeden, who was also a student in Scherman’s first 6th grade classroom. “As a teacher, Scherman is one of the rare, magical educators where every single kid feels like they’re his favorite. He knows what sports they play, who their families are, what lights them up, what they are working through. He always encourages the shy kids to speak up more and the boisterous kids to see themselves as learners,” said Breeden. “It is bittersweet to talk about our retirees. We have many of them this year because we did offer a retirement incentive,” said Superintendent Hawn. That retirement incentive offered eligible teachers one full year’s salary in compensation to retire. In doing so PUSD makes a youth movement at the front of its classrooms. The unwavering efforts of this unique retirement class will be felt for years to come. Their lessons may be emulated and sustained by colleagues next year and their phone numbers and advice will be priceless commodities for continuing staff. articles.text: There will a new administrative team at Piedmont Middle School (PMS) next year as Jamie Van Kleeck takes over as Principal. In his 12th year with the district Adam Saville moves from Tech Specialist to the role of Vice “We are in the midst of a generational shift of sorts at the middle school with many veteran PMS teachers retiring and many new teachers joining us,” said Saville and Van Kleeck said they will approach the opportunity with great enthusiasm and great humility. Change will come tangibly with electives for middle school students. A one semester Health class is being moved from 7th to 8th grade. During the April 15 school board meeting Van Kleeck explained that the health teacher agreed 8th grade is a “developmentally more appropriate time” for the Health content. Next year the middle school will pilot four new one semester elective courses: • Debate • Forensics • LEAD (Leadership, Empowerment, Action, Development) • Life Lab Next year’s Principal at PMS Jamie Van Kleeck (second from left) went on the Spring Break Trip to China with staff members PMS Core 6 teacher Lea Lotia (left), and PMS/PHS Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia (right). Supt. Jennifer Hawn and high school principal David Yoshihara also went on a hike through the rice terraces of Guangxi. New PMS Vice Principal Adam Saville LEAD will focus on personal leadership, collaboration on meaningful initiatives, and reflection on growth as leaders. Life Lab will focus on practical skills such as cooking, financial literacy, basic home maintenance and gardening. Next year the middle school will also introduce a “zero” period (before school) PE for 7th/8th graders. This creative solution allows middle school students the option to take P.E. during zero period to allot for more electives. “I think this is super innovative, and I want to take all of these electives,” said board member Lindsay Thomasson. “I really appreciate the out-of-the-box thinking.” Board President Ruchi Medhekar called the changes “a solution to a problem that has existed for a long time.”

articles.text: Since I’ve come home for summer break after finishing my first year in university, I have often found myself pondering how different my life would be if I had chosen UC San Diego over St. Andrews in Scotland. Swapping weeks of endless grey skies and sheets of bone chilling rain for constant sunshine and miles of idyllic California coastline, I get swept up in this day dream. Especially when my 20-minute walk back to my dorm from the library is pitch dark despite it only being four o’clock in the afternoon, or when I saw my friends who chose schools in warmer climates posting on social media about the college experiences they had had thus far. This thought of ‘what if’ prompted me to think about the differences of my Scottish university experience to that of any other American college. When I think about the American college experience I think of my sister and my closest friend. My sister graduated from UC Santa Barbara and my good friend will be a junior at the University of Oregon. When my sister went to college, I was just starting high school and had no idea where I wanted to go to college. But listening to my sister tell stories about the daily sunset pilgrimages at UCSB where all the students would walk along Isla Vista’s coastline with their friends to unwind for the night. Or what it was like to live in a college town inhabited by students and all the interesting and sometimes crazy happenings that came with it. But what I understood from my sister’s stories was that college had the potential to be some of the freest and best years of young adulthood. With that information firmly rooted into my mind, I made up my mind to work toward what my dad called, the ‘Santa Barbara Experience.’ For most of high school, especially junior year, whenever I was asked where I wanted to go to college, I answered UCSB because I wanted to experience what my sister did, I wanted to feel that sense of a never-ending adventure. When I entered my senior year at Bentley School, my closest friend had started her first year at the University of Oregon. During our facetime calls when I was done complaining about the college application process, she would tell me about her college life. And like my sister, she had many exciting stories about college, like joining the Kappa Delta sorority and meeting some good friends because of it. She would tell me about the Oregon football games, about the different musical artists that came to perform on campus, and other first-year experiences. At the time I wanted nothing more than to have that kind of college journey. Both my sister’s and friend’s stories fueled me for the final push of college applications. On my list of colleges was one school that was an outlier among the rest, St. Andrews. In contrast to the other schools it was much smaller, only about 8,000 undergraduates, and was a more specialised research university. More importantly it was on the other side of the globe. From the first time my parents took me to London, I was enamoured. It had been my far, far-fetched dream since that trip to eventually go to school in the United Kingdom. It was the kind of goal that would be an intense up-hill battle. It wasn’t until my high school theater class made a trip to Edinburgh to the Fringe Festival my junior year, that I had found out about St. Andrews. Its application system had been altered to help accommodate international students, meaning that the only requirement I needed to fulfill was to supply an AP test score above a three. Nonetheless, it was hard to get into despite its accommodation. When I finally submitted my final application in December, I kept my expectations low on getting an offer from St. Andrews. To my surprise, two and a half months later I found myself at a crossroads. I had been offered acceptance at St. Andrews and UC San Diego (ironically UCSB, my sister’s school, rejected me). UC San Diego had been the type of school that I had been working towards – a big public state school in Southern California, while St. Andrews was a school I knew next to nothing about. Despite that, I took one of the biggest leaps of faith, dug my heels in, and chose to go to university on a different continent. Despite the attempts at reconsideration by my family, I stood by my choice; it was my childhood dream on the brink of coming true. Yet despite that I had a sense of anxiety; I had no idea what kind of school St. Andrews really was. I only knew that the town had three main streets, the furthest walk was 25 minutes, and that it was renowned for its School of International Relations. So as graduation from high school came and went, as I went through the steps of applying for a student visa, and coming to terms with the fact that I would be incredibly far from my family, I researched St. Andrews. In hindsight I should have done that before I applied, but there’s a reason the saying ‘there’s no time like the present’ exists. Come September, and I was about to start at a college where I really did not think I would end up, I spent the first few weeks recalling the stories my sister and friend had told me and eagerly awaited having those exact same experiences. But as the weeks stretched on, I found that they didn’t necessarily happen. I was getting disheartened, I had worked for four years to have the classic American college experience, only to find myself in a place where everything seemed different. pages.text: Wednesday, July 1, 2026 11 US or UK? – A question of the college experience By Larissa Edel Since I’ve come home for summer break after finishing my first year in university, I have often found myself pondering how different my life would be if I had chosen UC San Diego over St. Andrews in Scotland. Swapping weeks of endless grey skies and sheets of bone chilling rain for constant sunshine and miles of idyllic California coastline, I get swept up in this day dream. Especially when my 20-minute walk back to my dorm from the library is pitch dark despite it only being four o’clock in the afternoon, or when I saw my friends who chose schools in warmer climates posting on social media about the college experiences they had had thus far. This thought of ‘what if’ prompted me to think about the differences of my Scottish university experience to that of any other American college. When I think about the American college experience I think of my sister and my closest friend. My sister graduated from UC Santa Barbara and my good friend will be a junior at the University of Oregon. When my sister went to college, I was just starting high school and had no idea where I wanted to go to college. But listening to my sister tell stories about the daily sunset pilgrimages at UCSB where all the students would walk along Isla Vista’s coastline with their friends to unwind for the night. Or what it was like to live in a college town inhabited by students and all the interesting and sometimes crazy happenings that came with it. But what I understood from my sister’s stories was that college had the potential to be some of the freest and best years of young adulthood. With that information firmly rooted into my mind, I made up my mind to work toward what my dad called, the ‘Santa Barbara Experience.’ For most of high school, especially junior year, whenever I was asked where I wanted to go to college, I answered UCSB because I wanted to experience what my sister did, I wanted to feel that sense of a never-ending adventure. When I entered my senior year at Bentley School, my closest friend had started her first year at the University of Oregon. During our facetime calls when I was done complaining about the college application process, she would tell me about her college life. And like my sister, she had many exciting stories about college, like joining the Kappa Delta sorority and meeting some good friends because of it. She would tell me about the Oregon football games, about the different musical artists that came to perform on campus, and other first-year experiences. At the time I wanted nothing more than to have that kind of college journey. Both my sister’s and friend’s stories fueled me for the final push of college applications. On my list of colleges was one school that was an outlier among the rest, St. Andrews. In contrast to the other schools it was much smaller, only about 8,000 undergraduates, and was a more specialised research university. More importantly it was on the other side of the globe. From the first time my parents took me to London, I was enamoured. It had been my far, far-fetched dream since that trip to eventually go to school in the United Kingdom. It was the kind of goal that would be an intense up-hill battle. It wasn’t until my high school theater class made a trip to Edinburgh to the Fringe Festival my junior year, that I had found out about St. Andrews. Its application system had been altered to help accommodate international students, meaning that the only requirement I needed to fulfill was to supply an AP test score above a three. Nonetheless, it was hard to get into despite its accommodation. When I finally submitted my final application in December, I kept my expectations low on getting an offer from St. Andrews. To my surprise, two and a half months later I found myself at a crossroads. I had been offered acceptance at St. Andrews and UC San Diego (ironically UCSB, my sister’s school, rejected me). UC San Diego had been the type of school that I had been working towards – a big public state school in Southern California, while St. Andrews was a school I knew next to nothing about. Despite that, I took one of the biggest leaps of faith, dug my heels in, and chose to go to university on a different continent. Despite the attempts at reconsideration by my family, I stood by my choice; it was my childhood dream on the brink of coming true. Yet despite that I had a sense of anxiety; I had no idea what kind of school St. Andrews really was. I only knew that the town had three main streets, the furthest walk was 25 minutes, and that it was renowned for its School of International Relations. So as graduation from high school came and went, as I went through the steps of applying for a student visa, and coming to terms with the fact that I would be incredibly far from my family, I researched St. Andrews. In hindsight I should have done that before I applied, but there’s a reason the saying ‘there’s no time like the present’ exists. Come September, and I was about to start at a college where I really did not think I would end up, I spent the first few weeks recalling the stories my sister and friend had told me and eagerly awaited having those exact same experiences. But as the weeks stretched on, I found that they didn’t necessarily happen. I was getting disheartened, I had worked for four years to have the classic American college experience, only to find myself in a place where everything seemed different. My first semester in Scotland was spent adjusting to a new system of learning, grading, and teaching with occasional weekend excursions or pub nights with new found friends. All the while I would see my friends at American colleges out enjoying the things I thought I too should experience. As winter break rolled around I was at home again reunited with my family and friends. I first thought ‘what if?’ San Diego seemed like a dream to me then, I was wondering if I had made the wrong decision. I talked about it with my mother extensively, I sought the advice of my sister and my friend at Oregon. I even tried to think what my late grandmother would say to me. It was only after speaking with my sister for the umpteenth time that I was reminded that the college experience isn’t something handed to you tied up neatly with a prim bow on top, it was something you made. And as obvious as that sounds, I had lost sight of that concept. I had been so caught up in trying to make St. Andrews fit into a mold when it was in fact a star, and in that process I had overlooked everything that had made it different and special. articles.text: With the new school year approaching, the Class of 2027 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. EMMA CHAN Tennis Staff Photos Cole Carnazzo has been a huge part of the swimming team’s success over the last three years and enters his fourth year on the varsity team. COLE CARNAZZO Swimming Emma Chan enters her senior year after making school history, winning the school’s only WACC doubles title in the individual tournament alongside Samantha Huynh. With Chan, the Highlanders won the league’s regular season title with a 13-9 overall record while going 7-1 against league opponents. At the WACC Individual Tournament, Chan and Huynh beat Alameda’s Natalie Wong and Sophie Featherstone in the finals, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3. They also took down Naomi Lin and Caroline Sue of Alameda 6-4, 6-4 in the semifinals, won 7-6 (7-2), 6-3 over No. 4 seed Fiona Wood and Sloane Kau of Bishop O’Dowd in the quarterfinals, and opened the tournament with a heated 4-6, 6-2, 14-12 win over Berkeley’s Esra Abarbanel and Vera Ertel. Chan earned an honorable mention for All-League honors and was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in November. Cole Carnazzo is a big part of the boys’ swimming team’s renaissance over the last few years, helping the 200 medley team reach the CIF State Championship despite not competing in the meet. At the NCS Championship, Carnazzo helped the medley relay team place fourth of 16 finalists in 1:32.91 alongside Asher Takazawa, Nik Costello, and his younger brother, Connor Carnazzo. To reach the finals, the team placed third of 37 teams in 1:32.10. Cole Carnazzo also helped the Highlanders set a 200 medley relay league record at the Western Alameda County Conference Championship with a time of 1:31.81 in a field of 15 teams. He was also a part of PHS’ league title in the 400 freestyle relay, winning the event with a time of 3:09.02 against 16 other schools. He was the second leg of the event alongside Takazawa, Costello, and Dima Secor. CONNOR FREDERICKS Lacrosse Connor Fredericks will be a four-year starter on the boys’ lacrosse team come his senior season in the spring. He earned first-team All-League honors as a junior, and second-team honors as a sophomore and freshman. In 2026, Fredericks helped Piedmont go 7-8 overall and receive the No. 6 seed in the D2 NCS playoffs. They beat No. 11 Las Lomas 12-11 in a thrilling overtime win for the first round of the postseason, but lost 7-6 to No. 3 Miramonte in a heated quarterfinal. Fredericks scored five goals, two assists, and 10 ground balls in PHS’ win over Las Lomas, including winning the opening faceoff of overtime to set up the winning Golden Goal. He also logged three goals, had two assists, five ground balls, and won 12 face-offs their playoff loss to Miramonte. He was our honorable mention for Freshman of the Year in 2024. Emma Chan returns this fall as the defending WACC Doubles champion and a senior leader on the tennis team. Connor Fredericks enters his fourth year as a varsity starter on the lacrosse team, He was our 2024 honorable mention for Freshman of the Year.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team ramped up its offseason training program with a 7-on-7 against San Lorenzo on June 24. Rising sophomore Cyrus Emanuelson is competing for the team’s starting quarterback role. Piedmont High’s football team is getting its summer training camp underway as they prepare for the approaching fall season. On Wednesday, June 24, Piedmont hosted San Lorenzo for a 7-on-7 scrimmage – scoring four touchdowns to SLZ’s three, while the junior varsity squad shutout the Grizzlies 2-0. The Highlanders are going through big changes in 2026. On top of losing nine seniors from last year’s team, they must replace quarterback Jimmy Lagios after he transferred to another school. “It’s my first time in five years that we won’t have a Lagios running the show,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We’re a really young team and lost a lot of guys to graduation, but now’s the time for the young guys to step up. It’s been fun.” Taking all of the reps in Wednesday’s 7-on-7 was rising sophomore Cyrus Emanuelson at quarterback. Seiden mentioned that Emanuelson will be competing with Jonah Cha-Foster for the starting job, making this an important offseason. “Cyrus is in contention. Jonah is a super talented baseball player and also a talented quarterback; he’s a great fit for our system,” Seiden mentioned. “I just have to keep competing and working, I’ve been training with a coach. I’m not really worried about whether I get the [starting quarterback role, I just want to keep competing. I’m learning how to throw a tighter spiral and just how to bounce back from mistakes,” Emanuelson said. Emanuelson threw two touchdown passes to Diego Hurwitz, and one to Mateo Long and George Saunders. Hurwitz missed a portion of last season due to an injury, and he’s set to move up the Highlanders’ depth chart after the team lost its top two receivers from last season in Cash Panico and Jack Meyjes. “Last year, I was injured for half of the year and it required a lot of rebuilding. Ever since then, I’ve just been stepping up and seeing what I can do. I’ve been taking the lead on offense and I think it’s rubbing off on everyone,” Hurwitz said. Hurwitz and the receiver’s performance will be important toward taking the load off the quarterback position, along with returning rising senior Rehan Mumtaz at running back. “It’s definitely been an offseason of building and working on chemistry. We’ve been out here putting in work and building that chemistry, now it’s just taking it onto the field. I think our offense looks better than expected, we’re progressing really far since the start of the summer,” Hurwitz said. “I just want to give all the support for Cyrus. He’s really stepped it up and is showing leadership. He really wants to get better and showing a lot of commitment,” Mumtaz added. Mumtaz will be stepping into the No. 1 running back role following the graduation of Xavier Henderson. He had some big games filling in for Henderson last season, including a 162-yard, two touchdown performance in the 39-35 win over Washington. “I’m really looking for more consistency. Football ramps up offseason program with 7-on-7 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s football team is getting its summer training camp underway as they prepare for the approaching fall season. On Wednesday, June 24, Piedmont hosted San Lorenzo for a 7-on-7 scrimmage – scoring four touchdowns to SLZ’s three, while the junior varsity squad shutout the Grizzlies 2-0. The Highlanders are going through big changes in 2026. On top of losing nine seniors from last year’s team, they must replace quarterback Jimmy Lagios after he transferred to another school. “It’s my first time in five years that we won’t have a Lagios running the show,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We’re a really young team and lost a lot of guys to graduation, but now’s the time for the young guys to step up. It’s been fun.” Taking all of the reps in Wednesday’s 7-on-7 was rising sophomore Cyrus Emanuelson at quarterback. Seiden mentioned that Emanuelson will be competing with Jonah Cha-Foster for the starting job, making this an important offseason. “Cyrus is in contention. Jonah is a super talented baseball player and also a talented quarterback; he’s a great fit for our system,” Seiden mentioned. “I just have to keep competing and working, I’ve been training with a coach. I’m not really worried about whether I get the [starting quarterback role, I just want to keep competing. I’m learning how to throw a tighter spiral and just how to bounce back from mistakes,” Emanuelson said. Emanuelson threw two touchdown passes to Diego Hurwitz, and one to Mateo Long and George Saunders. Hurwitz missed a portion of last season due to an injury, and he’s set to move up the Highlanders’ depth chart after the team lost its top two receivers from last season in Cash Panico and Jack Meyjes. “Last year, I was injured for half of the year and it required a lot of rebuilding. Ever since then, I’ve just been stepping up and seeing what I can do. I’ve been taking the lead on offense and I think it’s rubbing off on everyone,” Hurwitz said. Hurwitz and the receiver’s performance will be important toward taking the load off the quarterback position, along with returning rising senior Rehan Mumtaz at running back. “It’s definitely been an offseason of building and working on chemistry. We’ve been out here putting in work and building that chemistry, now it’s just taking it onto the field. I think our offense looks better than expected, we’re progressing really far since the start of the summer,” Hurwitz said. “I just want to give all the support for Cyrus. He’s really stepped it up and is showing leadership. He really wants to get better and showing a lot of commitment,” Mumtaz added. Mumtaz will be stepping into the No. 1 running back role following the graduation of Xavier Henderson. He had some big games filling in for Henderson last season, including a 162-yard, two touchdown performance in the 39-35 win over Washington. “I’m really looking for more consistency. articles.text: Yaxel Lendeborg speaks excitedly about the prospect of joining the Warriors and teaming up with Steph Curry. At the 2026 NBA draft, the Warriors walked away winners, drafting Michigan forward Yaxel Lendeborg in the first round (No. 11) and Florida State forward Lajae Jones (No. 54) in the second round. The Warriors got an experienced win-now player in Lendeborg who will be featured in big moments throughout the upcoming season. Draft expert and writer for The Athletic, Sam Veccine, “loved” the Warriors’ selection of Lendeborg. He believes Lendeborg is one of the most talented defenders in the class. His passing ability will make head coach Steve Kerr’s life much easier. His age is not a worry for the Warriors, who are trying to compete next season as Steph continues to age. “I think we’re excited to add Yaxel to the program,” said Warriors General Manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. “I think I said it a week or so ago that we felt like being at 11 we’d get a really good player, and I think we did. He’s a guy that we feel fits with our system right away. Obviously being a more older, mature player, those types of guys you can expect to come in and have more of an impact than maybe some of the younger guys.” Lendeborg averaged 15.1 points — on a 64.6 true shooting percentage — as well as 6.8 rebounds and 3.2 assists in his junior year at Michigan. He’s expected to make an immediate impact on the team next year. Lendeborg had this to say about joining the Warriors. “It’s a full-circle moment for me. In 2016, I was a big Kyrie Irving guy, so I used to hate Steph Curry,” said Lendeborg. “Now that I’m actually going to be able to be on the same team with him, play and actually learn so much from him, it means a lot. “He’s a very great guy, a genuine person. It’s going to be an honor to be able to watch what he does in person.” Curry responded on Instagram to Lendeborg, stating, “Let’s go! Welcome to the Bay! I’m going to work hard to be your new favorite player,” adding a cry-laughing emoji to the end. Many experts believed Lendeborg was a top-five player in the draft class, but he fell due to being an older prospect at age 23. The Warriors got an objective steal at 11th overall, a player who could be one of the most impactful role players in the NBA. The Warriors’ second-round pick is not as well known as Lendeborg, but still has the potential to make an impact. This past season, Jones averaged 12.7 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. His 3-point shooting went from 3.7 attempts per game at St. Bonaventure to 5.1 percent for Florida State, but his percentage dropped to 32.5 percent. He’s a 6-foot-7 wing weighing 220 pounds. With injuries to Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody, there is a hole in the Warriors’ wing depth, and Jones could fill that. Currently, the Warriors’ only wings on the roster are Gui Santos and Yaxel Lendeborg. Jones could immediately be that 3rd or 4th wing on the roster that could fill in if there is an injury to anyone above him. Given GM Dunleavy’s track record with second-round picks, I’m very intrigued to see if Jones can make a significant impact down the line. Overall, as a Warriors fan, I am very satisfied with the draft decisions and excited to see how they fit in next season.

articles.text: Men’s soccer team to face Bosnia-Herzegovina today Photo courtesy of US Soccer The United States is looking strong going into its Round of 32 match against Bosnia and Herzegovina today. The 2026 World Cup’s Group Stage has now concluded and we’re charging through the first few days of the Round of 32. The knockout stage has had a thrilling start, with two of the top European sides falling in penalty kicks after Paraguay stunned Germany 4-3, and Morocco took down the Netherlands 3-2 after both matches ended regulation in a 1-1 draw. As of Post time, Mexico vs. Ecuador was the only Round of 32 match to not concluded in Tuesday’s slate of games. So, how did the Post do with its Group Stage predictions? We successfully guessed 27 teams to reach the Round of 32, 11 of 12 group winners, seven runner ups, and four of eight thirdplace teams. The tournament’s expansion to 48 teams certainly paid off for FIFA, with Cinderella teams like Cape Verde, South Africa, Paraguay, and DR Congo reaching the knockout stage. Here’s taking a look at my predictions for the upcoming Round of 32 and 16 matches, starting with the United States. No. 15 United States vs. No. 61 Bosnia and Herzegovina (Wednesday, 5 p.m.) The United States’ potential route to the quarterfinals, which would be their farthest journey since 2002, got a little bit harder after Belgium took the lead of its group over Egypt. Initially, I had the U.S. losing to Belgium in the Round of 16, but as of this point, I’m buying the States’ stock. Belgium has looked mighty shaky through the Group Stage, and I’m unconvinced about the European side. But, the U.S. must first get through Bosnia, which is coming off a 3-1 win over Qatar to close the Group Stage. I think the Stars and Stripes will get it done in Santa Clara on Wednesday night in a 3-1 win. No. 4 England vs. No. 41 DR Congo (Wednesday, 9 a.m.) The DRC has been quite the story in this year’s World Cup, proving FIFA right in expanding this year’s tournament size. They reached their first World Cup in 52 years, and qualified for the knockout stage for the first time ever by taking third in their group after tying Portugal 1-1 and beating Uzbekistan 3-1. But, I think the Cinderella story is over. England win, 4-nil. No. 10 Belgium vs. No. 18 Senegal (Wednesday, 1 p.m.) This might be the most difficult game to predict. Both squads have underperformed and didn’t look its best until their final group stage match against their weakest opponents, where Senegal beat Iraq 5-nil and Belgium won 5-1 over New Zealand. Senegal has had the tougher route in its group against France and Norway, so I’m going with the upset. Senegal wins 2-1. No. 3 Spain vs. No. 23 Austria (Thursday, 12 p.m.) I’m still standing on my guess for Spain to reach the semifinals despite not looking as illustrious as expected. Spain wins 2-0. No. 8 Portugal vs. No. 13 Croatia (Thursday, 4 p.m.) This is another tough one to predict after Portugal underperformed to finish second in its group. Croatia is a scrappy bunch, but I’m taking the Portuguese in penalty kicks after a 1-1 draw through regulation and extra time. No. 16 Switzerland vs. No. 29 Algeria (Thursday, 8 p.m.) I like Switzerland’s depth here, although Algeria looked great in its 3-3 tie with Austria. I could see this going either way, but I’m taking Switzerland 2-1 in extra time. No. 26 Egypt vs. No. 28 Australia (Friday, 11 a.m.) Another toughie, but I like Egypt’s star-power with Mohammed Salah and Omar Marmoush. Egypt win 2-1. No. 2 Argentina vs. No. 64 Cape Verde (Friday, 3 p.m.) Cape Verde has been another great story, reaching the knockout stage by a nation of 550,000 for the very first World Cup appearance. But, they are running into a buzz saw with Messi and Argentina. Argentina wins 4-0, Messi scores two. No. 11 Colombia vs. No. 65 Ghana (Friday, 6:30 p.m.) I didn’t have Ghana making the knockout stage, so I’m not predicting them to go far. Colombia wins 2-nil. Round of 16; No. 6 Morocco vs. No. 30 Canada (Saturday, 10 a.m.) Morocco looked amazing in their R32 win over the Netherlands. The Dutch sat on their heels, seemingly looking to preserve its initial 1-nil lead and then make it to PKs. Morocco punished them, and I think they’ll dominate Canada. Morocco wins 3-1. Round of 16; No. 1 France vs. No. 34 Paraguay (Saturday, 2 p.m.) France is still my World Cup winners; Les Bleus win 3-1. Round of 16; No. 5 Brazil vs. No. 21 Norway (Sunday, 1 p.m.) This should be a fun one; both teams are high powered with Brazil’s athleticism and Norway boasting one of the world’s best scorers in Erling Haaland. Norway’s 2-1 win over Ivory Coast was its first knockout stage win, but I’m taking the Brazilians. Brazil wins in a thrilling 3-2 match. Photo courtesy of Olympics.com Paraguay stunned Germany by winning 4-3 in penalty kicks in the Round of 32.

articles.text: In this week’s Hiking with Jon column, the third of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe, we focus on Horsetail Falls Trail and its popular swimming hole. For Bay Area residents, the welcome sight of Horsetail Falls’ gushing waters off in the distance of U.S. 50 means you’ve nearly arrived at South Lake Tahoe. In Twin Bridges between Strawberry and the Sierra at Tahoe Resort along the El Dorado Freeway is a magnificent 500 foot tall waterfall cascading down Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from Stateline, Nevada and a worthy visit for readers considering vacationing in the area. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip. While hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek the trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The two mile mark puts you at around 750 feet in elevation gain while walking at over 6,100 feet. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks — proper footwear is required. Although our day ended at two miles, the trail continues up the mountain for another mile towards backpacking areas by the mouth of the falls. From there you can reach countless alpine lakes; Avalanche Lake is at the top of the falls. The entire trail is largely unmaintained, but keeping your Staff Photos Horsetail Falls in Desolation Wilderness is a 500 foot cascade down Pyramid Creek. It takes two miles of hiking, 750 feet in elevation gain. The hike along Pyramid Creek is just as majestic as the reward of reaching Horsetail Falls. Hikers can find countless areas to sit next to Pyramid Creek.
