Keep your eyes peeled for blue spray-painted trail markings on rocks, stumps, or the ground as you continue on the unmaintained trail. eyes on the beaten path is simple enough. There are also small blue-spray painted markings to keep hikers on the trail. Should hikers opt against making it all the way to the falls, there are countless areas to jump into the creek or sunbathe on the rocks. Beneath the falls is a popular swimming hole with ample space to jump, swim, or just wade. On a hot summer day, a dip into the cold fresh water is the perfect refresher before the return hike “The locals may be upset that you’re sharing this, it is really a treasured spot,” said Chad from Sacramento, who put on a display of dives into the swimming hole. Punch in “Pyramid Creek Trailhead” to access this hike’s parking lot, which is $10 for all day and overnight. This is the third of six features of popular trails around Lake Tahoe.

articles.text: Young Musicians Chorus: Collegium Musicum (USA) The female choral group Young Musicians Chorus will perform in this year’s Golden Gate International Choral Festival. Founded in 2020, the group has developed a reputation for strong musicianship, challenging repertoire, musical character, and subtlety of interpretation. Young Musicians Chorus’s spotlight performance will take place July 16 at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. Young Musicians Chorus Collegium, the most-advanced of Young Musicians Chorus’s 5 levels, has been featured as artists in concerts with the San Francisco Choral Society, Viva la Musica, SF Choral Artists, and San Francisco Boys Chorus, and was the representative choir for last spring’s Foundation for Kodály Music Educators demonstration and concert. Founder and artistic director Betsy Marvit has created high standards for youth choral singing through her tenure of over 25 years at San Francisco Boys Chorus. At the Crowden Music Center in Berkeley, she ran a choral program for over 12 years and developed a passion for teaching choral music to young musicians. Young Musicians Chorus is a community choir with a shared goal of musical beauty, fun, and challenge, in an atmosphere of acceptance. They pay special attention musically to the social issues their students care about. It’s a small organization supported by the local community and fueled by the enthusiasm and artistry of its students. The group previously participated in the 2023 Golden Gate International Choral Festival, winning silver in the contemporary division. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place locally from July 13 to July 18. articles.text: Into the Woods premieres July 11. Berkeley Playhouse brings the classic Grimm fairytale Into the Woods to audiences next month. The musical tells the story of a baker and his wife who attempt to lift a family curse and have a child. They are visited by a witch who promises she can fulfill the request, but on her terms only. The couple must travel into the nearby woods and search for four items: a cow as white as milk, a cape as red as blood, hair as yellow as corn, and a slipper as pure as gold. The production features a cast of familiar fairytale characters, like Rapunzel, Cinderella, Jack, and Little Red Riding Hood. Photo by Thomas Campitelli Music and lyrics are by Stephen Sondheim for this play adaptation of James Lapine’s book of the same name. Cast includes actors in grades 7 through 12, including Azalea Campbell, Mia Wong, Ernst Wang, Kimiko Bearde-Xisin, Sofie Donati, Brenda Gonzalez, Chase Wilcox, Lourdes Verde Lombardo, Taylor Petri, Nevo Naftalin-Kelman, Sawyer Ciruli, Harper Taylor, Piper Lilquist, Elise Talbot, Keila Reeves, Ella Smithers, Jayden McAdams and Maeve Dey-Toth. The play runs from July 11 through 19. Visit https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/event/into-thewoods/ to purchase tickets online. ®
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse Into the Woods premieres July 11

articles.text: Immersive exhibition “Creating Home” on view now Kids enjoy free admission with the purchase of an adult ticket this summer at Filoli. For a limited time, children under age 14 can visit Filoli’s historic estate and garden and view the nonprofit organization’s newest property-wide exhibition, “Creating Home,” which explores themes of home, habitat and belonging. “Creating Home,” on view throughout the summer, spans the historic estate’s gardens, house, redwood groves and natural campus, featuring interactive installations, storytelling experiences and educational programming designed to encourage visitors to engage with the people, animals and trees that shape the property. The centerpiece of the exhibition is a large-scale outdoor installation by California artist Jayson Fann. Constructed from naturally found wood and organic materials, the sculptural works are inspired by bird nests, tree hollows and other natural shelters found throughout the landscape. “This summer at Filoli is all about exploration, discovery, and inspiration,” Kara Newport, president and CEO of Filoli, said in a press release. “With ‘Creating Home,’ guests will uncover interactive installations inspired by the animals, trees, and stories that shape Filoli’s landscape, while ‘Kids Go Free’ makes it even easier for families to spend The centerpiece of the exhibition is a large-scale outdoor installation by artist Jayson Fann. the day outside together. From the gardens and historic house to the redwoods and trails, there’s something around every corner waiting to spark curiosity and joy.” The exhibition opens alongside Filoli’s Kids Go Free summer promotion, aimed at encouraging family visits throughout the season. Tickets must be reserved in advance online, and the offer is valid for daytime admission only. In addition to Fann’s outdoor installations, visitors will find immersive room displays inside the historic house highlighting the stories of staff members who helped shape Filoli. Other interactive elements include projected ballroom dance lessons, listening stations featuring imagined historic conversations and opportunities for guests to share family stories. Storytelling signage, daily staff talks and family-focused educational activities will also highlight local wildlife, notable trees and the ecosystems found across the estate. “I have worked with naturally found wood since early childhood, growing up along the Platte River,” Fann said. “This lifelong practice of listening deeply to the land, shaped by flowing water, wind, lightning, thunder, and the rhythms of the landscape, continues to inform my approach to nest building. In Creating Home, these elements come together to remind us that building, belonging, and care all arise through relationships with the world around us.” For more information, visit https://filoli.org/.
articles.title: Kids receive free admission at Filoli this summer

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is celebrating Agave in July, with speaker events, webinars, tours and workshops celebrating the iconic genus all throughout the month. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants, including Agave. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth when it was her private, personal garden. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. The garden is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Agave Fest celebrates one of Ruth’s most prized plants, native to the arid regions of North, South and Central Americas. See a list of daily events below. July 11 - Curator-led lector Ruth Bancroft Garden Curator Brian Kemble will share his insights on agaves as powerful focal point plants, the wide range of genera found in the nursery trade and the fascinating stories behind rare and unusual species. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees Brian Kemble thousands of agave and succulent species that grow in the garden’s three acres. Following the talk, a limited-capacity tour will offer an up-close look at select specimens, along with a special sale featuring rare agaves from Kemble’s private greenhouse. The lecture begins at 10 a.m. July 11 - Pop-up plant sale A curated selection of unique agaves from the private greenhouse collections of Ruth Bancroft Curator Brian Kemble and Garden Manager Walker Young will be available for purchase between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. July 18 - Mezcal tasting Join garden staff and agave experts for an evening guided tour focused on the “spirit” of agave. Produced primarily in Oaxaca and eight other regulated Mexican states, Mezcal is commonly made from the Espadín agave, but wild varieties like Tobalá and Tepeztate are also used. Kemble and Susan Coss, co-founder of Mezcalistas, lead the tour which precedes an assorted Mezcal tasting. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/agave-fest/ to learn more about Agave Fest.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft celebrates month-long Agave Fest in July

articles.text: Music at Kohl Mansion announced its 44th anniversary season, featuring eight performances by internationally acclaimed chamber music ensembles and artists from October 18, 2026 through May 2, 2027. The Burlingame concert series will present Sunday evening performances at 7 p.m., showcasing returning ensembles alongside debut appearances by several artists. Performances are held in the historic Kohl Mansion, also known as The Oaks, which was built in 1914 and is located at 2750 Adeline Drive in Burlingame. The mansion was listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its architecture and social and cultural significance to the local area in 1982, and provides a unique and intimate setting for chamber music concerts. “Our 44th season honors the rich traditions of chamber music while looking ahead to an exciting and dynamic future,” Music at Kohl Mansion Executive Director Patricia Kristof Moy said in a press release. “We are thrilled to welcome remarkable artists from across the United States and Europe and to invite audiences into the uniquely personal experience that chamber music offers.” Among the season highlights are the Music at Kohl Mansion debuts of the Neave Trio on November 15 and the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet on January 17, 2027. The Neave Trio will perform a program featuring works by early 20th-century Croatian composer Dora Pejačević, while the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet will present the local premiere of Hard Winter/ Holler and Stomp by violist and composer Kenji Bunch. The season will also include a holiday program by the Philharmonia Baroque Chamber Players and conclude May 2 with an encore presentation of Intonations: Songs from the Violins of Hope, commissioned by Music at Kohl Mansion and premiered in 2020. The work by composer Jake Heggie and librettist Gene Scheer will be performed by the Miró Quartet with mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz. “Every performance becomes a shared journey between artists and listeners,” Moy said. “Just as important, we remain committed to extending that experience beyond the concert hall through collaborations with community partners, bringing the transformative power of live music to people of all ages and backgrounds throughout our region.” Season tickets are available online at www.musicatkohl.org. Performances are held in the historic Kohl Mansion.
articles.title: Music at Kohl Mansion announces 44th chamber music season

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, July 1, 2026 The Musical Gourmet Adventurous dining By Joseph Gold Summer is upon us. Before we set out on the road to adventure, let’s have a look at some excellent cuisine with adventurous names. There are some pretty crazy foods out there. Some of the names can even scare you. Others will make you laugh. Some suggest a double meaning. Just to get you thinking, would you order Stinco if you see it on the menu? Despite its name, this is one of the most delicious dishes in Italy. It is a braised shank of beef, pork or lamb, and very similar to osso buco. In Scotland, there is a similar recipe which is known as Cullen skink. Fragrant yes…odorous, no. Some foods have a side story which is very humorous. When President Kennedy made a speech in the German city of Berlin, he said “today I am a Berliner.” The immediate reaction of some of The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet the people was a subdued laugh. Then they cheered. The reason that they laughed was because he actually said “today I am a jelly donut.” “A Berliner” is a jelly donut. What he should’ve said is: Ich bin Berliner. The Germans leave out the article “ein”. Other foods seem to imply personal characteristics. Two of them are “jerk“ and “haggis.”. Close on their heels are the violence of “poke and punch.” Animals might enter the picture when you are in Wales and you order Welsh rarebit (pronounced “rabbit”). This delicious cheese dish was a specialty of my mother. Some foods sound scatological. The eastern European Jewish dumpling known as Kreplach is notable. I was in a French restaurant and the Maître D pronounced crepe as “crap.” This is a Persian eggplant dish and he wasn’t Kuku. Other excellent foods have suggestive names. “Bulgur”, cock-aleekie, and matzah balls suggest other things. A woman who has served matzah balls wondered how large the animal was. Can you imagine how a mafioso would order mofongo. It sounds like an Italian insult. In reality it is a Puerto Rican type of plantain. Open the vindaloo for some fresh air. Your adventure is about to begin. What? You have objections? Well… If you don’t like it, you can “lumpia.” All of the above are “njoki” and that’s no joke, especially when you are in Yugoslavia. So enjoy your plate of dumplings. To paraphrase the advice of a noted travel expert… keep eating. Photo courtesy of Luca Trovato / Serious Eats Despite its name, stinco is a delightfully, fragrant Italian dish. It is a braised shank of meat similar to osso buco. The Neave Trio will perform a program featuring works by early 20th-century Croatian composer Dora Pejačević, while the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet will present the local premiere of Hard Winter/ Holler and Stomp by violist and composer Kenji Bunch. The season will also include a holiday program by the Philharmonia Baroque Chamber Players and conclude May 2 with an encore presentation of Intonations: Songs from the Violins of Hope, commissioned by Music at Kohl Mansion and premiered in 2020. The work by composer Jake Heggie and librettist Gene Scheer will be performed by the Miró Quartet with mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz. “Every performance becomes a shared journey between artists and listeners,” Moy said. “Just as important, we remain committed to extending that experience beyond the concert hall through collaborations with community partners, bringing the transformative power of live music to people of all ages and backgrounds throughout our region.” Season tickets are available online at www.musicatkohl.org. Coming up, Summer & Fall: Remember that we have many behind-the-scenes activities supporting the arts but not open to the public (rehearsals, trainings, etc.) as well as Recreation Department summer camps during the summer. However, we will have changing art exhibits back-to-back throughout the Summer and Fall months, as well as occasional concerts and events: Save these dates Thursday, August 13: Nathan and Jessie (swinging jazzy folk-style music with resonator guitars) Friday, August 14: Sonny Leyland and Danny Coots (with boogie-woogie, ragtime, stride & classic jazz) Sunday, August 16: Piedmont Chamber Players present Music for Summer Sunday, September 6: Sono-Musette brings Parisian singer Mimi Pirard to take us all back to 1900’s Paris Saturday, September 19: local star pianist Carl Blake presents a Mexican colleague, Ezequiel Barrera Sunday, September 27: Festival Opera Association’s first of three Vocal Salons Saturday, October 3: Mads Tolling returns, this time with Bruce Forman and his jazz guitar Sunday, October 25: Festival Opera Association’s second of three Vocal Salons Saturday, November 14: our first performance by Voci Women’s Vocal Ensemble, founded in 1991 Sunday, November 22: Festival Opera Association’s third of three Vocal Salons Watch this space and our website Join our mailing list & donate. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. 801 Magnolia Avenue • Piedmont, Calif. info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Performances are held in the historic Kohl Mansion.

articles.text: Movies about journalism often miss their mark. But The Post gets it just right, placing it in the same realm as what was a superb film about the Boston Diocese pedophilia scandal titled Spotlight. And there was, of course, a film that will be forever memorable, the iconic All the President’s Men. But what makes The Post so significant is, ultimately, not the story or the actors (Tom Hanks and Meryl Streep are excellent as Ben Bradlee, editor, and Katherine Graham, owner of the paper) but the timeless context. In other words, though it takes place in 1971, the importance of a free press today is as relevant as it was then. Perhaps more so. The press, also known as the Fourth Estate, is as essential to a vital and robust democracy as are the other three branches of government. In 1971, Richard Nixon loathed the press, especially the Post and the NY Times. As one character says emphatically (Bruce Greenwood as Robert McNamara), if you print the story you are now in possession of, Nixon will use all of the power of his presidency to destroy your paper. He spoke those words to Katherine Graham who understood that the decision facing her – whether to publish what became known as The Pentagon Papers, and, in the aggregate, demonstrated that the government had been lying about Vietnam for decades. Printing the story would clearly place the paper in harm’s way, a paper that had been in her family since the 1930s. The backstory/source was a Rand Corp employee, Daniel Ellsberg (Matthew Rhys), who stole and then leaked the Papers (commissioned by McNamara), initially, to the New York Times in June of 1971. After a fraction of their content was published over three days, the Nixon administration was granted a court order preventing the Times from continuing. It was then that Ellsberg turned to the Post and made Tom Hanks and Meryl Streep in The Post

Like NIMH, it’s a wonderfully animated adventure film, layered with award-winning songs and focused on a 7-year-old mouse named Fievel Mousekewitz. The year is 1885, and Fievel’s journey begins in Russia where his family – Papa Mouskevitz (Nehemiah Persoff), Mama Mousekevitz (Patricia Vohn), and Tanya Mousekevitz (Amy Green) – is attacked by Cossacks and cats; their home is burned down. Fleeing Russia, they manage to board a tramp steamer on its way to America, where they believe there are no cats. During a thunderstorm, Fievel is separated from his family and washed overboard. His family is distraught, believing that Fievel is lost forever. But remarkably he is safely ensconced in a bottle, and washes up in the harbor of New York City where his quest to find his parents begins. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) free community-gathering evening event series “Friday Nights” returns next week, July 10, with live music performances, food concessions and late-night museum access. OMCA hosts free community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax in the museum’s large outdoor space, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Blankets are available for loan from the museum. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and MXKA performs at OMCA next week. Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. San Leandro-based artist MXKA performs on July 10, delivering regional Mexican rhythms and R&B vocals. A Cumbia Wepa dance lesson led by Mireille Ruiz takes place throughout the evening. Visitors can also participate in an art-making activation led by artist Jason Powell-Smith, browse and purchase original artworks and special-edition pieces, meet other artists and staff, and learn more about NIAD Art Center’s work supporting professional artists with disabilities. The event is free, no advance registration is required. Visit https://museumca.org/about-friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid/ for more information.
articles.title: OMCA’s “Friday Nights” returns July 10

articles.text: July is beaming at the Bookmark bookstore, which plays a vital role in supporting the Oakland Public Library. The Bookmark’s brick and mortar location is in Old Oakland at 933 Broadway and has upcoming sales for books, comics and more physical media treasures. Speaking of sunshine, enjoy another extended shopping day with us during Old Oakland’s Summer Stroll on Friday, July 24, when the Bookmark will stay OPEN LATE until 7:30 p.m. alongside local merchants and food vendors. Check out the neighborhood’s family-friendly funtivities, and stop by the store to enjoy our “Buy 2, Get 1 Free” mix & match deal on dollar items, including books, media, comics, magazines, and more! We’re looking forward to our next Monthly Member Sale on Saturday, July 18. Save the date! Members receive 50% off on Saturday from 11 a.m.-6 p.m.; everyone receives 30% off on Sunday, July 20 from 11 a.m.-5 p.m.. Want a unique way to share your love of libraries this year? Give the gift of Membership with the Friends of the Oakland Public Library! Members receive 20% off at the Bookmark all year, plus 50% off at monthly Member sales. All proceeds support the Oakland Public Library. Please Note: Purchases are now limited to 100 items/day* per customer or party (no scanners permitted). The Monday after our monthly sale is Bulk Buyer Day, when customers may use scanners to buy unlimited items and receive 30% off when spending $500 or more (pre-discount). Our next Bulk Buyer Day is Monday, July 20. This July, we’re also excited about our Celebrating Inclusion curation at the store in honor of Disability Pride Month and the enactment of the Americans with Disabilities Act on July 26, 1990. DPM recognizes the history, experiences, and achievements of the disability community and also raises awareness of ongoing ableist barriers. Join us in commemorating this historic day and celebrating diverse abilities, neurodivergence, equity, and accessibility! Whether or not you’re feeling patriotic this Fourth of July, we’re celebrating revolutionary figures, movements, and inventions — including things that revolve in an actual circle — with our special in-store “It’s Revolutionary” curation. Snag a fascinating non-fiction find about innovation, rebellion, or something with wheels! Please note, the Bookmark will be closed on Saturday, July 4 in honor of Independence Day, and open again on Sunday, July 5 for our monthly Mahjong event: watch, learn, and play for FREE every first Sunday from 12-5 p.m. While we’re closed for the 4th, peruse our eBay store for more eclectic finds not available in-person at the Bookmark, and don’t miss our seasonal collections on bookshop.org. articles.text: Nuclear Physicist, Navy Captain, Lawyer, and Academic George Malcolm Moore was a nuclear physicist, a Navy Captain, a lawyer, and an academic. His unique combination of knowledge and experience allowed him to reach and impact people across the globe. He passed away peacefully on June 23rd, 2026, after a multiple-year battle with cancer with his family at his side at his home in Piedmont, CA. George was born in Berkeley, CA at Alta Bates Hospital, the same hospital where his mother and later his children were born. He grew up in a Navy family, living primarily in Oakland, Monterey, and Coronado and attending 13 different schools before graduating high school. As a young man he distinguished himself as both a scholar and an athlete. After graduating Coronado High School in 1962, he entered the U.S. Naval Academy where he finished first academically in the class of 1966, earning prizes for mathematics, chemistry, physics, and history. As an athlete he excelled at football, rowing, track and field, and golf. George had a lifelong enthusiasm for aviation and dreamed of being a fighter pilot before vision deterioration forced a change in his trajectory. George was a Fulbright Scholar at the University of Amsterdam, obtained a PhD in nuclear engineering from UC Berkeley, and served on active duty in Vietnam before transitioning to the Navy Reserve and working for the Department of Energy at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. In his lab career he focused on weapons design and countering nuclear and terrorism threats, taking particular joy in his work with the Nuclear Emergency Support Team. As a Captain in the Naval Reserve George led a Mobile Inshore Undersea Warfare Unit, a Commissioned Naval Unit, and a Fleet Training Group Detachment. George left the lab to obtain his law degree from UC Berkeley and pursued a career as a defense attorney in both energy and aviation litigation, practicing as an in-house counsel for the Pacific Gas and Electric Company and later as a partner at the aviation litigation firm Kenny and Markowitz in San Francisco. It was during this period he and his wife, Stella Kennedy, raised their children Greg and Sarah Moore in Piedmont, CA. Following 9/11 George returned to Livermore Lab and then transitioned to the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna, Austria, focusing his diplomatic work on nuclear nonproliferation and security. He later became a Scientist in Residence at the Middlebury Institute for International Studies in Monterey, CA where he taught and published on nuclear nonproliferation, security, and drone technology. His work during this period gave him the opportunity to travel the world with Stella which they enjoyed immensely. His contributions will continue through his students who now work in government agencies, the United Nations, universities, think tanks, military and law enforcement units, and nonprofits worldwide. As a father George was a devoted coach, scouting volunteer, and unfailing attendee of Greg and Sarah’s many sporting, scouting, and performing arts events. He was enduringly supportive of Greg and Sarah’s many pursuits and provided constant encouragement for their growth and exploration. He was noted by his family for possessing a remarkable ability to connect with animals and small children. George loved dogs and had a special affection for the Boxer breed, which he raised, bred, and showed. He was an avid amateur pilot and a licensed nuclear reactor engineer. George is survived by his wife of 46 years, Stella Kennedy, of Piedmont, CA, his son Greg Moore of Davis, CA, his daughter Sarah Moore of Falls Church, VA, and his Boxer Hattie. He will be laid to rest in Arlington National Cemetery. In lieu of a service, those wishing to share any memories or reflections on George for the family are encouraged to send any thoughts, photos, or recordings to george.m.moore.memorial@ gmail.com.
articles.title: George Malcolm Moore

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Janet Mendenhall died at her home in Walnut Creek on April 9, 2026. She was 105. Born on December 15, 1920 in Carbondale, Pennsylvania, she was the daughter of Orville and Elsie Ackerly. Her siblings were Helen, William, and Francis. During her elementary school years, the family moved to Piedmont, California, where Janet attended Wildwood Elementary School, Piedmont High School and ultimately graduated from the University of California in Berkeley with a degree in geography. After graduation, she joined the Marine Corps and was stationed at the weather station in Cherry Point, North Carolina working for the OSS. Upon return to Piedmont, she met Charles I. Mendenhall through the Piedmont Community Church choir. They married in 1951 and had two children, Bryce and Jan. Janet is survived by her daughter, Jan Moestue and her grandchildren Benjamin and Amylia. She was also blessed with three step great grandchilJanet Alice Mendenhall dren Brayden, Aiden and Ellie. She is predeceased by her husband, Charles and her son Bryce. Janet lived in Rossmoor for the last 23 years and was a strong supporter of the Diablo Valley Symphony. A memorial service will be held on Saturday, July 18 at 1 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church. Janet was a member of the church from age 16 to 105 years old. A life of love and strength, she was an inspiration to all who knew her.

articles.text: Tamra C. Hege, age 87, died peacefully at St. Paul’s Tower after a lengthy battle with congestive heart failure. She was born in Concord, CA June 18, 1938, to Florence Gertrude Kennerly Cummings and William Louis Cummings. Tamra graduated in 1960 from UC Berkeley with a zoology degree and later received a master’s degree in liberal studies from Mills College in 1997. She taught high school science at Hamlin’s School in San Francisco from 1962-1967. She moved to Piedmont in 1972 and was a lifelong volunteer for numerous organizations including Piedmont School Board (1982-1990), Piedmont Planning Commission (2001- 2007), Member of the Oakla nd Mu seu m’s Women’s Board (1999-present, President 2007-2009), Piedmont League of Women Voters (President 1980-1981, 1992-1994, 2010- 2012), and active member of Lake Merritt United Methodist Church. She was married to Dr. John Steele Hege for 56 years. They enjoyed a lifetime of backpacking, sailing, and raising three children. Tamra is survived by her daughters Laura Goodale (Michael) and Anne Hege (Grant Tompkins), and her five grandchildren Matt Goodale, Chris Goodale (Sydney), Dorothea Tompkins, Vera Tompkins, and Johnnie Tompkins. She was predeceased by her husband John Steele Hege in 2017 and her son John Raymond Hege of the Oakland Police Department who was killed in the line of duty in 2009. Tamra is also survived by two sisters Lana Laessig and Erin Wells (Larry), as well as her brother Ross Cummings (Andrea) and two nephews. A memorial service will be held on Saturday, July 11th, 2026, at 3 pm at the Lake Merritt United Methodist Church, 1255 First Ave, Oakland, CA 94606. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Friends of the Oakland Public Library or the Oakland Museum of California.
articles.title: Tamra Hege dies at age 87

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, July 1, 2026 Obituaries George Malcolm Moore 1944 – 2026 Nuclear Physicist, Navy Captain, Lawyer, and Academic George Malcolm Moore was a nuclear physicist, a Navy Captain, a lawyer, and an academic. His unique combination of knowledge and experience allowed him to reach and impact people across the globe. He passed away peacefully on June 23rd, 2026, after a multiple-year battle with cancer with his family at his side at his home in Piedmont, CA. George was born in Berkeley, CA at Alta Bates Hospital, the same hospital where his mother and later his children were born. He grew up in a Navy family, living primarily in Oakland, Monterey, and Coronado and attending 13 different schools before graduating high school. As a young man he distinguished himself as both a scholar and an athlete. After graduating Coronado High School in 1962, he entered the U.S. Naval Academy where he finished first academically in the class of 1966, earning prizes for mathematics, chemistry, physics, and history. As an athlete he excelled at football, rowing, track and field, and golf. George had a lifelong enthusiasm for aviation and dreamed of being a fighter pilot before vision deterioration forced a change in his trajectory. George was a Fulbright Scholar at the University of Amsterdam, obtained a PhD in nuclear engineering from UC Berkeley, and served on active duty in Vietnam before transitioning to the Navy Reserve and working for the Department of Energy at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. In his lab career he focused on weapons design and countering nuclear and terrorism threats, taking particular joy in his work with the Nuclear Emergency Support Team. As a Captain in the Naval Reserve George led a Mobile Inshore Undersea Warfare Unit, a Commissioned Naval Unit, and a Fleet Training Group Detachment. George left the lab to obtain his law degree from UC Berkeley and pursued a career as a defense attorney in both energy and aviation litigation, practicing as an in-house counsel for the Pacific Gas and Electric Company and later as a partner at the aviation litigation firm Kenny and Markowitz in San Francisco. It was during this period he and his wife, Stella Kennedy, raised their children Greg and Sarah Moore in Piedmont, CA. Following 9/11 George returned to Livermore Lab and then transitioned to the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna, Austria, focusing his diplomatic work on nuclear nonproliferation and security. He later became a Scientist in Residence at the Middlebury Institute for International Studies in Monterey, CA where he taught and published on nuclear nonproliferation, security, and drone technology. His work during this period gave him the opportunity to travel the world with Stella which they enjoyed immensely. His contributions will continue through his students who now work in government agencies, the United Nations, universities, think tanks, military and law enforcement units, and nonprofits worldwide. As a father George was a devoted coach, scouting volunteer, and unfailing attendee of Greg and Sarah’s many sporting, scouting, and performing arts events. He was enduringly supportive of Greg and Sarah’s many pursuits and provided constant encouragement for their growth and exploration. He was noted by his family for possessing a remarkable ability to connect with animals and small children. George loved dogs and had a special affection for the Boxer breed, which he raised, bred, and showed. He was an avid amateur pilot and a licensed nuclear reactor engineer. George is survived by his wife of 46 years, Stella Kennedy, of Piedmont, CA, his son Greg Moore of Davis, CA, his daughter Sarah Moore of Falls Church, VA, and his Boxer Hattie. He will be laid to rest in Arlington National Cemetery. In lieu of a service, those wishing to share any memories or reflections on George for the family are encouraged to send any thoughts, photos, or recordings to george.m.moore.memorial@ gmail.com. articles.text: In the heart of Napa Valley’s Calistoga region, Davis Estates represents the blending of Napa’s historic past with a modern vision for the future. Built on a century-old vineyard property along the Silverado Trail, the family-owned winery has transformed a historic site into one of Napa Valley’s newest destinations for fine wine, hospitality, and estategrown Cabernet Sauvignon. The story of Davis Estates begins with Mike Davis, whose lifelong connection to Napa Valley inspired a dream of creating a world-class family winery. In 2011, Davis and his family purchased the historic estate and began an ambitious restoration project, revitalizing the property while preserving its character and agricultural heritage. The winery officially opened as Davis Estates in 2014. Today, the 155-acre Calistoga estate showcases the dramatic diversity of Napa Valley’s northern landscape. Rising from the valley floor to elevations of more than 1,100 feet, the property includes volcanic soils, varied microclimates, and hillside terrain that provide ideal conditions for growing premium Bordeaux varieties, especially Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and Merlot. Davis Estates has earned attention for its commitment to producing elegant, age-worthy wines with a strong sense of place. The winery has worked with acclaimed winemaking talent, including Philippe Melka, whose Bordeau x-i nspi red approach emphasizes vineyard expression and careful craftsmanship. Beyond the wines, Davis Estates offers visitors an experience that celebrates Napa Valley’s history and hospitality. Guests can enjoy tastings overlooking the vineyards, explore the restored historic barn, visit the caves, and experience food-andwine pairings designed to highlight the estate’s wines. While many Napa wineries trace their roots back generations, Davis Estates represents a different kind of legacy: a family’s determination to restore a historic property and create something lasting. With its combination of heritage, sustainability, and world-class Cabernet, Davis Estates has quickly become a distinctive voice in the continuing story of Napa Valley wine. The Davis family uses them here to craft a highly aromatic charming rose. It is medium cherry-pink color and soft aromas of peaches, strawberries, watermelon and floral notions. The medium-bodied palate is packed with juicy berry flavors, and it finishes full of flavor. A perfect aperitif. • 2023 Davis Estates Sauvignon Blanc, $55 The Davis Sauvignon Blanc leads with a soft nose of honeysuckle and brine, green apples and pears. Davis Estates 4060 Silverado Trail N Calistoga, CA94515 (707) 9420700 • 2025 Davis Estates Lily Fleur Rose, $53 Pinot Noir grapes, because of their high cost, are not usually used for rose wine. The Davis family uses them here to craft a highly aromatic charming rose. It is medium cherry-pink color and soft aromas of peaches, strawberries, watermelon and floral notions. The medium-bodied palate is packed with juicy berry flavors, and it finishes full of flavor. A perfect aperitif. • 2023 Davis Estates Sauvignon Blanc, $55 The Davis Sauvignon Blanc leads with a soft nose of honeysuckle and brine, green apples and pears. In the mouth the wine The Davis Estates lineup is wide ranging. One of the outdoor seating areas for wine tasting. is tightly coiled and yet textured and plush. The length of flavor is long and lingering on the clean, supple finish. Perfect with any type of fish or shellfish. • 2024 Davis Estates Chardonnay, $68 The wine opens with streaks of jasmine and hay over a core of peach and apricot, and as it spends time in the glass it blossoms to reveal alluring spicy and herbal undertones. The medium-bodied palate is refreshing and gently creamy, with restrained apple and melon fruit and a long, floral finish. • 2024 Davis Estates Pinot Noir. $90 The Davis Pinot Noir comes from a vineyard in the Carneros AVA a very cool spot at the southern end of Napa Valley. It offers a complex nose of strawberries, cherries, and earth with underlying lavender, and dried herbs hints. Medium-bodied and elegantly styled in the mouth, it has a very fine structure of gentle tannins and refreshing acidity supporting the intense red fruit and earth flavors, finishing long and layered. • 2022 Davis Estates “Rhys” Merlot, $95 Rhys has a medium to deep ruby color and slowly blossoming aromas of black cherries and blueberries, sage, violet, cured meats, and thyme . The full-bodied palate has a fine, grainy tannic frame, detailed, perfumed fruits and a long, elegant finish. Very classy! • 2022 Davis Estates Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley. $90 The Napa Valley Cab blossoms in the glass to reveal scents of blackberry, cocoa , tobacco leaves, dried roses and spice. The full-bodied palate is bursting with nuanced, layered flavors. It’s framed by velvety tannins and vibrant acidity and has a long, succulent finish. It’s open and ready to drink, though it should age gracefully in the cellar over the next 10-15 years. • 2021 Davis Estates Cabernet Sauvignon Calistoga, $155 This is one of their flagship Cabernets and is a step up in intensity from the wine above. It’s full-bodied, rich and concentrated, a powerful and intense example of Calistoga AVA Cabernet that’s framed by plush tannins. The oak is perfectly balanced with the blackberry fruit and the wine shows great length and structure. Enjoy it over the next two decades. • 2022 Davis Estates “Zephyr”, $135 This Bordeaux blend is made from Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petite Verdot and Malbec. Wafting from the glass with a dramatic, perfumed bouquet of wild berries and cassis mingled with notions of violets, and licorice, framed by nicely integrated oak. Full-bodied, layered and seamless, it’s deep and multidimensional, with lively acids, beautifully refined tannins and a long, resonant finish. • 2014 Davis Estates “Pinwheel” Late Harvest Cabernet Franc, $85 The difficult thing when making dessert wine is to keep it from being cloying. They have succeeded here. This dense purple-colored wine possesses copious amounts of ripe, pure, blackcherry fruit, full body, excellent freshness and liveliness, and a long, clean, stylish palate. It should drink well for many, many years. Davis Estates is mostly known for its outstanding Cabernet Sauvignons.

Wishart founded the California Electric Crematory and California Memorial Columbarium on the present site, which had been a trolley station. Some walkers recalled of chapels, gardens, cloisters, atriums, and alcoves, including three terraced indoor gardens, blending Moorish, Romanesque, and Gothic elements complemented by European art. Throughout the columbarium, walls resemble bookshelves packed with urns shaped like books behind locked glass, their spines bearing names and dates that offer the most basic summaries of each life. articles.text: Alaska Mission Trip exceeds expectations What happens when you send a group of students more than 2,000 miles from home to serve others, experience a new culture, and grow in their faith? From June 5–12, a team of students and leaders from Piedmont Community Church set out to answer that question in Fairbanks, Alaska, as part of a pilot mission trip that may help shape the future of student missions at our church. Designed as a “beta test” for a potential new annual high school mission experience, the trip provided students with opportunities to serve the local community, learn about Alaska’s unique history and cultures, build lasting friendships, and discover how God can work through ordinary acts of service in extraordinary ways. For many years our Mexico Mission Trip was a cornerstone experience for students. However, increasing logistical challenges and changing policies among key partners led us to begin exploring new opportunities that would continue to provide meaningful service, faith formation, and cultural engagement. This year, a small group of students familiar with our church and community were invited to participate and provide candid feedback on whether Alaska could become the future home of our annual high school mission trip. Meri Schreiber splits firewood for a Fairbanks resident during Piedmont Community Church’s Alaska Mission Trip. Under the guidance of Next Step Ministries staff member Ava, students helped prepare and stack wood to help local residents stay warm through the Alaskan winter. Another important consideration was accessibility. One of our goals in evaluating future mission opportunities is ensurIncoming seniors Evie Hicks, Cora Brozowski-Schrader, and Clara Shum share a smile during Piedmont Community Church’s Alaska Mission Trip. ing that as many students as possible can participate. The Alaska trip was offered at a significantly lower price point than many traditional mission experiences, helping reduce financial barriers while still providing a meaningful week of service, spiritual growth, cultural learning, and community impact. As we look toward the future, creating opportunities that are both transformational and accessible remains a priority. Partnering with Next Step Ministries, a national organization that creates Christ-centered service experiences for students, our team spent three days working alongside residents and community organizations throughout Fairbanks. Students served at the Fairbanks Rescue Mission, where they power washed buildings, planted flowers, raked grounds, and sorted donations. They also worked directly with local residents, cutting, splitting, and stacking firewood, clearing brush, and helping prepare properties for the long Alaskan winter. One of the most memorable projects involved splitting and stacking approximately three cords of firewood at each of two homes. Both residents shared that the wood would help carry them through the harsh Alaskan winter—a powerful reminder that simple acts of service can have a lasting impact. One of the most meaningful aspects of the week was the opportunity to work alongside the people of Fairbanks rather than simply for them. Through conversations, shared meals, and service projects, students gained a deeper understanding of the community and the challenges many residents face. For Clara Shum, a soon-to-be senior who also participated in Piedmont Community Church’s Mexico Mission Trip, the experience highlighted the connection between service and community impact.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church tests new tradition

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers movies in a comfortable setting, with lively discussion afterwards. This July’s selection is American Graffiti, a coming-of-age portrayal of the 1962 teen hot-rod cruising culture. Director George Lucas wrote the film based on his experience during his high school years in Modesto. To develop a film from this period Lucas received encouragement from Francis Coppola to both direct and write the screenplay. Coppola agreed to produce the film and satisfy the financial concerns Universal Studios had for Lucas, then an unknown filmmaker. Written in just 3 weeks and filmed mostly in Petaluma, the film was nominated for 5 Oscars and grossed $61 million with a $750,000 budget. The movie uses little-known actors who later became major stars. The screenplay works well because it cleverly pairs up characters who are opposites. Terry the Toad (Charles Martin Smith), the lovable but clumsy nerd, spends the evening with Debby (Candy Clark), the “fast” girl, who isn’t exactly the sharpest tool in the shed. Meanwhile, John Milner (Paul Le Mat), tough guy, hot-rod cruiser, babysits Carol (Mackenzie Phillips), the funny, precocious, pre-teen. Then there’s Curt (Richard Dreyfuss), a cleancut kid and budding intellectual on his way to college, searching for the hot blond in a Thunderbird, but instead gets adopted by a group of hoodlums from the Pharaohs gang. pages.text: Wednesday, July 1, 2026 25 Piedmont Community Church tests new tradition Alaska Mission Trip exceeds expectations By Kerry Persichitte What happens when you send a group of students more than 2,000 miles from home to serve others, experience a new culture, and grow in their faith? From June 5–12, a team of students and leaders from Piedmont Community Church set out to answer that question in Fairbanks, Alaska, as part of a pilot mission trip that may help shape the future of student missions at our church. Designed as a “beta test” for a potential new annual high school mission experience, the trip provided students with opportunities to serve the local community, learn about Alaska’s unique history and cultures, build lasting friendships, and discover how God can work through ordinary acts of service in extraordinary ways. For many years our Mexico Mission Trip was a cornerstone experience for students. However, increasing logistical challenges and changing policies among key partners led us to begin exploring new opportunities that would continue to provide meaningful service, faith formation, and cultural engagement. This year, a small group of students familiar with our church and community were invited to participate and provide candid feedback on whether Alaska could become the future home of our annual high school mission trip. Meri Schreiber splits firewood for a Fairbanks resident during Piedmont Community Church’s Alaska Mission Trip. Under the guidance of Next Step Ministries staff member Ava, students helped prepare and stack wood to help local residents stay warm through the Alaskan winter. Another important consideration was accessibility. One of our goals in evaluating future mission opportunities is ensurIncoming seniors Evie Hicks, Cora Brozowski-Schrader, and Clara Shum share a smile during Piedmont Community Church’s Alaska Mission Trip. The Alaska trip was offered at a significantly lower price point than many traditional mission experiences, helping reduce financial barriers while still providing a meaningful week of service, spiritual growth, cultural learning, and community impact. As we look toward the future, creating opportunities that are both transformational and accessible remains a priority. Partnering with Next Step Ministries, a national organization that creates Christ-centered service experiences for students, our team spent three days working alongside residents and community organizations throughout Fairbanks. Students served at the Fairbanks Rescue Mission, where they power washed buildings, planted flowers, raked grounds, and sorted donations. They also worked directly with local residents, cutting, splitting, and stacking firewood, clearing brush, and helping prepare properties for the long Alaskan winter. One of the most memorable projects involved splitting and stacking approximately three cords of firewood at each of two homes. Both residents shared that the wood would help carry them through the harsh Alaskan winter—a powerful reminder that simple acts of service can have a lasting impact. One of the most meaningful aspects of the week was the opportunity to work alongside the people of Fairbanks rather than simply for them. Through conversations, shared meals, and service projects, students gained a deeper understanding of the community and the challenges many residents face. For Clara Shum, a soon-to-be senior who also participated in Piedmont Community Church’s Mexico Mission Trip, the experience highlighted the connection between service and community impact. PIEDMONT FLIX FEST American Graffiti shown July 9 at Center for the Arts By Gerry Gragg One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers movies in a comfortable setting, with lively discussion afterwards. This July’s selection is American Graffiti, a coming-of-age portrayal of the 1962 teen hot-rod cruising culture. Director George Lucas wrote the film based on his experience during his high school years in Modesto. To develop a film from this period Lucas received encouragement from Francis Coppola to both direct and write the screenplay. Coppola agreed to produce the film and satisfy the financial concerns Universal Studios had for Lucas, then an unknown filmmaker. Written in just 3 weeks and filmed mostly in Petaluma, the film was nominated for 5 Oscars and grossed $61 million with a $750,000 budget. The movie uses little-known actors who later became major stars. The screenplay works well because it cleverly pairs up characters who are opposites. Terry the Toad (Charles Martin Smith), the lovable but clumsy nerd, spends the evening with Debby (Candy Clark), the “fast” girl, who isn’t exactly the sharpest tool in the shed. Meanwhile, John Milner (Paul Le Mat), tough guy, hot-rod cruiser, babysits Carol (Mackenzie Phillips), the funny, precocious, pre-teen. Then there’s Curt (Richard Dreyfuss), a cleancut kid and budding intellectual on his way to college, searching for the hot blond in a Thunderbird, but instead gets adopted by a group of hoodlums from the Pharaohs gang. Finally, Laurie and Steve (Cindy Williams and Ron Howard), the Homecoming Queen and popular jock are in crisis mode regarding their high school romance. Steve is looking to spread his wings in college the coming year. The conflict almost turns into a disaster when Laurie gets into a hot rod driven by the reckless street racer Bob Falfa (Harrison Ford). Who was the personality that unified all the scenes and stories? Lucas recruited legendary late-night disk jockey Wolfman Jack, played by himself, as the beloved radio voice among teens nationwide. His mysterious voice throughout the soundtrack guided them as they cruised through the night, creating a sense of closeness as he called out dedications, introduced new sounds, and spun away rock-and-roll tunes. American Graffiti stands out because it used the 1960s Top 40 rock and roll hits to tell the story. By pairing each scene with a song, the soundtrack truly brings the spirit of the 60s to life. The film ends with an epilogue scroll that answers the question we all ask ourselves at our class reunions, “Whatever happened to….?” Common to each character listed are the role reversals they experienced after graduating from high school, matching Lucas’s own switch from auto mechanic to filmmaker. American Graffiti will be screened on Thursday, July 9, at 1 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone over age 18. The next movie will be Finding Forrester, a 2000 drama to be shown on August 13 at the normal time of 1 p.m. American Graffiti, written and directed by George Lucas, starring Richard Dreyfuss and Candy Clark.

articles.text: Happy July! One of Piedmont’s most popular and enduring events is coming right up. It is our annual FOURTH OF JULY PARADE. This year’s event, starting at 11:00 a.m, marks its 59th year of fun and celebration with the theme “Independence Day the Piedmont Way”. In 1965, Dick Johnson, chairman of the Recreation Commission, began the parade after noticing a lull in patriotism during the Vietnam War years. From the beginning, the parade included marching bands, our favorite being the bagpipe bands, antique cars, and neighborhood participation, sometimes with elaborate floats. The parade ends at Piedmont Park, with celebratory speeches, lively music, tasty food stands, and plenty of space to enjoy a holiday picnic with friends & family. Come out and enjoy the festivities! MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: If your home has an ADU, a pool, or a view, you’ve probably wondered what it’s actually worth. The honest answer is: it depends on what buyers in your neighborhood have proven they’ll pay for it. That’s how appraisers figure it out. They pull sales of similar homes without the feature, then pull sales of similar homes with it. The difference between those two numbers is what your feature is actually contributing to your value. Not what it cost to build. Not what you think it’s worth. What the market has shown it will pay. A pool in one zip code might add $40,000. In another, almost nothing. A view can swing value by 10%… or barely move the needle. If you’re thinking about selling, this is the question worth asking before you price it.

The goats eat for roughly 8 hours a day — 4 hours in the morning, then they rest, then another 4 hours in the afternoon. The Public Works and Fire Departments bring in grazing goats each summer to clear low-lying vegetation and eat dry grasses on difficult-to-navigate hillsides on either side of Moraga Canyon. This work acts in tandem with the large fuel-load reduction work the city did on the hillside early last year, clearing out shrubs and limbing trees up to a 6-foot clearance. In support of these efforts, Piedmont’s Fire Department encourages residents to manage their overgrown vegetation on their property to reduce fire hazards. articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike team will be riding in this year’s 4th of July Parade. Their first year in the parade was in 2023. The nonprofit organization’s focus is to get kids to have fun riding bikes. The group provides an opportunity weekly for high school and middle school students to learn to mountain bike. The umbrella organization for the team is called the National Interscholastic Cycling Association (NICA). NICA is a nationwide organization that started in Berkeley, CA, in 2009. The Piedmont Mountain Bike team is in the Central Conference of the Norcal league within NICA. The organization hosts two teams: a high school team and a development team consisting of kids in middle school or younger. Currently, the teams have 20 members each. The high school team’s season is four races from December to May with a championship race to end the year. This past season, the team finished 6th in their division at the 2026 NorZachary Carter, team co-captain in the upcoming season, racing at Exchequer near La Grange, CA. A picture of the team after participation in the 2025 4th of July parade. Development Coach Ode Bernstein and a parent hoist the wooden bike ramp that riders use for jumps during their parade appearance. cal High School Championships and 2nd overall. “It was just super awesome to see all the kids get really strong,” said Vanessa Oklejas, a representative of the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. “As the season goes on, they get in better and better condition, and they get faster and faster. So I remember towards the end of the season, the coaches were really sweating. They’re like ‘My gosh, they’re killing me.’ They’re just getting super fast.” Now that the season is over, the team focuses its attention on its participation in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade. The teams ride their bikes down Highland Avenue, doing tricks like a wheelie to excite the crowd. They usually bring a ramp to do jumps off of or a limbo stick to see how low they can go on their bikes. The team plans to hand out promotional material to highlight the team. “The crowd seems to like it. I think the middle school kids get the most enjoyment out of it. Getting them to do jumps and wheelies and the limbo is nothing. I think the bigger thing is getting them to the start line,” said Oklejas. Oklejas shared a memory of last year’s parade highlighting the importance of including everyone who wants to ride a bike. “What I really loved about last year was that there was a father who got in touch because his son wasn’t quite old enough to ride with the development team, but really wanted to be on that parade, and he had the best freaking time. He just loved it. He’s a fifth grader riding with big kids going off the ramp on, I mean, he just had a wonderful time,” she said. The mountain bike team encourages anyone interested to come and try it out. They host adventure rides before the season on Saturdays or Sundays. They offer loaner bikes to anyone who doesn’t have a bike. “It’s open to everybody. It’s really just come out and try it out,” said Oklejas. More information on the team can be found on their website: https://www.piedmontmtb.com/. Riders Mina Herrgott and Olivia Bailey on the race course at Six Sigma Ranch and Winery. The 2026 Piedmont High School Mountain Bike Team 2026 JV Girls Champion Josephine Schuetz, in a purple jersey, racing in a NICA race at Six Sigma Ranch and Winery.

PCSC took over the Pancake Breakfast in 2016 from the Piedmont Rec Department, and has done it every year since, except in 2020. When the event was threatened in 2021 due to COVID mandates, PCSC preserved the event by turning it into a Waldo Avenue block party. Prior to 2016 and Rec Department’s ownership of the event, Oakland Rotary members served up pancakes for the big parade crowd. The Pancake Breakfast fits in perfectly with PCSC’s initiatives. Around once a month, the crew cooks for the food insecure, which is where they spend the money earned at their fundraisers, like Pancake Beakfast. Making food for someone else has for as long as time has tested, been a primordial display of love and respect, another lesson learned and displayed by PCSC members. When putting on service events, crew members take turns being the event leader, Li explained they are “in charge of picking the menu, coming up with the detailed shopping list, meeting a budget, buying the PCSC will serve up pancake breakfasts in Veterans Hall on Saturday, July 4. articles.text: adjusting to being far from home again, but after the adjustment period. I found that everything about St. Andrews that I had been trying to change was what made it amazing. The sunset pilgrimages became walks along Lade Braes, a nature walk along a creek, Greek life became societies (fancy name for clubs) and sports teams, and formal events became society balls with ceilidh dancing. I soon began to experience the feeling of adventure and belonging I had been chasing. University was becoming something I looked forward to experiencing instead of dreading its contrasts to what my friends back home in the States had. While there are many aspects of upper education that differ between the US and the UK, what stays consistent is how much fun and growth you can have when you embrace the experience instead of fighting it. More importantly, the thought of ‘what if’ became a lighthearted gameplay scenario rather than the taunting threat it once was. I still think about San Diego, but now it’s a passing thought. As the fall term creeps closer to my second year at University, I find myself excited more than anything. Despite being in a place the opposite of where I thought I would end up, I find myself forging the experiences I have always wanted. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a former Piedmont Post intern.

PCSC took over the Pancake Breakfast in 2016 from the Piedmont Rec Department, and has done it every year since, except in 2020. When the event was threatened in 2021 due to COVID mandates, PCSC preserved the event by turning it into a Waldo Avenue block party. Prior to 2016 and Rec Department’s ownership of the event, Oakland Rotary members served up pancakes for the big parade crowd. The Pancake Breakfast fits in perfectly with PCSC’s initiatives. Around once a month, the crew cooks for the food insecure, which is where they spend the money earned at their fundraisers, like Pancake Beakfast. Making food for someone else has for as long as time has tested, been a primordial display of love and respect, another lesson learned and displayed by PCSC members. When putting on service events, crew members take turns being the event leader, Li explained they are “in charge of picking the menu, coming up with the detailed shopping list, meeting a budget, buying the food, bring it to the event and telling everyone else what to do.” Piedmont Community Service Crew is always open to interested youth and also to community adults that like working with youth and doing community service. The current Co-Presidents of PCSC are PHS senior Claire Aubrecht and junior Maddy Lee. PCSC takes on meaningful projects where members plan, fund, lead and execute service work not only locally, but throughout the world via service trips. Learn more about PCSC via PCservicecrew.org and reach out to Crew Advisor Ken Li Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net for a personal guide as to how PCSC can be a great experience. PCSC will serve up pancake breakfasts in Veterans Hall on Saturday, July 4. Where in the World Are We? College Experience Continued from page 11 adjusting to being far from home again, but after the adjustment period. I found that everything about St. Andrews that I had been trying to change was what made it amazing. The sunset pilgrimages became walks along Lade Braes, a nature walk along a creek, Greek life became societies (fancy name for clubs) and sports teams, and formal events became society balls with ceilidh dancing. I soon began to experience the feeling of adventure and belonging I had been chasing. University was becoming something I looked forward to experiencing instead of dreading its contrasts to what my friends back home in the States had. She was sixth of 20 in the 100 meter hurdles, fifth of 20 in the high jump, 18th of 22 in the shot put, 11th of 19 in the 200 meter dash, fourth of 20 in the long jump, 19 of 20 in the javelin, and 11 of 18 in the 800. Kim set UC Santa Cruz’s record in the pentathlon, 60 meter hurdles, and long jump at the Wolf Pack Classic in February. Her 3,439 pentathlon score was the No. 6 total in the country. She logged a winning time of 8.78 in the 60 meter hurdles in a field of eight at the Coast-ToCoast Athletic Conference Indoor Championships later on in February. She also won three events at the 2026 Coast-To-Coast Outdoor Championships in May, including the 100 hurdles in 14.19 over seven other finalists, the high jump in 1.57 meters against eight others, and the long jump in 5.77 meters in a field of 16. Kim was breakout star on Piedmont High’s track and field team in her only year as a varsity athlete after joining the squad as between the US and the UK, what stays consistent is how much fun and growth you can have when you embrace the experience instead of fighting it. More importantly, the thought of ‘what if’ became a lighthearted gameplay scenario rather than the taunting threat it once was. I still think about San Diego, but now it’s a passing thought. As the fall term creeps closer to my second year at University, I find myself excited more than anything. Despite being in a place the opposite of where I thought I would end up, I find myself forging the experiences I have always wanted. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a former Piedmont Post intern.
